SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump signs proclamation to try to prevent changes to gold-covered Oval Office
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday that he says will prevent future administrations from changing his design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, spaces which he declared as national monuments that should be preserved.
In the days since his party suffered historic defeats in the midterm elections, the president has seemingly turned his attention to the many renovation projects he has begun across the nation’s capital. Sitting behind the Resolute Desk on Thursday, Trump declared the Oval Office a “national monument”.
“I’m going to be signing a document which will make them into a landmark for the ages,” he told reporters in the gold-covered Oval Office.
According to the president, the proclamation would ensure the West Wing rooms would not be “touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape”.
“I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come and take it down and try and do something with it,” he said.
“Every once in a while they’ll look and they’ll say, oh, maybe what we’ll do is we’ll put some glass up that’s a little bit better or something, and I say no, you’re not going to do anything. We’re going to leave this as it is,” he continued.
“If anyone ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you’ll call me wherever I may be, and I will come back here and I will make sure it never happens.”
Since returning to office, Trump has embarked on a series of White House “beautification” projects, most notably the demolition of the East Wing to make way for a $600m ballroom, as well the building of a permanent granite helipad on the South Lawn.
Speaking to reporters from the Oval Office, the president defended his wider renovation work at the White House, saying the building’s exterior had suffered from years of deterioration. He pointed to cracked windows, damaged stonework and broken decorative features, saying he had paid for repairs and hired skilled workers to restore them.
“When you looked at that wall one year ago, it was badly damaged from years of service,” he said, adding that exterior columns had also been in “horrible shape”.
On the desk next to where he signed the proclamation was a red baseball cap emblazoned with the word “Veto” – an explicit reminder of his threat to block the legislative priorities and bills passed by the new Democratic-controlled Congress next year.
Democrats made significant gains in several traditionally Republican states where Trump had previously won, including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa, by campaigning on issues including affordability and tackling corruption, while also securing control of Congress.
Trump’s opulent redesign of the Oval Office has drawn criticism, including from former president Barack Obama, who recently joked that “he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”
Obama’s remark prompted a coordinated response from the White House, with treasury secretary Scott Bessent appearing to hit back by dining at a Cheesecake Factory.
In a final appeal ahead of the midterm elections, Trump held a press conference highlighting the delayed results of his $14m renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, while blaming Joe Biden for the algae that had accumulated in its waters.
“This was in the Biden era … Look, it’s not an easy thing. The algae is brutal. It forms easily. All you saw was dirt and filth and paper and everything else for years,” Trump said on Monday.
Two days later, as the scale of his party’s staggering losses came into focus, Trump led a media tour of the White House Ballroom construction site, where he marveled at the renovations to come.
“The whole thing is a miracle,” he said.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The real problem with Britain’s Political Traitors show is that no one is very faithful to anything for long | Robert Hutton
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
You join us on a steam train in Scotland as we head to the next episode of the BBC’s hit show Political Traitors. It’s like the celebrity edition, except that everyone is less comely – politics being the practice of show business for ugly people. For this week’s task, the players have to construct a “budget” of tiny crowd-pleasing measures, carefully balanced by invisible tax rises.
What makes the show so compelling is that the players don’t know the whole story. Only those of us on the outside can see what’s really going on. While John and Andy run around shouting about how they have faithfully met their “fiscal rules” in the third year of the forecasts, on our sofas at home we know that this incantation is entirely meaningless.
But people who’ve been on the show say that when you’re in the midst of it, it feels completely real. So much so that there are ongoing questions for the producers about safeguarding. Liz, who was a sensation of chaotic energy when she briefly appeared in 2022, is the most obvious example of someone who shouldn’t have been allowed to take part. She was last heard explaining her plan to colonise Mars.
If the series has any value beyond entertainment, it’s for the insights it offers into human psychology, especially the way people convince themselves of narratives that are objectively nonsense. Take Kemi, from the current run. After the banishment of Keir earlier this year, she could be heard explaining to anyone who would listen that this was the result of her brilliant inquisitions at the roundtable.
We could all see that the other players, after debating why on earth Keir hadn’t already been stabbed in the back, had concluded that although he was 100% faithful, he was also 1000% loser.
Nevertheless, there’s something rather charming about Kemi’s total conviction that she’s a masterly player on course for triumph. It’s easy for us to laugh, but you have to remember that she doesn’t have access to the information we do, such as opinion polls and byelection results.
That information gap is the joy of the show. Several times Nigel has seemingly revealed himself to be a traitor, and his close ally Nathan was actually unmasked as one, but still no one seems able to put two and two together.
Some players adopt a strategy of trying to fly below the radar to avoid being noticed. One current player, Ed D, has been so successful that many viewers have forgotten he exists and refuse to believe he is part of the game at all, even after his triumph in the water slide task.
Each morning, the players meet over breakfast TV for a heated discussion in which they all insist that whatever has just happened proves their theory is right. Then there’s the dramatic moment of discovering who has been banished, or simply walked off the set. In one compelling episode in 2022, almost all the players quit in the hope of forcing Boris to admit he’d been lying. Even then, to viewers’ delight, he still had the support of the loyal Nadine.
In last month’s “conference” task, the players were handed the severed head of a deceased teammate and had to mimic their distinctive cry. Kemi, predictably, chose Maggie, although her impersonation looked more like pastiche. Andy, on the other hand, reckons he can do a mean Harold. He’s rejected any suggestion that he should try copying Tony, one of the game’s most successful players, but he’s failed to brush aside the lingering suspicion that he’s simply doing an impression of Keir.
The format has been sold around the world, with changes for local markets. The French edition involves a runoff vote. The Israeli version is so complicated that no one understands anything about it except that somehow Bibi keeps winning. And the American one is louder, brasher and far more expensive. It also seems to be played entirely by idiots who have failed, despite an impossible number of very clear clues, to identify their obvious traitor.
Although the players change at an alarming rate, the one constant in the British show is the host, Lindsay. With his ridiculous outfits and his catchphrases – “Order! ORDER!” and “Mr Holden, I think you need to leave” – he is fast becoming a national treasure. And now, as he says at the end of every roundtable, the time for talk is over.
I’m joking, of course. In this version of the show, the time for talk never ends.
- 
  Robert Hutton is a journalist and author

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Can a £5.8bn scheme help revive Grimsby and other town centres?
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
“It is nice to see something happening for once,” says Jack Vincent, a Grimsby resident, as he considers a wave of change finally arriving in a town that had become a byword for deprivation.
In June, King Charles visited the Lincolnshire coastal town, celebrating the opening of a youth centre in a previously derelict Victorian warehouse building and a Care charity community drop-in centre in a vacant bank on the high street. Scaffolding also shrouds one end of the town’s shopping centre, part of which is being converted to house leisure facilities including a cinema and a food market.
“It is getting better and we have got the new cinema coming,” says Vincent, who is in town with his partner and two young children.
Linda Hooper, 75, who also lives locally, agrees: “They are generally making it nicer and there’s a good shopping centre.”
Once the world’s largest fishing port, Grimsby has been hit badly by the decline of its trawler fleet since the 1950s, and North East Lincolnshire council has spent the lion’s share of the £59m in government-backed regeneration funds awarded to it since 2021 trying to revamp the struggling town centre.
It is now beginning to spend a further £20m from the pride in place programme, the latest government attempt to support struggling communities. The scheme was launched under Keir Starmer as a revamp of previous Conservative plans, expanded to offer 284 deprived communities up to £2m a year for 10 years to help with regeneration.
On becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham made clear that reviving town centres would be one of his priorities and gave his backing to the £5.8bn national programme. It also fits within his wider devolution drive.
The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, says: “Our pride in place programme is a break from past approaches by putting local people in charge … no more ‘Whitehall knows best’. This is local people deciding what matters most to them.”
Residents in Grimsby feel the high street is the part of their town that has declined more than any other over the last decade, with household names such as Debenhams collapsing and shoplifting on the rise.
Henrietta Billings, the director of Save Britain’s Heritage, which campaigns for the preservation of historical buildings, says: “I think it is right the government is recognising that people are really fed up with seeing, at best, paint peeling off all the buildings … They see when no one cares about them and can feel let down.”
Despite hopes of further money for regeneration in John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October, and the announcement last month of another £210m to help turn boarded-up shops and other businesses into community spaces, the problem is bigger and more complex than just finding more funding.
Grimsby gives a glimpse into the challenges of how to adapt as more of us shop and bank online, amid years of central government cost-cutting and the decline of historical industries that once brought jobs and wages.
As in many other local authorities, the people of North East Lincolnshire registered their dissatisfaction with a big vote for Reform in the May elections, wresting minority control of the council. It is also a place that overwhelmingly supported Brexit, with the promise of a fishing revival, but which then lost processing jobs after the UK left the EU.
Despite its efforts at regeneration, many large commercial buildings, including a former Wilko and House of Fraser, and beautiful Victorian buildings such as the vast Victoria Mills and the Grimsby Ice Factory remain empty.
Local people say some empty office blocks and commercial buildings are vacant after being picked up for a song by out-of-town investors, who then realised redevelopment was more costly and complicated than they imagined.
The Covid pandemic and other hold-ups mean that, while three of Grimsby’s redevelopment projects funded by the predecessors to pride in place are complete, several more remain in progress.
As Spencer Hunt of the local council admits: “We still have issues.”
On a Friday in Grimsby, the Freshney Place shopping centre is busy with people popping into a revamped Marks & Spencer, a Primark and a good mix of other shops, while the nearby Abbeygate pedestrianised street is packed with independent boutiques and eateries.
However, the main high street is gap-toothed with vacant shops and has become a racetrack for local teenagers on bikes and scooters who join in lively banter with homeless people and daytime drinkers.
Hooper, Vincent and several other local people agree that something needs to be done to reduce what Hooper describes as “yobs going up and down the walkway”.
Some local teenagers agree that the town centre does not always feel very welcoming. “People need to feel more safe,” says Ewan Challender, 18, in town with Demi Sowerby, who says the shop where she works is frequently shoplifted.
Their scepticism about the redevelopment plans is fuelled by the struggles of previous efforts. The Riverhead building, which was built in the noughties and once home to a selection of bars, in September finally welcomed a new inflatable play park, after lying empty since 2024, while a revamped St James’ Square remains bordered by shuttered premises.
The effort to update town centres has been a long one. The rise of out-of-town retail parks and then internet shopping have been putting pressure on traditional retail-based high streets for decades.
In 2011, the David Cameron government commissioned the retail guru Mary Portas to come up with some solutions, leading to 10 pilot revamps. While a number of those towns – such as Margate, Stockport and Stockton – are now lauded as examples of regeneration, others such as Croydon and Wolverhampton continue to struggle.
A string of successors to the Portas scheme – including the town deals and the levelling up fund – have pumped almost £12bn into town centres in the past seven years, but so far failed to bring about widespread regeneration.
The towns fund wraps together the £2.3bn in the programmes money awarded to 101 places in 2019 with the future high street fund, under which 72 places shared awards worth £830m from 2020.
However, many recipients found that the pandemic and subsequent inflation, particularly on construction costs, as well as difficulties in securing sites or planning permission, forced them to scale back, pause or redraw plans.
A focus on investing in buildings and other infrastructure has also left projects stymied by a lack of resources for staff to run them. Continued weak high street spending has meanwhile led to businesses and entrepreneurs siphoning away cash once spent on improving stores towards selling online.
Almost £1.8m of town deals awards are only being released this year and next, according to a government evaluation report. At least £1bn of the £4.8bn levelling up fund launched in 2021 also remained “stuck in limbo” by 2024, according to the campaign group Power to Change.
The money from all these pride in place predecessors was incorporated into the local regeneration fund last year and the deadline for spending it was extended from March this year to March 2028 as many projects remained behind schedule.
Pride in place has tried to build on lessons from previous rounds of funding, which led to questionable decisions over allocation and funds going unspent. It has allocated funding based on published deprivation and community need data.
Its remit also stretches beyond doing up high streets, with the menu of automatically accepted spending options stretching to skills training for local people, modernising social housing and making space for nature. Communities can also seek approval for locally relevant alternatives.
Unlike many of the predecessor schemes, pride in place can also cover projects’ running costs. Local areas must also create neighbourhood boards, made up of residents, businesses and other members of the community alongside local authorities, to allocate the money.
In North East Lincolnshire, the council has brought in Our Future, a local group backed by Jason Stockwood, the entrepreneur behind Grimsby Town football club, to help catalyse community involvement in developing the town, backed by £850,000 to be handed out in grant funding to local projects to make the most of vacant buildings.
But Neela Parker Talwar, from the Centre for Cities , argues that “£20m is not so much money” and is unlikely to be able to fund major projects such as buying up large empty buildings for redevelopment.
She adds that communities might know their local problems better than central government, but the causes of high street vacancies may be beyond the reach of a local authority, things such as “access to jobs, transport, schools, things the local authority can have leverage over but only to an extent”.
“You can’t expect Blackburn to become Cambridge,” Talwar says.
Grimsby residents admit that perhaps its biggest hope for the future is not government-backed regeneration schemes but an improving local economy and entrepreneurship.
“For Grimsby the stars aligned when we stopped thinking about fishing and started thinking about wind. We stopped looking back and started looking forward,” says Mark Webb, who heads up the Grimsby 2025 group of local businesses aiming to invest in local regeneration. Local business niches include logistics, chemicals and food processing as well as renewables.
“We are a typical northern industrial town. We weren’t going anywhere, but now we are. People look at the town now and it is a bit of a mess, but it is a brilliant mess because someone is doing something behind those hoardings.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Burnham says ‘public will be the boss’ in any future decision about closer relationship with the EU – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Burnham says 'public will be the boss' in any future decisions about closer relationship with EU
Burnham confirmed that he wanted to open a discussion about the UK’s future relationship with the EU.
If we are serious, if we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have.
The status quo is not good enough for Britain.
Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away.
We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today to consider what is best for our country.
Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.
At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach like the one I am suggesting.
Andy Burnham has told MPs that it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to seek deeper partnership with the EU. In a long statement to MPs, he repeatedly refused to rule out taking the UK back into the EU single market after the general election. But he also insisted that the British public would be the “boss” at every stage of renegotiating the relationship. He critcised the Brexit deal negotiated by the last Tory government and said, if the opposition were genuinely committed to growth, they would accept the need to revise it. He said:
If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have.
Burnham says von der Leyen open to giving UK better access to EU databases which would help with migration control
Lisa O’Carroll
Lisa O’Carroll is a senior Guardian correspondent covering post-Brexit issues.
Labour’s Stella Creasy asked Burnham if he accepted that it was harder for the UK to control its borders because, after Brexit, it lost access to the Eurodac database, which contains biometric data about asylum seekers. Burnham accepted this was a big problem.
He told MPs:
We are in a weaker position when it comes to controlling immigration than we were, just over 10 years ago.
It is really important as we go into this next phase that all sides of the house support the British position when we go towards this negotiation.
Is any member of this house truly saying to me this afternoon that they do not want to have access again to that European immigration information?
If they are saying that they need to be honest about it.
Later Labour’s Chris Webb asked if the forthcoming EU-UK summit would allow the UK to regain better control of immigration. Burnham replied:
One of the most positive aspects of my meeting with [EU president Ursula] von der Leyen in New York was her openness to the conversation about restoring data sharing on immigration across the EU, across Europe. That is something that Britain has long sought in the decade since Brexit. It is the control that we lost, actually, at the time of the referendum.
It’s one of the issues that doesn’t get enough attention, and it should get more, and I can say to [Webb] I will work hard to see if we can get a practical arrangement on that very issue at the summit in November.
As well as losing access to Eurodac, which would allow the UK to swiftly identify if people claiming asylum in the UK had previously applied somewhere else in the EU, with Brexit the UK also lost access to the Schengen information systems, which provide alerts on criminals and stolen goods, and the European arrest warrant database, which provides immediate alerts about fugitives.
Burnham fails to rule out eventually accepting EU freedom of movement after being challenged by Labour and Tory MPs
The Labour MP Jonathan Hinder, who represents Pendle and Clitheroe, asked Burnham to confirm that, as long as he remains PM, “there will be no return to freedom of movement”.
Burnham said that he would fully respect the Labour manifesto which ruled out joining the single market during this parliament. Being in the single market would mean the UK having to comply with freedom of movement for EU nationals.
But he went on:
What we have to look at are the options that are available for the long-term relationship. This country in the next decade needs to know where it’s going.
There are no assumptions here. And as I said in my [opening comments – see 4.01pm], the British public will be the boss of whatever, whatever is decided.
A few minutes later the Labour MP Melanie Onn, who represents Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes, said Burnham was evasive in his answer to Hinder. She asked Burnham for an assurance that, in his proposed renegotiation with the EU, the UK would not have to accept freedom of movemment, and would not have to “capitulate” and join the euro.
Burnham again sidestepped the question. He said:
As I’ve said many times this afternoon, we will honour the manifesto in full, and the red lines are in place.
Later the Conservative MP Saqib Bhatti said Burnham was evading the question. He asked Burnham for a straight yes or no: in any future renegotiation, would freedom of movement be on the table.
Burnham replied:
The honourable gentleman is getting way ahead of himself. There is no proposal for a referendum. There’s no deal on the table. All I have said is, as we go towards this negotiation, it makes sense to consider also our longer term options because it helps our European partners if they know where Britain wants to go in the future. That is all that is being said at this moment in time.
Burnham ducks question from Richard Tice about whether any of RAF Fairford suspects had Iranian diplomatic immunity
Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform UK, has Burnham if he could comment on “serious suggestions” that some of those arrested and bailed in relation to the RAF Fairford suspected bomb plot had Iranian diplomatic immunity.
Burnham said he would not go into detail. But he said the home secretary would make a statement about this later.
Pippa Crerar and Jessica Elgot have been talking about the Brexit/Russia row on the latest edition of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast. You can watch it here.
Details of Burnham's meetings with Manchester City when he was city's mayor released
Andy Burnham had a formal meeting with Manchester City’s chair Khaldoon Al Mubarak at an investment summit, chatted to him in the stands at a star player’s testimonial game and was accompanied by staff from the club on official overseas visits, the Press Association reports. PA says:
Details of the prime minister’s contacts with the scandal-hit club and its Abu Dhabi owners during his time as Greater Manchester mayor were released by the combined authority.
Burnham told MPs that “all of my dealings” with Manchester City’s owners would be published.
A spokesperson for the Greater Manchester combined authority said:
In October 2021 Andy Burnham, in his role as mayor of Greater Manchester, had a formal meeting with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at the UK Government’s Global Investment Summit arranged by the Department for International Trade.
In his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City FC at home matches on a small number of occasions, including attending Vincent Kompany’s testimonial match in September 2019, where he met the chairman informally in the stands. These have been declared in the usual way.
Also during his time as mayor, representatives of Greater Manchester sporting clubs would routinely join business delegations as part of mayoral international visits. This included representatives from Manchester United travelling to Austin and Dublin, Lancashire Cricket Club joining a delegation to India, and Manchester City FC staff supporting visits to China and Japan.
In the Commons Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the business committee, asked Andy. Burnham to consider the case for new tariffs on Chinese imports.
He said:
The EU’s made-in-Europe proposals risks destroying any ambitions to re-industrialise our country. To avoid that peril, we are going to have to get serious with the EU in tackling unfair competition from China.
So will the prime minister reserve the right to introduce new tariffs on unfairly subsidised imports from China, so that British and European businesses have got a fair level playing field on which to compete?
Burnham replied:
I agree with him, though, that Made in Europe does present risks to British manufacturing, and I know he will have concerns about the automotive industry in the West Midlands.
I am raising those concerns with European partners. It is important that we get to an arrangement here that works for both the UK and the EU. After all, we are both trying to deal with the same issue, which is Chinese exports and the damaging effect that’s having on our industry.
So the way to approach this is to do it together, and that’s the case that we’re making to the EU.
In his response to Kemi Badenoch, Andy Burnham explicitly denied implying that the Brexit referendum result was illegitimate when he made his comment about Russian interference. (See 4.17pm.) The Conservative party has now issued a thoroughly misleading statement ignoring what he said. A spokesperson said:
The leader of the opposition just asked the prime minister, in light of his comments on Russian interference, if he thought the 2016 EU Referendum result was legitimate or illegitimate. Andy Burnham refused to answer.
There can be no doubt that his words to the Rest Is Politics were intended to cast doubt on the legitimacy of the referendum result. By not answering Kemi Badenoch’s question, Andy Burnham has all but conceded this was a deliberate ploy intended to sow more division, reopen the battles of the past, and bolster his own case for rejoining the EU.
This reads like the sort of statement which gets drafted in advance in expectation of one response in the Commons, and which then gets released anyway even though it doesn’t apply to what was actually said.
The former Tory PM Boris Johnson is also misrepresenting what Burnham said. He posted this on social media this afternoon.
This is just not true. As soon as I became foreign secretary I asked the security services the same question and they replied that there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power.
Either the security services have changed their view - which would be very odd - or Burnham is lying about what he has been told. After all Starmer was in power for two years and had access to exactly the same information.
You can read what Burnham did actually say on the Rest is Politics at 10.33am.
Burnham declines invitation to condemn Trump for his 'act of treachery' in buying diesel from Putin
Ed Davey also asked Burnham to bring together a coalition of countries willing to condemn President Trump for the deal he has agreed to buy Russian diesel.
Burnham ignored this question when he replied to Davey, but the Tory MP Roger Gale challenged him on it again later. Gale asked Burnham to unequivocally condemn “this act of treachery” by Trump.
Burnham replied:
I did make it clear in my statement that, when I heard news, I was immediately on the phone to President Zelenskyy offering any help that I could provide.
And I think where Britain can best provide help is in trying to bring people back together to get a solution that works for Ukraine. And you have to think about that more than anything in these circumstances - what will be most helpful?
Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, praised Burnham for his comments about Brexit. He said:
His predecessor turned a blind eye to the disastrous consequences of the Conservatives’ Brexit deal, so it’s welcome to hear him recognise that damage today.
We on these benches have consistently argued that their Brexit deal has made us all poorer, weaker and less safe.
So I’m glad the prime minister has arrived at the same conclusion as we have.
But now it’s time to do something about it.
Davey said that Burnham should not revisit the Labour manifesto red lines ruling out joining a customs union or the single market this parliament.
Burnham said he thought public opinion had shifted, and people now wanted a “pragmatic” approach to Europe.
But, he went on:
I also want to maintain trust in politics. And I’m afraid I’m not prepared to revisit the red lines. in our our manifesto.
Burnham claims he's not reopening Brexit referendum - but he says he wants to be 'pragmatic'
Edward Leigh, the Conservative father of the Commons, asked if Burnham would view this as a reasonable statement. This is the statement he asked the PM to endorse.
I’ve been elected by my MPs to serve a full term of government. I’m going to get on with bread and butter issues such as the care system, pensions, asylum. And of course we would like a good, close relationship with our partners on security in Europe.
But I say this to the people – this is the prime minister speaking – I am very wary about reopening the whole Brexit wars …
And I give this absolute commitment that I would not seek to join the EU unless there was a general election first and I offer the British people a full referendum.
Burnham replied:
Can I say to the father of the house that I stand by every single one of those words.
I am not reopening the referendum. I respect the referendum result … but what I will do is take a pragmatic approach.
When I can boost growth in the British economy, when I can increase cooperation to get a grip on the boat crossings across the channel, I will do those things where I believe they can be in the country’s best interests.
Burnham says Russian interference comment did not mean he was questioning legitimacy of Brexit referendum result
Burnham rejected Badenoch’s claim that his comment about Russia on the Rest is Politics podcast meant he did not accept the legitimacy of the Brexit referendum. He said “no such thing”, he told MPs. He went on:
It is a matter of record that Russian actors sought to interfere in the 2019 general election. And we think it is inconceivable that this was the first time.
Burnham says Tories shouldn't oppose revised deal with EU if they are serious about growth
In his response to Badenoch, Burnham said that her comments about the proposed EU-UK deal revising the Brexit settlement implied that she wanted to preserve the status quo.
He went on:
I’m sure I heard her say at her conference that increasing growth would be the operating principle of any government that she leads.
So how can she justify turning her back on a deal that is potentially on the table now to add billions to the UK economy? How can they justify turning their back on farmers and the food industry?
And referring to her attack on his negotiating tactics, Burnham added sarcastically: “Because the Tories were so good, weren’t they, at negotiating deals with our with our partners?”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise.
In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack, hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).
Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook.
Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage.
“It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux in Paris. “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.”
After removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.”
If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack.
Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio.
The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country in Europe.
Gérôme Billois, a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage.
“The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said.
“As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear.
“Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.”
The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms.
Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centre ANSSI confirmed supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted.
Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated.
“Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said.
“The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.”
She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.”
The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went into unscheduled defrost cycles overnight causing massive food loss.
France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management company Upguard.
In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks.
Billois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices.
“It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said.
In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry.
Supermarket boss Schelcher was quick to shift the blame for the attack on to unnamed refrigeration contractors who maintain the cold aisle equipment. “Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss,” he told RTL radio.
As yet, no individual or group has claimed responsibility for the supermarket cyber-attack; Paris prosecutors have instructed detectives from its anti-cybercrime unit but Billois says finding the hackers will take time.
“It’s possible they’ll be identified eventually, but it could take weeks if not months to be certain because hackers know how to hide their tracks,” Billois said.
Rybczyńska added: “Whether it’s possible to trace the hackers depends on their level of capability; if it’s a handful of youngsters, it’s easier because they probably won’t have thought to remove traces. If they are professionals it’s more complicated and will take longer. If they’re in a foreign country, it’ll be extremely difficult.”
The total cost of the cyber-attack has yet to be calculated but Thierry Cotillard, the CEO of Intermarché, said losses could run to “tens of millions of euros”, which store companies say is unlikely to be covered by their insurance.
“It’s a bizarre story,” Billois added. “There’s a shared responsibility between the supermarkets, the refrigeration companies who are sub-contractors and who maintain the material, and the software company. We cannot say who is to blame except, of course, the hackers.
“But in the end it comes down to freezers connected to the internet without being adequately secured. And that must be a wake-up call to everyone.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: These cruel new plans to ‘stop the boats’ show the government completely misunderstands refugees like me | Anonymous
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
I am a refugee and I am in shock at the home secretary’s announcement that people like me will now have to wait up to 30 years before they can apply for settlement in the UK – a sixfold increase on the current time period.
It feels like a pile-on at a time when asylum seekers and refugees are already facing a barrage of hostility in this country. Even before the announcement, refugees felt under siege. With the withdrawal of the right to ever become citizens for those of us who have “made a dangerous journey” and with frequent reviews of our refugee status to check if we are still deserving enough of protection or if we should be deported, our security in the UK is more vulnerable than ever.
According to the new rules, particular restrictions will be reserved for refugees who arrive in the UK on small boats or by other clandestine means such as in freight lorries. This is a punishment for fleeing war and using the only option open to us to reach a safe country. The government talks a lot about how asylum seekers will be treated differently if they arrive by safe and legal routes. The problem is that almost none exist: the largest scheme, refugee family reunion – which allowed about 20,000 women, children and other eligible dependents to join recognised refugees in the UK – has been suspended for more than a year.
The government has promoted other refugee resettlement schemes, such as one which will include Palestinians and Afghan women and girls, and another where refugees are supported and sponsored by individual communities. However, as well as only supporting small numbers of people, both have restrictions and limited scope, leaving those desperately trying to escape conflict zones with a binary choice: stay put or use an illegal method to reach safety.
Shutting the most vulnerable refugees out of settled status for 30 years places us in a state of limbo that will only deepen the trauma of fleeing our home country. This will cause refugees to disengage with the state, which will force more of us underground, working illegally for very low wages, and make us more vulnerable to exploitation. If more of us start to live under the radar, the government will ultimately have less rather than more control over irregular migration. This will also only hinder integration. It’s much harder to feel we belong in society if we’re shut out of settlement – even if we have a legal right to live here.
I arrived in the UK in 2017 after fleeing Syria. I protested against the Assad regime during the Arab spring and Syria’s civil war, and was twice imprisoned. When I was almost killed in a deadly missile attack in a suburb of Aleppo in 2017, I fled first to Turkey and then arrived in Calais in France and went on to the UK, where I joined my aunt, who raised me after my mother died. At that time I felt somewhat welcome in this country. In the almost decade since then, so much has changed.
Refugees are now increasingly scapegoated. The vast majority of us are law abiding. But because some corners of society encourage racism and anger towards us, many politicians are now scared to speak up for us. Like many other refugees, I have worked hard to integrate, to speak English well and to do voluntary work to help the community alongside my day job. But it seems that none of these things count in the political calculations the government has made.
If the government thinks that imposing a bar of up to 30 years on refugee settlement will stop the boats, it has fundamentally misunderstood refugees and the life calculations we make. The life of a refugee is filled with uncertainty – we are unable to make long-term plans, and instead move from one stepping stone to the next in the search for safety and security. We dream of a time when it will be safe to return to our home country but know that in reality this might never be possible.
While our priority is to find a safe place to live, the exact time we have to wait before we are granted settlement – whether it’s five years, 30 years or more – is not uppermost in our mind when we step into a dinghy on the coast of northern France. So the 30-year restriction is immoral, but it is also profoundly arrogant in attempting to sway the mind of a refugee. As long as people remain desperate to flee violent conflict, and without a proper investment in safe routes, the boats will continue to arrive.
- 
  As told to Diane Taylor

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: US carries out another round of ‘minor’ strikes on Iran, Trump says
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”
Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.
In an exchange with reporters on Friday, Trump said “they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”.
The US military had previously reported carrying out what it described as “defensive” strikes on Monday, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.
Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US.
The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the Iran war and elevated fuel prices – a byproduct of the war that has affected nearly every part of the global economy.
In the days since, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.
Differences with Iran about its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.
US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the US was offering “a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.
The post included a link to the state department’s Rewards for Justice program.
Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators’ discussions with Iran continue.
“We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump.
A flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the US military to carry out new strikes against Iran.
US defense secretary Pete Hegseth spoke on Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government. Qatar has been mediating between the US and Iran to end the war.
The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defence officials after confirming earlier that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to de-escalate tensions.
The telephone call between Trump and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani focused on international efforts to end tensions, according to a statement from the Qatari ruler’s media office.
With the Associated Press

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘They mobilized a whole government response to that joke’: Obama laughs off Trump attacks in rally for Ossoff
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Barack Obama, speaking at a Wednesday campaign rally in suburban Atlanta, offered a closing argument for Democrats in the final week of the midterm election campaign.
“These are not serious people,” he said of Donald Trump and the Republican party. “And we’re all paying the price for their lack of seriousness.”
Obama came to Georgia to support the campaigns of US senator Jon Ossoff, former Atlanta mayor and gubernatorial hopeful Keisha Lance Bottoms, and an array of down-ballot Democrats as part of his cross-country campaign tour before next week’s election. From 3,500 to 4,000 people filled the Discovery Center of Clayton county for the late election season stop, just south of Atlanta.
Obama has been casting caltrops behind him with each campaign stop, offering pointed criticism of Republican candidates and Donald Trump that has been unusual for the former president. He continued to do so on Wednesday, again invoking the image of Trump’s gilded renovations of the White House and noting Trump’s strident reaction to his crack last week likening it to Saddam Hussein decorating a Cheesecake Factory.
“The Saddam Hussein thing didn’t bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said. “I mean, it’s all crazy, but this is the crazy part: they mobilized a whole government response to that joke.
“The White House even called the secretary of the treasury,” the former president continued. “The guy who is trying to figure out how to lower inflation … they told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory.”
He also rebuffed Republicans’ accusations of snobbery for referencing the popular chain restaurant.
“I am the father of two daughters,” Obama said. “Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory?”
But he turned that discussion to the problems of affordability for American voters, in contrast with the corruption of the presidency.
“We have never seen a president so intent on selling favors,” Obama said. “The guy has made billions of dollars while in office. Understand that this has not been done in modern times.”
The construction of a new ballroom on the site of the former East Wing of the White House featured in the comments of many speakers at Wednesday’s rally, including Ossoff.
“Each day, Donald Trump digs the moral pit deeper,” Ossoff said, accusing the president of leading “the most corrupt administration of all time, and everybody knows it”.
“If you’re involved in any of this, next year you’ll be raising your hand to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth,” Ossoff said, in reference to Democrats pledging to impeach Trump if they take control of Congress next year.
The crowd chanted: “Lock him up!” in response.
Bottoms, meanwhile, contrasted her candidacy with that of her Republican opponent Rick Jackson, tying the billionaire healthcare executive to Trump and describing them as “two out-of-touch billionaires who want to keep getting rich on the backs of taxpayers”.
Invoking the legacies of US Representative John Lewis and Coretta Scott King, Bottoms characterized her candidacy as transcending politics. “They may have the money, but they will never overtake our movement,” she said.
Despite a broad wave of Democratic support buoying candidates across the country – and the eight- to 10-point polling lead Ossoff has on his Republican opponent, US Representative Mike Collins – Bottoms is statistically tied in polls with Jackson. If elected, Bottoms would break the state’s Republican trifecta – where the GOP has controlled both chambers of the legislature and the governor’s office – which began in 2004.
Rev Raphael Warnock, Georgia’s other senator, warned of “spiritual wickedness in high places” while describing the effects of deep cuts to Medicaid and Snap nutrition support for children.
“This is about the character of the country,” Warnock said. “This is about who we are and whether we are here for one another … I am concerned about the spiritual health of our country. There is brokenness, because only a broken nation could manage to elect Donald Trump twice.”
Trump, who was campaigning in Ohio at the same time as the Georgia rally, has also been on a national rally blitz, holding near-daily events in the final days of the midterm campaign. Trump has made two appearances in as many weeks in Georgia, both in what would otherwise seem to be congressional districts that are safe territory for Republicans.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Australia faces same issues that flipped control of US Congress in midterms, experts say
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Democrats’ stunning midterm victory should broaden Australia’s alliance with the US, observers say, even as a new power base emerges in Washington, affecting Aukus, datacentre development and relations with China.
Cabinet ministers, diplomats and Australia’s defence industrial sector closely watched the results this week, with control of the US Congress flipping to the Democrats and the outlook for Donald Trump’s final two years in office badly dinted.
Public fury over rising living costs, particularly fuel prices, and the impact of datacentres, were also two factors in the midterms results that carry warnings for the Australian government, analysts said.
Bruce Wolpe, a senior fellow at the United States Studies Centre, said Trump’s ability to rile up voters had been undermined by cost of living.
Wolpe said the Albanese government was taking a hit because of the economic fallout from the Iran war.
“I think a lot of people are wondering what does this [Australian] government do?” he said. “Have they lost control of the economy?
“In January, before the Iran war, the outlook looked pretty good. But now, after going through a budget process and the war … people are just very uncertain as to where this is going to end up.
“It is not an immediately solvable problem, and people really dislike it.”
Westpac’s head of international economics, Elliot Clarke, said the landslide midterms results had “dramatically changed” the outlook for the Iran war, which could affect the economy in Australia.
“It has changed the ‘atmospherics’ around the Middle East conflict,” he said. “It’s positive news.”
There was a steep drop in the global oil price as the election results filtered out. The Brent crude benchmark, which had threatened to pass its April peak, has instead plunged by 20%.
More confidence in a potential resolution in the Middle East would also help curb inflation and help central banks hold back on rate hikes, according to Clarke.
“It definitely changes the calculus,” he said.
Coalition frontbencher Andrew Hastie said the results showed economic messaging was critical.
“People feel worse off after tariffs and after the war in Iran, and Donald Trump has said a few times now that he doesn’t really care,” he told 2GB. “Our job is always to deliver better outcomes for the Australian people.”
The future of the alliance
Arthur Sinodinos, a former ambassador to Washington, said the change on Capitol Hill was a chance for Australian officials to progress policy goals with both US parties, and to consider the relationship beyond the 2028 presidential election.
“The main question mark is: ‘What is the impact on geopolitics across the world?’” he said. “Does this inject more uncertainty into American foreign policy? We’ve already had a lot of volatility in that regard.”
“The Congress may put more pressure on the administration to support Ukraine and pass measures that involve funding munitions to Ukraine.
“I think the Chinese will feel more emboldened, but I don’t think that translates into some sudden action on Taiwan. Trump has made it clear in the past that they won’t do anything on his watch, and I think he would feel bound to act if they did.”
Sinodinos praised Anthony Albanese’s professional approach to dealing with the often unconventional US president.
“I think the Australian government’s reaction after this vote is keep working with the administration, keep their heads down,” he said.
Trump claimed that Republicans had fared poorly because he was not on the ballot, despite repeatedly urging voters to pretend he was on the ballot. The vice-president, JD Vance, called Trump’s war in Iran “the obvious culprit”.
Ed Husic, former industry minister, wants a radical shakeup in the alliance.
“The moment to reset the relationship with the Trump administration is right now,” he said.
“A completely different Congress will require that administration to do things differently, including not hurting allies – friends, such as Australia – with tariffs.”
Abe Denmark, a partner at The Asia Group and an architect of the Aukus agreement in the Biden administration, warned against over-interpreting the results for Australia.
“What will change is how power is distributed in Washington,” he said.
“There will now be new centres of power to engage: Democratic chairs controlling authorisations and appropriations, Republicans more willing to break ranks, and 2028 hopefuls from both parties looking to stand out.
“While this gives Australia more points to engage, it also generates more noise. The challenge for Canberra, as with all allies and partners, will be to differentiate political positioning from durable policy.”
Denmark said the Democrats could take a different view from Trump on Aukus spending, as the US submarine industrial base needs a dramatic step up in production.
He said a government funding deal and passage of a key defence spending bill were urgent priorities for Congress.
A warning on datacentres
Husic also flagged possible changes to the US’s approach to AI regulation, and a flow on effect as the Albanese government prepare major legislation for 2027. Vermont senator Bernie Sanders has already called for a moratorium on new construction, warning that voters wanted the environment and humanity itself protected.
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said it was no coincidence that datacentre hotspots like Texas, Georgia and Ohio had shifted to support Democrats.
“Communities are being asked to hand over their land, water and power to some of the world’s wealthiest tech companies, yet the benefits for ordinary Australians remain remarkable difficult to identify,” she said.
The acting prime minister, Richard Marles, observed cost-of-living and datacentre anxiety was at play in both countries.
“What we are very mindful about here is that you’ve got to get the social licence right in respect of datacentres – where they’re built, and the place where they shouldn’t be built is in suburbs – and also making sure that the right power and the right water is brought to these datacentres,” he said.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Ukraine hit by deadly Russian strikes as ‘thanks’ for Trump diesel deal, Zelenskyy says
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine as “thanks” for a deal cut by Donald Trump with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, accusing Washington of helping fund Moscow’s war.
The Ukrainian president has expressed outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November’s midterm elections in which fuel costs are a key voter issue.
The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.
He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.
That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 20 people, including three children.
“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday.
“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.
There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.
Trump further stoked the fire on Saturday, saying it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end his country’s war with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in the US.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
Andy Burnham reiterated his “complete solidarity” in a call with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue talks.
The prime minister said he recognised the past day had been “difficult for Ukraine” and the two talked about the importance of keeping up pressure on Russia, No 10 said.
In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian news agency Interfax quoting an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”.
“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump.
The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.
Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationships with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.
The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.
Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied Luhansk region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four civilians and wounded five, the region’s Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said on Saturday.
Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.
Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The Financial Times reported that during the talks in Miami, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility that US intelligence sharing could be cut off if Kyiv did not halt the strikes.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeats Texas governor Greg Abbott in stunning upset
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
In a stunning political upset that would have seemed improbable only a few weeks ago, Democrat Gina Hinojosa has defeated three-term governor Greg Abbott on Tuesday, shattering the Republican grip on the highest and most powerful executive office in Texas.
Hinojosa’s historic victory – she will be the state’s first ever Latina governor – ended Abbott’s bid for an unprecedented fourth term, and delivered Democrats their most consequential victory in the state in a generation.
“We shocked the world tonight,” Hinojosa told a crowd of cheering supporters after the race was called. “We showed that anything is possible.”
It was an extraordinary reversal of fortunes for Democrats in the Lone Star state, which has long frustrated the party’s hopes of a political comeback. A Democrat has not won the Texas governor’s mansion since 1990, when voters elected Ann Richards.
But since then, Democrats have struggled to convert a growing urban population and changing demographics into statewide victories. Even high-profile challenges, including by Beto O’Rourke who sought to unseat Abbott in 2022, ended in defeat.
Hinojosa, a five-term state representative from Austin, entered the governor’s race with little fanfare after other prominent Democrats declined to run against Abbott, a staunch ally of Donald Trump with a formidable fundraising operation and record of easily dispatching with his Democratic rivals.
At the outset, Hinojosa’s candidacy was viewed as the longest of long shots, overshadowed by the campaign of fellow Democrat James Talarico, which attracted considerably more national attention and enthusiasm. But Hinojosa gradually fought her way into contention, with some polls showing the race neck-in-neck.
“It never bothered me that they doubted me. It bothered me that they doubted us,” Hinojosa said in her victory speech. “Hundreds and millions on attack ads, written off over and over again. But Texas, my faith in you never wavered.”
She said Abbott had called to congratulate her and extended a “generous offer” to assist with the transition. “Now I stand before you, humbled and grateful, and in awe of the incredible grace and power of God and of Texas,” she added.
In his election night speech, Abbott announced to supporters that he had conceded, prompting a brief moment of stunned silence in the crowd. “You all helped me to be your governor for 12 years – thank you very much,” he said, adding that he was proud of making Texas the “headquarters of business headquarters”.
“Know that we are leaving Texas in far better shape than it’s ever been.”
A former Austin school board president, Hinojosa has said public education is the issue that drew her into the race, but her campaign widened to focus on affordability issues and her opposition to the expansion of large-scale data centers. Under Abbott, Texas has become a leading state in the nation for data center construction.
Abbott, who maintained a large financial advantage, sought to portray Hinojosa as too “woke” for Texas, attacking her in Trumpian terms as “gender-bender Hinojosa”.
Hinojosa countered the culture-war attacks on her with an ad declaring her pronouns: “Mom, Texan and soon-to-be governor”.
She sought to capitalize on growing frustration with Trump’s presidency, courting traditionally Republican constituencies with a populist economic message.
Hinojosa grew up along the US-Mexico border. Her mother is an immigrant from Mexico, and her father served for several years as the state Democratic party chair. Her sister, Xochitl Hinojosa, is a long-time Democratic operative who previously served as spokesperson for the Department of Justice.
Trump responded to the flurry of bad results on Tuesday night with a social media post on his Truth Social platform deflecting blame.
“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” said the president, who had repeatedly told his supporters to “pretend I’m on the ticket”.
The president then directly attacked Abbott, saying if he had not “become a RINO [Republican in name only] in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost”.
“He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!” Trump added, months after endorsing him as an “exceptional Governor and man”.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Electricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivals
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
British steelmakers have been pushed further behind European rivals on electricity costs after the US-Israeli war on Iran caused a surge in global gas prices.
The premium paid by the British industry over its French counterpart has risen to almost £30 a megawatt hour (MWh), its highest level in three years, according to analysis by the lobby group UK Steel.
Energy prices have long been one of the main factors businesses cite when asked what is holding back British industry. For Andy Burnham they represent perhaps the biggest obstacle to his goal of “reindustrialising” the UK.
Analysts blame the UK’s high electricity prices on its reliance on gas for power generation, which is crucial for cleaner steelmaking with electric arc furnaces.
The way the market is set up means that the wholesale gas price determines the price of electricity even from other sources that cost much less to produce, such as wind or solar power, and Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz in response to Donald Trump’s bombing campaign has caused global gas prices to soar.
Electricity prices in France are mainly determined by its nuclear reactors, while in Germany heavily polluting coal still plays a large role in generation.
Comparisons with European rivals are particularly important for the UK because the EU is often the main market for British manufactured products, including about 75% of exported steel, worth about £3bn.
The gap with France had fallen in the previous three years to reach £18 a MWh last year, although it remains below the £153 reached in 2022 when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused a crisis in the global gas market. The gap with Germany this year fell slightly to about £12.
Under Keir Starmer most of the costs added by government policy to heavy industrial businesses’ electricity costs were removed last year. The main option to bring the price down further, however, would be to set up more cheap renewables – a challenge in the short term – or to directly subsidise prices.
The director general of UK Steel, Peter Brennan, said direct subsidies were the only option to help steelmakers. The lobby group has proposed a cap on prices that it estimates would cost about £51m a year. The government would pay the difference when prices go above that level, while the industry would pay the government if prices go below.
“British steelmakers are being asked to compete with one hand tied behind their backs,” Brennan said. “Despite welcome government action, our electricity prices remain vastly higher than those of our European and global competitors, and the gap with France is getting worse.
“The government has rightly made reindustrialisation a national priority. But we cannot rebuild British manufacturing while forcing our steelmakers to pay substantially more for electricity than their competitors.”
Separately, the government announced measures on Monday to support more than 100,000 workforce opportunities in the eight key growth sectors in its industrial strategy. The “jobs plans” are intended to help young people find work, with a focus on professional and business services, the defence sector and construction.
Similar plans for financial services, clean energy and life sciences have already been announced. Plans for advanced manufacturing and the creative industries are expected to follow shortly.
A government spokesperson said: “We are tackling industry’s number one concern head-on by reducing electricity bills by up to 25% for over 10,000 manufacturing businesses, and cutting costs for hundreds of our most electricity-intensive businesses by around £1bn per year – delivering on the prime minister’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The global economy “could soon test the limits of resilience”, as emergency oil stocks run low and government budgets become overstretched, the International Monetary Fund has warned.
In its twice-yearly World Economic Outlook, the IMF said global growth had withstood the Middle East conflict better than feared over the past six months.
It said the rerouting of oil supplies away from the strait of Hormuz, and the release of strategic energy stocks, had helped to contain the impact on oil prices from the US-Iran war.
However, it warned that emergency stocks are now depleted, and high debt levels and deficits in many countries could leave governments with little capacity to protect consumers from any future jump in prices.
“Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience,” it said. “Inventories in energy markets are dwindling and additional geopolitical shocks could still transmit rapidly through prices and supply disruptions.”
The International Energy Agency announced the largest-ever emergency releases of oil stocks on to the market in March this year, and promised to accelerate it after a meeting of oil ministers last month.
But in a sign of the system’s vulnerability, the US strategic petroleum reserve was recently reported to have fallen to its lowest level since 1982.
Last week, Donald Trump agreed a deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel in an attempt to bring down prices at the pumps, which analysts said would have little “meaningful” effect.
The World Economic Report was published on Tuesday in Bangkok, where the IMF and World Bank are holding their annual meetings this week, with finance ministers and central bankers scheduled to attend.
Launching the report in Bangkok, Silvano Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, warned, “the global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits”. She urged policymakers to “move from just coping, to rebuilding”.
Ahead of the gathering, the IMF managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged governments to tighten their belts, amid rising global debt levels. “We cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said.
In the report, the IMF revised up its forecast for global economic growth this year marginally, to 3.1% – against 3% in its last update in July. Next year’s forecast is unchanged, at 3.4%.
US growth remains unchanged at 2.3% this year and revised up to the same pace, 2.3%, for 2027 – from 2.2% at the last update.
The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year – up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July – in welcome news for the chancellor, John Healey, who is set to arrive in Bangkok later this week.
However, the IMF also warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027, “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.
The Fund cautioned that “risks are skewed to the downside” for the global economy. In particular, it pointed to the threat of “a prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East”, which would lead to higher energy and food prices.
“Further disruptions to energy infrastructure, cyber-attacks, or extreme weather events could amplify these effects,” the IMF added.
Trump has continued to insist that he could launch another wave of attacks on Iran in the coming weeks, with little sign of a peace agreement being negotiated.
The persistence of elevated oil prices means the spike in inflation is now expected to last longer than previously forecast.
Global inflation is expected to be 4.7% this year – the same level as forecast in July – and to decline to 4.1% in 2027 – up from 4% in the last update.
The IMF urged the world’s central banks not to overreact to short-term jumps in inflation, but to be ready to respond quickly if it appears to be becoming entrenched. “With economic conditions in flux, agility is at a premium,” it said.
As well as fresh turmoil in energy markets, the IMF pointed to the continuing risk to the global economy of an AI-driven market crash.
