SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Potholes, bus fares and headphone dodgers: will Burnham’s strategy of ‘everyday fixes’ succeed?
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
In the first episode of Armando Iannucci’s political satire The Thick of It, the hapless minister Hugh Abbot is in the back of a taxi, frantically brainstorming for an on-the-hoof policy he can announce to the assembled national press.
“So you want something sexy and eye-catching, and that is free and universally popular and instantly applicable. No one can possibly object to it,” says the addled junior adviser Ollie Reeder. “Well, really, you should have said something before then, because I’ve got a file about that fucking thick of that back in the office.”
After a three-month micro-policy blitz from Downing Street, the question now being asked is: did Reeder pass said file on to the government’s battalion of special advisers? In the past week Andy Burnham has vowed to clamp down on social pariahs blaring out TikTok videos on public transport, outlaw “rip-off” private car park fines and – on Thursday – fill in potholes in 7,000 miles of England’s roads.
Before that, as part of the focus on “everyday fixes”, the prime minister announced a plan to remove VAT from electricity bills, a £2 cap on single bus fares across England and take action on “auto-renew” subscriptions. There’s also promises to crack down on pricey branded school uniforms, ban specious discounts, limit vape and betting shops and stop airlines charging families to sit together on planes. At this rate all minor annoyances in the UK will be eradicated by Christmas.
The idea is simple, says one policy adviser. “People expect the government to be able to do something about things which are unfair – big or small,” they said. “It sends a message that the government is on people’s side, its ready to act, and it can genuinely make a difference.”
Government insiders say the policies are not the product of standing around in a circle, throwing a stress ball and shouting out ideas. “There isn’t someone with a whiteboard brainstorming new bicycles for special constables,” says one, furthering the Thick of It comparison. Instead, the everyday fixes were a central policy strategy from Burnham’s first day in office. “We did this sort of thing under Keir too,” said another source. “But under Andy it’s a whole different thing; he’s put rocket boosters under it.”
In the first days of his premiership, Burnham gave his close ally Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, the job of establishing taskforces for three core areas – cost of living, public control and regeneration. One government source said: “There is a very intentional drumbeat of those because they do make a difference, but also it’s constantly showing people that we understand where those frustrations and low-level pressures are.”
Ideas are “kicked around” between the cost of living taskforce in the Cabinet Office and the policy unit in No 10, with all departments encouraged to feed in. “There’s a sort of filtering up process,” the source said. “It’s quite a sprawling sort of cross-government approach.”
Another said that while some departments were better placed to find “not hugely spendy” fixes, every minister was encouraged to contribute. “I think a lot of people had sort of resigned any hope that the government can actually get things done – and this is showing them that, yes, actually, we can,” another source said.
The small policy announcements have been, one delighted adviser said, a roaring success. Another source said: “Some people are very snotty about it, but in a world where it’s really hard for a government to cut through, this is working. You put some ideas through the grid and you often don’t know if they’re going to fly. But when you see one go gangbusters, it’s kind of like Christmas morning.”
One single fact policy idea dominated the news cycle for an entire day. Another generated tens of thousands of posts on X. Burnham’s faintly hokey video on antisocial phone use garnered 2m views. “It helps that he’s just really good at it,” the source said.
The small-fix policies have not been appreciated by everyone. Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick said the UK was “going down the pan and our prime minister is faffing around tweaking parking tickets” – despite trying to implement the policy himself when he was a Conservative minister. The former Olympian Sharron Davies said: “As Paris burns our prime minister has stopped people playing loud music on buses & trains,” leading some to question whether she expected Burnham to invade the French capital.
Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, has been dismissive, saying in a speech this week that cracking down on loud music on public transport was a “job for ticket inspectors, not the prime minister”. Reprising the theme at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, the leader of the opposition implicitly accused Burnham of fiddling while Rome burns. “We are spending more on interest payments than we do on schools, the army and the police combined,” she said. “Meanwhile, the prime minister is worrying about loud music on trains. This is not serious.”
Across the dispatch box, Burnham hid his delight at her response behind a disappointed look. “I’m not going to apologise for doing the small things that help people have better lives,” he said sombrely, while his advisers likely high-fived in private.
Regardless of the reaction of Burnham’s opponents, the focus on minor grievances is a canny strategy that appears to be working, said the pollster Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common. In recent polling, when people were asked whether Burnham understood the pressure of high energy bills on ordinary people, 45% said he did. When the same question was asked about Starmer, that figure was 23%. “I think the Tories and Reform have got it dead wrong on this,” Tryl said. “People bring this sort of stuff up in focus groups all the time. It cuts across left- and rightwing voters. People care about immigration, about the NHS – but they also care about everyday frictions.”
But behind the scenes there is an acknowledgment that a focus on ticking off small things from the PM’s to-do list will be significantly more challenging in moments of crisis. There has to be a “twin-track” approach, said one insider. “It’s combining a big picture, long term, dismantling 40 years of neoliberalism and addressing questions about ownership and control, but at the same time tackling more immediate daily bugbears,” they said. “What you’ve seen so far is these smaller level interventions, but the bigger structural, longer term piece will be in the 10-year plan.”
While the everyday fixes may be popular, the sugar-high they produce could be short-lived, said Ed Shackle, the head of qualitative research at the policy consultants Public First Global. “The government should be under no illusion that as soon as any real substantive event rears its head, any small popularity boost will be instantly blown away,” he said. “Quick fixes are popular, but they are a poor substitute for fixing the big issues the public care about.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Climate academic Andreas Malm barred from entering UK
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andreas Malm, the climate academic and author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline, has been blocked from entering the UK before he was due to speak alongside a co-founder of the banned group Palestine Action.
Malm was told by immigration officials his presence in the UK “may not be considered to be conducive to the public good”. He said the decision was “scandalous” and urged the government to reconsider.
Malm, an associate professor of human ecology at Lund University in Sweden, was due to headline a conference organised by Tribune magazine next week on “Washington’s global reign of terror and Britain’s role in reinforcing it”.
He was due to speak alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action. They were expected to discuss the impact of the ban, including its effect on the author Sally Rooney, who has withdrawn her books from sale in the UK over her support for the group.
Rooney said the decision to ban Malm from the UK was a “sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm”.
The Tribune event was timed to coincide with the start of a supreme court challenge to the ban next Wednesday. While in London, Malm was also due to be interviewed for BBC Radio 4’s Radical With Gabriel Gatehouse programme.
Malm said: “I am deeply dismayed at this sudden ban on travelling to the UK. I have been going to the UK for decades – this is where I did my archival research for my PhD dissertation and lectured at dozens of universities and participated in even more conferences.”
Malm urged the government to think again. He said: “One was under the impression that the Burnham government had slightly more respect for the basic notions of freedom of expression and other democratic rights. I appeal for this decision to be overturned.”
The Home Office said it did not discuss individual cases.
Rooney said: “Andreas Malm is among the most brilliant and influential intellectuals working in Europe today. For the UK government to deny him entry to Britain is not only an outrageous attack on a respected climate expert, but a sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm.”
Earlier this year, the US leftwing commentators Cenk Uygur and Hasan Piker were also barred from the UK on the same grounds that their presence in the UK “may not be conducive to the public good”.
Tribune’s editor, Oliver Eagleton, said: “Ironically, Andreas was coming to London to speak at our event about the unprecedented attacks on free speech unleashed by the proscription of Palestine Action, including the effective ban on Sally Rooney’s books, but he has now been banned himself.
“He is being censored for speaking out about censorship, in truly Orwellian fashion. It is shameful that Andy Burnham’s government is continuing the authoritarian overreach we saw under Keir Starmer, and in this dystopian new reality it is now commonplace in Britain for authors and academics to be treated as terrorists because they support Palestinians facing genocide and the rights of people protesting that genocide.”
Malm’s books have won international awards and inspired many to take action for environmental justice and Palestinian rights. How to Blow Up a Pipeline inspired a film of the same name. He has travelled regularly to Britain to lecture at universities including Oxford, King’s College London and Cambridge.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘Realistic and reassuring’: UK public ‘responding calmly’ to Be Ready campaign
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
When the UK government launched its “Protect and Survive” public information campaign in 1980 on how to stay alive after a nuclear attack, it was met with a combination of scepticism, disbelief and derision.
The advice included how to build a “fallout room” at home, how to whitewash windows to protect from a blast, and how to store a dead body for up to five days.
You might expect this would have prompted widespread panic, but in fact it led to a political backlash, and was later lampooned on TV and in music.
It shows the risks governments take when launching such campaigns, and the fine balance that must be struck between hammering home a practical message without causing panic – or other unintended reactions.
The government’s new Be Ready campaign is advising the public to stock up on three day’s worth of supplies for use during severe weather or cyber-attacks, so help can be directed to the most vulnerable first.
In a concise, two-page document, it suggests people stock bottled water and non-perishable food for three days, a torch with spare batteries, a wind-up FM radio, a first aid kit and a copy of their passport. To stave off panic buying, it advises people to check their cupboards first and build up items gradually on regular shopping trips.
While there is no evidence the advice has triggered mass panic, the public is clearly responding. Jack Brown, who co-owns Sgt Prepper Shop, which stocks emergency food and survival tools, said he received a month’s worth of orders in the first 24 hours of the Be Ready campaign.
“I thought my phone was glitching or being hacked with the number of orders coming in,” he said.
Brown said the advice seemed sensible and proportionate. Three days was the “sweet spot”, he said, with most everyday emergencies like power cuts, a burst water main or flooding sorted within that timeframe.
It is also “realistic, affordable and fits in a cupboard”, he said, adding that asking people to stock up on a month’s worth of supplies would feel overwhelming and most people would do nothing at all.
A wind-up radio was also a sensible suggestion, and ones with a built-in torch and phone-charging USB port make them “one of the most useful bits of kit you can own”, he said.
Dr Sarita Robinson, associate dean for the school of psychology and humanities at the University of Lancashire, said there was little evidence to suggest these kinds of messaging campaigns cause panic.
“There’s this perception that if we tell people the truth we’re somehow going to panic them and it isn’t the case,” she said.
“When we use accurate messaging about emergency situations, the public will engage with that proactively. It’s when we start to hide information and there’s a void of information, that’s when things can go wrong for government.”
She said Be Ready was “realistic, quite low level, and should be reassuring because it’s basically treating the public like the grownups they are”.
Dan Goss, who runs Start Prepping UK, said traffic to his website was up 700% since news of the campaign emerged in August. He said he was glad to see the subject finally being taken seriously and spoken about in “plain language” by the government, and felt the risk of panic was low.
“The level of uptake required for that would be huge – you would need to have an enormous number of people all take the government’s advice very seriously and all jump on it as a priority,” he said.
“We’re definitely in a phase now where we’re seeing lots of more disruption to people’s lives – not necessarily apocalyptic disasters, but things that have a big impact on small areas, so this advice is very much needed.”
Robinson said the campaign showed how the perception of “prepping” has shifted, especially since the Covid-19 pandemic when most people will remember seeing empty supermarket shelves.
“We did a study during Covid that showed people who did mild levels of prepping, such as having food, masks and hand gel in the house a few weeks before the pandemic, had lower anxiety and depression, and less stress,” she said.
“The government really needs to portray that this is just normal, everyday, very common in other countries, and isn’t wearing a tinfoil hat and building a nuclear bunker in your back garden.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between members states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.
A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.
The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.
The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.
It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.
But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.
Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.
Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.
At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.
Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.
“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.
Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.
Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.
A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economics said.
Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.
Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
A previous draft statement had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, including an acknowledgment that defining the term would take another year.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort.
The British defence secretary, giving a speech before a meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity.
Taking questions after his address, Streeting acknowledged “the challenges of recent days”, a reference to the row over the sudden decision of the US government on Monday to limit the use of Starlink by Ukraine’s military.
He said it was “a reminder of two things – one is that American support in Ukraine has been significant and it has made, I think, a real impact in the Ukrainian war effort. And we and the Ukrainians would feel the absence of that.”
The second was that there was “an enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine”, a reference to the future “defence-industrial relationship” between the countries.
Streeting was speaking at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, before meeting Hegseth amid tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East.
Speaking to the BBC after the meeting, Streeting said he had been “reassured directly” by his US counterpart that access to the vital Starlink communications system had been restored. The defence secretary said it was not yet clear to the UK why the disruption occurred, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”
The two men were also expected to discuss the safety of US military bases in the UK, after an Iranian threat prompted the US to withdraw B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, and whether the two countries would come together to help Saudi Arabia, which has come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis.
But it is Ukraine that is the most urgent issue. A day ago, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he felt personally betrayed by Donald Trump after the US government appeared to have throttled a version of the Starlink satellite internet service used by Ukraine’s military.
Ukrainian officials have reported that the US has also threatened to cut the sharing of intelligence used by Ukraine to detect incoming missiles if it does not abandon its attacks on refineries, aimed at hurting the Russian economy.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, meeting Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday, said the UK would stand by Ukraine.
Developing the theme, Streeting made a direct appeal to the US audience, saying: “There’s rarely been a more important time for Britain and America to come together.
“The people of Ukraine are fighting for a principle that runs through the finest traditions of American political thought,” he said, which was “that a free people have a right to determine their own destiny”.
Trump has vacillated over supporting Ukraine against Russia since returning to the White House, while support among US Republicans for Kyiv has been mixed. But Streeting argued that helping Ukraine was also a matter of national self-interest for the US as well as the UK.
“Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent,” he said.
The change to Starlink happened without warning at about 1am, when Ukrainian soldiers reported that terminals on drones were no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph, rendering communications inoperable.
It led to a dramatic halt to mid-strike drone attacks on targets in Russian occupied territories on the frontline, and concerns about Ukraine’s ability to intercept new Russian jet-powered attack craft that are bombing its cities.
Trump has been trying to put pressure on Ukraine to halt its bombing of Russian oil refineries in a desperate attempt to reduce world oil prices before the US midterm elections. He agreed to buy diesel from Russia earlier this month.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Oriel College urged to cancel student group’s event with Jason Arday accuser
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The University of Oxford’s Oriel College has been urged to cancel an event featuring Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas that has been organised by student supporters of Reform UK.
Arday, 41, was found dead in August after resigning from his University of Cambridge professorship. He had faced intense media scrutiny after Cofnas made unproven accusations of plagiarism against him and said there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims.
Cofnas, a blogger and academic who has been accused of promoting pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference in his online writings, is expected to appear at an event called “An evening with Nathan Cofnas: Is DEI undermining higher education?” at Oriel’s Harris lecture theatre on 17 November.
The event has been organised by Oxon Universities’ Reform Society (OURS), a student group set up this year to support Reform UK.
Oxford campaign groups, British academics, members of the public and Oxford alumni have signed an open letter urging Oriel to “withdraw its facilities from the event”.
The signatories say the event “risks creating a hostile and exclusionary environment for students, particularly those of ethnic minorities” and “risks undermining Oriel’s role as a world-class educational institution” in 2026, the year of the 700th anniversary of its royal charter.
The letter accuses Cofnas of using his platform to assert discriminatory beliefs, and claims his blogging played a significant role in the coverage Arday faced.
Days before Arday’s death, Kehinde Andrews, the author and the UK’s first professor of Black studies, told the Guardian Arday was facing a “dedicated, coordinated smear campaign from the right, based on the premise that Black people should not be at Cambridge”.
Responding to news of the Oriel event, Andrews said in a post online that it was “despicable and disgusting”.
Oriel College said in a statement: “Oriel College is committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so. This includes the freedom to express views that many find deeply offensive. We are also committed to promoting inclusion and maintaining an environment that is free from all forms of discrimination and harassment, including racial discrimination.
“The college considers events booked by students who are committee members of registered societies according to our code of practice on freedom of speech. When an event is permitted, this does not imply endorsement by the college of the views of its speakers.
“When considering booking requests, the college takes seriously the security implications of events and the safety of its members.”
In a post on X, OURS claimed: “Nathan Cofnas and the event organisers have been subjected to a disturbing torrent of online hostility.”
In a statement, OURS said that since it was a registered student society at the University of Oxford, constituent colleges “are under a legal obligation to host events like ours”.
It added: “The Reform Society is committed to hosting Nathan Cofnas, and allowing attendees at the event to engage in respectful dialogue with the same.
“We find it strange that the University of Oxford or any of its constituent colleges should receive reputational damage in respect of this event. The decision to host Nathan Cofnas was made solely by the committee of the Reform Society, and responsibility for the event rests exclusively with the same.”
Cofnas was approached for comment.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Thousands march in Greece over public education failures as Macron blasts ‘stupid’ commentary on French protests – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Thousands march in Greece over public education failures and cost of living
Crowds are also marching in cities across Greece right now calling for better classroom conditions and higher pay for teachers.
Thousands of students, teachers and civil servants have shown up in Athens, with demonstrations also in Thessaloniki and other cities. Some protesters say they’ve been inspired by the rallies in France and Spain.
The primary school teachers union has launched a 24-hour strike while the high school teachers’ federation has also announced a three-hour stoppage, local media report.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
Thousands of people joined education protests across Greece, calling for better classroom conditions and higher pay for teachers, in demonstrations echoing demands seen in France (14:42, 16:00).
Two airports have run out of jet fuel, supermarket shelves across southern Italy are standing empty and pharmacies are running short of medicines as Italian lorry drivers continue to blockade roads in protest against soaring fuel prices caused by the war in Iran (13:49).
French president Emmanuel Macron blasted “unacceptable” and “stupid” comments on the protests and riots in France from foreign leaders, accusing them of “campaigning at our expense” (12:22).
More protests in France are expected this Saturday and on Thursday, 5 November.
In other news,
Russia has signalled its readiness to restart trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the war, despite calling the new proposals emerging from yesterday’s discussions in Oslo as lacking substance (11:19, 12:22, 16:15).
This signal came hours after US envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russia’s president Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg (14:06).
On the margins of the meeting, Russia released a US citizen held by Moscow on allegations of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine (11:24, 13:24).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
US, Ukraine discussed the worsening situation in Oleshky, Kyiv's negotiator said
Ukraine and US negotiators discussed the situation in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, Davyd Arakhamia – a member of Kyiv’s negotiating team – was quoted by local media via Reuters as saying.
“We discussed it yesterday, and the informal outcome of this meeting is that there should be some good news next week,” he told media outlet RBC-Ukraine.
Residents of the Ukrainian town, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, have reported a deepening food crisis as roads in and out are heavily mined and saturated by drones.
Last week, Pope Leo urged Russia’s Vladimir Putin to allow humanitarian aid to the city.
'Ukrainian conflict heading towards its conclusion,' Kremlin aide says, as trilateral talks earmarked for mid-November
We are still getting more lines from the Kremlin, with Interfax news agency reporting that a new round of trilateral Russia, US, Ukraine talks could take place in Abu Dhabi in mid-November.
Curiously, despite his less enthusiastic comments earlier, Interfax also has Kremlin’s Ushakov saying that “the Ukrainian conflict is heading toward its conclusion.”
Government, popular websites go dark as developers race to patch newly-discovered vulnerability
There is also a fascinating story unfolding online, as government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators scrambling to protect their systems, Reuters reported.
Developers of the PHP programming language said Tuesday they had identified two critical vulnerabilities and urged users to update their sites as soon as a fix was released. They said on Wednesday that a new version fixing the vulnerabilities was live.
But with reports that hackers were exploiting the flaws to break into websites, government agencies in the Netherlands and Finland were among those that took sites offline ahead of the fix as a precaution.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet, raising concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack.
Russia open to restarting trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US, but 'not much substance' in Oslo proposals, Kremlin says
Meanwhile, we now have a longer reaction from the Kremlin to the proposals US peace envoy Steve Witkoff relayed to president Vladimir Putin, warning they were “lacking substance.”
“Steve Witkoff briefed Vladimir Putin on the substance of the talks held in Oslo,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, referring to talks Witkoff held in Norway with Ukrainian and European officials on Tuesday.
“He mentioned some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv... but there wasn’t really much substance in them.”
(That’s very much not what Zelenskyy and the Europeans said last night.)
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the mentioned (trilateral) talks,” he added, saying they could take place in mid-November.
More than 10,000 join education protests in Athens
Helena Smith
in Athens
Back again to Greece where tens of thousands of students have joined the burgeoning youth movement demanding better education better prospects amid an ever worsening cost of living crisis in the Mediterranean EU member.
Greece is no newcomer to protests. The massive demonstrations that roiled the country at the height of its debt crisis are still remembered vividly by the parents of the Gen Z protesters now out on the streets.
But for the tens of thousands who marched through Athens, Thessaloniki and other cities today, it was France, as well as the perceived shortcomings of a long under-funded education system, that had spurred them into action.
“From Greece to France we’re fighting for public and free education,” proclaimed a giant banner erected above a stage in front of the Athens parliament in Syntagma Square.
Singing French partisan songs, Greek students participating in the Athens rally, said the French protests were not only admirable but had been an inspiration.
“No one is doubting their message or concerns, even if [media] coverage is mostly focused on the violence,” said Fotini, enrolled at a university in the capital.
“We’re here to say we’re with French youth. Our parents endured so many hardships, so much sacrifice, and they feel really upset and enraged that we, too, have so few prospects. A lot of us are still forced to live with our families, even after we graduate, because the cost of living and house rents are so high.”
The protests, which included a one-day ‘solidarity ‘ strike by teachers, have seen students erect tents infront of the Greek parliament to protest against the soaring costs of education.
Many have privately run colleges – a trend that has included British universities establishing branches in the capital – in their sights. “No to private universities. Free and contemporary studies for all,” read another boldly painted banner erected in the plaza.
Will Europe’s angry protests lead to real political change?
Ashifa Kassam
European community affairs correspondent
Much of the news coverage in recent days has focused on the violence that played out on the fringes of the protests in France and Italy.
The protests themselves, however, point to what seems to be a diverse response to a common crisis: the growing perception, particularly among younger generations, that governments are unable, or unwilling, to deliver when it comes to affordable housing, social equality and robust public services.
“This is the most powerful warning from Europe’s angry youth today, in France and across the continent,” the policy analyst Alberto Alemanno said.
The framing stands in sharp contrast to the many rightwing and far-right voices who have sought to exploit the violence in France and Italy, linking it without evidence to migration while brushing over protesters’ wider demands.
A student protest movement has gripped Serbia for two years. This weekend it will try to take power
Julian Borger
in Belgrade
On Sunday, a mass student movement, Student List, will represent the most serious challenge Aleksandar Vučić has faced in his 12 increasingly authoritarian years in power, by putting forward their own candidates in parliamentary elections.
They hope to emulate the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán,in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, in a domino effect that could bring a democratic resurgence to central Europe.
Opinion polls have varied wildly, but many expert observers say a close race is quite possible, with neither side prepared to accept a loss as a legitimate result, raising the risk of post-election unrest and clashes.
In order to win, the students’ list of 250 candidates would have to break the mould of Serbian politics, along with Vučić’s grip on the country.
He stepped down as president last month, five months before the end of his second and last term in office under the constitution, but only with the aim of extending his hold on power as prime minister at the head of his Serbian Progressive party (SNS).

Crowds are also marching in cities across Greece right now calling for better classroom conditions and higher pay for teachers.
Thousands of students, teachers and civil servants have shown up in Athens, with demonstrations also in Thessaloniki and other cities. Some protesters say they’ve been inspired by the rallies in France and Spain.
The primary school teachers union has launched a 24-hour strike while the high school teachers’ federation has also announced a three-hour stoppage, local media report.
Macron arrives in Saudi Arabia as he continues his Gulf tour
The Elysée has just announced that the French president Emmanuel Macron has arrived in Saudi Arabia.
As we’ve been reporting, Macron is facing major protests at home, but has embarked on a wider tour of the Gulf, arriving in Qatar yesterday.
His Saudi Arabia stop had not been advertised but it’s not a major surprise – France has recently pledged more military support to the kingdom which is currently fighting the Iran-backed Houthi rebel group in Yemen. France has committed some assistance to protect the state’s oil production facilities.
Q&A on French protests, riots on Friday - ask your questions
By the way, this Friday Guardian Europe’s France-based columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the riots and protests in France.
Southern Italy running out of jet fuel, products, medicines as lorry protest continues
Lorenzo Tondo
in Palermo
Meanwhile, two airports have run out of jet fuel, supermarket shelves across southern Italy are standing empty and pharmacies are running short of medicines as lorry drivers continue to blockade roads in protest against soaring fuel prices caused by the war in Iran.
Italy’s air traffic management agency, ENAV, said on Wednesday that airports in Crotone and Reggio Calabria had run out of aviation fuel because of disruptions to supplies caused by the protests. It warned that pilots would have to refuel at their departure airports or earlier stops, carrying enough fuel for subsequent flights.
The protests began last week, with lorry drivers blocking roads and slowing traffic across the country, particularly in the south, following strikes and sit-ins by farmers and fishers. The disruption has left supermarket shelves empty in several regions, with photographs showing entire aisles stripped of goods.
A video of a lorry driver’s teenage daughter breaking down in tears has gone viral after she said her family could no longer afford to go out at weekends because they were struggling to pay their bills.
Italy’s infrastructure minister, Matteo Salvini, has proposed €430m in financial support, but the motorway blockades and lengthy traffic jams continue, putting the government under growing pressure as anger over the cost of living mounts.
The protests have also sparked criticism of Italy’s public broadcaster, Rai, which has been accused of giving greater prominence to violent student demonstrations in Milan than to the economic hardship facing families and lorry drivers in the south. Critics say the coverage plays into the government’s increasingly hardline approach to protests while diverting attention from the growing cost-of-living crisis.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Charities condemn proposal to make some refugees wait up to 30 years for settlement – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
This announcement deserves recognition, but it cannot be the end of the story. We need protections that work in practice, certainty for workers and their families, and a system that allows care providers to retain the people our communities rely on every day.
But business organisations like the CBI expressed concerns (see 5.39pm), and charities were outraged by the proposal for some refugees to be made to wait up to 30 years for indefinite leave to remain (see 5.47pm). The Law Society also condemned the plans. Its vice president, Dana Denis-Smith, said:
The home secretary’s decision to change pathways to settlement retrospectively undermines the legal certainty that individuals, families and employers rely on. For those already on the path to settlement, the government decision to change the rules which people relied on when making important decisions about their future is unjust.
She also suggested the rules for refugees contravened the Refugee Convention.
Extending the qualifying period from five to 20 or even 30 years, for those that have no choice but to enter through unsafe means, backtracks on promises the UK has made under the Refugee Convention 1951 to help those seeking protection to integrate and build a new life. This obligation applies to all refugees, regardless of how they arrived.
Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey discuss the issue in the latest episode of the Politics Weekly UK podcast.
The TUC has welcomed Shabana Mahmood’s decision to revise her plans. In a statement, Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary, said:
This is a welcome rethink from the home secretary and shows the government has listened to care workers and their unions on key concerns.
Migrant care workers do valuable and essential work in our care sector. They work around the clock to provide care for our loved ones and keep the sector running - after recruitment and retention crises caused by years of underfunding.
That’s why it is important that the government has changed course. But this policy must now be put into place fairly.
We need a sector wide visa so workers can change employers, rather than having to put up with abuse, poor conditions and exploitation.
Sunder Katwala, director of British Future, a thinktank focusing on immigration, race and identity, has said that, in the light of its announcement today, the government should be more robust in confronting people calling for migrants to be deported. In a statement he said:
There may be no flagship government policy that has changed quite as much as this one as a result of public consultation. Those changes mean many thousands of people, anxious about losing legal status, will now have a pathway to settle in Britain.
Behind this complex policy debate is a political argument about whether people who have come to Britain should be allowed to stay and settle or not. The government has sided with the argument for settlement and integration. It will now need to make the case more publicly against opponents who are still voicing a politics of ‘send them all back’.
Voters more likely to support than oppose making migrants wait longer for ILR, poll suggests
Britons are more likely to support (47%) than oppose (35%) making most migrant workers wait longer before they can apply for ILR, according to polling by YouGov.
Charities condemn proposal to make some refugees wait up to 30 years for settlement
Charities working with refugees have strongly condemned Shabana Mahmood’s proposal to make some of them wait up to 30 years for settlement. (See 4.25pm.)
Imran Hussain, executive director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said:
Refugees are being asked to rebuild their lives on a status that expires every 30 months for what could be 30 years. That is unfair and unworkable.
These plans condemn refugees to decades of deep insecurity, unable to lay down roots in Britain and contribute their potential. And there is no evidence to suggest that harming refugee integration will act as a disincentive to refugees fleeing the Taliban or brutal conflicts like Sudan. It also creates another bureaucratic nightmare for a Home Office that already is struggling with poor quality initial decisions on asylum cases which is leading to avoidable costs and delays in the appeals system.
And Flora Alexander, executive director of International Rescue Committee UK, said:
A route to settlement that takes up to 30 years means people will be left in limbo for more than a third of their lifetime. Those who have fled conflict and persecution should have the chance to rebuild their lives, not put them on hold for decades.
Farage says anyone getting ILR before election under Mahmood's plan could have it removed if he becomes PM
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, has said that anyone getting indefinite leave to remain (ILR) before the next election as a result of the plans announced today could lose it if be became PM.
He was not in the Commons for the announcement. Instead, he held a press conference where he said this was “a very major U-turn”. He went on:
Normal countries don’t give out work visas, allow you to bring dependents, automatically give you indefinite leave to remain, and then one year later citizenship. We are uniquely stupid in doing this, and we’ve been uniquely stupid in doing this for far too many years.
Our position is very, very clear: Anybody under this scheme that’s been opened today, and I believe today is just the opening of the door, anybody that goes through to ILR and citizenship under this scheme, we will review each and every single one of those citizenships if they are granted.
CBI suggests care workers concession means rest of ILR reforms might be hard to justify
The CBI, one of Britain’s main business organisations, has suggested that Shabana Mahmood’s concession on care workers today means the rest of the measures announced might not be needed.
In a statement, Matthew Percival, the CBI’s future of work director, said:
Today’s announcement on settlement rules rightly recognises the importance of fairness and the contribution migrant workers make to the UK. But the decision to exempt health and social care workers fundamentally changes the case for the wider policy.
These proposals were introduced in response to a temporary spike in health and social care visas. If those workers are now outside the policy, the government should reconsider whether the remaining changes are still justified. Otherwise, the result risks being higher costs for the relatively small number of businesses using skilled worker visas, without addressing the problem the policy was originally designed to solve.
In the Commons, the first Conservative backbencher to speak in response to Shabana Mahmood’s statement was Edward Leigh. He accepted that the Conservatives were at fault in allowing immigration to soar when they were in office. In a jibe at the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, he said that “some of us don’t have amnesia” and that “anybody who was serving as a Home Office minister at that time should wear sackcloth and ashes”.
Home Office list of 'public service' jobs where foreign workers will get ILR after 5 years without having to earn £50,271
Here is the list of “public service” jobs where foreign workers will continue to be able to apply for ILR after five years, as now, instead of having to wait 10 years, which will be the new norm. Anyone earning more than £50,271 will automatically be in this category. But people earning less than that will be included if they are doing one of these jobs.
You will notice that care workers are not on the list.
Under the plans announced last year, care workers were going to be in a special category where they were going to have to wait 15 years for ILR (because of their low income). That idea has been abandoned, and instead they are covered by the new, 10-year norm. (See 4.39pm.)
But Mahmood has announced what she is calling “transitional arrangements” that will apply to most care workers. (See 4.11pm.) The Home Office says:
Care workers who entered, or switched into, the route before publication of the immigration white paper in May 2025 will retain the existing five-year qualifying period for settlement where they meet the applicable salary (£25,000 a year), sponsorship and employment requirements. They will also need to meet the strengthened minimum requirements that will apply generally under earned settlement, including on criminality and English language, unless an exemption applies.
Care workers who arrived before May 2025 who do not meet these criteria will instead be given the chance to apply for a second, five-year visa. (See 4.11pm.)
Mahmood says she does not accept her changes retrospective
Labour’s Diane Abbott told Mahmood she was in danger of creating another Windrush scandal. And she complained about the changes being retrospective. She said:
It is right that care workers are exempted from the new arrangements for [indefinite leave to remain]
But for the rest of the workforce, the retrospective nature of these new arrangements still seem to be unfair because you can come in legally, you can work legally and then have your residency rights turned upside down. How can that be fair?
Mahmood said she did not accept that the changes were retrospective.
On indefinite leave to remain and what she calls the retrospective nature of the changes, she will know I do not agree with that characterisation of those changes.
Any government needs to be able to make changes to immigration rules to reflect things that are happening, to reflect abuses that we can see in the system, to also be able to make additional changes based on assessment of numbers and costs.
Mahmood says 500,000 people will get settlement later as result of tighter rules
Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, responded to Mahmood on behalf of the Conservatives. He claimed she had performed a U-turn that would cost £10bn. (See 11.44am.)
The home secretary now proposes to allow every single care worker and their dependents who arrived prior to May 202 - a number running into hundreds of thousands – to stay in this country to stay in this country beyond the expiry of their visa, and in the case of 75% of them to stay permanently
How is it she can justify allowing people that she acknowledges arrived here fraudulently [to] stay forever, at a cost that she herself has admitted costs £10 billion? That is the cost. That is the cost of today’s U-turn.
Mahmood said her plans would save money, and lead to 500,000 people getting settlement later than planned. She said:
The cohort most likely to impose a cost will now, as a result of my measures, wait longer for settlement.
And that is why the [Department for Work and Pensions] say that these measures will save billions in the benefits bill.
And half a million people, 500,000 people, will settle later as a result of these reforms.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Officials confirm flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite found in US wildlife
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) said on Wednesday it had confirmed the first detection of flesh-eating parasite the New World screwworm in US wildlife in an elk in Pecos county, Texas.
The elk was located on a game ranch and was reported after being harvested by a hunter, the USDA said in a statement.
The Texas animal health commission will modify a previously established infested zone, and the USDA and the Texas parks and wildlife department is conducting additional wildlife surveillance in the area, the USDA said.
“We encourage all hunters and landowners to be vigilant for signs of New World screwworm while they are out in the field this season,” Texas wildlife division director Alan Cain said in a statement.
Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports.
The US halted livestock imports from Mexico last year to keep out screwworm, but resumed trade in August at an Arizona port as part of a phased reopening plan.
The halt has tightened US cattle supplies and pushed beef prices to record highs for American consumers.
Despite those efforts, the screwworm was detected in June on a calf in Texas’s Zavala county, located near the US-Mexico border. There have since been dozens of cases detected in the US this year, including on a horse and on a dog.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Judge dismisses Trump attempt to block Alaska Senate race results if Republican loses
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A judge has dismissed the Donald Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.
Trump said on 23 October that he had ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit in a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance.
The justice department argued in its lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before election day, that there could be “voter confusion” over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the November ballot, which Republicans fear could take away votes from the incumbent and influence the race’s outcome in favor of the Democratic nominee, Mary Peltola.
The justice department said it planned to appeal Sunday’s ruling: “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.
Sullivan, in an interview with CNN on Sunday morning, said that he would accept the results of his upcoming election.
According to a recent New York Times investigation, aides from Peltola’s campaign recruited another man who shared Sullivan’s name to join the race in a ploy to peel away votes from the Republican incumbent.
Since those revelations, Republicans, including Donald Trump, have called for Peltola to be disqualified from the race and criminally prosecuted. Peltola has continued to deny any knowledge of such a scheme on the part of her campaign, recently telling a reporter at a campaign event that she had “no idea” if any of her staff were involved.
Asked by CNN’s Jake Tapper if he would only accept the election results if he won, Sullivan responded: “No, I’m going to accept the election results.”
Earlier in his interview with Tapper, Sullivan also said he wasn’t focused on how Peltola’s campaign might be legally challenged. He was focused instead on winning the race outright. He nonetheless expressed doubt that Peltola had lacked any knowledge of the effort to put a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
“She’s continually lying to the Alaskan people,” Sullivan said. “And I guarantee you, she’s lying right now.”
Meanwhile, the Washington Post reported that Republicans tried to boost unviable Democratic candidates in the Alaska primaries as well. A Republican Super Pac boosted two candidates for Senate who did not live in Alaska, and praised them as “progressives” similar to Bernie Sanders.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Court blocks bid by Trump DoJ to stop California from counting mail-in ballots
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A US federal appeals court rejected the Trump administration’s move to block California from counting the ballots of 20,000 registered voters that the justice department claims are non-citizens.
The court on Monday ruled 2-1 against Donald Trump’s justice department in the dispute, denying the administration’s demand that election officials segregate the thousands of ballots until people on the list could verify their citizenship. The justice department had given the California secretary of state 48-hours to carry out the order, which state election officials refused – leading to the lawsuit.
The decision by the San Francisco-based ninth US circuit court of appeals marks a setback in Trump’s attempts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the 3 November midterms. Voting rights groups and Democrats have criticized the effort, saying the Trump administration is attempting to create uncertainty around the upcoming election results as Republicans vie to retain control of Congress.
The ruling is also the latest development in a conflict between California and Trump’s justice department. The DoJ additionally filed criminal charges against 28 green-card holders in California earlier this month over alleged voter fraud – including several people who court papers suggested were confused about their eligibility and agreed to voluntary interviews with investigators.
There is uncertainty over how the justice department developed its list of 20,000 non-citizen registered voters and its accuracy. Court filings from last week showed that Los Angeles election officials analyzed a sample of 200 people on the list and found that a “high percentage” were born in the United States.
The justice department claims about non-citizen voting in California have also faced backlash from state officials, who have said that the DoJ has not provided data or methodology to back up its allegations. California secretary of state Shirley Weber called the department’s claims “vague and unsubstantiated” in a letter earlier this month. Weber also stated that the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year claimed that California had 190,000 registered voters that “may be” non-citizens, but provided no further details on how it reached that number.
California’s attorney general Rob Bonta touted Monday’s decision as a victory for voting rights and rejection of the Trump administration’s “unlawful overreach”, while Governor Gavin Newsom accused Trump of carrying out an “assault on democracy”.
“Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the constitution and our country’s democracy,” Newsom said in a statement.
Trump has personally advocated for his supporters to seek out voter fraud in the midterm elections, posting on his Truth Social platform on Monday that he would issue a $1m reward for anyone whose report led to an arrest or conviction. He has long made unfounded claims that ineligible voting such as non-citizen voting is rampant, despite experts and data having shown it is exceedingly rare.
Associated Press contributed reporting

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK government to extend controversial Palantir NHS contract as it draws up plan for British alternative – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Palantir’s controversial £330m health contract is to be extended before ministers draw up plans to replace it with a British alternative, the FT has reported.
Health secretary Yvette Cooper has faced calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system.
The system aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements. But a review has concluded that removing Palantir from NHS data systems by triggering a break clause in its contract would be too disruptive, the FT reported.
Ministers instead plan to launch a procurement process for a UK tech alternative, with Palantir to potentially be replaced in two years.
Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”.
The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.
The plan is expected to be signed off soon but Green party leader Zack Polanski accused Labour of “betrayal” and said it was “allowing the corporate capture of our most beloved institution by a genocide and Donald Trump supporting tech corporation.”
He added:
The reports today that Labour is to keep Palantir in the NHS shows that the huge sums of money paid to the likes of former Labour ministers, Peter Mandelson and Tom Watson, looks to have paid off.
Any evidence of patient benefit is highly contested by NHS staff and many NHS trusts have rejected the use of Palantir’s platform.
That’s all from me, Tom Ambrose, and indeed the UK politics live blog for today.
Here is a round-up of the day’s main stories:
Palantir’s controversial £330m health contract is to be extended before ministers draw up plans to replace it with a British alternative, the FT has reported. Health secretary Yvette Cooper has faced calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system.
Employers will be forced to publish salaries on job adverts, Andy Burnham has announced, in the government’s latest “small fix” to help improve people’s lives. The prime minister said his government would bring in a legal requirement for companies to say what they pay when listing new jobs, which campaigners say will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay.
Andy Burnham has praised the victims who have come forward to speak about Russell Brand’s crimes, after he was convicted of rape and sexual assault against three women. Police have urged anyone with fresh allegations against Brand to come forward, with the head of Scotland Yard, Mark Rowley, saying he would not be surprised if “many more” alleged victims emerged following the former comedian and online influencer’s conviction on Thursday.
Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is considering a change to knife laws, following the murder of Henry Nowak. The home secretary said she had not “taken any options off the table”, after Nowak’s father, Mark Nowak, called for a clearer definition in law of what a Sikh kirpan looks like.
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has caused “profound anger, hurt and disbelief” among many black voters with her comments about transatlantic slavery, according to the chair of Operation Black Vote (OBV), who urged the prime minister, Andy Burnham, to apologise for Britain’s involvement without delay. David Weaver, a former government adviser, said the Labour and Tory leaders risked alienating black voters with their handling of the issue of a state apology for slavery, while saying Badenoch’s remarks showed a “troubling absence of moral leadership”.
Andy Burnham has joked that he was a bad driver after getting a quiz for primary-age children about braking distance wrong. During a visit to Siemens Rail Technology Centre in Chippenham on Friday, the prime minister was invited to take part in a lesson hosted by TV presenter Maddie Moate with year five and six pupils from the town.
The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month. At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.
An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy suppliers to do more to help households get on top of their unpaid energy bills this winter, before the government spends almost £2.5bn to help write off the country’s record high debts. Energy bosses were summoned to a roundtable meeting on Thursday to discuss the government’s plan to pay down the energy debts of about 2.4m of the hardest-hit households.
The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said. Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.
A Scottish government official warned there were “clearly significant impacts and risks” from plans to site a number of hyperscale data centres in Scotland, documents released under freedom of information (FoI) laws have revealed. The deputy director for domestic climate change said there were “various concerns about the way forward”, citing concerns about possible impacts on energy bills and on water usage, PA reported.
Staff at the Scottish government and four of its agencies are being balloted on potential strike action in a row over a mandatory level of office working.
The government has mandated that staff should work from one of their offices 40% of the time, which the PCS union – which represents civil servants – said is “unacceptable”.
The union is calling on the government to scrap the plan, with a ballot on potential industrial action opening on Monday and lasting until 14 December, PA reports.
Burnham says Brand’s crimes are 'horrifying' as he praises victims’ courage
Andy Burnham has praised the victims who have come forward to speak about Russell Brand’s crimes, after he was convicted of rape and sexual assault against three women.
Speaking to Times Radio, the prime minister said: “It’s horrifying what Russell Brand has done.
“I’d firstly like to praise the bravery of the women, the victims in the case, who’ve come forward and had the courage to speak out. But yes, the journalists too, who supported those who had been abused by Russell Brand and worse.
“So all of them deserve our praise for having that courage to stand forward.”
‘Profound anger’ among black voters over Kemi Badenoch’s slavery remarks
Chris Osuh
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has caused “profound anger, hurt and disbelief” among many black voters with her comments about transatlantic slavery, according to the chair of Operation Black Vote (OBV), who urged the prime minister, Andy Burnham, to apologise for Britain’s involvement without delay.
David Weaver, a former government adviser, said the Labour and Tory leaders risked alienating black voters with their handling of the issue of a state apology for slavery, while saying Badenoch’s remarks showed a “troubling absence of moral leadership”.
In a week in which the UK political agenda was dominated by postcolonial legacies, Badenoch said Burnham should not apologise for Britain’s historical role in slavery “because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash”, while criticising Commonwealth leaders on X.
Burnham, while saying he was open to making a formal apology on behalf of the British state, has ruled out reparations. Weaver said he welcomed the prime minister’s apparent willingness to apologise, but said the government’s “almost reflexive insistence” that any apology must come with assurances “reparations are off the table” was concerning.
Weaver said only the prime minister had the power to address the hurt felt by descendant communities and show Britain had the “moral courage to apologise without qualification”.

The deputy director for domestic climate change said there were “various concerns about the way forward”, citing concerns about possible impacts on energy bills and on water usage, PA reported.
The official, whose name was redacted in the documents that were released, said that depending on the location of data centres “there is a clear risk here that locals bear the brunt of increased electricity prices – or even a shortage of energy, or unreliable power – while seeing little direct benefit from ‘hosting’ the data centre”.
In the document, which dates back to March, they added that to mitigate against this “there needs to be a really clear system for protecting locals from increased energy prices and power shortages, as part of a deal to host the centre”.
Andy Burnham has joked that he was a bad driver after getting a quiz for primary-age children about braking distance wrong.
During a visit to Siemens Rail Technology Centre in Chippenham on Friday, the prime minister was invited to take part in a lesson hosted by TV presenter Maddie Moate with year five and six pupils from the town.
The host asked Burnham and the children a series of questions about the braking distance of moving vehicles, with the prime minister making light of his incorrect answers.
“That shows why I’m a bad driver, doesn’t it,” he joked.
He visited the manufacturing company in Wiltshire to highlight his plans to create more work experience opportunities for young people and tackle barriers to employment.
The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.
At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.
These member states oppose deferring agreement for another half-year. Many believe a failure to reach an agreement should delay the highly prized food and drink deal to cut Brexit red tape coming into force.
European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.
Andy Burnham will meet the EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on 20 November in Brussels, with the aim of signing three agreements – on food and drink, carbon markets and youth exchange – as well as pledging a “trusted partnership” on steel and defence industries.
But a longstanding dispute over whether EU students should pay costly international tuition fees at British universities remains unresolved and could delay the implementation of the food and energy deals, which are worth billions to the British economy.

Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”.
The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.
The plan is expected to be signed off soon but Green party leader Zack Polanski accused Labour of “betrayal” and said it was “allowing the corporate capture of our most beloved institution by a genocide and Donald Trump supporting tech corporation.”
He added:
The reports today that Labour is to keep Palantir in the NHS shows that the huge sums of money paid to the likes of former Labour ministers, Peter Mandelson and Tom Watson, looks to have paid off.
Any evidence of patient benefit is highly contested by NHS staff and many NHS trusts have rejected the use of Palantir’s platform.
UK government considers smart glasses ban over secret filming concerns
Nadeem Badshah
The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said.
Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.
Kaur said:
The benefits of smart glasses must be weighed against the harms they can cause. The government is already looking into options to restrict smart glasses in certain settings and restricting the sale to certain users.
The minister said people who used smart glasses for filming already risked breaking the law in certain settings, such as in a court where cameras are prohibited.
Kaur added:
Other settings, such as healthcare and education, have existing safeguarding or professional policies that are relevant to smart glasses and any kind of digital recording. NHS England and the Department for Education are currently looking into wearable technology in certain settings as well.
Anna Sabine, a Liberal Democrat MP and a culture spokesperson for the party, who held Wednesday’s debate, said:
Women are reporting waking up after nights out to find videos of themselves have gone viral online, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses.
To me, these devices not only have the potential to erode safety and privacy in public spaces, but raise really important questions about consent.
Minister tells energy suppliers to do more to help households tackle unpaid bills this winter
Jillian Ambrose
An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy suppliers to do more to help households get on top of their unpaid energy bills this winter, before the government spends almost £2.5bn to help write off the country’s record high debts.
Energy bosses were summoned to a roundtable meeting on Thursday to discuss the government’s plan to pay down the energy debts of about 2.4m of the hardest-hit households.
The debt relief scheme is part of a wider “circuit-breaker” strategy put forward by the chancellor in the annual budget statement last month. This includes measures to tackle household energy debt, which could reach £7bn by the end of the year.
The minister for energy consumers, Polly Billington, is understood to have told bosses from energy companies including Octopus Energy, British Gas and EDF Energy that suppliers would still need to play a “crucial role” in tackling the longstanding issue of problem debt alongside the government’s multibillion-pound support package.
Suppliers are expected to proactively identify customers who may be under financial strain and offer help such as debt payment plans or pointing them in the direction of debt advice services.
The government is also planning to work with the industry to make it easier to spot households that may need extra help, and to modernise payment systems to make it easier to pay. The government has backed the use of smart meters and smart pre-pay meters to help households track their spending and avoid getting into arrears.
Knife law changes not 'off the table', home secretary says
Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is considering a change to knife laws, following the murder of Henry Nowak.
The Home Secretary said she had not “taken any options off the table”, after Nowak’s father, Mark Nowak, called for a clearer definition in law of what a Sikh kirpan looks like.
Mark Nowak told ITV News: “I fully understand the need to carry a kirpan but surely that should be defined in law, in terms of size and type and whether it should be visible, and so on and so forth.
“And therefore, anything else should be made illegal.”
Asked about Mark Nowak’s suggestion, Mahmood told the same broadcaster:
I haven’t taken any options off the table. I’m also not going in with a fixed mind about what the right clarifications of the law might be.
It’s important to get the right balance between religious expression in this country, which is something that many of us of a faith, including myself, hold very dearly, but do so in a way that is within what we expect of our citizens for the purposes of the criminal law.
Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch said lawmakers “do need to look at” knife laws.
Burnham to force employers to publish salaries on job ads in latest government 'small fix'
Hello and welcome to the UK politics live blog.
Employers will be forced to publish salaries on job adverts, Andy Burnham has announced, in the government’s latest “small fix” to help improve people’s lives.
The prime minister said his government would bring in a legal requirement for companies to say what they pay when listing new jobs, which campaigners say will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay.
Burnham said the move would help deal with the frustration of applying for a job without knowing the salary, while officials say that publicising pay will help those in work know if they are being paid fairly in comparison with others.
The prime minister said:
Whether you’re a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it.
That’s why we will make it a legal requirement for all employers to say what you pay.
But breaking down barriers is only one part of the job. We also need businesses to open more doors and give young people the experience and confidence to take that first step into the world of work.
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said: “Anyone who’s searched for a job knows how frustrating it is to read ‘competitive salary’.”
Recent research by the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development found less than half of employers always published salaries ranges on job adverts, while less than a fifth always published specific salaries.
Experts say omitting pay details from job adverts makes it harder for young people to know which jobs to apply for, and makes it easier for employers to give lower pay offers to some candidates, including women.
