SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Liz Truss has brought our divided nation together – in mockery of her | Emma Brockes
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
In these times of social and political division, it’s worth doing a quick audit of what keeps us together. Where, as we fight over what constitutes “wealth” and whether or not to go back in on Brexit, are the key sites of consensus? The Celebrity Traitors and the gloriousness of Nigella on Bake Off may offer one area of unity; you can say the words “David Attenborough” to any sample of the population and elicit exactly the same murmur of approval. But, as the recent history of the internet shows, the most forceful bonds are those forged against, rather than in favour of, something. With that in mind, let’s turn to our old friend Liz Truss.
It’s an unusual position, isn’t it, wondering if we might owe a debt of gratitude to the former prime minister who, after tanking the value of the pound in 2022 and otherwise carrying on with the efficacy of someone stopped at random in the street and given the keys to government, is widely regarded as the worst ever to have held office. Truss has a book out this week, her second since leaving office, entitled Bank Job: A Short Book on How the Bank of England Broke the Bond Market and Brought Down the Government, and on the evidence of its early reception, it seems likely to prove even more successful in uniting disparate communities of Britain than her previous volume, Ten Years to Save the West.
The government to which she refers in the subtitle is, of course, Truss’s own, which faltered in the wake of her mini-budget four years ago, when she sought to put through £45bn of unfunded tax cuts. Blaming the crash that followed on the Bank of England and the Treasury, the author admits no error, rekindling in observers powerful feelings of fury, mockery, incredulity and shame, plus a release of energy so intense that, like someone kicking in an old TV in a rage room, it might be mistaken for joy.
The Independent’s reviewer called the book “dense, paranoid and peevish”. The Telegraph gave it zero stars and also called it “deranged”. Scottish tabloid the National called it “unhinged”. The Daily Star, which focused on the book’s failure to give an adequate account of the role played by the iceberg lettuce that outlasted Truss’s 49-day tenure, called it “loopy”. Writing on X, Truss’s own former trade minister Conor Burns called her “an international embarrassment with zero self-awareness”, and “financially illiterate”. And so on.
None of these opinions of Truss are new, but condensed as they are into a week of terrible reviews, they perhaps offer us an opportunity to come together to warm our hands around a single point of scorn. Even in a world dominated by horrible characters, this is a rare talent. President Donald Trump, for example, whom Truss has been unsuccessfully trying to suck up to for years, even going so far as to colour-scheme the cover of her last book red (for Republican) rather than blue (for Tory), can do no wrong in certain sections of the US electorate because of what he represents – white supremacy.
But Truss doesn’t represent anything. She is relieved of all political associations. She stands for chaos unrelieved by charm, deepened by the impression she gives of someone receiving orders at a frequency no one else can hear. As an experiment, I tried just now to see if, with a bit of effort, I could drum up some sympathy for Truss, as I have on occasion managed for Theresa May; then I tried to find her funny, as I can sometimes do with Boris Johnson. But no; with Truss it is simply impossible to summon anything but rage and derision.
In light of which, we might say this woman has become a national hero, achieving the seemingly impossible without even trying. In the first weeks after 9/11, Americans in large US cities enjoyed a brief improvement in civic behaviour as reported crime went down. I don’t mean to compare Truss’s premiership to the worst act of terrorism this century, but there is evidence to suggest that when people pull together in the wake of a universally recognised disaster, society briefly improves.
The question, given the damage done by Truss to this country’s standing in the world and to our own sense of political and financial security, is: was it worth it? Obviously not. Still, at the time of writing, as Bank Job sits in the Amazon top 20 and Truss’s belligerent expression stares out, across all media, provoking howls of laughter and explosive diatribes from everyone who looks on her, there are really only two words to say: thank you.
- 
  Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Repairing Brexit economic damage should be Burnham’s top priority, business chief says
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Repairing the economic damage of Brexit should be the top priority for Andy Burnham as he reconsiders Labour’s red lines on EU membership, the head of one of Britain’s leading business groups has said.
Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said she welcomed the prime minister reopening the Brexit battle lines despite the uncertainty it could create, arguing that the UK’s current trading relationship with the EU was bad for business.
“We do think it’s right, because of what we know from the evidence of how businesses feel it’s not working,” she said.
Highlighting the continuing economic hit from Brexit, Haviland said more than half of bosses surveyed by the business lobby group believed the deal negotiated by Boris Johnson’s government and enacted in 2021 was not helping them.
“We expected it to be very difficult at the beginning, when [companies] were getting used to the new rules, and then it would sort of get easier as it went to along. But actually, that has not happened,” she said.
Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far, with national income per head between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been had the UK not left the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a long-term hit of about 4% of gross domestic product.
At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” as he pledged to reassess Britain’s relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc, and this week he said failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty”.
In an interview with the Guardian in Norwich alongside the head of the Norfolk Chambers of Commerce (NCC) chief executive, Nova Fairbanks, Haviland said the government had to take into account business frustrations with Brexit.
She said the BCC would also consult its 50,000 members, who collectively employ more than 6 million people across the UK, on a range of options for Britain’s relationship, including rejoining the EU.
“We are 10 years since the referendum,” Haviland said. “We would say the language of Brexit needs to move on. That’s gone. What businesses understand is what we had before and what we’ve got now.
“We’re apolitical, it’s not a political question. It is an economic question. So we are going to set out the options, from the where we are to the most extreme. And in consultation with our chambers, and our partners, we will see where people are.”
Fairbanks said it was clear that some Brexit-backing bosses recognised the economic damage. “It would be very interesting to see how many businesses that were very much pro-Brexit are still pro-Brexit, because I’ve certainly not heard any change of heart from those that were against Brexit. I think they are still very much: ‘We need to be closer to Europe.’”
Speaking on the sidelines of an NCC trade fair at the Norfolk Showground, the business leaders said companies were coming under growing pressure from rising energy prices and other effects of the war in the Middle East.
Haviland called on the chancellor, John Healey, to take bold action at this month’s budget to support firms despite concerns at the heart of government about the pressure on the public finances amid jitters in the bond market.
“This rumour about a sort of ‘steady as she goes’ budget, and ‘let’s not upset the apple cart’. Business don’t really want just a ‘steady as she goes’. They want to see some action that will relieve some of those costs that will drive that fly wheel [of the British economy],” she said.
“You can’t just trot along in a crouch position effectively. And surely the markets will be happy to see some spending cuts by the government, and some investment in private-sector growth?”
Haviland called for action on energy bills, business rates and taxes on employment to help companies recruit more young people. “In your energy bill, about 40% of your energy is actually energy. The other 60% is about tax. So the government can get some of that out,” she said.
“The big test for the chancellor is to put his money where his mouth is for business at the budget. Just showing that he genuinely believes that the wealth creators are the job creators – which is business.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘There has to be a bolder shift’: retail and hospitality businesses assess relief in budget
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
“It is like letting the tyres down and then handing you a pump,” says James Nye, assessing the relief handed to businesses in John Healey’s first budget as chancellor.
The managing director of Norfolk’s Anglian Country Inns argues that the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but added more labour costs for already burdened companies.
Nye, who employs 500 people at the height of the season at its 10 venues across Norfolk and Hertfordshire, was among those business owners watching Healey carefully on Wednesday, after two previous Labour budgets under Rachel Reeves had loaded extra costs on to businesses.
Healey aimed to help high street operators by removing the business rates burden from more small businesses and limiting the rise in the minimum wage for younger workers.
The chancellor put a lid on increases to business rates, so they will only rise in line with inflation for two years, and clamped down on VAT dodging by online sellers, among other measures intended to help high streets. However, some businesses argued Andy Burnham’s chancellor could have gone further.
Pets Corner, family-owned retailer
Dean Richmond, the owner of the Pets Corner chain, says the chancellor has not fixed the “fundamental problem” that its costs are rising faster than it can increase sales.
The family-owned business, founded by Richmond’s parents in 1968, now employs 1,200 people and has 159 stores. He does not expect to get much benefit from the increase in the threshold at which business rates begin to be paid.
“It’s a bit ‘moving the deckchairs on the Titanic’ on rates. There has to be a bolder shift if the government is going to help offline retail,” Richmond says.
He welcomed the move to ensure that online marketplaces such as Amazon collect VAT from more sellers, but was disappointed that Healey did not bring forward the end of tax breaks for online sellers, such as Shein and Temu, importing cheaper items from overseas.
“It feels like the world’s against us. When offline retailers all but disappear the world will miss us,” he says.
While he says Reeves’s budgets had been “really damaging, this is safe but isn’t going to change anything”.
“It is not a good news budget with the minimum wage going up,” he says, on top of the previous changes to employers’ national insurance contributions (NICs) and big increases in the minimum wage for employers.
Richmond says the business, based in Crawley in Sussex, had been forced to make “pretty drastic cuts” to the number of people it employed and to reduce bonus incentives, and had shifted to hiring older, more experienced people as there was less incentive to hire new starters.
Herdy, independent retailer and brand
Spencer Hannah is the co-founder and owner of Herdy, which has five shops in Cumbria and sells its cartoon sheep-branded homewares and clothing online and to other retailers in the UK and overseas.
“The chancellor’s key narrative was that he wanted to support British businesses doing business with Britain and we applaud and support that,” says Hannah, whose business employs 28 people directly.
But Hannah says the budget lacked the “seismic difference” to help UK retailers and their local suppliers. He welcomed relief on business rates for smaller shops but says that was “not counterbalancing what’s happened in the last two years”.
“Like everybody else running small and medium-sized enterprises, life has got slowly harder over the last two budgets and some poor choices have been made by the [last] leadership in government.”
He says increases in national insurance contributions, the minimum wage and other costs such as rent and energy have weighed on the business directly, but the “most frustrating thing” has been the impact of the higher costs for his domestic suppliers. He has been forced to ditch some of them, such as its mug manufacturer in Stoke, and look abroad.
Anglian Country Inns, pub and hotel operator
Nye says the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but against a very tough backdrop.
He welcomes help on business rates for smaller venues but says this is unlikely to assist Anglian directly. He was disappointed that the chancellor had yet again put up the legal minimum wage from April, which will more than offset the rates change for most.
A failure to cut VAT for hospitality businesses or cut national insurance contributions for younger workers were further disappointments.
Nye hopes that Healey’s support for household energy bills “might help consumer confidence”, but added: “We were expecting a little bit more to offset the massive tax increases hospitality has faced.”
“We are being crippled by taxes as a sector and the cumulative tax burden is horrific. We pay 83% as a percentage of our profits in tax,” Nye says.
“I don’t mind paying people more, but we’re then being taxed on it because the NICs threshold hasn’t changed, and the rate of NICs has gone up, so every time that the national minimum wage goes up, we’re paying more and more in tax.
“The cost of going out is getting more and more expensive. My biggest fear is that hospitality starts becoming a luxury rather than a convenience.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of spying, in the latest sign of rising tensions between Moscow and Tokyo.
Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai, from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, adding that he had been accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
Imai, a reporter at the newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin, was reportedly preparing to return to Japan when he was arrested for allegedly collecting information on Russia’s defence capabilities, according to Russia’s Tass news agency.
Russia’s FSB security agency claimed the journalist had intended to pass the information on to Japanese intelligence.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Japan’s foreign ministry urged Moscow to extend “fair and impartial treatment” to the detained journalist. “The Japanese embassy … in Moscow and the consulate general in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk lodged a request with the Russian authorities for the prompt provision of information, as well as for humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” an official told Agence France-Presse.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said in a statement that it was aware of the announcement by Russian authorities but it was “still confirming the details”.
“Ensuring the safety of the journalist is our top priority, and we are responding accordingly,” it said.
Imai’s arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over sovereignty of islands belonging to the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido.
Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap.
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.
“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.
The Kurils have been under Russian control since the end of the second world war, when Soviet forces seized the islands in the final days of the conflict, forcing about 17,000 Japanese citizens to leave and, over time, replacing them with a similar number of Russians.
In 2022, Moscow scrapped a programme that allowed former residents to travel to the islands to visit the graves of their ancestors in protest at Japan’s support for Ukraine.
Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an uproar in Japan. Tokyo has said it would continue implementing sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
John Healey’s critics on the right and left accused him of dodging the big questions in his first budget. The chancellor failed to announce reforms that might tackle some of Britain’s chronic problems, they say.
Healey’s scatter-gun budget, as the Resolution Foundation called it, was more about politics than economics, and unapologetically so.
Housing was one area of policy that took up a considerable chunk of his speech. And yet the measures amounted to very little, if a test of his policy changes was to ask how different will the UK be at the next election. Or, as that date is only two and a half years away, 10 years from now.
Housing is more than a single element of a complex economy. It is both its driving force and a disease eating its way through the body, from the inside out.
More than 80% of global investment is in property and the vast majority of that is in residential. Countries that once had a more communitarian approach, such as France and Germany, with a highly regulated mix of social, private rented and home ownership, have succumbed to building wealth through property.
It doesn’t seem to matter that Japan was ruined in the 1990s by a vicious property price crash. And China is still suffering domestically after Beijing allowed a property Ponzi scheme to develop that enriched the already super-wealthy and left tens of millions of middle-income earners in negative equity.
Nowhere is the situation worse than in the UK, where property prices have cooled somewhat, but remain at levels that deny younger generations the chance to find a home at a reasonable price and some financial security.
UK property has also become the method by which Gen Xers pay for social care for their parents and release housing deposits for their offspring. Then there is the debilitating leasehold/freehold split that is both a source of angry disputes and stymies investment in solar panels and insulation (who should pay?).
The lack of regulation and ill-thought-out subsidies affecting new private housing means developers are incentivised to enter an arm-twisting contest with local authorities. Without robust planning guidelines, developers champion building on flood plains or erecting tower blocks that are later dubbed ovens for their lack of ventilation in hot summers.
And all the while the tax system is working to make the situation worse.
The Oxford academic John Muellbauer has spent almost 40 years researching the UK’s housing system. He calls it “one of the most dysfunctional in the world”.
In an academic article published in September by the British Academy, he says: “Many of the UK’s current economic and social problems, including its housing affordability crisis, can be traced to decades of land and housing policy failures. The role of land markets is strongly dependent on institutions, including land use regulation, financial regulation and property taxation.”
The Treasury and Angela Rayner’s Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government have considered proposals from Muellbauer and others that remodel council tax, turning it into a fairer annual levy on households and using the reform to abolish stamp duty on transactions, which has calcified the housing market.
Rachel Reeves’s mansion tax is a good start. It is only a start though, because the former chancellor was persuaded to keep the council tax banding system when she should have applied a percentage to the 150,000-odd homes valued above £2m that will be captured by the new policy.
There was the potential for a database of homes valued above £2m to be the beginning of a revaluation process, carrying on until all homes were logged. With a percentage tax of, say, 0.5%, applied to all homes, a £150,000 property would pay an annual tax rate of £750 while a £3m home would pay £15,000.
Of course, the real problem is not the £3m homeowner for whom policymakers will have little sympathy – it’s the professionals occupying £1.5m homes in London, the south-east and affluent suburbs around other big cities, who will see council tax rates more than double to £7,500.
The professional classes will be the worst affected in the short term. Yet there will only be progress when this powerful lobby group of owner-occupiers – working and retired – are prepared to accept the trade-off with stamp duty, which would disappear for those who sell.
There are plenty of people in government who understand the need to resolve housing market issues in a more fundamental fashion. The Treasury minister Torsten Bell is one. His book, Great Britain?: How We Get Our Future Back, talks about “our housing omnishambles”.
However, they have had little influence on policy in this area so far. In his first budget Healey revamped a much-discredited help-to-buy scheme for new-build homes, which will only boost prices and line the pockets of developers. He also gave some more money towards council housebuilding, slapped an extra tax on landlords (that will probably push up rents) and promised to tackle homelessness.
Healey and Andy Burnham put all their revolutionary zeal into a long, and possibly tortuous, process of devolution from London to the regions to kickstart growth.
However, it is tax incentives that are causing the problems, not whether policy decisions are made locally or centrally. Bad policy decisions can be made locally just as much as centrally. What makes the difference is a permanently reformed tax landscape that discourages treating housing as a store of wealth, allows people to move home cheaply – especially older homeowners who want to downsize – and supports the building of more truly affordable homes to buy and rent.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Healey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issue
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
John Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with a third runway at Heathrow despite the prime minister declining to back it.
Healey’s predecessor as chancellor, Rachel Reeves, put approval of the long-planned runway at the heart of her “growth speech” last year, saying it would “make Britain the world’s best-connected place to do business”.
However, since arriving in No 10 in July, Andy Burnham has ducked the issue of whether the runway should go ahead, suggesting it should be “a matter for London and Londoners”.
A recent Sunday Times report suggested the prime minister had told the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that he was “unconvinced” by arguments for the megaproject.
Asked for his views in Bangkok this week, Healey said the government would study responses to a public consultation, which recently closed. He appeared to strike a markedly more positive note than Burnham, however.
“I think in recent decades, and this is true in Heathrow and airports right across the UK, that they have been a big part of jobs and growth. And the case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth,” he said.
Healey has insisted economic growth is his and Burnham’s “number one mission” in government.
Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support.
 
 
 “Our shareholders would like to do this,” he said earlier this week. “They do think that things are taking a long time, and so far they have decided to be OK with that … But of course we cannot wait for ever.”
The airport’s owners include Qatar’s investment authority; the French private equity firm Ardian; Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, GIC. They are expected to decide in the coming months whether to apply for formal planning permission.
Healey voted in favour of the third runway when the question was put to the House of Commons in 2018.
The chancellor was in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund annual meetings but has returned to London to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.
The UK was praised by the IMF this week for taking action to cut its deficit, while other large economies have opted not to do so. The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged Healey to “stay the course” in his budget.
On Thursday, official figures showed the UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Reform UK braces for Farage standards verdict over undeclared £5m gift
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Nigel Farage’s Reform is braced for a negative report from the standards commissioner over his failure to declare a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne and plans to appeal against any adverse findings.
The party is on tenterhooks over the report, with multiple Reform insiders saying they are readying for a fightback through the appeals process and fully expect the initial verdict to find against their leader.
Any attempt by Farage to oppose a negative verdict could mean the process drags on for months, as an MP under investigation has the right to present further evidence to the standards committee as well as to appeal through the independent expert panel.
After any appeals process, and if parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from the House of Commons, Farage could end up facing a second byelection in his Clacton constituency. This would require a recall petition, triggered by signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over six weeks.
Farage was interviewed by the standards commissioner, Daniel Greenberg, last month and the party expects to be notified of the verdict at any time.
While it awaits the findings, Reform has been overhauling its HQ operations, having been destabilised by undercover investigations by Channel 4 and ITV in recent weeks and fallen in the polls.
The Channel 4 reporting with the investigative group Verbatim has led to a police inquiry into alleged attempts to orchestrate illegal overseas donations, as well as the suspension of James Orr as head of policy and Dan Jukes as Farage’s communications chief. They deny wrongdoing and an internal party report has cleared them, but the matter remains under police investigation.
The ITV reporting uncovered racist councillors and election candidates for the party caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.
One Reform insider said the ITV documentary in particular was extremely bad and showed the party’s vetting had not been up to scratch, despite its claims to have professionalised.
But they said the party was well on its way to bringing in changes in its organisation. Harvey Griffiths, Reform’s new treasurer, has been taking a central role in handling day-to-day party business, while Tom Waterhouse, its general secretary, has taken on the role of getting to grips with vetting.
There have also been departures. Aaron Lobo, its former head of operations, has moved to a new role running a Reform-focused TV channel, which is hiring dozens of “journalists” to increase communications directly to voters.
Amar Johal, a former government lawyer who had been working for the party as head of policy, has taken on the role of acting head of people operations and is said to be a rising force within the party.
Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s polling guru and former campaign lead, has been asked to return to play a role as an informal sounding board on strategy for the party. Raheem Kassam, a former communications chief for Farage now based in the US, has been playing an unofficial role as an attack dog mostly aimed at the Tories, including calling Kemi Badenoch a “Nigerian scammer”, which has been condemned by the Conservative chair, Kevin Hollinrake.
While Jukes, who was a longtime aide to Farage, was considered a loss, the party’s communications are now being handled by Ed Sumner, its communications director, and Miles Goslett, a former journalist.
The mood at Reform is said to be down but less bad than expected given its polling slide, partly because of the £72m gift from two donors, Harborne and Ben Delo. The Guardian reported undercover footage from Verbatim this week in which Orr suggested Harborne could be caught by the forthcoming overseas donor cap, given he has only been a registered domestic voter in the UK since June. However, Reform has insisted the money will not have to be handed back.
The party has begun a hiring spree since the windfall and is planning to take on 400 campaign managers in target seats. It has also sent a mailshot directly to voters – a move that may be repeated in the coming weeks.
Farage has been under investigation over the £5m gift from Harborne just before the last election in 2024 since shortly after the Guardian revealed it in May.
The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not a political one, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian.
Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.
The potential goals of the Russian campaign, according to an assessment seen by the Guardian that Ukrainian intelligence said it intercepted from Russia last month, range from “degrading the quality of life” of Ukrainians through power outages to fully shutting off the water supply, which the document cooly predicts would cause the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.”
The document does not specify which Russian agency developed the assessment, which is titled Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy, Housing and Utilities Sectors, includes vulnerable Ukrainian energy grid targets and even contemplates strikes against high-risk sites, including the switchyards at several nuclear power plants. But several European officials familiar with the document have said it is likely to have been produced by analytical departments linked to the Russian military or intelligence agencies, and that copies have circulated in Ukraine in previous years.
This year, however, Russia appears to be putting those plans into practice. On Tuesday night, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region – Combined Heat and Power Plants 4 and 5, and the Trypillya Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region – as well as a major electrical substation that transfers electricity from two of the country’s main nuclear power plants to the capital. Those, along with other substations that make up the “Kyiv energy ring” that helps bring electricity from across the country to the capital, have all been targets of a Russian barrage that, if it succeeds, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in a city of 3 million people.
Ukraine’s energy minister first briefed European allies last month about the plan, a copy of which was first reported on by the New York Times. Russia has stepped up its attacks on the Ukrainian power grid precisely as Washington and Kyiv are embroiled in a major political quarrel. The Guardian is withholding some specifics of the military assessment at the request of Ukraine’s energy ministry, which said it could aid in further strikes against the country.
“There are two large documents, written very coldly and very clearly, with tables showing the number of weapons needed for each facility to destroy it,” Ukrainian energy minister Denys Shmyhal said last month. “The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones. We understand how they are going to act.”
The leaked documents identify bottlenecks and prescribe the number of ballistic and hypersonic cruise missiles and jet-powered drones needed to knock out power plants and substations with brutal efficiency. If that was done, it could destroy more than 90% of the power that Kyiv is budgeted for each winter, the document predicts, plunging the city into the dark and cold. A worst-case scenario could lead to blackouts lasting up to 20 hours a day until damaged equipment is repaired, according to expert projections.
The strikes on Ukraine’s energy system have become the country’s new frontlines – and the country is badly outgunned, as its stocks of US-provided PAC-3 missiles have dwindled. Zelenskyy this week castigated city authorities for poor planning for the winter and for failing to protect the city’s energy infrastructure. Protests over heat and electricity blackouts are also planned for Saturday, highlighting how the difficult conditions in winter could provoke a political crisis for the wartime government.
Economic Pravda, a leading Ukrainian news site that covers business, reported on Thursday that the three major power plants in Kyiv no longer have the ability to generate electricity, leaving the city more reliant on electricity brought from elsewhere in the country (the government generally does not confirm specific damage to critical infrastructure). The outlets’ experts predicted that, given a moderate winter and quick repairs of damaged substations, Kyiv residents could face up to eight hours of blackouts a day. Its worst case scenario of frigid temperatures and frequent attacks would leave Kyiv in the dark for up to 20 hours a day.
This is no accident for the Kremlin, which has increasingly turned to punishing Ukraine’s population in major cities as the frontlines of the conflict have frozen. “Last year, we were really on the brink,” said Volodymyr Fesenko, a Ukrainian political analyst. “But the risk this year will be even worse, so the plan [to attack Ukrainian infrastructure] does seem realistic. There’s a very high chance that Russia tries to break us this winter.” If the Kremlin believed in the chance of a clean military victory before now, he added, it may now believe that not to be possible, and focus on destroying Ukraine’s remaining infrastructure rather than trying to capture it.
The secret plan, which officials here say was intercepted by Ukrainian intelligence and then briefed to senior European diplomats by Shmyhal last month, sets itself several goals: to destroy electricity generation, heating, water and sewage systems in such a way as to to make life in Ukrainian cities unliveable. Destroying electrical generation alone, it says, would lead to a “significant decrease in the quality of life of the population.”
To do so, it specifies the number of weapons that should be allocated – Geran 4/5 jet-powered drones and hypersonic or cruise missiles – in order to destroy key infrastructure such as thermal power plants, substations, water pumping stations and more.
Considering strikes against the basis of Ukraine’s water, sewage and heating systems, the document says it would create a “large-scale municipal infrastructure crisis.”
When contacted by the Guardian, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said that the document contained information that could aid in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. It did not reply to questions on how the current Russian bombing strategy matched with the proposals made in the document, or which Russian agency had developed the plans.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen | Zoe Williams
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
When the news broke that the UK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield, I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately, the theme suggested by readers was what can the public actually do in the face of what feels like paralysing climate doom?
There is so much going on that is hopeful: biodiversity tracking, river protection, rewilding. Shruti Suresh, from the independent watchdog Global Witness, told those in attendance that if they wanted to effect change, they should protest against Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project. The message was so well understood that it didn’t need labouring. The mood in the room when the news came in was one of audible dismay. People had just watched the minister for climate transition declare that she could see the challenges ahead and was ready for them. The Jackdaw announcement will face immediate protest and legal challenge, but it sends a very clear signal from the government: we don’t mean what we say about ending emissions.
It turns out you can take all imaginable personal responsibility to arrest the climate crisis, make lifestyle adjustments that even five years ago you wouldn’t have dreamed of, miraculously summon the energy to take collective action from what is often private despair, but it will be insufficient as long as corporations – assisted by the government – are working against you, in effect with impunity. At some point, you need to get the people you elected to do what we all know – and they acknowledge – is necessary.
The Jackdaw decision had been quietly parked during the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when the threat of the Greens seemed greater to Labour than it turned out to be. But while Labour successfully buried the issue during the campaign, the underlying issues surrounding Jackdaw – and Rosebank, which is yet to be decided upon – persist.
Since the 2015 Paris agreement, we have been committed to try to limit temperature rises to 1.5C, and we’ve known for at least five years that means the vast majority of fossil fuels have to stay in the ground. As of 2024, there’s been scientific consensus that the target of 1.5C is “deader than a doornail”, while this week’s emissions-gap report could not be clearer: the threshold will be breached and it will cause unimaginable damage, yet with urgent emissions reduction, there is a way back from the abyss. There is no workable argument that runs: “Everyone has to leave their fossil fuels in the ground, as a matter of the utmost urgency, except for us; everyone has to prioritise the long-term survival of a livable planet over energy bills, except for us; we all need to reach carbon neutrality and worry about high-skilled jobs later, except for us.” The Jackdaw field isn’t huge, will peak in a short time and won’t on its own reduce energy bills, which are determined by global markets. So it’s tempting to shuffle it off as a side-order issue, but it matters: it destroys our moral authority as a nation and it extinguishes hope.
The climate debate operates on two tracks that don’t meet. On the one hand, we talk about non-linear irreversible tipping points whose effects would be so seismic that the question of mitigation is too vast and, frankly, too painful to consider. The only bearable discussion of the collapse of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) – a system of currents within the Atlantic Ocean – is how to avoid it, and the contested matter of whether that is even possible. We talk about heat deaths across 854 European cities over the past summer, and we talk about areas in the UK of environmental deprivation, flood risks and poorly insulated housing. We also talk about food security both in the short term, with potato crops destroyed by the weather, and in the long term, with supply chains subject to the incomprehensible devastation of every country going through its own particular climate crisis simultaneously. We look at the social unrest across Europe – which is the fastest-warming continent – and ask to what extent the deprivation created by an unstable climate is being weaponised by a far right hell-bent on choking off climate action.
Then we gate off all that knowledge, all that anxiety, all that will to action, and turn our attention to the UK’s immediate energy compromises. The arguments here run that since we’re going to import gas from somewhere anyway, because any transition will take time, we may as well get it at home. Even though it’s well known that household energy prices won’t be reduced, the government can use the tax take to reduce VAT. Some categories of emission are lower from UK gas than they would be from energy imported from the Gulf.
We need to bring these conversations together, because what they describe is one shared reality. Alongside the carbon that Jackdaw and Rosebank would release, they’ve “sucked all the oxygen out of the debate around what to do about climate change”, Chris Stark, the former CEO of the Climate Change Committee, has said. A warm homes initiative would create vastly more jobs, research recently found, and by reducing bills would also bring far more prosperity, with the additional advantage of not undermining the climate goals we claim to hold.
Thinking of agriculture alone, the headroom, investment and planning we’re ploughing into carbon extraction could make an immeasurable difference to building resilience for an already uncertain future. The most meaningful way to reduce household bills is to reduce reliance on increasingly turbulent world markets, by separating the renewable price from the fossil fuel price, which would immediately boost the already flourishing wind and solar sectors.
Gas and oil proponents beg us to be pragmatic, while their own arguments are floridly impractical: conducted as though the outside world doesn’t exist; as though carbon emissions are tomorrow’s problem; as though there aren’t better solutions for high prices and insecurity everywhere you look; as though we have time to quickly exhaust all our bad answers before we move on to good ones.
One depressing aspect of the Jackdaw announcement – although by no means the most depressing – is that it’s all about the optics. Even its most trenchant supporters would admit that it’s not a long-term solution to energy security. Rather, it’s a flag to the fossil-fuel industry that the government isn’t an enemy. It’s a toxic smoke signal to the US that the UK might not be with it, but definitely isn’t against it. It’s a feeble attempt at domestic politicking by Labour, trying to deflate the Conservatives’ anti-net zero bubble. It’s a statement of intent to make no trouble, when the trouble is already upon us.
- 
  Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Oleshky evacuees reunite with families after truce allows crossing back into Ukraine
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have been reunited with their families after crossing into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.
The major rescue operation began on Friday and was carried out under the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago.
Evacuees wrapped in Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border to be reunited with family members. Volunteers with hand-drawn welcome signs handed coffee to the weary people who had travelled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. Residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and torches to greet the convoy.
Tetiana Leonidivna, 71, thanked the Ukrainian soldiers who helped her to flee. “We love them, we love them,” she said through tears. “We know that they are protecting us. And a deep bow to them, and a deep bow to their parents, for having such children. I am proud, I am simply proud.”
The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region began early on Tuesday and was expected to continue through Sunday evening. The White House said the first lady Melania Trump helped broker the localised deal, while Pope Leo XIV pressed Russia and Ukraine to allow aid deliveries and evacuations.
Relatives and volunteers with the Red Cross, Médecins Sans Frontières and World Central Kitchen welcomed the evacuees as they arrived at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets.
Holding a cigarette between shaking fingers, 48-year-old Ivan Yevhenovych described his last months in Oleshky. “It was very difficult. There were a lot of drones. It was hard to move around the streets,” he said. “Since spring, there hasn’t really been any staple food left. People had a little bit of their own reserves. We are thrifty people.”
He said landmines or drone strikes were killing residents every day.
An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of being evacuated to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
“Many people stayed behind and didn’t want to leave,” Yevhenovych said. “Some for their houses, some for their animals.”
Ukrainian authorities, seeking to protect those who remained and safeguard future humanitarian missions, have not said how many residents evacuated Oleshky and have restricted details of their route. Melania Trump posted on social media on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Liza Paliy, 19, waited at the border for her father, whom she last saw more than two and a half years earlier when she fled the occupied city with her mother and sister. “We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately two years have already passed,” she said.
Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, hailed the humanitarian mission as a win.
“This is an extremely important moment. Behind us are difficult negotiations, agreements, preparations, and an enormous amount of work. But most importantly, the people who waited so long to be rescued are finally safe,” he said in an online post.
Lubinets said evacuees ranged in age from just over one year old to 94, and they brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon. He said he hoped the Oleshky truce could be replicated elsewhere, saying it “could form the basis of a new mechanism for responding to the most difficult humanitarian crises”.
Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner, said both sides have agreed to conduct regular humanitarian missions in and around Oleshky. Lubinets did not mention this development.
“The mission has concluded, but, unfortunately, living conditions in Oleshky remain extremely difficult,” she said. “We will make every effort to support those residents who have made the decision to stay.”
Some Oleshky evacuees who chose to move to Russian-occupied territory were taken to a temporary shelter in Simferopol, Lantratova said. The city is in Ukraine’s Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
“After everything they have endured and a long journey, it is essential for these people to rest, recover and feel cared for. However, support should not be limited to just a roof over their heads and a hot meal,” she said in a social media post.
A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia’s western Bryansk region, the local governor, Yegor Kovalchuk, said on Saturday. Five others were wounded, he said.
Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region’s capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
The Russian defence ministry said on Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad apples | John Crace
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
It was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITV exposé of widespread racism and misogyny within Reform, you might have expected one of its MPs to have taken to the airwaves on Monday morning to defend the party’s honour. To try to persuade viewers that the real problem lay with the journalists who couldn’t stop themselves from investigating Reform rather than the fact that the party’s bigotry was endemic.
Instead, we got nothing. Every Reform MP was otherwise engaged. Were too busy having breakfast. Nothing from Nigel Farage. Nothing even from Robert Jenrick. Maybe he realised he had crashed and burned a few days earlier by suggesting it was just one of those things. One of life’s little mysteries. The BBC was riddled with paedophiles and Reform was awash with racists, said Honest Bob. No big deal. Every organisation had its crosses to bear.
The only MP to post on X in the morning was Richard Tice, who was feeling decidedly grumpy, having only just got married to Isabel Oakeshott. Perhaps he had a hangover. Though his main gripe was that British Airways was yet another failing British institution because it had mislaid at least one of his bags.
Dicky’s social media post had more than a touch of the “don’t you know who I am” to it. You can only imagine the baggage handler may have known exactly who Dicky was and had taken great pleasure in diverting one of the fake Louis Vuitton suitcases from Dubai to Manila. Via Buenos Aires.
The one person out and about for Reform was the one person you would have thought the party would want to keep hidden. Step forward Matt Goodwin, the party’s failed candidate for the Gorton and Denton byelection whose own views could easily pass off as borderline racist in polite circles. Matt is going through his own personal anti-growth agenda. Working hard to deconstruct himself from low-level academic to incredibly dim primate with low social skills. Almost every day, voters in Gorton and Denton thank their lucky stars for having dodged that bullet.
Matt’s defence of Reform was … unorthodox, to put it kindly. So much so that you began to wonder whether he was even conscious. Luckily for him, he was only allowed out on Times Radio. Though that was more than enough. To try to understand Matt is to make a category error. The whole point is to not understand him. That’s the way you stay sane. Because what he wanted listeners to believe was that Nige was a buffer zone against racism. That hordes of would-be racists begged to be allowed to join Reform, only to find out that Nige was a man of peace and love. The one politician who wanted nothing but good things for all immigrants.
It got better. Because Batshit Matt also wanted us to believe that the ITV documentary had just uncovered a few bad apples in the party. So in a way it had done Reform a favour. What were the chances? The ITV journalists had managed to uncover the only seven racists in the Reform ranks. Everyone else was Team Nigel. Never had a bad word for anyone. Except, there was another way of looking at this. That ITV had filmed about 10 Reform councillors and found that seven of them had views that included beheading King Charles for being a Muslim. Some statisticians might put that down as a 70% hit rate. Not so much a few wrong ’uns but a whole army of them. Poor Nige. Always the victim.
Over in the Commons, Wes Streeting was preparing for other threats during departmental defence questions. Though John Healey was not one of them. You’d have thought that Wes might have wanted to schmooze the chancellor before next week’s budget. To try to get the best funding settlement he could. Not a bit of it. Wes began by slagging off his predecessor as defence secretary for wasting money on unnecessary training exercises and then announced he was confident that Healey would reach the necessary 3% and 3.5% targets at next year’s spending review. So, no, Wes wouldn’t be resigning any time soon. Let’s hope his confidence is well placed.
Instead, Wes seemed more interested in persuading himself that there was absolutely nothing unusual in Donald Trump switching the Starlink satellite system on and off at random moments, thereby allowing Russian drones to do untold damage on Ukraine. This was just standard procedure. The only way you could tell the system was working properly was if you turned it off from time to time. Obvious when you think about. Wes was also totally chilled about Trump trying to lower US pump prices by allowing Russian imports of diesel. Fuel that the Russians had also imported from Iran and with whom, coincidentally, the US was at war.
All of this apparently made perfect sense not just to Streeting, but also to Labour and opposition backbenchers. Wes could reassure us because he had had a personal meeting with Pete Hegseth the previous week, during with the secretary for war had reiterated Trump’s claims that Nato forces had been a waste of space in Afghanistan and that the US troops had fought alone. A nice ice breaker. After that, Pete went out of his way to say Washington was totally behind Ukraine, just so long as Russia won the war.
Curiously, the shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, didn’t use his questions to talk up the four drones of the “Britannia shield” that the Tories were sure would protect the UK from nuclear war. So it remains a mystery. Almost as if it was a bullshit party conference announcement that was designed to be forgotten within days. Highlight of the day went to Sharron Davies, the former swimmer turned Tory peer, who demanded to know why Andy Burnham hadn’t invaded France to stop the rioting. Can you explain it to her?

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on apologising for slavery: a necessary process has at last begun | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
There was a risk, in the run-up to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) this week, that important discussions could be derailed by the UK government’s refusal to apologise for slavery and the slave trade, combined with its continuing rejection of calls for financial reparations. For the Caribbean governments and campaigners pushing for these steps, the siting of the biennial gathering in Antigua and Barbuda offered a vital opportunity to press their case and raise awareness of the challenges that they face.
That deadlock was broken when Andy Burnham wrote in the Guardian at the weekend of his “sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people”, and pledged to listen to calls for a formal apology as part of a structured dialogue. While he reiterated the UK government’s position that financial reparations will not be offered, he also indicated a willingness to discuss aid, investment and the restructuring of debt. King Charles did not say sorry when he addressed Chogm on Tuesday, but a very necessary process of reconciliation and redress has at last begun.
Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, pointed to continuing disagreement on the reparations question. Philip J Pierre, the chair of the Caribbean Community, said that “apology without repair is incomplete”. And while the new drive on debt promised by Mr Burnham is welcome, it is shamefully overdue. Last year’s UN development finance conference did not achieve the hoped-for breakthrough and the UK opposed proposals for a new process to tackle the worsening debt crisis. The context of rising climate threats and broken promises of climate finance to support a transition away from fossil fuels only serves to strengthen the Caribbean countries’ case.
Mr Burnham’s announcement of Gordon Brown’s involvement in debt negotiations was a promising sign, but so far there is no detailed plan. The difficulties are enormous. High interest payments have undermined the beneficial effects of earlier debt forgiveness, with record-high costs trapping poor countries in a cycle whereby they cannot afford to invest in the health, education and renewable energy that they desperately need. While problems with aid go back decades, the Trump administration’s defunding of USAID was a massive setback. Disappointingly, there is no sign that Mr Burnham will reverse the UK’s own aid spending cuts, which have hit Commonwealth countries and nature protection projects hard.
Historians continue to uncover new information about Britain’s involvement in slavery; William Pettigrew, for example, recently named King James II as “the most important English slave trader of the 17th century”. But while enslavers, investors and traffickers enriched themselves, and provided seed funding for the Industrial Revolution, the Caribbean was left impoverished by the cruel system that the colonists built. Now, demands for this legacy to be properly recognised are coinciding with the climate crisis, to which Caribbean islands are highly exposed through their vulnerability to hurricanes.
King Charles recognised as much when he spoke of the “monstrous injustice” of slavery and the “catastrophic reality” of global heating’s effects. But it falls to Mr Burnham to follow through on the statements of recent days. Structured dialogue is a step worth taking, but Caribbean countries are entitled to expect actions as well as words.
-

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Further bomb threats disrupt at least another 18 flights across Europe
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday but the affected aircraft landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices.
The latest alerts affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the UK.
Danish police investigated a threat against Copenhagen airport but the airport’s management said it was operating normally.
The warnings followed separate threats on Tuesday and Thursday that forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched, raising questions over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.
A number of European media outlets – including news organisations in Bulgaria, Ireland and the UK – have reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats sent an email to several outlets warning of further attacks on transport across Europe.
“This is only the beginning,” it reportedly said.
The latest threats affected at least nine flights to and from Prague, four flights over France, two flights en route to Sofia and a flight from Lisbon to Rome. Hungary scrambled fighter jets three times to escort civilian flights in its airspace, the defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said on Facebook.
The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny percentage – just 0.0674% – of the 26,709 flights that according to the air traffic control agency Eurocontrol were scheduled in Europe on Friday.
A separate spate of threats on Friday against media organisations in Ireland disrupted broadcasts and prompted staff evacuations and police searches of offices and newsrooms.
The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, told RTÉ Radio 1 after it resumed scheduled broadcasting that such threats had to be taken seriously and were an effort to sow fear and anxiety.
“It shows how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and undermine the normal operation of society,” said Martin, adding that European security agencies would seek to identify those responsible and hold them accountable.
The British broadcaster Sky said on Friday it had also received a security threat and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.
Earlier this week, cyber-attacks targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.
The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it was unclear whether the hoaxes and recent cyber-attacks were “all connected”.
She added: “But they definitely all tell us the same thing: today, what is under attack are civilian infrastructures.”
The Nato alliance continued to monitor the situation and was working closely with allies, according to a senior Nato military official.
Investigators have said there was no evidence that hoaxes against airlines and other targets were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, but that inquiries were continuing.
Several European media outlets in Bulgaria, Ireland, the UK and elsewhere reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats warned in an email of further actions against transport across Europe.
“This is only the beginning,” it reportedly said. The Guardian has chosen not to reproduce the email in full, given its unsubstantiated claims.
Some of the threats on Thursday were signed “fighters of the Male State”, a reference to a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016. In a Telegram post on Friday the group’s founder, Vladislav Pozdniakov, denied involvement and said the group had not existed since 2021.
Some officials suspect the waves of disruption are linked to European support for Ukraine in its war against the Russian invasion.
Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, said authorities needed more time to identify culprits but that there appeared to be a pattern.
“It cannot be mere coincidence that so many incidents with exactly the same modus operandi are happening across Europe,” he told the national broadcaster TVE.
“The most reasonable assumption is that we are facing an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare,” he said, adding that Europe must be prepared for more such challenges.
Mark Rowley, the chief of London’s Metropolitan police, urged a measured response, saying past experience with the paramilitary Irish Republican Army offered valuable lessons.
He recalled the phrase “10p terrorism”, when a hoax bomb call made from a coin-operated phone box could disrupt an entire city, forcing authorities to distinguish between genuine and false threats.
The authorities would need to adapt to an evolving threat landscape involving actors around the world, some backed by hostile states, he said.
“We are going to have to adapt to that same methodology to make sure that we don’t overreact to every message we get online,” he told BBC Radio 4.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Andy Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drilling
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, signalling Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry and threatening to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs.
Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey, the energy secretary and chancellor respectively, will make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning after more than a year of deliberations over whether doing so would violate the UK’s climate commitments.
The approval for drilling at one of the biggest undeveloped fields in the declining North Sea basin is a big boost for Britain’s oil and gas industry – and especially for Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor, which operate it.
It will be met with outrage from climate campaigners, who say it undermines Labour’s green credentials and will exacerbate the climate crisis.
Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.”
She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.”
When fully operational, Jackdaw will account for 6% of North Sea gas production, making it one of the biggest gasfields not yet under production.
Along with the Rosebank oilfield, its status has become symbolic of the government’s commitment to the oil and gas industry, which is facing heavy job losses as reserves decline and platforms become increasingly automated.
The field was approved by the Conservative government in 2022, with ministers arguing it would help shield the UK from the volatility in the energy market caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Labour came to power in 2024 on a promise not to grant any new licences in the North Sea, not expecting to have to make a decision on Jackdaw or Rosebank.
However both fields were cast into doubt last year by a landmark ruling that said their environmental approval had been incorrectly granted.
A judge ruled that when deciding whether the two fields would violate the UK’s climate commitments, regulators should have taken into account the carbon emissions generated by burning the oil and gas they would produce.
Shell and Equinor resubmitted their application for environmental consent last September. Since then, Fahnbulleh and her predecessor, Ed Miliband, have spent months deciding whether to use their ministerial power to block it.
Both the prime minister and his predecessor, Keir Starmer, have come under heavy pressure to allow the fields to go ahead in recent months, not least from Donald Trump, who urged both men to “open up the North Sea”.
Burnham signalled he was sympathetic to the US president’s arguments earlier this summer, promising to take a “pragmatic approach” to the decision.
“There is a resource there,” he said in July. “When people are struggling – you can’t ignore that.”
He told the Commons last week: “I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas. We will set out our decisions shortly.”
Several sources have told the Guardian that Fahnbulleh has decided not to block the field, allowing the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the industry, to give the go-ahead based on financial and logistical concerns.
Making the announcement alongside Healey and the NSTA’s chief executive, Stuart Payne, they will say that granting the environmental approval does not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment because it is not a new licence.
Fahnbulleh is understood not to have made a final decision on the larger Rosebank field, but energy department officials are looking at ways the tax proceeds from the project could go to green projects if it was given. A decision is expected later this year.
The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.
But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.
A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling.
That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and around half of 18- to 24-year-olds.
Ellie Mae O’Hagan, the UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer.
“If the prime minister wants a decade in power to change the country, he should invest in heat pumps and solar, not tax breaks for the oil and gas companies driving up our bills and polluting the planet.”
Officials say, however, that the Rosebank decision is likely to be the more sensitive one, partly because it will produce around seven times the CO2 emissions of Jackdaw and partly because most of the oil produced there will be exported.
Khan said: “The defining test is Rosebank. Burnham must deliver on his promise and prioritise affordable bills, genuine industrial growth and a safe climate over oil profits. That means rejecting Rosebank.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Youth mobility scheme may be delayed to ensure success of UK-EU summit
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A deadline for a youth mobility scheme between the EU and the UK could be deferred by six months in a bid to ensure Andy Burnham has a successful “reset” summit on 20 November, diplomats have said.
EU ambassadors in Brussels on Wednesday heard that the UK was still insisting on international tuition fees, quotas and an NHS surcharge for EU students. This has fuelled fears the summit could fail, just as the prime minister is promising to unveil a new vision for Britain’s long-term relationship with the EU.
Sources say the UK also continues to push for a cap of about 50,000 a year on the numbers of EU citizens allowed in the country for work, travel or study under the mooted youth experience scheme (YES) visas. Some EU member states want the cap much higher, at up to 500,000. Others want no cap at all.
The UK is also insisting that any YES visa holders pay the £1,035 NHS surcharge to cover potential doctor or hospital visits, although it is understood that a 25% discount has been suggested.
Negotiations on two other issues – a food and drink trade deal and the emissions trading system – are almost complete but views on the youth mobility scheme remain divided.
Sources say there is near-agreement on demands from the National Farmers’ Union that crops grown using fungicides yet to be approved in the EU could be sold in the bloc under a transition arrangement in the sanitary and phyto-sanitary agreement.
“A lot of member states were in favour of keeping the trio of issues together and not breaking the agenda up, but there are others that think it is acceptable to decouple them and there is no agreement yet on which approach to take,” said one diplomat.
But the reciprocal youth experience scheme designed to allow under-30s from both sides to work, travel or study in each other’s countries remains deadlocked.
Talks on a fourth issue, in relation to the reintegration of the UK into the EU’s energy market, will also, as expected, continue after 20 November. More time is needed to resolve significant barriers that have emerged, such as state aid and oversight frameworks, including a role for the European court of justice.
Tuition fees remains the thorniest problem, with UK universities putting pressure on the Labour government to maintain full international student fees for EU citizens – which can run to £69,190 a year at Oxford.
One diplomat said there was an “emerging consensus” at the meeting in Brussels around a European Commission proposal to take tuition fees out of the package altogether, with wording in a joint statement on 20 November committing both sides to negotiating a solution by May 2027.
It was thought that the landing zone was somewhere between home fees of £9,790 and the average international fees, but universities outside the elite 24-strong Russell Group have told the UK government they cannot afford to drop fees for EU citizens.
According to several diplomats, the bloc is still divided on whether to remove tuition fees from the table. There are also divisions over how a cap on numbers would work amid fears in the UK that voters – particularly in “red wall” constituencies – would see it as opening the gates to workers coming from economically less wealthy countries such as Bulgaria.
A proposal to cap the figures per country has been suggested, although how that would work in practice has not been detailed.
Some countries such as France are still arguing for an “all or nothing” approach, with all three topics on the table, arguing if the UK cannot agree tuition fees now, 17 months since the last EU-UK summit, “why would they do so in six months?”.
Others say with pressure to move on from three “significant but modest” issues to the bigger issues of deeper economic, security and defence ties, they cannot risk a failure on 20 November.
“YES is politically, emotionally and diplomatically very important. But if we can get an agreement at the summit by removing one element from the agenda it is a price worth paying,” said one diplomat.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Democrat Rob Sand wins Iowa’s gubernatorial race as party plans rebuild
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Democrat Rob Sand has been elected governor of Iowa, the Associated Press projects, a milestone as his party seeks to rebuild its political standing in the midwestern state.
Sand, the state auditor who is the sole Democrat holding statewide office in Iowa, triumphed over Republican Zach Lahn, a political newcomer backed by Robert F Kennedy Jr’s “Make America healthy again” movement.
It’s a significant victory for Democrats in Iowa, which twice backed Barack Obama but has voted for Trump all three times he was on the presidential ballot, while the GOP has come to dominate state politics. Sand is the first Democrat to win the governor’s office since 2006.
Sand’s victory comes as Democrats netted historic victories in gubernatorial elections nationwide, including in states where they have struggled in recent years. In Georgia, former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms has become the first Black woman elected governor in the country.
Sand, 44, is a native Iowan who has cast himself as a unifier who would restore balance to the state’s politics.
“To Iowa Democrats, we’ve had a hard few years here in Iowa, but balanced government has been restored,” Sand said at his victory party on Tuesday night as the crowd cheered.
He had the crowd sing America the Beautiful together, a feature of his hundreds of town halls as he criss-crossed the state. He thanked the state’s voters, and emphasized on how he intends to bring people to the table to improve water quality, accountability and the political process.
“Come January, we will be forced to work together,” he said of the political parties, later adding: “Left wing, right wing, same bird.”
Sand had been leading in the polls ahead of election day. Lahn, who won the Republican primary over a candidate endorsed by Donald Trump, had been accused by Iowa Democrats of spending a disproportionate amount of time in Kansas, despite wanting to be governor of Iowa. The New York Times reported in October that although Lahn voted in Iowa in the 2024 general election, he had his ballot mailed to him in Kansas.
Lahn had also faced scrutiny for his complicated ties to the Koch family, the Republican billionaire mega-donors.
An emphasis on bipartisan, balanced politics had been a hallmark of Sands’s campaign, with a focus on the need to return to Iowa as a “commonsense state”.
“I think a big piece of that was because we elected both Democrats and Republicans, and they had to work together to get anything done,” Sand said at a rally on 28 October.
“We have had 10 years of one-party control in the state of Iowa, and that is what led us to where we are today.”
At his victory party, Carol Sand, Rob’s aunt, said that as a public school teacher, she was relieved that her nephew – a product of the public education system himself – would be in the governor’s office.
“He’s going to right the ship in Iowa and bring some accountability,” Carol Sand said.
Rachel Leingang contributed reporting
