SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: IFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK’s £35bn spending pressures
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures.
As the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade.
Against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, the thinktank warned Healey that failure to address the issue at his 28 October budget risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans.
Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.”
Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at Jeremy Hunt, the former Conservative chancellor, who before the 2024 general election was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans.
Publishing its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances before Healey’s speech to the Commons, it called on the chancellor to avoid announcing a “steady as she goes” budget that delayed decisions until next year’s spending review.
“If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said.
Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.”
Miller said the Treasury adopting an assumption that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility.
“We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.”
Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30.
With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement.
Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash.
The IFS said that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue – meaning Healey could see headroom cut by only £4bn.
However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services.
Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing.
The IFS said a choice to leave spending totals unchanged at the budget would implicitly mean allowing the quality or quantity of public services to fall. However, it said compensating for the inflation shock, and funding Healey’s pledge to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, would require tax rises or benefit cuts of about £35bn.
“Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said.
“It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.”
She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within.
A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “The chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.
“The Office for Budget Responsibility will publish its updated forecast alongside the budget in October and we will not comment on rumour, speculation or proposals about its contents ahead of then.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Budget briefing: the key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa Crerar
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content: The Guardian’s political editor, Pippa Crerar, and economics editor, Heather Stewart, examine John Healey’s first budget and how it will be received by voters. Photograph: Jill Mead, Andy Hall/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s political editor, Pippa Crerar, and economics editor, Heather Stewart, examine John Healey’s first budget and how it will be received by voters. Photograph: Jill Mead, Andy Hall/The GuardianExplainerBudget briefing: the key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa CrerarOur economics and political editors dissect John Healey’s maiden budgetThe Guardian’s economics editor, Heather Stewart, and political editor, Pippa Crerar, assess the chancellor’s budget: what he said, why – and what he left out.Did the chancellor’s budget panic the financial markets?Not at all. Reassuring febrile financial markets appeared to be one of Andy Burnham’s motivations in putting Healey in No 11, and this ‘steady-as-she-goes’ budget seems to have met that brief, for now.The chancellor promised to keep Labour’s deficit-reduction plans on track, albeit at a slower pace in the early years of the forecast – raising taxes modestly to do so.The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) now expects him to meet his crucial first fiscal rule – to balance day-to-day spending with revenues – with a margin of £15bn to spare. That’s a slimmer cushion than the £24bn Rachel Reeves had at the spring statement, but investors appear to have taken it in their stride, with barely a flutter in the bond markets. Healey stressed that he plans to rebuild his headroom back to £22bn by 2030-31. “That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can,” he said.However, the OBR’s forecasts underlined the significant hit to Britain’s public finances from higher borrowing costs – which it said had cost the government an additional £14bn in interest costs alone. Partly as a result, borrowing is set to be £8bn higher than expected this year, before heading back to target over time. And Healey has delayed a series of knotty decisions on tax and spend for a critical spending review next year.Has Healey done enough to reassure restive Labour MPs and the public?Government insiders had briefed that the budget would be “low key”, with tough decisions over public spending – including on defence and welfare – put off to the spending review. But that didn’t stop Labour MPs asking “Is that it?” when Healey sat down from the dispatch box.While they welcomed support for energy bills – the only rabbit in the budget – and other cost of living measures, they are impatient for Burnham to deliver the radical change he has argued the country needs. “That won’t end 40 years of neoliberalism, will it?” one MP remarked to the Guardian.Healey’s decision to increase taxes on banks is likely to land well with the public – it is an industry which has made massive profits and does not elicit much sympathy from voters – but some Labour MPs are already questioning why he did not go much further to give himself more room for manoeuvre this winter.For now, though, MPs aren’t kicking up a fuss. The polls – some of which put Labour eight points ahead – suggest the public is on board, and Burnham’s approval ratings remain high. He has won them a second hearing. Whether the public expected more than a signal of intent will become clear in the coming days. But questions over the timing of the next general election have not gone away. After the budget, Burnham ruled out calling one in the next 12 months (he’d previously said there wouldn’t be one soon). Labour’s prospects at the ballot box remain very much on the mind of its MPs. And if there are suggestions the public is getting impatient, the pressure on Burnham will grow.Has the budget really given consumers a “breathing space” amid the cost of living crisis?Higher energy prices as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran have made the UK – an energy importer – poorer, as well as raising the cost of government borrowing. Healey’s key challenge was to decide who should have to bear the pain.He announced a more generous package than expected to contain energy costs this winter, costing the Treasury about £4bn in total. That included sending £100 to every householder in council tax banks A to D; cancelling Rachel Reeves’s planned fuel duty rises; and extending the VAT cut on electricity bills until next summer.But households will still be hit by a sharp rise in the energy price cap in January – which EDF predicts could be as much as 27%.And because the cost of energy feeds into the cost of making almost everything, higher oil prices will push up economy-wide inflation, which the OBR now reckons will be 3.5% next year, instead of the 2% it expected in March. The Bank of England is expected to respond by pushing up interest rates, perhaps as soon as its meeting next week, causing fresh pain for mortgage-borrowers.Despite the government’s interventions, the OBR reckons higher energy costs will make the outlook for living standards even worse than it previously feared. On its preferred measure, real household disposable income, living standards are expected to fall slightly this year as the impact of the war takes its toll – and then to climb gradually, to just 2% above pre-Covid levels by 2030.What does it tell us about the relationship between Healey and Burnham?John Healey and Andy Burnham have had regular Sunday night curries in the No 11 flat in advance of the budget. While they are both of the soft left and agree the north is in need of investment, they haven’t fought in the political trenches together or shared a joint project, like Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.Healey wasn’t even Burnham’s number one choice for the role. However, he was seen as capable and trustworthy and – crucially – more likely to sign up to the Burnham project than other figures touted for the role. Even so, there were early concerns that the chancellor could be “captured” by the Treasury, which still wields great power despite Burnham’s attempts to rebalance the government machine. But the budget – a low key, defensive one which was small in scale and ambition – suggests the prime minister has had to accept the fiscal constraints to his ambition for more radical change. For now. Healey did, however, lay the groundwork for more significant reform in his boss’s priority areas: devolution and housing.For his own part, he still has plenty to prove on defence spending – having quit Keir Starmer’s government over the failure to commit to 3% of GDP on defence by 2030. Healey signalled he will hit the target – but can’t say how until next autumn’s spending review. His own political reputation relies on it.What big decisions have been postponed by the breathing space budget?Higher inflation will make it more expensive to deliver public services. Many Whitehall departments were already facing a tight spending squeeze towards the end of this parliament, on the plans Healey inherited from Reeves. The darker global backdrop is only likely to make that worse.In its pre-budget analysis, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) suggested that, alongside the £11bn he would need to find to hit the 3% of GDP defence spending target by 2030, these additional pressures amounted to £35bn a year.Healey gave little indication of how he intends to respond – though he did suggest that more digitisation of service delivery, and a significantly slimmed-down civil service at the centre as additional powers are devolved, would help to cut the government’s costs, and expressed the hope that better-than-expected economic growth might help.“I believe Britain can beat the forecasts again,” he said. If not, next year’s spending review looks formidably challenging.Will people accept that the economic pressures aren’t the government’s fault?Healey’s speech was littered with references to the difficult international picture, with Donald Trump continuing to wreak havoc on the global economy with his war in Iran. “Analysts like to speak of economic headwinds, but what we face today are global economic storms,” the chancellor told MPs.The main risk identified by the OBR to its fiscal forecast is the evolution of the Middle East conflict and its implications for energy prices, interest rates and inflation. The US midterms are a key moment – and the big unknown is what the US president does next, which Downing Street is watching anxiously.For now, however, the public appears willing to accept that the government is not to blame for resulting cost of living pressures. No 10 sources say their own research shows that most people still see the global context as a justifiable reason for their current plight, rather than an excuse. But government insiders are concerned this might change this winter, as soaring bills and costs really start to bite.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyLabourEconomicsEconomic policyexplainersShareReuse this content

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham appeared to suggest he had been given new information on Russia’s role in the vote in excerpts from a podcast interview. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Reuters
Andy Burnham appeared to suggest he had been given new information on Russia’s role in the vote in excerpts from a podcast interview. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Reuters
How significant are Burnham’s remarks on Kremlin interference in Brexit vote?
Prime minister has reopened the debate over whether Russia sought to influence the 2016 referendum
Andy Burnham unexpectedly reopened an old Brexit debate when he said he had been told after becoming prime minister that Russia had interfered in the 2016 EU referendum.
It was a contentious issue in the second half of the previous decade, but one that had largely been forgotten about as the UK finally adjusted to the reality of leaving the EU. Now Burnham’s comments have given the topic a fresh impetus.
What did the prime minister say, and why could it be significant?
The Russia topic came up as part of a wide-ranging interview Burnham gave to The Rest is Politics, excerpts of which were released on Sunday, in which he appeared to suggest he had been given new information about the Brexit vote.
“I asked the question coming to Downing Street: ‘Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia?’ And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” he said.
The prime minister did not say whom he had asked, or set out in detail what the answer was. But his comments suggest he had been given new information of some kind, although he then switched to talking about Russian disinformation in general.
“These things are important now to put clearly on the record, and I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia,” he said.
What could Burnham have been told?
It was hard to decipher from the interview.
One possibility is that he was given a summary of a recent assessment by the UK’s intelligence agencies. Another is that it was a relatively informal conversation with officials, where opinions were exchanged.
The difference is significant – if there was a fresh assessment it would run counter to the position established under a succession of Conservative governments in the aftermath of the Brexit vote.
Later on Monday, in the Commons, Burnham did not share any extra information, saying instead: “It is a matter of record that Russia has sought to interfere in elections, the 2019 general election, and we think it is inconceivable that this was the first time.”
What was the conclusion of previous inquiries?
There were no serious official investigations into Russian interference attempts in 2016, not least because the Conservatives had no appetite to order them. As time passed, it became increasingly difficult to do so.
The topic was addressed by parliament’s cross-party intelligence and security committee in its Russia report, published in July 2020, which took evidence in secret from the UK’s intelligence agencies before publishing a partly redacted report.
It concluded that the government “had not seen or sought evidence of successful interference in UK democratic processes”. No formal post-referendum assessment had been made, the committee added, and the UK intelligence community was accused of taking its “eye off the ball” when it came to the Russian threat.
What could have happened in 2016?
This is an old controversy with three main elements. First, that a “troll army” of state-linked Russian accounts tweeted about the referendum in the run-up to the vote, though estimates of numbers have varied wildly from 54 to 150,000 (many of which were deleted).
Second, that the Russian English-language media outlets RT and Sputnik published a large amount of anti-EU and pro-Brexit content, which had a wide reach. The digital campaign group 89up said the two broadcasters had published 261 articles that achieved 134m potential page impressions.
The third aspect were claims that Arron Banks, a donor to the pro-Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage, had links to Russia. Leaked emails showed he met Alexander Yakovenko, then the Russian ambassador to the UK, three times – a figure he later revised up to four – and that he was offered the chance to participate in a goldmining deal in Russia.
A subsequent investigation by the National Crime Agency into £8m of loans Banks provided to Brexit campaigns run by Farage concluded the money was legitimately his and there was no evidence of wrongdoing.
But the EU referendum was also a complex, closely fought campaign in which many points of view were in play. The idea that one country, with an interest in weakening the UK and the EU, could have had a decisive influence in a vote of 33.5 million people is debatable.
So what’s going on?
The prime minister is making a broader argument that Britain needs to reconsider its relationship with the EU, arguing that Brexit has not delivered what was promised. Highlighting that there could have been Russian efforts to interfere with the vote raises questions about the outcome, though Downing Street insisted on Monday it regarded the result as legitimate.
Burnham has also proposed creating a National Centre for Information Defence to detect, attribute and disrupt disinformation coming from overseas – and it appears that his comments about Russian interference were also intended to justify that.
However, when he appeared in the Commons, Burnham was careful to limit his remarks. He emphasised that he had not said that Russia had altered the result of the Brexit referendum, only that the Kremlin had tried to interfere. But with little new to back up his initial statements about Russian interference, the prime minister risks being accused of exaggeration.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Business secretary says UK needs to understand direction of EU before signing up to closer relationship – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Jonathan Reynolds says UK needs to know more about where EU heading before it opts for much closer relationship
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has suggested the UK needs to know more about where the EU is heading before it signs up to a much closer relationship.
He made the comment in an interview with the Sun, a day after John Healey, the chancellor, also hinted that he might have reservations about Andy Burnham’s ambitions for a new relationship with the EU undoing the damage done by Brexit.
Burnham is attending a summit with the EU next month where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus. There is strong support for all these initiatives in cabinet.
But Burnham also wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election, when – if it wants – Labour will be able to dump the 2024 manifesto pledges ruling out joining the single market or the customs union.
Burnham has not said what he wants to propose in Labour’s next manifesto, and he insists ultimately the public will decide, but he has said that he would like the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime and he seems open to trying to rejoin the single market in the next parliament.
Asked by the Sun if he shared Burnham’s dream of rejoining the EU, Reynolds replied:
I genuinely can’t answer that, because I don’t know what the future of the EU is – because [of] some of the very strong political currents in member states.
For me, it’s an approach to issues. What is their approach to how they regulate technology, AI? How dynamic will the economy be?
In a bid to stop ministers disagreeing in public about the EU, Burnham sent them a letter earlier this week telling them to stay “disciplined” and not to “advocate for specific options” as the debate on the future UK-EU relationship gets under way.
Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, has claimed that Andy Burnham has now accepted in principle the case for the Welsh government to get greater borrowing powers. (See 3.59pm.) He was speaking after they met at the national economic council meeting in Glasgow.
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has suggested the UK needs to know more about where the EU is heading before it signs up to a much closer relationship. (See 1.28pm.)
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.
Ap Iorwerth claims Burnham has now accepted in principle that Welsh government should get more borowing powers
Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, has released his readout from his meeting with Andy Burnham. Breaking with convention (these readouts are normally rather bland), he has included some news in his.
Ap Iorwerth claims Burnham has now accepted that Wales should greater borrowing powers. Under the current rules, the Welsh government’s borrowing powers are extremely limited. “This has led to the bizarre situation where it has been forced to rely on local authorities to do its borrowing for it (such as a school-building programme),” Will Hayward said in a recent Guardian column.Ap Iorwerth said:
There was an encouraging consensus that the fiscal and borrowing powers which have for so long put Wales at a disadvantage compared with other UK nations must be revised as a matter of urgency. I welcome the prime minister’s comments that this is now a matter of how and when.
He said he told Burnham that “further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd” – which sounded like a rather blunt ‘stay in your lane” response to Burnham’s “regional empowerment” proposals.
Ap Iorwerth said he asked Burnham to lean on the Treasury “to enable the Welsh government to press ahead with our Cynnal weekly child payment pilot to support the poorest families”.
Ap Iorwerth urged him to back rejoining the EU single market and customs union “as a priority”.
The Downing Street readout did not mention any of these issues. It just repeated some of what was in the Swinney one about the NEC meeting (see 3.28pm), and said Cardiff would host the next NEC meeting in spring 2027.
Burnham and Swinney agree 'Westminster doesn't work' - but remain divided over what sort of devolution offers solution
John Swinney, Scotland’s first minister, has now issued a statement about today’s national economic council [NEC] in Glasgow, and Downing Street has issued a readout about Andy Burnham’s bilateral meeting with Swinney. Reading them together, three points emerge.
Swinney and Burnham were both positive about the meeting, and sounded keen to be constructive not confrontational. No 10 said both leaders agreed the NEC meeting had been “extremely positive”, and Swinney said it was “a welcome start of work to develop the UK government’s new principle of ‘devolving by default’”.
But there is still a problem because, although they both want devolution, it’s not the same devolution.Swinney’s statement is all about the devolution of power from Westminster to Scotland. No 10’s is mostly about “regional empowerment” (devolution within Scotland), although it does say the PM agreed to “review and respond to a range of issues raised by the first minister”.
They agreed to differ on independence. The No 10 statement restates Burnham’s position that a second independence referendum is off the table. Swinney could have chosen to have a row about this, but he didn’t. While not at all resiling from his pro-independence position, he politely said: “While the prime minister and I disagree on independence, we do agree that Westminster does not work for people in Scotland.”
For the record, here is the full readout from the No 10 spokesperson.
The prime minister met with the first minister of Scotland in Glasgow following a meeting of the National Economic Council today.
The prime minister and first minister agreed the meeting at the NEC had been extremely positive. They said it had been a valuable exercise in starting the process of exploring how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode.
They agreed that now there would be a policy sprint led by No 10 North, involving officials from both governments, to take this agenda forward.
Outside that process, the prime minister said the UK government would review and respond to a range of issues raised by the first minister.
This would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland, which the prime minister has repeatedly made clear is off the table.
While the prime minister and I disagree on independence, we do agree that Westminster does not work for people in Scotland. And when the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will come about.
To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with him to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland – as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living.
Today’s meeting of the national economic council was a welcome start of work to develop the UK Government’s new principle of ‘devolving by default’ and the prime minister has been clear that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour.
I welcome that commitment, and look forward to our governments jointly developing a plan to consider further devolution to Scotland that will boost economic growth.
Rise in rough sleeping numbers for London 'stark reminder' of challenge facing Burnham, campaigners say
A rise in rough sleeping in London is a “stark reminder of the huge challenge” Andy Burnham faces in his pledge to get people off the streets, campaigners have said. As the Press Association reports, data shows there were 4,678 people recorded as sleeping rough in the capital in July to September this year. PA says:
While this is a slight drop of 1% on the same three-month period in 2025, the figure has risen by almost a fifth (18%) on the previous quarter this year.
The Combined Homelessness and Information Network (Chain) figures, published today, showed that there were 819 people classed as living on the streets (a separate category) – a rise of 8% on the same time last year and up by a fifth (20%) on the previous quarter.
Rick Henderson, chief executive of Homeless Link, the national membership body for frontline homelessness services, said: “The increase in rough sleeping across London, and particularly of those spending longer on our streets, is a stark reminder of the huge challenge London and the wider country face in turning the prime minister’s ambition to end rough sleeping into action.”
Burnham says he does not want Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to be 'left behind' as England embraces fiscal devolution
Speaking to reporters after the national economic council meeting, Andy Burnham said he did not want Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to lose out on the changes that will give more financial powers to mayors in England.
The agenda is moving quickly in England. There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind. I don’t want to see Wales left behind, but also crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.
So it’s really important that we all move at the same pace together. And I won’t allow anything to delay that. Growth can’t wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK.
Referring to the absence of Northern Ireland’s first minister and deputy first minister, he said:
It’s disappointing that the first minister and deputy first minister of Northern Ireland weren’t here. There was some representation, but we will continue the discussions too with Stormont about how do we take forward the same ideas.
Burnham says UK government to consider further devolution of employment support to Scotland and Wales
Andy Burnham has said the UK government will consider further devolution of employment support to Scotland and Wales.
Speaking after chairing a meeting of the national economic council, Burnham said:
We had a good discussion today on two fronts.
One around reindustrialisation, and the offer of more devolution of innovation funding to the regional level. It’s about creating those structures at a regional level, and that’s a matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries.
It’s not for me to impose or try to interfere there. But once there is a vehicle, that can be backed by the Scottish government, it can be backed by the UK government …
Secondly, we had a conversation about employment support, and particularly young people. There are too many young people out of work here in Scotland, in Wales, and in England too.
It’s a very big agenda that’s coming towards us. We need to localise as much as we can support for young people, employment support to help them back to work.
Now, as part of those discussions that will follow this meeting of the national economic council, we need to look at what are [the] arrangements for further devolution of employment support, particularly for young people in both Scotland and Wales.
Jonathan Reynolds says UK needs to know more about where EU heading before it opts for much closer relationship
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has suggested the UK needs to know more about where the EU is heading before it signs up to a much closer relationship.
He made the comment in an interview with the Sun, a day after John Healey, the chancellor, also hinted that he might have reservations about Andy Burnham’s ambitions for a new relationship with the EU undoing the damage done by Brexit.
Burnham is attending a summit with the EU next month where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus. There is strong support for all these initiatives in cabinet.
But Burnham also wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election, when – if it wants – Labour will be able to dump the 2024 manifesto pledges ruling out joining the single market or the customs union.
Burnham has not said what he wants to propose in Labour’s next manifesto, and he insists ultimately the public will decide, but he has said that he would like the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime and he seems open to trying to rejoin the single market in the next parliament.
Asked by the Sun if he shared Burnham’s dream of rejoining the EU, Reynolds replied:
I genuinely can’t answer that, because I don’t know what the future of the EU is – because [of] some of the very strong political currents in member states.
For me, it’s an approach to issues. What is their approach to how they regulate technology, AI? How dynamic will the economy be?
In a bid to stop ministers disagreeing in public about the EU, Burnham sent them a letter earlier this week telling them to stay “disciplined” and not to “advocate for specific options” as the debate on the future UK-EU relationship gets under way.
At the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson was asked to give more details of the sort of “regional empowerment” that could be offered to Scotland and Wales on the basis of today’s summit. The spokesperson did not give any detail beyond what No 10 has said already (see 9.11am) and, like the PM (see 12.05pm), he said it was ultimately up to Scotland and Wales to say what they wanted. It sounds like we won’t be getting specific proposals today.
Patrick Stewart 'one of the very best', says No 10 in tribute
Downing Street has paid tribute to Patrick Stewart following the actor’s death. At the daily lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson gave a comment that was a bit more extensive than the usual No 10 contribution when a great British celebrity dies. The spokesperson said that was because Andy Burnham feels strongly about the importance of actors.
The spokesperson said:
The prime minister was very sad to hear of the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart.
As a former culture secretary he knows how much Britain’s greatest actors mean to the country, and Sir Patrick was one of the very best.
He never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots. He brought joy to millions, and he always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.
Our thoughts are with his family and friends.
Here is our story, by Adrian Horton and Benjamin Lee, about the death of the Star Trek star.
Burnham wrong to think Manchester-style regional devolution would work for Wales, says former Welsh Labour minister
Lee Waters, a former Labour minister in the Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until May this year, thinks it is a mistake for Andy Burnham to think Manchester-style devolution (greater powers for mayors) will help in Wales. Referring to posts earlier summarising Burnham’s thinking (see 9.11am, 9.33am and 12.05pm), Waters sent me this note.
Just a reminder that when it comes to Wales, we are not comparing like with like. The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas. The Swansea Bay city region captures some 700,000 people, and similarly North Wales around 690,000 people. In Mid-Wales sheep outnumber people by 7:1. Only the Cardiff city region is comparable to English tiers, and even then at the lower end: around 1.5 million people.
Transposing an English mayoral worldview onto a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends.
Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government. Powers over skills, employment support, economic development, housing investment and major spending programmes sit at an all-Wales strategic level (covering a similar population size to Greater Manchester.)
His argument for England is that powers should flow from Westminster to city regions because they operate at an economically meaningful scale. Yet when the PM turns to Wales, he seems to suggest that powers already devolved to Cardiff Bay should be dispersed further down the system.
But notably he is not calling on his successor as the mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, to fragment the powers of the Greater Manchester combined authority and redistribute them amongst its ten constituent councils. On the contrary, the whole logic of the Greater Manchester model rests on concentrating strategic authority at a regional level.
Yet the implication of his comments is that Wales should move in the opposite direction.
Burnham tells devolved governments he wants to 'draw a line', leading to better relationship
Andy Burnham delivered his opening remarks at the national economic council meeting in Glasgow on camera. Here are the key points.
Burnham stressed that he wanted to be cooperative. He said:
What I want to do is set the tone which is one of positive offer to work with both the Scottish and Welsh governments, in terms of looking at a model of deeper devolution in Scotland and Wales.
Referring to John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth using their first names, not their titles, Burnham also said that he hoped they had seen enough of him as PM to know that he was serious about wanting “problem solving rather than point scoring”. He also said he wanted to “draw a line”, implying previous relations with the devolved governments weren’t ideal.
He said that, while he wanted “deeper devolution” (see 9.11am), “obviously, it’s for the devolved governments to determine the shape and the structure of that”.
He suggested his experience as mayor of Greater Manchester had made him more inclined to see Westminster the way Scotland and Wales did. He said:
Obviously, speaking as a former mayor, I saw how Greater Manchester was able to go on a very different track to the one that we’d been on pre the arrival of devolved powers in Greater Manchester.
I’ll be honest, I looked at the world differently, and perhaps more from Scotland and Wales’ point of view, when we were making that case for a greater level of power.
He said, using devolved powers, as mayor he was able to set “high ambitions” for Manchester – “and a decade on the results are there to see.”
He said he wanted Westminster to work “in a more collaborative way” with the devolved governments.
He said that Britain in the past had not been particularly good at handling “industrial transition” and that he wanted to change this. He recalled visiting the site of the Ravenscraig steelworks near Motherwell recently, saying:
I was on the site of Ravenscraig and … I used to hear that word in the news when I was growing up. I only then, when I was there, understood the scale of what that industry once was, and how the country didn’t help those communities through industrial transition.
You could say the same of Port Talbot in south Wales, he said. He said what was happening in Port Talbot was a model of industrial transition.
He expressed regret that Northern Ireland’s first minister and deputy first minister weren’t at the meeting.
John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, and Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, arrived together for the national economic council meeting in Glasgow. The SNP and Plaid Cymru are sister parties, and recently Swinney, ap Iorwerth and the Sinn Féin leaders Mary Lou McDonald and Michelle O’Neill held a meeting in Cardiff that was characterised by opponents as a summit to dismantle the UK.
Voters regard Healey's budget as one of fairest for years, poll suggests
Yesterday the Institute for Fiscal Studies (see here) and the Resolution Foundation (see here) delivered fairly negative assessments of the budget. But mostly the gloom was triggered by the thinktanks said about the overall state of the economy and the public finances; they were critical of John Healey for deferring difficult choices, but less hostile about the decisions he did actually announce.
However, according to YouGov, voters are quite positive. They regard it as one of the fairest budgets for years.
The public’s initial reaction to John Healey’s first budget is in some key respects broadly positive, with nearly half of Britons (45%) regarding the budget as being fair, relative to just 20% seeing the measures announced as not fair.
This is a notable improvement on last year, when Rachel Reeves’ second budget was declared ‘not fair’ by a near-inverse margin of 48% to 21%. In fact, on this measure, this is one of the most positively received budgets in recent times. In data going back to 2010, only George Osborne’s first budget in 2010 and Rishi Sunak’s Covid budgets of 2020 and March 2021 have been judged ‘fair’ by a greater proportion of Britons (50-55%).
The Covid budgets were both giveaway, rescue budgets, and so it is not surprising they polled well. Osborne’s first budget was an austerity budget, and it is not a model popular with Labour MPs, but it probably polled well on fairness because the pain was spread across all groups in society.
The YouGov figures also show that only 15% of people think their family finances will improve as a result of the budget. That may not sound much but, as Difford says, “this is a sharp and favourable contrast with last November’s budget, which 50% of Britons believed would leave them and their family worse off, compared to a mere 3% feeling they’d be better off.”
In fact, Healey and his first budget outperform Rachel Reeves and her budget last year on every measure assessed in the polling.
Yesterday one of the criticisms of the budget from the Resolution Foundation was that the energy cost of living support package helped the rich almost as much as the poor. That meant it was “poorly targeted”, said the RF, applying a progressive, social justice definition of fairness. What the YouGov poll suggests is that voters as a whole judge fairness differently; it is probably precisely because most households get the £100 energy payment that people regard it as fair.
In their London Playbook briefing for Politico yesterday, Sam Blewett and Megan McElroy said Healey used focus groups extensively before finalising his measures.
Government officials say they focus-grouped all this relentlessly. Playbook was told these sessions helped convince ministers to go for wider support payments for council tax bands A-D rather than the initial plans to go with something more targeted. It was the supposedly better-off voters who were complaining about the pinch as well.
MoD says under new offset policy foreign firms will only get big defence contracts if they spend equivalent amount in UK
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, was on the interview round this morning, announcing a new aspect of defence procurement policy. The Ministry of Defence is now saying that, if overseas suppliers win UK defence contracts, they will be required to spend the equivalent amount in the UK.
British workers, businesses and apprentices will benefit from major changes which will see more defence work carried out in the UK thanks to the launch of a world-leading Offsets policy.
Under the new rules, overseas companies that win significant UK defence contracts will be required to invest back into Britain, through new British jobs and apprenticeships, opening UK factories, investing in domestic suppliers, transferring technology and innovation know-how.
This means contracts worth over £50m will be considered for offsets. The contractors will be required to deliver such benefits to the UK that could reach the same value as the contract, for example a £100m contract could see new jobs, facilities, or skills training up to the same £100m value in the UK.
The government is prioritising buying British defence contracts wherever possible. Where it must buy defence equipment from overseas, this new approach will ensure British workers and businesses still benefit.
John Healey, the chancellor, and Streeting are formally announcing this on a visit to BAE Systems Scotstoun in Glasgow today.
The MoD says countries like Poland, Norway and the Netherlands use similar offset policies. Further details of how this will work are set out in an offset policy paper published today.
Streeting said:
Every pound we invest in defence should be judged by what it does for Britain. That’s why we are backing British by buying British wherever we can.
Even when that is not possible, we are acting to ensure that any investment brings jobs, skills and investment back home, strengthening our national security by boosting our domestic industry.
In the past, the conventional globalist, free market approach to defence procurement operated on the basis that cost and quality were all that mattered and that, if a foreign firm could supply kit better and more cheaply than anyone else, that was enough. But the US is not the only country that has become protectionist in recent years, and this is a good example of Europe prioritising local employment in government procurement.
John Swinney urges Burnham to devolve more powers to Scottish government
In his statement ahead of the devolution summit in Glasgow today, Andy Burnham made it clear that he is interested in transferring more power from Edinburgh to Glasgow. (See 9.11am.) But John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, would rather talk about devolving further powers from London to Edinburgh. He issued this statement ahead of the meeting.
The prime minister has made devolution a central focus for his government. However the UK government must ensure that any devolution proposals respect devolution in Scotland. That means working with the Scottish government.
The Scottish government has put forward substantive proposals to the UK government on areas where further devolution would help grow Scotland’s economy and I will press the prime minister, and his government, to work with us to deliver those proposals.
The SNP wants Scotland to be fully independent (the ultimate version of devolution). But, pending that, it is also calling for the Scottish parliament to have power over policy areas currently reserved to London. Greater control over taxation, immigration, employment law and energy policy are particular priorities.
Burnham admits he would have liked more radical first budget
Andy Burnham has admitted his first budget as prime minister was not as radical as he would have liked because of the economic uncertainty facing the country, Kiran Stacey reports.
Burnham says he wants to offer more ‘regional empowerment’ ahead of devolution summit with Scottish and Welsh leaders
Good morning. Andy Burnham is in Glasgow today for a meeting with the leaders from Scotland and Wales and he says he wants to use it to talk about “the next stage of devolution”. According to the overnight briefing from No 10, he is less interested in giving more powers to the devolved parliaments and more interested in promoting “regional empowerment” in their countries.
In his pre-summit statement, Burnham says:
Through No 10 North, we are rewiring the state. I want to make sure every city and region in the United Kingdom is part of that.
Today I’ll be making an offer to the governments of each nation. Put politics aside and work in partnership with the UK government to develop models of regional empowerment that ensure communities can use their own strengths to unlock their potential.
This is the next stage of devolution. Together, there is no limit to what we can achieve.
Burnham is speaking at a time when Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have since the May elections (when Plaid Cymru won in Wales) for the first time had first ministers from nationalist parties that want to break away from the UK. John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, and Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, will be at the meeting today. But Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minister from Northern Ireland won’t be there. She holds power jointly with a DUP deputy, and both of them have to stay away because the DUP has vetoed their attendance due to an ongoing row about Drumcree. Some officials will attend instead.
Downing Street says at today’s meeting Burnham “will say that devolution by default shouldn’t be about the transfer of powers from one parliament to another but should go deeper within nations to empower all places and communities who know best what they need to grow and access opportunities.”
Here is the agenda for the day.
Morning:Andy Burnham chairs a meeting of the national economic council in Glasgow.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
Afternoon (UK time): Ed Miliband is attending a meeting of G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta in the US.
I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Putin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian version of Starlink
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine.
The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation.
“Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Russian leader said, according to the Tass news agency. “How many of these [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we’re only taking the first steps.”
The true number of active SpaceX satellites is estimated at about 10,000, which provide the high-speed internet service that has been the subject of a diplomatic row between Musk, the US and Ukraine earlier this month.
A military version of Starlink, called Starshield, was suddenly restricted one night in the middle of October, preventing Ukraine from conducting medium drone attacks and hampering some of its anti-drone air defences.
Initially, Musk, an ally of the US president, Donald Trump, denied that he had ordered a throttling of the internet connection, before saying at the end of last week that he had closed a loophole in which the civilian Starlink had been used by the military.
Putin appeared to be trying to flatter Musk, whose control of the communications technology has raised questions about the US billionaire’s leverage over the White House and the impact he is able to have on Ukraine’s war effort.
“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.
Starlink does not work in Russia and its use by Russia inside Ukraine was restricted earlier this year. Meanwhile, Moscow has begun to develop an alternative system, though, with an estimated 26 working satellites, its capacity is limited.
Last week, after about 10 days of restriction, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, announced that “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored” and that the speeds were “now where they need to be”.
Few believe the issue is permanently settled, with relations between Zelenskyy and Trump fraught in the run-up to the US midterm elections next Tuesday. Trump has also reached out to Putin, agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow early in October in an effort to reduce the oil price before Americans go to the polls.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he hoped proposed trilateral peace talks, involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, would take place between 6 and 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, shortly after the midterms.
“We are waiting for the American side. I think that they’ll be ready with all the answers after the elections,” the Ukrainian leader said at a press conference in The Hague with the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten.
Earlier, Zelenskyy said he had spoken to Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, as it emerged that Britain would provide £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over the next three years – and an immediate £500m for air defence systems.
The additional aid was, Zelenskyy said, “a truly strong and very timely step” that came “as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone” as the war heads towards what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet.
John Healey, the UK chancellor, announced the extra funding as part of the government’s annual budget. “The prime minister and I called President Zelenskyy to tell him about our commitments in the budget today. He told us: ‘You’ve made my day’.”
The Dutch government also said it would provide €500m in military support for the winter, and a further €1.2bn in non-military aid, partly to help fund urgent repairs to Ukraine’s utilities and manufacturing.
Kyiv has been relentlessly attacked by Moscow this autumn as Russian forces fail to make progress on the frontlines in the east of Ukraine.
Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since the middle of October, Zelenskyy said overnight, hitting power plants and other key targets in an effort to cause a humanitarian crisis in the capital.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die | Andrew Roth
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
They say the first casualty of war is truth. For the Trump administration, the road to peace with Russia now encompasses some extraordinary lies.
Steve Witkoff delivered one as he sat down with Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday, aiming to close the deal on Russia’s land grab in Ukraine with the White House’s strategy of maximum pressure on Kyiv and saccharine flattery of the Kremlin.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” said Witkoff, a real-estate mogul who, thanks to being Trump’s friend, is now the US’s senior envoy and diplomat to end the largest European conflict since the second world war. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”
In Putin’s 26 years in power, it is a rare moment when he has been granted that specific honour. Skim through Russia’s past wartime exploits – from the bombing campaigns in Chechnya and Georgia and Syria, to the thousands of Russian citizens jailed for dissent, to the violent deaths of prominent opposition journalists and politicians in barely disguised assassinations and poisonings – and it will be difficult to identify Putin’s credentials as a humanitarian.
And that is before looking to Ukraine, where Russia chose to launch a full-scale invasion that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. The Guardian recently obtained a Russian strategy document showing the Kremlin’s potential to black out Ukrainian cities this winter, cutting off up to 90% of electricity to cities such as Kyiv and Odesa and Kharkiv – where millions of people live – to intentionally create a humanitarian catastrophe. And judging by the nightly barrages levelled at power plants for cities across Ukraine, the Kremlin has decided to move forward with that strategy until Kyiv surrenders.
As Witkoff met Putin on Wednesday, schoolchildren in Kharkiv hastened down a reinforced stairway, sirens announcing the arrival of Shahed drones overhead. This is no ordinary bomb shelter; it is one of 10 underground schools Kharkiv has constructed because of Russia’s regular bombing of the city less than 20 miles from the border.
Parents had welcomed the schools because they were safe, said teachers, and this was the one way that young people could have an uninterrupted school day during a war that could last years more – and reignite even if a shaky peace deal is reached.
“We all believed in Trump. We all really had hopes for America and for Trump to stop this monster Putin,” said Olena Svytlychna, the head of the education department of the Novobavarskyi region in Kharkiv, sitting in the school’s cafe on Wednesday.
“And now we have doubts, we don’t believe them. And we are very scared.”
As Witkoff spoke, the families of six people killed in a drone strike in a park near Kharkiv this week were holding funerals. The youngest victim of the strike was a one-year-old girl, Anhelina, who was killed as she was sitting strapped into her stroller in a playground. Her mother, Inna Mariukhna, a local schoolteacher, was also killed in the strike. The final death toll was four adults and two children, Anhelina and an 11-year-old girl.
Those lives have barely earned a mention from the White House as it pushes for Ukraine to capitulate as quickly as it can this week – and crucially before the 3 November midterm elections when voters will deliver a referendum on Trump’s leadership for the last two years.
Shortly after the bombing, Trump told reporters on the White House lawn that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine”. After taking criticism for that remark, he mentioned the attacks in passing just to downplay the shelling of civilians: there were “some people in a town that got hit or whatever, but mostly young soldiers” died, he said from the Oval Office on Tuesday.
For the White House, those words cost little. Witkoff’s goal was to bring home a US citizen, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, who had been detained in Russia. But if Witkoff wants to buy a peace deal by 3 November through flattering Putin, then this will only be the White House’s opening salvo in its war on truth.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source says
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Federal authorities investigating the Minnesota representative Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the inquiry.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities investigate potential fraud in Omar’s immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar’s Washington DC home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
On Tuesday, Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and that her office is also looking into issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.
“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.
The search of Omar’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests, which will determine control of the House and the Senate, was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the representative for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement”.
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
A phone message seeking comment was left on Wednesday with a representative for Omar.
Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election. The justice department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s fifth district, including Minneapolis. She is part of “the Squad” of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Burnham wants to ‘recast’ Chagos Islands deal after US resistance
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham has said he wants to “recast” the UK’s deal to cede control of the Chagos Islands after resistance from Washington, which said the agreement could instead be modelled on America’s Greenland deal with Denmark.
The prime minister told the Economist he wanted “a new discussion” with the US over the disputed islands, which are home to the Diego Garcia military base.
The original deal, which was struck by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and would have given sovereignty of the islands to Mauritius, has been in limbo since Donald Trump made clear he opposed it.
Burnham said: “We are in discussion with our US friends to see how we might recast the arrangement that better meets their concerns.
“We look at the Greenland deal and obviously there was a solution reached there. Now, maybe there is something there we can take from that to see if there’s a solution that works in relation to Diego Garcia. But that is something that we’re very engaged on. We’re working hard on it, but it is challenging.”
Starmer’s government signed a treaty to transfer sovereignty to Mauritius while keeping control of the joint UK-US base on Diego Garcia under a 99-year lease. Under the agreement, Mauritius would have received £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year.
The agreement was thrown into uncertainty when Trump voiced his opposition to it. Speaking in September after a bilateral meeting with Burnham in New York, the president said: “I don’t support it – I think it’s a terrible deal.”
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has since said the British government had suspended payments to Mauritius while the UK and US worked on a compromise.
He told the BBC: “This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support. So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government.”
While Trump was expressing his unhappiness at the Chagos deal, he was striking an agreement with Denmark over Greenland, after months of threats towards the island.
Under that agreement, Greenland will remain a Danish territory but the US will be allowed to develop a significant military presence there, while its adversaries will be banned from building their own bases on the island.
Burnham was speaking on his return journey from Antigua, where he attended the Commonwealth heads of government (Chogm) summit. Much of the trip was dominated by demands from Caribbean countries for Britain to pay reparations for slavery, but Burnham insisted his government had helped move the issue on by opening up the possibility of a government apology.
“I think we have done something, we’ve achieved something out there,” he said.
Burnham will host his own international summit next year when the G20 meets in Manchester. Burnham said the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, would be barred from that meeting, though the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, would be welcome.
“There are sanctions against leading figures in the [Russian] administration,” he said. “[Putin] will not be coming because of an outstanding sanction.”
Asked about Xi’s presence, he said: “President Xi visited Manchester in 2015, and I spoke to him and we had a good conversation about that, and he was warm about that visit. And obviously he’s coming back 12 years later and he will see a big difference in Manchester. And some of that has been done in partnership with China.”
Over the next few weeks, Burnham will prepare for the EU summit in Brussels, which the prime minister says will be a moment for the UK to begin thinking about its longer-term relationship with the bloc and whether it should rejoin.
He will also pull together his “10-year plan”, which aides say will lay out his long-term vision for how the UK should change over the next decade, including public control over key parts of the economy.
Burnham said the plan, which had been promised for this year, could be delayed until January. He denied recent reports that it would be relatively brief and lacking in detail. “It will be substantial, and it will also be – well, in my view, it will be compelling because I am weaving the different threads together,” he said.
“We may go into the new year, to be honest … December or January. I think we will need to leave that open.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Dozens injured and buildings damaged as tornadoes hit Sicily
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Two tornadoes have struck the coastal town of Marsala in western Sicily, injuring dozens of people, damaging buildings including a school, and overturning cars.
A series of videos began to circulate on Friday morning showing two waterspouts approaching the Sicilian town from the sea as people braced for their arrival.
Dozens of people were reported injured, with at least 11 taken to hospital after being struck by flying debris and shattered glass. Among the most seriously injured was a 70-year-old man admitted to Mazara del Vallo hospital in a critical condition with several fractures.
A school was also hit by the powerful winds, leaving six children with minor cuts and abrasions. At the time the tornado struck, 273 pupils were inside the building, all of whom were safely evacuated. Drone footage showing the aftermath revealed extensive damage to the school, with windows shattered and desks and chairs overturned.
In recent years, people in southern Italy have been bracing for the arrival of a “medicane” – a rare Mediterranean storm with hurricane-like characteristics, capable of producing winds exceeding 60 miles an hour and waves reaching five metres in height.
The weather system developed amid intense heat over north Africa and unusually warm Mediterranean waters. Scientists have warned that rising sea temperatures, driven by the climate emergency, can provide additional energy for powerful storms in the region.
According to experts, record temperatures in the Mediterranean contributed to the freak storm that sank the Bayesian, a super yacht off the coast of Sicily, in August 2024, killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UNHCR criticises UK’s 30-year ‘earned settlement’ plans for refugees
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The UN refugee agency has said a government plan to make refugees wait up to 30 years before they get permission to settle in the UK “raises significant concerns”.
The strategy was unveiled earlier this week by Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, as she announced a softening of aspects of her immigration plans, but kept some of the rigorous rules drawn up by her office last year.
Mahmood introduced a carve-out for care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years, but maintained rules to make those who arrived by irregular means such as small boats having to wait up to 30 years.
UNHCR, which has international responsibility for refugees, told the Guardian that the plan to increase the time people had to wait for those who arrived by irregular means was “likely to be detrimental”.
Some refugees can reduce the upper limit of 30 years if they enter work or study, but there is a 10-year penalty for those who arrive on small boats or concealed in lorries rather than arriving via safe and legal routes. The government has significantly reduced the latter, and although it has announced some legal routes, these will only be able to be accessed by a small minority seeking sanctuary here.
The UNHCR welcomed the legal routes but said: “An extended qualifying period for settlement for refugees raises significant concerns, particularly when considered alongside the introduction of short-term stay arrangements and changes made last year that would preclude many from ever accessing citizenship.
“Taken together, these measures are likely to be detrimental to refugees’ sense of security, belonging and stability, and to impact their ability to contribute and become part of their new communities.
“Refugees are not migrants: they have fled their countries because they cannot rely on their protection nor safely return home. For refugees, safety means more than a grant of asylum and settlement has an important role to play.”
Kamena Dorling, the director of policy at Helen Bamber Foundation, also raised concerns about the 30-year rule. She said: “We are deeply alarmed and disappointed by the government’s announcement on ‘earned settlement’. It will cause profound and lasting harm to refugees, including survivors of torture, trafficking and other forms of extreme cruelty.
“The government had an opportunity to change its approach after receiving extensive evidence about the devastating consequences of this policy, but instead has doubled down on its approach that will damage the lives and futures of thousands of men, women, families and children, as well as harm wider integration and social cohesion.
She said that extending the qualifying period for settlement “is simply inhumane”.
She added: “This will not deter people fleeing war, persecution, torture and violence, who are fighting for their lives and seeking safety in the UK. When legal routes are so severely limited, people will continue to take desperate measures to reach safety. It will punish people who have already endured unimaginable harm, leaving those recognised as refugees facing decades of uncertainty, insecurity and fear.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: EHRC raises concern with Reform about ‘racial and sexual remarks’ in documentary
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The official equalities watchdog has written to Reform UK to raise concerns after an undercover TV documentary showed councillors and candidates for the party expressing racist and misogynistic views, with one of the party’s MPs complaining about ingrained sexism.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said it had written to Nigel Farage’s party in the wake of revelations in ITV’s Undercover: A Year in Reform, which was broadcast in October.
While Farage has said the party’s vetting procedures have improved greatly, footage in the programme included Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, making Islamophobic remarks, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.
Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues.
In another section, the Reform MP Sarah Pochin was shown complaining that the party was “chauvinistic” and riven with “alpha male shit”.
An EHRC statement said its letter had asked Reform to provide information, “including what action the party is taking to comply with the Equality Act”.
In the wake of the documentary, the statement said, the EHRC “received complaints alleging unlawful activity under the Equality Act 2010, including concerns about racial and sexual remarks expressed by councillors, prospective councillors and members”.
It went on: “As with every complaint we receive, we will assess the information provided carefully and, following that consideration, take action where appropriate.
“Political parties, like all duty-bearers, must comply with the Equality Act and take steps to avoid discrimination or harassment including on the grounds of race, religion or belief and sex. We have guidance advising parties on their responsibilities under the act and urge them to consider it. This could include reviewing party policies or practices to identify areas of potential discrimination, harassment or victimisation that need to be addressed.”
It comes weeks after the EHRC wrote to the Greens in England and Wales to seek more information about a new party policy which equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.
Reform has said it reported ITV and the reporters concerned to police, with separate threats of civil legal action against the broadcaster.
Responding to the EHRC letter, a party spokesperson said: “We are confident we have fully complied with our obligations under the Equality Act. There is no room for racism in Reform UK.”
