Trump says he will have spent $400m to support Republican candidates in midterms
Donald Trump said that he will have spent $400m supporting Republican candidates in midterm races by the time election day rolls around on 3 November.
The staggering amount will be spent through his political operation and aligned Super Pac, Maga Inc.
“More than 300 Million Dollars has already been spent on Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity, and more. It is my Great Honor to do so on behalf of the Republican Party, which has done so much to bring our Country back from the Edge of Oblivion,” he wrote on Truth Social.
He cited his belief in the Republican party, but also the riots that have swept through France, as his reasons behind the spend. A reminder, Trump has repeated baseless claims that the demonstrations, which have descended into chaos and seen thousands arrested, are the result of mass migration.
We’re wrapping up our live coverage of US politics. Here are some of the day’s key developments:
Donald Trump rallied in North Carolina as part of a week-long tour to stump for Republicans ahead of the midterms. He mostly stuck to a familiar script, repeating conspiracy theories about paid protesters, lies about Roy Cooper’s tenure as governor and complimenting men’s bodies.
Trump said that there will be “no money” to settle claims related to water contamination at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune if Republicans are not victorious in the upcoming midterm elections.
Trump loyalist and rightwing influencer Laura Loomer tore into the Department of Justice on Tuesday, saying the agency was belittling veterans, who were exposed to contaminated drinking water at the Marine Corps base decades ago, with “lowball” settlement offers.
Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, announced new investment to support semi-conductor production in North Carolina, telling Trump supporters at a rally in the state that Sibelco would build silicon manufacturing.
Donald Trump said that he will have spent $400m supporting Republican candidates in midterm races by the time election day rolls around on 3 November. The staggering amount will have been spent through his political operation and aligned Super Pac, Maga Inc. Meanwhile, former New York City mayor Mike Bloomberg is donating $80m to Democrats ahead of the upcoming elections.
Trump says he will pay settlement money to veterans affected by contaminated water at marine base only if Republicans retain control of Congress
Donald Trump said that there will be “no money” to settle claims related to water contamination at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune if Republicans are not victorious in the upcoming midterm elections.
“If we win the House and the Senate, I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible, and get it off the books and get it finished,” he told supporters during a rally in North Carolina. “If we don’t win, there’s no money. If we do win, you’re getting it and it’s gonna be finally over with, that nightmare that’s been going on for so many years.”
Camp Lejeune was built in the early 1940s, and from the early 1950s to the late 80s, its drinking water was contaminated with industrial solvents. Trump said his administration has so far delivered $1bn in settlements to impacted veterans and their families.
His remarks were only the latest instance of the president suggesting he would punish Americans if they fail to vote the way he wants them to. While in Kansas on Monday, the US president also said he will not allow year-round sales of gasoline containing higher volumes of ethanol if the state’s voters elect a Democrat over Republican senator Roger Marshall.
During his rally in North Carolina, Donald Trump has mostly stuck to a familiar script, repeating conspiracy theories about paid protesters, lies about Roy Cooper’s tenure as governor and complimenting men’s bodies.
Several demonstrators were removed from the event, including one who protested high gas prices. Trump called them “losers” and claimed that their parents were likely his supporters and would physically punish them for the disruptions.
He also erroneously suggested crime in North Carolina rose under Roy Cooper, the Democratic Senate candidate, because some 3,500 inmates were released during the pandemic while he was governor. His administration agreed to the release as part of a settlement with civil rights groups.
Trump spoke at length about Ohio Senator Jon Husted who he described as a “football stud.”
“I’m studying his body. I’ve never studied the body of a man before, it’s not my thing,” he said. “But I looked at his ass and then I looked at his legs and I said, ‘His ass — it’s like a pile of muscle.’ Then I looked at his legs and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’”
Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, briefly came on stage during Trump’s North Carolina rally to announce new investment to support semi-conductor production in the state.
“We’re announcing Sibelco is going to build silicon manufacturing. It’s quartz manufacturing. It is basically the foundation of semiconductors,” he said during the event.
He said the investment would amount to “hundreds of millions of dollars”.
Donald Trump has taken the stage at a rally in North Carolina as part of a seven-day tour to stump for Republicans ahead of the US midterms.
He’s in North Carolina to support Michael Whatley, the Republican nominee for US Senate, who is polling behind candidate Roy Cooper, the state’s former Democratic governor.
We’ll keep you updated on anything notable from the president’s remarks.
FEMA to states: Prepare to handle your own disasters, Politico reports
The Trump administration wants states to shoulder more of the financial responsibility for disasters, Politico reports.
“Federal dollars should be building greater capability, not creating greater dependency,” Federal emergency management agency (FEMA) administrator Cameron Hamilton told state officials at an Arkansas conference, in a recording exclusively obtained by the Politico. He said each state should have the “appropriate financial reserves.”
“A future that I hope we would shoot for is one where we wouldn’t require as many disasters because the capability of states is so high and so substantial,” Hamilton also said, noting that changes could begin in the next six months.
Under Trump’s second administration, FEMA has seen deep cuts in funding and the exodus of over 2,400 personnel. Former employees and emergency response experts have voiced concern over its capability to respond to future natural disasters.
Trump loyalist and rightwing influencer Laura Loomer tore into the Department of Justice on Tuesday, saying the agency was belittling veterans, who were exposed to contaminated drinking water at a Marine Corps base decades ago, with “lowball” settlement offers.
“This is a political disaster waiting to happen. Let’s be clear: Democrats are 100% going to weaponize this against President Trump and try to hurt him with veterans heading into the midterms in two weeks,” Loomer wrote in a X post, blaming associate attorney general Stanley Woodward Jr.
In a thinly-veiled rebuff, attorney general Todd Blanche appeared to suggest Loomer’s diatribe was financially-motivated.
“You should be transparent with your followers, and you are dead wrong about Stanley,” he responded on X.
“We love our veterans and we want to get these cases right. Find a different obsession other than going after one of DOJ’s best fighters.”
Loomer shot back, saying Trump wanted to fire Woodward, but took pity on him “because his lefty wife is divorcing him,” she claimed.
Some outlets, including Bloomberg, reported earlier this year that Harmeet Dhillon, an assistant attorney general in the DOJ’s civil rights division, would be promoted to Woodward’s post. She was not.
Trump's use of an antisemitic slur for a second time draws belated, indirect criticism from ADL
The Anti-Defamation League, which calls itself the world’s “leading anti-hate organization”, founded in 1913 “to protect the Jewish people”, denounced the use of the term “shylock” as antisemitic on Tuesday, without explaining that the slur had been used one day earlier by Donald Trump in a speech in Kansas.
The ADL’s brief social-media post made no mention of Trump at all and offered no explanation as to why the group found it necessary to explain, today, that anyone equating an avaricious person to Shylock, the villainous Jewish moneylender in Shakespeare’s Merchant of Venice, is using an antisemitic trope.
“The term ‘Shylock’ is rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype,” the ADL posted on X but not its other social media accounts. “Regardless of intent, its use can reinforce harmful tropes about Jews and normalize language that has long been used to target the Jewish community.”
Critics who accuse the ADL of using accusations of antisemitism selectively, to attack people who are critical of Israel, suggested that the Jewish-American civil rights group was going easy on Trump because of his support for Israel.
Matt Duss, a former foreign police adviser to senator Bernie Sanders, the most prominent Jewish American politician, responded to the ADL’s failure to mention Trump by suggesting its president would have been more direct had someone else used the slur. “If a Democrat said it Jonathan Greenblatt would be knocking people over to get in front of a camera to condemn them by name, but it was Trump so it’s just a general public service announcement,” Duss wrote.
In 2014, after then vice-president Joe Biden described people who take financial advantage of American service members as “shylocks”, the Anti-Defamation League’s national director accepted his apology and called the remarks “a teachable moment”.
Trump’s use of the slur, at a rally in Kansas on Monday night, came just one day after he had endorsed Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Monday, ahead of Israel’s elections.
Trump invoked the antisemitic stereotype as part of his defense of the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, a doctor who has been criticized for filing lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills, leading to 18 of them being arrested.
The president began by claiming, falsely, that Marshall had been required by law to take legal action over unpaid bills, even one for just $101.
Marshall, Trump told supporters at a rally outside Wichita on Monday, “was given a bum rap because he was mandated by law to request strongly, money owed from patients. You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people.” There is, in fact, no such law.
Turning to Marshall’s critics, including his Democratic rival, Adam Hamilton, who featured some of Marshall’s patients in a campaign ad, Trump said: “they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy.”
“If he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law,” Trump said again, repeating the falsehood he based his defense on. “He would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability,” the president claimed, falsely.
Trump’s use of the antisemitic slur came 15 months after he was made aware of its meaning when he used it at a rally in Iowa. Speaking on 3 July 2025, Trump Trump told supporters that eliminating the taxes on inherited family farms would save farmers from “going to the banks and borrowing from, in some cases a fine banker, and in some cases shylocks and bad people”.
The day after that Iowa rally, the ADL called the president’s use of the term “very troubling and irresponsible”, but Trump claimed ignorance when he was asked by a reporter if he had intended to use the word “shylocks” to refer to Jews.
“No, I’ve never heard it that way,” Trump replied then. “To me, a shylock is somebody that’s a, uh, a moneylender at high rates. I’ve never heard it that way. You view it differently than me. I’ve never heard that.”

The staggering amount will have been spent through his political operation and aligned Super Pac, Maga Inc. The president will continue his campaign blitz with a rally in Greenville, North Carolina on Tuesday.
Beyond Washington, Trump’s special envoys – Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – wrapped up a meeting with Nordic leaders and Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo. The Ukrainian president said that the talks covered security guarantees, among others, and he hopes to hear Russia’s response tomorrow. Witkoff is set to head to St Petersburg on Wednesday to relay to the new peace proposals discussed with Ukraine to Moscow.
Zelenskyy also said that US intelligence sharing with Ukraine is working again, after sustained disruptions. Earlier, the Ukrainian president said he had a “substantive conversation” with US secretary of state Marco Rubio.
Meanwhile, Rubio told reporters in India today that “there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine”. He called the assertion that people in Ukraine are dying because the US is denying them information “scandalous” and “outrageous”. However, in an interview with CNN, representative Eugene Vindman, the Democratic congressman from Virginia, slammed the secretary of state’s comments. “He [Rubio] is lying and so is the president when they say that they are not restricting intelligence in violation of the law,” Vindman said.
And Trump continued to blame the riots in France on mass migration, without providing any evidence. “It’s an immigration problem. You have people that poured into France, and they were also unchecked, unvetted, like with Biden when he was doing. We don’t do that,” Trump said. Even though French authorities have not tied the upheaval to immigrants, that hasn’t deterred the president from insisting that similar chaos would be the US’ fate if Democrats win control of Congress in the upcoming midterms.
Also in the Oval Office today, Mehmet Oz – the director of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that the health department would be deferring $1.2bn more to California.
This comes after the Trump administration already paused almost $1bn in Medicaid funding to the Golden state in July.
“They just got the note, and we’re doing that because the growth of personal care services in California,” Oz told reporters on Tuesday. “That one little area where you’re paying someone to carry groceries upstairs for your mom, which many of you would carry groceries upstairs for your mom for free, I would think. But in California, they’ll pay you a lot of money for it, and it’s actually run by the counties. But California has been growing that program 24% in the last three years.”
Once again, Trump launched into a racist attack against Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar, and the Somali-American community.
This comes after the justice department launched a raid on the Minnesota representative’s Washington DC home. Reports citing sources familar with the probe said the search earlier this month was related to a criminal fraud investigation concerning Omar’s immigration paperwork. Omar’s father filled out that paperwork when she was a child. The raid has been met with widespread condemnation, particularly so close to the midterm elections.
However, Trump today doubled down.
“I think she’s a sick, a very dishonest person, but who hates our country. And she comes from a country that is essentially not even a country, Somalia. It’s a real shit house,” he said.
“Somalians vote for her … Most of them shouldn’t be here. You know, they have like a 98 % unemployment rate. They don’t work,” the president added, an incredible statistic given the fact that the census doesn’t actually track the unemployment rate for Somali-Americans specifically.
Donald Trump was not optimistic about whether peace talks appear to be back on the table ahead of Steve Witkoff’s meeting in St Petersburg, Russia tomorrow (following his summit with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Nordic leaders in Oslo).
“Russia is a big machine. They just keep grinding forward, and that’s what they’ve done. They’ve taken a very large piece of land, and you know you can say that Ukraine is doing well or poorly, but the land gets bigger and bigger all the time, week by week,” Trump said, before repeating his insistence for Zelenskyy to cut a deal.
“We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We’ve got nothing back, other than high diesel,” Trump said, without acknowledging that the price of diesel and gasoline jumped at the beginning of the Iran war in February. “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal … In my opinion, it’s just really just going to get worse.”
On France, the president once again said – without providing any evidence – that the riots are due to mass migration.
“It’s an immigration problem. You have people that poured into France, and they were also unchecked, unvetted, like with Biden when he was doing. We don’t do that,” Trump said.
However, the French authorities have not tied the upheaval to immigrants, but that hasn’t deterred the president for insisting that the chaos would be a fate the US is destined for if Democrats win control of Congress in the upcoming midterms.
Donald Trump announces incentive program for people to report fraud, after conservative YouTuber Nick Shirley's allegations
In the Oval Office, Trump announced an incentive program for people to report fraud, in honor of conservative YouTuber Nick Shirley – who, you may remember, posted a video last year alleging fraud by daycare centers servicing Minneapolis’s Somali American community.
The video, initially posted in December, resulted in a deluge of anti-immigrant and anti-Somali content across social media, including in Truth Social posts by Donald Trump.
In July, Fahima Egeh Mahamud, the CEO of the daycare center that appeared in Shirley’s video, pleaded guilty to wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the US.
Under the administration’s proposed program, people who submit information through that results in a fraud conviction could receive up to $30,000.
In the Oval Office today, Trump presented Shirley, 24, with a check for $10,000 for his work.

It is my Great Honor to do so on behalf of the Republican Party, which has done so much to bring our Country back from the Edge of Oblivion,” he wrote on Truth Social.
He cited his belief in the Republican party, but also the riots that have swept through France, as his reasons behind the spend. A reminder, Trump has repeated baseless claims that the demonstrations, which have descended into chaos and seen thousands arrested, are the result of mass migration.
Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932 – does Adam Hamilton have the courage, brain and heart to cause an extraordinary upset?
Just two years after Donald Trump won Kansas by 16 points in his fight to regain the White House, Republicans in the state are scrambling to retain their dominance. The battle for one of its two seats in the US Senate is too close to call, setting the stage for a potentially extraordinary upset.
Some recent polls even put Democrat Adam Hamilton on course for a historic victory. Kansans have not sent a representative of the party to the US Senate since 1932.
On the campaign trail, Hamilton regularly points to one of his state’s most famous residents: Dorothy from Wizard of Oz. Recalling a visit he made to Liberal, Kansas, and its Oz museum, he asks the audience to recall what Dorothy’s companions on her journey need. The lion needed courage, the scarecrow a brain and the tin man a heart.
Washington needs more of all three, he says, and he can deliver it. He decided to run for office after seeing the Trump administration act in ways that were “not good or kind or compassionate or humble”, Hamilton – in the energetic cadence of the pastor he is – told a crowd of business leaders in Topeka on Friday. He was waiting for Roger Marshall, the state’s Republican incumbent senator, to stand up for his state and its people.
“I would have arguments with Roger Marshall in the shower. He was not in the shower with me,” Hamilton joked. “And I would just say, Roger, please stand up for your people. You were not hired to be a spokesperson for the White House. You were hired to fight for your people.”
Hamilton’s role as senior pastor of the country’s largest United Methodist congregation comes with name recognition and speaking skills. But Marshall’s liabilities as his opponent – namely, the fact he sued hundreds of his patients for unpaid bills, resulting in the arrests of dozens of them – have contributed greatly to Hamilton’s prospects of flipping the seat.
Electorally, he’s trying to win over independents and Republicans, calling himself an independent-minded Democrat. It would be valuable, he told the business leaders last week, for Kansas to have a Democrat like him and a Republican in Jerry Moran representing them in the US Senate – working both sides of the aisle.
Mike Bloomberg is donating $80m to Democrats ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
Speaking to the New York Times on Tuesday, Bloomberg’s advisor Howard Wolfson said: “He believes in participation in our democracy. And obviously the scale of his participation, given his resources and his means, is greater than other people’s financially. But other people are participating in different ways.”
“He is of the view that resources matter in campaigns,” Wolfson said, adding that Bloomberg “expects a result.”
The outlet reports that the former New York City major, now 84-years old, is focused on securing a Democratic majority in the House of Representatives, with at least $50m of his doantion to be spent on House races.
In response to Bloomberg’s donation, House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries said: “Mayor Bloomberg played an incredibly instrumental role in the decisive midterm election in 2018. The extraordinary support from Mayor Bloomberg will once again help Democrats flip the House,” the outlet reports.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Fugitive businessman taken into US custody in Venezuela bribery case
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A businessman wanted for years in the US for allegedly paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts in Venezuela has been taken into custody.
Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro. The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the state department had been offering a reward of up to $10m for information leading to his arrest.
Pulido, 62, was taken into US custody after an investigation led by the DEA, FBI and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agencies, American officials said on Sunday.
It was unclear how Pulido ended up in US custody. He was scheduled to make his initial court appearance on Tuesday in Miami.
“His alleged actions show a blatant disregard to the Venezuelan people by corrupting government programs intended to provide critical food, medicine, and housing for personal enrichment and exploiting the American financial system to do it,” the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, wrote in a social media post Sunday.
“No amount of time or distance will stop” the justice department “from working with our federal law enforcement and international partners to pursue these criminals and bring them to justice in an American courtroom,” he wrote.
Venezuelan authorities have so far been silent about the arrest, reflecting the challenge that Venezuela’s acting president Delcy Rodríguez faces in appeasing elements of the ruling coalition that want her to resist attempts by the Trump administration to round up scores of Venezuelan insiders wanted by the US, sometimes for years, for serious crimes ranging from corruption to drug trafficking.
The Colombian-born Pulido was arrested in Venezuela in 2023 as part of a sprawling crackdown on corruption inside state-run oil company PDVSA that was led by Rodríguez while she was serving as Maduro’s vice-president. She took over as Venezuela’s acting president following the US military’s ouster of Maduro in January.
Prosecutors allege that Pulido, together with Saab, created a network of offshore shell companies to funnel bribes to top Maduro allies in exchange for more than $2bn in contracts to import food, medicine and low-cost housing at a time of widespread hardship in the South American country.
Prior to these alleged offenses, Pulido had a prolific history of drug trafficking, including a 1997 conviction in Italy under the alias of German Enrique Rubio, the US attorney’s office for the southern district of Florida said in a statement.
Saab, who also hails from Colombia, was deported to the US by Rodríguez in May. In September, he pleaded guilty in a related bribery case, agreeing to cooperate against Maduro and other individuals and forfeit $195m in criminal proceeds from the corruption scheme.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Andreas Malm condemns UK travel ban as ‘drift into authoritarianism’
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Swedish climate academic Andreas Malm has condemned a travel ban imposed on him by the UK government as a “drift into authoritarianism” amid criticism of the move.
Malm, the author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline, said he had been “kept in the dark” by the UK’s immigration authorities over the reasons for his electronic travel authorisation (ETA) being revoked.
He said he had only been told that his presence in the UK was “not considered to be conducive to the public good”, as the Guardian revealed.
Speaking to Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday, he speculated that the only plausible rationale for the ban was his advertised appearance at a conference next Wednesday alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed group Palestine Action.
He said: “I cannot see any other explanation than the scheduled appearance of me on stage for a panel on Wednesday evening in London, together with Huda Ammori. That … makes me somehow a terrorist or associated with terrorism, and therefore barred from travelling to the UK. That’s pretty scandalous.”
He added: “What I am going through here is just a very small part of a major trend: this drift into authoritarianism that is targeting the Palestine movement, the climate movement, and others who oppose the destructive forces that are in control of this world. And that’s a very sad thing.”
Malm confirmed to the Guardian that he would speak via video link at the event organised by Tribune magazine.
In his BBC interview, he denied supporting or helping to finance Palestine Action. But Malm, who has long campaigned for Palestinian rights, added: “You might be able to guess my opinions and sympathies.”
The Home Office said it could not discuss individual cases. However, a source said: “Decisions to refuse or cancel an ETA on the grounds that presence in the UK may not be conducive to public good are based solely on an assessment of the potential risk an individual may pose to UK society.”
Malm said: “I don’t have any concrete evidence for what this is all about. I’m left in the dark. I have asked for clarification, explanation. I haven’t received any.”
Malm was challenged on Today over whether his description of the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023 as an “act of liberation” could be the reason for the ban.
He replied: “It could be. But my views about what happened on 7 October and in Palestine have been in the public realm for a long time. I was most recently in the UK in May.”
Malm added: “I’ve done nothing in public that is associated with Palestine Action. I have not publicly supported them or promoted them in any way.”
Malm said he was invited to speak alongside Ammori to discuss the war in Iran.
“So, what they’re preventing here is for us to have a discussion about the drivers of the imperial aggression in the Middle East,” he said.
“The only link to Palestine Action is her [Ammori] as a person. If you continue with these guilt-by-association links, then presumably if I am a threat to the public good in the UK by dint of talking to her, then someone who talks to me presumably is also a threat to the public good. Where does that end?”
The travel ban has been widely criticised. The author Sally Rooney said it was a “sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm”.
In a post on X, the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said: “This all feels very much Starmer’s Labour government 2.0. An extraordinary attack on free speech from Andy Burnham.”
The Labour MP Clive Lewis, who last year offered to stand down from his Norwich South seat to allow Andy Burnham the chance to return to parliament, said: “When any government starts barring academics for their political views, alarm bells should be ringing.
“If ministers have evidence Andreas Malm is dangerous, produce it. Otherwise, this looks like political censorship dressed up as public safety. That’s a dangerous road for any democracy.”
Ammori said in a post on X: “Banning academic and author Andreas Malm from entering Britain to stop him from speaking alongside myself, a Palestine Action co-founder, is another disgusting attack on free speech as a result of the draconian ban. The ban must be overturned.”
Neal Lawson, the director of the thinktank Compass, tweeted: “This makes me ashamed to be British and ashamed of an @UKLabour government that enacts illiberal attempts to stifle legitimate voices.”
The former shadow chancellor John McDonnell wrote: “You would have thought there was someone in government to appreciate the irony of effectively censoring someone who wanted to come here to discuss censorship. Home Office policy-making has degenerated into dangerous farce.”
How to Blow Up a Pipeline, which inspired a film of the same name, argues that sabotage and destroying property are morally and strategically justified forms of activism.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Tap water no longer drinkable in Norwegian town as climate-related thawing releases heavy metals
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Residents of a remote town in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost.
Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard, gets its main drinking water supply from a 1.5 mile-long (2.5km) dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond”. Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond.
Longyearbyen, 800 miles from the north pole, is warming at between five and seven times the world’s average rate, with autumn temperatures rising at up to 4C a decade.
Heavy metal contamination of the water supply is likely to be linked to two factors, researchers say: the thawing of permafrost – rock-hard ground that remains frozen all year apart from a so-called “active layer” that thaws in summer – and the geology of the former mining town.
“The combination of the thawing permafrost and the shale bedrock, which contains a mineral called pyrite, or fool’s gold, is causing contamination of its water supply,” said Marjolaine Verret, a permafrost expert and associate professor in Arctic geology at the University Centre in Svalbard.
When pyrite came into contact with water and oxygen, it oxidised and generated acidity, she explained. “The acid produced can now leach heavy metals from these rocks into the waterways. The issue we’ve been having here in Longyearbyen is manganese, but other contaminants can be leached out from the rocks.”
The municipality, Longyearbyen lokalstyre, first alerted its 2,600 residents after manganese levels in the water supply were found to be 25 times higher than the 50 micrograms per litre recommended by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, in September last year. The mayor of Longyearbyen, Terje Aunevik, said that while drinking water quality had never been good, due to sediment, the manganese levels had “gone ballistic”.
Prolonged exposure to high levels of manganese can cause neurological problems, particularly in children and infants.
Emergency, temporary measures were rolled out, including the installation of a central tank of free purified water, filtered by the local brewery, for residents to refill containers at the local supermarket, and an investigation was launched.
Manganese levels have since dropped, but earlier this year sulphate and nickel levels were found to exceed recommended drinking water limits. As a result, the ban remains in place.
Aunevik said that while manganese levels were “not dangerous”, government guidelines had to be followed. The drinking water crisis had created a lot of “noise”, he admitted, with some residents angry at the inconvenience.
The mayor, who has commissioned an investigation into water quality, said a “completely new water mains supply” may be needed. Potential solutions being considered were installing a filtration system to Isdammen and having a desalination plant as a backup, or the other way around. Either way was “extremely expensive” and, due to the extreme temperatures of Svalbard, with water temperatures often below zero, would include technical challenges, Aunevik said.
“In Norway, where we have always taken for granted that we can drink the water from the tap, it is challenging to start thinking that we need to carry our water like we do now. Other small communities should be precautious and start thinking of what to do if it happens to their sources.”
Verret and other scientists have warned that the contamination of water sources in Longyearbyen could be a foretaste of what is to come for Arctic communities.
“These ingredients [bedrock rich in pyrite and heavy metals] and thawing permafrost are present in other parts of the Arctic so this could be a first example of how climate change can impact freshwater, for example in northern Canada and Alaska,” Verret said.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump says government to ‘terminate’ Biden-era methane emissions rules
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Donald Trump announced his administration is “terminating” Biden-era regulations holding oil and gas companies accountable for large leaks of planet-warming methane during a rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday evening.
Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas that the change would save consumers and energy producers $45bn and unlock 210 million barrels of oil – equivalent to about 10 days of US petroleum consumption. “Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators.
The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices stemming from the US war in Iran.
In a press release, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator, Lee Zeldin, praised what he called Trump’s move “to end the war on oil and natural gas” by revising oil and natural gas regulations under the Clean Air Act.
According to the EPA, the proposal is expected to save $45bn in costs to consumers and businesses, including small businesses operating marginal wells, and produce an estimated 210m additional barrels of oil and 1.41tn cubic ft of natural gas.
Although some oil and gas executives spoke publicly in favor of the landmark methane rule, industry trade groups and corporations worked behind the scenes to gut the methane regulations, according to trade association materials and records obtained via the Freedom of Information Act by Fieldnotes, an oil and gas watchdog organization.
The 2024 methane rule required oil and gas operators to eliminate and minimize leaking, flaring and venting of methane and of volatile organic compounds, which are harmful to human health.
It was the first time the federal government had set nationwide requirements to limit methane emissions from existing oil and gas facilities. An earlier rule finalized under the Obama administration in 2016 applied to new and modified sources. Under the rule’s super emitter program, companies had to investigate major leaks near oil and gas facilities detected by third parties using EPA-approved remote sensing technology.
In March 2025, EPA administrator Lee Zeldin announced that the agency was reconsidering the Biden-Harris regulations “to ensure that they do not prevent America from unleashing energy dominance and continuing our trajectory as a leader in clean energy and emissions reductions”.
Last year, the US emitted more methane from its oil and gas sector than any other country in the world. Methane is responsible for at least a quarter of today’s warming.
Julia Kane, a researcher for Fieldnotes, said the Trump Environmental Protection Agency was giving oil and gas corporations exactly what they want. “The oil and gas industry says it’s a ‘good-faith’ partner eager to help craft regulations, but time and time again it’s worked behind the scenes to delay and weaken them,” she said.
Records obtained by Fieldnotes, including calendar events, presentation slides and meeting request forms, show that industry groups and companies met with the EPA to discuss methane regulations at least 38 times during the current administration’s first year.
“I do think it’s just an extraordinary level of access,” Kane said, adding that industry groups themselves were pleasantly surprised by their access under Trump. For example, during a conference call with industry representatives last year, Independent Petroleum Association of America executive Lee Fuller described a discussion with EPA staff, saying: “It was one of the more fascinating meetings that we’ve ever had, just because they were suddenly willing to talk to us. And they were also suddenly willing to talk about things that we’ve been trying to get them to do for years, and they’ve never even let it come on to the radar screen.”
At a Trump rally in Corpus Christi earlier today, Trump shouted out Harold Hamm, saying the founder of Continental Resources was in the audience. In April, Continental Resources wrote a letter to the EPA pushing back against measures in the methane rule that prohibit routine flaring of associated gas.
Since the EPA announced it would no longer enforce oil and gas regulations in March 2025, oil and gas operators have leaked, vented or flared $7bn worth of natural gas, according to calculations by the Environmental Defense Fund.
Rosalie Winn, senior director and lead counsel at the Environmental Defense Fund, said the Trump administration was seeking to curtail the federal government’s ability to do anything to address climate pollution across all of the largest sectors responsible for emissions.
“What this administration is doing is enabling the worst polluters in the industry to continue to make ever more money off the back of American consumers while they’re wasting energy,” she said.
Robert Mackey contributed reporting

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Disquiet grows in Albanese’s back yard as Grayndler artists unite against ‘insane’ AI proposal
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The prime minister is facing growing discontent within his own electorate as creatives push back against the federal government’s proposal to allow AI companies to scrape everything Australians create online.
Anthony Albanese’s seat of Grayndler in Sydney’s inner west is home to more than 3,000 cultural and creative businesses, and 10% of its workers are employed in cultural and creative fields – compared with 4.2% nationally.
He has held it on a safe margin for three decades, and has spoken of its high representation of live music, theatre and artist spaces with pride.
But now, as Labor considers giving AI companies access to Australian creatives’ works by default as it pursues a compromise with US tech giants, locals are reacting with dismay.
Labor is mulling over the copyright changes in a suite of reforms surrounding AI, including datacentres, energy and the economy. While Albanese has promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train their models using Australian material.
Some AI companies have said making licensing agreements under existing copyright law would be too difficult, while Anthropic has suggested an “opt-out” model which would allow it to scrape content unless a rights holder objected, prompting warnings from Coalition senators and the recording industry that this could amount to an acquisition of property by the government.
The federal government’s draft laws are expected by the end of the year, with consideration in parliament due in 2027.
Pete Strong is a screenprinter and Greens councillor for Bayside. His business is based in Grayndler, with his solar-powered wheelie bin sound systems a fixture around the inner west.
He said AI could be “good for humanity” but is now an “extraction industry mining for profit for the few”.
“I’m completely against [the federal government’s proposal],” he said.
“There’s obviously an AI gold rush at the moment, it’s the wild west and we really need to push back. It’s hard enough being a starving artist these days without having all your work taken and used in these nefarious ways.”
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
This year Strong curated a show called “overthrow the algorithm”. He has also been a vocal critic of a proposed datacentre at Cooks Cove.
“I’ve seen a backlash [to the government] already,” he said. “It started with the datacentre uprising.”
Labor’s proposals were leaked in September as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, met Labor ministers and warned that Australia’s copyright laws were preventing the company from training models locally.
For the inner west designer and artist Lu Campbell-Smith, AI has been useful in her practice. But she said having to opt out was “outrageous”.
“It just really pinpoints how Australia’s [a] test market and they’re happy for us to just be a little resource to be exploited,” she said.
“Why would anyone want to make anything and post anything online if … you’re creating free content for an AI machine?”
Grayndler has always been an ultra-safe Labor seat. Albanese’s face as a much younger man is plastered on to cans of Albo Pale Ale at Willie the Boatman brewery in St Peters. For the past few elections, he has won on first preferences alone.
But at the next federal election, he will be challenged by 28-year-old Hannah Ferguson, the co-founder of Cheek Media, who will run as an independent.
No sitting member has lost their seat from such a margin at a federal election. Were it not for the longstanding popularity of Albanese, Grayndler would have been a prime target for the Greens and progressive independents.
Now, Ferguson is betting that his popularity is waning. And polling indicates the same. Guardian Australia’s latest Essential poll shows Albanese’s disapproval rating at 56%, the equal highest since he took office.
At Tortuga Studios and the aerie, one of the longest-running artist-led spaces in Sydney which operates out of an old brick factory in St Peters, the frustration is palpable.
H Morgan-Harris, an author, curator and director of the space, said there was a risk the Australian creative ecosystem could be “decimated”.
“This whole conversation always comes back to money,” she said, adding: “The artistic ecosystem is the bedrock of human interaction and human connection. And you risk our societal value by threatening it.”
Morgan-Harris’s copywriting industry has already been “heavily impacted” by AI, she said. Asked what her response was to the federal government’s latest proposal, she said it wasn’t “one you can print”.
“I just feel like artists are the first to be thrown under the bus,” she said.
“I think a lot of people were really excited when [Albanese] got into government, but there’s a yawning chasm in terms of the recognition, consideration and protection of the value of this sector. This honestly feels like the end of times to a lot of us.”
Jason Zoidberg, a co-founder of Monster Mouse Studios in Marrickville, said the AI industry had already “without consequence” stolen the “collective labour” uploaded by artists. He said it was “utterly crazy” that the government was considering giving companies the green light to do so.
“It just feels insane that they’re like, ‘Yeah, please come and we want to invest in you,’ when we’ve seen all these horrible things that they’re doing,” he said.
If there is a flipside, Zoidberg said, he is witnessing a surge in interest in traditional, hands-on art forms.
“There’s a backlash in the inner west against social media and AI,” Zoidberg said. “So our workshops are actually getting more participants. But it is also just a niche, a little inner west bubble.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Democratic lawmakers demand ICE data on detainee miscarriages
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
US lawmakers are urgently demanding that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) disclose how many pregnant immigrants have experienced miscarriages, stillbirths and pregnancy-related hospitalizations while in the its custody, after the agency admitted it lost count last year.
US representatives sent the request following a recent Guardian investigation revealing that the Trump administration is detaining a record number of pregnant women and teens, and at the same has lost track of how many suffered miscarriages.
In a letter sent this month to ICE’s acting director, David Venturella, Democratic representatives Brittany Pettersen, Joyce Beatty and Robin Kelly also asked the immigration enforcement agency to explain what – if any – steps have been taken to recover any missing data about these cases.
Government documents obtained by the Guardian found that ICE had placed more pregnant immigrants in detention last fall and winter than at any time over the previous year. The agency recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration, the documents found, but the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.
Detained pregnant women said that they were struggling to access routine and emergency medical care. Medical experts told the Guardian that lapses in care both during pregnancy and during and after miscarriage could escalate treatable conditions into life-threatening emergencies.
In their letter, the representatives also cite a 2021 directive instructing ICE to wholly avoid detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants “unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist” – and ask the agency to clarify on what grounds it is detaining pregnant immigrants. The directive also requires ICE to closely monitor and document the health of all pregnant people in its custody, and continuously evaluate whether it is medically advisable to keep them detained.
“ICE’s inability to follow agency directives, provide adequate medical care and maintain accurate records of pregnancy-related medical outcomes is unacceptable,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter, which was cosigned by 64 other representatives.
In an interview, Pettersen said it was “deeply concerning” that ICE had failed to account for a full year of pregnancy outcomes. “I’m just devastated for the people who have gone through this, who’ve lost pregnancies unnecessarily, who have been left without the medical care that they need after miscarrying,” she said. “It’s hard to imagine how we are ever going to right these wrongs.”
In internal agency documents, ICE said it had no data on miscarriages because the agency changed medical billing providers in October. The agency’s medical claims processing has been delayed for months. Immigration attorneys and former government officials told said it was odd, but plausible, that ICE was keeping track of miscarriages solely via its medical billing provider.
In response to follow-up questions about its tracking practices after 3 October 2025, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, first said that the agency was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports. But later, the spokesperson confirmed what was in the ICE internal documents – the agency does not have data on miscarriages between October 2025 through June 2026.
The DHS did not confirm to the Guardian whether it had received the letter from Congress members. “Claims that any pregnant detainees are receiving subprime care are FALSE,” an agency spokesperson said.
In their letter, lawmakers asked ICE’s acting director to detail when “ICE leadership first became aware of concerns regarding miscarriage reporting and deficiencies in agency tracking systems”. They gave the agency until 6 November to respond.
Prior to the Guardian’s reporting, the agency had never acknowledged that it had lost count of miscarriages – not even when US senators asked the agency for the data.
The Guardian filed a Freedom of Information Act request and then filed suit in collaboration with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press to obtain data on the number of pregnant people in ICE detention, and the health outcomes for this population.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Andy Burnham says he has emergency stockpile of beans, soup and Twiglets
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham has said he has stockpiles of beans, soup and Twiglets in case of a civil emergency, as he said a new government campaign was not a reason for panic buying.
The prime minister was questioned on his domestic supply situation after the Be Ready campaign advised households to have enough bottled water and long-life food to keep going in case of an emergency, such as one caused by a weather event or a cyber-attack.
Asked on BBC Radio 5 Live whether, like Angela Rayner, he would make sure his emergency supplies included a bottle of sauvignon blanc, Burnham said: “I’m not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you’re in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you’ve done the hard work.
“I’ll stick to the basics, I think. I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup. I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets. I’m not sure I can get by for too long without those.”
The campaign says people should ensure they have at least three days of supplies, including water, in case of an emergency, which is similar to advice given to citizens in some other European countries.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the nation also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.
The advice was general and longer-term, Burnham told 5 Live, rather than urgent. “It’s not about panicking, is it? It’s just about being prepared and having a sensible amount of supplies in the home … These events, sadly, in the world that we’re in are becoming more likely, and therefore it’s just sensible to be prepared.”
Asked about a message from a listener who was worried about supplies running low as people tried to stock up, Burnham said: “It’s not about panic buying. I understand what your listener is saying there, but it’s about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation.”
Speaking earlier to the BBC, the Treasury minister James Murray admitted to being less prepared. He said: “I’ve got quite a lot of coffee in my house … it’s for individual people to take choices. I’m not going to say: ‘Here’s a government shopping list.’” He added: “I’m not going to pretend I’ve followed all that advice myself yet.”
He said the advice was in part a matter of bringing the UK into line with other countries. He told BBC Breakfast: “If you look at, say, Ireland or other countries in Europe like France and Netherlands, they’ve had this system for quite a long time, the idea of having a bit of stuff at home to protect yourselves in case something goes wrong.
“So it’s quite normal in other countries. I think it’s a bit more interesting here because we haven’t really talked about it as a country in recent years.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Middle East peace held back by US insistence that Iran is a threat, Oman’s foreign minister says
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Middle East’s ability to solve its problems has been held back by America’s 50-year insistence that the Gulf states should view Iran as a security threat, Oman’s foreign minister said on Monday in a significant speech designed to break the deadlock over the region’s future.
Badr Albusaidi called for a non-aggression security pact involving all six Gulf states as well as Iran and Iraq. The US would in future no longer be the primary provider of security, he said.
He was speaking on the day high-level defence and intelligence officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent a renewed outbreak of fighting between the US and Iran.
Tehran said the meeting also explored future security arrangements in the region. The high stakes were underlined by the sight of the Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, in Tehran weeks after Iran had struck Saudi infrastructure and as Iran-backed Houthis continue to send missiles towards Riyadh.
Albusaidi is the first Gulf leader to break ranks so explicitly by calling for the mainly Sunni Gulf states to form a security alliance with Iran, a long-term aspiration of Tehran’s.
Speaking at Girton College, Cambridge, he said the talks might be difficult and the proposal appeared counterintuitive, but “issues such as the strait of Hormuz have become impossible to resolve because external powers continue to define the terms of engagement, while regional powers are unable to take collective responsibility for making their own security arrangements and reach a consensus on them”.
He added: “What holds us back is that issues which ought to be handled at a regional level by the states of the Gulf themselves, are made more complex, more intractable and sometimes simply impossible to resolve because the region’s security arrangements are insufficiently developed.
“And they are insufficiently developed because they have relied for too long on the involvement of external powers.”
He said that for half a century Iran “had been systematically excluded from playing any meaningful role in the security arrangements of the region”. This had led to “profoundly negative consequences, not just for Iran, but for the region as a whole”, including the imposition of priorities on the region by external powers such as “the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf”.
He added: “Perhaps the most damaging of the priorities imposed on the region from the outside has been the requirement that Iran be excluded. Not just excluded. Worse. Positioned as the threat against which regional security had to be organised.”
Oman is on the southern side of the strait of Hormuz, with Iran on the northern shores. The two countries have reached a temporary agreement on how shipping traffic should be managed in the strait, but the plan is on hold until the US and Iran lift their respective blockades of the waterway.
Albusaidi also indirectly challenged Donald Trump’s case for a further attack on Iran by saying he believed the previous round of talks between the US and Iran in February, which Oman mediated, were “making significant progress, and that an agreement was within reach. We still stand by that judgment today.”
The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role. The US-Iran conflict may have reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.
No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attacks on Iran last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.
The meeting in Tehran was taking place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.
Israeli media reports claimed that the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday.
Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that the US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity.
The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners increasingly say Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb.
A pact that is likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: He promised fresh hope and delivered doom, but Dr Death’s budget succeeds in doing no harm | John Crace
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
It was as if John Healey was taking the Hippocratic oath. First do no harm. For your first budget, this may be no bad thing: we can all think of plenty of chancellors who have done untold damage. Take a bow George Osborne. It might just have been better if the doctor that Healey had chosen to impersonate was not Dr Death.
John can’t help looking like the last man you would want to stop by your hospital bed. Not everyone can have a naturally sunny disposition. His face seems to be carved out of despair. But it would be a big help if, when called upon to make his most important speech of the year, he didn’t reinforce the impression when he opened his mouth. A one-way journey to the slough of despond.
“I’m very sorry to let you know, Mr Crace,” he would say with Voldemort delight. “But your cancer is now terminal. You have months to live.” And just when you are trying to process what he’s said and are preparing to say your goodbyes, he would let you know he had made a mistake. You only had weeks to live after all. He would then smile wanly, pat you on the shoulder before moving on to kill off his next patient. You wouldn’t be seeing him again.
Healey began with a few cheery words. Cheery by his standards, that is. This was a budget for working people. People often talked about global headwinds. John was here to let us know that these headwinds were more like a storm. Make that a hurricane. One we’d all be lucky to come out of alive. The wars in Iran and Ukraine, the rising cost of energy. The whole world was basically screwed. He knew the government had suggested we all stockpile food and water ahead of the apocalypse, but frankly we might as well not bother. Why prolong the agony?
“Fresh hope for Britain’s future,” he said. The word hope died on his lips. Only Healey can send you into a vortex of existential futility with an attempt at optimism. Even the normally upbeat Andy Burnham who was sitting next to him looked lost in his own sense of pointlessness. Not even a glimmer of a smile. The main reason he had appointed Healey was because he could be relied on to do his bidding. To deliver the kind of budget Andy had in mind. Ed Miliband was far too much his own man. But Burnham hadn’t factored in the aura of gloom.
The one consolation was that even John couldn’t be as depressing as Rachel Reeves. But Healey was working on it. Give him time. Most budget statements try to tell a story. To create a coherent narrative of the state of the economy, the government’s plans to stimulate growth and fix the problems they inherited. Even when the problems the chancellor is inheriting are the ones they created. But Healey was going to try a different approach. Just a series of unstructured, random spending announcements. Dr Death’s Seven Last Words on the Cross.
Most budget speeches also contain the odd joke. Or what passes for a gag in the minds of MPs. None of them are going to get gigs at the Edinburgh fringe. But on the few occasions that the mirror cracked and Healey’s mouth tried to form a rictus grin, his words fell flat. Turns out that not everyone finds telling people they have nothing to live for quite as funny as John. Worse still, he is a man with no sense of timing. He makes Ed Balls sound like a comedy giant.
There was the obligatory reference to Liz Truss’s mini-budget, and the hand that the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, played in it. That should have been fertile comic ground as it has the benefit of being true. Four years on, we are all still suffering PTSD. Everyone apart from the Trusster, who believes the real problem was that she was forced to reverse £70bn of unfunded tax cuts. But Healey couldn’t land the punchline. Labour backbenchers were willing him to succeed, but they still couldn’t bring themselves to laugh.
The only really funny moment was completely unintentional, when Healey said that the energy secretary had opposed Jackdaw. That was supposed to be kept an open secret, not broadcast to the world. The Tory benches couldn’t contain themselves with forced laughter. The chancellor tried to redeem the situation by ad-libbing that at least the opposition was still awake. Which was more than could be said for many Labour backbenchers.
Fresh hope and breathing space, Healey said again. It had become his only leitmotif. And, yet again, it felt like another nail in the coffin. The world was in turmoil, the country bouncing from crisis to crisis and the chancellor was doing not very much. Or rather he was doing a lot – he announced 98 different measures – but none of them amounted to a lot. Not that anyone was going to complain about getting £100 off their council tax or not having to queue up at the post office for your Amazon returns. These things do make a difference.
It was just that we were waiting for the big reveal. The major surprise. But time passed. And passed. And none came. There was a promise to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, but no details of how. It was the miserabilist’s dream. Growth baked in at less than 2%, living standards predicted to fall.
A sense of drift. But maybe it was all deliberate. A country put on palliative care because it wouldn’t survive extreme surgery. Healey had said he had called an early budget because it was time to inject some urgency into the public finances. But many of the really big decisions had been kicked into the long grass. He had said the budget was to give the country some breathing space. It felt as if the government were the ones who needed the breathing space.
Kemi Badenoch’s response was similarly underwhelming. Then she had rather shot herself in the foot by admitting that the country had been paralysed and miserable under the Tories. She even found herself agreeing with some of Healey’s measures but her overall assessment – Was that it? – was echoed by many Labour MPs. Not that Kemi had any answers herself. None to be taken seriously, at least. At his own press conference, a disinhibited Nigel Farage had just sounded mad. There is no appetite for the Tories or Reform. So a breathing space it is.
-

Will Healey’s budget tackle the cost of living? – podcast
John Healey has delivered a ‘steady as she goes’ budget, with help for the cost of living a big theme. The chancellor promised a £100 energy payment for some households, extended the VAT suspension on electricity bills to next July and confirmed the scrapping of gas standing charges.
But after months of the same old message of ‘hope in difficult times’, and many of the big decisions on tax and spending delayed until next year, what should we take away from today?

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Minister says Mahmood’s migration policy will ‘prolong integration’
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, appears to have criticised Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy in a post on her constituency website, in which she suggested she had concerns that a longer settlement process could affect integration.
Fahnbulleh has since removed the critique, which appeared in a write-up of a community meeting in Peckham, her south London constituency, in September, saying it was not a true representation of her views.
In the original write-up of her comments at the town hall meeting, first highlighted by the Telegraph, Fahnbulleh was reported to have said: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.” Her office said the remarks had been paraphrased, and would be rewritten to reflect a more accurate description of what she had told residents.
The government has proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain from five years to 10, though it is likely to make concessions for some professions, including care workers.
The changes will also mean the pathway to permanent settlement for refugees is extended to up to 20 years, with reviews every 30 months. The government is yet to publish its long-anticipated final response to a consultation on the proposals – though the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he is committed to the bulk of the changes.
Tensions in the cabinet have already surfaced over the proposals. Last month the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said in an interview that the proposed changes – if left unamended – would unfairly penalise care staff who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”.
Fahnbulleh came to the UK as a child after fleeing the civil war in Liberia. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast last month, she admitted her family would have found Mahmood’s changes “tough”.
“I represent a constituency which is hugely diverse, where we’ve got first, second, third-generation immigrants, and how we navigate this landscape has been tough,” she added.
With Mahmood believed to be considering changing her plans, Fahnbulleh said she wanted the government to recognise migrants’ contributions.
“I think we ultimately need to get to an immigration system that has control … but actually then recognises the contribution that people have made. And if you’re in this country and you’re working – I say this as a refugee – and you’re doing your bit, and you’re part of your community, you’re working in our health service, then actually this should be a country that welcomes you,” she said.
“I wouldn’t be here if that wasn’t the way that we structured our immigration system. It has always been the case that this country is a welcoming country, and I’m sure it will continue to be that way.”
In her address to her Peckham constituents, Fahnbulleh said the debate had become “increasingly depressing and toxic”. She said there needed to be “a more compassionate immigration system. The asylum process is broken and needs reform. Ultimately, I want to see a system based on control and compassion, with a much stronger focus on integration.”
She continued: “Peckham is a good example of what can happen when communities are built deliberately, and people are given the opportunity to integrate and participate. If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.
“We need to raise the level of the debate, challenge divisive political rhetoric and make the case for communities like the one we have in Peckham. That means talking about immigration with care, control and compassion.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Andy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave trade
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham has gone further than any previous prime minister towards offering a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, in a Guardian article ahead of a Commonwealth leaders’ summit where the subject is expected to dominate.
As he prepares to fly to the Caribbean next week, the prime minister said he was open to calls for an official apology on behalf of the state and offered formal talks to those affected, including individual countries and campaign groups at home and abroad.
Burnham wrote: “The Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”
While any formal statement will depend on that dialogue, Burnham gave what amounted to a personal apology, saying he wanted to share his “sorrow and regret” for the pain and suffering of millions of people, and to recognise the way the slave trade still shapes the world now.
However, he rejected demands from Caribbean countries and campaigners for the UK to pay financial reparations for its role in the slave trade, maintaining the position of successive governments that British people today could not be held liable for the past.
He wrote that reparations were not the “right answer”, adding: “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, which happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”
Instead, Burnham said he would launch a new drive to restructure debt for the poorest Commonwealth countries – led by former prime minister Gordon Brown and expected to eventually include organisations such as the IMF – helping them repay debt over a longer period and with better interest rates.
Debt servicing costs for the poorest and most vulnerable Commonwealth countries are at their highest in more than 25 years, he added, with more than 40% of those spending more on interest repayments than on health.
Burnham’s intervention follows years of pressure from Caribbean states, backed by some African countries, for European nations including the UK, France and Spain to offer reparations – including monetary compensation, a full formal apology, support for health and education and debt cancellation.
As recently as last week, the Commonwealth secretary general, Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey, said a formal apology for slavery from King Charles, who will attend the heads of government summit, “wouldn’t hurt” and the “time has come” for a serious conversation on reparations.
Writing for the Guardian, Burnham said: “The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths.
“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.”
He added: “We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.”
Burnham’s intervention received a cautious welcome from leading figures in the Caribbean. Dorbrene O’Marde, the chair of the Antigua and Barbuda reparations support commission, said his organisation welcomed the statement as “a movement in the correct direction in the interest of reparatory justice and humanity generally”.
But, he added: “We reject the decision that financial reparations will not be on the table.”
Ralph Gonsalves, former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the Repair campaign, told the Guardian that an apology was the first point in the Caribbean community’s 10-point reparations plan but “though necessary, is insufficient”.
He added: “We are pleased to hear that [the UK] comes into a conversation. But it can’t be a conversation about nothing. It has to be a conversation about something. If they are not going to entertain reparations, what is the conversation about? Nothing.”
Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the Caricom reparations commission, said he believed Burnham “is carrying the broad middle of British opinion on this matter”.
He said the call for financial reparations need not be a stumbling block to progress: “There are much broader issues that can occupy that dialogue. So you don’t know what you will emerge out until you have a conversation of decency.
“I think the prime minister will find that Caribbean leaders are very reasonable people on the matter of developing a new Anglo-Caribbean bond … words are important, but the spirit of collaboration is more important.”
Caribbean leaders have been reacting to Bunham’s announcement. In a statement, the prime minister of Barbados, Mia Mottley
thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground” but said she and the UK government “are not yet on the same page on every element”.
“On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully. Honest disagreement on some questions should not hold back progress on the many others where we can readily agree.
“An apology, a commitment to eradicate a mindset that is anchored in Afrophobia and against all things “black”, investment in health and education, development partnership that fights systemic poverty and institutionalised inequality, and fairer terms on debt for vulnerable states, as called for by the Bridgetown Initiative, are a few of the areas where we believe understanding can be reached and settled,” her statement said.
“I thank prime minister Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, for breaking new ground and recognising that this is the right thing, and the moral thing, to do by ensuring that we move to the next stage of engagement on this difficult and emotional issue,” it added.
Antigua and Barbuda’s prime minister Gaston Browne, who is hosting this year’s CHOGM, welcomed particularly Burnham’s offer to assist with debt restructuring and a transition to renewable enegry.
“The Caribbean’s longstanding position on reparatory justice remains unchanged. Differences over financial compensation should be addressed through dialogue, but they need not prevent progress in areas where agreement is possible,” he said in a statement.
Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, also welcomed Burnham’s willingness to discuss a formal apology. In September, Jamaican officials lodged a landmark petition to the king seeking legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations, which will be heard by the privy council in March.
“We have always been open to having full and meaningful dialogue on this important issue. We welcome this development, coming in the wake of our legal petition which is now before the privy council,” Holness said in a statement.
Similarly, the Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, commended Burnham’s decision to agree to a dialogue and consider an apology. “The Bahamas approaches this dialogue with a clear understanding that the issue is not simply one of historical remembrance. It concerns the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress for the generations of Africans and their descendants who continue to live with its legacy,” he said.
The UK government has taken a cautious approach to the issue amid pressure from leftwing MPs to offer a formal apology and engage in reparatory justice, alongside concerns over the potential fiscal and electoral impact, with polls suggesting most voters are opposed to financial compensation.
The Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm), which King Charles will also attend, runs from Sunday 1 November until Wednesday 4 November.
At the previous Chogm summit in Samoa two years ago, Britain’s former colonies agreed “the time has come” for a dialogue about reparations – even though then-prime minister Keir Starmer said it would not be on the agenda.
Some inside the UK government had questioned whether Burnham should even attend after the reparations row dominated the 2024 gathering. But his decision to address the issue head-on is likely to be welcomed in Antigua and Barbuda.
Campaigners see the summit as the culmination of decades of advocacy from Caribbean leaders for a deeper acknowledgment of the UK’s historic responsibility for the enslavement of millions of Africans.
Advocates say the UK had been under increasing pressure to act after a UN resolution in March which described the trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity.
The UK was among the 52 countries that abstained, saying that while it recognised the gravity of the issue, it disagreed with the fundamental proposition of the text which it said risked creating a hierarchy of historical atrocities.
In June, Mottley, announced a new manifesto from Caribbean leaders asserting the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations over damage caused by hundreds of years of enslavement.
The 10-point plan argued that repair could include international debt cancellation and that climate justice and slavery reparations were “inextricably linked”.
Burnham also referred to the history of Manchester as “the cotton capital of the world” which grew in part thanks to cotton picked by enslaved people.
In 2023 the owner of the Guardian apologised for the role the newspaper’s founders had in the transatlantic slave trade, and launched the Cotton Capital series and a 10-year programme of restorative justice.
