SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on schools: the hardest questions for Lucy Powell are about priorities | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
There is a good case to be made for the increased importance of speaking skills in our new age of machines. With the UK economy’s stronger-than-expected recent performance widely linked to AI investment, it is vital that people are equipped for the kinds of in-person, public-facing jobs that are least likely to be automated. A concerning decline in children’s language development, both in the UK and internationally, has been linked to high screen use. There is a grim irony in a situation where tech companies both compete with humans for contracts and undermine our ability to talk to one other.
The Guardian has previously backed efforts to more strongly embed speaking skills, or oracy, in British schools. In a speech on Thursday, Lucy Powell promised to give them equal status to reading and writing in English (education is devolved, so her main responsibility is for England, but there are parallel initiatives in the other nations). Yet with promised updates to the national curriculum postponed, and plans for special educational needs reform causing deep anxiety to families, schools and councils, the hardest questions for the education secretary are about priorities. Following negative feedback from schools, she has also asked Ofsted to look again at its new inspection framework.
The curriculum review completed last year was deliberately cautious, reflecting the Starmer administration’s overall tone. Since then, England’s high scores in maths and science, in international tests, have shown that standards in some subjects have risen. But in English, an overly prescriptive and grammar-obsessed curriculum is putting pupils off. This is the obvious place to start with new speaking skills. The delayed curriculum revisions should set out how it is going to be done.
The energy that Ms Powell brings to the education brief is welcome. She is right to refuse to “sit still and polish the status quo”, especially as the Conservative party seeks to take credit for improvements to English schools that were a legacy of New Labour. The decline of the arts in schools must also be tackled. An improved vocational offer is arguably most urgent of all.
But there is no point denying the challenges around implementation. The government is already committed to the introduction of new maths and English qualifications, to replace demoralising GCSE resits. Reform of the special educational needs system will need to be carefully monitored. Many experts in the college sector believe that the scrapping of BTec qualifications, in favour of T-levels and V-levels, is a mistake. This too needs to be closely watched. A stronger steer from government on universities is also needed. Bridget Phillipson’s decision to unfreeze fees after eight years has only slightly eased their funding difficulties. Reform of unfair student loan terms must come sooner rather than later.
Ms Powell is not unique, among Andy Burnham’s new brooms, in facing a daunting set of challenges. Her pledge to go “further and deeper on curriculum reform” is welcome; the world is changing fast and schools need help to keep up. A strengthened emphasis on the spoken word is just one part of this. But in the coming months, she will need to make decisions about where to put her energies. There are only so many changes, on top of special educational needs reforms, that schools can be expected to cope with.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Homes across UK to get low- or no-interest loans to fund solar panels and heat pumps
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Households across the UK can now cut their energy bills by hundreds of pounds a year at no upfront cost by applying for interest-free or “low-interest” loans to fund upgrades such as heat pumps, batteries and solar panels.
The government-backed Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, could mean thousands more households are able to access low-carbon energy alternative technologies, thanks to loans ranging from £7,500 to up £35,000.
Energy suppliers including British Gas and E.On have partnered with lenders from Tandem Bank and Homeserve respectively to offer the loans directly to customers at a discounted rate compared with those offered by high street lenders.
People interested in swapping their gas boiler for an air-source or ground-source heat pump could secure loans of up to £10,000 or £35,000 respectively, while also drawing on the government’s existing scheme which offers grants of up to £9,000 a year for households installing the replacements for fossil fuel heating.
Installing a heat pump, battery and solar panels could save households up to £550 a year on their energy bills, rising by a further £300 a year with a time-of-use tariff, according to the government.
Soaring energy costs have led to record demand for low-carbon home energy upgrades over the last year, and the government believes the loan scheme means “thousands more households” will be able to cut their energy bills by fitting clean energy technology and spreading repayments over many years.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “Energy is an everyday essential that must be affordable for everyone. These government-supported loans will help families across the UK upgrade their homes with no upfront costs to make them warmer and cheaper to run.”
Chris Norbury, the chief executive of E.On UK, said that a recent trial showed that fuel-poor customers in Coventry were able to save more than £250 a year on average by combining a home battery with a time of use tariff that charges lower rates for using energy outside peak demand hours.
He said the Warm Homes Loan scheme was “an opportunity to take that further” by “removing barriers to low-carbon technologies”.
The government set out the terms of the new scheme a day before the chancellor, John Healey, delivers his first budget on Wednesday, which reportedly will include plans to scale back heat pump grants made through its boiler upgrade scheme.
The scheme is not expected to be scrapped altogether, but sources say hundreds of millions of pounds will be cut from its £2.7bn five-year budget because Treasury officials consider it a subsidy used mainly by middle-class households.
It has typically provided grants of up to £7,500 to help meet the £13,600 cost of installing a heat pump, meaning households have still required a significant outlay to make up the difference.
The Guardian understands that grants of up to £9,000 a year are likely to remain available to households that are not connected to the gas grid and are forced to rely on high-cost heating oil. These grants could be used alongside the low-interest loans to cover the full cost of a heat pump.
Other lenders taking part in the Warm Home Loans scheme include HTG Finance, Propensio, Secure Trust Bank, Selina Finance, South Manchester Credit Union, Sunsave, The Money Co-op and This Bank.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Flu cases rise on west coast earlier than usual as US health experts encourage vaccine
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Flu cases on the west coast are on the rise months earlier than normal, prompting US health experts to stress the importance of the annual vaccine.
Flu activity typically ramps up in December, hitting its peak in February. But this season has kicked into action earlier this year, with higher positive cases than normal recorded.
Several experts have credited the early seasonal start to a new mutation of the influenza A strain H1N1, which was behind the 2009 swine flu pandemic.
This strain has accounted for 242 of 300 influenza viruses reported by public health laboratories to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to date (CDC).
In California, during the past two flu seasons, influenza test positivity hovered slightly above 1% in early October. As of 10 October, that rate is 9.65%, according to data from the state’s department of health.
As of 11 October, Utah has recorded 242 influenza A cases, up from 10 cases this time last year, according to Germ Watch, an Intermountain Health database.
Parts of central Oregon have also seen an influenza A surge.
Influenza vaccines can reduce severe illness and hospitalization, according to the American Medical Association, which recommends flu shots for all people 6 months and older.
The 2026-27 flu vaccines, approved by the FDA in August, target H1N1, H3N2 – the dominant strain last flu season – and one influenza B virus.
Scott Hensley, a microbiologist at the University of Pennsylvania, said two of the three components of this year’s vaccine appear to be very well matched to circulating flu strains.
However, the H1N1 mutation might affect antibodies in younger people, and with flu season picking up steam, “it is probably a good idea to get vaccinated early”, Hensley said via email.
Promotion of flu shots has been reduced under US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has engineered an overhaul of long-standing childhood vaccine schedules.
Reuters contributed reporting

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Farage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide says
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides.
The apparent admission came in undercover footage seen by the Guardian in which Dan Jukes says that it is “priced in” for Farage to profit from politics.
The footage raises fresh questions about the party leader’s statements that the gift was solely for security purposes.
The Reform UK leader is awaiting the outcome of a parliamentary watchdog investigation into whether or not the £5m from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, should have been declared under parliamentary rules.
Farage told the Sun on 14 May: “And this [£5m] was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years.”
Now, previously unpublished footage from the undercover reporting group Verbatim, shared with the Guardian, has revealed a conversation between Jukes, a longtime close aide of Farage, and an undercover reporter.
“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said of Farage’s admission that the funds were a political reward, appearing to suggest that it was an on-air accident.
The subject of Farage’s funds arose when Jukes quipped that if a US limited liability company could not make a donation because of electoral law, perhaps the reporter posing as a donor could just make him a £5m unconditional gift instead.
After discussing if Jukes could think of any ways other than secret polling – foreign-funded polls that appeared to be orchestrated by Reform officials but which were not publicly attributed to the party – for the party to benefit from money from a US LLC, Jukes replied: “I’m happy to take a £5m personal, unconditional gift, of course.”
The undercover reporter said: “That seems like it’s [the £5m] been quite tough.”
“I’m a realist and I bat straight and it’s a little bit awkward,” Jukes said, appearing to admit that Farage was not meant to change his explanation from the £5m being intended for security costs to say it was a reward for Brexit.
“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said. “So I think now the line is it was a thank you for Brexit to pay for security so he is safe for the rest of his life.”
The undercover reporter suggested that people did not mind if Farage “makes a few bob [from politics]”.
Jukes replied: “Well it’s a bit priced in with our Nige, isn’t it, no one’s voting for him to be the pope.”
If the funds were not given unconditionally but rather as a way to circumvent donation rules, as the footage appears to suggest, it could also trigger questions about whether it was a payment for work and therefore subject to tax.
Jukes left Reform after the original Verbatim/Channel 4 investigation was aired. He had worked closely with Farage for more than a decade.
An internal Reform investigation concluded that neither Jukes nor another senior party official, James Orr, had broken laws that ban foreign donations. A police investigation is ongoing.
Harborne has previously said of the gift to Farage that it was “to support Nigel’s security not just now, but for the rest of his life”. Lawyers for the crypto-billionaire have previously said he “expected nothing in return” and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.
The timeline for the gift is disputed.
Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024.
According to financial industry sources, some of the £5m was not received until the end of May, just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP.
The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election.
Farage has given a wide variety of reasons for accepting the £5m including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit. He has refused to say how much, if any, of the £5m has been spent on security, adding it was nobody’s business what he did with the money and he could “spend it on Ferraris” if he wanted.
A spokesperson for Farage did not address several of the points put to them by the Guardian, including the claim that Farage had deviated from the press office line by admitting the £5m was a reward for Brexit.
Farage’s spokesperson said Jukes “accurately describes that the gift was for his security for the rest of his life”.
Lawyers for Jukes referred back to a previous statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals, using selective editing, who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.”
They added that Jukes denied any wrongdoing and pointed to the outcome of Reform’s internal investigation.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Cuts like a knife: Canadian rocker Bryan Adams trolls Trump with new song
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Lake Ontario, the vast body of water that straddles the US-Canada border, has gone by many names over the centuries: Lac Saint-Louis, Lacus Ontarius, Skaniadorio, Cataraqui Lake. But one thing it will never be called, says the Canadian rock star Bryan Adams, is Lake America.
In his new song Lake Ontario, Adams takes aim at the US president, Donald Trump, accusing him of “breaking the peace” between the people who live on the lake’s shores.
Trump signed an executive order in August directing US federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”, echoing his earlier, widely mocked decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico “the Gulf of America”.
The move further escalated a feud with Canada that has strained the longstanding alliance between the two countries. Trump’s decision has largely been met with derision in Canada, with some pointing out that the province of Ontario is named after the lake, not the other way around. Adams’s lyrics emphasise the roots of the name:
 The ‘lake of shining waters’ is what the Iroquois called her
It’s a First Nations name – not an executive order.
Adams’s lyrics also suggest that Trump’s naming stunt was intended to deflect from the president’s other political problems, including the war in Iran and renewed scrutiny of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
 But things weren’t going his way in Iran
So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram
But it feels like another distraction
While the Epstein files were getting traction
The song is part of what Adams described in a recent interview as a broader “love letter” to Canada: a songwriting project that began with an invitation from a film company to write about the Maritimes provinces of Canada and has since morphed into the upcoming album How’s It Goin’.
“After finishing the first song, I moved on to that one, and then moved on to another one, and then started thinking maybe I should just carry on with my theme,” he said.
As well as homages to Canadian heroes, the album also includes 51st State, released on 1 July – Canada Day – as another repudiation of Trump, in this case his efforts to annex Canada.
 You can push us to the brink
But where the open road divides
You’ll find a wall of maple
With us on the other side.
The first time he played the song in public was in the US.
“We weren’t sure how people were going to respond to it,” he said. “But we got a standing ovation every night for it. It made me think: perhaps, finally, the tide’s turning.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost amid warnings of public finance shortfall
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.
Experts rounded on Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget on Thursday, with the Institute for Fiscal Studies saying he had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking big tax and spending decisions.
In a damning analysis, the IFS said Healey would need to have set aside an additional £28bn a year, to offset the impact of inflation on future spending plans and hit the target of spending 3% of GDP in defence by 2030.
Instead Helen Miller, the IFS director, said Healey had opened the way to “a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments” – including real-term budget cuts.
“Public service spending plans look extremely tight. They don’t look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver,” she said, adding that meant Healey could face “another season of damaging speculation about tax rises”.
The welfare bill will not be part of the spending review, which focuses on departmental budgets. But in a bid to underline his determination to balance the books, the chancellor pointed to plans for reform, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We have to bring the benefits bill down.”
He had earlier appeared to say cuts would be made in this parliament, when asked if there would be a reduction in the bill before the next election. “There will be. There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Healey. “We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progress to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.”
However, Treasury officials clarified that he had not meant to give a timeline and Healey later told Channel 4: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.”
Instead, he pointed to forthcoming reviews from Alan Milburn on employment support for young people, and from Stephen Timms on disability benefits.
Milburn is expected to recommend additional spending upfront, aimed at bringing down costs over the longer term by helping more young people into employment.
The Office for Budget Responsibility has said total welfare spending will grow from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030 – with about half of that being spent on pensioners and a quarter on sickness and disability benefits. The overall forecast spending has risen by £8bn since March.
With a tough global economic backdrop, Healey has said the single biggest driver of better prospects for the UK would be an end to the Iran and Ukraine wars.
But in his interviews, Healey appeared to take a more cautious view than the prime minister on the potential for growth from rejoining Europe or the single market. Asked by LBC if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU or the single market, Healey replied: “Well, I don’t actually accept that. Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union. The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient.”
Asked later by Channel 4 if he, like Andy Burnham, hoped for the UK to re-enter the bloc in his lifetime, Healey said: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.”
The chancellor put measures to ease the cost of living at the heart of his first budget, including a £100 winter cost of living payment for most households. However, critics lined up on Thursday to accuse him of taking a “scattergun” approach – and of not hitting Britain’s banks hard enough to fund the package.
The Resolution Foundation thinktank said Healey had failed to target energy support to the households that need it most ahead of a difficult winter, with bills expected to rise sharply in January and the Bank of England to raise interest rates next week.
Ruth Curtice, Resolution’s chief executive, said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain.
“Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.”
Paul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, has strongly advocated for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. He said he welcomed Healey’s approach, but would be pushing for him to go further.
The chancellor has doubled the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months. Novak said: “It was right to tax banks to help people with their energy bills, but I think banks could have been asked to pay a fairer share. He’s going to review it in 15 months. We’re going to be looking as part of that review – if banks are still making windfall profits – for him to extend and increase the bank tax.”
As well as casting doubt on whether Healey’s future spending plans are realistic, the IFS said the £15bn headroom, or buffer, he has left himself against Labour’s fiscal rules could easily be eroded by higher than expected energy costs.
The chancellor allowed the buffer to absorb some of the impact of the Iran war, which has driven up the government’s cost of borrowing. At the time of the spring statement, Rachel Reeves had built up headroom of £24bn.
Miller said that was a “reasonable” decision to make, but “a lower buffer leaves the chancellor more exposed to future bad news”.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of pressure from Donald Trump ahead of the US midterm elections, as a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky ended on Sunday night.
Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast overnight, soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy giant Rosneft.
The Wall Street Journal had reported that Ukraine had given in to pressure from the White House to stop bombing Russian energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials, however, told the Kyiv Independent newspaper that they never agreed to a demand from Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, to pause refinery strikes for 30 days. The raids on Russia restarted on Friday, Kremlin officials said, complaining that Kyiv was now “simply ignoring” US wishes.
Trump has blamed the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the rise in global fuel prices, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel.
Zelenskyy has not acknowledged the latest refinery attacks, in an apparent attempt to avoid angry US reprisals. Instead, he said his armed forces had hit a defence industry enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region that made missiles. A Pantsir missile system was destroyed, he said, as part of Ukraine’s continuing “long-range sanctions”.
Zelenskyy said his country was obliged to retaliate because of a remorseless campaign by Moscow, using drones and ballistic missiles, against vulnerable city-based energy facilities. Four Ukrainian regions were hit by Russia overnight, with electricity cut as a result in hundreds of thousands of households.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said on Telegram. Kyiv experienced power cuts lasting eight to 10 hours on Sunday after a critical thermal power plant was damaged.
Zelenskyy said Russia was suffering record losses, with 54,400 military personnel killed and wounded in October – the highest monthly figure since the full-scale war began. He said Ukraine recaptured 96.2 sq km (37 sq miles) of its territory last month, 10.4 sq km (4 sq miles) more than Moscow managed to seize, and emphasised: “Russia is losing.”
The latest attacks came before a six-day local ceasefire brokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump, came to an end in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Hundreds of residents were reunited with their loved ones over the weekend in northern Ukraine, with both sides hailing the evacuation mission as a success.
“The ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended,” said Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, hailing what had been an “important step in our joint humanitarian efforts”.
Ukrainian observers say the Russian military used the truce to reinforce its positions and to swap hungry and exhausted troops garrisoned in Oleshky. The town sits on the left bank of the Dnipro River, to the east, and is opposite the larger city of Kherson, which Ukraine recaptured in autumn 2022. A renewed Russian onslaught is inevitable, the observers believe.
The pope said on Sunday he hoped cooperation between Russia and Ukraine in implementing the Oleshky ceasefire – the most significant since 2022 – would pave the way for broader peace efforts.
“I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian gesture possible, will strengthen their willingness to engage in dialogue,” he said during his Sunday prayer.
Later on Sunday Ukraine’s air force and anti-disinformation centre said they suspected the country’s air raid alert system had been hacked, after false alerts of a radiation threat appeared on the application. The announcement came minutes after the end of the truce.
A separate app, which deals specifically with the Ukrainian capital, is still working normally, the Kyiv city authorities said.
Hours later, Russia’s emergencies ministry claimed that a “massive cyber-attack” had hit its own application designed to warn people of incoming drone attacks and other threats.
Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US are likely to take place later this month, and Kremlin officials said on Sunday that Vladimir Putin was willing to talk directly to Zelenskyy by phone. They added that European leaders who support Ukraine should not be involved in any such call.
There is little prospect of a wider breakthrough, however, as the Russian president’s maximalist demands remain unchanged.
He is insisting that Ukraine give up all of the eastern Donetsk oblast – which Russia has been unable to seize since 2014 – as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces, which the Kremlin does not control but says it has “annexed”.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Reform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarks
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Alan Feeney has resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after backlash over racist comments that were captured in an undercover investigation.
In a Facebook post on Friday, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”
Earlier this week, an ITV investigation revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.
Feeney has apologised for his comments. “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said,” he wrote in a Facebook post.
“The comments do not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report. These are communities I have supported countless times in my personal and professional life over many years, many of whom I have been lucky enough to call friends.”
Earlier this year, Feeney won seats in the Shard End ward of Birmingham city council and the Castle Bromwich ward of Solihull metropolitan borough council, and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull.
Following the ITV investigation, which is part of a longer series on Reform UK, Feeney announced on Facebook that he was leaving Reform for “personal reasons”, but kept his seats as an independent councillor before resigning.
In a Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “Byelections will be held on a timescale laid out by those councils in the due course. I hope that in time these councils, and the communities they serve can heal and move on.”
Secretly filmed footage showed Feeney making racist remarks alongside two other Reform candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, while canvassing during May’s local elections. Both Campbell and Whelan have also resigned after the fallout from the investigation.
Nigel Farage has repeatedly pledged to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots”. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.
The clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Feeney calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.
In a Facebook post Feeney wrote: “I understand that my words have caused hurt and anger, particularly among those from the communities I serve. For that, I am deeply sorry. I will be undertaking intensive personal analysis to understand how these sentiments could have taken root, and ensure they can never do so again.”
Alan Feeney and Reform UK have been approached for comment.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘Man, I loved that’: Trump cheers South Carolina rally attender who hit protester
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Multiple protesters were removed from Donald Trump’s rally at South Carolina’s Clemson University on Wednesday, including one who was apparently punched by a rally attender – to the US president’s delight.
“That was great, man. Wow. Man, I loved that. I watched that,” Trump said. “That was incredible. Wow. That was unbelievable. Is everybody OK?
“Who’s the guy that threw that punch?” he continued. “You know, you reminded me of Evander, the real deal, Holyfield,” referring to the former heavyweight champion, who was also in attendance at the rally.
“You gotta give them credit. It takes courage to do that at a Trump rally,” he said. “He got whacked.”
According to a pool report, the president was interrupted at least nine times by hecklers. The crowd chanted “USA” as security guards escorted the protesters out of the arena.
One protester who was removed by security was followed by a rally attendee, who appeared to slap the demonstrator on the head.
Trump was in South Carolina to support Darline Graham, the sister of late senator Lindsey Graham who died suddenly in July from a heart condition. Graham, elected to her brother’s seat in a special election, is facing Democratic challenger Annie Andrews in her bid for a full six-year term.
Protests have frequently erupted at Trump rallies in recent weeks, as the president has ramped up his campaign stops in the final weeks before the 3 November midterm elections. The president often brushes off the demonstrations as being carried out by “paid protesters”.
Trump’s 32-day campaign blitz has largely taken him to Republican-leaning areas that he won comfortably in previous elections, underscoring the challenges facing Republicans as they try to retain control of the US Senate and the House of Representatives.
The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, published on Monday, found that 31% of Americans approve of Trump’s performance in office, a record low for the president.
Reuters contributed reporting

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Most NSW homes destroyed in black summer bushfires were within 100 metres of vegetation
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Almost every home destroyed in New South Wales during the black summer bushfires of 2019-20 was inside the 100 metre buffer zone used to identify properties most at risk, new research has found.
The findings are an endorsement of the risk maps used by authorities, but the research warns that as global heating generates ever-worsening fire conditions, firefighters may have to extend the recommended distances between homes and vegetation to keep properties safe.
The NSW rural fire service said the findings reinforced how homes in high risk areas should be built to higher fire standards as it prepared for a potentially “challenging” fire season.
More than 3,000 homes were lost across the country during the unprecedented fires six years ago that took 33 lives and killed or displaced almost 3 billion native animals.
Of the 2,475 homes lost in NSW, the research, published in the International Journal of Wildland Fire, found 94% were less than 100 metres away from flammable vegetation such as trees.
The 100 metre buffer is a key part of the widely used maps of bushfire prone land that firefighters use to plan local outreach activities, and planning authorities use to assess how bushfire-resistant new homes and renovations should be.
Associate Prof Owen Price, an expert in bushfire risk at the University of Wollongong who led the research, said the findings showed a key aspect of the method to identify buildings at risk from bushfires was “more or less spot on”.
“That’s reassuring. Distance to vegetation is really important and that 100 metre rule that they apply is pretty good,” he said.
But the research also examined fire danger ratings – an index that combines temperature, wind, humidity and the dryness of fuel – on the days when each home was lost.
When the fire danger ratings – known technically as the forest fire danger index – reached extreme or catastrophic conditions, “houses further away [than 100 metres] were burning,” Price said.
“That’s a warning sign, because we know that index is going to get worse [from global heating]. We know the direction of travel.”
He said wildfire researchers were alarmed by the increasing number of fires around the world hitting and moving through urban areas, including the 2025 Los Angeles Eaton fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged thousands of homes and businesses.
Part of his own research was aimed at understanding if similar events could be replicated in Australia.
“Being very close to another house [that is on fire] is another risk factor, which is why it’s important we stop houses from burning,” he said.
The research warned that the “current regulation may become less useful over time” as the climate crisis increased the risk of homes being lost.
Melissa O’Halloran, responsible for work on bushfire planning at the NSW rural fire service, said the research showed that “houses in that [bushfire prone] area should be built to a higher construction standard”.
“The conditions in 2019 were extreme and outside what we would usually prepare for and, even under those conditions, our policy has stood up pretty well.
“This reinforces why we want people to have bushfire protection measures in place.”
O’Halloran said investigations carried out after previous fires had shown that not all residents knew they were actually living in a bushfire prone area.
Homes within bushfire prone land in the state are allowed to remove trees within 10 metres of a house and clear understory within 50 metres.
She said the service was reviewing its main bushfire protection policy that would consider the increasing climate risk.
“We’re seeing the impacts of climate change already. It isn’t just temperatures, it’s also about how quickly the landscape dries out, as well as extreme pyroconvective fires,” she said.
Insp James Morris, of the NSW rural fire service, said there was already heightened risk this year for fires in northern parts of the state, in the central west and the far south coast.
“They’ve had high rainfall, and it does not take long for those fuels to dry out. It is important residents do their bit and prepare,” he said.
“We could be in for a challenging fire season.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Thank you, Brazil, for demonstrating how the far right can be trounced while protection for the Amazon is strengthened. In a world where nature and democracy appeared to be bleeding out in tandem, voters and forest defenders in this global south powerhouse have shown it is possible to staunch the flow. This should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France.
The astonishing comeback victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff against his extreme right challenger Flavío Bolsonaro has brought oceans of rapturous supporters on to the streets, while also thrilling conservationists, climate activists and social justice campaigners across the world.
Coming just weeks after the Lula administration announced a record fall in Amazon and Cerrado destruction, they hope Brazil can now go on to achieve its target of zero deforestation by 2030 and continue to support a global transition away from fossil fuels. That would provide a huge boost to flagging global efforts to stabilise the climate and protect degraded ecosystems. It would also set a remarkable example of leadership by the global south.
Big battles lie ahead. In the Amazon region itself, far-right members of Bolsonaro’s party have won the governorships of seven of the nine states and a large number of municipal mayorships. Brazil’s congress is now dominated by agribusiness and mining interests that have set the political agenda in recent years, and will push hard to allow more extractivist industries in indigenous lands, expand road-building, privatise rivers, weaken environmental protections and possibly attempt to impeach the president.
In the regional sphere, Lula, alone among the leaders of main South American nations in not aligning with Donald Trump’s so-called Shield of the Americas, will face pressure from Washington to channel critical minerals and other natural resources to the US, rather than selling to China or Europe, or leaving them in the ground. And, on the planetary level, Brazil faces the threat of accelerating global heating, which is pushing the Amazon ever closer to the point of no return.
So although Sunday’s result will hopefully provide a little breathing space for the Amazon and other crucially important biomes, the joy and hope that Brazil has gifted the world will quickly fade unless it inspires political change in other countries. In that sense, the biggest environmental impact of Lula’s victory may be the lessons it provides for campaigners elsewhere. Here are some initial takeaways:
1 Politics matter. There is no higher environmental priority than defeating the far right, which is a Trojan horse for extractivist – and often criminal – groups to capture states and erode protections for people, democracy and the environment. Just look at the 59.5% surge of Amazon deforestation under the 2019-2022 term of Jair Bolsonaro – the highest level of any four-year presidency in Brazil. Compare that with the 71.2% fall during the Lula administration. Over the past year, forest loss was 3,335 sq km, the lowest level since the start of satellite measurements in 1988. And Lula is not, by any means, an environmentalist. He has approved several destructive projects himself, but he is a people person who listens to the voice of social movements.
2 Don’t give up. Lula was largely written off by the markets and some polls after his first-round defeat. No first-round loser had ever previously come back to win the runoff. Lula was able to do so by securing an extra 10m votes over three weeks. The energy for this came from the streets and the forests. Social movements organised giant rallies in cities. In the Amazon, indigenous, riverine and quilombola groups travelled by hours – sometimes days – to reach polling stations by boats or buses.
3 Mobilise a campaign army. The first round of Lula’s campaign had been stodgy, old-fashioned and defensive – three traits that are also often applicable to environmental campaigns. This was transformed during the runoff, when federal deputy André Janones launched a “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp group that used humorous memes, live streams and algorithmic outreach to seize digital territory that had long been dominated by the right. By voting day, this army had 10m “soldiers”, about 8% of the electorate. Volunteers devoted hours posting stories and spreading messages across social media, speeding up the Lula campaign’s response time and emotional impact. Everyone was instructed not to share or respond to posts by the opposition camp.
4 Go on the offensive against US tech giants. Lula’s campaign accused Meta, which runs the Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram social media platforms, of political favouritism towards Bolsonaro in its algorithms and AI tools. Meta denied bias but acknowledged technical failures. Brazil’s electoral court ordered corrective action. Among the most popular chants of Lula supporters was “Hey Meta, vai tomar no cu!” (Hey Meta, take it up the arse!). Many on the left have blamed US social media platforms for spreading rightwing disinformation and fearmongering, causing recent electoral defeats in Colombia, Chile and Peru. Lula made clear that would not be allowed in Brazil: “We had to overcome foreign interference through digital platforms, which we will have to regulate. We cannot have a monstrously large corporation earning millions and billions paying no taxes to this country and trying to steer our election results.”
5 Reclaim the flag. Brazil’s green, yellow and blue national colours had been associated with Bolsonaro’s movement in previous elections. This time, Lula seized it back by posing in a national football team strip while his “army” launched a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours”. Before voting day, millions of people across Brazil and the world – from Indigenous leaders in the Amazon to Hollywood celebrities and European football stars – flooded social networks with images of themselves in Brazil colours making an L (for Lula) sign with their thumb and little finger extended.
6 Increase social spending. Amazon protection may have galvanised conservationists, but the far greater motivations for many Lula voters were record low unemployment, robust wage growth, a 15% increase in “bolsa familia” poverty relief payments and a promise to raise the minimum wage. The importance of combining social justice with climate and nature action is widely recognised by Brazilian environmental groups. Without it, elections are lost and protests can erupt in the streets – as the world learned from France during the violent gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrations of 2018.
7 Defend sovereignty, democracy and sustainability. Lula and his army called out the interlinked threats posed by the Bolsonaro family’s fealty to Donald Trump (now doubly confirmed by Flávio’s post-election flight to the US). They highlighted the interlinked threats posed by the obsequience to Trump, Bolsonaro’s desire to change the constitution and his promise to open up exploration of the Amazon and other biomes. This reflects a global phenomenon. Now that seven of the planetary boundaries essential for the flourishing of life have been breached, more and more people are affected by business activities that make the situation worse by destabilising the climate, damaging ecosystems and polluting the air, soil and rivers. This makes it harder for extractive companies to secure a social mandate so they become more inclined to either break the law or support extreme politics that override democracy.
The former environment minister Marina Silva pulled these threads together during the victory celebrations, saying Brazil had come together against these threats: “Long live the people who emerged from every corner of Brazil to sow hope for a future that is socially just, sovereign, democratic and sustainable.”
Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action. Now it needs others to follow.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘No indications’ PHP code flaw has led to government systems being hacked, cyber security official says – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Cyber security official says there are 'no indications' PHP code flaw has led to government computer systems being hacked
Ollie Whitehouse, chief technology officer at the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, told Radio 4’s the World at One that incidents like today’s computer system shutdowns because of a coding problem were likely to re-occur. He explained:
[This] highlights to a lot of organisations that technology is not a one-time purchase now, that it needs that continuous investment throughout its operational lifetime.
We’re in an era now of digital dependency, coupled with heightened cyber threat, coupled with increasing capability, which means all organisations are going to likely have to revisit their risk assumptions and work out how they are able to invest in technology to be able to meet the contemporary era.
Whitehouse said there were “no indications” that the PHP flaw now being fixed had been successfully exploited by hackers.
He also said that the problem that had led to 32 government websites being temporarily shut down (see 12.54pm) was originally identified months ago. He said the NCSC had been conducting a “coordinated disclosure process” to warn organisations of the vulnerability, until a leak meant that the process had to be accelerated.
A UK cyber security official has said that there are “no indications” that the PHP computer coding flaw, that has led to 32 government websites being taken down, has been successfully exploited by hackers. (See 4.46pm.)
MPs pay tribute to Diane Abbott as they debate black history month
MPs debated black history month earlier today. Politicians are often fairly unpleasant to their opponents, but there was a surprise moment near the start of the debate when Joy Morrissey, the Tory spokesperson for women and equalities (and not someone known for being particularly woke or leftwing), paid a moving tribute to the veteran Labour MP Diane Abbott. Morrissey said:
In 1987, the very same year black history month began here, a young woman from Paddington walked into the House of Commons as Britain’s first black female MP. Today, she is the mother of the House.
When she arrived, there were only 41 women in the entire Commons. She was told in a hundred ways that she didn’t belong. She stayed anyway.
For nearly four decades, she has represented the people of Hackney, championed black children in London schools, and chaired parliamentary groups on West Indian and sickle cell disease.
She has faced more abuse than almost any politician of her generation, and she has never stopped turning up.
You don’t have to share her political her politics to recognise what her presence meant. For millions of black Britons, especially black girls, she was proof that the doors of power could open and that someone who looked like them could walk through.
Florence Eshalomi, the communities minister, opened the debate, and she also paid tribute to Abbott. She said she remembered when Abbott was elected in 1987, along with Paul Boateng and Bernie Grant. They were the first black MPs. Eshalomi said:
I was just six years old when [Abbott] was elected, and I remember that quiet hope I felt in watching TV and seeing her in parliament to see that, yes, a black woman can have that voice and that we don’t have to stand by when decisions are made to us and not by us. That gave me the confidence to stand for public office as a local councillor in the borough where I grew up, and later for the London assembly.
Voters significantly more likely to back progressive coalition led by Burnham than Tory/Reform UK one, poll suggests
YouGov has published some interesting polling on what voters think about various coalition options. Here are some of the key points.
Voters are significantly more likely to support a progressive coalition than a rightwing coalition. The most popular coalition option polled was a Labour/Lib Dem one, with Andy Burnham as PM. Some 42% of people would support that. Other progressive options, with Burnham as PM, would get the support of more than a third of voters. But only a quarter of voters would back a Conservative/Reform UK coalition, with a Kemi Badenoch-led version only marginally more popular than a Nigel Farage-led one.
Conservative supporters would rather see the party go into coalition with the Liberal Democrats than with Reform UK. In its write-up, YouGov says:
Most current Conservative supporters would support either arrangement, though more are in favour of the party forming a coalition with the Lib Dems (68%) than Reform (60%), and with at least 28% opposed to either coalition. Lib Dem supporters do not return the favour, with 58% of those currently intending to vote for the party opposed to a repeat of the Cameron-Clegg government, although 36% are in favour.
This is interesting because, on immigration, Brexit, and the European convention on human rights, Badenoch has shifted her party to a position where its policies are near identical to Reform UK’s. Recently there have been signs she has started to steer back the other way.
Most Conservative supporters would not be in favour of a coalition with Reform UK, with Nigel Farage as PM, if the two parties combined could form a majority government. In December last year Conservative supporters (defined as people who voted Tory in 2024) were narrowly in favour of this option. They would still favour a Conservative-Reform UK coalition if Badenoch were PM, but by a narrower margin than last year. YouGov says:
Britons have become less inclined towards a Farage-led Reform-Tory coalition, with net support for such a government falling from -27 to -41 since last December. This includes 2024 Conservative voters going from being effectively divided on the question (+5) to being clearly opposed (-13).
Conservative voters have also become less receptive to a Badenoch-led Tory-Reform coalition, with net support falling 15 points since the end of last year to +23, even if those who voted Reform at the last election have become more open to the idea, with net support doubling to +22.
Fahnbulleh says ministers won't 'faff around' in getting rid of gas standing charges, implying decision coming in budget
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, has heightened speculation that a government announcement about getting rid of the standing charges on gas bills will come in the budget on Wednesday next week.
Andy Burnham implied this strongly yesterday when he said he had asked John Healey, the chancellor, and Fahnbulleh to look at this idea and to report back to MPs “at the earliest opportunity”. The “earliest opportunity” is Wednesday next week, because that will be the first time either of those two MPs gets to address the Commons.
Today, speaking to a press gallery lunch, Fahnbulleh confirmed that an announcement is likely very soon. She said Burnham had made it clear the government “can’t faff around”.
She explained:
I love working with him because Andy is very clear … in his mind about the sorts of things that he wants us to do, and he’s really impatient with change.
And so, if you ask the department, ‘Oh, you know, standing charge reform’, they’re like, ‘Oh, we’d have to consult. This is a 10-year proposition’. And Andy’s like, ‘I want you and John to look at it and come back with an answer’. So we’re looking at the options.
Fahnbulleh said getting rid of standing charges would be popular.
The thing I do know is that the public absolutely hates standing charges, and it’s a control question. People just find that really egregious, and their ability to manage their energy bills by deciding how much they want to use on their terms is essentially taken away from them. So, even shifting it into the unit rate gives people that agency.
She said modelling suggested the move could reduce the bills of “a big stack of low-income through to middle-income households”.
She went on:
There are some people that will be impacted negatively because they are essentially low-income, high users, and so you need to think about mitigations. But we’re looking at all the options.
But the thing that he is very clear on is we can’t faff around. We need to get on with this. So watch this space.
According to research by Nesta, a research foundation, 64% of households would benefit if the government got rid of the standing charge and instead loaded those costs onto the unit charge. But households using large amounts of gas would pay more.
Our analysis shows that, on its own, abolishing the gas standing charge would save the typical dual fuel household £27 per year, and that 64% of dual fuel households will be better off under this policy.
Because the distribution of gas consumption is skewed by a small number of (predominantly wealthy) households, the average and median household are quite a way apart. The threshold at which this policy would start to increase bills is around 12,400 kWh, but a majority of homes (64%) use less gas than this. This is why the typical household (using only 9,500 kWh of gas) would expect to save around £27 per year under this policy.
TDCV stands for typical domestic consumption values – a figure for how much gas and electricity an average household is using at any point.
Burnham has flu jab, as NHS encourages those eligible for free injection to get one
Andy Burnham has had his flu jab. He has posted about it on Instagram, and at the same time the Department of Health and Social Care is launching a publicity campaign to encourage people eligible for a free jab to get one.
James Frith, a health minister, said:
Vaccines save lives. It has never been easier to find out if you are eligible and get vaccinated, helping protect yourself and reduce pressure on the NHS during the winter season.
Eligibility is focused on those most vulnerable - from young children to older adults and people with long-term health conditions - so if you are eligible, please come forward this winter.
In England, most children under 17 are eligible for a free flu jab, as well as people over 65, people with some long-term health conditions, pregnant women, carers and people living in a care home, people living with someone with a weakened immune system, homeless people and frontline health and care workers.
The latest edition of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast is out. It features Jessica Elgot and Alexandra Topping talking about whether or not the government will allow the Rosebank oilfield development to go ahead, after the less controversial Jackdaw gasfield was approved yesterday.
Starmer granted core participant status in grooming gangs inquiry
Keir Starmer may be summoned to give evidence at the grooming gangs inquiry, the Press Association reports. PA says:
The former prime minister, who ordered the probe last year, has been listed as a core participant for the inquiry’s hearings which are due to begin in December.
This means he is among people, groups and organisations formally granted special status by the chairwoman under public inquiry rules, giving him rights to participate in the investigation.
While this does not automatically mean he will be required to give evidence, many core participants are asked or compelled to do so.
Victims and their families, charities, whistleblowers, police chiefs and government departments are among those also listed as core participants.
The scandal-hit probe is looking at how grooming gangs operated in England and Wales and the actions of police, councils, health and social care services, schools and other public bodies.
An inquiry spokesman said the decision on core participant status “considers whether a person played, or may have played, a direct and significant role in relation to the matters to which the inquiry relates, whether they have a significant interest in an important aspect of the matters to which the inquiry relates, or whether the person may be subject to explicit or significant criticism during the inquiry proceedings or in the report, or in any interim report”, adding: “Nobody is beyond examination or transparency, and that the inquiry is following the evidence, wherever it leads.”
Starmer was prime minister when the grooming gangs inquiry was announced last year. But he was also director of public prosecutions from 2008 to 2013, at a time when the CPS was being accused of being too reluctant to prosecute in many cases of alleged child sexual abuse. As DPP, Starmer set out to change this – ordering prosecutors to be more sympathetic to victims, and less inclined to disbelieve them or to drop cases because victims might not make compelling witnesses.
According to Christopher Hope from GB News, Kemi Badenoch is unhappy about Andy Burnham going on Gogglebox (see 2.35pm) – but only because she wants an invite too! Hope says:
A political row has broken out over Andy Burnham’s decision to go on Channel 4’s programme ‘Gogglebox’. A Tory source tells me that Kemi Badenoch should be invited on to the show. One says: “It’s Channel 4’s job to ensure political balance.”
Cyber security official says there are 'no indications' PHP code flaw has led to government computer systems being hacked
Ollie Whitehouse, chief technology officer at the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, told Radio 4’s the World at One that incidents like today’s computer system shutdowns because of a coding problem were likely to re-occur. He explained:
[This] highlights to a lot of organisations that technology is not a one-time purchase now, that it needs that continuous investment throughout its operational lifetime.
We’re in an era now of digital dependency, coupled with heightened cyber threat, coupled with increasing capability, which means all organisations are going to likely have to revisit their risk assumptions and work out how they are able to invest in technology to be able to meet the contemporary era.
Whitehouse said there were “no indications” that the PHP flaw now being fixed had been successfully exploited by hackers.
He also said that the problem that had led to 32 government websites being temporarily shut down (see 12.54pm) was originally identified months ago. He said the NCSC had been conducting a “coordinated disclosure process” to warn organisations of the vulnerability, until a leak meant that the process had to be accelerated.
Burnham to appear on Gogglebox with Steve Rotheram
Kemi Badenoch has been routinely complaining about Andy Burnham spending time on supposedly trivial things, like discussing how he makes his tea in a summer Q&A, or doing a social media video about pork scratchings. So God know what she is going to say when she finds out he’s on Gogglebox tomorrow night.
The PM will be appearing on the show tomorrow night for a Gogglebox for Stand Up To Cancer special. He will be on the sofa with his friend Steve Rotheram, the Liverpool city region mayor.
As Max Goldbart writes in an article for Deadline, there is some precedent for his appearance.
Seen as something of an everyman, Burnham will now get the chance to broadcast his thoughts on the week’s TV to millions. An Instagram reel teasing his appearance shows him offering crisps and beer to Rotheram.
Burnham is the first prime minister to appear on Gogglebox. Jeremy Corbyn, who was leader of the opposition at the time, came on the show a decade ago, while former PM Boris Johnson’s father Stanley Johnson appeared two years later.
“Nearly 7,000 miles of road resurfacing – the equivalent of travelling between London and Singapore – will be completed this year,” the Department for Transportis saying. It says councils in England are doing 10% more resurfacing than last year, because they are getting more government funding.
Mahmood condemned by Unison for refusing to let care worker attend private meeting about her 'nasty' proposed ILR changes
Andrea Egan, the Unison general secretary, has criticised Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, for not letting her bring a care worker to a meeting to discuss Mahmood’s plans to tighten the permanent residency rules for foreign workers.
Egan described the proposals as “nasty”, and said Mahmood’s failure to engage with people affected by the rules was “totally unacceptable”.
The Unison leader was commenting in a post on social media that referenced a story by Arj Singh for the i, which said talks between Mahmood and Unison “broke down after the home secretary refused to allow a migrant care worker to attend the meeting”. Singh said:
The meeting was cancelled by Unison after Mahmood refused Egan’s late request to bring a migrant care worker who will be affected by the “earned settlement” changes, The i Paper understands.
Mahmood is under pressure to water down her proposals, particularly those relating to care workers, and Unison, which represents many workers in the care sector, has campaigned particularly forcefully against the plan.
In her social media posts, Egan said:
Shabana Mahmood’s failure to engage properly with the migrant workers whose lives her nasty proposals will devastate is totally unacceptable.
These are brilliant, committed workers who hold our public services together. UNISON won’t tolerate them being attacked and ignored.
I’ve changed UNISON’s political approach to put members first. That includes taking members with me to government meetings.
Engaging directly with workers should be standard for Labour cabinet ministers, not something they run away from.
In his report, Singh says:
The care worker who Egan wanted to bring to the meeting has completed an NVQ level 3 and is set to do further qualifications so that he can develop his career in the sector, and was planning to tell Mahmood about why he and many other Unison members had chosen to work in the sector.
Singh quotes a Home Office source as saying that Egan had been invited to a private meeting with Mahmood and that it was Unison that chose to cancel it. The source also said that it would be wrong for Mahmood to prioritise the views of just one care worker when 200,000 responses to the government’s consultation were being considered.
In a social media post commenting on the same story, the Labour MP John McDonnell said:
The work visa issue is causing totally unnecessary division in the Labour Party at a time when the new leader is settling himself into the job. Listening to numerous workers employed on work visas in the care sector has been essential in gaining an understanding of what they face and the effect on our public services of the proposed rule changes. All Unison wanted was to ensure the home secretary had the opportunity to appreciate fully the concerns of the people who will be affected by her proposals. I urge her to think again on this decision not to meet.
32 UK government services offline while work carried out to sort out PHP programming flaw, minister says
Some 32 government services are offline and four are partially unavailable while work is carried out to address potential cybersecurity issues, a minister has said.
As the Press Association reports, organisations around the world have been scrambling to fix a critical security flaw in the programming language PHP used by the majority of websites.
Downing Street on Thursday said no large UK public-facing critical services have been affected, but some “limited” government websites have gone dark while issues are resolved. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) experts are working with OpenAI, whose technology was used to discover the vulnerabilities, and partners around the globe to address potential problems, a No 10 spokesperson said.
In the House of Lords, Liz Lloyd, the tech minister, said:
The information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable.
Lloyd said that “has largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied”.
The No 10 spokesperson told reporters:
Work has already taken place across government to identify and fix potential exposures to our systems, and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue.
Here is our story about the global impact of the problems identified in the PHP programming language. It’s by Robert Booth and Aisha Down.
Steve Witkoff wrong about Putin being a 'humanitarian', says No 10
Yesterday Steve Witkoff, the property developer appointed by Donald Trump as his lead foreign policy envoy, described Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian”. Andrew Roth has more about that here, in a piece pointing out that this is an extraordinary lie.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish secretary, was giving interviews this morning. Asked if he agreed with Witkoff’s description on LBC, he was reassuringly blunt. He replied:
No, we don’t.
We see him as somebody who illegally invaded Ukraine at the start of this conflict, who has been responsible for conduct by his government that included attempted assassinations on UK soil.
So we simply do not recognise the description of Vladimir Putin as a humanitarian.
In contrast, we are crystal clear that we stand foursquare behind Volodymyr Zelensky and the people of Ukraine in their battle for freedom.
At the No 10 lobby briefing, a No 10 spokesperson also argued that Witkoff had got it wrong. Asked about Witkoff’s comment, the spokesperson said:
We do not recognise that characterisation … Putin has killed thousands of people, Ukrainians and his own. He’s starving children and the elderly of heat and warmth and destroying critical national infrastructure.
Tories claim crime figures 'spiralling out of control' - and why the data doesn't back this up
The Conservative party seems to have missed the bit in the ONS report on the crime figures where it said “crime against individuals and households has generally decreased over the last 10 years”. (See 9.54am.) Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, has issued a statement saying:
Crime is spiralling out of control under Labour. Record numbers of sexual offences, knife crime and shop theft show what happens when criminals know they can get away with it. This is a direct consequence of Labour cutting police numbers by 2,000 and letting thousands of prisoners out of jail early.
The Tories justify this claim by looking at the ONS report and picking out all the worst bits (a technique not unfamiliar in the world of journalism). Their briefing highlights four figures in particular. Here is an extract.
Sexual offences have reached the highest level on record under Labour, with the police now logging around 600 of them every single day. Police in England and Wales recorded 218,994 sexual offences in the year to June 2026, the highest annual total since the series began in 2002-03 …
Police are recording more rapes of women than at any point since records began, at a rate of around 142 every day. There were 51,731 recorded rapes of women aged 16 or over in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2004-05 …
More people are being caught carrying knives and blades than at any point since records began. Police recorded 30,216 offences of possessing an article with a blade or point in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2008-09 …
Thefts and robberies from shops have reached a record high under Labour, with more than 1,500 recorded every single day. Police recorded 519,516 shoplifting offences and 31,089 robberies of business property in the year to June 2026, a combined 550,605 and the highest total since the series began in 2002-03.
But these claims are highly selective – to the point of being misleading.
On sexual offences, and rape, the ONS report points out that much of the increase over time is due to more offences being recorded, and not necessarily more of them taking place. It says “there has been a general increase in police recorded sexual offences over the last decade, largely because of improvements in police recording practices”. And it includes a specific warning about drawing the wrong conclusions from the figures.
Police recorded sexual offences are not a good indicator of trends over time. Improvements in police recording practices, the introduction of new offences, and increased reporting by victims have contributed to the level of offences in recent years.
On knives, while more people may be carrying them, the Tories have ignored the figures suggesting fewer criminals are actually using them. The ONS says:
Knife-enabled crime recorded by the police decreased by 6% in year ending (YE) June 2026 (to 48,615 offences), compared with YE June 2025 (51,567 offences). Levels remained 12% lower than YE March 2020 (55,170 offences).
And, on shoplifting, the Tories are again presenting the data in a misleading way. The ONS says:
Following a period of increases in shoplifting, there has been a 2% decrease (to 519,516 offences) in YE June 2026 when compared with the previous year (530,336 offences).
The Tories have justified their “record high” claim by combining the shoplifing figures with the figures for robberies from business properties. They describe this as “shop crime” – even though many business properties are not shops. And the ONS has a caveat about these figures too.
The number of robbery of personal property offences fell by 7% (to 57,193 offences) compared with the previous year, however, overall robbery increased by 10% (to 88,282 offences) mainly because of improvements to recording practices for robbery of business property.
And the ONS says, with shoplifting, more offences are also now being recorded than in the past.
Recent increases in police recorded shoplifting likely reflect both growth in offences and improved reporting resulting from closer engagement between police and retailers. Reporting rates for shoplifting are known to be very low and police are actively encouraging the reporting of all incidents and the submission of supporting evidence, such as CCTV, to strengthen intelligence, identify offenders, and link related offences.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Altering copyright law to allow AI companies to scrape music, books and journalism could trigger a constitutional breach, Coalition senators and the recording industry have warned, as they raise new fears it could open Australia to massive legal action and compensation claims from rights holders worldwide.
The attorney general’s department admitted it was “extremely alive” to the issue, and Australia’s leading constitutional expert, Anne Twomey, agreed there was “potentially” a concern – depending how legislation was drafted – that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material from the internet could amount to an acquisition of property by the government.
In a simmering debate centred on the same legal point as the movie The Castle, the question of acquiring property “on just terms” is emerging as a key concern amid furious lobbying from tech companies and rights holders ahead of a looming federal government announcement on AI.
“We could be liable for ‘just terms’ compensation for acquiring that property for every rights holder on Earth,” Ross Cadell, a Nationals senator, told Guardian Australia.
Michaelia Cash, the shadow attorney general, said the government should not “sell out Australian creators and rights holders in the rush to entice AI investment”.
Labor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of reforms around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.
Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model which would allow it to scrape content unless a rightholder deployed digital protections signaling an objection.
A fresh concern being aired by sceptics and creatives is that any weakening of copyright to benefit AI could represent a breach of section 51 of the constitution, which allows the commonwealth to make laws about “the acquisition of property on just terms”.
“If they go ahead with an opt-out model, it does raise a real question of whether the government is acquiring the intellectual property rights of others,” said Cadell, a member of the federal parliamentary committee on AI.
“How we support property rights is core to this.”
A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.
Anne Twomey, professor emerita of law at the University of Sydney, said the issue was exceedingly complex and noted no legislative proposal had been aired. She said numerous cases had come before the high court relating to copyright and acquisition of property, including about video games, cigarette plain packaging and cassette tapes, with varying outcomes.
Twomey expected the federal government would be hyperaware of such concerns, but said granting a new right to AI companies to use copyrighted material and diminishing the rights of copyright holders could “potentially” trigger constitutional issues.
“The high court has recognised a number of exceptions to section 51 … One would want to be quite confident before enacting the legislation about whether or not section 51 would apply,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.
She said any change allowing Australia to host AI companies training on international data could potentially create grounds for global rights holders to take legal action here.
Cadell told Guardian Australia he worried about such a development opening the federal government to liability for “the biggest compensation rights case in history”.
Cadell raised his concerns about the constitution in a committee hearing with the attorney general’s department on Friday, in which officials said they were conscious of those issues.
Officials did not directly answer when Cadell asked about international implications and liability for compensation to foreign rights holders.
Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association, claimed any proposal to allow AI companies to scrape data was “clearly an acquisition of property”.
“It’s hard to imagine what kind of compensation would make up for the fact that they’re basically taking our right … and trading it away to the AI companies to then monetise themselves, and that appears to be a clear path to a constitutional challenge.”
Chris Maund, CEO of Mushroom Records, said current copyright law was working and that AI companies should use existing licensing arrangements, noting companies such as Spotify were already making AI-related deals.
He also raised concern about international ramifications were Australia to change copyright law, saying it would not only apply to Australian artists and copyright owners.
“The AI company could do their training here in Australia and circumvent the copyright laws that apply outside of Australia, and that’s why the international creative industries are watching this very closely,” he said.
Maund said international rights holder groups had been urging Labor not to weaken copyright law. Guardian Australia has provided submissions to the Joint Select Committee as a member of Australia’s wider rights holder community.
“The Australian government has been really great to the music industry, particularly Prime Minister Albanese and Tony Burke. They’ve set up Creative Music Australia, which companies like us and our artists have done very well out of, but it feels like they’re out of step with artists and copyright owners on this point,” he said.
Cash said the Coalition welcomed the benefits of AI and wanted investment, but also raised the constitutional concern.
“That is the prime minister’s own test, and the government should be held to it,” she said of compensation to rights holders.
“The constitutional question of property rights and their acquisition on just terms is also a live issue we will be examining depending on what the government puts forward.”
Cadell said while AI had benefits, he worried about its risks.
“There’s lots of talk about what the benefits may be and what may happen. But if we take these rights away, we know what will happen,” Cadell said.
“I don’t want to hurt people for a ‘may’.”
