SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Surgeon faces deportation as Home Office revokes refugee status for Syrians
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A Syrian plastic surgeon is facing deportation from the UK after the Home Office revoked his refugee status, declaring it is now safe for him and his family to return to their home country.
Despite Foreign Office guidance advising against all travel to Syria because of the “volatile” security situation, the government has classified it as a safe place for refugees to return to.
Although some European countries are strongly promoting voluntary return to Syria, the Home Office’s decision to actively remove refugee status for Syrians is thought to be the first of its kind in Europe since the fall of the Assad regime.
The surgeon, who fled the Assad regime and arrived in the UK in 2016, now lives in London with his wife and six children, three of whom are studying at university. He is understood to be one of the first Syrian refugees in the UK to have his refugee protection cancelled.
The move is believed to be the first time the Home Office has cancelled refugee protection for a particular nationality, and thousands of Syrians settled in the UK are likely to be affected.
“I am so shocked by the Home Office’s decision to withdraw refugee protection,” the surgeon said. “I brought my family to what I considered to be a safe place. We have integrated well but now my refugee status has been cancelled.
“I worked as a plastic surgeon in Syria, converted my medical qualifications here so that I am registered with the General Medical Council to work as a doctor here. I am currently working in a GP surgery but am hoping I will be able to continue my practice as a plastic surgeon soon.
“I don’t believe Syria will be a safe place for me to return to. I was targeted by certain radical groups in Syria who are still operating there. They are capable of doing many things to me. And I don’t believe that the current Syrian government would be able to protect me from these groups.
“I have heard of a few other families who have also had their refugee status taken away from them on the same basis as me – the Home Office says Syria is now a safe country for us to return to.
“After I received the letter from the Home Office I delayed telling my family because I wanted to protect them from sadness for a few more days. But now I have given them the news. Like me, they are all in shock and are only just starting to absorb this. My three older children are all studying at university: one is doing neuroscience, another cybersecurity and a third pharmacy.
“It’s unsafe for all of us to go back to Syria. By revoking our refugee status the Home Office is depriving us of the right to live our lives.”
The Home Office letter states: “Your refugee status has been ceased. Although officials accept that the situation in Syria remains ‘complex’ they consider that changes in Syria are so significant that your fear of persecution and serious harm can no longer be regarded as well founded.”
The technical term is “cessation” of refugee status. The UN’s refugee agency, UNHCR, in its most recent guidance about the safety of Syria, found that governments should not be returning refugees there.
It said: “UNHCR calls on states to refrain from implementing cessation exercises until such time as the situation in Syria has seen significant improvements in overall stability.”
Foreign Office guidance states that the security situation in Syria “remains volatile” and adds: “Fighting and violence may occur around the country and is highly unpredictable. This includes artillery and airstrikes.” The guidance also states that there is a humanitarian crisis in Syria including lack of infrastructure, water, sanitation and health services.
The family’s solicitor, Manini Menon of Duncan Lewis, said: “It is regrettable that the home secretary has seen fit to target Syrian refugees and their families as part of her pledge to reduce net migration figures. This is a cynical and unprecedented step which will have devastating consequences for a group of people who have rebuilt their lives in the UK with considerable effort, contributing to their communities and putting down roots here.
“The evidence in relation to Syria is clear: the circumstances in the country do not allow the home secretary to lawfully conclude that they have stabilised to the extent that refugees can be safely returned there.”
The Home Office said: “Britain will always provide protection to genuine refugees, and we will never return anyone to danger. When it is safe for someone to return to their home country, they will be expected to do so. We continue to work closely with governments around the world to develop and maintain returns agreements, including with Syria.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on Labour’s budget: bold ambitions and welcome first steps | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
John Healey’s first budget was a Rorschach test. Supporters saw dozens of measures offering “breathing space” to a public worn down by rising prices. Critics admitted to a slew of announcements but countered that each was modest in value. Underlying both views is that the budget was more ambitious on how a state can do more to protect the public than on how much it spends. The chancellor has taken a small step in the right direction – a tricky feat in a turbulent world. But an economy marked by entrenched inequality and more than a decade of stagnation will need a bigger stride.
The Office for Budget Responsibility’s “pretty grim picture” of living standards exposes the budget’s central weakness: its relief is temporary, while the squeeze on households persists. As the government deficit shrinks and company profits recover, households are expected to move from saving roughly £50bn in 2026 to borrowing roughly the same amount in 2031. By then, mortgage repayments are expected to reach 4.25% of household disposable income – the highest level since 2009. The OBR expects growth to recover from 1% in 2027 to 1.8% in 2029, while weak worker “bargaining power” allows firms to rebuild profit margins. That sits uneasily with Mr Healey’s promises to working people.
Admittedly, the budget’s ambitions – shaping energy markets, ending rough sleeping, devolving tax and spend decisions – go beyond its winter relief package. Mr Healey is also right to ask banks, gambling companies and landlords to contribute more. Preventing hardship is better than repeatedly paying for its consequences. In ringfencing homelessness prevention in local government spending, even though the savings are experienced in the NHS, he is making both moral and financial sense.
The problem, however, is not that Mr Healey’s budget lacks ambition, but that it lacks firepower. The bank tax raises just £1.5bn over 15 months, against the projected £11bn that a Thatcher-style levy on interest-free deposits could have yielded. The Resolution Foundation has a point when it says that 80% of homes get a £100 energy payment, while 1.4 million poor families miss out. Relying on revenues from the giant Rosebank oilfield before its approval is settled would be reckless. So would treating the export of its oil as an answer to the climate damage caused by burning it.
The choices that Mr Healey makes all too often reflect the fiscal constraints he opted to retain. Is it really “credible” to claim that there will be £11bn of cuts to “unprotected” budgets (those that aren’t defence, the NHS, schools or international aid) in 2031-32? Many experts think not. Should the defence budget be funded by “reprioritising” other departments’ capital spend? Mr Healey thinks so. The prime minister called the 2009 Marmot review his bible on reducing inequalities – it advocates for widescale economic rebalancing. But devolving tax revenues without adequate redistribution risks giving the wealthiest places the most to spend, rather than giving the poorest the help they need. Mr Healey has yet to explain how he will prevent that.
Global events could make Mr Healey’s life much tougher. Prolonged disruption in the strait of Hormuz would further squeeze real incomes. But the chancellor has in his budget sketched the outline of a social-democratic active state: taxing rentiers, protecting vulnerable people and investing in prevention. The question is whether those commitments have enough resources to succeed.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: US military says strike on alleged drug vessel in eastern Pacific kills five people
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The US military said on Tuesday it killed five people after an airstrike on a suspected drug-trafficking vessel in the eastern Pacific.
Tuesday’s strike was among more than 70 such attacks since the beginning of Donald Trump’s second presidency, according to media tallies. Collectively, they have killed more than 240 people.
The Trump administration has maintained the people and boats were involved in trafficking. Trump has said the US is locked in armed conflict with Latin American cartels while justifying strikes as necessary to stem the flow of drugs into the US.
But the Trump administration has not provided definitive evidence to back up its contentions of drug trafficking and has prompted debate about the legality of the strikes.
Legal experts and rights groups argue the strikes could amount to extrajudicial killings because they have apparently targeted civilians who do not pose an immediate threat to the US.
More details soon …
Reuters, the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: National Grid to site biggest substation in UK near planned Teesside datacentre
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
National Grid has taken a step towards building Britain’s biggest electricity substation on Teesside, which could supply power to a vast neighbouring datacentre as the UK races to expand its AI infrastructure.
Last week, the company agreed to purchase 29.5 hectares (73 acres) of land at Dorman Point on a site owned by Teesworks, a local private-public partnership. The deal was first reported by Sky News.
The deal followed reports last year that the UK government had picked Teesworks as the site for a new artificial intelligence datacentre, and planning applications had been submitted for a project that would span nearly 500,000 sq metres.
The deal “reflects the constructive work between all those involved to enable this vital infrastructure … and will support the growth of AI and digital technologies, and enable the region’s next phase of industrial and economic development”, Matt Pearce, the head of land at National Grid, said.
 
 
 “We are committed to working closely with our partners to progress the development as quickly as possible,” he added.
Ben Houchen, the mayor of the Tees Valley combined authority, told Sky News: “Everyone who has tried to build a datacentre in this country knows the biggest problem is getting enough power to the site quickly.
“While we’ve been stuck in the queue, the US, the Gulf and parts of Europe have been getting on with it and hoovering up the investment. Having up to 3.2GW of capacity here means we can finally compete for those projects.
“If Britain is serious about having its own AI capability, with sensitive data stored safely on British soil, it needs somewhere to physically put it, and I’d much rather that was Teesside than Texas or Abu Dhabi.”
Last week, the government published a draft national policy statement on datacentres, describing them as “as fundamental to our economy as the railways and electricity networks on which we have long depended”.
“We must take control over the development of datacentres in this country and ensure that the country and host communities benefit from them,” it said.
However, the rapid construction of datacentres in the UK has been met by strong opposition, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging from Auchtertool, a village north of Edinburgh, to Brick Lane in east London.
In October, the Guardian reported that AI companies told ministers they had 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.
The London-listed infrastructure services group Balfour Beatty was reported to be in line to deliver the Teesworks substation for National Grid, with the utilities firm Steel River Power (SRP) also heavily involved in the project.
Balfour Beatty and SRP were approached for comment.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm push
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
In races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support them have released ads accusing Republicans of protecting pedophiles by voting against legislation to release files related to Jeffrey Epstein.
The ads appear intended to evoke an emotional response by accusing candidates of “protecting” Epstein, a notorious pedophile accused of running a sex-trafficking ring involving minors.
An analysis from CNN found that candidates and outside groups have spent more than $35m on Epstein-related ads. Another from the Washington Post found that Democrats spent more than $40m on Epstein-related ads across six key Senate races.
In Colorado, ads targeting Republican Jeff Crank note that the lawmaker voted against releasing the Epstein files. In one, the family members of Virginia Giuffre, a woman who survived abuse at the hands of Epstein and died by suicide last year, claim Crank “covered up Epstein’s crimes to protect Donald Trump”.
Ashley Hinson, a Senate candidate in Iowa, was accused of voting to “protect her donors” by refusing to vote to release the Epstein files.
“This week I had to explain to my boys, ‘No, Mom does not protect pedophiles,’” Hinson said in a campaign ad responding to attacks over the Epstein files.
An ad targeting Mike Collins, the Republican running for a Georgia Senate seat, says “Mike Collins voted against releasing the Epstein files even after he knew Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation exploited 14-year-old girls for sex”.
Florida Republican Jimmy Patronis faced an attack from his Democratic opponent, claiming he called investigating Epstein “a waste of his time”.
A spokesperson for Crank’s campaign accused the Epstein-related ad of being “intentionally vague”, in a statement to the Washington Post, because his position was that he would vote against the file’s release until he could be confident that victim information was properly redacted. The campaign also said it was “unfortunate” that his opponent, Jessica Killin, was “preying on a grieving family with the help of the Washington Democrats”.
Crank’s staff invited and met with Giuffre’s family, though Crank himself did not meet with them in person, the New York Times reported. Crank’s campaign also said it offered to meet with Epstein victims before the vote on the legislation.
Last year, Democrats and a select few House Republicans tried to force a vote on the Epstein files through a discharge petition – a procedure used in Congress to bypass the traditional steps of legislation and force a vote on the House floor.
Donald Trump, who knew Epstein in the 1990s and early 2000s, opposed the discharge petition for the files, reversing his campaign promise to increase government transparency. House Republicans largely aligned themselves with him, prompting anger from high-profile Trump voters.
Eventually, under pressure from allies, Trump supported the legislation, giving Republican lawmakers the go-ahead to vote for it. All but one House Republican voted for the Epstein Files Transparency Act.
Many of the ads omit the fact that nearly every House Republican voted to release the Epstein files when the Epstein Files Transparency Act came to the floor, although at that point Trump had agreed to sign the legislation and release the files. Instead, the ads refer to Republicans opposing early attempts to force the legislation to the floor.
Republicans have pointed to this fact when disputing the attack ads.
“Of course I voted to release the Epstein files,” Hinson said in a direct-to-camera ad, accusing her opponent, Josh Turek, of lying. While Hinson voted for the final Epstein Files Transparency Act, she did not sign on to the discharge petition.
Patronis, meanwhile, never called the investigation a “waste of time”, but told a local radio station that while he had “no problem getting everything all released”, the issue was a “massive energy and time suck at the end of the day”.
Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for Patronis’s campaign, highlighted his work with Trump to obtain disaster funding after Hurricane Isaias and said his opponent, Gay Valimont, was “still talking about a dead pedophile in a sad web video than helping the people of [the first congressional district] recover.”
Some Republicans and groups supporting the GOP have sought to flip the script, accusing Democrats of taking money from donors who had ties to Epstein.
During a Georgia Senate debate, Collins accused his opponent, Jon Ossoff, of accepting campaign donations from Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire who had ties to Epstein. Hoffman has said he only knew Epstein through fundraising relationships and regrets it.
“You can claim to fight against the Epstein class, but I’m going to tell you, this call is coming from inside the house and the Epstein class is on stage right now and it’s you,” Collins said.
In New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, an outside group released an ad accusing Democratic candidate Deb Haaland of accepting a ride on Epstein’s private jet and taking “tens of thousands of dollars from Epstein businesses” and then “asking for more”.
Haaland did not fly on Epstein’s jet, but did take a flight booked by one of Epstein’s companies in 2014. Haaland has said she was unaware the chartered flight was owned by an Epstein-owned company.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Houthi attack on Riyadh airport forces swift rethink of Trump’s new strategy
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month.
The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Saturday. It was to blame what he described as “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – on the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying his attacks on Russian oil refineries were the cause. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms.
In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska.
Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold.
For all the talk of the Gulf becoming responsible for its own security, it is doubtful that Saudi Arabia can be left to fend for itself after the carnage in Riyadh. One of the the 12 dead is an American and there may be more among the severely injured. Something is clearly wrong with Saudi defences since the Houthis are firing rockets from 500 miles away, and they are reaching their target too often.
The US has had a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, and once the hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis recommenced in the summer, the pact was quietly renewed. Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Can he spurn them three times? The pressure to act as allies are expected to may prove overwhelming.
But “the blame Zelenskyy, trade with Russia” strategy is anyway unlikely to work. The amount of additional diesel Vladimir Putin will put on the market is not enough to bring down prices at the pump. Russia accounted for about 12% of global diesel shipped by sea. Exports have fallen by about a third, according to calculations by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
The deal has also reawakened Europe’s worst fears about Trump’s relationship with Russia only weeks after Congress had passed a sanctions package against Moscow authorising Trump to penalise buyers of Russian energy.
Europeans know full well that the inflation problem helping to drive populism is caused by the Iran war and not by Zelenskyy’s tactics. The only question is who will say so. The former UK Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson did not hold back, writing: “It is sickening that the USA is now lifting sanctions on Russian fuel, and transparently ridiculous to blame Ukraine for the spike in prices that obviously began with the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Putin is murdering innocent Ukrainian civilians every day. The Ukrainians are fighting for their lives. And yet the White House is apparently determined to force American drivers to bankroll Putin’s slaughter.”
The German education minister and a member of the CDU, Karin Prien, said: “For a few litres of diesel. What moral bankruptcy.”
Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general and Trump ally, will this week travel to Estonia, one of the countries most supportive of Ukraine. He will have some explaining to do. Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, vowed that EU foreign ministers on Monday will impose the biggest package of sanctions in its history, and he, along with Sweden, now wants to revisit using frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine.
What is worse, it looks as if the political damage to the Republicans caused by the Iran war is irrecoverable. Polls show the ship has sailed. The war has already been weaponised as a pocketbook issue by every Democratic candidate in every TV debate. Republican candidates, challenged to disown the war, are scrambling for the relative safety of identity politics.
The Iranians are also trying to maximise the damage they cause in the strait of Hormuz, countering the Trump narrative that the blockade has been broken. Scenes of tankers on fire are proliferating.
So Trump post-Riyadh needs to rethink. He can rejoin the war against the Houthis, ending the unilateral US ceasefire, but, if so, he knows from experience this will be costly. The first three weeks of the war against Iran cost $1n a day. Many of the US president’s advisers say he may as well also attack Iran, the Houthis’ backers, as Tehran expects him to do. The Iranian military nevertheless still believes it has escalation dominance, and what happened in Riyadh can be repeated across the Gulf.
The alternative is that his team can negotiate discreetly and indirectly with Tehran as is occurring in Doha. Some Iranians are urging their leadership to seize the chance, arguing Trump is uniquely vulnerable in the run-up to the midterms.
A deal could be done, including on uranium enrichment, but it would not be palatable for the US – or for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election chances.
China and Russia are trying to sort out the Houthis diplomatically, but the Houthi objectives are broadening, while the south of Yemen is split about its future inside the country, a division that harms the country’s ability to be the ground component that Saudi Arabia needs to supplement its air-power dominance. Taiz, the third city of Yemen, is struggling to overcome a Houthi siege. The Saudis can deliver retribution, but retribution is not a solution to a decade-long civil war.
So for the moment the twin Trump strategy – to park the Iran and Yemen conflicts while blaming Zelenskyy – is now so transparent, so morally craven, and in its own terms so ineffective, that it looks unsustainable. The only question is whether the strategy will be jettisoned by the president or instead just rejected by the American people at the ballot box.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
John Healey is poised to tax Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget, to help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, the Guardian understands.
The chancellor is in Bangkok, where the International Monetary Fund has praised the UK’s progress towards balancing the books, urging him to “stay the course”.
To keep the Treasury’s deficit reduction plans on track in the face of rising government borrowing costs, the Guardian understands Healey has decided to tap the financial sector for additional revenue.
One option understood to be under discussion – reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt – would raise upwards of £2bn a year.
Lenders have been logging strong earnings on the back of rising interest rates, with the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group – alone having generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years.
Thinktanks and trade unions have repeatedly urged Healey to tax Britain’s banks more heavily, an option considered but rejected by his predecessor Rachel Reeves, who was wary of deterring future investment.
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), said: “Britain’s big four banks are making a billion pounds a week, while bonuses have hit a post-crash record. These are bumper profits, driven by high interest rates and households’ mortgage misery. It’s time to make sure banks pay their fair share.”
Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, Healey praised the banks as crucial to supporting economic growth. “People too often see them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects,” he said.
But he is nevertheless believed to be minded to increase the surcharge banks pay on their profits, over and above corporation tax. Industry figures believe that will probably mean raising the surcharge back to 8%, from 3% at present.
The UK’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as bond markets have responded to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the Middle East conflict.
Analysts have suggested that could as much as halve the £24bn cushion Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules at the time of the spring forecast in March.
Healey is understood to be willing to accept a narrower “headroom”, but is also keen to convince bond markets he is wedded to deficit reduction.
Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against tax rises since narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. UK bosses of lenders including HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and Santander met Healey last week but were given no reassurance that bank tax hikes had been ruled out.
 
 
 Their lobby groups – including UK Finance and TheCityUK – wrote to Healey days later, saying that on top of “weakening investors confidence and damaging UK attractiveness”, higher taxes would force them to move staff and business out of the country.
 
 
 That echoed warnings by the chief executive of JP Morgan, Jamie Dimon, who said in May he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks. News of the tower – which will house more than half of the US investment bank’s 23,000 UK staff – was came days after Reeves spared the sector further tax rises in her 2025 autumn budget.
One industry source said banks were resigned to a rise in the surcharge. They believe Healey is minded to reverse Hunt’s cut – taking it back to 8% – but not go further. Such a move would raise £2.25bn a year, according to analysis by the TUC.
Another industry source said they were caught off guard by the change in messaging, having come just hours after Healey hailed banks as a “jewel” in the crown of the British economy. “We’re surprised to see this following earlier comments which appeared to be more supportive of the sector.”
When asked about how much the banking industry might be able to absorb in terms of tax rises, the head of policy at TheCityUK, John Godfrey, said banks “do not want to get into debating the menu of taxation. The fact is that we don’t want to eat in that restaurant.”
Healey has also been “listening to representations” from specialist banks, including Revolut and Shawbrook, that want the profit threshold at which the surcharge kicks in to be raised from £100m to £500m.
One government source said Labour was mindful of the UK needing to offer a positive environment for startup banks, especially the lending they offered to small businesses.
The TUC has lobbied for a much more punitive increase, to 16%, saying that could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years.
Healey said he wanted his first budget as chancellor to give “breathing space” to both consumers and businesses in the face of rising energy prices.
There will be little additional funding for other Whitehall departments, however, which he stressed would have to stick to the budgets Reeves set out at her spending review in June 2025.
“It’s important that they do manage within what they’ve got, and it’s part of the job,” Healey said. “You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things, or more.”
The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said Reeves’s plans could result in real-terms spending cuts for some departments in the later years of the spending review period.
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, used a visit to a financial services firm in Edinburgh on Thursday to caution against further banking tax rises, saying the sector already faced a higher effective tax rate than in many other big global financial centres.
Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Britain needs growth. But a raid on the financial services sector will stifle it. Labour should be backing businesses and wealth-creators, not making their lives even harder. Rather than hiking taxes yet again, Labour should cut spending.”
As well as an energy support package for households and businesses, Healey’s first budget is expected to set out more details of plans to devolve income tax to mayoralties, and explain how the government will fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced by Keir Starmer before he stepped down as prime minister.
Healey is expected to duck the longer-term question of when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence, the issue over which he resigned as defence secretary in June, contributing to Starmer’s downfall.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
AI companies have told ministers they have 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.
Successive dry summers and rising energy bills are increasing public scrutiny of plans for the huge computer warehouses that are used to train and run AI models, says a submission to the Labour government from a group including the AI infrastructure companies Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco.
Amid increasing anti-datacentre activism in the US and Europe, they are calling on ministers to create a “compact” that would show how communities can benefit from hosting datacentres, including allowing councils that host them to retain more tax revenues.
The move by the Sovereign AI Leadership (SAIL) taskforce reflects rising concern among tech companies that arguments that have blocked datacentre developments in parts of the US are taking hold in Britain. Microsoft has promised to invest $30bn (£22bn) in UK AI infrastructure.
Microsoft has built a datacentre in Acton, London and another is under construction in Newport, but wants to build several more facilities and is engaging with local and national leaders, including the prime minister, Andy Burnham, over the balance between the potential benefit of AI to the economy and public opposition to datacentres.
The SAIL group said: “In the United States, organised local opposition has stopped fully permitted datacentre projects, and moratoriums have been announced even in states that are otherwise pro-growth.
“Reporting from those places shows that AI itself is only a surface-level concern; distrust of corporate and government promises, fear of stranded assets and electricity costs run deeper. The same arguments have begun to appear here.”
It added: “Britain has a window – we think of roughly 12 months – to build a compact that earns public consent before that pattern takes hold.”
The taskforce is calling for the government to create a clear framework for councils and mayors to follow that will set out recommended terms for local benefit, including an indicative contribution – likely to be financial or in terms of facilities – scaled to a site’s size.
Opposition to datacentre construction is being fuelled by widening public concern about the safety of AI systems, after a summer in which some of the largest companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google appeared to lose control of some of their most cutting-edge AIs. Some protesters have begun resorting to direct action and the membership of anti-AI campaign groups has been growing rapidly.
The datacentre companies are determined to head off that opposition. The chair of the SAIL taskforce, Steve Rigby, said: “By establishing a clear prosperity compact between government, industry and local communities, we can build the infrastructure we need, equip our workforce with future-ready skills, and ensure Britain’s digital destiny. This taskforce’s goal isn’t another strategy document, but high-impact actions that materially accelerate the UK’s transition to an AI-enabled economy.”
It has not calculated the cost to central government finances if councils that grant permission to datacentres are allowed to keep all of their business rates.
Responding to the proposals, Joseph Miller, the director of PauseAI UK, which campaigns for a global pause to datacentre buildout, said: “People are going to feel it is undignified to be bought off by huge tech companies who do not share their interests.”
He said tech companies were “absolutely right to be worried” about US-style public opposition to datacentres growing in the UK. Kat Jones, the director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland, which campaigns against datacentres, said tech companies had already “missed the boat on containing community opposition to hyperscale AI datacentres”.
“In Scotland, we have 15 community campaigns already working incredibly hard opposing these environmentally destructive developments locally, and a growing national campaign,” she said. “Even the titanic lobbying efforts of US big tech are going to find it a real challenge to change the winds of public opinion, which have already shifted solidly against hyperscale AI datacentres.”
Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at the tech equity campaign Foxglove, said: “Big tech firms have spent years trying to force vast, highly polluting datacentres through the planning system under a blanket of secrecy and misleading information. Now, with the public waking up to the fact that these facilities plunder resources and wreck the climate, the US tech giants have decided that there’s a problem.”
He warned that incentivising councils to back datacentres by allowing them to keep more of their business rate revenue would mean “these wealthy tech giants would not pay a penny more” while boosts to council funding would “come from the pocket of central government services like the NHS”.
A government spokesperson said datacentres “should create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built, as well as prioritising clean power, using water responsibly”.
“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes,” they said. “We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on the Liberal Democrats: now is not the time to change leader | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Will the first victim of the political conference season be the Liberal Democrats’ Sir Ed Davey? It might seem quixotic, given that he is the most successful liberal parliamentary leader in a century. Yet a meeting of Lib Dem MPs on Tuesday night could see them collect the 18 signatures needed for a confidence vote. It’s hard to see what a putsch would achieve, apart from giving the party’s opponents a stick to beat it with. That may be the point: weakening Sir Ed in an internal war of attrition so that he walks away would be easier than removing him via a no-confidence vote passed by a majority of all Lib Dem MPs.
“Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake,” said Napoleon Bonaparte. With populists slipping in the polls, Lib Dem plotters should remember this, especially as Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives are looking to advance at the Lib Dems’ expense. The Tory economic pitch is to end the 60% marginal tax rate on earnings between £100,000 and £125,000, and let couples pass on the family home plus another £1m tax-free. It’s a clear bid to win back affluent southern voters in England’s “yellow wall”.
In the face of such an offensive, Sir Ed’s £17bn tax giveaway looks like a pre-emptive strike aimed at disillusioned Tory voters. His strategy has its detractors. Discontent has moved over the past year from private complaints to public criticism from council leaders, and frontbench resignations last week. At the heart of the row is how the Lib Dems turn their MPs into a more potent force. Sir Ed wants to expand from the party’s geographic base, mobilise tactical voters and firmly establish the Lib Dems in seats they can win as the best bet to stop a rightwing government headed by Reform UK.
His opponents argue that parliamentary heft counts for little if voters barely notice it. Critics point to polling saying that Lib Dems don’t “own” any one issue. It’s true that the Lib Dem leader has trained his fire on the Tories and Reform, not Labour. But that’s no bad thing. Sir Ed’s team pointedly argue that a more populist strategy would be as exhilarating as a plane in a nosedive. Just ask the Greens: no one knows if their pilot will be able to pull out before hitting the ground.
An upmarket Gail’s bakery on the high street is the best predictor of a Lib Dem vote. It marks the party’s affluent electorate: Lib Dems hold five of Britain’s 10 most prosperous seats, but just seven in the poorest half. For the Lib Dems, taking chunks out of Labour in their urban strongholds at the next election simply helps Reform by splitting the opposition. Sir Ed’s pro-Europeanism is a selling point. Although Mrs Badenoch denies it, the Tories and Reform could form a “marriage of convenience” coalition to run the country after the next election. Sir Ed’s strategy may be low-key, but it is ruthlessly efficient: the party’s 3.7m votes won 11 seats in 2019, whereas 3.5m votes won 72 seats in 2024. The Lib Dems must help to keep the right out of Downing Street. Sir Ed’s critics risk handing the Tories and Reform the keys to No 10 by chasing headlines rather than seats.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: John Healey pledges to use budget to harness power of AI to bolster Britain’s security
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
John Healey has pledged to use Wednesday’s budget to harness the power of artificial intelligence to bolster Britain’s security and prosperity against the risks in the accelerating global technology arms race.
As he prepares for his debut budget, the chancellor said that Andy Burnham’s government would commit hundreds of millions of pounds to develop a “distinctively British” approach to AI that would capitalise on the benefits of the frontier technology.
At a fork in the road as AI developments pose both existential threats and transformative economic potential, Healey said he would be making the biggest ever investment to guard against cyber risks and the disruptive potential of the technology.
As part of the measures in his tax and spending statement, he promised fresh investment for Britain’s AI Security Institute and other critical institutions, alongside allocating public money to support the use of the technology for good.
“AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school and every aspect of our economy can benefit,” Healey said.
“I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI – one that doesn’t leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country.”
Three months into Burnham’s premiership, Healey is poised to deliver a budget against an increasingly volatile backdrop as the war in the Middle East sends shock waves through the global economy, putting pressure on public finances and reigniting the cost of living crisis.
The chancellor has vowed to use his first budget to provide households and businesses with “breathing space” as the global surge in energy costs triggered by the war hits millions of families this winter. On Friday, the latest tensions in the Gulf sent the oil price to its highest level for six months, rising above $117 a barrel at one point.
However he will also use the opportunity afforded by the critical speech to the Commons to flesh out Burnham’s policy priorities for government after he replaced Keir Starmer this summer, and to spell out a vision for Britain amid the increasingly turbulent global economic outlook.
Aiming to harness the opportunities of AI to raise living standards, back UK businesses and support economic growth, the chancellor said he wanted to seize the opportunities of the technology as a central plank of Labour’s plan for growth.
It comes after official figures show AI investment has helped the UK outperform gloomy economic forecasts as the Iran war pushes up inflation and drags down business confidence, powering the country to the strongest growth performance in the G7 in the first half of this year.
However, there are growing fears over the security of the nation and critical industries as the technology opens up the danger of cyber-attacks, IT systems turning rogue and devastating job losses as companies invest in machines rather than humans.
It comes as websites around the globe went dark this week after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web, in a development made possible by rapid AI advances. It also emerged this week that Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of cost-saving plans identified by bosses as the rollout of AI across the bank helps it make efficiency gains.
Healey said he wanted to use his budget to protect against risks while also nurturing homegrown businesses and talent, in order to cut Britain’s dependency on other countries that were also making strides in AI technology.
New investments would be made in AI chip design capability in Edinburgh, alongside a new AI Centre of Excellence in Manchester that it said would enable the UK to harness the technology’s benefits.
The government would also spend £10m a year to lead the UK’s work on understanding how AI will reshape jobs and industry, aiming to address concerns about potential job disruption.
As part of the plan the Treasury said it would back up to £300m in public-private investment in a new AI Biosecurity Lab, designed to serve as a world-leading institution bringing together scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats.
It comes after the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, warned on Thursday that UK households should make preparations against the mounting risks from weather, cyber or other serious emergencies.
The advice to stock up on supplies to last 72 hours, in a campaign called Be Ready, comes as Silicon Valley bosses sound the alarm over the increasingly existential threats AI could pose, and amid growing official concern over the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.
Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said: “I’m proud the UK has repeatedly been at the forefront of global efforts to use AI for the benefit of humankind.
“Today’s investment will help the UK seize the opportunities AI presents to strengthen our national security, while staying one step ahead of those who seek to use AI to do us harm.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump tells Iowa rally crowd he encouraged Ramaswamy to keep running widely criticized campaign ad – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
'You’ve got to ride with it'. Trump says he encouraged Ramaswamy to keep running ad featuring Acton's estranged mother
Speaking in Iowa on Thursday, Donald Trump told supporters that he had personally encouraged Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for Ohio governor, to keep running an attack ad featuring the mother of his Democratic rival, Dr Amy Acton, who had lost custody of her daughter at age 12 because her husband was charged with raping the young girl.
“They did an ad of the mother saying the daughter is incompetent, a liar and disgusting unreliable person,” Trump said, adding some claims that were not, in fact, in the ad.
“My mom would not say that about me - even if she believed it,” the president added, making light of the testimony of a woman who sided with the man charged with raping her own 12-year-old daughter.
“When I first saw it, I said, ‘Wow, that means Vivek easily will win the race’. And then I got a call from Vivek,” Trump said. “He said, ‘What would you recommend? Because I’m getting killed in the press.’ Why? He said, ‘Because they think I should immediately take the ad off.’”
“The mother said horrible things about your opponent,” Trump said. “I said, ‘You’ve got to ride with it’”.
The president made no mention of the fact that the Republican Senate candidate he was there to support, Ashley Hinson, denounced the ad earlier on Thursday. “I think it’s absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down,” Hinson told ABC News ahead of Trump’s appearance.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:

Iowa Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson broke with the president by denouncing the attack ad, saying: “I think it’s absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down.”
Attorney general Todd Blanche did not rule it out a scenario in which the justice department would try to block states from certifying midterm election results.
… or at least the stage, exiting to the live-blogger’s favorite tune, YMCA. The president just wrapped up 90 minutes of remarks, saying very little that he has not said before, but he did devote an extended portion of the speech to defending the attack ad his ally, Vivek Ramaswamy, is running in Ohio, to the dismay of many Republicans, including Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson – the person Trump was there to promote.
'I am, really, on the ballot', Trump says, without offering to resign if Republicans lose the midterms
“I’m asking you to pretend that I’m running… pretend I’m on the ballot,” Donald Trump told supporters in Iowa on Thursday, as he has at each stop on his “midterm blitz”.
“Remember, I’m on the ballot,” he said later in the speech. “Because I am on the ballot. Really, it’s our stuff, it’s going to be taken away. If we if we don’t win, it’s going to be taken away. So I am, really, on the ballot.”
Of course, if the president really wanted to make the midterms a referendum on himself, he could take a page from the leaders of parliamentary democracies and pledge to resign from office should Republicans lose the House and Senate, something he has not done.

Describing cognitive test, Trump recites math problem he claims he solved, but does not provide the answer
As he frequently does at campaign rallies, Donald Trump boasted to supporters in Iowa on Thursday that he “aced” what he called “an aptitude test” that is, in fact, a screening for mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer’s disease.
While the test does include a short test of basic mathematical ability, in which patients are asked to perform serial subtraction by 7 starting at 60, Trump claimed on Thursday that the mathematical test was much more complicated.
“The first question easy. The second question is easy. And by the time you get up to number 30, there are many people that can answer those questions. I’ll tell you,” the president said.
“They’ll say like: ‘Take a number, any number’. Say, 49, ‘triple it’, and they go pretty much in this speed, ‘triple it and divide by four; add 2,019; subtract 87; divide by three; multiply by nine. What is the number?’”
As supporters shouted out numbers, Trump just asserted that he solved the problem without saying what the answer is. “Not a lot of people are going to be able to do that,” Trump said. “Not a lot. I did it. I did it three times,” the president said.
The president has given similarly detailed descriptions of mathematical problems he says were on the test, and claims to have solved, in previous speeches, but never once provided an answer.
“These are tough questions, you know,” Trump told elderly supporters at The Villages in Florida in May. “They say, ‘Take a number, any number.’ Okay, I’ll take 99. ‘Multiply times nine.’ Okay. ‘Divide it by three.’ Good. ‘Add 4,293.’ That’s good. ‘Divide by two; subtract 93; divide by nine. What is your answer?’ Now they go a little slower than that, but not much. I don’t want to waste a lot of time, but there aren’t a lot of people that get it right. I got it right.”
Trump tosses conspiracy theories about Ilhan Omar to Iowa crowd, prompting chants of 'Lock her up!'
Despite the fact that he is in Iowa, ostensibly to support Republican candidates, Donald Trump quickly turned to attacks on two candidates running in other states, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, repeating false claims he has made before about two prominent Muslim Americans.
Making no effort to conceal the anti-Muslim racism and fear-mongering he has put at the center of his pitch to Republican voters, Trump claimed that El-Sayed is “a jihadist”.
He then recited multiple falsehoods about Omar, including the false claims that she married her brother and that she told an interviewer this week that she did not, “as far as I know”, which she did not.
Trump begins Iowa rally in support of Republican candidates with heaps of praise for himself
Donald Trump started speaking, about 40 minutes late, to supporters in Sioux City, Iowa on Thursday by boasting about how well he had done in the state in his own three runs for office.
Unusually, the president acknowledged that his term in office is drawing (slowly) to a close. “You know, we only have a little more than two years left. Can you believe it?” Trump said, before adding: “But I’m going to have a lot of power when I leave.”
He then turned to reciting a litany of lies about Josh Turek, the Democrat running against Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, casting him as a supporter of “taxpayer-funded transgender brutalization surgeries and in favor of men in girls bathrooms.”
Lebron James mimed a golf swing and took an imaginary jump shot, as the national anthem was performed during Tuesday’s Philadelphia 76ers and New York Knicks match-up. His gestures provoked the ire of Donald Trump, who berated him as “no good” and a “TOTAL DISGRACE” on social media.
“LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!” Trump wrote in a Wednesday Truth Social post.
The NBA star and Trump have been at odds for several years.
In 2017, Trump rescinded a White House invitation to the Golden State Warriors, after Stephen Curry indicated he would not want to go. James famously called Trump a “bum,” saying his presidency took away from the customary honor.
The feud appeared to rekindle this summer, when in July, Trump suggested James was a “racist,” without much further explanation, after being asked to compare his career to that of Michael Jordan’s.
As Trump travels to Iowa, Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson denounced Ohio ad he supports
Donald Trump is expected to speak soon at a rally in Sioux City, Iowa in support of Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, who broke with the president on Thursday by denouncing an attack ad he has supported in the Ohio governor race.
As Trump defended the ad, from Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, in which the estranged mother of the Democratic candidate, Dr Amy Acton, calls her daughter “a liar”, Hinson joined the bipartisan backlash against the ad triggered by the fact that Acton was removed from her mother’s custody at age 12, after her stepfather was charged with raping her.
In an interview ahead of today’s rally, Hinson was asked by Jonathan Karl of ABC News about the ad from Ramaswamy’s campaign. “It’s terrible,” Hinson said. “I think about it as a mom, and you think about kid surviving childhood sexual abuse and having to relive that trauma on TV again. I think it’s absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down.”
Hinson also called the comment from vice-president JD Vance, that he was disgusted by Republican criticism of the ad, “ridiculous”.
“Again, I think it’s wrong and should come down.”
Hinson, who currently represents Iowa in the House, is campaigning to replace Republican senator Joni Ernst, who revealed in 2019 that she was a survivor of sexual assault who had been raped in college.
Hinson spoke at the rally on Thursday about 90 minutes before Trump’s schedule arrival time.
Student IDs will not be accepted at New Hampshire polls, Supreme Court rules
Uwa Ede-Osifo
The US supreme court ruled on Thursday that New Hampshire students cannot use their school-issued ID cards as proof of identity to vote, handing a victory to the state’s Republicans.
The high court cited a previous ruling, “lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election,” in its decision to keep intact an April state law that struck high school and college IDs from a list of acceptable voter documents. House Bill 323, signed by New Hampshire’s Republican governor, Kelly Ayotte, requires government-issued IDs, such as a passport or driver license.
The Coalition for Open Democracy, a New Hampshire-based nonprofit, had sued to block the legislation, arguing that it raised unconstitutional barriers for the state’s young voting bloc.
Republican legislators nationwide have embraced stricter voter ID laws, framing them as a safeguard against alleged voter fraud. Voting rights groups have argued that the narrow range of acceptable forms of identification disenfranchises millions of voters.
According to the Brennan Center, “more than 49 million American adults don’t possess an unexpired driver’s license with their current name and address. Seniors, people of color, people with disabilities, low-income voters, and students are especially likely to lack such documents.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Mahmood’s migration changes may harm women and children, Labour MP warns
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Shabana Mahmood’s changes to the migration system could harm women and children, a Labour MP has warned, as members of her own party continue to raise concerns with the home secretary’s proposals.
Olivia Bailey, the chair of the women and equalities committee, has written to Mahmood warning about the possible damage that could be done by plans to make it harder for migrants to achieve settled status in the UK.
Mahmood has said the changes are designed to deter both economic migrants and asylum seekers from coming to the UK, and to minimise the impact on British taxpayers of those who are already here.
The home secretary softened the proposed rules for care workers and their families on Monday after unions, cabinet members and backbench Labour MPs voiced their concerns.
But many in the Labour party and in the charitable sector are still unhappy with the plans, claiming they are unfair to those who have already arrived in the country, and risk pushing people into destitution.
Writing on behalf of the committee, which is dominated by Labour MPs, Bailey wrote: “The committee is particularly concerned about the implications for children and young people whose parents are now on significantly longer routes to settlement, including on refugee routes. We heard compelling evidence of potentially adverse impacts on children, not least where the parent is on a longer route to settlement.”
She warned against plans to including children in more rigorous testing of migrants’ claims of having been trafficked. And she called on Mahmood to make it easier for victims of domestic abuse to get settled status.
Calling for a full impact assessment of what the changes might mean for equality, she added: “Witnesses at our evidence session raised concerns that the cumulative impact of these changes is likely to have a disproportionate equalities impact, in particular on race, class and sex.”
The Home Office has been contacted for comment.
Earlier on Thursday, the Refugee Council accused the home secretary of causing “distress and uncertainty” to hundreds of thousands of refugees by quietly introducing plans to force them to wait up to 30 years before getting the right to settle.
The Refugee Council said Mahmood’s hardening of plans came despite her personal reassurances last year that only “illegal entrants who are not refugees will face a 30-year wait for settlement”.
In a further tightening of the rules, a cohort of 200,000 successful asylum applicants who were told they could apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years will now face reviews of their status every 30 months.
Refugees who arrive by irregular means, for example, by small boat, will face a 30-year wait for settlement in the UK under the new plans.
Last year’s consultation included a proposal that people who arrived irregularly would face a 10-year penalty for having done so. However, this was not expected to apply to those who had been granted refugee status.
An explanatory memo at the time said: “Adults and accompanied and unaccompanied children granted five years’ leave as a result of an asylum claim or further submissions made by 1 March 2026 will remain eligible to apply for settlement after five years.”
In a social media post last year, Mahmood said: “Illegal entrants who are not refugees will face a 30-year wait for settlement.”
That guarantee has been quietly dropped in the small print of the government’s latest immigration plan which was released on Monday.
Instead a footnote says: “Those refugees, not on safe and legal routes, who claimed asylum before 2 March 2026 will move to core protection.”
 
 
 Under the Home Office’s core protection scheme, adults and their children receive an initial period of only 30 months of permission to stay, which must then be renewed. If conditions in their home country are considered safe, their refugee status can be revoked.
Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “Keeping changing positions on what refugees should expect will cause distress and huge uncertainty. Thousands of refugees who thought they were just weeks or months away from being able to access settlement could now have to wait for another 25 years.
“It is impossible to expect people to start new lives while living with a temporary status that expires every 30 months for 30 years. That’s decades of fear and uncertainty for people who have already faced war, conflict and persecution and simply want to be safe here.
“These plans will also cause chaos for the Home Office, which will now have decades of repeated extra applications to process at enormous cost to the public purse.
Responding to the Refugee Council’s analysis, the Home Office said there had been no policy change since last year’s proposals but declined to comment further on Mahmood’s comments on X or the footnote in the Home Office’s recent document.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ICE agent who crashed into man in Texas was targeting suspect who died years ago, family says
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A federal officer slammed a vehicle into a Houston construction worker and broke his leg, believing him to be a man who apparently died years ago, the dead man’s family said on Friday, further calling into question the account given by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
The worker, 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez of Mexico, remains hospitalized with multiple leg fractures and needs reconstructive ankle surgery, according to FIEL, a Houston-based immigration advocacy group. At a news conference on Friday, the group said the alleged suspect’s family had shared documentation proving his death.
After the episode on 10 October, ICE said in a statement that officers had observed a suspect they were targeting, identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, enter a vehicle with Parra Hernandez.
But on Friday, Rafael Lemaitre, spokesperson with the Harris county district attorney’s office, told the Associated Press that Mendoza-Cervantes was not in that vehicle.
ICE did not respond to requests for comment on Friday.
“ICE is lying,” said Cesar Espinosa, FIEL’s executive director. “Either somebody is not telling the truth or all of a sudden these two ICE agents have developed a sixth sense and are able to see dead people.”
ICE released a photo of a man it identified as Mendoza-Cervantes. But the man in the photo is actually Jose Hector Jimenez, who died years ago while being pursued by federal immigration authorities as he was trying to re-enter the US, according to FIEL.
The man’s daughter provided his death certificate from the Mexican government, which has been turned over to the district attorney, Espinosa told the AP. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) did not respond to a request for comment.
Jimenez’s daughter, Jamie Jimenez, did not respond to requests for comment from the AP. Her husband, Andres Rendon, confirmed to the AP that Jimenez was his wife’s deceased father.
Criminal charges against the ICE officer who drove the vehicle are being considered by Harris county district attorney Sean Teare, who has said surveillance footage contradicts ICE’s claim that Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the vehicle.
The video shows a black SUV speeding over a median and driving toward a man who is running away. The video does not show the car hitting him – that view is blocked by another vehicle – but it shows the SUV inches from the fleeing man. The video then shows him on the ground.
US House member Sylvia Garcia, a Democrat who represents Houston, said that ICE appears to be lying about what happened.
“If ICE was pursuing a man who died years ago, it raises serious questions about how these operations are being carried out and whether agents are even verifying who they’re looking for before putting people’s lives at risk,” Garcia said in a statement to the AP. “It’s outrageous – but frankly, not surprising.”
ICE has been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for its aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.
Just in 2026, the second year since Trump returned to the White House, more than 30 people have died during interactions with immigration officials, the Guardian reported in late September.
Parra Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, told reporters that her client was suffering from depression in federal custody, especially after learning that he was not the target of the operation.
“This never should have happened in the first place,” Bruno said.
Miguel’s brother, Roberto Parra, said the two would work construction all day together and he just wants his brother treated with humanity. He said Parra Hernandez has a family to support, and his only crime was coming to a country out of necessity.
FIEL is seeking Parra Hernandez’s release before he is moved from a hospital to a federal detention center.
Nidia Delfín, the sister of Luis Enrique Delfín, who was detained in the ICE vehicle that hit Parra Hernandez, called for her brother’s release from federal custody so he could serve as a witness.
“He’s still very concerned, still very afraid,” she said. “He’s not the same guy that was out” before Parra Hernandez was struck on 10 October.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Canva layoffs: design giant to cut or relocate more than 1,200 jobs in major restructure
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Canva is cutting or relocating more than 1,200 jobs, representing 22% of its global workforce, as part of a major restructure that includes laying off staff who helped build the Australian-founded design platform.
The changes mirror a trend across the technology sector, where software companies are fighting to stay competitive against cheaper artificial intelligence disrupters while aggressively embedding AI tools themselves.
Canva’s chief executive, Melanie Perkins, said in an email to staff on Wednesday that the restructure was “without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history”.
“For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs,” she said. “Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today.”
The restructure will affect 1,271 people, according to the company, as it focuses on “collapsing layers” and bringing “more teams together in person”.
“We know relocating is a big decision for those being asked to consider it, and we’re committed to making the process as smooth as possible with comprehensive support,” said Perkins, who did not specify the exact number of job losses.
Those leaving Canva will receive at least six months of salary and retain healthcare coverage for a further 12 months in countries where workers receive that benefit. They can also keep their laptops.
Those leaving can also apply for US$10,000 (A$14,000) grants to start their own ventures.
The graphic design company is one of Australia’s most successful startups and has long been touted as a candidate for a blockbuster listing on the Nasdaq.
But it has now added to a wave of restructures in the technology sector, which has included 1,600 redundancies at the software company Atlassian, and job losses at Afterpay’s owner, Block, and at WiseTech Global, another software company.
While established software companies have rejected the threat of a “SaaS-pocalypse”, a term used to describe the idea that AI becomes so advanced that specialised software becomes redundant, many have overhauled their business models in response or aggressively adopted AI tools.
Unlike Atlassian, Block and WiseTech, Canva did not mention AI in its restructure announcement.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: When you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month matters  | Hugh Muir
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Pity Black History Month UK, assailed on all sides. Those on the right seek to end the celebration on the basis that it amounts to special treatment for a group that doesn’t deserve it. History should be colour-blind: society should not differentiate, they say. We are not racist, we just want fairness. But often, they are – and they really don’t.
On the other side of the argument are the progressives, notably minority progressives, who say the idea of a month to consider Black history is demeaning because it should already have a year-round place in our teaching and consciousness. There is a further view that any beneficial effect the month once had has been diluted by unimaginative repetition and commercially motivated virtue signalling. Players taking the knee in the Premier League? Been there, done that: yawn!
I have long taken the glass-half-full approach. The ideal would be for Black history to be incorporated into the social and educational culture – and perhaps one day it will be. But in the meantime, I’ll take a mandated, month-long focus on the Black contribution to the way our society has evolved. And it seems very necessary this year, when the very notion of belonging in Britain and other major western countries has been so under attack.
A year in which we have clearly seen that a political party, with pretensions to lead the country, attracts activists with ugly racist and nativist views – at national and local level – with the same efficiency that magnets attract iron filings. Our expectations are different now. When transcripts of the things Reform folk say in private reach the public domain, the old-fashioned Tory dog-whistle seems comparatively quaint.
This is a year in which we have again seen the confidence and daring of those who cuddle close to pseudo-scientific theories asserting white superiority and black inferiority. The racial eugenicists are back from the fringes, championed down their venal path by Donald Trump, whose leadership of the free world gladhands nativists, targets Black officials and routinely belittles Black enemies as “low IQ”.
It’s been a year in which toxic politics and the mainstreaming of intolerance – against minorities of many categories – has led to racist unpleasantness on our streets and in the workplace. There is a snapshot from the Royal College of Nursing: racist abuse of NHS nurses – including use of the N-word – up 86% in the recent past. All part of what one NHS official called “a rising tide of racism”.
Another snapshot of the increasingly hostile environment is from parliament. What happened, via social media, when Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy posted a video in support of Black History Month? Vile abuse, of course: “Some of a kind that I had not necessarily seen in that volume before. I had people calling me the N-word, people telling me to eff-off and go back to where I came from, and people sending monkey photographs.”
Another snapshot from Chichester, Sussex, where a diverse group of actors recently went to perform A Midsummer Night’s Dream and were shamefully menaced. “I don’t know if I have witnessed and/or experienced as much racism, xenophobia and homophobia as I saw in those six weeks,” said the actor and comedian Munya Chawawa. Britain is a good place. The vast majority of our fellow citizens are decent and kind. But it’s now easy, far too easy, to unwittingly enter hostile territory.
So in years like this, when there are obvious, concerted, targeted, and well-funded attempts to undermine Black people and the Black experience – not least the targeting of books by Black authors by “anti woke” crusaders – it becomes more difficult to be sanguine about concepts such as Black History Month. It then becomes a good thing, perhaps an essential one, to remember and to highlight – if only over a calendar month – who we are, who has shaped us and how we have indisputably helped to shape Britain as a vibrant, diverse, first world power.
Today, at the end of this Black History Month, Guardian Opinion has asked Black Britons representing four generations to tell us how their own Black British identities have evolved, for we have been here long enough now to compare notes on the different stages of our lives on this island. A twentysomething sees the joy and pain of being here very differently to their elderly siblings, to their parents, to their grandparents.
Call it reflection with a purpose. In a time like this, it seems more vital than ever to know who we were, who we are – and the foundations on which we all stand.
- 
  Hugh Muir is executive editor, Opinion

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: AI ‘godfather’ Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
One of the “godfathers of AI”, Geoffrey Hinton, has said it could turn out that humans would have been better off never developing the technology as he warned it could trigger a large-scale incident this year or next, such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems.
The Nobel prize-winning computer scientist told the Guardian he is not a “doomer” about the technology that is underpinned by his groundbreaking research into artificial neural networks and believes AI has the potential to lead to a “wonderful future” but he said “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it”.
Hinton, 78, said that within a decade and possibly sooner, humanity will know whether it can manage the technology’s risks and enable what he called “radical abundance” or whether “we fail to manage the risks and … have a huge gap between rich and poor, huge cultural problems, massive unemployment, just society being torn apart”.
Hinton was speaking before a screening of a new feature-length documentary, AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About – a title suggested by an AI chatbot – featuring him and his former Google colleague Demis Hassabis. Hinton tells the documentary makers: “I feel I have a duty. I’ve got a reputation that makes me a spokesperson and I need to burn it all on this.”
Speaking to the Guardian, Hinton took aim at the risk-taking by the leaders of some of the major AI companies who continue to release ever more powerful AI models as they race for supremacy and market-share, saying he didn’t trust Sam Altman, the chief executive of the ChatGPT maker, OpenAI, “at all”. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a shit. They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.”
The London-born computer scientist, who grew up in Bristol and spent much of his career at the University of Toronto, said it was “extremely worrying” that Altman was in charge of one of the handful of frontier US AI companies currently leading a race with China to develop the most powerful AI. Altman insisted in September: “the world should trust we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing and because we feel the magnitude of this”.
Hinton has been working on AI for about 44 years and in the 1970s coined the concept of the neural network – a mathematical system that could learn and gain experience much like humans do. In 2023 he quit Google to speak freely about AI risks, warning: “If these things get carried away with getting more control, we’re in trouble.”
He said he viewed incidents this summer in which OpenAI AI agents conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website as akin to 1979’s partial nuclear meltdown at the Three Mile Island power station in Pennsylvania – effectively a warning shot.
“Either later this year or next year we’ll see Chornobyl, and that may be enough to make people really pay attention,” he said.
This Chornobyl-type of event would not be a nuclear incident, according to the examples he gave, but rather could include an AI-enabled attack on the electricity-generating system that “causes a massive brownout” or an incident that brings down the financial system for a week.
“Can you imagine what would happen? We could recover from it [but] that would make them sit up and take notice.”
Asked who “they” were, he said: “world leaders other than Trump”.
The US president, Donald Trump, has said he “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” to control AI and wants frontier AI companies to regulate themselves, amid concern that rules could hinder the US in its AI race with China. Hinton backs a tougher plan endorsed by the president of Finland and 32 other countries, including Singapore, Germany, Canada and Australia, for mandatory testing of frontier AI models, independent evaluation and intergovernmental common standards.
The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he will use the UK’s G20 presidency next year to seek agreement on a “single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks”.
Hinton said: “We need something like the American FDA for drugs where the companies have to give very good statistical evidence to an independent authority that [the AI model] does more good than harm before it is released. We discovered with thalidomide [a drug developed in the 1950s that caused severe birth defects] that releasing and then suing them isn’t the right way to do it. What the big tech companies are saying is treat it like we treated thalidomide.”
Hinton’s role as one of the progenitors of AI has led to comparisons to Robert Oppenheimer, who was central to the creation of nuclear weapons. One of Hinton’s friends even bought him an Oppenheimer-style hat. But he insists: “I was not Oppenheimer”, citing the thousands of other scientists also working in the same field of neural networks.
Despite his warnings, Hinton remains, on balance, hopeful that catastrophe can be averted.
“My gut is that we’re still in control,” he said. “We might well be able to do something. It’ll only work if we put a big effort into it, but we might well put a big effort into it.”
