SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The UK-EU food produce deal: what was agreed and will it affect shoppers?
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content: Lorries are parked on the motorway heading towards Dover. The new agreement will reduce paperwork and checks on exports. Photograph: Neil Hall/ReutersView image in fullscreenLorries are parked on the motorway heading towards Dover. The new agreement will reduce paperwork and checks on exports. Photograph: Neil Hall/ReutersExplainerThe UK-EU food produce deal: what was agreed and will it affect shoppers?Two sides agree deal to remove some Brexit checks on food and animal product exports to EU Andy Burnham to unveil EU trade deals worth billions of pounds The UK and the EU have finalised their deal to remove red tape for food producers and agreed first drafts on joint positions on migration, youth mobility and electricity trading before a summit on 20 November.The draft text of a joint statement has emerged 17 days before the summit, an indication of the consensual state of play between two sides previously at loggerheads during the Conservative government era.What is the overall deal on 20 November?The food deal is one of three main issues identified by the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, for his “reset” of relations with the EU.Andy Burnham promised to stick with them and the focus on food, electricity and a youth travel scheme for British and EU citizens between 18 and 30 years old.What else is in the deal?“Cooperation built on strong foundations” is the title of the draft statement which sets out plans for deeper relations on migration, the possibility of a youth mobility scheme, continued joint support for Ukraine, furthering the strong defence and security relationship and cooperation on hybrid threats such as recent drone incidents at European airports linked to Russia.What are the practical implications of the food and drinks reset?The details announced on Tuesday mean exports of fresh meat, fish, shellfish and seed potatoes, largely from Scotland, can resume without costly paperwork proving they comply with EU standards.Exporters will no longer need the £200 veterinary certificate proving their produce is safe to eat or use in the EU, nor will they need a £25 plant health certificate proving they are free of pests and diseases, paving the way for easier exports of trees, shrubs and wooden or leather goods.A youth mobility scheme will also start, possibly next year, with travellers between 18 and 30 years old able to get a special visa to work, study or simply travel.So if this is being announced on 20 November, what happened on Tuesday?The draft statement appears to show that the remaining loose ends in the food and drink deal, which was largely agreed and announced in May, was finally agreed by both sides.Negotiators are still thrashing out the details of the youth mobility scheme, with the EU insisting that the UK allow EU students study in British universities on home fees.What does it mean for exporters?In practice, the agreement will mean exporting is easier, but the food sector will be looking for substantial financial and marketing support from the UK to get British food back to the continent at scale.As the National Farmers’ Union president, Tom Bradshaw, said earlier this year: “There are no empty shelves in the EU with signs saying waiting for British products to return”. Food exports, particularly poultry and eggs, have collapsed by a third since Brexit, NFU analysis of trade data showed last month.The food deal is expected to be implemented in early 2028 as it needs legislation on the British side to align with the EU.Will shoppers notice the difference?Yes. It should mean the variety of fresh produce such as cheese from France and elsewhere is restored in British supermarkets, along with a wider range of wine.Since Brexit, supermarkets have reduced the range of fresh produce from the continent because of the red tape, while small artisan producers of cheese, wine and olive oil have stopped selling into the UK for the same reason.What about pet passports?As of April this year EU pet passports can no longer be used or held by residents in England, Scotland or Wales to travel to the EU, causing headaches for families holidaying abroad, mainly with pet dogs.Before Brexit, a single EU pet passport (issued by an authorised vet in the UK or another EU country) was valid for multiple trips into the EU, provided the pet’s rabies vaccination remained in date. Under the new agreement, this system should be restored.What about fish?Scottish salmon producers were among the first to devise a way of centralising exports to cut the red tape, but the risk of having a truckload of fresh fish being detained in Boulogne (where the fish checks take place) meant many producers of shellfish gave up.The new deal would reopen the door for exports of Scottish langoustines and molluscs that could be fished then served on restaurant plates the following day.View image in fullscreenScottish salmon. Photograph: Karen Appleyard/AlamyHow will it affect the Northern Ireland border?Checks and paperwork of fresh produce were controversially introduced on goods going from mainland Britain to Northern Ireland in a trade-off designed to ensure there were no checks on the border with the Republic of Ireland.The Democratic Unionist party vehemently opposed what they saw as a border in the Irish sea and on Tuesday said the SPS did not go far enough because it did not get rid of all checks. But it does get rid of most.The deal will bring an end to physical checks and veterinary certificates on farm produce and the “green” and “red” lanes for trucks bringing food from Great Britain. It will also mean those who sell into Northern Ireland will no longer need to label their food “not for EU”, which has been a significant problem for wholesalers.But checks on anything that comes with excise duty, such as wine and cigarettes, will continue, to prevent smuggling into the Republic of Ireland.What about youth mobility? The EU and the UK will agree a deal whether the dispute over the level of tuition fees paid by EU students who want to study in the UK is settled or not.The draft statement allows for the fees to be decoupled from the summit pact with a stated aim to conclude negotiations within six months.Explore more on these topicsBrexitEuropean UnionEuropeTrade policyexplainersShareReuse this content

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Man in custody after being found in vehicle near White House with guns
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The US secret service said a suspect has been taken into custody and charged after officers found him in a vehicle near the White House with multiple guns, claiming he heard voices in his head telling him to kill Donald Trump.
The arrest Thursday night happened after secret service officers approached a man “acting suspicious” in a parked car, according to a Homeland Security statement. US officials said the suspect – Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos – went on to describe voices in his head that were telling him to come to the nation’s capital and kill the Republican president.
Shortly after, officers discovered the suspect’s vehicle had been reported stolen and he had three firearms and dozens of rounds of ammunition. This is the latest in a series of arrests the secret service and other law enforcement agencies have made against individuals who have threatened Trump or his family members’ lives since he returned to office last year.
The statement described Chrinos as an immigrant from Venezuela who is in the country illegally after entering the US through Texas in March 2024. DHS said he had been charged and was in US Marshals Service custody.
The White House did not provide comment, instead referring to DHS and the US secret service.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Ebola cases in Kenya highlight US failures amid Trump cuts to key services
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region.
It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.
The US created a controversial quarantine center at Kenya’s Laikipia airbase, where Americans returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo would be required to quarantine. The center, opposed by locals, has stirred distrust in the Kenyan government, leading to protests and a Kenyan court ordering a halt to the center.
“Many Kenyans were concerned about the fact that there was no information and people did not know why the quarantine place was being set up, who was actually going to use it, and what had informed that,” said Allan Maleche, executive director of the Kenya Legal & Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids (Kelin). The litigation will be decided in November, he said.
In the meantime, Kenyans were “very cautious around any information that is being given by the government around Ebola”, Maleche said.
Americans who questioned whether the US has the legal authority to quarantine Americans on foreign soil and prevent them from returning home are pushing back against the quarantine center as Kenya faces its first Ebola cases.
“Is this still a viable solution for the US?” asked Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the pandemic center at Brown University school of public health. “Are we posing not only an undue burden on the Kenyan government to be able to handle this, but also is this the safest place to be bringing Americans?”
The US already has “world-class” Ebola treatment units, Nuzzo pointed out.
“American taxpayers built these units for precisely this purpose, and it’s mind-boggling to me that we’re going to leave them empty,” she said. In previous outbreaks, actively ill patients have been evacuated safely to these centers, where they have recovered without further spread of the virus.
The unease follows sweeping cuts to US health support across the world, with the demolition of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cuts to funding and staff at health agencies like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
On 1 October, the CDC closed HIV prevention offices in Angola and South Sudan, with plans to close offices in Zimbabwe. The US has slashed programs across the world – including DR Congo, where the Ebola outbreak is centered, and other countries, like Kenya, bracing for cases as the outbreak widens.
“We have had a lot of concerns after the US first cut funding for HIV promptly without any direction,” Maleche said. “It led to clinics closing. It led to a lot of anxiety among people.”
The US is now negotiating bilateral agreements with each country, including Kenya – a process that has been mired in secrecy, Maleche said. “It’s not very clear what’s the plan, who’s rolling it out, and what will be involved.”
Cuts to decades-long programs mean the affected countries and the US have less insight into what’s happening, in addition to a lessened ability to prevent and stop outbreaks. “When you pull back on those, not only do you leave those countries less prepared to deal with that day-to-day threat, but it also means that they’re less prepared to deal with future emergencies,” Nuzzo said.
The US officially left the World Health Organization (WHO) in January, making it much harder to collaborate on the response to crises like these. When the US left the WHO, it also “pulled out a substantial amount of funding”, said Maleche. That means the WHO’s response had also been “weakened”, he said.
A Kenyan man fell ill in DRC before traveling by road to Uganda and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October, where he died in a hospital two days later. Since then, seven close contacts have tested positive.
Patrick Amoth, the director-general for health, confirmed on Sunday the total number of infections in the country was eight.
Kenya’s ministry of health pointed to the success of contact tracing and quarantine. About 108 people have been quarantined in Nairobi.
“The general feeling is that the contact tracing systems are working,” Maleche said. But Kenyans are also wondering why there were “many lapses” that resulted in a sick person traveling across countries. The border between DR Congo and Uganda has been closed since May. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August after earlier reporting 20 cases and two deaths.
A French doctor who returned from DR Congo in June tested positive, and several Americans have been evacuated from DR Congo to Europe for Ebola treatment or monitoring.
In Kenya, “the biggest fear is around how will other countries react” to the outbreak, with travel bans a particular worry, Maleche said. The US put travel bans in place from DR Congo and neighboring Uganda and South Sudan once the outbreak was detected in May, but it would be “very ironic” if the US instituted travel bans, given its quarantine center in Kenya, Maleche said.
Raphael Warnock, a Democratic senator from Georgia, and Bill Cassidy, a Republican senator from Louisiana, penned a letter in June to the Senate appropriations committee opposing the Trump administration’s plans to cut back on HIV prevention and monitoring.
Dismantling of USAID, withdrawing from the WHO, and abruptly cutting foreign aid cuts was “degrading our outbreak preparedness” and had “seriously weakened our ability to keep Americans safe from infectious disease”, Warnock said in a statement.
“These cuts to global health funding have led to the erosion of international disease-monitoring infrastructure that helps us catch threats like Ebola before they reach our shores, at a time when the world needs American leadership most.” The US should be strengthening these systems, not abandoning them, he said.
Nuzzo agreed. “It’s about having an understanding of the systems and the conditions in other countries, and eyes and ears in those countries to detect when something out of the ordinary happens, and to get that information as early as possible,” she said. That benefits the US and the countries themselves, she said.
Work such as HIV prevention “can be repurposed”, she added. “You have connections with clinical care, the ability to move medicines, the ability to conduct laboratory tests, the ability to move specimens around – all of those capacities are things that you would use in other disease emergencies.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: This civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than ever | Jonathan Liew
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Kapow! In a warmly received conference speech, Kemi Badenoch turns her fire on Reform UK, describing it as “weird”, and ruling out an electoral pact. Slap! Not to be outdone, her former colleague Robert Jenrick derides Badenoch as a champion of the wealthy, which is quite rich for a guy who looks like he’s just accidentally ingested a bundle of £50 notes through his sphincter. Bosh! Reform’s Richard Tice and Restore’s Rupert Lowe clash online over the result of a council byelection in Derbyshire, in which the Greens profited from a split rightwing vote. “Vote Restore get Islamists,” Tice chides. “Vote Reform, get some random Bangladeshi bloke,” Lowe responds.
Meanwhile, the Conservatives are back. The Kemibounce is real. The Keminaissance is true. We’ve all got a severe case of the Kemirrhoids. And you may wonder why much of the media are talking about a Badenoch revival in a year where her party lost 563 councillors and 40% of its councils, remains about four points below its apparent nadir of 2024, and in which the leader herself appears incapable of doing a broadcast interview without looking like a restaurant diner who received exactly what she ordered and is inexplicably furious at it. The point is that the Conservatives are a serious party of government again, and the reason is that we all said so.
And even if we take into account Badenoch’s curiously resilient personal polling, this does feel like a largely arbitrary volte-face. There was a soft-focus interview in the Financial Times, a warm editorial in the Sun, and generally positive coverage of the Tory conference in the rest of the rightwing press. Tom Tugendhat, the new shadow foreign secretary and once regarded as a party moderate, had a sympathetic platform in the Observer to defend the party’s opposition to net zero and the European convention on human rights.
From a safe distance, it is possible to regard these realignments in a fairly optimistic light. The right is tearing itself to shreds, potentially allowing a leftwing alternative – or failing that, Labour – to clean up. And in the continuing scrap between Lowe and Nigel Farage, or the series of aggressive Telegraph editorials aimed at Restore Britain, it is tempting to glimpse a reassertion of basic, consensual values in which, for all our many disagreements, certain voices will always be beyond the pale.
Occasionally you will even hear it said on the progressive left that a strong centre-right is a necessary, welcome bulwark against the extremist far right. That while we can disagree strongly and vehemently with Badenoch’s party, we can also recognise the ways in which a moderate right can act as a kind of cordon sanitaire against the nativists, ethnonationalists and race theorists who may otherwise get their hands on the levers of government. All of which would probably be true, if that were actually what was happening. But is it?
Let’s start with the Tories, who appear to be rapidly pivoting towards a demographic that one insider has described as “Waitrose Woman”: affluent, socially liberal, turned off by culture-war rhetoric but laser-focused on tax and the economy. “We have done a ton of opinion research over the last 18 months,” a Conservative source told the Mail on Sunday. “You do have to appear reasonable.” Or, as one shadow cabinet minister told the Guardian: “We have outsourced our toxicity to Reform.”
But in the real world, beyond superficial branding, how different are the two platforms? Shadow cabinet member Nick Timothy called Islamic prayers in Trafalgar Square un-British, “an act of domination”, “straight from the Islamist playbook”, and Badenoch backed him. Badenoch advocates a ban on pro-Palestine marches, but argued Tommy Robinson should not receive the same treatment. Another shadow cabinet member, Katie Lam, advocated mass deportations of legally settled immigrants in order to make Britain a “culturally coherent group of people”.
The Conservative police and crime commissioner Donna Jones responded to the masked vigilante protests in Portsmouth by blaming the government for failing to control our borders. A former neo-Nazi activist was selected as a local election candidate for the Tories, and subsequently appointed as an adviser. In the Telegraph, Badenoch wrote that anyone committed to net zero targets is no longer welcome in the party.
As for Reform, Monday’s announcement that it would immediately suspend the UK asylum system brought the party further in line with Restore, both of whom advocate ICE-style raids, the stripping of citizenship from people who thought they were here permanently, and the cessation of aid and visas to countries who refuse to take back migrants. Suella Braverman, a former Tory, now says she can “understand why some people are drawn to Restore”, and suggests people of colour cannot be English.
Indeed, you can argue that net zero, welfare, tax cuts, Israel, Brexit, defence spending, trans rights, Donald Trump, the obsession with grooming gangs and Islam, immigration and, most importantly, their common enemies, there is barely a sheet of nori to separate the three parties. And yet at the same time we are expected to believe that these parties engaged in an eternal blood feud, rather than three heads of the same army, pursuing different strategies towards a common cause.
Naturally Westminster will fall for this narrative wholesale, focused as it is on divisions over alliances, personalities over ideas. The Conservatives will be allowed to carry on decontaminating their brand without decontaminating their platform. Farage will continue as flag bearer for the movement, sweeping up donor money and airtime. Meanwhile Restore serves an equally important role as the engine of change, the pressure group, the brains trust: shifting the rhetorical window to the right while allowing Badenoch and Farage to look reasonable in comparison.
The civil war on the right is in fact a charade, a fake fight being enacted for our benefit. The right bloc is now a single basic substance, responsive and carefully calibrated to the different audiences it needs to capture. Reform, already in informal talks with Restore, can now tailor its offering to the post-industrial north, Midlands and Wales, leaving the rehabilitated Conservatives – the acceptable face of the project – to concentrate on their southern and rural heartlands. And if, after all the bickering and infighting, a coalition should be required? Do we really expect a Conservative party founded entirely on the gain and exercise of power to suddenly turn it down?
To those on the left, the idea of a rightwing meltdown feels vaguely reassuring. But in reality nothing here is being repudiated. The personalities may butt heads for our entertainment, but the ideas and politics are largely common among them all. The parts are being divvied out, but ultimately the production remains the same.
- 
  Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.
The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.
The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.
Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.
Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.
It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.
Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.
The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.
Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”
Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.
However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: From the US midterms to the hard right in Britain, empathy has become a dirty word in politics | John Harris
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Towards the end of the summer, the Tory-Reform defector Robert Jenrick authored an op-ed piece for the Daily Telegraph about the seemingly impossible economics of rising benefits bills because of mental ill-health. In his capacity as Reform’s Treasury spokesman, his task was to big up its plans to cut 25% of so-called welfare spending by 2030, and thereby tackle what he called the state’s “suicidal empathy”.
Straight away, I wondered where this most opportunistic politician had borrowed that phrase from, and instantly found out: a book with the same title, published this year by the Canadian academic Gad Saad, whom the dust jacket describes as having particular expertise in “the use of evolutionary psychology in marketing and consumer behaviour”. It comes with an endorsement from Elon Musk. “Western civilisation is doomed unless the core weakness of suicidal empathy is recognised and actions are taken that are hard but necessary for survival,” says the world’s richest man. “All of Gad’s books, including this one, are great.”
Unfortunately, Suicidal Empathy is not great. It is, in fact, a baggy mess, glueing together absurd straw men (“suicidal empathy can cause people to care more about rapists and other felons than their victims”) to familiar arguments about immigration, Covid lockdowns and whether the word “imbecile” is offensive. One of its most head-turning claims is that the west’s supposed embrace of degenerate woke-ism is largely traceable to the fact that “women are much more likely to succumb to such emotional and ideological capture”. At a push, its most useful function is as a meandering guide to the soup of ideas simmering in the minds of hardcore Maga voters as they prepared for this week’s midterms.
There is a huge amount of this stuff around, crystallising the philosophical core of Trumpism and its adherent movements across the world – roughly, the idea that might is right and compassion is for wimps. We are now well beyond the culture wars and the US right’s long history of (to put it politely) Christian revisionism, and into the very serious prospect of a decisive western moral counter-revolution that may already be under way. That’s certainly the intention of the slew of voices responsible for podcasts, social media posts and other Maga potboilers – witness 2024’s Toxic Empathy: How Progressives Exploit Christian Compassion, by the Christian podcaster Allie Beth Stuckey, or last year’s The Sin of Empathy: Compassion and its Counterfeits, by the rightwing pastor Joe Rigney.
But here’s the crucial thing: the same moral push is also supported by alarming numbers of regular people. According to polling by the Public Religion Research Institute, while 84% of registered US Democrats support the proposition that empathy helps build a healthy society, only 54% of Republicans agree. Perhaps most strikingly, to quote from the survey’s accompanying blurb: “White evangelical Protestants are the only religious group in which a majority does not agree that empathy is a foundational moral value (42%). Instead, a majority (54%) say empathy can be dangerous.”
Much the same seems to be true of that possible Trump successor, JD Vance – a Catholic convert who now has the rare distinction of having locked horns with two popes. In April, Leo XIV plainly decried the US’s attacks on Iran, insisting: “Anyone who is a disciple of Christ, the Prince of Peace, is never on the side of those who once wielded the sword and today drop bombs.” Vance’s response? “I think it’s very, very important for the pope to be careful when he talks about matters of theology.” Only a few months before, the vice-president insisted his “old-school” notion of Christian compassion descended in priority from “your family”, “your neighbor” and “your community” to “your fellow citizens in your own country”. Then and only then, he said, could you “focus [sic] and prioritize the rest of the world”.
Soon after, our era’s most pre-eminent moral philosopher was interviewed by the podcaster Joe Rogan. “The fundamental weakness of western civilisation,” said Musk, “is empathy, the empathy exploit.” Progressives, he said, have set themselves on “exploiting a bug in western civilisation, which is the empathy response”.
At that point, I went straight back to one of my favourite modern books: the classicist and historian Tom Holland’s bestseller Dominion, that brilliant history of Christianity and its global impact that illuminates how an emphasis on what we now call empathy (the word was only created in 1908, as the English translation of the German “Einfühlung”, or “in-feeling”) was one of that religion’s philosophical revolutions.
“Across the Roman world,” Holland writes, “wailing at the sides of roads or on rubbish tips, babies abandoned by their parents were a common sight.” Such everyday barbarism was also reflected in official attitudes to poor, disabled and infirm people – until a moral up-ending began with Rome’s conversion to Christianity under Constantine. As Holland writes: “Every week in churches across the Roman world, collections for orphans and widows, for the imprisoned, and the shipwrecked and the sick had been raised … Entire systems of social security had begun to emerge.” But there was an additional element of this sea change – which, in a modern context, stands in sharp contrast to everything from ICE detention camps to Musk’s vandalism of USAID and the 700,000 deaths it is reckoned to have already caused. As Holland puts it, “divine love for the outcast and derelict demanded that mortals love them too”.
No one would claim Christian countries and institutions stuck to those ideas in the centuries that followed, but the modern US is surely now moral light years away. And there is a British story here, too, bound up with the changes brought to our politics by Margaret Thatcher – who was raised as a strict Methodist, and occasionally blurted out quite remarkable opinions about Christian teaching and questions of morality: in January 1980, for example, she claimed that “no one would remember the Good Samaritan if he’d only had good intentions; he had money as well”.
In this and so many other respects, she was way ahead of her time, opening the path to the kind of moral contortions we hear not just from Jenrick, but both his new comrades in Reform and his former Tory colleagues. Some have gone even further: let migrants drown, they say, while others accuse the lifeboat service – the lifeboat service! – of complicity in a supposed invasion of untouchables, barely pausing for breath before they mourn the decline of “Judeo-Christian culture”. In the States, a proper Republican drubbing on Tuesday might give the anti-empaths the kind of shock they deserve, but Musk’s power and influence alone shows that it will take a lot more than a single round of election results to really push them back. Meanwhile, all over the world, compassion, kindness and other such virtues gather a thick layer of dust, like old hymn books in a long-deserted church.
- 
  John Harris is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: How irrational are Labour’s plans for migrant workers? To find out, read the small print | Frances Ryan
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
If you want to see the senselessness of Britain’s immigration debate play out in real time, look no further than the crackdown on care workers’ visas that came to a head this week.
As part of its plans to force low-paid migrant workers to wait 15 years before settlement in the UK, the Home Office has been in a battle behind the scenes for the past six months to controversially include care workers in the policy. This is despite the social care system already facing critical staff shortages and the number of British citizens and immigrants taking the jobs dwindling.
After a fierce backlash from health unions and Labour cabinet members, this week the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, announced a partial U-turn: an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependents will be exempt and allowed to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) after five years.
It’s a welcome reprieve from a policy that should never have been on the table. But check the fine print and this “watering down” will not protect every care worker. Only carers who earn £25,000 a year and entered or switched on to the care staff visa route before the white paper’s publication in 2025 will be eligible.
Those who don’t meet the strict requirements will have to get another five-year “health and social care” visa before applying for ILR – a move campaigners are warning will leave vulnerable workers open to exploitation from unscrupulous employers.
Ministers have not established what benefit any of this is meant to bestow on the British people, millions of whom rely on migrant carers to help them or their elderly parents wash and dress. Nor has anyone explained how Labour’s upcoming care reforms will work while alienating – rather than actively recruiting – more international staff, as recent tightened immigration rules already have.
Or, to put it another way: the government has simultaneously pledged to fix social care while creating a hostile environment for the migrant staff who keep the system afloat. It sums up not only the nastiness of it all, but the deep-seated irrationality that now plagues almost any mainstream conversation about immigration, with politicians across the spectrum seemingly contractually obliged to ignore basic common sense as well as decency.
Few things demonstrate this more than the obsession with the “contribution v cost” framing that dominates these debates, and which Labour has now threaded through its visa policy. On paper, it appears to many a fair and logical way to allocate visa rights. In practice, it rewards the wealthy and dismisses the value of working-class and predominantly female labour: while care workers will have to wait five or 15 years for ILR, a solicitor on £125,000 can get fast-tracked in only three. It is blatant classism, sure, but also fundamentally misses the very obvious tenet of capitalism that a worker’s “contribution” to a society and economy is not necessarily reflected in their wage packet.
That Mahmood has been doing the rounds in recent months using disputed figures to claim that granting ILR to care staff and their families for the next few years would cost the public purse £10bn over a lifetime suggests how unreliable – and outright ludicrous – the cost v contribution binary is. These are the people keeping our loved ones alive for the minimum wage and we’re still debating whether they’re a burden on the taxpayer.
Of course, evidence shows care workers are, to use that favoured phrase, “net contributors”. The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found this week that skilled migrants – including care workers – and their families due to settle in the UK under current rules are expected to boost the public purse by a staggering £115bn through taxes.
Such a figure doesn’t even include the many other ways care workers save the country money: by enabling family members to keep paying income tax rather than quitting their jobs to be an unpaid carer; supporting younger disabled people to get to the office and stay in work; or keeping older people out of expensive hospital beds by reducing their risk of falls.
And yet we are losing something if we accept the idea that a migrant’s “contribution” is only in economic terms, as if the Home Office can scan a human being at the border and put a price tag round their neck. Anyone who has ever relied on a good carer knows there is value that can’t be measured on a spreadsheet: the security of knowing there is someone to help you get out of bed in the morning; the dignity of having a regular shower; the laughter that comes with a shared joke as you write the shopping list together.
You won’t see many of these people on front pages or hear their voices on radio call-ins. But the people providing care and those who rely on it will “contribute” considerably more to the debate than the non-disabled white contrarians who so persistently dominate it.
If it is a “legitimate concern” for the public to worry about immigration, it is legitimate for a disabled person to be afraid there will be no one to help them cook dinner, or for a migrant to worry about where they’ll live next year.
Because here’s the thing about fears: some are irrational, and others are not. Labour would do well to remember which ones it should listen to and which it should challenge.
- 
  Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.
The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so.
British officials insist, however, they will only make concessions on fees if the EU allows Britain entry to its proposed protectionist industrial scheme, which will impose trade restrictions on countries outside the bloc.
On Sunday the former chancellor Rachel Reeves praised the prime minister, Andy Burnham, for a willingness to think boldly about the UK’s relationship with Europe – saying she believed Britain’s future was within the EU. But in her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.
Ministers hope if such an agreement is reached at a Brussels summit later this month it will unlock millions of pounds’ worth of benefits for British companies looking to do business in the EU, and show that the prime minister’s attempts to forge much closer ties with the bloc are paying off.
But giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically, especially when many graduates are calling for changes to their own student loan repayment plans.
One person with knowledge of the talks said: “We are willing to give the Europeans what they want on fees, but we will have to get something significant in return. The biggest prize we are pushing for right now is access to Made in Europe, so there is a deal to be done there.”
A government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”
Negotiators have been thrashing out a series of deals for months to be finalised at the long-awaited summit on 20 November. Burnham wants to use it to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU and to lay out options for how the relationship could develop in the future, including full re-entry.
In a speech at Harvard on Monday, Reeves will say the UK’s “economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe”. Praising Burnham’s “willingness to face reality head-on”, she will say it is vital the British government can “prove to the public the benefits of a closer relationship and prove to Europe that we are serious and open to compromise”.
Before the summit, agreement is understood to have largely been reached in a number of areas, including on emissions trading, agricultural products and a youth mobility scheme, with reports suggesting up to 80,000 young Europeans could be allowed to come to Britain to work, live and study. EU member states had demanded between 100,000 and 150,000, with some arguing in favour of no quota.
The two sides are also nearing agreement to allow Britain access to European biometric databases, the Guardian has learned, which could help the UK government track asylum seekers.
British access to the Made in Europe scheme, which is due to be finalised next year, and European demands for cheaper fees for students at British universities are the two remaining hurdles.
EU officials say they want their students to pay fees of just over £9,000 a year rather than international fees, which can rise above £60,000. The demand briefly brought negotiations to a standstill this year, with British officials saying they had been blindsided by its inclusion in talks.
The first draft of a joint statement will be presented to EU ambassadors on Wednesday with room for text to be added or deleted up to 20 November. The agreement will include fresh commitments to strengthen efforts to end the small boat crossings in the Channel, including commitments to explore the possibility of restoring the UK’s access to EU databases.
EU diplomats say top of the UK’s shopping list is access to Eurodac, an EU database that holds fingerprints of all asylum seekers from the age of six. But they also warn there will be challenges for the UK as the database was not built for law enforcement, and sharing data with a non-EU member may not be supported by all states.
Member states are pushing for firm language on fees while the UK holds out for guarantees on Made in Europe. France dropped its opposition to the inclusion of the UK in the Industrial Accelerator Act with a proposal any country in the single market on 1 January 2020 could be involved as along as it dynamically aligned on trade measures.
Ten days ago, with talks still deadlocked, the EU discussed “decoupling” the discussion on fees from the joint statement at the summit entirely, deferring any agreement for six months. But EU diplomats still hope for an agreement to allow talks to flourish for what one called “the real reset”.
Sources have told the Guardian the government is willing to concede on fees and is prepared to pay cash-strapped universities for the income they will lose. Treasury officials have been drawing up estimates for how much such a policy will cost under various scenarios, including different levels of discounts for European students and different levels of demand for British university courses.
Two sources who have seen the costings have told the Guardian that under the most expensive scenario, which involves reducing fees to the same level as domestic students’ and very high levels of demand, the government could end up paying £450m a year. Another source said the true cost was likely to be lower, while a government official described the figure as “speculative”.
Mark Corver, an analyst of university funding and director at Campus Numerics, previously calculated it would cost the sector £140m in the first year and £400m across the three-year period of a typical course.
UK negotiators are only willing to give way on fees if they get a guarantee that British companies will be treated the same as those from the EU under the new industrial scheme.
The UK was excluded from the definition of “European” for the purposes of the scheme, prompting warnings from the British government and the UK car industry. More recently, however, France – which was the principal opponent of Britain’s inclusion in the scheme – shifted its position with a new proposal to allow British manufacturers into the system as long as the UK accepted “dynamic alignment” on EU tariffs.
This could cause a problem for the UK, which has much lower tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles than in the EU. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, recently told the Guardian he would not set tariff policy in response to pressure from Brussels.
The UK is also working on securing access to the Schengen Information System II – a database holding records of fugitives, missing persons and stolen goods, which gives real-time alerts on their cross-border movements.
The EU commissioner responsible for migration, Magnus Brunner, had been due to meet the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in London two weeks ago to flesh out that text, but after a last-minute cancellation, work has continued between officials at the Cabinet Office and the European Commission.

Andy Burnham has asked countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape a formal apology through a ‘structured dialogue’. During the prime minister’s visit to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, Downing Street said affected countries would play an indispensable role in crafting an enduring message. SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Department of Justice opens criminal investigation into Corey Lewandowski
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Corey Lewandowski, a former political adviser to Donald Trump and top aide at the Department of Homeland Security, is under criminal investigation over allegations he profited off his role in the US government, three US officials and a fourth person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Thursday.
The investigation began with a criminal referral to the justice department from the internal watchdog at DHS, according to the four people. The DHS inspector general’s office has been investigating Lewandowski’s involvement in the handling of certain government contracts, according to one of the people, a DHS official.
A lawyer for Lewandowski, Adam Trigg, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The investigation was first reported in the Wall Street Journal, which quoted Lewandowski’s lawyer as saying that his client denies all allegations of wrongdoing.
The DoJ has not yet issued subpoenas or other legal demands in the criminal investigation, according to one of the people. All four of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The justice department under Trump has investigated several prominent critics of the president, including the former FBI director James Comey and the New York attorney general Letitia James, but investigations of people close to Trump have been rare. The department has also moved to dismiss several existing cases involving Trump allies, including supporters charged in connection with the 6 January 2021 attack on the US Capitol.
Asked about media reports on the investigation, Trump told reporters that he did not know the specifics of the investigation, but said: “I want my people to be honest.”
“And if they’re not honest, I’ll have my DoJ go and do whatever they have to do,” Trump added.
Lewandowski served as a top aide to the former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem during her tenure leading DHS. Trump fired Noem in March after months of controversy, including the fatal shootings of two US citizens by federal officers in Minneapolis and lawmakers’ questions over a $220m advertising contract promoting Noem that was awarded without a standard bidding process.
Lewandowski had signed some DHS contracts despite having questionable legal authority as a special government employee, according to the DHS official. Certain grants and contracts, including those involving the Federal Emergency Management Agency, were put on hold at Lewandowski’s direction, according to two of the people, both of whom are DHS officials.
Lewandowski previously served as a campaign manager during Trump’s first presidential run in 2016 and advised his 2024 campaign.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
In February 2016, days after David Cameron announced the UK would hold a referendum on leaving the EU, he told workers in Slough not to imagine they could change their minds a few years down the line if they did not like how things panned out. Voting to stay in or leave was a once in a generation thing, he said. “This is a decision that lasts for life.”
Well times change, as the last prime minister but five could testify. A decade after Britain told Brussels where to go, Brexit is back on the political agenda. After years in which many politicians avoided any mention of the B-word, Andy Burnham broke the omertà in his party conference speech last month, saying he would look again at Britain’s relationship with Europe.
This week he went further, insisting the current arrangement must change: “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain.” Among a range of options on the table, he has been clear, is the possibility of going “all the way” and rejoining the EU.
There are pressing economic reasons Burnham has been talking up closer alignment, as the EU works out its position on the UK’s access to its protectionist “Made in Europe” legislation, which the prime minister has said could hurt British manufacturing.
But after years of bitter division and political dysfunction in the fallout from the vote, are the British public really ready to talk about Brexit again – and even to contemplate reversing it?
Polling evidence may suggest so. A “megapoll” of more than 11,000 people published this month found that half of Britons now support rejoining the EU, with only 28% opposed, and the remainder undecided. Almost 60% think it was wrong to leave.
Sliced some ways, the numbers are even more striking: a More in Common survey in June to mark a decade since the vote found that if another referendum was held today across Britain’s 632 constituencies, just 11 would vote to leave (even in Clacton, Nigel Farage’s constituency, 52% supported rejoining).
What changed? To the polling expert Rob Ford, a professor of political science at the University of Manchester, there are several key reasons, from demographic change to buyers’ remorse. Brexiters are fewer in number – “a lot of leave voters have died, bluntly” – and both young people entering the electorate and those who did not vote in 2016 skew heavily in favour of Europe. And with the project widely considered a disappointment at best, a proportion of those who opted to leave have switched positions.
“Although each is a relatively slow moving and relatively small incremental force, add them together over a decade and it adds up to quite a lot of change,” said Ford.
Given the divisiveness and turbulence of the past decade – and the fact many Labour MPs represent constituencies that voted to leave – it is little wonder that some senior Labour figures have expressed nervousness about reopening the debate. “[Burnham] definitely needs to proceed with caution because we don’t want to restoke division,” one cabinet minister told the Guardian.
But the view from formerly Brexit-supporting areas is not necessarily what it was. “Hull East voted 74% leave in the referendum, however I believe the mood has changed,” said Karl Turner, the Labour MP for the constituency since 2010 (he now sits as an independent after having the whip withdrawn).
“Constituents tell me they expected Brexit to improve their lives; instead many face higher costs and fewer opportunities.” As a result, he said, they were “increasingly ready to consider the practical benefits of rejoining the EU”.
Ford added: “Andy Burnham looks at the data and says, well, I’ve got an electoral coalition that’s 80% remain and becoming more so. The parties to my left that I need to squeeze have a [position] that is even more remain than that.
“And the overall balance of opinion in the country is now nudging up towards 60% in favour of remain, sometimes even higher in terms of how many think Brexit is a mistake. Why wouldn’t I move in a pro-remain direction? It’s the direction of travel of the country. The art of leadership is getting out ahead of the trends that are happening and using them to your advantage.”
Sara Hobolt, a professor in the department of government at London School of Economics, agrees that the polling data today suggests Brexit could be an effective general election rallying cry for Labour. “This is an issue that a lot of people were quite upset with Keir Starmer and his government for not talking about it. It is something that definitely mobilises the base.”
While Labour supporters and those the party wants to win back from other progressive parties overwhelmingly support remain, she points out, the Conservative party is now much more divided on the issue, having lost many of its hardline Brexiters to Reform. “That means that [by putting Brexit back on the agenda] you can potentially do more damage to the right than the left.
“But I think probably the main thing for Andy Burnham is that this has been seen in his electoral base as something [that has been overlooked]. ‘You talk about growth? Why are you not talking about Brexit?’ Because overwhelmingly remainers think that a lot of the economic problems we’ve faced over the last decade are due to Brexit.”
But if uniting the left before a Westminster election is one thing, winning a future Brexit referendum is a whole other challenge, as the experience of 2016 showed. “There clearly is support for rejoining the EU,” says the More in Commondirector, Luke Tryl, “the question is, how resilient would that be in the face of a referendum campaign?”
One factor is, inevitably, Brexit weariness, he says. “The British public are tired. They’ve lurched from crisis to crisis, from row to row, and I think, for some, just the idea of reopening the wounds [is unwelcome]. I think in a campaign rejoin, if it got to that, would start ahead, but I don’t think the headline polling we are seeing now would remain where it is once it was subject to a full back and forth.”
Ford agrees – noting that the EU will be resistant to serious discussions so long as there is the prospect of a wholesale reversal under a future Reform government. The risk of bringing up Brexit is not just because the subject is neuralgic to many, he says. “One of the problems during the Brexit years was it was just simply impossible to get a conversation going about all the other pressing issues that mattered.
“There is a risk for Burnham, if this thing starts to take life of its own yet again, that the big difficult conversations he wants to have about some of the longstanding structural problems in British society will be harder to have because for a lot of people in the political conversation, Brexit is like catnip – they’ll run straight to it. And then you’re not able to get them to pay attention to the issues you want them to pay attention to.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company.
In an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control, the prime minister is urging his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a new list of policies for the utility.
One option being looked at is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run.
Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames, which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn, but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.
Sources familiar with the prime minister’s thinking say he has now told policy officials across Whitehall to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that means spending taxpayer money and going to court.
One government source described the fate of the company as a “litmus test” on whether the government could deal with challenges in the medium term, rather than just immediate cost of living support and longer-term structural changes.
“There are more options than people have assumed to date including ones that have never been properly considered,” the source said.
Another said the prime minister had told his officials to “look at all the options and not feel constrained”, in a departure from the advice under Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.
Burnham has promised to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism” and has instructed his ministers to draw up a 10-year plan for government later this year, including detailed proposals for bringing utilities under public control.
Meanwhile, Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, is working on a water bill that will lift a Thatcher-era cap on government ownership of water companies and could rewrite how the bankruptcy regime works for the industry.
Government advisers believe changes to the “special administration regime” (SAR) would make it easier to take companies such as Thames into state control in the future.
But Burnham is also looking for a more immediate solution to Thames’s problems.
When the prime minister came to office, government insiders say he was presented with two main options for Thames: strike a bailout deal with the American hedge funds that own its debt, or pursue an SAR.
Thames’s creditors had proposed a £10bn rescue plan for the company, but Emma Reynolds, the previous environment secretary, made clear her opposition to such a plan before Burnham became prime minister.
Government lawyers also believe it will be difficult to have the company placed into SAR given that it is being kept afloat financially by its creditors and has managed to keep services running.
Among the other options being discussed is the waiving of the approximately £100m in environmental fines the company still owes and taking a stake in it instead. Then, if and when the company is fined again, the government would automatically increase its share rather than collecting the cash.
While some believe this would be a relatively straightforward way to give the government a say in how the company is run, many also believe it would fall short of Burnham’s promise to nationalise the company outright.
The prime minister is under pressure to go further, for example by stripping Thames of its licence, pushing for it to go into SAR immediately and then taking it out of administration without offering anything to the existing creditors.
Such a plan will inevitably be challenged in court, but Burnham is understood to be more willing to take on legal action than Starmer was. One adviser said: “Litigation was always a 100% certainty.”
The prime minister’s advisers also believe they can go further with Thames than with other companies because international investors see the company as a unique case, and not an indication of how the government intends to treat every water company.
Officials say other water companies are likely to be dealt with in different ways, through a mixture of stricter regulation and increased oversight by elected officials such as mayors.
Ewan McGaughey, a professor in law at King’s College, London, said: “The government’s best option is to start a special administration process for Thames Water before it runs up more debts, and sends billions more overseas.
“An orderly transition to public ownership does not require that banks in control are bailed out – on the contrary, the law says polluters should pay.”
Lena Swedlow, deputy director of the Compass campaign group, said: “The obvious solution is to put Thames Water into SAR, and then brought into public ownership so it truly works for everyone.
“While reform of the failing regulatory mechanisms is welcome, any recapitalisation and debt-to-equity schemes that do not seek to permanently wrestle the company from private hands will fail to be in the interests of the workers, stakeholders, and the 16 million people Thames serves. Everything else is noise in the wind.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: What’s the future for the Green party? Should it be ecosocialism? | Joe Todd
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
It’s a strange time to be a Green. We have just held our largest conference ever, but it was overshadowed by a controversial motion that was attacked by the media as racist. Then, when we lost a byelection in a Camden seat that is so Labour it has estates named after Blair-era ministers, the headlines called for Zack Polanski to resign.
It does, however, mark the end of phase one for Polanski’s Greens. Polanski burst on to the political scene in 2025 and ate up attention, enjoying an easy monopoly on hope while Labour was sucked into the black hole of Starmerism. Labour has since escaped, with Andy Burnham giving social democracy with Mancunian characteristics a half-hearted go. But Burnham’s honeymoon already seems to be ending. John Healey’s budget of “difficult decisions” and “fiscal responsibility” is likely to disappoint everyone but the financial markets, and a winter energy bill crisis driven by a possible El Niño deep freeze is just one of many problems he’ll soon have to face.
One school of thought says Polanski can carry on as before, focusing on points of difference with Labour. Healey announces a no-change budget; Polanski calls for a tax on wealth to fund public services. Angela Rayner sides with landlords over renters; Polanski proposes an emergency rent brake and explores Berlin’s plan to expropriate the properties of corporate landlords.
These interventions matter, especially in our attention-driven politics. But on their own they are only tactical manoeuvres in response to the politics of Labour. If we act like we’re only a Labour pressure group, that’s what we will become. And in doing so, we will neglect to answer the deeper question: what are society’s fundamental problems and what is our plan to fix them?
In practice, Burnham’s “radical vision” promises only modest regulation of public utilities, limited devolution and reform of the voting system and of social care after the next election. Weighed against the crises we face – climate breakdown, bankrupt public services, rampant inflation, runaway rents, an epidemic of loneliness, a billionaire-owned media, a deranged elite of tech oligarchs who literally want the world to end – his vision reads more like the managed decline of a system in crisis.
If phase two of Polanski’s Green party is about anything, it should be about breaking this spell. Part of this is naming capitalism as the root cause. Naomi Klein made the best-selling case more than a decade ago that the fight of our times is capitalism v the climate – that a livable world and continued resource extraction are fundamentally incompatible.
But Burnham will not go there. He names neoliberalism as the problem and then neglects to fix it, unceremoniously dumping any intention to expand public ownership and shrink the role of the market.
Polanski should go there, rooting his day-to-day interventions in a credible programme to transition away from capitalism – not only imagining the end of capitalism and what might come next, but planning in painstaking detail just how we are going to get there. He must build a credible Green party vision that shows Burnham’s to be meek and hollow.
Don’t get me wrong, the Green party isn’t there yet, nor anywhere close. We have 5 MPs, 10% of the vote and we’re still learning to be a mass of 230,000 members. But if we don’t start taking ourselves seriously, why would anybody else? Trust in political parties is on the floor, and that affects the Greens too. Why should people put their faith in us and dare to hope if we don’t have a programme that is honest, rigorous and credible?
We only need to look to the French leftwing party La France Insoumise to see what this looks like. In 2016 Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s movement published L’Avenir en Commun, which went straight into the bestseller list and has been read by hundreds of thousands of people. It is a visionary, comprehensive programme that would be written into the constitution so that companies can never take more from nature than they give. It’s a plan to provide free water and energy to every household, to redraw France’s regions around river basins, mountain ranges and forests, and to organise ecological planning. It is more extensive and detailed than any manifesto for ecological transition in Europe, and polls suggest Mélenchon could lead the French left into next May’s presidential runoff against Marine Le Pen.
The Green party’s programme must be similarly full of strategy and vision: reckoning honestly with the forces arrayed against us and setting out precisely what we’d do in our first year of government. It should also talk about the good life and what we’re fighting for, in words that resonate with voters, rather than dry policy. Written in a big open process where lots of groups are involved: unions, community groups and thinktanks, farmers watching harvests fail, pensioners battling fuel poverty, renters priced out of homeownership and workers whose jobs are vanishing – it should become a comprehensive point of unity that can provide an answer to those who aren’t voting Green because they doubt our credibility, and fill the void currently occupied by single-issue policy motions.
Polanski is correct when he says that Burnham isn’t serious about socialism. But we have to be honest: right now, neither are we. If Burnham’s vision is meek and hollow, ours is still being formed. And as Labour faces the tests of governing, now is the time to write it.
- 
  Joe Todd is a senior fellow at the Autonomy Institute, the co-host of the Life of the Party podcast and a Green party member

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Alaska prosecutor investigates alleged Democratic plot to confuse voters with second Dan Sullivan
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal and a civil investigation into an alleged scheme by Democrats to confuse voters by recruiting a spoiler candidate on the ballot for US Senate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, senator Dan Sullivan.
Speaking at a news conference in Anchorage on Friday, US attorney Michael Heyman cited reporting by the New York Times which suggested that the Senate campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola and national Democrats had, in his words, “orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J Sullivan as a sham candidate”.
Both Dan Sullivans – one a Republican senator and the other a retired schoolteacher with no prior political experience – qualified for the ballot.
“We are taking that extremely seriously,” Heyman said.
“This new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska,” he added. “As we speak, law enforcement around the country are taking investigative steps with respect to a criminal investigation on these matters.”
In a separate filing, the Department of Justice asked a federal judge to order state elections officials to isolate ballots ranking Dan J Sullivan to investigate potential voter “confusion” with the incumbent Dan Sullivan.
E. Bryan Wilson, an assistant US attorney in Alaska, in a filing, said the government “seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary”.
The justice department on Friday also asked a federal judge to issue a preliminary injunction that would block Alaska from certifying its Senate election result if the incumbent senator loses to Peltola due to the presence of Daniel J Sullivan on the ballot.
Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into. It is highly unusual for federal prosecutors to confirm the existence of an open criminal investigation, much less discuss it publicly.
“The civil lawsuit is publicly faced, and is focused on preserving the ballots,” Heyman said, referring to a Department of Justice suit filed last week.
A day earlier, Peltola denied any prior knowledge of the alleged effort, telling supporters in Juneau, Alaska’s capital: “I am not interested in tricking voters.”
“I just want to clear the air,” the Democratic Senate candidate said on Thursday at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about.”
Peltola is running against Dan Sullivan, the two-term US senator. A person familiar with the matter told the Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after the New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J Sullivan Jr as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters.
The race is considered one of the most important contests of next week’s midterm elections, and will be key to determining control of the Senate. Alaska is one of a handful of states with Senate races this year that Democrats are targeting as they try to win back a majority in the chamber, where they hold 47 seats to the Republican party’s 53, and recent polls have shown Peltola in the lead.
More subpoenas were expected, according to the person who spoke to the Associated Press. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the number of them were immediately clear.
Republicans have condemned the presence in the race of two candidates named Dan Sullivan, calling the newcomer a ploy by Democrats to cost the incumbent re-election by splitting the GOP candidate’s supporters.
Before the August primary, election authorities in the state attempted to disqualify the other Dan Sullivan, but the state supreme court ruled that he could appear on the ballot. Together with Sullivan and Peltola, the challenger was one of the top four vote-getters in the non-partisan primary.
On the general election ballot, the senator will be listed as “Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent” and the challenger “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.”
Since the New York Times published its report, Mike Dunleavy, Alaska’s Republican governor, separately announced plans to launch a criminal investigation, saying the story revealed “disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates – including one with the same name as an incumbent US senator – to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes”.
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the report “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Donald Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate if she won the election.
“Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Later, as he rallied for Darline Graham, a Republican senator, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted”.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Home Office denies British baby living in Thailand chance to meet great-grandfather in UK
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Home Office has denied a great-grandfather from Lancashire the chance of meeting his five-month-old British great-grandson, who lives abroad.
William Cross was born in Thailand on 30 April to parents Matthew Cross, 31, who is from Burnley in Lancashire, and Khin Thant Zin, known as Jue Jue, also 31, a refugee who fled persecution in Myanmar to Thailand.
The family live on the island of Koh Tao, famous for its diving schools and a centre for turtle conservation. It is a popular tourism spot and Cross, a mechanical engineer, opened a steakhouse restaurant there 15 months ago. He met Zin on the island and the couple are now engaged. She works in the restaurant managing social media and human resources.
Cross’s parents have visited the family in Thailand and have met their grandson. But William’s great-grandfather George Kerr, 74, who lives in Clayton-le-Moors in Lancashire, has multiple health problems and so is unable to fly out to Thailand to meet the baby. Instead, a large family gathering was planned in Burnley for Christmas.
Cross said: “My grandfather suffers from ill health and sadly he is unable to travel. He and I have been extremely close all my life and I’m desperate for him to meet his grandchild.”
The family have just signed a lease on a new home and have bought some land on the island for later development.
They assumed that organising a short trip to the UK for a family Christmas would be straightforward. But the Home Office refused Zin’s visitor visa application, which means the family will be unable to travel.
Officials said they were not satisfied she was a “genuine visitor”, and that there was no evidence Zin would return to Thailand because she had not shown evidence of significant family ties there, and she was unable to show sufficient evidence of her income.
“Jue Jue has never had a bank account,” Cross said. “Her brother and sister both live on Koh Tao and her mum is planning to move here when her younger sister has finished school in Myanmar.”
The visitor visa application process is expensive and cumbersome. “They required documentation from my family to be financial guarantors while we’re in the UK. Passport photos of my grandfather, my mum and dad and me, a typed letter from each of us confirming our commitment to sponsorship, a formal letter of invitation from my parents saying they would be comfortable with my partner being in my home,” Cross said.
“We had to travel to Phuket, a journey of two nights and three days from Koh Tao on a ferry and buses, which cost us £400, to complete biometric screening required for the visitor visa application.”
There is no right of appeal against this visa refusal so the couple are preparing a new application, although the Home Office refusal letter warns that future applications are likely to be refused “unless the circumstances of your application change”.
They also need to buy and provide evidence of return flight tickets even though they don’t know whether the new visa application will be granted. They have to make the long journey from the island on ferry and buses a second time to repeat the biometrics.
“By the time we send our next application, the whole thing will have cost us £3,000 with no guarantee of it being accepted,” Cross said.
The family are still hoping that baby William will be able to meet his great-grandfather at Christmas. Temperatures on the island rarely fall below 25C, so back in Burnley his relatives have bought warm baby clothes in the hope he will get a chance to wear them.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on individual cases. All visa applications are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the immigration rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant.”
