SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Burnham tells Zelenskyy’s UK’s support for Ukraine ‘will not change’ – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Burnham praises Zelenskyy for showing 'leadership' after Trump's energy ceasefire comment
Here are fuller quotes from the public statements by Andy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelenskyy before their main meeting.
Burnham said:
MrPresident, it’s a great privilege for me to welcome you to Downing Street today. And you’ve just seen the reaction [a reference to the crowd cheering as he arrived]. Obviously, you’ve seen the solidarity and the support you’ve got from everybody here in Britain. We’re behind you. And that will not change.
We know that the last few days, the last few hours, have been very dark and difficult days for Ukraine. We know that the country sustained heavy bombardments in the last 24 hours in Kyiv, particularly. And we would want to extend our condolences to all of those people in Ukraine who’ve lost loved ones as a result of what has been happening.
President Trump made a call at the weekend for an energy ceasefire. And, Volodymyr, you have shown your leadership in saying that you would be prepared to sit down and discuss what that looks like, to make sure we protect people from a very harsh winter that lies ahead in Ukraine.
Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine. It’s clear to the world, again, who the aggressor is in this conflict.
However, in these moments, Britain will continue to provide you with whatever support that we can. And today I’m announcing that we are accelerating the delivery of British-made air defences for you, and we will make sure that they’re in place as soon as possible. (See 9am.)
I’ve also asked all of our ministers here in the government to do whatever they can, extra, to support you, and they are looking at all possible avenues …
All of the people of Ukraine have our support. There are such connections between our two countries. We will forever stand by you through this difficult time.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, is holding talks with Andy Burnham in No 10 now, where he said he would be discussing with the PM “difficulties” caused by Ukraine getting less intelligence and reduced access to the Starlink internet access in the light of Washington striking a diesel deal with Russia. (See 5.31pm.)
Andy Burnham has ruled out Labour doing deals with the Green party after its conference voted for a motion saying “Zionism is racism”. (See 12.57pm.)
Dominic Cummings has not received much coverage for his appearance at the Lords constitution committee this morning, where he was talking about constitutional safeguards, and I’ve afraid I have too much other stuff on to give it much attention. But if you want to listen to a better expert on the constitution, Peter Hennessy, the historian and crossbencher peer, has given an interview to the Lord Speaker’s Corner podcast. The transcript and audio are here.
Hennessy said constitutional safeguards could quickly crumble. He said:
So much would go wrong.
If we had a government that came in, if it was a Reform government, and the first thing they did was sack the cabinet secretary, and got rid of the career officials who came in under the Northcote-Trevelyan merit, not partisanship rubric of selection, and had a go at the judges, too – it would be very easy if they had a big enough majority for them to take away the fundamentals … as the first act that they were doing week one.
We have a major competitor for power now in this country who said what they’d do. In effect, they would rip up the constitution, and the way we recruit and promote our senior civil servants, and indeed would interfere in the choice of judges.
And so much would go … We’d crumble, and it would be very hard to get it back.
Government says 900,000 people could get stronger rights under crackdown on bogus self-employment loopholes
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has told published a consultation paper on employment status reform. This sets out how the government proposes to implement plans he announced at Labour conference to close the “bogus self-employment loopholes” that deny workers basic rights.
Explaining the plans, the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade says:
Bogus self-employment is a practice whereby some businesses mislabel staff as self-employed to avoid statutory obligations.
However, the day-to-day reality is that many of these people are treated as workers, not self-employed. External estimates suggest that as many as 900,000 people may currently be affected by this and could be missing out on core employment rights.
The proposals to be consulted on could provide greater clarity to businesses and workers, levelling the playing field for those businesses who are already doing the right thing and clamping down on abuses. This could help workers such as parcel couriers, delivery drivers, hairdressers and gig economy workers.
But, in a good article on this topic for LabourList, Tom Berger points out that the plans don’t include a firm commitment to create a single status of worker in employment law – something that in opposition the party did commit to.
Meri Ahlberg, a senior policy adviser at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, a thinktank that has argued for employment status reform, said:
The measures in the government’s consultation are a step forward for making sure people have the rights and protections everyone deserves. But without putting single worker status and tax reform on the table for the near future, it will still be cheaper to employ people in less secure jobs and millions of workers will be left without sick pay and parental pay. It’s time basic protections were in place for everyone, however they work, and that existing protections are enforced properly.
Zelenskyy says he will be discussing intelligence sharing 'difficulties' and Starlink access with Burnham
And this is what Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, said in reply to Andy Burnham.
We are very thankful, all our people in Ukraine, we absolutely thankful to your nation. You are strong people, a very supportive nation …
[This is a] terrible war. Absolutely terrible as.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was being attacked by ballistic missiles and hundreds of Iranian drones.
There was no energy ceasefire, he said. It looked like “escalation from Russian side”.
He said he wanted the war to stop.
We have massive attacks today, and it’s a pity that we had also some difficulties. What I want to discuss with Andy – about Starlink and about intelligence. There are lot of different surprises on which you can’t count.
He said UK was one of Ukraine’s strongest partners.
A reporter asked Zelenskyy if he could confirm that the US had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, and if it had slowed down Starlink – meaning Ukrainian weapons lose access to the internet at very high speeds (making them inoperable). Zelenskyy did not answer.
Burnham praises Zelenskyy for showing 'leadership' after Trump's energy ceasefire comment
Here are fuller quotes from the public statements by Andy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelenskyy before their main meeting.
Burnham said:
MrPresident, it’s a great privilege for me to welcome you to Downing Street today. And you’ve just seen the reaction [a reference to the crowd cheering as he arrived]. Obviously, you’ve seen the solidarity and the support you’ve got from everybody here in Britain. We’re behind you. And that will not change.
We know that the last few days, the last few hours, have been very dark and difficult days for Ukraine. We know that the country sustained heavy bombardments in the last 24 hours in Kyiv, particularly. And we would want to extend our condolences to all of those people in Ukraine who’ve lost loved ones as a result of what has been happening.
President Trump made a call at the weekend for an energy ceasefire. And, Volodymyr, you have shown your leadership in saying that you would be prepared to sit down and discuss what that looks like, to make sure we protect people from a very harsh winter that lies ahead in Ukraine.
Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine. It’s clear to the world, again, who the aggressor is in this conflict.
However, in these moments, Britain will continue to provide you with whatever support that we can. And today I’m announcing that we are accelerating the delivery of British-made air defences for you, and we will make sure that they’re in place as soon as possible. (See 9am.)
I’ve also asked all of our ministers here in the government to do whatever they can, extra, to support you, and they are looking at all possible avenues …
All of the people of Ukraine have our support. There are such connections between our two countries. We will forever stand by you through this difficult time.
Burnham tells Zelenskyy's UK's support for Ukraine 'will not change'
Andy Burnham told Volodymyr Zelenskyy Britain’s support for Ukraine “will not change”, as he welcomed the leader to Downing Street.
In public remarks before their main meeting got under way, Burnham said:
You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change.
He added that recent days had been “dark and difficult” for Ukraine, which has suffered “heavy bombardment in the last 24 hours”, and he extending the UK’s condolences to those who had lost loved ones.
Burnham said Zelenskyy was “prepared to sit down and discuss” the energy ceasefire proposed by Donald Trump, but added: “Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine.”
He said:
In these moments, Britain will continue to provide you with whatever support we can.
Zelenskyy said he was “thankful” for British support, saying:
Our people, we survived and continue to do this because we have strong partners and I’m very proud that we have one of the strongest partners in our history and it’s your people, Andy.
Andy Burnham has welcomed President Zelenskyy to Downing Street.
As they posed for pictures outside No 10, there was a loud cheer from Foreign Office staff who were there watching. (The Foreign Office is next door to Downing Street.)
King Charles meets Zelenskyy, before Ukrainian president's meeting with Burnham
Another ‘show of support’ feature of President Zelenskyy’s visit is the fact that he was invited to meet the king at Buckingham Palace. Foreign leaders coming to Downing Street for a political visit don’t normally get to meet the king at the same time. But Charles and Zelenskyy have met many times before, and the king is a strong supporter of Ukraine.
Thank you to His Majesty King Charles III for the audience. For me, it is important to have the opportunity to personally thank him for the unwavering support of Ukraine. We appreciate all the assistance from the United Kingdom.
While Andy Burnham has been relatively guarded in what he has said in public (see 12.40pm) about Donald Trump buying diesel from Russia and declaring that Volodymyr Zelenskyy should be replaced as Ukrainian president, this is a way of using the apparatus of the state to send a visual signal that the UK is very, very firmly on Zelenskyy’s side on this one.
President Zelenskyy is expected to arrive in Downing Street shortly. Unusually, there will be a ceremonial military guard there to greet him. According to Sky News, Downing Street has not laid on one of these for a visitor since Donald Trump visited Chequers.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Nigel Farage's exit from the Telegraph may be cause for cheer. But there’s a sobering side to this story | Jane Martinson
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Nigel Farage has been writing columns for the Daily Telegraph since 2016, most of which have promoted the previously Brexit and now Reform UK party he leads, or accused his rivals of going soft on immigration. For this privilege the paper’s cash-strapped bosses paid him around £4,000 a month, adding up to nearly half a million pounds over the past decade.
News broke this week that Farage’s services are no longer required by the Telegraph’s new German owners, Axel Springer, though sources close to Farage say that he resigned. The paper is also reported to be negotiating the exit of Allison Pearson, who has been complimentary of far-right activist Tommy Robinson’s “rough-diamond charisma”, which together have prompted rumours that Springer has called a halt to the paper’s rightwards shift, calling it back to the basics of its Conservative party bible past.
All the attention so far has focused on the departure of these controversial columnists: subscribers have threatened to leave in posts on X, with mutterings about Springer’s pro-EU stance and the existence of its internal LGBTQ+ network.
Yet, while there are signs of a tonal shift away from some of the more outre Telegraph rantings, most of the outrage misses the main cause of the change. “This wasn’t politics,” one insider told me. “It was just money.”
The Telegraph is just the latest example of the trend for media organisations: while still attracting trophy prices such as the £575m Springer paid to acquire the newspaper in June, many no longer have the money to pay for journalists. As new Telegraph Media Group chief executive Carolin Hulshoff Pol told staff in announcing the cuts, the Telegraph’s print sales continue to decline, its search traffic is under pressure and AI is changing everything.
In total, more than 100 people are said to be facing the axe before Christmas, almost 20% of editorial and commercial staffing. The company has not confirmed numbers but sports and culture, two departments considered the mainstay of Telegraph coverage, are expected to be harder hit than comment.
Some journalists have already announced their departure. A post by Liam Halligan, who has written a well-regarded economics column for 27 years, prompted sympathy as well as some outrage on X about the possible left turn. Few mentioned the fact that Springer boss Mathias Döpfner is said to be a fan of the platform’s owner, Elon Musk, and encouraged him to back Germany’s far-right AfD party (as reported by the Telegraph itself).
Others to leave include the head of long reads, Lisa Markwell, a former editor of the Independent on Sunday, who no one would accuse of swivel-eyed bigotry.
The perceived toning down of anti-migrant, pro-extremist content in recent weeks is more likely to be a reflection of the current zeitgeist, with both Reform and the Maga right having seen better days. Besides, as one senior Telegraph journalist told me: “As for singling out Brexiteers, they’re all Brexiteers here (bar one or two notable exceptions).”
Before the Springer takeover, during the three-year ownership limbo after Lloyds Bank seized assets from their former owners, the Barclay family, staff had been expecting cuts under a new owner. Other prospective owners, which included RedBird IMI and the owners of the Daily Mail, were all expected to cut costs, especially when the price rose to a level that defied economic reality. This is partly because the independent directors brought in to sell the business were apparently more focused on decorating rather than selling off the top floor.
Media owners in this prolonged time of crisis, facing a business model savaged by the internet and a collapse in trust, have tended to cut jobs slowly, over time. But Springer, obviously in a hurry, having waited 22 years since its first offer for the Telegraph, was not prepared to wait any longer.
Yet Döpfner had cheered a depressed newsroom in June, when he spoke of using the Telegraph to push into the US market as a centre-right, pro-free speech challenger to the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times. His words seemed to echo those of another media mogul with global ambitions: Rupert Murdoch. Amid a legal battle about the future of the Murdoch family trust, Murdoch said that his papers would be the “protector of the conservative voice in the English-speaking world”.
Yet Springer’s expansion plan, we now learn, is based on greater use of AI. Though details of how this technology will be used are yet to be revealed, there is talk of it being utilised to streamline the content produced across all Springer’s outlets, which includes Politico and Business Insider. The lack of a human editor, if not touch, seemed to be evident in an official email jointly signed by Hulshoff Pol and Chris Evans, the paper’s editor; if anything screams “written by ChatGPT”, it’s announcing job cuts with ambitions to turn your company “into a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”.
It is hard to feel sympathy for Nigel Farage, who appears to have no trouble getting people to pay him ridiculous sums of money for various jobs. The same cannot be said for more than 100 journalists who face the possibility of Christmas with no job at all.
- 
  Jane Martinson is an academic and Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group, and writes in a personal capacity

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Russian society being ‘systematically crushed’ says Novaya Gazeta as newspaper announces closure
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent media outlets, has announced it will permanently close next month. The newspaper, whose former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov won the Nobel peace prize in 2021, cited intolerable pressure, including being stripped of its newsroom, its donation platforms and its legal right to publish.
“This is not just our own story; it is the story of a country and a society that are being systematically crushed,” wrote its editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, on the newspaper’s website.
Launched in the 1990s and for many years partly funded by the late Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, Novaya made its name through dogged, long-form reporting on corruption, rights abuses and social issues. Over the years, six of its journalists have been assassinated, including Anna Politkovskaya, who was gunned down in the stairwell of her Moscow apartment block in 2006.
While Novaya always swam against a tide of repression, the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made independent reporting almost impossible and decimated the Russian media landscape. Novaya was one of the last critical voices still operating from inside the country.
“For nearly five years of ***, we managed to keep working while being completely encircled by the security services. Now it’s over. We have found ourselves in a ‘kill zone’,” wrote Sokolov. The stars were used in place of the word “war”, as under Russian law, journalists must refer to the war in Ukraine as a “special military operation” or face consequences.
The newspaper’s first response to the invasion was to put out a special bilingual Russian-Ukrainian edition in the days after Vladimir Putin launched the invasion. It described the war as “madness” on its front page. Soon after, the Kremlin implemented draconian new censorship laws, which forced media outlets to publish only the Russian official narrative about the conflict.
“We said it’s not journalism and we’re not going to do that,” said Nadezhda Prusenkova, the head of Novaya’s press service. The newspaper published blank white spaces instead of euphemisms and false information, to provide a visible reminder of the censorship laws.
By the end of March 2022, Novaya decided to stop publishing its print edition altogether, but the threats and pressure only increased. In April that year, Muratov was doused with red paint while on a train, an attack that damaged his eyesight and that US officials say was carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence agencies. In September that year, the newspaper’s official licence was taken away and soon after their website was blocked in Russia.
Novaya’s journalists, long used to operating in a hostile environment, found ways to circumvent the bans. Many left Russia, and a number of exiled former employees set up Novaya Gazeta Europe, a legally distinct outlet. Muratov and a core team stayed behind and continued to publish a series of magazines with a print run of 999 copies, taking advantage of a law that means magazines with under 1,000 copies do not require an official licence. Novaya’s website continued running, too, although the Russian state hit the outlet with various new legal threats.
“The fact Novaya kept working for this four and a half years after everything that happened was a miracle, but it was not just a miracle, it was also the daily choice of people who continued to go to work even when it was very scary,” said Elena Kostyuchenko, a former Novaya journalist who spent 17 years at the newspaper. “Today I feel very inspired by my colleagues, but also very painful and sad for them, and for all of us.”
In recent months, Prusenkova said the pressure had become intolerable. In April, the journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”. He is under house arrest awaiting trial and last month Sokolov’s home was searched as part of the case.
This month, the newspaper’s landlords informed Novaya staff that they must vacate their longstanding office premises in central Moscow by 9 November. The newsroom has been the hub of the newspaper for decades and houses a memorial museum to Politkovskaya in the former office of the murdered journalist. Prusenkova said the exhibits would be taken down and put into storage, for now.
On top of the eviction notice, all the outlet’s donation platforms have been shut down, leaving the paper without any source of funding. The court case, combined with the eviction and the lack of funds, gave the newspaper no choice but to close, said staff.
“Sometimes it happens that your enemies win. At this moment in time, it seems like they have won, and we have no options left,” said Prusenkova. But she said it was probable Novaya’s journalists would try to find some way to continue their work. “After all, we don’t know how to do anything else,” she said.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”
Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”
Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.
The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.
Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.
“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.
When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.
Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”
US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.
Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.
US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.
Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.
Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.
His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.
Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.
The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.
Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.
“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.
Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.
Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.
Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.
Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”
Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.
“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”
Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.
Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.
Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.
Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.
David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”
The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”
Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.
Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.
Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.
Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”
In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.
Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.
El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.
Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.
Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.
For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.
“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.
Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety efforts
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Companies building the most advanced AI systems must increase safety efforts, the UK’s AI minister will say, as he announces a strengthening of Britain’s cyber defences.
Kanishka Narayan will call on companies developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. He will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models and will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.
Narayan’s speech in west London will be the first since Andy Burnham made AI a cabinet-level brief. It comes as Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which tests the most powerful AI models, raised fears enemy states could steal unreleased cutting-edge models. Amid increasing global concern at dangers posed by AI, Irving told the Guardian: “The AI companies do not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models.”
He cited a recent incident at OpenAI where it was “hacked” by cybersecurity researchers, who said “the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge”. The attack was carried out under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers testing its systems. OpenAI says it has multiple protections against theft of its models, including encryption and continuous monitoring.
Irving, a former employee at OpenAI and Google DeepMind who now runs an AI safety research body, has warned there is a “50% chance” of humanity being wiped out by superintelligent AIs and the only answer, for now, is to stop development of advanced systems as soon as possible. Irving is concerned by the rate of progress in alarming attributes shown by models, which could lead to them becoming highly advanced in traits such as concealing their actions and manipulating humans.
“It is possible we [will] get superintelligence in less than 12 months, on the current path,” he said.
Narayan’s speech will be watched closely for signs the UK may join a call for international governments to coordinate common safety standards for AIs, which has been signed by leaders of nations including Finland, France, Germany, Australia, Singapore, the UAE and Ireland, but not the UK and the US, where Donald Trump has said he wants the leading AI companies to “self-police”. The international alliance calling for strict rules comes after a wave of recent incidents with misaligned advanced AIs hacking into private and government systems.
In one of the latest cases, Anthropic on Friday revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model the AI contacted police claiming it could help solve a murder. It had landed on a page containing a police department tip form and a mention of an unsolved homicide. It wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Although Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, its instructions did not rule out form submissions.
Last week UK intelligence leaders from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ briefed the cabinet on AI’s threat to national security, according to the Sunday Times. The warning from the spy chiefs is being seen by some as encouragement for Burnham to grip the AI safety issue more firmly.
The prime minister told the UN last month that Britain would use its G20 presidency next year to champion agreement on AI safety with “a single set of global principles and standards”. But safety experts are calling for faster action to avert the most serious risks, which range from advanced AIs being used to mount a cyber-attack on essential infrastructure to the creation of novel bioweapons.
Meanwhile, Satya Nadella, the chair and chief executive of Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is an OpenAI shareholder, on Saturday called for AI models to be designed with an “emergency brake”. He said people needed to start from the principle of assuming advanced AI models posed an insider risk.
“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: My advice for Burnham’s first budget? Hit the banks – and hit them hard | Polly Toynbee
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Vibes matter. We live by how we feel – an idea that orthodox economics gets wrong and Andy Burnham’s first budget looks set to get right.
This walking good-vibes maestro is spreading a confetti of small good deeds. These may not shift the dial yet on 40 years of neoliberal economics, but they show the way he’s heading. Eyecatching everyday things – from capping bus fares to that small but resonant sum of £45 VAT on average off electricity bills – get people talking, alongside bigger plans for a national care service, electoral reform and a possible journey back to the EU.
Though his first budget is billed as unradical, one tax rise stands out for its Burnham vibes. After years of no penalties, no apologies, no payback for their bailout from the crash they caused, banks face a tax rise. The Tories’ cuts to the bank levy and bank profits surcharge were left in place by Rachel Reeves. No longer.
UK profits from the country’s four biggest banks were reportedly £13bn for the first half of this year, 16% up on last year.
Don’t undervalue the toughness it takes to ignore bankers’ intimidation, as the boss of their pressure group UK Finance writes to the chancellor saying a tax rise will encourage banks to move to competitor countries. The group’s claim that London has the highest bank taxes is a fabrication: only Ireland has a lower rate among western European countries. Paris’s is far higher, according to the authoritative Tax Policy Associates.
Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said that any move against bank profits could cause him to scrap plans for a £3bn London headquarters, a tower in Canary Wharf to house more than half of the bank’s 23,000 UK staff. He threatened Reeves likewise, and announced the tower go-ahead only after she left banks in peace in her 2025 budget.
Pause here to examine Dimon, the essence of the business power that Labour governments are always up against. Forbes lists his net worth as $3.1bn, and he took home $43m last year. In 2009, when the then chancellor, Alistair Darling, imposed a 50% levy on bankers’ bonuses over £25,000, Dimon called him to protest. In his memoir, Back from the Brink, Darling recalled that a “very, very angry” Dimon had threatened that JP Morgan might reconsider its UK investments. “He said that his bank bought a lot of UK debt and he wondered if that was now such a good idea.” And, yes, again Dimon reportedly warned that he might not build a new London office.
This year, documents released in the Epstein files revealed how the then business secretary, Peter Mandelson, had urged Dimon to “mildly threaten” Darling over the tax. That’s their milieu and how they operate. But Darling didn’t back down, though he was besieged by bankers with identical scripts. He stood firm, and JP Morgan built its London office and didn’t stop buying UK government debt. The BBC’s Faisal Islam recounts that episode as told him by Darling as “an incredible live example of the relative power of government and financial markets, of the actual dynamics of the ‘bond vigilantes’”.
The bank payroll tax raised an estimated £2.3bn in four months. But it was dropped. Are you surprised to learn that what was billed as a bonus levy was paid by the banks, never by the bankers? Or by their lack of shame or collective responsibility as they bargained squalidly over bonuses even in the aftermath of a crash they caused?
Officially the bank bailout cost the public £23bn, after some asset sales. But that’s trivial compared with the colossal lasting damage right across the economy. Official estimates cite a loss of up to 7.5% of GDP; others suggest double that amount.
Bankers hiss at any hint of plucking a few feathers off them, but we wait to know how much John Healey dares take. Dimon visited No 10 last month to warn them off a tax raise, but Burnham only “dropped into the meeting briefly”.
So, how much? Returning the corporation tax surcharge on banks to its original 8%, from the 3% to which the Tories cut it, would yield £2bn. It’s a puny sum, and the banks owe the country much more. But nonetheless, Burnham resisting their bullying would send a self-confident message.
TUC polling finds strong support for a bank windfall tax, as it does for higher gambling and wealth taxes. Raising capital gains tax is popular, too. In the air, more long-term, is a money-raising idea backed by the Institute for Fiscal Studies and Resolution Foundation, to merge national insurance and income tax and no longer exempt pensions, rent and share income from NI.
Burnham knows the trick to raising tax is linking it to good spending, such as ending the triple lock to invest in social care. So banks, shedding jobs by the thousand, could be funding Alan Milburn’s upfront costs to get Neets (young people not in education, employment or training) into work.
Good vibes greet this budget. Though inflation is up, so is employment, growth, business investment and average pay. Earnings inequality jumped up for the first time in a decade, but from Friday, trade union reps get the right to recruit in every workplace, a gamechanger in anti-union companies. Union membership is the surest way to raise pay, by a reported 4-5%, so ignore Tories raging about the “red tape” of workers’ rights.
A budget signals a government’s way forward. Willingness to defy bank bullying, even a bit, is a good early sign. Watch out for more Burnham emblems.
- 
  Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Non-profit group leaks data of more than 40,000 homeland security workers
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Data identifying more than 41,000 employees and contractors for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was released on Wednesday in an unprecedented leak that reveals how the agency is organized. The records, which were made public by the transpaency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets reference operation names, surveillance programs and information on undercover initiatives.
DHS did not immediately return a message seeking comment.
The leaked data unveils the names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from various DHS agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
Most of the agents in the leak – more than 21,000 – work for CBP, and about 6,600 work for ICE.
The data also includes job titles, email groups and other details that show which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work.
It was made public at a time when DHS, in turn, has aggressively sought to unmask critics on social media, and obtain records on protestors and journalists – even as it moves to keep its own agents anonymous, defending agents’ rights to hide their identities and faces while conducting enforcement.
In a statement, Emma Best, a Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder, said the hacktivist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight.
The Department of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data, it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”.
The disclosure – which the non-profit data transparency group says draws on information obtained by an entity calling itself “Department of Peace” – is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.
In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the defense department was hit with a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.
The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors.
Best’s statement said Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”
Reuters could not immediately verify the authenticity of the entire data trove but it was able to match personal information of about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs. In other cases, Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach.
In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Burnham says long-awaited 10-year plan may be delayed until January – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Burnham says long-awaited 10-year plan may be delayed until January
Andy Burnham has confirmed that his long-awaited 10-year plan may be delayed.
In his speech outside No 10 on the day he became PM, Burham declared that “later this year” he would “bring forward a new plan for Britain, a 10-year plan, laying out a path from where we are now to where I believe we all want Britain to be”. The document has been described as the core policy statement coming from No 10 this year, with some insiders briefing that the budget was relatively low-key because key announcements were being held back for the 10-year plan.
But we may have to wait a little longer then expected until we see it. In an interview with Hugo Gye from the Economist, when asked when it would appear, Burnhamsaid:
We may go into the new year, to be honest ... December or January, I think we will need to leave that open.
Burnham was speaking after Ailbhe Rea in the New Statesman published an article yesterday suggesting that, even when the initial 10-year plan announcement comes at the end of this year (or in January), that won’t be the final word. Rea said:
Yet, with expectations high, some familiar with the process are already worried that the Ten-Year Plan may be another kicking of the can. I can reveal that it may not be the long, comprehensive document that we might have expected, and will be the beginning – not the end – of a long consultation process.
It will be a speech, delivered by the prime minister before Christmas, to tick the box of a plan delivered “later this year”, accompanied by a document that may be “slimmer than expected”. It will mark the beginning of a six-to-nine-month process of consulting with the public, think tanks and everybody else about government priorities – as well as kickstarting work across government to define what some of its plans will look like in more detail. That process, in turn, will set the priorities for the spending review, itself a procedure that will take months. Suddenly, critics fear, we are looking at a government spending well over a year discussing its plans without taking the major action to address them.
Yvette Cooper says she hopes much of health budget can qualify for new 'preventative DEL' protected spending status
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has said her officials are “extremely excited” about one of the more obscure, but potentially most significant, changes in last week’s budget – the creation of a new category of “preventative” spending.
Internal government spending negotiations are all about DEL (departmental expenditure limits), and standard government accounting differentiates between resource DEL (day-to-day spending) and capital DEL.
Last week John Healey, the chancellor, announced that he would create a new category of ringfenced spending in the spending review next year – preventative DEL, or PDEL. This will ensure that budgets are protected for measures involving early intervention to create savings in the long term.
Giving evidence to the Commons health committee yesterday, Cooper said that her public health officials were “extremely excited” about this announcement. She said:
We think a lot of our investment across not just public health but across the NHS has benefits in terms of keeping people healthy and in work. A lot of those treatment budgets have a consequence in helping people work as well as in the direct prevention.
Cooper said that, as a former Treasury minister, she knew that preventative programmes designed to deliver benefits in the long term were “the areas that always come under shortest-term pressure”.
Asked how rigorous her definition of preventative spending would be, she replied:
Mine would be quite broad; we do not yet know what the Treasury’s will be …
A lot of our treatment services have an impact, in saving money elsewhere. Mental health is a really good example, as we know that a lot of young people who are not in work could benefit from mental health support.
Cooper is already in a better position than most other cabinet ministers because the health budget is one of the few that it nominally protected from real-terms cuts.
Heather Stewart, the Guardian’s economics editor, wrote a good column on the potential benefits of PDEL at the weekend.
Peter Walker has also posted these on Bluesky about what Angus MacIntyre said when Peter asked him why he did not mention Ukraine in his first speech as Reform UK’s armed forces spokesperson.
In a 16-minute speech on defence, Reform’s new armed forces spokesperson did not mention Ukraine or Iran once.
Worth noting that I asked MacIntyre about this after and he said this was simply as his speech was to introduce him and his role, and that Ukraine/Iran are very much a focus
Farage claims polling figures showing Tories catching up with Reform UK are 'nonsense' and due to pollsters' 'jiggery-pokery'
Peter Walker
Peter Walker is a senior Guardian political correspondent.
Polling numbers which have seen the Conservatives climb above Reform UK are not credible, Nigel Farage has said, claiming that there had been “jiggery-pokery” intended to restore the two-party system.
Farage made the claim unprompted while speaking to reporters after a speech when he was asked if Reform UK had failed in vetting, given the number of councillors and candidates found to have said offensive things or, in some cases, charged with serious offences.
The Reform UK leader said that while politicians from other parties had been arrested for alleged offences, it was only those connected to his party – notably this week’s charging of George Madgwick, its leader on Hampshire county council, with 12 counts of rape and other offences – that led to “a BBC push notification – the others don’t”.
Digressing into polling, he said:
What I will tell you is this: the jiggery-pokery that is going on with polling is utterly astonishing. And if you believe the polls you’ve seen this week, you’re not understanding what’s going on out there. On the raw data, we’re four points higher, and the Conservatives are nearly four points lower than the reality.
And I know there’s a desperate push from the establishment – let’s get back to two-party politics, let’s get back to Tweedledum and Tweedledee. Let’s get back to total failure. Let’s make sure there’s no change.
It simply isn’t true. What you’ve seen from the polling industry is nonsense, and I mean that.
He did not offer any evidence for the claim.
Farage adopted a different line in a recent GB News appearance when he said he did not mind being behind in the opinion polls because he thought that would make campaigning easier. (See 1.51pm.)
Farage says Repubicans lost US midterm elections because Trump broke promise to end foreign wars
Peter Walker
Peter Walker is a senior Guardian political correspondent.
The main lesson for Reform UK from the Republicans’ huge defeat in the US midterm elections is “keep your promises”, Nigel Farage has told reporters in his first comments since the results.
Speaking after a media event at which the party unveiled their new armed forces spokesperson, Angus MacIntyre, a former RAF officer, Farage said Trump was also being punished for the “bizarre” decision to wage a long-term conflict with Iran.
Asked if he had learned something from the US results, Farage said:
Yes, keep your promises. Trump was very good in the first term and the second term in keeping his promises, but he broke a promise. That was no more foreign wars, and we’re eight months in, and the resultant rise in gas and diesel prices, more than anything else, is what did them in.
The key focus must be keeping your promises, and the cost of living, of course.
Asked if the Iran war – which Farage did not initially oppose – was a mistake, Farage said:
No question about it. I mean, to have quick tactical strikes from Diego Garcia, to try and maybe not halt, but at least slow the nuclear weapons programme, I totally agree with that …
But would I have said to them, ‘Yes, come on, let’s go to war for the next eight months or three years’? No, of course not. And that is so bizarre.
The government has announced it is spending £13m on another wave of Valour-recognised support centres for military veterans and their families. In the first round, 14 organisations got funding earlier this year, and another 21 organisations are now getting money. “An estimated one million veterans and their families in the UK will benefit from easier access to local services, thanks to the Valour network expanding,” the government says.
Mahmood accused of hardening rules for 200,000 successful asylum applicants
Shabana Mahmood has been accused of causing “distress and uncertainty” to hundreds of thousands of refugees by quietly introducing plans to force them to wait up to 30 years before being granted the right to settle in the UK, Rajeev Syal reports.
The latest episode of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast is out. It features Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey talking about the US midterm elections results, and what lessons they may offer to Labour.
After MacIntyre finished his speech, Farage did not take questions on camera in the main hall where the rally was taking place. But he is speaking to journalists in a “huddle” shortly.
MacIntyre says, if Reform UK wins the election, it will end ongoing prosections of veterans.
And future prosecutions would only be allowed with the consent of the defence secretary, he says.
(This is not that different from the situation that will apply under the Northern Ireland Troubles bill, currently going through parliament. It says any Troubles-related prosecutions will only be allowed with the explicit consent of the attorney general.)
New Reform UK defence spokesperson says prosecutions of veterans amount to 'Marxist rewriting of history'
MacIntyre complains about the prosecution of veterans over alleged war crimes. Veterans should be treated as heroes, but they are treated as criminals, he says.
Human rights lawyers dissect the decisions taken by servicemen in the heat of battle, life and death situations that no civilian can imagine.
Government lawyers use the luxury of hindsight, often decades on, to drag our veterans through the courts, treating them as criminals at every stage.
This is unjust and immoral.
We are witnessing the Marxist rewriting of history’s narratives, calling evil good and good evil.
A functioning society celebrates, not criminalises, its armed forces personnel.
My colleague Peter Walker is at the Reform UK event. He has posted these about Angus MacIntyre.
I am at a Reform UK event at which they are about to unveil their new armed forces [spokesperson], a just-retired RAF officer called Angus MacIntyre. As someone who ended a 40-year military career just last week he has no apparent social media presence, which must be useful for Reform.
Note he is armed forces spokesperson, not the main defence brief. Two years-plus from the election, that brief for Reform is still unfilled, as are a few other fairly key ones eg health.
MacIntyre seems like a real believer. This is him on asylum: “Uncontrolled illegal migration has brought hundreds of thsouands of undocumented fighting-age males, many with combat eperience and operatives from hostile states into the heart of our communities.”
He also says that zet zero has “collapsed our industrial base, and they put our energy sovereignty at risk”. He is a confident speaker, so my guess is we’ll see a fair bit more of him. But he is also a complete political novice, so there is always a risk of something going wrong.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Revealed: French police used UK-funded 4x4 vehicles to charge student protesters
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
French police have used 4x4 vehicles paid for by British taxpayers to charge at student protesters during the school protests that have swept the country.
The French government has confirmed that an investigation has been launched into why the cars, funded by the UK government specifically to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel, were used during a protest involving school students in Dunkirk.
School protests have been taking place across France for a third week with an estimated 160,000 people involved, with protesters raising concerns about crumbling schools and teacher shortages. Demonstrators have criticised policing tactics after teargas was fired at protesters in two areas.
The incident involving the UK-funded 4x4, a land cruiser known as Masstech VEZI (Vehicule d’Eclairage de Zone d’Intervention), was reported by French media outlet BFM TV on 10 October.
The report included footage of the VEZI driving at speed, reversing then driving forwards again with a bin caught under a front wheel being dragged along. Students can be heard screaming as they scatter from the path of the vehicle.
According to reports, a 14-year-old girl was injured by the vehicle and was taken to hospital, sustaining a haematoma. She was later discharged from hospital. She is now recovering, but she told reporters that what happened to her was “unacceptable”.
The VEZI was earmarked for UK-funded operations on French beaches to stop asylum seekers boarding dinghies, part of an Anglo-French border agreement signed in January 2018 and known as the Sandhurst treaty.
This treaty specifies cooperation between France and the UK in combatting irregular immigration and secures UK financial support for French efforts through the “Sandhurst funds”.
These funds enable France’s national gendarmerie (police service) to acquire additional resources such as all-terrain vehicles suited to dunes and beaches, including the VEZIs, which are reinforced with grilles.
According to a recent French parliamentary cross-party inquiry into Anglo-French border agreements, nine of these specialised VEZI vehicles have been bought under the terms of the Sandhurst treaty. The inquiry report states that to be eligible for Sandhurst funding, the equipment must contribute directly to combatting illegal migration in the UK.
A spokesperson from the office of Laurent Nuñez, France’s minister of the interior, when asked why a vehicle funded by the UK and specifically earmarked for border control was used to counter a schools protest, said: “We can confirm the opening of an investigation into this.”
Sources close to the investigation said: “I don’t think the British are aware that their money is being used to beat French kids.”
Another expressed concern about the expanding militarisation of French policing to support authoritarian policies.
A spokesperson for Utopia 56, a French association that provides support to asylum seekers in northern France, said: “In Dunkirk, the 4x4 that ploughed into high school students during the protests is a vehicle funded by the British Sandhurst fund – money earmarked for combatting Channel crossings.
“The practice of using 4x4s to chase people in the student protest is the same one used on the beaches.
“Disproportionate force is employed to silence, intimidate and deter. The repressive tactics being tested at the border to prevent crossings should serve as a warning to everyone.
“These are surveillance, control and repression methods that will be replicated in other contexts. The incident involving the vehicle in the student protest is proof of this.”
The UK Home Office declined to comment.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Canadian publisher Boréal ends relationship with novelist Thélyson Orélien over alleged use of AI
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The publisher of top-selling Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien, who was removed from France’s most prestigious literary prize list last month, has confirmed the author used artificial intelligence to help write his novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was Either That or Die).
Orélien has denied allegations that he used AI on his breakthrough novel and, last week, Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer.
But on Wednesday, Boréal said it had conducted a further investigation into the allegations.
“New information, confirmed over the past few days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process” of the novel, a statement from Boréal said.
The publisher announced it was “ending its professional relationship” with Orélien.
Boréal said it did not know the extent of AI’s use in the writing process “and we will likely never have a definitive answer”.
It said it gathered all the working versions of the novel and hired an outside party to analyse various drafts.
“The results obtained this week revealed traces of AI tags in the metadata of certain documents,” Boréal said.
Before conducting this analysis, the publisher said it had tried to work with Orélien to gather the evidence necessary to prove his innocence.
That effort was inconclusive, and Orélien “subsequently announced that he would not provide any further information,” the publisher said.
The novel about migration had been scheduled for translation in more than 20 countries.
The book was shrouded in suspicion and withdrawn from the list for France’s book prize the Prix Goncourt, after tests with AI detector Pangram indicated a 100% probability it contained computer-generated text.
In a statement to Agence France-Presse earlier this month, Orélien called the allegations “slander and heresy”.
“Here and there I did use tools for research, particularly for foreign idioms,” he said in a statement sent exclusively to AFP.
“But not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine, nor the meaning or the structure of a story that comes from my gut.”
He stood firm on Wednesday, telling the French newspaper Libération he used AI “in the creative process” for “historical research”.
“I’ve explained everything to those close to me, but at the moment I don’t think my words count for anything,” he said, adding that what he is now experiencing has “gone way too far”.
Orélien said he started writing the book in late 2017 “on the corner of a table” and completed a first draft in 2019 of more than 300 pages, several years before the advent of AI services such as ChatGPT.
The author fled his native Haiti after a 2010 earthquake that struck the Caribbean island, already ravaged by poverty and unrest.
In response to separate allegations of plagiarism, Orélien admitted to making “unacceptable mistakes” in the past in his writing, without mentioning specifics.
“I was just over 20, I was probably a little too impatient, without really understanding how much I still had to learn. I wanted to write, I was reading a lot,” he wrote.
“But admiring someone does not give you the right to take, to claim as mine texts that are not my own.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners.
The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person.
Unlawful settlement activity will be captured through a breach of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva convention on occupation.
The Israeli government closed the UK consulate last week in protest, forcing the it to withdraw 21 diplomats and downgrade the consulate to the status of a mission. But the Israeli punishment does not appear to have deterred the UK government.
The proposed new powers also extend government reach beyond direct perpetrators of wrongdoing to those who facilitate, incite, promote or support qualifying conduct, provide it with finance, goods or technology, conceal evidence of it or benefit from it.
Banks and commercial entities could also fall within this remit as designation only requires reasonable grounds to suspect involvement.
The proposed sanctions measures include asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, travel bans and director disqualifications.
A new urgent procedure will allow ministers to mirror designations already made by the EU, US, Canada or Australia for up to 112 days while a specific separate UK case is prepared.
The new global sanctions regime will come into force on Thursday but will need endorsement by MPs and peers within 28 days.
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is pushing through the measures at speed because the Israeli government has vowed to press ahead with an E1 settlement containing 1,234 homes in the West Bank – a development that many observers say would sever a contiguous, viable Palestinian state, so making the so-called two-state solution to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict near impossible.
The E1 bids close on 19 October but the Israel Land Authority has confirmed that the tender box will not be opened, nor the bids considered, before 19 November, which is after the Israeli election on 27 October.
The British Palestinian Project said the Israeli deferral “does not remove the need to deter commitments being made now, since bidders and their backers commit on 19 October, contracts could still be signed before a new Israeli government is formed”.
The project welcomed the addition of the right to liberty and security of person in the new laws, saying it opens a route to sanctions for serious arbitrary or unlawful detention, including of Palestinian children, and of those responsible for or enabling it. Save the Children estimated in November 2023 that 10,000 Palestinian children had passed through Israeli military detention over the preceding 20 years.
A UN 2026 report on children and armed conflict verified that 981 Palestinian children were detained by Israeli forces in 2025 and 180 of them remained in administrative detention without charge or trial at the year’s end.
The UK has already applied sanctions designations for restrictions on humanitarian aid in Sudan and South Sudan but this is the first time this general power is being applied as part of a new worldwide regime including Israel.
Refusing permits or blocking convoys will be sufficient grounds to apply sanctions, without requiring the obstruction to constitute a formal breach of international humanitarian law – thereby lowering the threshold for action.
Separate work is under way by UK officials in conjunction with European partners on how to outlaw British trade with unlawful Israeli settlements.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Repressive, secretive and highly militarised: Eritrea, the east African country facing UK visa ban threat
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Eritrea, the east African country embroiled in a row with the UK over its refusal to accept the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals, is considered one of world’s most secretive and repressive states, with reports of arbitrary detention and severe restrictions on freedom of expression, opinion and religion.
Situated in the Horn of Africa and bordering Sudan, Ethiopia and Djibouti, it became a sovereign state after gaining independence from Ethiopia in 1993 following a 30-year war.
The country is run by an authoritarian regime under Isaias Afwerki, who led separatist forces to defeat Ethiopian forces in 1991 and became president in 1993. He has served as president since independence and heads the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice, the country’s only legal political party.
Eritrea has not held a national election since independence. A constitution that was ratified in 1997 by the constituent assembly has still not been implemented nearly three decades later.
In 2001, the government shut down all independent newspapers after the publishing of an open letter by senior ruling party officials calling on the government to implement the constitution and hold elections.
A highly militarised state, Eritrea runs a compulsory national service system that requires students to study at a military training centre in their final year of secondary school. They undergo military training and political education before working in either military units or civilian national service roles that can last decades.
The repression and conscription has forced many Eritreans to risk harsh punishment for evading, deserting or escaping the military by fleeing the country. It is estimated that up to one-third of the Eritrean-born population lives abroad.
Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat to the UK in the year ending June 2026. Earlier this year, Eritrea abruptly withdrew cooperation with the UK on migrant returns, and on Thursday the UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said all Eritreans could be stopped from coming to the UK unless the country agreed to accept more rejected asylum seekers and criminals.
Eritrea’s political, economic and social framework has been defined by a doctrine of economic self-reliance, with the country notably rejecting foreign aid.
It was an Italian colony and parts of the country feature early to mid-20th-century Italian modernist architecture. The capital, Asmara, was inscribed as a world heritage site in 2017, with Unesco describing it as “an exceptional example of early modernist urbanism at the beginning of the 20th century and its application in an African context”.
A multi-ethnic country, Eritrea is mainly made up of the Tigrinya people. Its extensive Red Sea coastline (1,388 miles) gives it a strategic position along the Red Sea corridor.
The country has been in the spotlight in recent weeks because of fears of war with Ethiopia. Both countries have accused each other of aggression. Ethiopia has claimed Eritrean troops crossed up to 60km (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, while Eritrea has said the accusation is a fabrication to create a pretext for war.
The escalation is linked to renewed fighting between Ethiopian government forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), an armed opposition group, in Tigray, which borders Eritrea.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, a claim that Eritrea has denied. On Tuesday, Ethiopian forces advanced to Zalambessa, a town on the border with Eritrea that was under Tigrayan rebel control.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Firefighters voice growing concerns over water supplies to tackle UK wildfires
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Concerns have been raised about how drought affects the UK’s ability to cope with wildfires after MPs were told firefighters struggled for water supplies during this year’s record summer.
The government has been urged to set out water companies’ statutory responsibilities during major fire incidents to improve the country’s preparedness for the years ahead.
The UK experienced its hottest-ever summer this year, with prolonged dry periods and extreme heat fuelling wildfires across the country. Figures released earlier this month showed a clear upward trend in the number of fires recorded each year.
The chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFFC), Phil Garrigan, told MPs on the environment, food and rural affairs (EFRA) committee that fires developed more quickly because of limited water supplies. He said concerns about water availability had grown during his 37 years in the fire service.
During a wildfire in Stourbridge in the West Midlands that destroyed several homes, replenishing a water carrier took almost 40 minutes because of reduced water pressure.
In tackling a separate wildfire in the New Forest in August, the fire service said maintaining water supply had been a significant challenge.
Fire services take water from mains and open sources such as lakes and rivers. With levels in the latter extremely low as result of the drought, the fire service’s access was restricted. It also faced pressure to limit its use of mains water to avoid shortages for paying customers.
“In summers like this year, we would normally ask for more resources, but those resources aren’t always available and we’re having to wait longer for additional resources or we’re having to find other ways to deal with the fire,” said Dave Swallow, the NFCC’s deputy lead on wildfires.
A survey of UK fire and rescue services in the summer found that 81% of respondents had changed their emergency response plans in areas where access to water was a concern.
The NFCC, which conducted the survey, said growing pressure from climate breakdown, population growth, housing development and emerging infrastructure such as datacentres, was increasing demand on an already stretched water network.
“Firefighters cannot fight fires without water. That sounds obvious, yet our evidence shows four in five fire and rescue services have had to change response plans because of concerns about firefighting water supplies,” Garrigan said in the summer.
As the climate crisis worsens and demand for water increases, the Environment Agency estimates that England’s public water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055 without urgent action to future-proof resources.
The EFRA committee has called for water for firefighting to be recognised as a critical public safety requirement. It said the government should establish a statutory framework and national protocol setting out water companies’ responsibilities during major fire incidents, including minimum expectations for water supply and pressure, communication and operational coordination with fire and rescue.
The committee also said water companies should be required to assess, test and verify their ability to support firefighting operations.
“Water companies must be relied upon for adequate supply,” the committee chair, Alistair Carmichael of the Scottish Liberal Democrats, said.
A government spokesperson said: “Improving wildfire preparedness is a major government priority. That’s why this week we are holding a summit with government ministers, fire and rescue leaders, land managers and other partners to understand how we can strengthen the response to this increasing risk.”
A government-funded UK wildfire conference is scheduled to take place in Leeds on 10 and 11 November.
