SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Imagine if, for once, Labour decided to tell the truth about immigration | Gaby Hinsliff
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
My mum’s carer was uncharacteristically late one morning. She didn’t want to say why at first, but it turned out she’d found her previous client – an elderly lady living all alone, with no family to visit – collapsed on the floor, barely alive. It was a lot to cope with for someone only in their early 20s, a reminder of the heavy responsibility this job carries. Watching the carers who helped both my parents in their respective final weeks taught me that while the work itself might seem mundane, the emotional and social skills needed to do it well – to coax some sense out of the confused, to jolly along the lonely, and to soothe the dying, to walk in and out of unfamiliar houses all day long without quite knowing what you might find – are anything but.
Yet like so many jobs predominantly done by women, care has long been relentlessly undervalued. That means lousy pay, little public recognition, and now – at least for the disproportionately large chunk of this workforce who are migrant workers – the disorientating realisation that the government can snap its fingers and all your life plans are upended overnight.
Under the latest attempt by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, to ratchet immigration numbers ever further down, “low-skilled” foreign workers will now have to wait up to 15 years for the right to become permanent residents. The new rules would be backdated to 2021 to catch what the right dubbed the “Boriswave”, that unexpected surge of workers who came to Britain in the Boris Johnson years – many on health and care visas – and would under the old five-year rule have started qualifying for settlement in 2027. What has unsettled some of Mahmood’s own cabinet colleagues is the sense of the state reneging on what was understood to be the deal when those workers came here. Having to be continuously employed for 15 years instead of five without a break means in practice that some will have to leave, while others will live in mortal fear of losing a job. A growing cabinet revolt against Mahmood’s reforms is now becoming the first real challenge to Andy Burnham’s authority as prime minister, but also more broadly a test of where he really stands on immigration.
This month’s budget throws a problem that governments have been trying to ignore for a decade into sharp relief: kneejerk hostility to foreign workers is costing Britain dear, and not just because public services would fall apart without them. Last month, the Institute for Fiscal Studies warned that falling immigration would inevitably mean falling tax revenues, shrinking John Healey’s headroom at the budget by about £4bn. So much for the rightwing myth that migrants are a drain on their host country: if anything, they’ve been bailing Britain out.
It’s not just taxes, either. Immigrants pay a surcharge on top for the right to use the NHS if needed while they’re here, which is now raising £2.5bn a year, according to new research from the Nuffield Trust. It seems all those pesky liberals who argued that migrants are generally healthier than the average Briton – and therefore less likely to need a GP – were right after all: the trust estimates that migrants are on average paying in 60% more in surcharge per year than they take out in healthcare services, a handy little revenue stream that for some reason we never talk about. But immigration crackdowns threaten that income too. The trust notes that falling immigration can lead to “a sharp drop in income” for the NHS, much as slashing foreign student visas has hurt universities that were reliant on their fees.
As the Office for Budget Responsibility spelled out in 2024 – when it calculated that the surge of immigration under Johnson that so offended Tory voters at the time would help knock more than £7bn off projected government borrowing by 2028-29 – economically speaking, immigration is basically good news. If the country really wants it to fall, then something else – higher taxes, lower spending or more borrowing – is going to have to plug the resulting hole in the finances. Yet for years now, successive governments, fearful of confronting leave voters, have tried manfully to pretend that that choice does not exist.
Mahmood’s plan is essentially yet another attempt to square the same old circle, gearing the system around letting in as few people as possible – in keeping with what a furious public has for the last decade seemed to want – while trying to cherrypick those most likely to make an outsize economic contribution. Under her reforms, the highest paid workers (who are likely to pay lots of tax over their lifetimes) would be fast-tracked to settlement, while those judged more likely to be an economic burden on the state overall would be pushed away. What she doesn’t seem to have bargained for, aside from the fact that the rest of the world is in hot competition for high-skilled migrants, is the sense of deep disquiet that engenders. As the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, has pointed out, endlessly prolonging settlement risks undermining social cohesion. A country that makes very clear its foreign workers are here at best on sufferance, even if they do hold lives in their hands at work every day, does nothing to encourage them to integrate and put down roots.
The logic of Burnham’s announcement that a future Labour government might consider rejoining the EU, meanwhile, leaves Mahmood’s reforms looking strangely like the relics of a bygone era. If rejoining the single market or customs union would inevitably mean accepting freedom of movement again, what’s the point?
The truth is that grimly ratcheting immigration down to next to nothing has come at extraordinary fiscal and social cost, and if the aim was to destroy Reform’s raison d’etre then it hasn’t worked. The mainstream right has switched seamlessly from the pre-Brexit days of complaining that Polish plumbers were taking Britons’ jobs, to a much darker post-Brexit stage of painting migrants as rapists and criminals. The far right, meanwhile, has simply moved on from cheerleading for deportations to insisting that even people who were born here aren’t English unless they’re white.
Legal migrant numbers are at a historic low and small boat crossings have halved, yet that didn’t stop anger at asylum seekers spilling on to the streets again this summer. There is no level of migration low enough to satisfy some people. There is, however, very much a level of migration low enough to make us all even poorer, and the angry somehow even angrier. And right now, we’re living with it.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn, but Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned deliveries could take years and stockpiles were needed now to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the US state department said in a statement on Friday.
The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision by the US state department” but said in a post on X early on Saturday: “However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors.
“Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day.”
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
On Thursday, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
Zelenskyy said US and European allies had sufficient stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to provide to Ukraine now, which could be replenished in the coming years through contracts already paid for by Ukraine and its partners.
He said this would “be the right approach” and was “entirely feasible”.
Delayed missile deliveries have added to Kyiv’s tensions with Washington after US president Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelenskyy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will probably not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense was encouraging the Pentagon to bring forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US Jumpstart, along with national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, the state department said in a statement.
The programme uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defense and precision-guided weapons.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on drilling in Jackdaw: a truly pragmatic approach would focus on Britain’s green transition | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
This week a report from the UN Environment Programme concluded that holding global temperatures to a 1.5C warming limit – the centrepiece commitment of the Paris climate agreement – is no longer achievable. If the disastrous consequences of a significant overshoot are to be mitigated, it argued, governments must start delivering the short-term actions to meet long-term targets on reducing fossil fuel consumption.
Disappointingly, Andy Burnham and his energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, took a different view of short-term priorities on Wednesday. Before the November Cop summit, where regaining lost momentum on climate action will be crucial, their decision to approve new drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield sent a dismal signal. The prime minister justified it as a pragmatic move “at a time when people are really struggling”. But the pragmatic arguments don’t stack up.
Going ahead with Jackdaw will have no impact on bills this winter and little in the longer run. It will deliver only a small number of jobs for a very limited period. Tax revenues from new drilling will be substantially negated by the various concessions and breaks enjoyed by the oil and gas industry. Claims that Jackdaw will enhance the UK’s national energy security are hugely overblown, given that it will satisfy a mere 2% of national demand. The country’s heavy reliance on natural gas imports will remain unaltered.
So why? Mr Burnham would doubtless have preferred not to be landed with the judgment call on either Jackdaw or the much larger Rosebank oil and gas field (on which an announcement has yet to be made). Both were already in the licensing system, having been approved by Rishi Sunak as he sought a dividing line with Labour. A successful legal challenge meant the final decision fell in the present prime minister’s lap.
On Jackdaw at least, Mr Burnham appears to have judged that political expediency, particularly in Scotland, was best served by waving it through. A failure by governments to invest gamechanging sums in the green transition has made the politics of net zero more fraught. The recent Tory byelection victory in Aberdeen South followed a campaign focused on reviving oil and gas production in the North Sea. One of the first acts of Scottish Labour’s new leader, Michael Marra, has been to back both the Rosebank and Jackdaw developments.
Mr Burnham inherited this complicated set of circumstances. But rather than rubber-stamping a regressive rearguard action by the fossil fuel industry, he should be using his rhetorical gifts to make the pragmatic case for Britain’s green energy future. As research by the E3G thinktank has laid out, the dubious benefits of drilling for disappearing oil and gas reserves are dwarfed by the potential economic impact of insulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps. The government’s warm homes plan, it estimated, would significantly reduce household energy bills and generate 50,000 new jobs. Yet Ms Fahnbulleh is reportedly under pressure to find cuts so spending can be diverted to defence.
The best way to achieve energy security, back British workers and bring down bills – the three imperatives identified by Mr Burnham in his statement on Wednesday – is to invest ambitiously in the country’s climate goals. Proceeding with Jackdaw does not, in itself, signify a prime ministerial reluctance to do that. But this decision suggests there are grounds for concern about which way the wind is blowing in Downing Street.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
US midterm elections 2026 live: Democrats eye historic upset in Mississippi Senate race as Republican blame game begins
Democrat Scott Colom is leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in the southern state; JD Vance pointed to the war in Iran as the ‘obvious’ culprit for Republicans’ loss
Mississippi count continues with Democratic candidate ahead by a razor-thin margin
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the 2026 midterms where almost 24 hours after Democrats secured their historic sweep of the US Congress, two Senate seats remain in play.
Counting in Alaska is expected to continue into Thursday, while in deep red Mississippi, Democrats could be close to pulling off another almighty upset. Currently, Democrat Scott Colom is leading his Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 1,138 votes with almost 96% of the vote counted.
In the last few hours, votes for Colom have been outpacing those for his Republican opponent, although new batches of votes have not been reported for several hours now.
Although a race this close would automatically trigger a recount in some states, Mississippi has no law on the books for initiating a recount.
Democrats haven’t won a US Senate seat in Mississippi since 1982, and Donald Trump carried the state by 22 points in 2024. It’s been much longer – not since 1875 – that the state elected a Black person to that office.
Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian, whose father was a Republican who campaigned for Ronald Reagan and was friends with Thad Cochran, a longtime state politician. In 2015, he unseated a nearly 30-year incumbent when he was elected the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit. As district attorney, he had a 94% success rate for convictions.
Meanwhile, after Democrats secured their historic wins in last night’s midterm elections, Republicans are beginning the blame game:
Donald Trump claimed Republicans fared poorly because he was not on the ballot – after repeatedly urging voters to pretend he was on the ballot.
JD Vance pointed to Trump’s ongoing war in Iran as the “obvious” culprit for the loss.
Pete Hegseth’s role leading the unpopular war could lead to him taking the fall – despite Trump publicly backing him. Republicans including Trump foe Thomas Massie have criticized the defense secretary.
Ron DeSantis, Florida’s governor, said the “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” was caused in part by his party failing to target their ad spending on issues that would motivate voters.
According to exit polls from the Associated Press, voters said the cost of living and government corruption were their two top issues. But how will Trump cope with this new political reality?
The Guardian’s David Smith explores that – and whether these elections mark the beginning of the end for Trump – this analysis piece here:
Across the US, editors worked into the night on Tuesday to get out late editions of their papers. In Chicago, the Sun Times captured newly elected Senator Juliana Stratton as she celebrated her party’s victory, under the headline “Dem-olition”.
Keisha Lance Bottom’s win was described as “historic” by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution – an online publication which produces a daily front page. The paper notes that the governor-elect has shattered “racial and gender glass ceilings” on a day the US elected “four Black governors”.
Highlighting the end of the Republican party’s “stranglehold on Texas politics”, the Dallas Morning News captured two of the night’s biggest wins under the headline “Wave of change”.
Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa shared the front page, after a night that saw the Democrats sweep to victory in deep red Texas.
With the results showing hispanic voters swinging away from Trump, California’s Spanish-language daily La Opinión produced one of the more memorable front pages.
Above a picture of a battered Maga hat, the paper’s headline simply reads “National punishment”.
How papers across the world reacted to Trump's midterm loss
The results of America’s historic midterm elections reverberated around the world on Wednesday, with front pages reflecting on a night that saw Donald Trump dealt a punishing blow by the US electorate.
“Trumped” was the Guardian’s headline on Thursday’s edition, with reporter Ed Pilkington noting that, with the president’s party stripped of control of Congress, the country was waking up to a “radically altered political landscape”.
A late edition of the New York Post captured the scale of Trump’s defeat on Wednesday. Riffing on Hokusai’s Great Wave artwork, the paper notes it was a “historic romp for Democrats”, under the headline “Blue Tsunami”.
The English-language Tehran Times, which is closely aligned with the government, said in its headline: “US hegemony crumbling; Iran will never surrender”.
With a selection of midterms stories across the front page, the paper quotes senior figures under a subhead that reads “Iranian officials link Republican election defeat to US war against Iran”.
Mississippi count continues with Democratic candidate ahead by a razor-thin margin
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the 2026 midterms where almost 24 hours after Democrats secured their historic sweep of the US Congress, two Senate seats remain in play.
Counting in Alaska is expected to continue into Thursday, while in deep red Mississippi, Democrats could be close to pulling off another almighty upset. Currently, Democrat Scott Colom is leading his Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 1,138 votes with almost 96% of the vote counted.
In the last few hours, votes for Colom have been outpacing those for his Republican opponent, although new batches of votes have not been reported for several hours now.
Although a race this close would automatically trigger a recount in some states, Mississippi has no law on the books for initiating a recount.
Democrats haven’t won a US Senate seat in Mississippi since 1982, and Donald Trump carried the state by 22 points in 2024. It’s been much longer – not since 1875 – that the state elected a Black person to that office.
Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian, whose father was a Republican who campaigned for Ronald Reagan and was friends with Thad Cochran, a longtime state politician. In 2015, he unseated a nearly 30-year incumbent when he was elected the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit. As district attorney, he had a 94% success rate for convictions.
Meanwhile, after Democrats secured their historic wins in last night’s midterm elections, Republicans are beginning the blame game:
Donald Trump claimed Republicans fared poorly because he was not on the ballot – after repeatedly urging voters to pretend he was on the ballot.
JD Vance pointed to Trump’s ongoing war in Iran as the “obvious” culprit for the loss.
Pete Hegseth’s role leading the unpopular war could lead to him taking the fall – despite Trump publicly backing him. Republicans including Trump foe Thomas Massie have criticized the defense secretary.
Ron DeSantis, Florida’s governor, said the “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” was caused in part by his party failing to target their ad spending on issues that would motivate voters.
According to exit polls from the Associated Press, voters said the cost of living and government corruption were their two top issues. But how will Trump cope with this new political reality?

Why did Andy Burnham recently intervene to defend Manchester City’s beleaguered Abu Dhabi owners, days after they were found guilty of one of the biggest cheating scandals in British sporting history?
Today in Focus presenter and city resident Helen Pidd walks through modern Manchester – where Burnham was mayor for nearly a decade – and charts its transformation wrought by Emirati money.

Who ultimately has benefited from the UAE’s investment in Manchester? And, as the prime minister is keen to export his model of “Manchesterism” all across the country, what does it tell us about Burnham’s time as mayor?

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
As Republicans confront mounting political headwinds ahead of November’s midterm elections, Donald Trump is attempting to turn unrest in France into a cautionary tale for American voters, recasting the demonstrations that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the soaring cost of living as evidence of the dangers of immigration and the erosion of western civilization.
At a rally in Kansas on Monday evening, Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”.
“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” he said.
Nationwide protests in France on Saturday were called over rising fuel prices and falling purchasing power, and in several cities they erupted into looting and clashes with police that left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests. On Monday, overnight curfews were issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris.
“This is what’s happening to France – they want to happen to our country. It’s never happening here,” Trump declared, drawing loud cheers from the thousands-strong crowd in ruby-red Kansas where the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Earlier in the day, Trump repeated his baseless claim that migrants had “taken over” France, writing on Truth Social that the country’s leaders must “CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!”
The rhetoric echoes France’s far-right National Rally, whose president, Jordan Bardella, described the violence as a convergence of ultra-left extremism and delinquent populations from the suburbs. Trump and Vance have both publicly backed Marine Le Pen, and the unrest has added pressure on Emmanuel Macron six months before an April election to choose his successor.
As Trump set off for the Kansas rally on Monday, the US president told reporters at the White House that he had warned Macron he was “making a big mistake”.
“The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal,” he said, adding: “We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
Before Trump arrived on stage in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes’ of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities, which included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.
The demonstrations in France began weeks ago, when high school students began marching for teacher shortages, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. The CGT, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the movement and called for lower prices, higher pensions and better wages. The anger has since widened to fuel prices, which have climbed since US strikes effectively shut the strait of Hormuz, and other economic grievances.
As the midterms loom, the unrest in France offers Trump a familiar politcal opportunity: the chance to transform a crisis on the other side of the Atlantic into an argument in favor of the hard-line immigration policies that helped propel Trump’s return to the White House.
“If you import the third world, you become the third world,” the official White House X account posted earlier in the day..
JD Vance and array of Republican politicians have lined up to make a similar argument.
Sharing a video that showed the historic city hall in Limoges alight, vice-president JD Vance argued that the rioting was the result of what he called a liberal failure. “Western liberals imported the third world into France,” he wrote on X, adding that the country had “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”.
House Speaker Mike Johnson posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS — just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”
Not all protests have drawn the same attention from Washington, as young people have taken to the streets across Europe, in Spain, Portugal and Italy, over underfunded schools, housing costs and a wider squeeze on living standards.
Neither has the president commented on protests in Albania, where demonstrators have targeted both the government and a luxury tourism development backed by an investment firm founded by Trump’s close familyson-in-law, Jared Kushner.
But Republicans are eager to keep the attention on France, as they warn of threats to the national identity and seek to rally support for Trump’s Make America Great Again movement.
The vice president said he hoped Americans were paying attention as they cast their ballots.
“This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” Vance concluded.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Rosebank oilfield would not breach UK emission targets, say government insiders
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The giant Rosebank oilfield can be approved without breaching the UK’s emission targets, according to government insiders, in a boost to those in the cabinet who are pushing for it to be given the go-ahead.
The Guardian revealed last week that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, was leaning towards rejecting the project, but her position has put her at loggerheads with cabinet colleagues, including the chancellor, John Healey, who are lobbying for an approval.
Government insiders have told the Guardian the project can be approved on a strict reading of Britain’s climate obligations, in part because once the oil is exported, the emissions from burning it no longer count against domestic targets. “Miatta has more latitude than you might think,” said one.
A decision to approve the oilfield would be met with dismay from climate campaigners and some Labour backbenchers who view it as a harmful step away from prioritising net zero – and may see the shift of emissions from one country to another as a trivial distinction.
On Tuesday, Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth wrote to the prime minister urging him to consider the cumulative impacts of big decisions on North Sea drilling, Heathrow expansion and grants for heat pumps – rather than viewing each in isolation.
But sources say the Treasury has already accounted for billions of pounds’ worth of tax revenue from Rosebank and so would be faced with a shortfall should it be rejected.
“The climate case against was never the direct emissions,” one source said. “Instead it was the leadership position … the power of a G7 producer seeking to put that into action is the climate point, not the direct emissions.”
Greg Muttitt, a climate researcher at University College, London, said the government was wrong to approve the Jackdaw gasfield last week and would be wrong to approve Rosebank, which would generate around seven times the emissions.
But he added: “It is true that the UK government is not going to find itself in any international court if it approves Rosebank. Approving it is not inconsistent with what the UK has committed to firmly, because most of the oil will be exported and so will count towards other countries’ emissions.”
Fahnbulleh has been forced to make a decision over Rosebank because of a legal judgment that the previous environmental consent was incorrectly given by the Conservative government at the time.
A judge ruled in 2024 that ministers should have accounted for emissions not just from drilling for oil at Rosebank, but also from those which will be generated by burning it.
Given most of that oil will be burned abroad, however, the resulting emissions will not count against the UK’s carbon budgets. Experts estimate that Rosebank could emit 1m additional tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2042, against an overall limit of 90m tonnes.
Fahnbulleh is under an obligation to take into account Britain’s commitment under the Paris agreement to take action to prevent global temperatures rising more than 1.5C.
In her decision to approve the Jackdaw scheme last week, however, she noted Jackdaw would account for about 0.01% of global greenhouse gas emissions created by the oil and gas industry in 2035.
Some experts believe Rosebank could be approved without meaningfully adding to global temperature changes. But others insist that any new oil and gasfields are harmful to the goal of staying within safe carbon budgets.
Downing Street insiders insist the decision rests with Fahnbulleh, rather than with Andy Burnham. However supportive ministers have interpreted the prime minister’s promise to take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas as a signal he would support giving the green light to Rosebank.
He has also talked of “reindustrialisation” in a speech in Motherwell, North Lanarkshire, this month, language often associated in Scotland with the North Sea. Scottish Labour MPs are believed to be overwhelmingly in favour of approving the oilfield.
Fahnbulleh told the Guardian last week that while she had approved the Jackdaw gasfield on the grounds of national energy security, the same concerns did not necessarily apply to Rosebank.
Her allies say she is leaning away from approving it because the climate damage it would create, while arguably not enough to violate legal limits, would not be overriden by the potential benefits, which those who support its approval argue includes tax take, jobs and investment.
In recent days, however, people close to the chancellor have said he wants Fahnbulleh to approve the project.
The Guardian has learned that part of the reason for this is the Treasury has already accounted for the tax benefits, which Adura, the company operating the field, estimate would be £500m a year by the end of this parliament.
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Any decision will be made through the quasi-judicial process, taking into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received as part of the regulatory process.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘I felt disgusted’: MEP speaks out over nude deepfakes and urges EU action
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
An Austrian MEP has spoken out about her experience of being “stripped naked” online without her consent and has urged the EU to take action, as a report found that one in six female MEPs had been targeted by sexualised AI-generated content.
Lena Schilling of the Green party said she had learned last month about nude deepfakes of herself circulating online. When she opened the links, she found herself staring at images from one of her first ever press conferences – but the images had been digitally altered to remove her clothing.
It was a shocking twist on a defining moment of her career. “I felt disgusted,” she said. “I remember how nervous I was and how much I had prepared for the press conference. And then to see someone using this image in a way aimed at harming and humiliating me was really hard to grasp.”
Schilling is one of 50 MEPs – 46 of them women – who have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes, according to a report by Agora Digitale Transformation (ADT).
The Berlin-based thinktank, which alerted Schilling to the presence of the images online, said the finding laid bare how deepfake pornography had become a “systemic threat to women in European politics”.
An earlier ADT report found that 138 female parliamentarians from 22 EU countries had been affected, and that women were 33 times more likely than their male colleagues to be depicted in or associated with deepfake pornography.
Schilling described the images as a form of “digital violence against women” piled on top of the already disproportionate amount of sexist abuse, harassment and violence that women in politics faced.
The result was a potent threat to democracy, she said: “These things make going into politics even harder than it is already. Just imagine what would happen to our society if more and more women disappear from public life.”
Schilling said she had spoken to some of the other female MEPs targeted, but they had expressed fears about coming forward. “But there’s nothing to be ashamed of. People misused your photos, you did nothing wrong,” she said. “And I think that’s the moment when you say: ‘OK, this has to stop.’”
The sentiment was captured in a recent letter to the EU initiated by Schilling and the German Green MEP Terry Reintke. Signed by 119 MEPs, it called on officials to ensure that a forthcoming ban on apps and websites that use AI to undress women, scheduled to take effect across the EU on 2 December, would be paired with mechanisms capable of enforcing the prohibition.
“A ban on paper protects no one until it is enforced,” the letter said, pointing to the widespread use of “nudifier” apps in which photos of women can be undressed with just one click.
“Its purpose is humiliation and control over women’s bodies, and its effect is to make public life more hostile for female politicians,” the letter said. “Every young woman considering a political career now must factor in that this could happen to her.”
Schilling said the aim was to push national authorities to close any loopholes or workarounds that would allow the apps to continue to function in the EU. “We were stripped naked without our consent,” she said. “This cannot become the new normal.”
The call for action was why she had decided to speak up, she said, in the hope that sharing her story would convince member states to crack down on tech companies for which this sort of digital violence could be a viable business model.
“It’s quite simple,” she said. “Every woman who wants to run for office should be able to do so without being afraid of being undressed against her will.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Serbia wakes up to new reality after student-led movement ousts Vučić – as it hapepned
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Morning opening: Serbia wakes up to new reality after Vučić
Jakub Krupa
Serbia wakes up to a new reality this morning after a grassroots opposition movement led by students ousted the country’s former authoritarian president Aleksandar Vučić, raising hopes for a new opening in relations with the EU and other partners.
The latest CeSID projection suggested the students will have 140 seats in the new parliament, well clear of the 126 required for majority, with 103 for Vucic’s bloc. No other party crossed the 3% threshold, with national minority parties taking the remaining seven seats.
We are likely to get more reactions to the vote today, with international observers set to present their preliminary report on the vote in the early afternoon.
I will also pick up the latest on the first round of the presidential vote in Bulgaria, which saw a record-low turnout of just 22%. The second round will be held this Sunday.
Elsewhere, I will be looking for updates from France and Italy after another rocky weekend of protests. French PM Sébastien Lecornu is going to meet with the student unions in the afternoon for what could be pivotal talks on the future of the demonstrations.
And E5 defence ministers – that’s France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and the UK – are meeting in Paris for discussions on Ukraine. Oh, and Slovakia’s foreign minister Juraj Blanár is in Moscow for energy talks with Russia.
It’s Monday, 26 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
International observers issued an overall positive assessment of the Serbian election, despite major underlying structural issues on state capture, polarisation, and misuse of state resources that require urgent addressing in the future (15:10, 15:15, 15:19, 15:37, 15:54)
The largest domestic group of observers also urged the incoming new government to “re-establish the integrity of elections” as one of its top priorities (13:31).
The focus now shifts to the government formation process as we wait for the official results to kick off the constitutional timeline (16:31).
Former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić is seen as a possible future prime minister, but the consultative and decentralised nature of the student movement makes it tricky to pinpoint who will get the top job (17:17).
Several EU leaders offered their congratulations for the student movement as they hoped for renewed engagement between the EU and Serbia (10:21, 12:15).
Russia said it hoped for cooperation with the new Serbian authorities, despite their preferred candidate Aleksandar Vučić losing the election (11:18).
Elsewhere,
In France, it is make or break time for the government on high school protests, which continued over the weekend, with the government now expected to set out new proposals to address the key demands in the late afternoon (13:02).
Bulgaria will head to the polls this Sunday in a runoff of the presidential race, with the list of candidates narrowed to two main favourites (12:59).
Sweden shows how complicated the government formation process can get as it remains stuck in finding a new parliamentary majority, 43 days on from the election (12:50).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
One thing to watch out for is how the Student List will pick its top figures, including the next prime minister and their presidential candidate.
One of the key features of the movementso far is that everythinghas been covered by very extensive and time-consuming consultations with student plenum meetings across the country, including the vetting of all candidates on the electoral list.
That may, of course, not always be possible in the future given the urgency some decisions will demand. The students will quickly need to figure out how to streamline these decision-making processes and make them work at the pace governing demands.
It may be easier to run a similarly complex process to choose their presidential candidate, as there is still some time to go until the vote in late December, but less so when it comes to the top jobs in the government, starting from the prime minister, and his key ministers.
“There is almost certainly going to be a complex process. It will not be decided by a small group of people sitting somewhere in a room. It’s only a matter of how complicated it will be,” Nikola Burazer, programme director at the Belgrade-based thinktank Centre for Contemporary Politics explained.
“It will have to be sped up because the process of choosing candidates for the list actually took a long time, months, to finish … [and finished] literally one day before they submitted the list. So, it has to be shorter.”
And the constitutional deadlines (16:31) will “force them to choose their candidates more quickly,” Aleksandar Ivković, a researcher at the Centre for Contemporary Politics added.
Former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić, who in 2012 resigned two years into the job in protest against alleged interference with his independence,is widely seen as the frontrunner for the job of the prime minister, but let’s see what other names can come up and who can emerged unscathed through the vetting process.
“After people are done celebrating and thinking about what happened yesterday, we will focus a bit more on what’s coming up, and how the government will look. 24 hours ago that all seemed like a fantasy to us,” Burazer said.
In terms of next steps in Serbia, here is what we know for now.
We are still waiting for the final election results: more than 97% polling station are now counted, but there are some localised issues that may even, in extreme cases, prompt a revote in some individual polling stations.
None of this will affect the overall result, but may cause a delay of a week or two from today.
Once the results are published, the National Assembly needs to meet for the first time within 30 days – that gets us to early to mid-December at the latest – starting the 90 days deadline for forming the new government.
This in itself will be fascinating as we have no idea who could emerge as the next prime minister given the leaderless nature of the Student List. Expect lots of speculation on this in the coming weeks, with former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić often mentioned as a possible candidate.
It’s worth saying that given the Student List will have a majority in the new parliament, they are very unlikely to need to run the clock down, and so the process can be well accelerated: manyexperts expect the new government to take over in December at the latest.
That timing is convenient for one more reason: following Vučić’s resignation as president to run for parliament, Serbia must hold a presidential election to choose a new head of state before the end of the year (well, by 27 December).
A close Vučić ally, Ana Brbabić, is currently the acting president as the last speaker of the parliament. Once we have a new speaker – presumably from the Student List – he or she will take over that interim role from here until the new leader gets elected.
That should make for an exciting end to the year in Serbia, with all change at the top going into 2027.
Serbian election marred by 'grave misuse of public resources' and 'intimidation of voters,' observers say
The preliminary report from international observers is also now out in writing, if you fancy reading it in full.
“Serbia’s 25 October early parliamentary elections saw active citizen engagement, with high voter turnout and vigorous competition between two main contenders, but unfolded in an atmosphere of profound polarisation, with equality of campaign opportunities seriously compromised, international observers said in a preliminary statement released today.
Entrenched advantages enjoyed by the ruling party, including the grave misuse of public resources, together with intimidation and pressure on voters, alongside disruptions of campaign activities, further marred the electoral environment, the statement says.”
International observers warn of issues with social media's impact on elections
Ireland’s Eoghan Murphy, who heads the ODIHR’s mission, goes into much more detail than other politicians on various technical issues in Serbia.
He talks in detail about the abuse of state resources for campaigning purposes, instances of intimidation and confrontation during the campaign, and serious issues spotted on social media and in traditional media.
This last point is particularly relevant as it feels it could just as well apply to most countries with elections coming up.
He warns that online campaigning “remains largely unregulated,” with “no dedicated oversight mechanism, safeguards … or accountability.”
“We don’t know how social media platforms prioritise and amplify such content, which harms transparency, and this reinforces the need for oversight and for safeguards.”
Sounds familiar?
He also makes it very clear that Serbia’s state media were way too involved in the election, with “pronounced imbalances in exposure and treatment of contestants, contrary to its legal obligations and public service mandate.”
“Overall, most monitored broadcasters failed to provide voters with the substantive and impartial information necessary to make an informed choice.”
“The arrangements for voting abroad raised concerns about the disproportionate inconvenience of voters in certain countries due to the absence of clear and objective criteria regarding polling stations, locations, and voting hours.”
Austrian MEP Andreas Schieder, head of the European parliament’s mission, also flags this problem, and says “this needs to change in the future.”
Italian MP Pierro Fassino, head of the parliamentary assembly of Council of Europe’s delegation and an Italian MP in his own right, is up next.
He says the election took place in a “calm and responsible manner … despite the polarised” atmosphere, with the electoral process passing the assessment at 96% of the polling stations observed.
The press conference continues along these lines, so I will flag if anyone disagrees with this view – or say anything particularly exciting about their experience of monitoring the vote.
International observers conclude with preliminary 'positive' assessment of Serbia vote, despite major structural issues
Special coordinator and Luxembourgish MP Gilles Baum is now speaking at the presentation of the international observers’ preliminary verdict on the election.
He says the election “unfolded in the atmosphere of profound polarisation, with the equality of campaign opportunity seriously compromised” through “entrenched advantages enjoyed by the ruling party.”
He also talks about the suspected “misuse of state resources together with intimidation and pressure on voters, candidates and civil society, as well as disruption of campaign activities.”
He warns that despite previous recommendations, “widespread distrust in the integrity of the voter registration persisted.”
But the mission’s on the day observation concludes with “positive” assessment of all stages of the election day process “in the vast majority of polling stations observer.”
“Nevertheless, reported incidents of physical violence raised serious concerns, and some procedural shortcomings were noted,” he says.
The main group of international observers – including OSCE’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and the European parliament - is about to deliver their preliminary verdict on the Serbian election, with a press conference in Belgrade.
I will keep an eye on this and bring you the key lines.
Most of the student list’s 250 candidates were experts from fields including academia and the arts with little political experience.
We are still waiting for the official confirmation of the exact names that will sit in the new parliament, but given their roots in academia they may very well have a chance to be among the best educated parliamentary caucuses in Europe. More than 160 of the 250 candidates held a PhD!
(But, perhaps a little-known fact, none of them were actually students; they were picked by students.)
As explained yesterday, the movement has a broad platform, centred on a pledge to fight corruption.
It evolved from demands for a transparent investigation into the Novi Sad tragedy into calls for an early election.
The movement deliberately kept foreign policy issues, including Serbia’s relationship with the European Union and longtime ally Russia, in the background.
‘This is a symbol for Europe’: streets of Belgrade resound with joy after Vučić defeat
Ana Milosavljevic in Belgrade and Ashifa Kassam
Standing on the streets of Belgrade, as passing cars honked excitedly and revellers high-fived police officers, Sara, 24, gestures to the streets around her to explain just how much things had changed for Serbia’s student-led movement.
Moments earlier, the country’s longstanding leader, Aleksandar Vučić, had conceded defeat to the student movement, ushering in a seismic political shift in the Balkan country.
It was a surreal reversal of fortunes for the hundreds of thousands of people who had spent nearly two years peacefully protesting against a ruling power that had become increasingly authoritarian.
“It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors.”
If you want to catch up with last night’s wild celebrations in Belgrade, here are two quick videos for you to get an idea of what the party atmosphere on the streets of the capital was like.
CRTA’s Raša Nedeljkov is currently presenting the organisation’s preliminary findings on last night’s elections, with a long list of reasons and issues that essentially make the Student List’s win against the incumbents even more impressive.
He says that “systemic manipulation at the polling stations was largely prevented” by the record-high number of domestic observers – up to 15,000, three times more than in 2023 – and usual citizens getting involved in running polling stations.
He says international observers also played a role in the process, but they had a “different role,” without permanent structures in place to observe broader, systemic abuses.
Summing up yesterday’s vote, he says there were still clear issues with voter identification, the use of UV lamps (we explained what they use them for yesterday), and how polling stations were set up, and calls for an urgent reform of the system.
“Re-establishing the integrity of elections should be among the top priorities of the new legislative and executive authority and seen as the foundation for the recovery of democratic institutions in Serbia,” he said.
“Serbia should never again participate in elections that … were marked by the misuse of state and public resources,” he said, with “significant efforts to bring the flow of information under the total control of the government,” with attacks on media and social media as well as attempts to discredit election observers.
He says that he still believes the state capture by Vučić’s ruling party influenced the result of the election, given voter intimidation and state-media propaganda.
“You had one political leader [Vučić] who had public addresses in our media more than 500 times, on camera, live, on average 30 minutes. Give me a country in the world, except North Korea, that has this kind of [single-party] dominance in the media.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: I’d all but forgotten my ‘altercation’ with Nigel Farage. But since he mentions it, here’s what happened | Caroline Voaden
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
I got an unexpected message last week from a former colleague whom I haven’t heard from in 20 years. I was all over her TikTok, she said, so she reached out to say hi. Such was the furore caused by Nigel Farage bizarrely raising an incident that took place in the House of Commons nearly six months ago that I suddenly found myself trending on social media. That had not been on my bingo card for budget week.
I was at home, having just got back from London, when I received a message telling me that Farage had referenced “the incident”. I looked at the footage of his press conference and was completely dumbfounded. Because this “physical altercation”, as he described it, was something I’d chosen not to discuss in public at the time, and something that, if I were him, I’d have kept quiet about.
But, no, not Nigel. Here he was, scrabbling around for excuses to explain why he wasn’t in the chamber for the budget, and this had to be the strangest one he could possibly have used. And it made absolutely no sense.
For clarity’s sake, this is what happened.
On the day of the king’s speech, MPs process through to the House of Lords to listen to it. Leaders of all parties, including smaller ones, lead the procession, but on this occasion Farage didn’t seem to get into place in time. So he was stuck behind a load of MPs also trying to join the procession.
I was on a flight of stairs and he demanded to get past. I told him to wait his turn like everyone else and he clearly didn’t like that, so he grabbed me by the arm and I ended up shoved to one side so he could push through. My colleague thought I was going to fall down the stairs, so he grabbed Farage and had a word with him about his behaviour. I reported it to the parliamentary authorities and they asked him to apologise in writing. That never happened – of course – and I chose not to say anything about it publicly.
So, yes, there was an altercation. Was it caused by “aggressive” Lib Dem MPs, as a Reform UK source later claimed? Hardly.
The whole thing makes me wonder: why bring it up now? Why bring it up at all? I think it’s a perfect reflection of the type of politics that typifies Reform UK. The politics of grievance, the repetitive mantra that the “establishment are out to get us”, but, more importantly, the disdain for parliament and its traditions.
For a man who claims he wants to become prime minister, Farage’s aversion to spending time in parliament means that he will go into the next election with very little knowledge about how the place works, how to leverage its power and what lies behind its traditions. He has spoken less in parliament than any other comparable party leader and voted about half as much as the average MP. He is a stranger in the place he aims to command.
I’ve never believed Farage would be PM, even when his party was polling in first place. Because much of what the PM does is the hard yards behind the scenes – the kind of stuff Farage hates – and, in reality, very little of the job is the glory bit in the media.
As leader of the Lib Dems in Europe, I worked “alongside” Farage in the European parliament – though he barely showed his face in Brussels. He attended just one out of 42 fisheries meetings, despite being the member chosen to represent the UK fishing industry. For all his bluster about being on the side of UK fishers, he hardly ever showed up to be their voice at the table because that seemed too much like work – too boring, too mundane, not glamorous enough for a man who loves the limelight.
And it’s much the same in London. Last Thursday he showed up at business questions, where MPs can ask the leader of the house about the following week’s Commons business, and had to ask a colleague how it worked. We’re halfway through this parliament, and Farage is still apparently getting to grips with the basics of what happens in the House of Commons.
It’s a sign of the disdain in which he seemingly holds parliament and the work we do there. Yes, it’s old-fashioned. Yes, there are traditions that have probably seen better days. And, yes, we could – and I’d argue should – modernise the way we work. But if you want to be PM, or even leader of the opposition, it’s fundamental to understand what goes on there and respect how the place works. And part of that is respecting your colleagues – all of them, regardless of party or political persuasion, age, race or sex.
I’ve been asked whether I thought Farage would have acted in the same way if I’d been a man. I think it’s highly unlikely. We’ve all heard what Sarah Pochin MP has said about the alpha males at the top of Reform UK and the problem they have with women, and the boorish behaviour I’ve experienced pretty much sums this up.
For Farage to float the idea that he chose not to go into the chamber to listen to the budget in case he got involved in another altercation is quite simply laughable. There may be nine Lib Dems to every one Reform MP, but we’re not spoiling for a fight. We’re just getting on with the day job – which does involve sometimes being in the chamber, Nigel.
- 
  Caroline Voaden is the Liberal Democrat MP for South Devon

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK politics: Burnham says US midterm results have created ‘opportunity’ for world to focus on cost of living and ending Iran war – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Burnham says US election results have created 'opportunity' for world to focus on cutting cost of living and ending Iran war
Andy Burnham has said that he hopes the sweeping losses for Donald Trump’s Republican party in the US elections will give the world an “opportunity” to focus on ending the Iran war and easing the cost of living pressures.
In an interview at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua, asked if he was worried the results might make Trump more unpredictable, Burnham replied:
President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living.
That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we’ve made moves.
But I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved. The conflict in Ukraine started by Russia.
These are the things we have to focus on now, and I hope the world has a moment to do that. And certainly, in my calls with leaders, that is what I will be asking everybody to do.
Some politicians and commentators have interpreted the results as evidence that rightwing populism is in retreat around the world. But when asked if he thought the elections were part of a global pattern, Burnham was reluctant to make that claim. Instead, he replied:
I think people want to see the world coming together and focusing on the things that matter to people, and that’s what the voters, in my view, are saying in the United States.
Let’s get focused in a laser-like way on those cost of living issues. And I think around the world there’s a recognition that countries can’t do that on their own, and can’t do that when we have division between nations.
I’ve been working hard as prime minister to bring a new approach, a new approach in the Middle East, and the foreign secretary set that out [with the announcements about sanctions on illegal Israeli settlement in the West Bank].
A new approach to Europe, and we believe that will help us get growth back up and reduce those cost of living pressures. But a new approach with the Commonwealth too.
Asked if Britain would be pushing for de-escalation in the Iran war, Burnham said:
I’ll be working for de-escalation. To make it very clear, we want to see a resolution, the Strait of Hormuz fully opened again. That’s what we will be working towards.
Andy Burnham has said that he hopes the sweeping losses for Donald Trump’s Republican party in the US elections will give the world an “opportunity” to focus on ending the Iran war and easing the cost of living pressures. (See 1.53pm.)
The government has said that the visitor levy bill, legislation giving powers to local leaders to impose a levy on visitors staying overnight that was introduced in the Commons today, is “the most significant step in making fiscal devolution a reality”.
The government has also introduced into parliament the energy independence bill, which it says is “a down payment on longer-term reforms that will fix Britain’s broken energy system, putting affordability at its heart, while unlocking barriers to deliver clean power”.
How accurate were Haigh and Burghart's facts at PMQs?
The Press Association’s QuickCheck service has been looking at some of the facts cited by Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, and Alex Burghart, the deputy Tory leader, at PMQs. Here are three figures that it suggests are potentially misleading.
Burghart claimed the OBR report said 215,000 jobs were at risk from the government’s tax rises.
PA says he seemed to be quoting a figure that applied to the impact of the tax threshold freezes that started when the Tories were in office.
The OBR said: “Following our standard approach, we have estimated that, taken together, the threshold freezes in income tax and NICs from 2022/23 to 2030/31 could decrease labour supply by 215,000 in average-hours equivalent (AHE) terms by 2030/31.”
£183bn spent on working-age welfare?
Burghart asked Haigh how much the government was spending on working-age welfare and, when she refused to answer, he said the figure was £183bn.
PA says he seemed to be referencing a figure that covered spending for children and pensioners. It says:
The OBR forecasted total welfare spending to reach £352.7bn in the current fiscal year.
This figure falls to about £182.8bn when excluding certain spending on pensioners. This might be the figure Mr Burghart was referencing, however it includes £13.7bn of child benefit spending.
This figure also includes attendance allowance, which is a disability benefit paid to those of state pension age.
Separate data show the Department for Work and Pensions spending on benefits for working-age people is set to reach £136.1bn in 2026/27. This does not include welfare spending from other departments, such as HM Revenue and Customs.
Welfare spending rising £88bn under the Tories?
Haigh said welfare spending rose by £88bn in a decade under the Tories.
PA says this is close to what OBR and DWP figures say. But those are cash figures, it says. “In real terms, a measure which offsets for inflation, the DWP figure rose by a more modest £21.8bn,” PA says.
UNHCR criticises UK’s 30-year ‘earned settlement’ plans for refugees
The UN refugee agency has said a government plan to make refugees wait up to 30 years before they get permission to settle in the UK “raises significant concerns”. Diane Taylor has the story.
Legislation aimed at ensuring more major sporting events are held in the UK is poised to become law after being approved by MPs this afternoon. As the Press Association reports, the sporting events bill is modelled on bespoke laws passed for the London 2012 Olympic and Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games and creates a framework for future events. It will support competitions such as the upcoming Uefa European football championship in 2028, in addition to future bids, such as the UK’s application to host the Fifa Women’s World Cup in 2035.
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, told MPs the bill would allow the government “to stand ready to host the biggest events in the world”, and added the UK had already bid to host the 2029 World Para Athletics Championships.
The bill has already gone through the House of Lords.
Andy Burnham tried his hand at playing the steel drum during his trip to the Caribbean, the Press Association reports. PA says:
The PM played Mary Had A Little Lamb while in Antigua for the Commonwealth heads of government meeting. After his performance of the nursery rhyme, he was told by director Khan Cordice of the Hell’s Gate steel orchestra “you’re a musician”, to which Burnham modestly replied: “I play a little music.”
He was later joined by foreign secretary Ed Miliband for a duet of the nursery rhyme.
Burnham has previously shown off his musical skills on the guitar, including playing a song by The Smiths after being handed an instrument by a Ukrainian soldier on a visit to Kyiv.
Swinney rejects call for review of law saying people with limited rights to live in UK can stand as MSPs
Severin Carrell
Severin Carrell is the Guardian’s Scotland editor.
John Swinney, Scotland’s first minister, has rejected calls from MSPs for a review of laws which allow people with limited rights to live in the UK to stand for Holyrood.
Yesterday the standards, procedures and public appointments committee, chaired by the Scottish National party MSP Jenni Minto, said the reforms could undermine “fragile” confidence amongst voters in the country’s institutions.
Swinney told LBC he had no plans to review the provisions, which first came into force this year in the Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Act 2025. He said:
We don’t intend to do so, no. The parliament voted unanimously for the provision for foreign nationals to be able to stand for elections in certain circumstances.
The reforms came under intense scrutiny after the May election after the Conservatives and Reform UK protested about the election of Q Manivannan, an Indian citizen, for the Scottish Greens in Edinburgh and Lothians East region.
A post-graduate student at St Andrews, it emerged their student visa was due to expire at the end of 2026. They have since been granted a three-year graduate visa, given them right to remain until the end of 2029.
Swinney’s government is bidding to expand the provisions of the act by including Commonwealth citizens, who were excluded as a category last year. Swinney told LBC “the government will press ahead with that.” Manivannan only qualified because they were on a student visa, not because they were a Commonwealth citizen.
The act covers elections to Holyrood and Scottish councils; Westminster contests in Scotland are reserved to Westminster and excluded.
The Department for Work and Pensions’ report released today on the employment of disabled people (see 2.41pm) says that the financial year ending 2026 was the first for more than a decade where the number of disabled working-age people in the UK fell. It says it is too early to know if this was just temporary. It explains:
This (FYE [financial year ending] 2026) is the first full year since financial year ending (FYE) 2014 where the number of disabled people and disability prevalence have decreased, by 0.5% (around 50,000) and by 0.2 percentage points, respectively. It is too early to determine whether this is a temporary change, also as the latest quarterly data for April to June 2026 reports a year-on-year significant increase in the number of disabled people (250,000).
OBR tells MPs it is not in position to confirm Tory claim ILR U-turn will cost £10bn
The Commons Treasury committee has started taking evidence from officials from the Office for Budget Responsibility about the budget. Harriett Baldwin, a Conservative member of the committee, asked about Shabana Mahmood’s announcement on Monday axing some of the restrictions to indefinite leave to remain (ILR) that had been planned by the Home Office.
The Tories claim this U-turn will cost the exchequer £10bn.
Asked what impact this announcement would have on the OBR’s fiscal assumptions, Tom Josephs, a member of the OBR’s budget responsibility committee, said the OBR would have to review this for its next forecast in the spring. He said he could not give an answer now.
Asked if he thought it really would cost £10bn, Josephs said “that is not an estimate that we produced”. He said that was a government estimate for the lifetime cost of some migrants.
Asked if the change on Monday would be "material enough” to require a change to the OBR’s forecast, Josephs just said the OBR would assess the policy as a whole. “If we think [the Monday announcement is] significant enough to adjust the forecast, then we will do so.”
Mahmood originally produced the £10bn figure to justify the plans she originally announced last year. She said making it harder for migrant workers to get ILR would save the government £10bn over time.
This claim backfired when Mahmood U-turned on a large part of her plan, leading the Tories to claim she was now in effect raising spending by almost £10bn (because the savings were forgone).
Almost half of Neet young people classed as disabled, DWP figures show
Just under half of young people not in work, education or training were classed as disabled in the year to March – a proportion which has more than doubled in just over a decade, the Press Association reports. PA says:
The government is currently working on reducing the number of 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training – known as Neets – with a review expected to be published in the coming weeks making recommendations for changes in the system.
The number of Neets topped a million earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade, fuelling calls for more help to get young people into work.
Government data published today showed 45.3% of Neets were classed as disabled in the year to March.
The Department for Work and Pensions said this was a rise of 24.2 percentage points since the proportion of 21.1% in the 12 months to March 2014.
The latest data showed disabled young people were more than three times as likely to be Neet compared to non-disabled young people – 30.2% compared with 8.6%.
Depression, bad nerves or anxiety was the most common main health condition reported by disabled Neets, accounting for almost a quarter (23.8%), followed by autism (22.7%).
Burnham claims there's 'solution' to Poundland's problems, as he urges its bosses to work with government on rescue plan
Andy Burnham has urged Poundland bosses to work with the government on trying to find a “practical solution” to the problems that have left the company on the brink of administration.
In a pooled interview, asked if he had a message for Poundland executives, Burnham replied:
Focus on the people in your employment, meet with the business secretary because we are setting up that meeting, come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores because many of them are viable propositions, they’re on high streets, they matter in our communities. There is a solution to be found here, sit down with us and let’s find it.
When it was put to him that there was a limit to what the government could do if the company was not profitable, he replied:
There’s always a limit, but we’re prepared to find what we can do. We believe in this instance there is a solution. There are many viable outlets here. Other retailers are expressing interest. Get around the table. Let’s find a solution.
Here is an initial take fromPippa Crerar, the Guardian’s political editor, on what the US election results might mean for the UK.
While the public here in the UK - which overwhelmingly believes his presidency has been bad for Britain - may welcome the ‘blue tsunami’, ministers and officials will be watching nervously for how Trump reacts.
The US president acknowledged overnight the Iran conflict - which has pushed up the cost of living globally - had cost the Republicans votes and has previously suggested a deal could be struck with Tehran post-midterms.
But there are concerns here that a bruised Trump - whose domestic agenda is constrained after losing control of Congress but who still wields a veto and significant power over foreign policy - could now lash out like a caged animal.
There could be a backlash on the world stage as he tries to cement his legacy during his last two years, potentially including more military action in Iran, Ukraine and even Cuba; more trade tariffs; and more unhelpful interventions in UK and European politics.
But for now, there is also relief that the US has cast its verdict on Trump and his combative style of politics, and hope that if the Democrats get their act together (for this was a referendum on the US president rather than a ringing endorsement of his opponents), the 2028 election could transform the special relationship.

If you are deputising at PMQs, it may be nice to get a good write-up from the sketchwriters, and satisfying to craft a line that will play well on the TV or radio later, but, frankly, one task matters above all others: don’t mess up. And, in that respect, Louise Haigh and Alex Burghart both performed well – in exchanges likely to be quickly forgotten.
For Haigh, this was her first time, but it did not particularly sound like this. She sounded confident and authoritative, without being brash and hubristic. She did not have anything very new to say about welfare, and Labour does not have a firm answer yet to the question as to when it will cut the benefits bill, but Haigh swerved this quite adequately with attacks on the Tories’ record and by making the Labour argument about now wanting welfare spending on failure. She said:
We have been repeatedly clear that we cannot afford to pay for failure and must invest in success – and that is how we will bring the welfare bill down.
We will make support more conditional on taking up opportunities, ensuring young people get help they need earlier, tackling the long-term drivers of welfare spending, including high housing costs, and we will do all this in a Labour way.
She would not rule out tax rises to pay for more welfare spending (see 2.16pm), but that was the sort of question opposition parties ask when they can’t think of a proper, specific one and so instead have to resort to simplistic politics-by-slogan.
Burghart has done PMQs before, and he was a bit more polished. His pre-scripted riffs about “two 10-year plans in 10 months”, and John Healey’s Today programme welfare gaffe last week, were elegantly done, but not quite withering or funny enough to be truly damaging. He didn’t fail, but he didn’t score.
The most interesting question came from the Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper, who is probably the first MP to get a ‘Trump might be a rapist’ allegation into Hansard. (See 12.29pm.) Rather ingeniously, she tried to suggest there might be some sort of UK government angle. But there probably isn’t. This is one for Congress.
If anyone had a bad PMQs, it was probably Lindsay Hoyle. It was not clear who he was referring to when he delivered his ‘don’t shout a woman down’ bollocking to some Tory MP. (See 12.20pm.) But it sounded a bit chauvinist. Haigh is the second most senior person in government; she seemed perfectly capable of coping with a bit of heckling; and if shouting down a minister is unacceptable, it should not matter what sex they are.
Munira Wilson (Lib Dem) says Haigh recently said the government would give local leaders more power to invest in things that matter. But it is cutting funding for Richmond council by more than £100m over the next four years, 60% of its budget? Will Haigh meet her to discuss this to find a solution.
Haigh says the government inherited an unfair council funding system. She offers Wilson a meeting with a minister.
Bobby Dean (Lib Dem) asks if the government will back legislation to make US tech companies pay fair compensation to victims of online scams. He says, given the US election results, the government should be tougher with the US administration.
Haigh says the Online Safety Act requires tech companies to take robust action on online scams.
