Andy Burnham is preparing to announce billions of pounds of trade deals with the EU covering everything from youth visas to pet passports under his vision of a much closer relationship with the bloc.
With the prime minister scheduled to meet his European counterparts in Brussels on 20 November, officials have all but agreed three deals that would allow farmers to sell freely to the continent and travellers to take their animals abroad more easily.
Although parts of the agreement will not be put in place until 2028, those close to the talks insist the process will not be derailed by disagreements on European industrial policy or UK university fees.
Elements of the deal, which will see the UK pay the EU for access to its emissions trading scheme, face criticism from those who argue Britain is signing up to the same rules it was seeking to avoid when it left the bloc.
However, Burnham said on Tuesday that the agreement would boost the UK economy by £17bn – an increase of 0.4%. His advisers believe it will also strengthen his attempts to forge much closer ties with, and even potentially rejoin, the bloc.
The prime minister told the Economist on Tuesday: “A deal could add up to 0.4% to GDP. Now that is a number that you cannot ignore.”
And he told ITV: “Public opinion has changed nationally. But I want to be really clear on this issue. I will not run ahead of public opinion. The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit.”
Burnham will meet Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and António Costa, the president of the European Council, in Brussels later this month when the leaders are expected to announce the deals.
They include an agricultural agreement, which the government believes will be worth over £5bn to the UK economy by 2040; access to the EU’s emissions trading scheme; and a youth visa scheme for tens of thousands of people under 30.
Officials on both sides say the final text for all three deals is close to being agreed, though some key details need to be finalised. These include how many young people should be allowed to travel under the mobility scheme.
Both sides are understood to have agreed that each European member state should get its own quota under the scheme, to spread out the benefits and potential costs.
Under the proposed agricultural deal, UK companies and travellers would no longer have to get a certificate to transport live animals, including pets, into Europe. Those wanting to bring domesticated animals into the bloc would be issued with a pet passport, eradicating the need for complicated paperwork each trip.
UK producers would be allowed to continue selling some products that are banned under EU law, such as certain pesticides, for a “transition period”. Trade in other products, including live molluscs and Scottish salmon, would be freed up.
Under an agreement on emissions, the UK will pay the EU billions of pounds to avoid a cross-border carbon tax, which comes into place next January. Under a separate agreement the UK will join the EU emissions trading scheme to avoid being trapped.
And under the “youth experience scheme”, Britain and the EU would issue visas to people under the age of 30 to live, work and travel in each other’s territories. The UK is negotiating an emergency brake-style mechanism to make sure that if a member state refuses to issue its quota of visas, the UK will restrict the number of their nationals looking to travel to Britain.
Officials on both sides have now started talks over a separate joint statement setting out areas of future cooperation, including on industrial policy and tuition fees. A draft of that agreement seen by the Guardian would seek to conclude an agreement on charging European students lower fees within six months.
The Guardian revealed earlier this week that the UK was willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities for any financial loss as a result – but only if the EU agreed to grant Britain access to its protectionist Made in Europe scheme.
The draft statement, which has been prepared by the EU and not yet agreed by the UK, describes the two sides as “trusted partners” – language which the UK believes will allow it to participate in Made in Europe.
But European countries are pushing Britain to sign up to higher tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, a move UK ministers and businesses are resisting. The European draft text says both sides will “cooperate closely and explore further solutions”.
It also says the UK is likely to pay a financial contribution to the EU’s “cohesion” budget to help poorer member states – though this has not been signed off by the UK and is understood to be more likely as part of a future agreement.
The EU has also raised concerns about the UK’s plans for an accelerated programme to deport “foreign national offenders from the UK to the EU”, which it is pushing London to drop.
The agreement being announced later this month forms one half of Burnham’s attempts to reset the British conversation over Europe.
The prime minister is also planning a major announcement setting out his vision for how the UK could interact with the union in the future, including possible re-entry.
Downing Street has said this would take place “around the time of the summit” – though it has not yet been decided whether it will be before, during or after.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Farage accused of ‘protecting’ Reform candidate over racist slurs against David Lammy
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Nigel Farage was told by a senior Reform official that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about David Lammy, an undercover investigation has revealed.
The latest footage from an undercover investigation by ITV also shows Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”.
Other footage shows Farage himself discussing the case of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party.
The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged that he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds do not have a primary loyalty towards the UK.
However, while Reform eventually suspended him in March after the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, clips from an ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier disucussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”.
“He needs to go, I’m getting rid of him,” Sumner was filmed saying when the controversy broke last December. However, Parry was still the candidate three weeks later, while Farage told a press conference that the candidate could stay if he apologised.
In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said that Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate.
“He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.”
To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.”
Parry was suspended on 26 March after the Guardian reported that he had described members of a Jewish neighbourhood watch group as “cosplayers” and likened them to “Islamists on horseback”.
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said these “latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform”, adding: “Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.”
The revelations are the latest in a number of recent controversies for Reform. The full ITV documentary, Undercover: A Year in Reform, airs on Sunday.
A number of councillors have already stood down after segments from the investigation aired on Wednesday showed them making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.
The undercover reporter for ITV also met Pochin, Reform’s MP for Runcorn and Helsby, at a time when she was the party’s only female member of parliament.
When Pochin was told that a new female press officer was starting work, she was recorded as saying: “Oh thank fuck for that. God! We so need women press officers … They are so fucking chauvinistic.
“I go out on all the shows and go: ‘Oh no, it’s lovely, oh they’re all so welcoming.’ Shit … they just exclude you if you’re a woman. It’s really tough being a girl with all of this alpha male shit going on.”
Pochin did not provide a statement when approached by ITV. Reform UK used a statement issued on Thursday to accuse ITV and the company behind the documentary, Hardcash Productions, of using “extreme methods of deception”.
It said: “They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees.
“That same journalist did not limit themselves to recording candid conversations in the workplace. That journalist also sought to find out sensitive security information, travel arrangements, and financial information outside of the scope of this investigation.”
Reform went on to claim that ITV had failed to address this in correspondence, despite this conduct being drawn to its attention. “This is at a time when Nigel Farage and other members of Reform are being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation,” it added.
“There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.”
When approached for comment, Parry referred the Guardian to a statement given to ITV. In it he said: “I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government. They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Israel blocks construction of key Gaza base created by Trump peace board
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned.
In early August, the Board of Peace, the international organization authorized in 2025 by the UN and chaired by the US president, issued its first construction contract for Gaza: Louisiana-based Arkel International would construct a military outpost for 150 international troops that would be the vanguard of an international stabilization force.
Two months later, Israel has still not permitted the contract to move forward, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. Contractors and trucks are not being allowed to cross into Gaza and begin the work. “Israel won’t open the border,” they said.
A Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment. The Israeli Defense Forces and the Israeli government declined to comment.
Israel’s war in Gaza is one of the eight wars Trump claims to have resolved. He listed it again last week in a screed on social media, protesting that it was unfair he had not won the Nobel peace prize.
The Board of Peace, formed in the wake of an October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, is central to Trump’s claims to have ended the conflict.
Arkel’s planned “mission support site temporary outpost” is decidedly rudimentary: a fortified position of about 100 meters by 100 meters, at a site that was once part of the controversial and now defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, according to the person familiar with the matter. The US-backed GHF operated in Gaza from May 2025 till October 2025 to deliver aid protected by private contractors.
The base would host short rotating deployments of a well-armed force of 150 troops in Gaza, the person said. They would come from a larger component of 500 sent already from Morocco and Kosovo.
But without this contract, the source said, the rest of the Board of Peace program cannot launch. Israel’s refusal to allow Arkel, the contractor, to build the base, essentially cuts the Board of Peace off at the legs.
“You can’t get in without [an international stabilization force (ISF)]. You can’t rebuild,” the person said. “There’s no security. There’s no deliveries of construction equipment. You can’t even start putting utilities. You can’t start putting in basic life-support facilities you know because without the ISF you can’t go in.”
The person familiar with the matter said the Board of Peace believes that Israel’s government will let the project proceed after the Israeli elections, which are scheduled for 27 October.
The controversial Board of Peace has a unique structure. Trump is designated as chair for life. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, is an executive board member, as is real estate developer Steve Witkoff, whom Trump has appointed as a mediator in various international disputes.
Though many western democracies have kept their distance from the Board of Peace, 28 countries joined as founding members earlier this year. Kushner has unveiled renderings of a futuristic vision of Gaza, where the city was envisioned as a pristine luxury waterfront resort city with hi-tech skyscrapers looking out over the Mediterranean.
On 23 September the group unveiled what it said was a six-month, $2.45bn plan, as the first step towards reconstruction with a 10-year estimated cost of $71bn.
There were lofty promises and requests for contributions. “Today we can point to real progress,” announced Witkoff.
A US senior adviser to the board, Aryeh Lightstone, announced a new fund would be started. “Your high net-worth donations will go directly to the Palestinian people,” he said. Lightstone has traveled in Trump circles since the president’s first term. He officiated as a rabbi at the 2020 wedding of Trump adviser Stephen Miller to Katie Miller.
Israel has continued strikes in Gaza since the October ceasefire, killing about 1,400 people over that time, according to Gaza health authorities.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Andy Burnham launches campaign against ‘headphone dodgers’ on public transport
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham has announced a crackdown on “headphone dodgers” who play loud music on public transport, as he extends his promise to give voters “breathing space” in the confines of a train carriage.
The prime minister will unveil a campaign against nuisance behaviour on public transport on Monday, alongside guidance allowing local transport authorities to levy fines of up to £100 for non-compliance.
The move makes him the latest senior politician to promise action against people who play videos or music out loud in public spaces, something that about 60% of voters back.
Burnham said in a statement: “We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey.
“So, we’re launching a nationwide campaign reminding passengers to use headphones on trains. On top of that, we’re giving local leaders new powers to tackle loud music, vaping and littering on buses.
“It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.”
Under the plan, ministers will issue guidance to local transport authorities advising them on how they should use new powers granted under the Bus Services Act, which allows them to set and enforce their own rules on board.
The guidance will say authorities should issue fines of up to £100 if bus passengers refuse to comply with a request to stop certain nuisance behaviour.
Officials said drivers would not be expected to enforce such rules. That job would be left to transport safety officers or police officers. Train operating companies already have the power to issue fines of up to £1,000 for similar behaviour.
Alongside the new powers, the government is launching a poster campaign to discourage people from playing videos or music on their phones out loud on public transport.
Under the slogan “share the carriage, not the noise”, passengers will be encouraged to use headphones, avoid making calls on speakerphone and watch videos quietly.
The campaign makes Burnham the latest in a series of politicians to promise to tackle headphone dodgers.
The London mayor, Sadiq Khan, unveiled a campaign in the summer urging passengers to “travel kind”, including by wearing headphones. The Liberal Democrats have called for bus travellers to face £1,000 fines as well as those on trains.
The scramble for politicians to react comes as polls show noise on public transport is a major annoyance for British people.
A recent poll by YouGov found voters would back £1,000 fines for people playing music out loud on buses and trains. A separate survey by the same company found that voters listed people talking on speakerphones as one of their top three irritants.
Unions, however, said the new enforcement regime would do little to protect transport workers.
The general secretary of Unite, Sharon Graham, said: “The government’s proposals are well-meaning but wholly inadequate to tackle the challenges and violence bus workers are facing on a daily basis. The proposed penalties are not going to deal with the issues facing workers.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Rachel Reeves and the Starmerites are back – and they’re pointing out how little has changed | Gaby Hinsliff
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Rachel Reeves wants you to know she thinks Britain’s future belongs in Europe. She would also like to mention that she “absolutely” got all the big calls right as chancellor, even if there were a few things she would have done differently, and that John Healey’s budget last week would have been far harder for him if she hadn’t put in so much of the groundwork.
The gist of her argument in last weekend’s Sunday papers – previewing a lecture at Harvard University today, reflecting on her time in power – was essentially that if anyone imagines Andy Burnham somehow invented pro-Europeanism and putting more money in people’s pockets, they can think again.
Reeves was clearly devastated by losing a job she loved, and her return to the fray after a summer of quietly licking her wounds has inevitably sparked speculation over whether she now seeks a comeback. But her timing is acute enough to suggest that this goes a little deeper, coming as it does days after a deliberately low-key budget that left some Labour MPs wondering what happened to the much-hyped end of neoliberalism.
How much of the Burnham agenda is really new, and how much is essentially the old Starmer one, repackaged with rather more warmth, charm and political skill?
Inside what’s left of the old inner circle, loyalists point out that Reeves and Starmer were both fervent remainers at heart and of course they would have loved to be back inside the EU one day; it’s just that the time wasn’t yet right to talk about it when they ran for office.
Similarly, the package of sanctions on Israeli settlers that the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced in September, alongside an apology for what he considered Starmer had got wrong on Gaza, wasn’t a dramatic break with the past but essentially the measures his predecessor, Yvette Cooper (now health secretary), had spent her last weeks at the Foreign Office working up, which couldn’t be published until a new prime minister was formally in place.
Starmer’s former close lieutenant Darren Jones, meanwhile, is openly arguing that this administration’s answer to a looming crisis in defence spending – basically shunting the hard questions about funding it into next year’s spending review – is “what Keir and Rachel were going to do”, if only they hadn’t been forced out by the very same John Healey resigning as defence secretary in protest at something remarkably like the strategy he’s now pursuing. Starmer himself, who has kept his counsel over the summer, made a rare public intervention in Dublin last week to warn pointedly that the US withdrawal from European defence will outlast the Trump era, and Europe cannot afford to be left exposed.
If the Starmerites are understandably smarting at what some see as history being rewritten by the winners, some are also failing to recognise their part in their own downfall. Starmer was ultimately ousted by his own MPs because they wereexasperated by his failure to lead and sensed the country had turned inexorably against him.
Burnham has shown not only that he can take decisions – across Whitehall there seems to be more clarity now about what Downing Street wants – but that he can build the emotional bond with the public his predecessor couldn’t, without which even the boldest moves wouldn’t have worked. He might only have moved the needle fractionally on issues such as Palestine or Europe, where the manifesto red lines effectively mean nothing significant can change that wouldn’t have under Starmer, at least this side of a general election. But each time he has done just enough to achieve the political impact that Starmer was seemingly chasing but couldn’t pull off. Where his predecessor could never quite get the dosage right, Burnham seems to instinctively know how far to go: it’s the difference between a novice cook clinging fixedly to a recipe that isn’t quite right, and an experienced one who tastes and adjusts the seasoning as they go. And judging by the polling, it’s working.
Yet still some MPs are anxious to hear a bigger vision of where Burnham wants the country to go than fixing social care and banning people listening to loud music on the bus. Since there wasn’t one in the budget, all eyes are on the 10-year plan, now expected some time in December.
Burnham has made much of promising to give Britain some breathing space after years of rolling crises and financial struggle. But the small, popular changes he has offered so far – £100 off your energy bills, a No 10 North office in Manchester – have also been in part about buying some breathing space for himself while he gets to grips with bigger and potentially more controversial challenges, from welfare reforms to defusing a Labour revolt over Shabana Mahmood’s plan to make migrants wait longer for the right to settlement.
A confident and relaxed debut has masked the fact that transitioning from mayor to prime minister was always going to be a steep learning curve, and that he didn’t get the long summer of planning that his team had wanted to prepare for power. But now that period of grace is coming to an end, along with a period of silence from those he ousted, some of whom are keen to defend their legacies. By Christmas we should know whether Burnham is offering genuine new thinking in British politics, or something more like the old kind, regifted.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggests
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Doctors have developed an artificial intelligence tool that can predict a cancer patient’s chances of survival from a single photograph of their face.
The AI system was custom-built by experts at Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit, integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, to estimate biological age and directly predict survival outcomes in patients diagnosed with cancer.
It is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations to date of how AI analysis of a selfie could help assess a patient’s health and potentially guide their medical care, and was trained on data from more than 40 million facial photographs across a range of ethnicities and ages.
Details of the breakthrough were published in the Lancet Digital Health journal.
The system can estimate a person’s biological age – the age a person looks, rather than their actual, chronological age – and predict the chances of survival for cancer patients from an ordinary photograph of their face, according to the results of a study that examined the model.
Doctors used the technology to develop two complementary tools. FAHR-FaceAge estimates a patient’s biological age, and predicts cancer survival. FAHR-FaceSurvival predicts survival from a facial photograph directly, rather than inferring survival through biological age.
Although FAHR-FaceAge and FAHR-FaceSurvival were derived from the same model, they captured different and complementary information about a patient’s health.
Each algorithm also relied on distinct parts of the face to make respective predictions of age and mortality risk. FAHR-FaceAge focuses on the creases that run from the sides of the nose down to the corners of the mouth, the forehead area just above the eye sockets, and the temples. FAHR-FaceSurvival, meanwhile, evaluates the region below the eyes and around the nasal bridge.
“FAHR-FaceSurvival advances the field of facial health recognition AI a step further by learning survival risk directly from facial photographs of patients with cancer,” said Hugo Aerts, a co-senior author of the study. “To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that an AI model can directly predict cancer survival from a simple photograph.”
Among cancer patients treated with radiotherapy in the US, the people who, according to FAHR-FaceAge, looked five or more years older than their actual age had a 21% higher risk of dying during the average four-year follow-up than the rest of the group. The patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk.
“The key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images, which can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival,” said Aerts. “This foundation-model approach gives us a scalable way to develop multiple facial health biomarkers rather than training each model from scratch.”
The results of the study suggest people’s biological age estimates are closely linked to their physical health, which could reflect their ability to survive certain treatments.
The breakthrough could pave the way for AI facial analysis to assist doctors in making difficult decisions about the best way forward in terms of treatment for their patients.
The tool could help better predict the risk of death or complications after major surgery or other treatments for cancer.
Dr Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham, said: “As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy.
“Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment.”
Researchers found lifestyle factors were associated with facial ageing. For example, heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking were linked to looking biologically older in AI analysis of facial photographs.
“Another surprising finding was how consistent FAHR-FaceAge was across common real-world photo variations, including pose, lighting, facial expression and makeup,” said Mak. “It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty.”
Doctors cautioned that while single facial photographs could offer an easy, low-cost way to support personalised treatment decisions, more research was needed before the tool could be widely used.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK officials discussing options including free movement with EU ahead of summit
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
British officials have begun discussions with the EU about a long-term relationship that could include a return to free movement, the business secretary has said while promising the British people “are the boss” when it comes to what the UK will accept.
Jonathan Reynolds said the focus for British negotiations was the EU summit in November to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But he said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, had made it clear he wanted to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc.
“They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be. But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we’re going to make,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.
He said the changes announced at the EU summit, including a food and drink deal and on emissions trading, would make a significant difference. But he added: “What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us, and we need to get as little uncertainty as possible.
“We need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be, and he is going to set that out after the summit. And he is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are.”
Reynolds said there had been “no assumptions made about the next stage after that. It’s the prime minister quite rightly saying he wants to set out to the British people what the options are to resolve some of the tensions that exist.”
He said no decision would be made without voters being given a say, without specifying whether this would be through a general election or a referendum. “No assumptions have been made on this. The British people are the people who will decide this. They’re the boss on this,” he said.
A number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.
The Labour MP for Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes, Melanie Onn, was among those urging caution. “I am still not over the kind of very divisive debate that we had when we were leaving the EU post the referendum, and I don’t think that the scars have healed for many people around the country,” she told Today. “So I do think that this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time.”
The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the programme it would be “very, very poor indeed” to begin discussing freedom of movement. “Five months ago, Andy Burnham says to leave-voting Makerfield: ‘I’m not going to reopen these arguments.’ Two and a half years ago, a Labour government got a massive majority in parliament saying we will not be re-entering the single market, the customs union, or opening up the debate on the free movement of people,” he said.
“What I am saying is this: this prime minister has no mandate, and to hear that his officials are negotiating in Brussels already is really very, very poor indeed.”
Burnham made his plea for an “honest discussion” about freedom of movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.
Burnham also shared his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in its manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.
The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].
“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: France drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
France has dropped its opposition to the UK being included in the EU’s “Made in Europe” legislation as long as the British government aligns with the bloc’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs.
In a breakthrough for Andy Burnham, France on Thursday came round to backing Germany, which has always supported the UK’s calls to be designated European for the purposes of the Industrial Accelerator Act. The legislation, which is in its draft stage, is designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition.
According to a joint Franco-German paper seen by the Guardian, the two countries are now proposing that for the car industry specifically the UK could be included in Made in Europe.
“For the automotive sector, ‘Made in Europe’ should comprise the EU27 and an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 01/01/2020, subject to an agreement on full reciprocity – i.e. adopting the European preference scheme relevant to the automotive sector,” it says in a clear reference to the UK, which was still in the single market as an EU member in January 2020.
It would also include Norway, which is in the single market but not a member of the EU.
The paper added that the opt-in would come with conditions, including alignment on trade defence measures, which have included tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the EU in 2024 and any future trade barriers, such as the quota deal being finalised with China on its exports of hybrid cars.
The paper says that “as well as relevant anti-circumvention measures”, these “opt-in” countries would have to accept “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the UK’s business, innovation, science and trade committee, said he believed aligning with the EU on trade defence measures was a small price to pay to save British manufacturing.
“Sometimes politics is the least worst choice – aligning with Europe on trade defence against an over-subsidised China is the way we deliver for all of us,” he said.
“Tariffs on these would be a small price to pay for the protection of a European manufacturing industry which safeguards jobs across supply chains in the UK and makes us less prone to coercion from China in the future.”
On Wednesday the head of Mercedes implored EU leaders to let the UK join the package.
Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial Made in Europe legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz said.
The UK has been under pressure for weeks to align with the EU on tariffs on Chinese vehicles, but this week the business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK was locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Earlier on Thursday trade minister Anas Sarwar hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs.
He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
Bernd Lange, the chair of the European parliament’s influential international trade committee, told the Guardian the UK should “of course” be included in the Made in Europe legislation, calling France’s opposition “not rational”.
A Downing Street spokesperson said it had yet to see the detail but saw the development as positive. “This is a Franco-German proposal and there is still a European process to run, but if confirmed, we welcome the objective to have UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act and this would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Seven oil tankers carrying 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel sail towards US
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Seven oil tankers carrying an estimated 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel are now sailing towards the US, though it is uncertain if the vessels will be able to unload amid a political row about the legality of the shipments.
The transport, tracked by the pressure group Greenpeace, is the first phase of a contentious supply deal negotiated between presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin earlier this month, reversing years of sanctions on Russia oil.
Previous reports had counted three tankers that had departed Russian oil terminals in the Baltic Sea, but using a range of sources, including shipping tracking websites, Greenpeace believes its monitoring exercise is the most complete yet.
Shaun Burnie, an energy specialist with Greenpeace Ukraine, argued that now the location of the tankers could be plotted on a map, the shipments should be halted by Congress or local authorities in the US.
“Instead of rewarding Russia for its vile war against Ukraine, there needs to be more punitive sanctions against Russia,” he said. “These shipments can be stopped”.
One of the seven tankers, Taurus, is relatively close to the US, but at the time the map was first published, five of the others were close to the UK, and three were sailing through or into the English Channel.
In Ukraine, 14 people were reported killed on Thursday morning when a Russian drone struck a crowded train platform in the central city of Dnipro. Five others were reported killed in daytime strikes in two other cities, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk.
Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway company, said a high speed jet-powered drone had struck as a commuter train was preparing to depart Dnipro’s main station. Bodies lay scattered after the relatively unusual daytime attack, which took place at around 11am.
Putin agreed to supply the US with 1.8m tonnes of diesel in a surprise deal announced on 9 October, starting with 300,000 tonnes immediately. Trump announced a six-month waiver on existing sanctions to allow the shipments to proceed.
Russia had been hit by waves of economic sanctions from the US, EU, UK and other leading western economies since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. But this autumn, Trump has altered course and tried to work more closely with Putin, even though Russia has not stopped attacking its neighbour.
Earlier this week, a group of US lawmakers, led by a handful of Democratic senators, warned banks and port authorities that they could face congressional investigations and other legal action if they handled the Russian diesel.
Mikie Sherrill, the Democratic governor of New Jersey, said she was looking at how to prevent the diesel from being unloaded, if an attempt was made to do so in her state. She described the deal as “corrupt and illegal”.
There have been reports that the White House has been trying to encourage US firms to take the oil, though it is not clear buyers are forthcoming, given the legal risks so close to next Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Trump’s popularity has waned as fuel prices in the US have soared since he attacked Iran in the spring. Polling suggests a high likelihood that control of the House of Representatives could pass to the Democrats in the elections, while the battle over the Senate is considered too close to call.
The US president had argued that the Russia deal would help lower diesel prices, though the price per gallon has risen from $6.28 at the time the agreement was announced to $6.33, according to the American Automobile Association.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, denounced the agreement because the money raised would help the Kremlin fund the ongoing war. “Backroom deals” gave Putin more chances on the battlefield, he said.
The Kremlin has been trying to keep information about the latest oil exports secret. A presidential decree from the end of September restricted the publication of information about oil exports in an effort to evade international sanctions.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The David Attenborough-narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said.
Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hit BBC series is returning with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed “stonefish” cam.
Since the first Blue Planet, TVs and cameras have evolved to give viewers sharper, higher definition pictures. But the combination of the rise in AI and the extraordinary sequences and fantastical creatures captured by BBC Studios’ natural history unit for this series led producers to include what they called more “organic” footage and less polished shots, to show that the animals were not AI-generated.
The executive producer, Elizabeth White, said AI, “makes us want to be even more authentic”, adding that the creatures filmed in the deep ocean “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real”.
She said that in the past “the amount of plankton and things that are in the water in the sequences” would usually mean they might be excluded, and previously, “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’”
But now such things are being left in as “we’re really leaning into that authenticity … As AI booms we will probably lean more into the more organic”, murkier and less polished footage.
For the first time, the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle, assured journalists at a press screening: “No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame. It’s all real photography.”
Bootle added that as we live in a “golden age of natural history-making … sometimes people feel like they’ve seen it all before [so] this series is bursting with novel behaviour”.
That includes never-before-seen action of dolphins using sea sponges to block holes in coral to trap fish, captured using underwater CCTV – developed by the programme’s producer and director, Yoland Bosiger.
Over the four years of filming across five oceans, BBC Studios “continually innovated”, said the series producer, Lara Bickerton, creating a “mini-dome” camera to follow an octopus, a “deep-sea selfie stick”, camera operators wearing leg-mounted scooters to create immersive TikTok-style diving footage and using lasers to film deep-sea creatures.
Other remarkable animal behaviour captured in the programme includes grouper communicating with another species of fish; 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed; sea urchins using shells as sun hats; and footage involving penguins that echoes the Planet Earth II, ‘iguana v snakes’ sequence.
Threats to the ocean as well as its resilience are addressed in the series. Episodes show how the climatecrisis is killing off the sea where anemone clown fish live and what they do to try to fix their homes, and the issue of plastics raised in Blue Planet II continues with a story about pollutants [and] forever chemicals, said White.
Bosiger said Attenborough, who is 100 years old, was “very much involved” and made changes to scripts.
White added: “What’s wonderful is he hasn’t lost his curiosity … he’s still that little boy … who gets excited … when you show him a new piece of footage.”
Asked if the BBC’s £500m cost-cutting drive would affect BBC Studios’ renowned natural history reputation, White said she could not comment on that but pointed out that Blue Planet III made savings by using more local crews on location than in previous series.
- 
  Blue Planet III starts Sunday 1 November on BBC1 and iPlayer

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on probation: overcrowded prisons need an outlet | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The early release of thousands of prisoners was bound to be awkward for a new prime minister. Politically speaking, Andy Burnham’s decision to exclude those convicted of manslaughter and some other offences made sense. But with about 2,000 offenders being freed this month, the risk is that by cutting the numbers, he has added to overcrowding problems inside. With the prison and probation services under huge pressure, and a ballot on industrial action expected, there is an urgent need for moves from the government to strengthen both.
Shielded from view as prisons are, and despite the efforts of campaigners and writers such as Jimmy McGovern to draw attention to them, conditions have been allowed to deteriorate to a shocking extent. The latest annual report from the prisons watchdog drew a dismal picture of rampant drug use, organised crime and governors wasting time on form-filling. It warned that the Prison Service’s managers appear to favour crisis management over improvement.
Criticisms of the probation service of England and Wales contained in the latest report by the Institute for Government’s (IfG) appear measured, by comparison. Probation’s problems are less attention-grabbing, and senior leaders are not singled out for blame. But analysis of the impact of sentencing reforms, combined with ongoing staff shortages and tagging failures, are cause for very serious concern all the same. This is a vital public service that was already facing serious difficulties before its caseload was massively enlarged.
Problems date back to the failed part-privatisation of the service. The IfG highlights the toll of “near-constant organisational change”. One result has been de-skilling, with staff increasingly reliant on risk-management protocols rather than judgment. The number of recalls to prison due to breached conditions, rather than new offences, undermines rehabilitation and worsens overcrowding. But an overstretched workforce seems unable to break this cycle. There is simply not enough time to build relationships.
The failure to fit 45% of tags on time is obviously unacceptable; ministers need to get a grip and explain what is happening. The IfG also recommends further sentencing reforms aimed at making the system clearer. Rightly, it points out that the growing gap between jail sentences imposed in court and time actually served risks undermining trust and angering victims. Similarly, licence periods should end at the point where supervision ceases. Currently, there is a pretence that more people are serving community sentences than is actually the case. This places the probation service in a false position.
The pay dispute is the immediate challenge. As part of a settlement, ministers should pledge to rebuild capacity and fill vacancies. Looking further ahead, probation needs closer links to the local services that can help offenders to get back on their feet. The merger with the Prison Service has failed to deliver promised gains.
Managing risks to the public must remain a priority. But Enver Solomon, who leads Nacro, the criminal justice charity, is right to argue for a more “person-centred” style of probation work. No one who knows anything about prisons thinks that they are fulfilling their rehabilitation remit. A renewed focus on purposeful activity inside jails is needed. But as increased numbers of prisoners are diverted towards probation, the service needs resources to deliver what is asked of it.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Cut benefits to fund work support for young people, says Neet review author Alan Milburn
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Ministers should cut welfare spending to fund more employment support if it wants to end the youth Neet crisis, the author of a government-led review has said.
Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, told the Guardian he believed ministers should reduce benefits payments to help pay for more employment support, opening a potentially contentious debate within the Labour party over welfare cuts.
His intervention comes in the run-up to John Healey’s first budget, at which the chancellor is under pressure to explain how he will reduce a multibillion-pound black hole in the country’s finances and pay for more cost of living support without increasing borrowing.
“We’ve got to have a different conversation about the welfare system, it just isn’t working for young people,” Milburn told the Guardian. “We need to redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support if we are going to end the Neet crisis.”
Milburn’s review of why so many 18- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training calculated that a record 1 million young people are now classed as Neet. The former cabinet minister said this was far more than a cyclical youth unemployment problem – it was a “youth detachment” problem, pointing to the fact that 60% of these Neets have never had a job.
Ministers have pushed back Milburn’s final report until after the budget, at which Healey is expected to use a tax raid on banks to help pay for cost of living schemes such as a new energy support package.
The chancellor has signalled his willingness to spend more money on youth unemployment programmes in the short term, however, even if the welfare savings take longer to be realised. He announced a £100m “local apprenticeship service” at last month’s Labour conference, calling it “a downpayment on Alan Milburn’s work”.
In a joint interview with Peter Fonagy, the chair of the government’s landmark independent review of mental health, ADHD and autism, Milburn said his final recommendations were not just about tackling youth unemployment but also improving wellbeing.
“The Neet crisis is a health crisis,” he said. “We’re in this vicious cycle where ill health is driving higher Neet rates. Non-participation is a disaster for young people’s mental health.”
Milburn’s review is likely to recommend that employment, health and benefits support become more integrated. “We have got to change how the wealth, health and welfare systems work and how they interact with each other, because right now they’re plunging far too many young people into a life on benefits, which is ruinous to their life chances, rather than the opportunity to work,” he said.
“No one [in government] is responsible for ensuring that young people both avoid the trap door of becoming Neet and get support to get them out of being Neet.”
Fonagy’s review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s. It recommended providing help at the point of need, not after a diagnosis.
“The current system is based on identifying disability, why a person can’t do something,” Fonagy said. “We need a system that actually addresses their potential and what it is that they can do.
“If nothing is done, and the trends go on as up till now, then there will be not one in five young people with diagnosable mental disorders, but one in four,” which, he added, increased the chances of them becoming Neet.
While there will always be a group of young people whose physical or mental health mean work is not an option, “for the vast majority of young people with autism, ADHD, anxiety or depression, the starting point has to be what could you do, what would you like to do, and how can the state help them do it,” Milburn said.
Young people with health needs should get prompt needs assessment, a personalised health plan and a wider “participation plan”, the review is likely to recommend.
The kind of transformation Milburn and Fonagy describe would cost hundreds of millions of pounds in investment, sources believe. While they would not comment on the level of funding required, both were clear that upfront money would be crucial. “I think everybody in government is very, very well aware of the need to invest behind this priority,” Milburn said.
“Over the medium term, it is entirely possible that you can reduce the benefits bill, but in order to do that, you’ve got to provide the support for young people. You’ve got to increase the opportunities that are available for young people and then provide the support for them to enable them to grab those opportunities.”
“This is not a workshy, snowflake generation, you know, who are making mental distress up,” Milburn added. “If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that’s what they want. The system isn’t delivering what young people want, which is a job.”
But Milburn also hinted at possible consequences for those who don’t engage. “Equally, there has got to be an obligation on young people to take up those opportunities, of course,” he said.
The problem with the system was that it was “over-indexed to cash” and didn’t provide enough support, he added. “The consequence is calamitous for young people who could be working and are not being helped to do so, who then end up on a trajectory to a lifetime on benefits.”
But intervening earlier and providing better support would in turn help relieve the pressure on the mental health waiting list. “I would hope that, for the first time, we could also introduce a maximum waiting time for mental health services, particularly for young people,” said Milburn.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Most Israelis think settlements policy should change to avoid more sanctions, poll finds
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The UK government’s decision to impose a ban on trade in goods from illegal settlements was not decisive in how Israelis voted in their general election, but a majority think the Israeli government’s settlements policy should change if it is going to lead to further sanctions, a new poll of Israelis shows.
There had been fierce criticism of the UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s decision in September to impose a trade ban and wider sanctions on illegal settlements, with some claiming it would drive Israeli voters into the arms of Benjamin Netanyahu.
A survey last month by Israeli social research group aChord shows overall support for foreign sanctions on violent settlers in the West Bank, but there was little support for the UK’s ban on trade with goods from illegal settlements, with many fearing it would end up being extended across Israel.
The survey is unique in showing how much the tougher line on Israel adopted by Britain and some foreign states was affecting the thinking of Israeli voters, and the extent to which Israelis thought it was a response to Israel’s actions or born of hostility to Israel, or even antisemitism.
The survey showed that three-quarters of supporters of the bloc backing Netanyahu said UK sanctions and trade ban policies towards Israel did not affect their vote at all, and to the small extent that they changed anyone’s vote, they shifted voters both ways, leaving no detectable net effect.
Just over three-quarters of all those surveyed (76) – had heard of the UK government announcement on settlements, even if 18 % had only heard the broad headline. Four-fifths of those that were aware of the announcement knew that the policy applied to the West Bank, and not the whole of Israel.
Israel’s relations with the west were “important or very important” to 60% of the supporters of the Change bloc of parties backing Gadi Eisenkot in deciding their vote. But even then these relationships came fifth in importance in a proffered group of six motives for voting. Only 30% of supporters of the Netanyahu bloc said relations with the west mattered in the same way.
But 71% of voters for the opposition Change bloc said the Israeli government should adapt its settlements policy to avoid an escalation of sanctions. Only 14% of Netanyahu bloc voters agreed, most saying instead that the government should continue the policy “whatever the price”.
A plurality of the public – 50% – said the settlement and construction policy in the West Bank should be adjusted to avoid sanctions escalation and international isolation, with 71% of Eisenkot bloc supporters agreeing to this proposition. Support for a change in the policy is strongest among supporters of the Arab parties.
The finding prompted Hannah Weisfeld, the director of the British-Jewish organisation Yachad, to claim the research “illustrates that the Israeli public certainly recognises that if there is not a policy shift in relation to settlement enterprise, the international community is likely to try to create an incentive to shift things from the outside. If anything, that highlights the importance of UK and other allies taking action that targets the occupation.”
The survey also showed that concerns about foreign sanctions are highest when voters feel they will suffer a high personal price. Only 36% of all those surveyed agreed that the settlement policy should continue even if sanctions on banks that finance construction in illegal settlements led either to higher interest rates, difficulties in transferring money abroad, or using credit cards abroad. The poll suggests that the more people feel they will be damaged personally, the more they oppose the settlement policy.
A majority of all Israelis surveyed (52%) support sanctions on individual violent settlers, so long as the sanctions are imposed only on those acting violently, but 70% of Netanyahu bloc supporters oppose foreign sanctions in all circumstances.
There is much less widespread support for the policy of banning the import of goods from the illegal settlement, with 63% of all those surveyed opposing the ban and 26% either supporting the measure outright, or saying they would if it were underlined that the ban would not apply to goods from outside settlements.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Saudi Arabia strikes oil depots in Yemen and says missiles launched toward location of Saudi Aramco HQ
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco.
The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces. Before its offensive on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population before the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure.
The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often hold substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack.
Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed at immobilising the Houthi army as it continues its push south, including towards the city of Taiz.
Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.
The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left 300 injured. The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.
A Houthi spokesperson responded to the attack on its oil storage by warning “all employees and citizens present near any facility affiliated with Aramco Petroleum in Riyadh to evacuate it and stay away from it, as it is a legitimate target for our forces”.
Later in the day, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired at Dharan, the location of the headquarters of Saudi Aramco. It said fragments from the interception fell on a residential area. Witnesses reported hearing loud booms. An evacuation order for the building had been issued, four sources told Reuters. There was no official comment or confirmation from Aramco.
The incident underlined how Saudi Arabia has complete air dominance over Yemen while the Houthis have to reply using drones and missiles which can be intercepted.
Baraa Shiban, a Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), warned “Saudi Arabia is struggling to respond to the Houthi’s improved arms technology. Until relatively recently Houthi missiles and drones fell in desert areas or if they got through were intercepted. They have learned how to deploy drones that fly lower and are smaller, and are less easy to detect. They are cheap and it does not take many to get through to be effective”.
But the two sides’ dramatic threats to set ablaze the enemy energy infrastructure symbolised how the conflict is escalating rather than blowing itself out.
Donald Trump complained that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and said he would “never forget” their attacks, which he suggested were an attempt to influence the US midterm elections next month. But he stopped short of announcing any new military action.
The latest phase of the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transportation of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen.
This week, the Houthis have come closer to throttling the southern city of Taiz, drawing close enough to the city edges to fire rockets into residential areas. City leaders have made repeated appeals to the Yemeni government for military equipment while public health professionals warned of a shortage of medicines for patients in intensive care.
Government-aligned forces sent reinforcements to the south-western district of Al-Mudarabba in Lahij governorate as well as the mountain district of Al-Waz’iyya.
But anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen are not themselves united: a group known as the Southern Transitional Council has been taking a more prominent role in the fight against the Houthis – even though its main objective is to secede from the country’s north.
On Tuesday, Aidarous al Zubaidi, the exiled STC leader, gave a rare address declaring “a popular mobilisation in defence of the south, and its national liberation project” – including by repelling the invading Houthi militia.
Al Zubaidi, now based in Abu Dhabi, made clear he still supported a plan to eventually hold a referendum on the independence of South Yemen.
Zubaidi’s organisation remains banned in Yemen and he has been charged with treason, but there are incremental behind-the-scenes talks under way testing whether the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman is prepared to legitimise the STC and even permit Zubaidi to return. Reinstatement of the STC would be seen as a betrayal by the current Yemen president, Rashad al-Alimi, but his usefulness to Saudi Arabia is reduced if he does not have the same military forces at his disposal as Zubaidi.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Minister insists she backs migration policy after joking she couldn’t lie about supporting it
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The energy secretary has been forced to clarify that she backs Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy, after earlier joking that she had not been able to “lie” about supporting a key element of the changes.
Miatta Fahnbulleh made the original remarks to a journalists’ event in Westminster, referring to an “awkward” Sky News interview in which she repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
She told the event: “I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments, including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge yesterday.”
The implication that she could not bring herself to lie about supporting the changes appears to have gone down badly among colleagues in government, although No 10 refused to be drawn on whether they requested her to issue a clarification.
Fahnbulleh posted a statement on social media on Thursday evening saying: “Today I made what was meant to be a lighthearted, self-deprecating remark. I didn’t get it right and it hasn’t come off as I intended.
“I fully support our home secretary and the government’s position on migration reform. As I said earlier this week, it’s absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship.”
The clarification represents a twist in the cabinet split over the issue of the migration changes, with Fahnbulleh and Angela Rayner among those not keen on elements of the original plan.
Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.
She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule.
However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”
This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”
And earlier this year, Rayner, the housing secretary, publicly criticised the plans, while dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.
One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.
“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.
MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.
No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the planned changes.
Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.
“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”
Earlier this week, a Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK accused of giving people of Gaza false hope over new refugee safe route
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Home Office is facing claims it gave false hope to the people of Gaza after it emerged that a new safe route for Palestinian refugees will only be open to those who have already escaped to Lebanon or Jordan.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, announced the reopening of a resettlement scheme for refugees at Labour’s annual conference last month. A statement from her department said: “Around one in four referrals will be for Afghan women and girls and Palestinian refugees, fleeing war and persecution.”
But the body administering the scheme has confirmed it would only refer “a very small number of extremely urgent cases”, all of which would be processed in Jordan and Lebanon.
The umbrella alliance Communities for Palestinians (CFP) said this crucial detail was not in Mahmood’s speech or subsequent Home Office statements, giving people in Gaza and their supporters the belief that they could also apply.
Vicky Moller, a co-founder of CFP, said: “The applause at Shabana’s announcement at conference was at the prospect of a resettlement scheme for Palestinians fleeing war and persecution. People understood that would mean rescuing people from Gaza.”
The Home Office has pushed back at the claims, saying the UK resettlement scheme that Mahmood has reopened has always been for people from outside their country of origin.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “To qualify for refugee status under international frameworks, individuals must be outside their country of origin.
“Palestinians who remain in Gaza would not initially be in scope for these routes. However, Palestinians who have fled Gaza could be referred to the UK through the International Refugee Assistance Project [Irap].”
Restrictions on eligibility for the scheme emerged after an exchange of emails between the CFP and Irap, which has been tasked with making referrals.
According to Irap’s website, it will refer “a very small number of extremely urgent humanitarian cases to the UK for consideration for resettlement”, adding: “These cases will be referred to Irap by humanitarian organisations in Jordan and Lebanon and Irap will then hold interviews to determine if these cases can be referred to the UK government.”
The programme focuses on “extremely vulnerable refugees whose lives have become unsustainable in Jordan or Lebanon”.
The non-profit’s website added: “Irap does not know how many people the UK government will accept under the Palestinian resettlement programme. This is ultimately a decision for the UK government and depends on funding as well as local authorities’ capacity.”
Other safe and legal routes administered by the UK have allowed small numbers of people to enter the UK from their country of origin, including previous schemes for Afghan refugees.
Palestinian refugees fall outside the remit of the refugee convention and UNHCR.
Unrwa was instead set up to serve Palestinian refugees who were defined as any person whose “normal place of residence was Palestine during the period 1 June 1946 to 15 May 1948 and who lost both home and means of livelihood as a result of the 1948 conflict”.
As a result, Palestinian refugees live in what refugee charities and NGOs refer to as Palestine – in other words, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip – as well as second countries such as Syria, Lebanon and Jordan.
Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said ministers should recognise the particular circumstances that meant Palestinians could be refugees while living in their own country.
“The government is right to commit to safe and legal routes. They provide a vital way for refugees to reach safety without having to put their lives in the hands of smuggling gangs,” he said.
“But the warm words have to be accompanied by ambition, and that means supporting people in the thousands, not the hundreds. They must also recognise the particular circumstances of Palestinian refugees and be accessible to them no matter where they are in the world.”
A renowned expert in asylum systems has said resettlement programmes are usually designed as a solution for people who have already left their own country.
Dr Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said the UK government’s safe and legal route was always going to mean taking Palestinians from neighbouring states such as Egypt, Jordan or Lebanon.
“The Syrian scheme worked the same way: the roughly 20,000 people resettled to the UK between 2014 and 2021 all came from countries around Syria, with nobody to my knowledge being flown directly from Syria,” he said.
“Bringing people directly out of Gaza would be a different kind of programme, closer to an emergency evacuation … And crucially, such an emergency evacuation in Gaza would depend on Israel and Egypt letting people leave and on the Home Office finding a way to do security and biometric checks with no visa centre in Gaza.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Haley Stevens advised to stay away from Abdul El-Sayed campaign events to limit ‘distractions’
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s tightly fought US Senate race, wants Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens to stay away from his campaign events.
“I don’t want any distractions,” El-Sayed told reporters after a campaign rally, according to the New York Times. “It seems as though other folks are more interested in making this race about things that it’s not about.”
The two had planned to appear together on Sunday at a church service in Detroit, but Representative Debbie Dingell later told CNN she had spoken to Stevens and told her “This isn’t working.” Dingell added that the tensions between the two were a distraction and that “there’s nothing to be gained by the two of them being in the same place.”
The public rupture between the progressive El-Sayed and the more moderate Stevens, whom he defeated in a bitter primary, has cast Democratic tensions into the spotlight in one of the most consequential elections in the party’s campaign to retake control of the Senate.
Stevens endorsed El-Sayed shortly after he won the primary election in August, and planned to campaign with him on Sunday.
But Stevens had until now avoided appearing publicly with her former opponent, whom she has criticized publicly for weeks. Her fiance, Jason Turkish, has campaigned on behalf of Republican candidate Mike Rogers.
And just two days before they were scheduled to campaign together this weekend, Stevens demanded that El-Sayed denounce an outside group’s political ad that blamed higher prices on US support for Israel’s war in Gaza.
“Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago,” El-Sayed shot back in a statement, which noted that the American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent heavily to defeat him in the primary.
“Let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics, putting money in pockets, and passing Medicare for All,” the statement said.
The open feuding worries many Democrats, who see the tight race as a must-win for the party to win back the Senate.
“I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing,” Michigan state senator Mallory McMorrow told CNN Friday. “This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes. People are not talking about ads. They are not talking about Haley Stevens. They are talking about the price of gas and groceries.”
