SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump rallies for Mike Rogers – and Nicki Minaj’s derriere – in Michigan
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Donald Trump reiterated his apparent love for buxom bums during a rally in Michigan on Sunday where he encouraged the crowd to compliment rapper Nicki Minaj’s behind.
Trump’s cheeky comments about Minaj’s derriere came as he explained his recent observation on the Republican Ohio senator Jon Husted’s rear end. Earlier in October, Trump said of the former college football player: “I don’t do this with men very often. I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass and I looked at the whole – and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He’s got these, like, claws.
“You are a great athlete,” Trump also said to Husted. “Congratulations.”
Trump was speaking at the rally to support Mike Rogers, the Michigan Republican Senate candidate. The Michigan race between Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed remains neck and neck as both political parties scramble for control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections. But he couldn’t resist his purported other favorite topic.
This afternoon, Trump said the media buzz about these comments was “fake news” neglecting the athletic context of his statements. Trump said he had just learned Husted was a college athlete when he was “looking at him up and down, and I’m studying him”.
Trump insisted his subsequent crack was “in fun”. “I said: I looked at his ass, and I’ve never done that with a man before. It’s true. Off the record, women yes, men no, OK.”
Trump then shouted out Minaj, who the New York Post said was donned in “head-to-toe Gucci” today. Minaj, the paper also reported, was seen walking with Trump after leaving Air Force One.
“By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before – Nicki Minaj,” Trump said, prompting celebratory woos from the crowd. “That’s hard to miss. That – stand up! That’s hard to miss.
“OK, I’m going to get back to my story, Nicki,” Trump continued following still more cheers. “I hope Nicki wasn’t insulted, but we love Nicki. She’s been with us for a long time.”
Trump made statements about Husted’s tush just over a week ago in Kentucky.
“I examined his ass,” Trump said of Husted, who was not at the event. “And then I looked at his shoulders. I looked at his feet. I looked at his hand. I looked at his jawline. Studied him. He’s got a jawline.
“I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I’m still recovering,” Trump said.
Trump also recently praised the appearance of Ed Gallrein, theRepublican congressional candidate from Kentucky.
“I needed somebody good, and this guy walks through the door,” Trump remarked of Gallrein, in describing his efforts to find a replacement for anti-Maga incumbent Thomas Massie. “I said, look at this beautiful guy.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment about why Trump has been discussing others’ bodies.
Trump’s comments come amid criticism of his language style, which some have likened to grotesquerie.
During a Saturday rally for El-Sayed, Barack Obama joked about Trump’s White House renovation efforts.
“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” the former president said.
Meanwhile, Trump said that the US-Canada trade war would soon be in America’s rear view.
“Canada has been ripping off the US for years. I had to do it,” Trump said of tariffs during the rally. “We’ll have that settled pretty soon. They’re willing to give us anything at this moment.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Labour faces accusations of breaking manifesto pledge over minimum wage for young people – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Labour faces accusations of breaking manifesto pledge over minimum wage for young people – as it happened
Greens say Labour has ‘no respect for young people’ amid reports chancellor will pause equalisation of minimum wage for under-21s with that paid to older workers
Greens accuse Labour of breaking manifesto pledge, after minister signals minimum wage age equalisation being paused
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has not contested reports saying that, in the budget tomorrow, John Healey, the chancellor, will pause the process of equalising the lower national minimum wage paid to people under the age of 21 with the more generous national living wage that applies to older workers.
In an interview on the BBC this morning, Reynolds was asked to respond to a story suggesting the equalisation process has been put on hold because of concerns about youth unemployment.
John Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for young people after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs.
The Times has been told that the national living wage, which applies to those aged 21 and over, is expected to rise from £12.71 to around £13.20 – an increase of 3.9%.
However, Healey has decided not to repeat the big rises of the past two budgets in the national minimum wage, which applies to those aged 18 to 21. It will rise broadly in line with the rate for older workers – from £10.85 to around £11.27, an increase of 3.9%.
In its manifesto, Labour said it would raise the level of the national minimum wage to the level of the national living wage to “so all adults are entitled to the same minimum wage, delivering a pay rise to hundreds of thousands of workers across the UK”. The manifesto implied this would happen during this parliament, but in May Torsten Bell, the pensions minister, said implementation of this commitment could be delayed until after the general election – implying the government is worried equalisation now could increase youth unemployment.
Asked about the Times story on the Today programme, Reynolds insisted the new national living wage and national minimum wage rates would be announced tomorrow.
But he went on:
The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies, but it was always clear it would happen over time and we would take into account, as the minimum wage uprating each year always does, the relative strength of the labour market and other pressures …
Of course, you want not just good wages, but good work. And the way this has always been done – it is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account. That is the approach you will see confirmed [in the budget].
The Green party has accused Labour of breaking a manifesto promise. Responding to the Times’ story, and Reynolds’ comments in effect confirming it, Mothin Ali, the Greens’ co-deputy leader, said:
Anyone doing a day’s work, needs to be paid the same rate for the same job. A young person’s rent and food bill is no less because they are young, so they need to receive the same wage.
Healey and Burnham are now breaking a manifesto pledge to young people that even Starmer managed to keep. Labour have no respect for young people, who appear to just be there for cheap labour for the wealthy and their corporate donors.
Ali said the Greens would introduce a £15 minimum wage for workers of all ages.
Labour has been accused of breaking a manifesto pledge to raise the minimum wage for younger people up to the level that applies to workers over the age of 21 after a minister signalled that the process of equalising the two different rates will be paused in the budget. (See 12.52pm.)
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, has said Nigel Farage is “completely unfit for public office” after the Reform UK leader in interviews this morning said he would not block a candidate for liking Tommy Robinson (see 12.13pm) and refused to condemn a former aide who called Kemi Badenoch a Nigerian scammer. In response, Phillipson said:
Nigel Farage is desperately trying to drag politics further and further into the gutter. It seems there is no low he won’t stoop to – he is completely unfit for public office.
Failing to call out blatant racism against the leader of His Majesty’s Opposition despite being given at least ten opportunities to do so and then giving his activists the green light to support Tommy Robinson shows just who he really is.
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.
Minister opens National School of Government and Public Services
A National School of Government and Public Services has opened, the Cabinet Officehas announced. Mark Ferguson, a Cabinet Office minister, formally opened it today. The government says:
Regional hubs will be developed across the country, with the first opened in York this week, alongside digital access routes to give civil servants access to modern learning facilities close to where they live and work.
It will provide civil servants and public sector leaders with the world-class learning and development they need to meet the challenges of the future.
The school will build a curriculum around the skills all servants need, including training on devolution, national security, leadership and innovation. Training will also be offered in AI, covering the full range of skills needed now and in the future, from implementing practical solutions at the frontline to cut clerical workloads to cloud engineering courses to develop and deploy the latest technology across government, the School will equip Civil Servants with the tools to build a world-class Civil Service.
Security minister says Britons far less ready for emergencies than other Europeans as he defends Be Ready campaign
Last week the government launched a Be Ready campaign to publicise advice saying people should stockpile water, food and other supplies in the event of an emergency. The announcement attracted a lot of attention, although many Britons probably sided with Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, who signalled that she was not going to get too alarmed by it all by joking about how she would include a bottle of sauvignon blanc and mascara alongside her government-mandated survival supplies.
Dan Jarvis, the security minister, gave a statement about the advice to MPs this afternoon. In his opening comments, he did not pass judgment on the usefulness or otherwise of a bottle of wine, but he did have some points to add.
Jarvis dismissed claims that the advice was an “overreaction”. Anyone who did think that should have been with him when he met victims of Storm Goretti earlier this year, he said. He said 50,000 homes, schools and businesses were left without power, communities were cut off because of blocked roads and families experienced having “the basic necessities of everyday life”, like power, water and the internet, taken away from them.
He said government research shows only 13% of people in the UK feel they are prepared for an emergency, like having power cut off after a storm. He went on:
This figure is far lower than our European neighbours. The very same research showed that 84% of people in the UK want the government to share more information about the steps they can take to increase their preparedness.
He said the last government launched a website giving preparedness guidance, but there was no proper publicity campaign and “not enough people noticed [the advice], and those who did found the guidance hard to follow”.
He said the publicity campaign was not being launched in response to a specific threat.
He said there were two main things people are being asked to do.
The two main actions are ensuring that you have three days of water and non-perishable food, and signing up to the Priority Services Register if you or someone in your household is eligible for extra support in a utility outage.
He said the government would be encouraging communities to get involved in emergency planning.
He joked about how, before he was in the Parachute regiment, he was a Boy Scout where the motto was “Be Prepared”.
UK government to give £15m to anti-misogyny fund amid ‘manosphere’ concerns
John Healey, the chancellor, will give £15m to a dedicated fund to tackle misogyny in workplaces, schools and public places amid concerns in government about the rise of “manosphere” influencers, Jessica Elgot reports.
Burnham says he wants to be PM who ends 'decade of division', as he stresses support for British Muslims
Andy Burnham has said that he wants to be a prime minister who brings to an end “a decade of division”.
He made the remark at a meeting with Muslim leaders in Downing Street this morning, where he said British Muslims were particularly likely to be victims of hate.
Without giving examples, he also said some of the language used by opposition parties about Muslims was “completely unacceptable”.
Speaking at the opening of the meeting, Burnham said
Where I want to start is just to talk a little bit about the style I’m trying to bring into my role.
I’m really clear in saying that we cannot have another decade of division like the one we’ve lived through.
It’s easier said than done, of course. But I did try on the steps outside Downing Street to talk very directly about that, drawing a line on it and building a more positive, hopeful feeling within the country. I’m going to stick to that path and try and move the country beyond some of what we’ve all lived through in the last 10 years.
And I know Muslim communities across different parts of the country have really in many ways lived through some of the worst examples of division and the hatred that people experience.
Burnham said that he wanted to be a PM “alongside the [Muslim] community, visibly so, very much sending that message, particularly to younger Muslims across Britain, that this is their country, this country is behind them, working to support them.”
As the Press Association reports, attendees included crossbench peer Lady Gohir, who leads the Muslim Women’s Network; Shabir Randeree and Akeela Ahmed, chair and chief executive of the British Muslim Trust; Bibi Khan of the London Islamic Cultural Centre; and Javed Khan, managing director of the Equi thinktank.
Shabana Mahmood urged to grant visa to former Weather Underground activist
Human rights activists and celebrities including the lawyer Helena Kennedy, the actor Harriet Walter and the theatre director Phyllida Lloyd have urged the Home Office to overturn its decision to refuse a visa to a former member of the radical US group the Weather Underground, saying her decades of rehabilitation should count in her favour. Nadia Khomami has the story.
SNP claims Burnham's 'minuscule announcements' are 'insulting' to voters
The SNP is also making a last-minute budget submission to the chancellor. It is calling for VAT on petrol and diesel to be removed.
Kirsty Blackman, the SNP’s economy spokesperson at Westminster, said:
In the face of a cost-of-living emergency, Andy Burnham has broken his promise to cut bills and is insulting voters with minuscule announcements that won’t scratch the surface. [See 9.07am.]
The fact is every major household bill has risen under Burnham.
He is treating voters like fools by pretending he is delivering ‘breathing space’ when energy bills will soon be £1,000 higher than the Labour party promised, mortgage rates are up at 6%, and the price of petrol, diesel, food and shopping has gone through the roof on his watch.
At the UK budget on Wednesday, the chancellor must finally deliver meaningful help for the majority of households by cutting energy bills by at least £300 and by removing VAT from petrol and diesel for the remainder of the fuel price crisis.
It could save households in Scotland £500 as prices soar under the Labour government.
(Describing statements like this, and the Lib Dems’ (see 2.20pm), as budget ‘submissions’ is journalistic fiction in some respects, because the budget has already been written. But opposition parties feel it is important to set out their views.)
UK rejoining EU's Erasmus student exchange scheme in January, with applications open next month, minister tells MPs
The government has confirmed that the UK will rejoin the Erasmus+ student exchange scheme from the start of January, the Press Association reports. PA says:
Foreign Office minister Hamish Falconer said applications would open next month for young people who will be able to study, train or get work experience in the European Union.
Speaking during Foreign Office questions, Falconer emphasised to MPs that the opportunities would be open to “educational institutions of all kinds”.
Work on the UK joining the Erasmus programme was announced as part of Keir Starmer’s post-Brexit reset deal with Brussels in 2025.
The UK left the scheme under Boris Johnson’s Brexit deal in 2020, with the then-prime minister arguing it did not offer value for money.
It was replaced by the Turing Scheme, which was ended when the government announced the new deal over Erasmus plus.
The government has previously said it expects more than 100,000 people to be able to benefit, and that disadvantaged students tend to benefit highly from taking part in the scheme.
Lib Dems call for business rates to be scrapped as they highlight their budget proposals
Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, and Daisy Cooper, his deputy, visited an MOT garage today – for the sole purpose, it seems, of providing a picture to illustrate his pre-budget soundbite.
In a statement, he said:
Labour has put the handbrake on the economy. Growth is in the slow lane and hardworking business owners like Bob are facing higher costs, a jobs tax, and a broken business rates system.
The economy desperately needs a tune-up. The Liberal Democrats would scrap business rates, replace them with a fairer system, and negotiate a proper growth and defence deal with Europe, so we can turbocharge our economy by joining the EU single market and customs union.
In a briefing on their own budget proposals, the Liberal Democrats said they would:
• Turbocharge economic growth and spur investment and job creation across the UK, through a new growth and defence partnership with Europe, including joining the EU Single Market and a customs union.
• Scrap business rates and replace them with a fairer system. The Liberal Democrats would replace business rates with a commercial landowner levy. Firms would no longer be taxed on the value of the building or machinery they use, which penalises investment and hits independent businesses hardest.
• Boost skills and tackle the Neet crisis. The party would guarantee every young person 100 hours of work experience and professional enrichment before they turn 18 to tackle the Neets pipeline before young people fall out of education and work. This would also help tackle the growing number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets), by making it cheaper for small employers to offer first jobs. According to latest ONS figures, there were an estimated 981,000 young people aged 16 to 24 years in the UK who were Neet in April to June 2026.
Streeting signs defence agreement with Poland, describing it as 'one of UK's closest allies'
Britain and Poland have agreed to work together to build a new generation of air defence missiles, as the west gears up its defence efforts against Russia, the Press Association reports. PA says:
A new agreement, the Warsaw Defence Plan, will also see the two nations work together to build new drones and anti-drone measures, as well as collaborate closely on more traditional land, sea and air defence.
Defence secretary Wes Streeting signed the pact in Warsaw today, where he met his Polish counterpart Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.
Streeting said: “Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies – from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century.
“The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger Nato.
“From collaborating on Nato exercises that deter our adversaries to working together to support Ukraine in its fight for freedom, we are committed to standing together for European security whilst boosting our economies with stronger defence industries.”
Under the pact, the two nations will share their experiences of developing new warships. Britain’s Type 31 frigate and Poland’s Miecznik are based on a common design.
The allies have also agreed to increase shared patrols in the Baltic Sea, to protect vital communications cables on the seabed.
The agreement comes ahead of a major coalition of the willing exercise next month, which will see British, French and German forces join Warsaw’s soldiers in Poland for training to prepare for a peacekeeping mission in Ukraine once the war is over.
No 10 says Burnham to set out 'next steps' for long-term relations with EU around time of 20 November summit
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said this morning that British government officials would be talking to their EU counterparts about possible changes to the UK-EU relationship. Possible options include the UK joining the single market, and so free movement would be part of that discussion.
The government seems to be nervous about suggestions it is already in talks about the UK signing up for free movement rules and, at the Downing Street lobby briefing this morning, a No 10 spokesperson insisted free movement was not part of the current talks with the EU.
Those talks are “focused solely on next month’s summit, and the practical agreements that we hope to make there that will add billions to the economy and cut the red tape that holds back British business,” the spokesperson said.
She added:
Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements, on what is realistic for both sides, and, crucially, on what the British public supports. And the prime minister will set out the next steps when it comes to our longer term relationship around the time of the summit.
The summit will take place in Brussels on Friday 20 November.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Nancy Pelosi’s office latest recipient of letter containing white powder
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
California representative Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious letter” on Wednesday in what appears to be the latest incident of ill-intentioned mailings targeted at US Congress members before the midterm elections.
The offices of more than three dozen members of Congress across the political spectrum have received envelopes containing white powder in recent days. One lawmaker’s office said preliminary tests indicated the powder was not hazardous.
A spokesperson for Pelosi said the letter was “consistent with mailings reported by other congressional offices” and that everyone in the office was safe.
“Speaker Pelosi remains focused on serving the people of San Francisco and is concerned for the members and staff whose offices have experienced similar incidents,” Nicholas Martin, a spokesperson for the speaker emerita, said in a statement.
“She is grateful for the efforts of the US Capitol police, the San Francisco police department and other law enforcement agencies to thoroughly investigate this series of intimidation across America.”
More than 100 letters thought to contain white powder were reportedly thought to be circulating in the US mail system. Election offices across the US have also reported receiving suspicious mail.
The mailings are under investigation by the FBI, the Capitol police and the US Postal Inspection Service. The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement earlier this week: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.
The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.
“A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events.
“First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”
Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.
He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.
Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.
“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.
“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”
His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.
Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.
Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.
Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.
“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.
“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”

Top Senate Democratic Super Pac pours millions more in Michigan and Maine races
The top Super Pac for Senate Democrats will pour more than $7m into two marquee races this cycle: Michigan and Maine.
The Senate Majority Pac has reserved $3.7m for its campaign in Michigan, to support the Democratic nominee , Dr Abdul El-Sayed, against the Trump-backed Republican, Mike Rogers. The group is also investing $3m in Maine, to boost Democrat Troy Jackson’s chances against Susan Collins – the five-term moderate GOP incumbent, who Democrats see as increasingly vulnerable in a cycle where anti-Trump sentiment has colored much of the election.
This comes after reports that the Senate Majority Pac has also paused ad spending in North Carolina and Georgia. Semafor was first to report on the updated spend.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Donald Trump traveled to Bullhead City, Arizona and Kalispell, Montana for campaign rallies today. In Arizona, Trump urged voters to elect Andy Biggs, a GOP congressman who’s running to unseat the state’s Democratic governor, Katie Hobbs. In Montana, Trump rallied for Kurt Alme, a Republican and the former US attorney for Montana, who is facing Alani Bankhead, a Democrat and a retired air force officer, as well as Seth Bodnar, an independent and US army veteran former president of the University of Montana.
The president traveled to campaign rallies today onboard the new Air Force One, a luxury Boeing 747-8 aircraft gifted by the Qatari government. Speaking about the plane during his appearance in Arizona, Trump said, “When you’re giving gifts, you take them, right?”
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv. The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by the US agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow.
The top Super Pac for Senate Democrats will pour more than $7m into two marquee races this cycle:Michigan and Maine. The Senate Majority Pac has reserved $3.7m for its campaign in Michigan, to support Democratic Senate nominee Dr Abdul El-Sayed. The group is also investing $3m in Maine, to boost Democrat Troy Jackson’s chances against Susan Collins.
Federal authorities investigating the Minnesota representative Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the inquiry.
The justice department has threatened California over alleged noncitizen voters. In a letter addressed to the California secretary of state, Shirley Weber, on Tuesday, the acting deputy attorney general, Trent McCotter, said the justice department gave Los Angeles county officials a “password-protected thumb drive” with names of people that the federal government “believes are likely noncitizens”.
US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living.
A record number of Georgians cast ballots in the first day of early voting this midterm cycle. According to Brad Raffensperger, Georgia’s secretary of state, there were 188,600 votes cast on Tuesday – an increase of more than 53,000 voters over the 2022 midterm election, which saw 134,962 early in-person votes.
Kamala Harris, the former vice-president and 2024 presidential nominee, will travel across the country in support of several Democrats facing competitive races in the final two weeks ahead of the November midterms, according to her office. During a podcast appearance yesterday, Harris said ‘I haven’t decided’ about a 2028 presidential run.
Before his rally speech, Donald Trump blamed Joe Biden for provoking the Russian invasion of Ukraine in remarks to a reporter back stage. “I have to make deals with people, so I don’t go around calling them names,” the president said. “I don’t go around mocking people. Part of the reason you have that war in the first place is Biden went around mocking Russia.”
Katie Zacharia claims she misheard question about where she passed the bar exam, but still has no answer – report
Robert Mackey
Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, told the New York Times on Wednesday that she misheard reporters who asked her on Tuesday where she had passed the bar exam.
When reporters asked Zacharia, as she left the White House with Donald Trump on Tuesday, where she had passed the bar exam, since she has described herself as a lawyer, she replied, oddly: “I moved to China”.
In a brief phone interview with the Times, she said: “I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’
“That’s all I could hear over the sound of Marine One,” she said, of the helicopter that was about to bring her and the president to the airport for his flight to Alaska. “And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question.”
According to the Times, she added that when she first began appearing on television as a pro-Trump commentator, the president of Pepperdine law school, where she obtained her law degree in 2011, warned her not to call herself “attorney” or “esquire,” but said that using the term “lawyer” was allowed.
That answer suggests that Zacharia simply did not pass the bar exam in any US state, before or after moving to China to work in a Chinese law firm.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday night that Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school at Pepperdine in 2011, but failed to pass, according to a source it did not name.
Donald Trump began his remarks in Montana tonight focused largely on gun rights.
Kurt Alme, the Republican candidate for US Senate that Trump is campaigning for, has an A rating from the National Rifle Association, which endorsed him last month.
Donald Trump has arrived in Montana an hour after he was slated to appear. We’ll bring you newsworthy lines from his second campaign appearance of the day.
James Talarico downplayed a past remark about God being non-binary, after being questioned about his social stances.
In 2021, Talarico, a state legislator, came out against a bill restricting transgender athletes, saying then “God is both masculine and feminine and everything in between. God is nonbinary.”
His comments have since surfaced as fuel for his opponent Ken Paxton’s attack ads.
“When I said that, I was being provocative and I want to admit that and come clean about that,” Talarico said during the CNN town hall. “What I was saying is actually not controversial theologically: the idea that we can’t define God using human categories. Not only did I say that, but the late Charlie Kirk said that – the late Pope Benedict said that.
“Preachers often will say something shocking in a sermon to get your attention and that’s something I’m still learning how to do in a responsible way.”
James Talarico, the Texas Democratic candidate for Senate, once again debunked rumors in the conservative media that he had a clandestine stint at a mental health facility.
Before his CNN town hall kicked off on Wednesday evening, Talarico said, as he has before, that he took a hiatus from in-person campaign appearances after coming down with the flu.
“My decision to stay home for a week sent my opponent and his conspiracy theorists spiraling. I opened up social media and learned I had apparently dropped out of the race, had flown to a mental hospital in Ohio – that I had died,” Talarico said.
“False claims got millions of views online and this is an example of what I call the ‘rage economy.’ Billionaires who own these platforms get rich. We all get angry and nobody’s life gets any better. Conspiracy theories don’t put food on the table, put gas in the tank, or improve our communities.”
Trump lies that Abdul El-Sayed once said he was 'a member of the Muslim Brotherhood'
Robert Mackey
Speaking to reporters in Arizona on Wednesday, Donald Trump was asked about the allegation that Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s relatives in Egypt once supported the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist opposition movement.
The president responded by lying that El-Sayed had called himself “a member of the Muslim Brotherhood”.
“Abdul, or as I call him, Mohammed El-Sayed, he’s a member of the Muslim Brotherhood,” Trump said in a false statement posted on social media by the White House. “He said that years ago, he was a proud member,” the president continued, also falsely. “And you can’t have a member of the Muslim Brotherhood in Congress, being on one of our security committees.”
Despite Trump’s blatant lie, there is no evidence that El-Sayed is or ever has been a member of the group. The allegation he was being asked to respond to, which has become a centerpiece of the Republican campaign against El-Sayed, is that his mother and members of her family in Egypt might have once had sympathy for the group, based on three tweets posted in 2012 and 2013 by the candidate’s half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, in response to political developments in Egypt after the revolution there.
The social media posts from El-Sayed’s half-sister were reported this week by the Washington Free Beacon, a partisan, rightwing news site funded by a major Republican donor. The rightwing site was invited to accompany Trump on his trip to Arizona on Wednesday by the White House.
On 24 June 2012, the day that a former Muslim Brotherhood leader, Mohamed Morsi, was elected Egypt’s president, with the support of secular pro-democracy activists who celebrated in Cairo’s Tahrir Square, Abdelhadi posted criticism of the Islamist group while saying that her family had supported it during its long years of opposition to the ousted dictator Hosni Mubarak.
The same day, as secular supporters of the revolution that deposed Mubarak expressed relief that Morsi had defeated a military-backed candidate, Abdelhadi also posted: “Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college.”
On 3 July 2013, when Morsi was deposed in a military coup by Gen Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, starting a bloody crackdown on Islamists and secular activists that lasts to this day, El-Sayed’s half-sister posted that she was praying for family members in Egypt who supported the Muslim Brotherhood.
El-Sayed, who was raised by his father and stepmother – and grandparents – told NBC News on Wednesday that his half-sister’s tweets did not contradict his repeated statement that he has no ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. “I wasn’t raised by my mother,” El-Sayed said, adding that he has never talked to her about her days as a student activist in Egypt a decade before his birth in the US.
Donald Trump is scheduled to begin speaking soon at a rally in Montana.
Here, Kurt Alme, a Republican and the former US attorney for Montana, is facing Alani Bankhead, a Democrat and a retired air force officer, as well as Seth Bodnar, an independent and US army veteran former president of the University of Montana.
A Trump administration raid on Ilhan Omar’s home this week is part of an investigation intended to build a case to strip her of her US citizenship and deport her, the Wall Street Journal reports, citing US officials and other people familiar with the investigation.
During his second term, Donald Trump’s administration has aggressively pursued work to denaturalize US citizens. Since returning to office, the president’s administration has filed more than 200 lawsuits against people it is seeking to denaturalize. Previously, the government filed denaturalization cases fewer than a dozen times a year, the Journal reports, citing the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.
Kamala Harris says 'I haven't decided' about 2028 presidential run
Kamala Harris said she has not decided whether she will run for president in 2028, the former vice-president told Keke Palmer during an interview on the actor’s podcast Tuesday.
At the end of the interview – which covered the midterm elections, the Trump administration and Black voters – Palmer asked whether Harris was considering a 2028 presidential run.
“I haven’t decided. I haven’t decided yet. I will, I promise,” Harris said.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on Labour’s fiscal devolution: the future of Burnhamism will play out in municipal England | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Following Wednesday’s budget, the Treasury minister, Torsten Bell, was challenged by the BBC’s Evan Davis on whether its modest series of “breathing space” measures could truly be said to have ended “40 years of neoliberalism”. This line of questioning is becoming a familiar one. Andy Burnham’s ringing declaration of long-term intent is now being regularly deployed by commentators to suggest an emerging gulf between rhetoric and action.
Mr Bell’s response was a good one. Recalling how “Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s hugely hollowed out local government [and] tried to emasculate our big cities”, he called the fiscal devolution roadmap unveiled in the budget a step change and a really big deal.From 2028, mayoral strategic authorities will for the first time receive a share of income tax receipts, and from next year they will be allocated 20% of business rates revenue. That figure will potentially rise to 100% by the end of the decade, while a new overnight visitors levy will add another local income stream.
These are structural changes that will transform the relationship between local government and a notoriously overly centralised state. They have so far failed to generate anything like the coverage that accompanied the Conservatives’ levelling-up programme, which degenerated into a tawdry pork barrel exercise for “red wall” Tory MPs. But it is on this municipal terrain that Mr Burnham’s aspiration to rebalance the country, reduce regional inequality and “roll back” the 80s will be played out.
Replacing government grants with guaranteed income streams will give strategic authorities more certainty over future revenue – against which they will be able to borrow – and the ability to plan flexibly according to locally set priorities. The devil will be in details to be announced in next year’s spending review, in particular regarding mechanisms to ensure poorer areas with a smaller tax base do not lose out. But the roadmap is a first move towards restoring proper agency to local authorities struggling to cope with the disastrous twin legacy of deindustrialisation and austerity.
Further steps will need to be taken if, as the prime minister intends, local government is to drive “good growth” that improves general living standards and prospects throughout communities. As the Local Government Association pointed out, cash-strapped councils on the frontline face a £7bn funding gap by 2028-29, and are in a perennial struggle merely to meet their statutory obligations on social care. Strategic authorities need to be given the capacity to gradually reassume control of priorities in sectors such as care, housing and the utilities. That will take time and investment at scale in forms of community provision that can offer an alternative to a model in which services have been outsourced and profits offshored.
Devolution will not of itself reduce inequalities or restore a degraded public realm. But this week’s budget measures began the necessary process of rewiring British politics. Mr Burnham’s core conviction is that radical devolution can redistribute power to those who know their own community best, and allow councils to rebalance the relationship between the public and the private sector. After decades in which the latter has profited hugely from calling nearly all the shots, that is very much the right direction of travel. The starting gun has been fired in a process that can lead to a genuine renaissance of municipal England.
-

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: EU presses UK to guarantee discounted university tuition fees for European students
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.
At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.
These member states oppose deferring agreement for another half-year. Many believe a failure to reach an agreement should delay the highly prized food and drink deal to cut Brexit red tape coming into force.
European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.
Andy Burnham will meet the EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on 20 November in Brussels, with the aim of signing three agreements – on food and drink, carbon markets and youth exchange – as well as pledging a “trusted partnership” on steel and defence industries.
But a longstanding dispute over whether EU students should pay costly international tuition fees at British universities remains unresolved and could delay the implementation of the food and energy deals, which are worth billions to the British economy.
The EU wants a return to the pre-Brexit status quo where European students paid the UK domestic rate of university tuition, rather than international fees, which can be about four to six times higher for an undergraduate degree.
European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing an agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.
But at least six member states, including in central and eastern Europe, want the university fees issue settled by the summit, while many are seeking a firmer commitment on the issue from the British government, according to four EU sources.
One EU diplomat told the Guardian: “Having a youth experience scheme without an agreement on tuition fees has very little added value,” noting the much lower cost of university education in many EU countries and therefore potential greater advantage to British students.
A second EU diplomat said there was cautious optimism about the November summit, but “a large majority” wanted “a more convincing British commitment” on tuition fees.
A government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on leaks or provide a running commentary on live negotiations. We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”
For the EU, the creation of a youth experience scheme, known as Yes, which will enable those aged 18 to 30 to live, work and study on both sides of the Channel is a high priority. The erosion of people-to-people links is seen as one of the big losses of Brexit, and many European officials studied in the UK, making the issue especially resonant.
EU officials argue the bloc has leverage, saying the food and drink deal – a Labour manifesto pledge estimated to be worth £5.1bn a year to the British economy – would come into force only if there was a satisfactory agreement on tuition fees.
Similarly, the agreement to relink emissions trading systems sundered by Brexit, which would protect British exporters from European carbon taxes, could also be delayed pending agreement on tuition fees.
A leaked version of the summit statement hints at the link between the trio of agreements, looking forward to “their joint and timely entry into force”.
Separately, EU sources have suggested without a deal on tuition fees, the EU could delay talks on British reintegration into the European electricity market that are expected to intensify next year. To secure its return to the market, the UK would have to pledge an “appropriate” contribution to European cohesion funds aimed at boosting economic development in poorer regions.
This week the Guardian reported that the UK was prepared to spend up to £450m a year to give EU students discounted university tuition fees if Brussels allowed Britain access to the Made in Europe industrial programme.
The EU said there would be no deal on Made in Europe at the November summit because the bloc was still finalising its position on the key draft law, the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).
Targeted at strategic industrial sectors, such as electric cars and renewables, the law would mean public subsidies and contracts would only go towards products made in Europe.
France, supported by many lawmakers in the European parliament, is pushing for a narrow definition of Made in Europe, while Germany leads a larger group of countries that don’t want to exclude trade partners including the UK.
While Britain is keen to resolve the issue, EU lawmakers are not expected to finalise the IAA text until next spring. In a significant milestone, France and Germany struck a compromise on Made in Europe favourable to the UK, but it only applies to cars, not the other industrial sectors in the IAA such as renewables and nuclear technology, or other draft proposals aimed at promoting European preference.
In a win for the UK, the draft summit statement proposes a “trusted partnership” on strategic industries, starting with steel and defence. The aim is to stop either side becoming collateral damage of the other’s trade defence measures targeted at China’s heavily subsidised imports.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.
The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes “all the way” and rejoins the EU.
Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.
In an interview with the Sunday Times, he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”
The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.
The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it”, but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.
“It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he told the Sunday Times.
“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.
“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.
He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.
The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.
In the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000, according to the Office for National Statistics.
Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however.
Net migration peaked at a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic.
It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at 171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016.
Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.
But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.
Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.
The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”
Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.
“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Fine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to Japan | Emily Bratt
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
There are two types of people who listen to music in public: those who wear headphones and those who … are a word I probably can’t use here. “Loudcasting” – playing audio, watching videos or talking on speakerphone in public spaces – is a form of antisocial behaviour that drives eight in 10 of people in the UK crazy, and I’m glad Andy Burnham is one of those eight. But while I welcome his policy to fine “headphone dodgers”, I’m not convinced it will solve the problem.
This behaviour isn’t only a nuisance, but a grave indicator of a deeper societal issue: the erosion of empathy. You can’t legislate civic pride into an individualistic culture where feelings of social disconnection are widespread.
From 2019 to 2021 I lived in Japan, where keeping the peace is paramount and you can be reprimanded just for talking on the bus. When I returned to England, I felt shock and shame at how we treat one another and our public spaces. I still do. We watch our dogs defecate in the street and walk away. We use public bathrooms as if we’re feral two-year-olds. We inflict the soundtrack of our mindless social-media scrolling on an entire train carriage.
Japanese society is not without its flaws; I often chafed at the level of deference I witnessed. But living there also highlighted to me just how selfish we can be in Britain. Last week, I saw someone had smeared dog poo into the communal carpeted entrance of their own block of flats. Some on the far right love to cast other cultures as primitive, but I think we need to look at ourselves.
We could learn from Japan. As a broadly collectivist society, it favours social harmony and group responsibility. One guiding principle is meiwaku wo kakenai: the idea that you should avoid inconveniencing others.
I worked in Japanese state schools and was astonished when students as young as five diligently began stacking chairs and clearing apparatus as sports day wrapped up. Nobody told them to. Additionally, Japanese schools don’t completely rely on cleaners: the students sweep the halls, wipe down desks, empty bins and even disinfect and scrub the bathrooms. This cleaning practice, a component of tokkatsu (special activities), forms part of a wider approach to holistic education and teaches children personal responsibility for, and pride in, their environment.
It’s important to add that a teenager is still a teenager, no matter the country. It’s a myth that all Japanese children are innately disciplined perfect little angels. But the wider impact of these social ethics is obvious. Crime rates in Japan are (comparatively) low, public spaces are meticulously maintained and litter is a rarity. It’s not a myth that Japanese streets are so clean you could lick them. Lick an English street and, bam! Dysentery.
The UK government’s crackdown on content-blaring can only work in conjunction with a wider effort. First, fines have to actually be imposed by those in authority – and they need to feel safe and incentivised to do so. Train managers have been hot on calling out fare dodgers for years (one made me cry when I was 19 for not having my student railcard, such was his wrath). Now they need to bring the same resolve to headphone dodgers. Burnham’s policy states that drivers would not be expected to enforce such rules – it’s a job for safety officers or the police. But unless someone is there to enforce the rules in the moment, the policy becomes little more than an empty threat.
Second, we need to rebuild social norms so that consideration for others is instinctive. The word etiquette seems antiquated, but given that almost half of us in the UK play content from our phones without headphones – and that this behaviour bothers most of us – etiquette education is still necessary. Maybe, so we don’t feel we’re in a Jane Austen novel, we call it something else. Perhaps in schools, it’s civic responsibility class, or lessons in caring about others, or simply learning how to not be a twat. It doesn’t require major educational reform. Copying Japan’s approach to school-cleaning, for example, could be a good (and easy) place to start.
The onus, of course, isn’t only on schools – parents have to lead by example. But imagine the ripple effect if British schoolchildren were given the responsibility of caring for their classrooms and corridors.
Unfortunately, there’s also a deeper issue. Some loudcasters are simply oblivious, but others are deliberately rage-baiting. The latter is a product of a disaffected society, which Burnham’s fines by themselves could exacerbate. Nobody likes being told off, but especially not angry people.
We don’t need to become Japan. But in an increasingly divided world, consideration for others and respect for our surroundings are what can still hold us together.
- 
  Emily Bratt is a freelance journalist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.
The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.”
To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones.
In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August.
Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader, and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”.
Trump is an often wayward ally for Ukraine, and Zelenskyy has expressed anger at the diesel deal, saying subsequent Russian attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine amounted to a “thanks” from Vladimir Putin.
UK governments have previously welcomed Zelenskyy after difficult experiences with Trump. He met Keir Starmer at Downing Street the day after Trump and his vice-president, JD Vance, publicly berated the Ukrainian president in the Oval Office 18 months ago.
During that trip Zelenskyy was also hosted by King Charles, who, in a pointedly personal touch, saw the Ukrainian president at Sandringham in Norfolk, which is a royal family home and rarely used for such visits.
Announcing the latest Downing Street meeting, No 10 said part of an ongoing £1.6bn package to deliver more than 5,000 LMMs to Ukraine would be sped up to help combat attacks by jet-powered drones.
These are quicker and higher-flying than the propeller-driven Shahed drones previously used, making them much harder to shoot down, allowing Russia to strike more targets in Ukraine, including in Kyiv.
The chancellor, John Healey, will separately use meetings at the ongoing International Monetary Fund summit in Bangkok to push other countries to ban Russian LNG.
In a statement before his meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.
“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer: we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe.
“It is not just the right thing to do, but it’s the necessary thing to do. Russia’s aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Elon Musk’s nearly half a billion dollars in midterms spending was a flop
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Elon Musk set a record for election spending this year after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans in the US midterm elections. It turned out to be a poor investment.
The SpaceX and Tesla CEO contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress. He outdid his own 2024 spending of nearly $290m. Yet as Democrats swept to power across the country on Tuesday night, it became clear that Musk would get nearly nothing in return for his hundreds of millions in spending.
Democrats won every one of the five Senate races where Musk’s America Pac spent the most money backing Republican candidates. In Texas, where Musk’s empire is based and where he directed most of his political efforts, Republicans lost the Senate race, governor’s office and are expected to relinquish control of the state house.
After months of Musk posting attacks on Democrats and amplifying election conspiracy theories on X, the tech mogul was unusually quiet on election night. He jokingly posted “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” but the top Republican mega-donor was otherwise largely silent on the results.
Musk’s losses from midterms go beyond the enormous sums that he dumped into failed campaigns, however, potentially ending an era of lax regulation and cozy relations with state officials that has benefitted his companies. The world’s richest person will soon face a House, Senate and Texas government filled with Democrats that have vowed to take a tougher stance on tech and specifically scrutinize his operations in particular.
Altogether, Musk’s political spending this midterms flowed into at least eight Republican-aligned Super Pacs that targeted races across the country, with the largest donation of at least $216m going into his own America Pac. He also gave $168m to the Senate Leadership Fund, which backed a series of candidates that included the Texas Republican Ken Paxton.
Out of all of Musk’s political activity in midterms, the contest where he put the most money and focus was the Senate race in Texas between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico. America Pac spent at least $28m on anti-Talarico ad buys and messaging alone, while Musk repeatedly posted attacks on X, his social media platform, such as “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”
After Talarico achieved a commanding win on Tuesday night, the Democratic senator-elect referenced Musk in his victory speech.
“We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas,” Talarico said. “We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor.”
Senate races in Michigan, Maine, Ohio and Iowa similarly went for Democratic candidates after America Pac spent tens of millions supporting Republican campaigns. The Pac’s money had gone into attack ads that focused on transgender rights or accused Democrats of being radical socialists.
Even if Musk’s spending was not successful, it doesn’t mean it wasn’t impactful. Musk and the Super Pacs’ expenditures created several of the most expensive races in US history and set a potential precedent for how much spending will take place in the 2028 presidential election. It will also probably spur months of analysis around the limits of what money can buy in politics.
Musk’s businesses have benefitted greatly from lucrative contracts with the Trump administration, as well as Trump’s hands-off approach to regulating artificial intelligence. In Texas, the state legislature and Governor Greg Abbott have provided him a friendly environment to do business while passing laws backed by the billionaire’s lobbyists.
Gina Hinojosa, the incoming Democratic governor in Texas,will probably take a more critical stance towards Musk and his businesses. Hinojosa has called for a datacenter moratorium and has been in a legal battle in recent months to gain access to unredacted emails between Abbott’s office and Musk. Meanwhile, House Democrats have called for launching investigations into Musk’s conduct while he was leader of the so-called “department of government efficiency” last year and vowed to scrutinize federal funding for his companies.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Revealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regime
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic.
Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum.
He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party.
The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America.
Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardian sheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016.
It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links to another Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson, an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year.
Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being a bigger danger to the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.
The French judgment reveals that Ghandehari was the major investor behind a deal to supply and build a fibre-optic cable to carry telecoms traffic across Iran in a joint venture with a state-linked Iranian partner.
The businessman’s HP Trust was the ultimate owner of Ori Group, which took a 49% stake in the venture, called Omran Razavi International Co, in 2015.
The other 51% of the venture was owned by Astan Quds Razavi (AQR), a multibillion pound religious foundation in Iran’s second city of Mashhad.
AQR’s leader at the time was ayatollah Abbas Vaez Tabasi, who was appointed custodian of the foundation by the first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and served from the 1979 revolution until his death in 2016. Vaez Tabasi had been an ally of some reformers but remained close to the next supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and, according to the BBC, was reported by state media in 2009 to have said of opposition protest movements that those behind “sedition” in the country were “enemies of god” who deserved to be executed under sharia law.
The joint venture ended in about 2016, with the Ghandehari-backed entities being pushed out of the deal as a hardliner was appointed to replace Vaez Tabasi.
The US imposed sanctions on AQR in 2021, saying it controlled “large swaths of the Iranian economy, including assets expropriated from political dissidents and religious minorities, to the benefit of supreme leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian government officials”. It describes it as a bonyad, one of the “opaque, quasi-official organisations generally controlled by current and former government officials and clerics that report directly to the supreme leader”.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said it would be misleading to characterise him as “working with Iran” without the context that, after 2016, he was targeted by Iran’s supreme national security council with the false allegation that he was working with hostile western powers. They also said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information, which he believed was why the US and French authorities authorised the project.
Tom Keatinge, the director of the Centre for Finance and Security at Rusi, the foreign affairs thinktank, said dealing with Iran “has always been a risky business as a financial institution because of this blurring between kind of state and the private sector. The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail.”
He said there was clearly a range of positions among ayatollahs but it would be “pretty difficult to operate in an industry like telecoms” without the acceptance of the core leadership.
The judgment also revealed that, until 2016, Ghandehari’s HP Trust was the owner of Orico General Trading LLC, which was contracted to supply telecoms equipment from France’s Alcatel-Lucent and transport it from Dubai to Iran. After 2016, this company was transferred to Simpson, the administration professional, who was responsible for winding down Orico’s operations and taking hundreds of staff out of the region.
Simpson told the Guardian he acquired the company after Iranian extremists took over AQR, when the project’s assets were seized and those involved faced political persecution on national security grounds, including accusations of working for hostile western governments. He said his plan was to wind down the business, adding that he carried out detailed checks before acquiring Orico.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said AQR was independent and respected, and therefore the only viable choice for a joint venture in Iran. They said Ghandehari had never met Vaez Tabasi and that he did not regard him as an advocate for freedom or human rights but had believed him to be the only force in the Iranian hierarchy capable of holding back the hardliners in order for the project to go ahead.
The original contract for the deal was awarded to the Omran consortium in 2012 by the Iranian state-owned Telecommunication Infrastructure Company of Iran.
According to Iranian corporate filings, Omran Razavi International Co also owned stakes in two majority state-owned banks, Bank Mellat and Bank Tejerat, in 2013. Both were subject to sanctions over involvement in Iran’s nuclear programme at that point.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said Omran Razavi disposed of the small stakes in the banks before HP Trust’s Ori Group signed its agreement for a 49% stake in the venture in December 2014. They added that the deal was fully approved by authorities in France and the US.
In 2016, AQR took over the whole of the joint venture. Around the same time, the project’s chair, Mohammed Reza Noory, ended up in Iran’s infamous Evin prison, serving an 18-year sentence.
Ghandehari and Noory are both named on leaked judicial papers published by the hacktivist group Edaalat Ali as having being under investigation in Iran after the deal collapsed. Ghandehari’s lawyers say he first became aware of the “bogus allegations” during French court proceedings and that the intelligence services had not given him any further details. Ghandehari’s representatives said fabricating financial and social cases against its targets to discredit them was part of the Iranian regime’s playbook and had been widely documented and recognised by western governments, human rights organisations and independent journalists.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said he had not been to Iran for 30 years and his wealth had no connection to the country, since his ancestral property and assets were confiscated in 2016.
Farage has been highly critical of Iran’s government this year, supporting Donald Trump’s war against it, and attending a protest outside the Iranian embassy with pro-democracy activists in the spring. Last week he warned about Iranian agents entering the UK via small boats across the Channel.
In a joint interview with Farage and Ghandehari in July, the Telegraph described Ghandehari’s business deal in Iran without mentioning its connections to Iranian regime-linked companies. It described it as a project to bring access to high-speed internet to Iran that would help drive reform, but that it later went wrong and resulted in Ghandehari’s assets being confiscated.
It is still not clear how Ghandehari and his family have built up their extraordinary wealth. His fortune is said to have gone from an estimated $2bn, when his late mother bought a property on London’s “billionaire’s row” in 2008, to a reported $10bn now.
In a recent court case over a Picasso painting, Ghandehari was asked to provide proof that he could afford £1.5m in legal costs. His lawyers pointed only to a brochure from his Davos trip with Farage, with a description that he controls a trust with a “collective investment value in excess of $10bn”.
At one point, he offered a letter from a “partner in a leading accountancy firm” confirming he was the principal beneficiary of HP Trust, and drawing an annual income from it. However, this was later withdrawn, as Ghandehari decided he did not want its contents to enter the public domain.
