SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Nige seems tired and bored of himself as Kemi conjures a telepathic budget | John Crace
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
If you’re worried about next week’s budget, then now is your time to chill out. Because Kemi Badenoch has all the answers. The chancellor, John Healey, has been living rent free in the leader of the opposition’s head for the past few weeks. Lucky man. More than that, she has been perched on his shoulder while he sits at his desk in the Treasury and tries to make the sums add up.
And – SPOILER ALERT – Kemi has now read the whole speech that hasn’t yet been written and is in a position to give her budget reply more than a week ahead of time. Opposition by telepathy. Or wish fulfilment. If things don’t work out for her in her current job she could apply to be the next Mystic Meg.
In a plush room in Westminster on a wet Tuesday morning, Kemi was giving her verdict in front of an adoring crowd of invited Tory members. They cheered every word. Which was kind. Because she won’t be getting that kind of reception next week. Nobody could be worse than Rachel Reeves, she began. Rachel had been the She-Devil who had implemented £70bn of tax rises. But wait. There was someone worse than Reeves. And that was Healey. Logic is not Kemi’s strongest point.
No matter. Healey would be worse because he would do less. Fiscal dialecticism. Yup, the chancellor was going to stand up for an hour and say absolutely nothing. Make no changes to anything. This didn’t seem very likely, but we had to take it on trust.
Kemi was John Healey’s brain. And Healey doing nothing was worse than Rachel doing something. It sounded as if Kemi rather missed the tax rises after all. But she had a further warning. The Marxist International Monetary Fund were completely wrong to praise the government for its efforts to reduce the deficit. At best, they had been duped by Healey, at worst they were trying to bankrupt the country.
Here’s what was going to happen. Labour were going to introduce some fictional cuts to benefits that would never be implemented. Because deep down what Labour MPs really wanted was for everyone to live in a country where they could pick up £80,000 a year in benefits. The sign of a functioning nirvana was a world where everyone could be paid not to work. It didn’t seem to have occurred to Kemi that the reason the benefits bill was so high was primarily because the Conservative government in which she had served had increased them substantially during her time in office. And also because many benefits, such as pensions, she was unwilling to cut herself.
Labour was doing the wrong things for the wrong reasons, she said. This opened up several philosophical lines of inquiry. Ontologically speaking, was it better to do the wrong things for the right reasons, even if the results were the same? Or what happened if you did the right things for the wrong reasons? Would you then have to negate everything regardless of the outcomes?
It turned out that I wasn’t the only one struggling with Kemi’s reasoning. When it came to the questions from the media, several reporters wondered why, if the welfare cuts that she was proposing were so easy to make, previous Tory governments hadn’t got round to making them earlier. And was it just our imagination, or were the same cuts being used to pay for several different items on the country’s balance sheet?
Kemi didn’t miss a beat. The cuts she was proposing were the ones Rishi Sunak would have made if he hadn’t been interrupted by the general election that he himself called. It was all very unfortunate. The Tories had been on the brink of success and if only they had had another couple of weeks, everything would have been hunky dory. Tax breaks for the wealthy and benefits cuts for those that need them, that was the Tory way.
Then the reverse ferret. Although she had been in previous Conservative governments, she had never inhaled. She had kept her fingers crossed and her mouth shut. Previous prime ministers had taken wrong steps. But sometimes the bravest thing a cabinet minister can do is to do and say nothing. And no one had been braver than Kemi.
“In case you hadn’t noticed,” she said patronisingly to one journalist, “we are under new management.” Only it feels very much like the old management. Kemi was still saying nothing her predecessors wouldn’t have said. It was just one of life’s sadnesses that the scales had only fallen from her eyes when the Tories had been booted out of office.
Down in Plymouth, Reform was regrouping after yet another weekend of bad headlines. And the party members who had assembled for the rally didn’t look entirely enthused when the first person sent on stage to act as cheerleader was the charisma-free Danny Kruger. The man who is meant to act as the brains of the party, despite appearing spectacularly dim.
“I don’t want to whine,” he said, before going on to do just that. The ITV exposé was just a bit unfortunate, he went on, because he was sure most Reform supporters weren’t racist. “There is no room for that kind of behaviour in the party.” Some of the audience looked a bit disappointed by that. They thought they had been guaranteed a welcome.
After a brief and entirely forgettable number from Honest Bob Jenrick – even Reform members think he seems a wrong ’un – out came Nigel Farage. He seemed like a man with the cares of the world on his shoulders. A man who could sense the tide was going out. There was no energy about him as he rolled through a collection of his greatest hits. Forgetting where he was, he even called Plymouth, Portsmouth. That drew a few boos. People like to think they matter a little bit.
Nige was just tired and bored of himself. Disappointed with a world that had promised him so much and was now crumbling before him. Hell, why hadn’t the riots even spread to this country? Then he could blame lefties and foreigners. He tried to pass off the stories of racism and financial unorthodoxy as just one offs. Every self-respecting party has a few racists. He didn’t sound as if he believed a word of it. And ITV had exposed a 70% hit rate of undesirables. Those aren’t outliers.
Come the end, Nige couldn’t wait to see the back of Portsmouth. Or wherever he was. And it felt as though for much of the audience the feeling was entirely mutual.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Reform’s Zia Yusuf is sounding more and more like Trump every day | Zoe Williams
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Had Reform merely announced its intention to suspend the asylum system for an entire parliamentary term, I’d have just ignored it. Even to dignify its policy platform with a response is to enter its alternate universe, in which it’s preparing for government. I prefer, if only fractionally, this universe we’re in, where the party hangs by a thread on the results of a parliamentary inquiry into Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from a disinterested well-wisher.
Had Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, gone on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme merely promising a British version of ICE, I still would have ignored it, not due to complacency, more due to a bone-penetrating despair that anyone, even he, would look at the US’s shadow militia, performing staged acts of unfettered violence and inhumanity, and think: “That looks cool – I bet I could get some political capital out of that.”
However, as Yusuf laid out his arguments, they were so dumb, so random, disconnected, hammy and cliche-riddled, just so unremittingly stupid, that it turned out to be impossible not to react. I cannot let his nonsense slide. It would be an insult to words.
An elderly woman, he said, waited 23 hours for an ambulance and the coroner found this contributed to her death. A Welsh 15-year-old’s educational attainment is below the OECD average. Many young people have to live with their parents into their 30s and 40s because they can’t afford rent. How does any of this relate to asylum seekers? Are they displacing elderly people in ambulance-demand? It seems unlikely, although if they are an immediate fix would be to stop masked gangs surrounding their living quarters and scaring the hell out of them. Those are ethno-nationalist thugs, of course, and nothing to do with Reform.
High private rents, meanwhile, are not driven by asylum seekers, who have no right to work even if they arrive through a formal route, and as for Welsh 15-year-olds … well, we have some data here. They’re underperforming compared with English 15-year-olds, who are above the OECD average, indeed, above every other European nation, except Estonia and Ireland. If migrants destroy educational standards, how is Ireland managing to thrive? Why, with its very low number of asylum seekers, is Slovenia full of 15-year-olds who (no offence) suck at reading?
None of it makes sense because none of it was meant to. It’s bilge punctuated by soothing mantras (“Charity begins at home”, Yusuf repeated), aimed at the half-asleep mind dreaming of a whites-only yesteryear. It had that in common with a Trump rally, but lacked his pizzazz. Reform can’t even do neo-fascist mimicry right.
A word entered my social-media lexicon recently, which I wish I’d never had cause to look up, because I wish it wasn’t so useful: “agnotology” is the deliberate creation of ignorance, confusion and doubt. You can do it with misinformation and fake news, or you can do it with half-truths pouring out of bot factories, then leave an entire body politic tearing chunks out of itself as it seeks to establish whether the discursive environment has been deliberately polluted, or whether people are just mean and wrong nowadays. But you can also do it by simply talking nonsense, which we’ve seen writ large in party conference season and its aftermath.
“Let’s build an impenetrable and state-of-the-art defence dome for £10bn, and call it the Britannia Shield, even though that’s already the name of a Oxfordshire roofing company,” says the party that spent vastly more than that trying and failing to build the HS2 train line. “Let’s stop all refugees coming from everywhere, until the conditions for every single Briton at every conceivable stage of life have been improved,” from the party whose only discernible allegiance is to its billionaire donors.
The policies don’t even matter. Florid, premeditated stupidity is an end in itself, to clog the collective consciousness with nonsense, chase down every citizen who woke up in a good mood, with a scintilla of confidence about the future, and kill their mojo. The only defence is to hold your line. Insist on the difference between truth and untruth; guard your precious mojo with everything you’ve got.
Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: That Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything is a big help to the PM | John Crace
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Little things please little minds. And minds don’t come much smaller than some of those in Westminster. If a researcher had come up with a study that showed one element two points higher in value than countless other experiments, it would almost certainly be marked down either as an outlier or “within the margin of error”. At the very least, no conclusions would be drawn until many other experiments had been conducted which had produced similar results. Serious scientific journals would just laugh at you if you asked them to publish your findings.
And yet. In one – just one out of many – recent opinion poll, the Tories have increased their ratings by a couple of points and are now for the first time in years in second place, ahead of Reform. And all of a sudden, Kemi Badenoch is insisting this is incontrovertible proof that the Tories are back in business. All the sins of its 14 years in government have been wiped clean. All hail to Kemi, the new chief. She is the chosen one. And the Conservatives are a government-in-waiting.
You need a certain amount of self-confidence to make it as a party leader. Not to say a touch of the Panglossian. The ability to insist all is well when it is turning to shit. But you can have too much of a good thing. You must at least be within touching distance of reality. And it appears that once again Kemi has jumped the shark. The one good poll has gone to her head and she now believes she is invincible. Nothing can touch her narcissism.
In her early days as Tory leader, Kemi used to crash and burn every week at prime minister’s questions. She considered preparation and research to be beneath her. Instead, she peddled the latest conspiracy theories she had seen on X with a series of scattergun questions. She only started to improve when her minders tried to get her to concentrate for 10 minutes of sustained questions on one subject. Yet over the conference break, Kemi has undergone a brain wipe. She is back in her happy space of making it up as she goes along. No one knows better than Kemi.
Sadly for the Tory leader, Kemi’s approach is also Andy Burnham’s happy place. Much more of this and the prime minister is going to look forward to his Wednesday lunchtime encounters in the Commons. Never look an easy win in the eye. Not because he’s word perfect – there are still a lot of unanswered questions about his involvement with the Manchester City owners – but because there’s an engaging openness to him you seldom find in other politicians. A willingness to answer the questions and to appear as if he’s listening. Mr Congeniality.
It’s also a big help to Andy that Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything. Arguments are always so much simpler when your opponents are deluded. Indeed you couldn’t escape the irony of her insisting that it was Burnham who was consistently mistaken about everything. Even the head of MI5, Ken McCallum, had slapped the prime minister down for suggesting hostile actors had interfered with the Brexit referendum. Kemi can’t bear the fact she might have had the backing of the Russian state in 2016.
Burnham chose to respond to Kemi in the most hurtful way. With kindness. No anger. Just a gentle reiteration of the facts. It was incontrovertible that Russia had tried to influence both the 2019 general election and the EU referendum. The evidence was in front of our eyes. Russian bots selling misinformation all over social media. It was a non-story. And far from correcting him, McCallum had gone out of his way to confirm this.
What the MI5 boss had gone on to say was that it would be better for everyone concerned if we all just dropped the story as it would only give the Russians further encouragement. And who had been keeping the story alive for a third day by bringing it up at PMQs? Take a bow, Kemi. The Tory leader seemingly content to carry on doing the Russians’ dirty work for them. At least Nathan Gill, Reform’s former leader in Wales, had the sense to get paid for this. Kemi was doing it for free. Andy ended by saying he would be delighted to debate whether Brexit had done more harm than good. Kemi shook her head. This isn’t an argument the Tories are keen to have. Their feeling is Brexit is something we all just have to suck up.
After that, Kemi looked a bit lost. Clueless. Scouring her file for something to ask. Instead she just wasted her own and everyone else’s time. First by asking about the budget. As if Burnham was ever going to say: “You know what? Since you’ve asked I might as well give you a heads-up two weeks early.” All Kemi achieved was to make herself look half witted. She ended up sounding a bit hurt. She had hoped that Andy would have spent more time problem-solving than point-scoring. There are days with Kemi when even giving a straight answer comes across as point-scoring.
Earlier in the day, Dominic Cummings had been giving evidence to a Lords select committee on how to prevent rogue actors from entering No 10. That should have been a very short session. Just stop morons like Boris Johnson from appointing people like Dom as his special adviser. Curiously this hadn’t occurred to Dom, nor to the dopey peers interrogating him.
It was a bizarre hour and a half. The sort that gives you mild PTSD. Your mind goes back to all the damage he did to the country during the Brexit referendum and during his year in No 10 and suddenly the horror floods back. Just when your brain has done its best to forget all about him. To consider him a footnote in history. For the record, Dom is as deluded as ever. His main thesis seemed to be that Boris was right to allow him to do whatever he liked but no one else in No 10 should ever be allowed to do what he did. Some things never change. We are well rid of him.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Failing Grayling double reports for duty as Reform’s armed forces spokesperson | John Crace
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
You can make a good case for Nigel Farage having been one of the most consequential British politicians of the 21st century. Without him there would have been no Brexit. And yet it is now beginning to look as if his time has come and gone.
The narcissistic qualities that have served him so well now threaten to finish him off. His skin is becoming thinner by the day. All that’s left is reflexive lashing out. A raging against the dying of the light. You’d need to have a heart of stone not to laugh.
On Thursday, Nige was at the old Billingsgate fish market in central London for a press conference – not another one – at which he was to unveil his new armed forces spokesperson. Only this would turn out to be a press conference with a difference. Nige would not be taking any questions for the cameras.
You couldn’t help but think he was struggling to shake off the humiliation of insisting the pollsters were wrong about the Republicans in the US midterms. Trump would not be smashed, he said. The American voters saw it differently. And now The Donald was proving to be a liability.
It’s not just Nige who is suffering. He’s taking his whole team down with him. Not least those former Tory MPs who had thought the Conservatives were dead in the water. Danny Kruger was supposed to be the sensible one. The one who could provide a veneer of intelligence to the Reform project. Yet Nice Danny is rapidly morphing into Desperate Dan: a man now thinking he may have been a bit hasty and made the wrong call.
Desperate Dan had been roped in as the warm-up act. Usually the sort of meaningless gig that is delegated to Dicky Tice. It probably wasn’t in the script for Dan to use his five-minute gig to unload his full existential meltdown, but that was what he got. Angry Dan is a sucker for any conspiracy theory. The polls had been rigged to make it look as if Reform was in third place. And John Healey had only resigned as defence secretary so that he could get the job as chancellor in order to dismantle all the armed forces.
The madness apogee was reached when Desperate Dan declared that no politician in the whole country knew more about defence than Nige. In a war, Nige would be the first person trying to escape the draft with ingrown toenails. Reform have never even got round to naming a defence spokesperson or showing the slightest interest in the subject. Reform’s attendance in parliament for defence-related matters is pitiful.
Nige took centre stage to a standing ovation. There are still a few hardcore believers left. He craves the attention despite the ever-diminishing returns. “The world is more dangerous now than it has been for 80 years,” he said, with his trademark grin. He could be right, though he hadn’t stopped to consider whether Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump – two leaders whom he has openly admired – might have contributed to that. Nige has blamed the Ukraine war on Nato and was all up for joining the US in bombing Iran.
The 3.5% of GDP by 2035 was paltry, he continued. Though he didn’t commit to spending any more or saying how the increase would be funded. But help was at hand. Nige had tracked down the one man in the entire armed services who could save the country from its darkest hour. No matter that the RAF had rather overlooked the talents of the wing commander with 40 years’ service. Meet Angus MacIntyre, who last week resigned from the RAF to become Nige’s official wingman.
Cue a spectacular double take. Because the man who walked on stage was a dead ringer for Chris Grayling, the former Tory minister who had never yet found a job he couldn’t do worse than anyone else. Failing Grayling made a career out of his own incompetence. Mediocrity was a level of achievement to which he could only aspire.
Being Failing Grayling’s double is a cross no man should have to bear but Angus was determined to do his best. He was happy to report for duty as Reform’s shadow minister for the armed forces. This was Angus’s first lie in his new role. Start as you mean to go on. He is not and is never going to be a shadow minister. That role can only ever be done by a Tory as the official opposition. But maybe no one had yet got round to explaining such things to him. Angus was a grunt who operated on a need to know basis.
MacIntyre quickly moved on to his CV, which includes spells in the US and at Nato HQ. More lanyard class than man of action. Nor did he quite explain why he had finished his career only as wing commander despite four decades of service. You couldn’t help thinking Angus might have been passed over for promotion several times and that the RAF hadn’t quite appreciated his talents as much as he would have liked.
Still, Angus looks as if he has landed in the right place, sounding suitably swivel-eyed about net zero and condemning current attitudes towards the armed forces as “Marxist ideology”. However, it was a little weird that Reform’s new man from the military had nothing to say about either Ukraine or Iran. It would have been good to know if he shared Nige’s admiration for Putin and Trump and whether he, too, looks on not joining the Iran war as a missed opportunity. Nor did he say whether he intended to stand as an MP or who was paying him. Questions, questions.
“Have I got the right guy?” Nige asked the audience, as he joined Angus on stage for a last group hug. We will find out soon enough. But my bet would be that Angus may soon be feeling buyer’s remorse. Nige looks as if he is running on empty.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
“I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare.
It was Labour conference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader.
But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy.
One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors.
Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast.
In his conference speech, Ed Miliband was the most strident about the “daunting” dangers of AI, making the case that politicians could not and would not allow the profits of tech companies “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.
And it has not taken long for these alarm bells to ring even louder, with the last seven days looking like the week Westminster fully woke up to the warnings.
A flurry of activity started on Monday with Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, stating it was “likely, if not inevitable” that rogue agents would hack the British state, and saying the UK was looking to strengthen its forthcoming cybersecurity legislation.
It was the main topic of discussion at cabinet on Tuesday, and that was followed by the MI5 chief Ken McCallum warning AI was “supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders”. He said the biggest threat was extremist groups using the technology to unleash bioweapons – toxins used to cause death and disease.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the business, innovation, science and trade committee, said the change of government from Keir Starmer to Burnham was partly behind the increased focus on protecting the UK from AI threats but more still had to be done. “The reality is that the Starmer administration was much too close to the big tech companies,” Byrne said. “And Burnham is not, frankly, so there has been a change of posture. Those things, plus the security services issuing their warning, that is what has changed the weather on this.”
One senior Labour government figure agreed that Burnham’s government was taking AI safety warnings more seriously. “I do feel there has been a shift. Under the last lot, too many of them had drunk the tech-bro Kool-Aid,” he said.
Byrne’s committee held an evidence session this week with civil service leaders in charge of AI security and executives from the key companies – Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind and Meta – with a split between them about whether government testing of new models should be mandatory.
He said his committee was “lighting up” the issue, particularly in terms of working with the US to regulate and monitor new models. It had been reported that Donald Trump’s administration had asked AI companies not to share their latest models with the UK’s cutting-edge AI Security Institute for testing, though Narayan confirmed this week that they had managed to retain cooperation.
But Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation, particularly if Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections to the Democrats.
“I think the government is still caught in a dilemma between how to keep model access, given a capricious US president, and the safeguards that the industry itself now says are essential. It’s make-your-mind-up time, I would say,” Byrne said.
“The companies want to cooperate … It’s not in their commercial interest to issue models which are lethal. Now they too have got to navigate the White House. So I just think this is a moment when the government has actually got to do what is right for the country because Congress is about to change the dynamics on this in the US.”
The UK’s upcoming G20 presidency will be the key moment to push for international action to rein in AI. Geoffrey Irving, the former chief scientist at AISI who spoke at this week’s parliamentary hearing, believes Whitehall concerns are justified. OpenAI and Anthropic’s technology has already shown its hacking capabilities but their models are released with safety guardrails in place that at least mitigate against the threat of malicious behaviour.
However, so-called open source AI models are freely available and can be adapted. Typically, they caught up with the paid-for models such as OpenAI’s within less than a year, said Irving, although they could cause disruption already.
“It’s very likely that open source models are already powerful enough to do serious damage,” Irving told the Guardian, adding that he expected open source technology to reach the capabilities of OpenAI and Anthropic products “soon”. Safety guardrails “either don’t exist or can be trivially removed” from open source models, he added.
The business committee heard this week that AI-enabled bioweapons could become the next serious threat to manifest itself, in the wake of cybersecurity, as models become more powerful and therefore capable of designing novel bio-harms – although experts suggest there is a gap between designing dangerous pathogens and weaponising them.
Concerns over cybersecurity and bioweapons can escalate rapidly to fears about AI wiping out humanity in a variety of scenarios – a concern that is widespread within the AI community, and is shared by Irving.
However, some experts argue that the government should focus on immediate risks from AI. Prof Elena Simperl, a co-director of the Institute for Artificial Intelligence at King’s College London, said the existential risk argument had “no evidence” and was a “theory” rather than a credible threat.
“There are bigger, more immediate risks that AI technology is posing now and are actually evidenced, like hacking and signs that AI can be as addictive as social media,” Simperl said.
In the absence of international AI regulation, there are some in Whitehall worried about whether the UK is doing enough preparation to defend against AI warfare and attacks.
Defence sources said there was concern about the cancellation last year of the AI programme at the government’s Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), based at Porton Down, with worries that this was shortsighted given the need for cutting-edge research on advancing the nation’s capabilities and defending against its risks.
This was countered by an MoD spokesperson who said AI was “transforming defence from industry to the battlefield and will play a decisive role in how we fight and defend” and that it must be “integrated across all workstreams, rather than a standalone programme”. They pointed to a £400m investment in AI-focused capabilities over the next four years to “prepare the UK for the future of warfare”.
Others in Whitehall have the opposite concern: that worries about safety could become too dominant – and end up holding back the government’s adoption of tools that could be transformative for productivity and solving longstanding problems in public services, from medical care to reducing waiting lists.
The former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell told the Guardian that ministers needed to be as aware of “the risk of being left behind” when it came to AI as being aware of the need for guardrails.
Launching a Global Government Forum report on AI with the tech firm Cognizant, O’Donnell told the Guardian: “There is a big need to get it better and to really push on. I’m really optimistic, but the challenge for us, obviously, is managing the risks along the way, making sure that we don’t make mistakes, which reduce people’s trust, which means that that sets us back.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.
“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.
China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.
The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.
But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025, a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.
The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.
Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.
The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.
A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships.
 
 
 “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Macron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrest
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Emmanuel Macron has accused Donald Trump and other foreign leaders of making “stupid comments” about France’s street unrest for political gain, as the country prepared for more protests this weekend.
Speaking during a visit to Qatar, the French president did not name names but said “manipulation of information” after Saturday’s riots had led to “comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders”.
Asked if he was referring to Donald Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.” The US president has blamed France’s violence on “migrants, jihadists and communists” as he campaigns for his Republican party before midterm elections.
Macron told reporters in Doha that some leaders “in the middle of election campaigns, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic” were “naively spreading narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote”.
They were “using our country for their own political campaigns”, the French president said. “And we don’t need that. We already have difficulties to deal with.”
He said AI-generated images were circulating “depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.”
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections next weekend, has also said that France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam”. Analysts have dismissed claims that migrants were the main factor in France’s protests.
Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has erupted six months before presidential elections to choose his successor. The government has admitted it “lost control” over widespread rioting on Saturday.
Largely peaceful demonstrations over the cost of living rapidly descended into rampant violence and extensive looting, especially in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Limoges, where the town hall was set on fire and partly destroyed.
Police said that protests would be banned in parts of Paris on Thursday as the city braced for more demonstrations.
The ban, from 8am to 8pm, will apply to key landmarks, including the Elysee presidential palace, both houses of parliament, and tourist havens such as the Louvre museum and the Champs-Elysees.
Other areas where rallies will be prohibited include the Bastille and République squares, and the Châtelet-Les Halles shopping area which was heavily targeted by looters over the weekend.
The unrest has prompted several countries to issue travel warnings for France and rattled already nervous financial markets, with the yield on the French government’s benchmark 10-year bonds passing 5% on Wednesday, its highest since 2002.
Macron pledged to prevent any repeat of last weekend’s convulsions, as the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) grassroots protest movement formally filed plans for a march through the centre of Paris on Saturday that is likely to be the government’s next big test.
Student groups have also called for protests on the same day to push demands for greater investment in education. The gilets jaunes activists aim to revive their nationwide 2018 campaign against rising living costs and declining public services.
“Those who want to cause disorder in city centres next Saturday will be prevented from doing so,” Macron told reporters in the Gulf, where he was seeking energy deals to help offset rising fuel costs. “There must be no wavering at the top of the state.”
Government ministers have promised a “massive” and vastly reinforced security operation after acknowledging shortcomings in their initial response last weekend, with some troops expected to be deployed alongside police reinforcements.
Partial night-time curfews imposed on Monday and Tuesday in areas prone to violent protests and looting in cities around France, including Paris, Marseille and Lille, have helped ensure relative calm and were expected to be renewed on Wednesday.
France’s main trade unions have separately called a nationwide mobilisation for 5 November. Sophie Binet, the head of the CGT union, said: “There is huge and legitimate anger, and the answer to that situation is not repression. It is a political response.”
Macron insisted France “doesn’t need a state of emergency”, saying it “has the means” to control any further unrest. Union representatives met the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on Wednesday but no concrete announcements followed.
Justice minister Gérald Darmanin said on Wednesday that, of the 2,500 people taken into custody during and after the protests, 174 had been jailed. Another 917 had been formally prosecuted, he added.
Sometimes violent protests in European countries including Italy and Belgium have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading across the continent where with many nations, including France, face budget problems.
Italy’s government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: What can Britain learn from backlash to Dutch slavery apology?
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham’s pledge to seek a “structured dialogue” with former colonies to help shape Britain’s first formal state apology for slavery marks the UK’s first tentative step down a path the Netherlands set out on five years ago.
The prime minister’s attempts to initiate a historic shift alongside the royal family – whose customary expressions of “profound personal sorrow”, falling short of an apology, was repeated by King Charles this week – echo a process begun by the Dutch state in 2021.
As London weighs its words, while firmly ruling out any support for reparations, the Dutch experience may provide a preview: in the Netherlands, apologising did not draw a line under the past for everyone, and prompted a political backlash, disillusion among many descendants, and a row over what justice really means.
That is not to say it was not the right thing to do. The apologies were “sensitive, the right words, the right gestures … You could feel the sincerity,” said Linda Nooitmeer, the then chair of the National Institute for the Study of Dutch Slavery and its Legacy (NiNsee).
It was about “restoring the humanity of the ancestors”, because a key historical element had been “the dehumanisation of people of African descent”, she said. “But when it comes to real change, the rights of people of African descent, we have another issue.”
Merchants of the so-called Dutch Golden Age trafficked an estimated 600,000 enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to brutal plantations in Suriname and Curaçao, as well as between 660,000 and 1 million across the Indian Ocean and East Indies.
By the 1770s, slavery-derived wealth generated more than 10% of the GDP of the province of Holland. Even the crown was enriched: Willems III, IV and V made what equates to €545m (£465m) in modern money from the trade between 1675 and 1770 alone.
The Netherlands was among the last European colonial powers to outlaw the practice, legally abolishing it in Suriname and the Dutch Caribbean on 1 July 1863, 30 years after Britain and 15 after France. The actual end – freedom – came in 1873.
Afro-Surinamese and Afro-Caribbean community campaigners started demanding accountability in the 1980s. NiNsee was founded in 2002, and slavery entered the school curriculum in 2006.
The political trigger came in 2020, with the wave of protests that followed George Floyd’s murder in the US. If many had tried to ignore Dutch history, said the activist Patrick Mathurin at the time, “through our activism, we forced them to look”.
On 1 July 2021, Amsterdam’s mayor, Femke Halsema, broke ranks during the annual Dutch Keti Koti (“breaking the chains”) commemorations marking the anniversary of abolition, delivering a direct apology on behalf of the municipality.
Amsterdam’s involvement, Halsema said, had been “direct, worldwide, large-scale, multifaceted and protracted”, and the city’s immense past wealth and commercial legacy were “indivisible from persistent racism that still festers”.
Amsterdam’s apology was followed by those of Rotterdam, Utrecht and The Hague, and by the Dutch central bank. The then prime minister, Mark Rutte, who had insisted as late as 2020 that a national apology would only “polarise society”, began to waver.
In December 2022, Rutte delivered a landmark speech at the Dutch National Archives recognising slavery as a “crime against humanity” and admitting the Dutch state had “enabled, encouraged, and profited from slavery” for more than 250 years.
“Today, on behalf of the Dutch government, I apologise for the past actions of the Dutch state: posthumously to all enslaved people worldwide who suffered from those actions, to their daughters and sons, and to all their descendants down to the present day,” he said.
Six months later, on 1 July 2023, in Amsterdam’s Oosterpark, King Willem-Alexander also asked forgiveness: “As your king, and as a member of the government, I make this apology myself. And I feel the weight of the words in my heart and my soul.”
Afterwards, however, there was anger among activists, advocacy groups and descendants, who criticised Rutte’s apology in particular as hasty, paternalistic and made without real consultation.
Roy Kaikusi Groenberg, of the Honour and Recovery Foundation, called the prime minister’s declaration a “neocolonial belch”. Caribbean intellectuals pointed out the obvious and painful irony of European politicians dictating the terms and timing of reconciliation.
While the Dutch government explicitly ruled out direct financial reparations to individuals or former colonies, it did back its apology with a €200m fund and an initial commitment towards a National Slavery Museum.
The money was divided between state-led educational and awareness programmes, such as overhauling school curriculums, funding historical research and preserving colonial heritage, and social initiatives and community grants to grassroots groups.
Nooitmeer, who has since set up Deeeni, a grassroots organisation focusing on economic initiatives in the African-origin community, said at the time there was a danger of apologies becoming the “mirrors and crystals of the 21st century”.
Mirrors and crystals, she noted, were the symbolic, empty trinkets with which enslaved people were once bought and sold. “Slavery was an economic system,” she says now. “If you say all this was wrong, when are you ready to talk about the economic side: reparations in the broader sense?”
Community ownership of the whole process “was completely lacking”, she said. While apologies might be made, “as long as the community is excluded from the decision-making process, the old mechanisms of inequality simply remain”.
A key lesson from the Dutch experience, Nooitmeer said, was that people of African descent today need some kind of “agency over what reparations should look like – and when they are considered sufficient”.
The Netherlands also witnessed a conservative political backlash. In 2021, only 31% of the Dutch public said they supported the idea of a national apology for slavery, said Sjoerd van Heck of Ipsos I&O, while 55% opposed it.
The numbers converged somewhat, reaching 38% in favour and 49% opposed in 2022 and, after the Rutte and Willem-Alexander apologies, 40% for versus 46% against, Van Heck said, but added: “It’s clear that the subject remained one that sharply divided the population.”
That was grist to the mill for Geert Wilders, who, like Europe’s other populist far-right leaders, has long ridiculed state apologies for past wrongs and pledged to rewrite school textbooks to emphasise their nation’s achievements. His Freedom party (PVV) won a shock victory in 2023 elections.
The National Slavery Museum, conceived with Surinamese, Caribbean and Dutch community participation and backed by €80m from Amsterdam city hall and the national government, is due to open in 2030.
But for Britain, the Dutch experience suggests that state apologies, while plainly welcome, may prove not so much a neat final settlement with colonial history as the opening of a new and almost certainly contested phase of reckoning.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: AI-powered malware ‘highly likely’ to be used to hack UK infrastructure by 2028
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028, according to the state cybersecurity body.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said AI will probably enable a ransomware attack against critical national infrastructure [CNI] between now and 2028. The UK’s definition of CNI covers a range of facilities and services across sectors including energy, transport, defence, food, health and finance.
The warning from the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was published in the organisation’s annual review, which also warned that Russia and China will start using AI “routinely” in cyber-attacks.
“It is … highly likely that between now and 2028, AI-powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI,” said NCSC.
Ransomware has become a cornerstone of the criminal hacker’s repertoire and is a signature ploy of gangs that typically operate out of former Soviet Union states.
After gaining access to a victim’s IT systems, the attackers then encrypt files with bespoke malicious software – or malware – and then demand a payment in cryptocurrency to unlock the crippled systems and return any stolen data. UK ransomware victims include Royal Mail, outsourcing firm Capita and various public bodies, including councils.
AI is set to enhance the ransomware threat by helping attackers with tasks such as scouting targets, locating weaknesses in IT networks and writing malicious code, said the NCSC.
Last month, the government urged Britons to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in order to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said as the Be Ready campaign was launched that Britain needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.
NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, will warn the public in a speech accompanying the review on Tuesday that AI is going to unleash a wave of cyber-attacks imminently.
“In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” he will say.
Horne will attribute the threat to the technology’s ability to uncover weaknesses in IT systems that have been “tolerated for far too long”.
An example of AI’s capacity to root out previously undetected vulnerabilities came last month, when the technology helped discover a critical weakness in PHP, a computer language used by almost 70% of the world’s websites.
Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at Surrey University, said NCSC’s warning underlined the need for nation states and companies to access cutting-edge AI technology.
“AI can help people find these flaws and patch them, but if we don’t get the access the bad guys will beat them to it,” he said. So far, leading AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have given some companies advanced access to their most powerful models in order to help them identify serious IT glitches.
Horne will also say in his speech that communications networks used by the British military are subjected to daily attacks that are “persistent” and “sustained”.
Horne will say Russia was one of the perpetrators, but the attacks have deliberately not crossed the line into warfare, with Moscow carrying out “notable campaigns” that “intentionally fall below the threshold of armed conflict as they escalate their attempts at hybrid warfare”.
Horne will add that recent cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in Europe, which have seen fridge temperatures raised by hackers to more than 50C, are a warning to companies and organisations to invest strongly in cyber resilience.
“For decades we have collectively got away with tech on the cheap,” he will say.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Retired Michigan teacher released from Russian prison believed he would never be freed
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
In his first comments since recently being released from a Russian prison, a retired Michigan teacher said he only believed he would be freed when he got new clothes.
Stephen Hubbard, 74, remarked on Friday that he had heard many times previously that he would be released – but never really trusted what he was told, adopting a philosophy of “seeing is believing” and “actions speak louder than words”.
“Only when they started giving me new clothes and leading me to the exit of the prison,” Hubbard said in his first public remarks since his 21 October release, which came during a visit at the White House with Donald Trump, “I went out and I saw the car, and I was accompanied by a couple of Russians, then I believed, finally believed, on the drive from Moscow to St Petersburg, ‘I’m really going somewhere.’”
Hubbard had been behind bars for more than four years on charges that he fought as a mercenary in Ukraine, which Russia invaded in February 2022. His legal team has denied the Russian accusations and said he was not involved in any military activity.
Trump has previously said that he had asked Russian leader Vladimir Putin to free Hubbard – and that the US did not have to release anyone in return.
“He was somebody I wanted to get back,” the US president said as he hosted Hubbard on Friday in the Oval Office.
The White House allowed a limited pool of journalists into Trump’s meeting with Hubbard, allowing primarily news photographers and a television crew.
Many in the international community perceived Hubbard’s release to be Russia’s latest maneuver to bring Trump closer to Putin’s position on the war in Ukraine. It also offered Trump a diplomatic victory ahead of the 3 November midterm elections, when his Republican party is expected to lose seats in Congress.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Zelenskyy says ceasefire 'was news for me' but Kyiv would accept it if Moscow does
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy has said the “energy ceasefire” was news to him.
He told the news outlet Axios that he was not aware of an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia announced by  Donald Trump, but added that if Moscow agreed to such a ceasefire, Kyiv would accept it.
“The ceasefire announcement was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree. If president Trump negotiated it with Putin — please tell us when the ceasefire begins — we are ready and we will accept it,” Zelenskiy was quoted as saying by Axios.
Donald Trump’s call for Zelenskyy to make way for a new Ukrainian leader drew criticism from his own party.
Don Bacon, a Republican Nebraska congressman and former military officer, suggested Trump was not fit to lead.
Reacting to Trump’s statement that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president’”, Bacon wrote on: “We need a president who is up to the task of leading the free world.”
The latest acrimonious row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump warned that Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukraine’s society to chose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to bow down to US demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” sixty-day ceasefire.

Just hours before Donald Trump claimed the two sides had agreed a ceasefire on energy strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy rebuffed his demand that Ukraine stop bombing Russian oil refineries.
Zelenskyy demanded Moscow has to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on Ukraine and its energy infrastructure.
Ukraine’s president said any deal to end his country’s long-range drone strikes on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to stop attacks on energy infrastructure
Donald Trump has claimed Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an ”energy ceasefire”, though the US president gave no details of the purported agreement.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social network.
Trump made the announcement on his Truth Social account shortly after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told ABC on Sunday that Ukraine was ready for a ceasefire, including on energy infrastructure.
This announcement follows Trump’s criticism of Zelenskyy for attacks on Russian diesel facilities, which he blames for global shortages.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on EU ‘Made in Europe’ rules: a fatal blow to Brexiter delusions | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The EU is a constantly evolving institution. The rules keep changing and, since Britain is destined by geography to want a close economic relationship with the bloc, there will always be something to negotiate in Brussels.
Most of those discussions over the past two years have been uncontroversial, except in the eyes of dogmatic Eurosceptics. That doesn’t mean the talks have been easy. They never are with a club of 27 nations. But later this month, at a summit with the EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, Andy Burnham is expected to complete a treaty covering closer cooperation in a wide range of areas, including elimination of customs barriers to agricultural goods, a youth-mobility programme and integration with the EU’s carbon emissions trading scheme.
The agenda was set by Sir Keir Starmer as part of his intended “reset” of EU relations. Mr Burnham has since pledged to move further and faster towards closer ties, although he remains bound by his predecessor’s manifesto prohibition on membership of the single market and customs union this side of a general election.
What the prime minister can achieve in that space will be determined partly by his judgment of what domestic public opinion will allow, but more immediately by the terms of the European Commission’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act. This legislative package, more commonly called “Made in Europe”, mobilises public procurement rules to insulate continental industries from what many EU political leaders see as unfair overseas competition – chiefly from China. Industrial policy and protectionism on such a scale is a symptom of the way a once-globalised trading system has in recent years fractured into rivalry between continental blocs. China’s colossal trade surplus, causing panic among European car manufacturers, for example, is one side of that story. Donald Trump’s capricious tariff wars are another.
Britain looks perilously isolated in such a world, which is why Mr Burnham is keen to find some accommodation within the Made in Europe regime. That isn’t straightforward, given that the essential purpose of the new rules will be to benefit enterprises in the single market to the deliberate disadvantage of those on the outside, which includes Brexit Britain. Some compromise is available, with the UK recognised as a “trusted partner”, but that status won’t be accorded simply as a reward for pro-European vibes from Labour. Mr Burnham’s declarations of strategic intent are helpful, but there will be a lot of hard bargaining ahead on the terms of a deal. Without one, Britain’s carmaker and other industries would face crippling new trade barriers.
For that reason, the “Made in Europe” question has shot up the government’s agenda. The Eurosceptic opposition parties, meanwhile, are silent on the subject. To acknowledge the existence of a problem would mean recognising Britain’s disadvantaged status outside the single market, which is a refutation of the founding case for Brexit. Mr Burnham will not find it easy to negotiate the next stage of Britain’s reintegration with the EU, but those who resist his direction of travel will find it ever harder to pretend there is any alternative.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Reform candidate filmed saying asylum seekers should be put in ‘concentration camps’
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A would-be Reform UK MP told an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers should be put in “concentration camps”.
The comments were recorded as part of the undercover investigation by ITV that has already seen Reform accused of “appalling behaviour” and “extreme racism”.
Reform has said it had opened investigations where activists or members had “clearly behaved inappropriately”, adding there was “no room for racism” in the party.
In footage due to be broadcast on Sunday, a Reform activist and aspiring MP, who has yet to be publicly identified, described himself as “pretty hardline about Islam”.
He said: “If a Muslim’s prepared to de-convert, I’m happy.
“But if they want to remain faithful to Islam, then this would be, I would have disagreements, especially with, um, I mean, as far as I understand, [Reform home affairs spokesperson] Zia Yusuf is a Muslim … to me … you cannot be a Muslim and British … it’s like oil and water.”
Discussing people crossing the Channel in small boats, the same activist said: “In the first week of election, build concentration camps, and everyone who comes across on the Channel, you’re in there.”
Excerpts from the investigation released earlier in the week included councillors and candidates within Reform using racist language.
In one excerpt, black children were referred to as “animals”, while in another a Reform member said his area had become “infested” with Asian families.
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said Nigel Farage’s response to the revelations showed he was “completely unfit to lead”.
She said: “Bad apples don’t fall far from the tree. The sleaze, scandals and appalling revelations of racism and rank misogyny piling up by the day go right to the top of Reform UK.
“Nigel Farage is incapable of taking responsibility and getting his house in order because he himself shares culpability.”
Speaking earlier in the week, Farage said that while Reform carries out vetting, “you can’t vet people for what they say in the future”.
In a statement to ITV, the party said: “Reform UK has improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting.
“This is the same for all organisations. However good the vetting, one cannot vet a future comment.
“There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.”
On Friday, Alan Feeney resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after racist comments he had made were uncovered in the investigation.
ITV revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.
In a subsequent Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”
He added: “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny | Nils Pratley
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Two winners in the budget are known already. They are the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, state-funded investment bodies that have rapidly become central to the government’s growth strategy.
The former chancellor Rachel Reeves handed extra slugs of capital to both and now John Healey is going further. The NWF will get another £15.4bn over the next half decade, on top of its existing £27.8bn, and there’ll be another £5bn for the BBB, which already has £25.6bn.
Expect a fanfare about “over 100,000 jobs across the country to be created” via the extra capital for these so-called PuFins. The term means public financial institutions. They invest in private sector assets, either directly or through third-party funds, with the aim of making a profit for the taxpayer – or, at least, earning a return that matches or beats the government’s cost of borrowing.
Cue, also, another round of debate about whether Healey is engaged in fancy financial footwork to get around the constraints of his fiscal rules. Reeves rewrote those rules in her first budget in 2024 to allow the value of financial assets – such the NWF and BBB’s loans and stakes in companies – to be netted off against the public debt.
To fans, the principle makes sense. As long as the PuFins’ assets maintain their value and cover the interest on the government’s extra borrowing (a critical condition), it’s a way to boost investment. More critical projects can be built sooner, and possibly more cheaply; more companies may prosper to the eventual benefit of the public purse.
Critics, such as the right-leaning Centre for Policy Studies in a report last week, see a “financial wheeze” that disguises the true level of government borrowing and stores up trouble, as the Blair-era private finance initiative did. The thinktank called for the wings of the PuFins to be clipped.
Healey, it is safe to assume, will ignore that advice. The PuFins fall squarely within his theory for growth – the idea of “crowding in” private investment and spreading money around the regions.
In Healey’s support, one can say state-backed co-investment vehicles are not new. Governments of all hues have used them. George Osborne even launched a Green Investment Bank. And the NWF, despite its misleading name (it’s not a Norway-style wealth fund), to some degree merely replaces infrastructure lending that might have been done by the European Investment Bank in pre-Brexit days. As for the BBB, its focus on “scale-up” capital for young, fast-growing companies is designed to address a gap that has been a source of grumbles for decades. Both institutions are useful.
There are questions, however, about potential overuse. Are the NWF and BBB sticking in all cases to their core role of “additionality”, the idea that PuFins should bring something extra to the party? They are not meant to be substitutes for private capital. They must crowd in rather than crowd out.
The line can appear blurry at times. This column has questioned the £25m that BBB invested in Kraken Technologies, the software firm being spun out of Octopus Energy. How was that a case of “helping smaller businesses get the finance they need”? Kraken was valued at a thumping £6.45bn, so wasn’t a small firm; and £25m was a rounding error within a wider $1bn fundraising.
Similarly, the Centre for Policy Studies surely has a point when it wonders why the NWF lent to Scottish Power, “an investment-grade company with an investment-grade Spanish parent” on projects to upgrade to the electricity grid. The NWF’s ability to make long-dated loans probably helped the financing, but regulated utilities are supposed to be big enough to stand on their own feet. Weren’t there better targets for the NWF’s loans?
To be fair, the websites of both the NWF and BBB are stuffed with case studies that fit the government’s priorities uncontroversially. For example, the latter’s follow-on £100m investment in Oxford Quantum Circuits, a quantum computing firm, was big and on-message.
And, so far at least, the promise of gilt-like returns is intact, or not disproved. The BBB cites a “3.9% five-year adjusted return” but says the number would be higher if one was counting only its commercial activities. In the case of NWF, it’s too soon to tell: last year’s return on equity was -2.6% but a gilt-like number was only ever promised in 2030-31. The requirement to co-invest with hard-nosed private investors is probably helpful.
But there’s still the issue of being additional. “Assessing additionality is not a precise science, but rather an exercise in judgment,” concedes the NWF in its impact framework. An Office for Budget Responsibility-style body to scrutinise those judgments is starting to look essential. As the allocations from the Treasury increase, there is a risk that the definition of “additional” gets stretched. At the moment, the PuFins are only ultimately answerable to their sole shareholder, the Treasury.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies, in its pre-budget assessment, said: “If the government follows the spirit of the guidelines, and aims to construct a portfolio of investments that align with government priorities and generate a profit, the cases where investment can occur through PuFins may turn out to be relatively limited.”
That sounds like good advice. For the time being, there’s a fair argument there is room for more. The Resolution Foundation argues that, notwithstanding the extra £5.8bn from Reeves, the NWF’s capacity has “barely kept pace with inflation”. But policing the PuFins, and ensuring they stick to their “additionality” brief, is surely equally important. There will be problems if they behave like gannets.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of improper conduct
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, are considering firing US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
A senior US official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s federal holiday.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.
In a series of stories, the Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the US embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her.
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied.
A second US official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the state department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG investigation had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The state department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
The top two Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House committee for oversight and government reform, Robert Garcia, Democrat of California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Has Healey’s military-style budget secrecy really played out so differently to past budgets?
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The public has been told repeatedly that John Healey is so concerned about budget leaks that he has set up defence-style “compartmentalisation” to prevent the Treasury’s financial secrets escaping.
The macho military analogies began in mid-August when Healey was said by the Telegraph to be “on a war footing” to stop the drip of information that he believed had beleaguered Rachel Reeves.
The Financial Times added that “military-style protocols” were being deployed, while the Spectator was excited about the use of “classified computer systems” and the i newspaper described a process where officials could sign in to only their parts of the document and could not access the sections they were not working on.
This weekend, the Observer reported that Healey was “flabbergasted” by the lack of security around financial information when he became chancellor and “it was so different to how we did things in the MoD”.
The chancellor is known to have been worried that market-sensitive leaks cost Britain billions in the run-up to the last government’s budgets. But has this time around been so different after all?
Despite the heightened “security” around Wednesday’s budget, many of its announcements have been leaked already from a clear mixture of authorised and unauthorised sources.
It emerged well in advance that there will be a higher tax on banks – a deeply market-sensitive policy – and a package of energy support for the most vulnerable.
There will also be billions of pounds in extra defence spending, directed towards the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund, as well as a £1bn crackdown on online VAT sales, with big retailers such as Amazon, eBay and Temu to be responsible for collecting what is due from smaller merchants selling on their platforms.
On top of that, there have been stories indicating the level of headroom the chancellor will be looking at – in the region of £15bn – known in the political trade as “pitch rolling” to avoid alarming the markets or the public.
The Treasury and No 10 have also undertaken their traditional stream of embargoed announcements by press release in the days before the fiscal event, such as a new £1.5bn borrowing facility for local authorities and £1bn for social housing, as they seek to build a sense of action and momentum about what the government is trying to achieve.
Former Treasury advisers believe the rigamarole around budget security is partly designed to deter civil servants and gossiping MPs from thinking they can embark on unauthorised chatter before a policy is ready.
But they also say it is unhelpful for the chancellor to produce a hermetically sealed budget, which could cause a backlash over surprise measures – in the markets, the media, among the government’s own MPs and the wider public.
It is often the less-trailed policies that have tended to go wrong, from George Osborne’s pasty tax in 2012 to Philip Hammond’s surprise national insurance hike for the self-employed in 2017 that had to be abandoned within seven days after a furore among Conservative MPs about breaking their manifesto promise.
Aides say there is a balance to be struck – and it’s not always a good idea to hoard information until budget day. “If everything is kept tight, then you end up surprising people. And that’s called a Liz Truss situation,” says one former strategist from the Tory years.
Healey has been shutting down speculation about various tax rises, from higher capital gains tax on certain assets to lowering the mansion tax on properties worth more than £1.5m – showing he has begun to see the virtue in expectation management and limiting surprises on the big day.
There may still be a few fiscal “rabbits out of the hat” on the day, as Healey seeks to combine a “steady-as-she-goes” budget with some eye-catching measures designed to show the public that the government is on their side.
But if the Treasury really has aimed for military levels of secrecy around its budget, the Ministry of Defence might have something to worry about.
