SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
MI5 chief Ken McCallum confirms Russia did interfere in Brexit referendum - but says it had little impact
Dan Sabbagh
Dan Sabbagh is the Guardian’s defence and security editor.
MI5 chief Ken McCallum said today that Moscow did attempt to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media and via troll social media accounts. But there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”, he added.
The head of the Security Service said that he agreed strongly with what the prime minister had said on Sunday and Monday, when he raised the issue of attempted Russian interference a decade ago – though Burnham then backed off when he was challenged by the Conservatives as to whether this meant he regarded the Brexit vote as illegitimate.
McCallum did not put any new evidence into the public domain but cited already known concerns about Russian broadcasters who “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” in favour of Brexit. He also said that “there was a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”.
However, he argued there was no evidence to suggest the result of the Brexit vote had been swayed as a result of the effort, which is generally believed to have been marginal, and said that it would be to Russia’s benefit if the issue was talked about further.
He explained:
It is up to us how far we allow our adversaries to divide us.
I’m a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, the Russian trolls who didn’t appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they’ll be delighted they are front page news once again despite the comparative unimpressedness of what they do at all points along the journey.
I am a little bit anxious that we don’t play into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.
UPDATE:McCallum said:
There is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed … It’s quite important to focus on the difference between what may have been attempted and what actually resulted.
It is a matter of public record including in select committee reports published in 2019 – the DCMS [digital, culture, media and sport] committee did a bit and the intelligence and security committee did a bit also – that in 2016, before you even get to any secret intelligence … it is openly on the record that Russia Today and Sputnik and other Russian media organisations came in pretty strongly around the referendum.
And it is also a matter of open source record that there was a certain amount of interference attempted through trolls and bots and so forth.
I agree strongly with what the prime minister said yesterday, we did see a hack and leak thing inside the 2019 general election campaign.
Ken McCallum has said that Moscow did attempt to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media and via troll social media accounts. But there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”, he added. (See 1.15pm.)
Streeting says, if Sinn Féin opposing new Troubles bill as 'veterans' charter', he's 'delighted'
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, is still giving evidence to the defence committee. Asked about the Northern Ireland Troubles bill, he said that the new amendments being tabled (see 2.34pm) considerably improved it from the point of view of the armed forces. He went on:
And so we are in a much stronger place, to the extent that I think Sinn Féin have condemned these amendments and the bill as a veterans’ charter, which as far as I’m concerned is the highest plaudit possible, and I’m absolutely delighted that that’s where we’ve got to.
We have worked intensively with the Northern Ireland secretary [Chris Bryant] and his team to get this bill to a much better place, that deals with what I think is my personal moral obligation to people who’ve served.
Ed Davey under pressure to defend his leadership at meeting with his MPs
Liberal Democrat MPs are holding a private meeting later where they are expected to thrash out disagreements about Ed Davey’s leadership. For months there has been persistent, low-level grumbling about Davey’s supposedly ineffectual leadership. This is a long way off the sort of firing squad revolt the Tory 1922 Committee used to specialise in. So far only two relatively junior frontbenchers have resigned.
But it must be a bit serious because at the Times they have activated a loyalty spreadsheet. This is fromAubrey Allegretti on the state of play.
Lib Dem leadership showdown:
- 4-hours has been carved out in MPs’ diaries for their meeting at 5pm today, to accommodate requests from more than 40 people to speak (and breaks in proceedings for votes). Roz Savage, as chair of the parliamentary party, will chair the meeting.
- So far, I’ve counted 21 MPs who’ve explicitly - or at least appeared - to back Ed Davey. That leaves a *lot* still undeclared. The rebels need 18 (or 25% of MPs) to force a no-confidence vote.
- Davey’s critics are digging in - and hoping his performance tonight swings sceptics in their favour. They say even if he survives tonight, it’s a matter of “when, not if” he goes.
- Davey’s allies accuse the rebels of “trying to create chaos at a pivotal moment, with the timing of the next general election up in the air”. He has spoken to some MPs to encourage them to speak in support of him tonight.
- Some MPs privately think Davey should go, but are divided over who should replace him - further splintering the rebels.
But my colleague Peter Walkerreckons Davey is safe for now.
From what I hear there is almost no chance of Ed Davey facing any kind of no confidence vote at tonight’s meeting of the Lib Dem parliamentary party. Some MPs are dissatisfied with him, even if it’s hard to gauge how many. But there seems a willingness to listen to what he has to say
Two other reasons why anything dramatic feels unlikely:
• There is no consensus among the malcontents - or anyone else – about who they might want to replace Davey.
• The Lib Dems aren’t generally very good at this sort of thing.
Streeting tells MPs committing to spending 3% of GDP on defence without plan to fund it would risk Truss-type backlash
The government could trigger a Liz Truss mini-budget-type economic incident if it committed to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 without saying where the money will come from, Wes Streeting has suggested.
Streeting used the argument as he gave evidence to the Commons defence committee, where he as pressed to confirm that the government will raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.
The defence investment plan (Dip) currently sets out a path to spending 2.7% of GDP on defence by the 2027-28 financial year. John Healey resigned as defence secretary when Keir Starmer refused to commit to 3% by 2030. Healey is now chancellor, but he has not yet explained how he will raise defence spending to the 3% level he treated as a resignation issue.
Streeting told the committee he never expected Healey to set out a pathway to 3% at the budget later this month and that plan was always due in the spending review, now reportedly expected next autumn.
And he defended the chancellor’s decision not to rush. He said:
We have had very bitter recent experience of a former prime minister making unfunded commitments to spend more, tax less, and borrow more all simultaneously, and it led to enormous loss of confidence, people’s mortgages going up, and a level of fundamental loss of confidence in Britain among investors, and this country is still recovering from that.
But Streeting also said that he was “confident that we will get there”, arguing that this confidence was justified “from the choices that Labour’s already made in government through to how strongly, as a matter of principle, the chancellor felt about this”.
Pat McFadden accuses Tories of hypocrisy over pensions triple lock, saying many of them accept current version unsustainable
Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, has claimed he has a file “as thick as my morning porridge” with quotes from Tories arguing against the pensions triple lock.
He made the claim in a Commons statement explaining the plan announced by Andy Burnham at Labour conference to replace the current triple lock with an adjusted version that will be less generous.
The Conservatives opposed the move when it was announced and, in the Commons, McFadden’s Tory shadow, Helen Whately, claimed this policy was a “U-turn in waiting” and that it would be abandoned by Burnham because of its unpopularity.
But McFadden told Whately that plenty of her colleagues were in favour of the Labour policy. He told her:
The shadow foreign secretary [Tom Tugendhat] has called it simply not affordable and described it as a Ponzi scheme. The shadow justice secretary [Nick Timothy] actually wrote the 2017 manifesto that pledged to replace it with a double lock.
But my favourite is Lord Gove, who told LBC that if Andy Burnham changed the triple lock, he would, and I quote, “declare that I will be campaigning at the next general election exclusively for Stella Creasy in Walthamstow”. So I look forward to seeing him at the end of the Victoria line at the next election. with a red rosette on.
McFadden said these were not isolated examples.
I have a file as thick as my morning porridge full of quotes from the Tories saying that the triple lock is unsustainable and will have to be changed. They say it in private, they say it before they join the frontbench, and they say it after they leave it.
McFadden also said that, if the Tories remained committed to restoring the triple lock in its current form, they would have to explain at the next election how they would fund that. (Labour plans to legislate before the next election to change the triple lock uprating mechanism from 2030.)
Foreign Office minister tells MPs nearly 240 Iranian people and entities now subject to sanctions over hostile acts
Stephen Doughty, the Foreign Office minister, told MPs earlier that the UK has now sanctioned nearly 240 individuals and entities in relation to threats to the country posed by Iran.
A further two Iranian officers from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) were sanctioned yesterday, he said.
In response to an urgent question, Doughty also confirmed that 34 other foreign ministers have joined Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, in issuing a joint statement condemning “in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners”.
And Doughty said that yesterday he had summoned the Iranian ambassador to the Foreign Office to tell him, “candidly and forcibly” that Iran’s activities were unacceptable.
Doughty said:
We have sanctioned nearly 240 individuals and entities in relation to Iran whose actions threaten our people and security and will continue to keep all those tools under review and will not hesitate to take further action where appropriate.
Veterans to get more protection under significant amendments to Northern Ireland Troubles bill, ministers claim
Later in the Commons, MPs are expected to pass a motion allowing them more time to consider the Northern Ireland Troubles bill before it has to be passed. The bill was introduced in the last session of parliament, which means it is subject to the carry-over procedure.
The bill replaces legislation passed by the last Tory government which in effect gave immunity to terrorists and members of the armed forces accused of crimes during the Troubles, provided they gave evidence to a Legacy Commission trying to establish the truth about unsolved Troubles-era murders. The Conservative law was hugely unpopular in Northern Ireland, and the Labour alternative – which is similar – has also been widely criticised.
In an article in the Times today, Chris Byrant, the Northern Ireland secretary, and Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, highlight amendments being made to the bill which they argue will reduce the risk of retired soldiers being subject to vexatious investigations. Under one change, in future the attorney general would have to approve any serious, Troubles-related prosecution.
They say:
By setting up a fair, workable system to deliver as many answers as possible, we will help communities to heal so that we can finally turn the page on one of the darkest periods in our recent history.
More than a quarter of the families seeking answers from the Legacy Commission are veterans’ families. Nearly one in five are the families of police officers. No one should be in any doubt how important this is.
And describing the way the legislation has been changed, they say:
Over the last few months, we have listened to veterans, victims’ groups, including those representing service families, and the wider defence community to hear their concerns. We are responding by making sure the Troubles bill properly protects all those troops who served with honour.
Under the previous government’s scheme, terrorists would have enjoyed the same immunity as veterans – something so abhorrent it should never have been considered in the first place. And so we will not only repeal it, we will make clear – in black and white – that there is no equivalence between paramilitaries, who waged campaigns of violence, murder and destruction, and the lawful actions of our armed forces sent to stop them.
For too long, our servicemen and women have had to fear the knock at the door, the call from an unknown number or the ping of an email notification, as they bear the brunt of incidents being reinvestigated years or decades after the events in question. The bill spells out that there can be no duplication of previous investigative processes unless it is essential, and that witnesses cannot be contacted unless it has been clearly demonstrated that there is compelling new evidence. Nor will veterans be forced to traipse to Northern Ireland to attend hearings. And any decision to prosecute a serious Troubles-related crime will now require the consent of the attorney general.
Reoffending 'off the charts' because of prisoner early release scheme, Tories claim
The Tories have claimed reoffending is “off the charts” due to the prisoner early release scheme.
In an urgent question in the Commons, Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, said the majority of prisoners were not being tagged before release, despite assurances from the government that the tagging system would be the “toughest in history”.
He said:
The justice secretary [Alex Norris] told the country that proper safeguards would be put in place with a presumption that all released prisoners would be tagged.
He called it the toughest tagging regime in history, but that was nonsense.
I have some advice for him and his ministers – it is better to work out how to implement your policy before it starts, not after. We know a majority of prisoners are not being tagged before release, and we know reoffending is off the charts already.
Jake Richards, a justice minister, said that Timothy should be showing more contrition because prisoners were having to be released early as a result of the Tories leaving a system where the prisons were full.
Kemi Badenoch has welcomed a poll giving the Tories a three-point bounce since their conference, and putting them just one point behind Labour.
In its write-up of its latest regular, weekly poll, YouGov says:
Our latest figures show Labour on 24% of the vote, down three points on last week’s poll, while the Conservatives are up three points to 23%, their highest level since we restarted our voting intention tracker in January 2025. Reform UK take a 21% share in this week’s poll, their joint-lowest on our tracker this parliament.
Speaking to reporters today, Badenoch suggested the fall in Reform UK’s ratings showed the public had been taking a “long look” at Nigel Farage’s party and “don’t like what they see.”
Asked whether she was confident her party could continue to rise in popularity, or whether it was just a temporary, post-conference blip, Badenoch told the Press Association:
I am confident that the momentum will continue, because people are seeing the Conservative party has changed under my leadership and there’s much more to come, this is just the beginning.
We left office two years ago, it was a historic defeat for the Conservative party. We made a lot of mistakes.
I have been showing the public that I understand what went wrong; apologised and acknowledged those mistakes. But we are the only party with common sense and a plan to unite the country.
Asked what she thought the poll suggested about Reform UK, she said:
I think the public have been taking a long look at Reform and they don’t like what they see. What I need to show them is that if they don’t want a Labour Government there is only one credible alternative.
And this is fromLuke Tryl, the More in Common pollster, on the significance of the YouGov poll figures.
Few interesting things here of which the most important thing I’d say is the level of volatility should be a further warning of risks a snap election. Lab’s conference bounce disappears in a week. Second conferences still matter at least short term. Third battle for the right is now wide open.
How MI5 chief's comments undermine Tory claim Burnham was spreading 'conspiracy theories' about Brexit referendum
The statement from Ken McCallum confirming Russian interference in the Brexit referendum is a bit awkward for Katie Lam, the shadow communities secretary. On Sunday she wrote an open letter to Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, about Andy Burnham saying Russia did interfere in the 2016 vote. Lam said in her letter these claims were “unproven” and in a post on social media she said: “The prime minister is spreading conspiracy theories about the Brexit referendum.”
(You can argue that the claim Russia decided the outcome of the referendum is a conspiracy theory, but this is not something Burnham did say in his Rest is Politics interview, or ever has said.)
Ken McCallum, the head of MI5, has also said that extremists holding anti-immigration opinions are becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels in the UK. Dan Sabbagh has the story.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump’s pause on Russia sanctions is ‘reward’ for Putin, Zelenskyy says
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has described Donald Trump’s decision to roll back sanctions on Russia as a “reward” for Vladimir Putin and warned it will embolden the Russian leader and intensify the Kremlin’s war, as Moscow launched one of its worst strikes yet on Ukraine’s power plants in an attempt to black out the country’s cities before winter.
The Ukrainian president also said he expected the Trump administration to lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.”
In a social media message, Zelenskyy wrote: “A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground.
“We must keep trying to end the war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely.”
In the Trump administration’s latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, the US president announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.
The act, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the legislation, would have introduced tough new sanctions on Russia including a 100% tariff on major importers of Russian oil such as China and India, as well as sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, financial institutions and shadow fleet of oil tankers.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said the decision to waive the sanctions would encourage Vladimir Putin to intensify the war in Ukraine and called for support in the US to resurrect the bill.
“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he wrote in a statement. “This law could have – and still can! – help a great deal. But the law needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”
US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Saturday said Trump’s sanctions waiver would be a 60-day pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy.
“The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.
The move was greeted by the Russian presidential envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”
The legislation, which sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps the country’s energy supplies moving, was due to be implemented in two days.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Zelenskyy also said the military-grade Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian forces still had limited functionality, and would disconnect from the network when travelling at more than 161km/h (100mph), interfering with drone operations.
The service was throttled inside Ukraine without warning on Tuesday, and Zelenskyy said his government had determined that the restrictions were a “deliberate operation … to prevent us from defending ourselves”.
 
 
 By sending vehicles with the terminals into EU countries, the Ukrainians found they operated at speeds of more than 180km/h, in effect proving that the terminals were only experiencing restrictions in Ukraine.
 
 
 “The conclusion is clear: the restrictions are in effect within Ukraine but do not apply within the European Union,” he said. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
Trump’s announcement that he would pause US sanctions came a week after he said Washington had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1m tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
The Trump administration’s decision to waive the sanctions is the latest consequence of a brutal quarrel between Trump and Zelenskyy. Several times this week, the US did not provide intelligence of impending ballistic missile attacks to Ukraine, in addition to the White House reportedly ordering the Pentagon to throttle the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet network used by Ukraine’s armed forces.
“We very much hope – and I personally hope – that the president of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops the strikes on our energy infrastructure, and stops this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But once again, you cannot achieve this by restricting Ukraine’s responses to Russia for killing our people. And even less so by lifting sanctions.”
Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he has blamed the war in Ukraine, rather than the closure of the strait of Hormuz, for the worldwide spike in diesel prices. Ukraine unilaterally halted the strikes after Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, but resumed them when it became clear that Russia was stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian power plants and substations.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had launched one of its worst strikes yet against the country’s energy infrastructure, hitting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities and causing “severe consequences”.
He also indicated that Ukraine’s dwindling stock of anti-air weapons made it difficult to shoot down many of the loitering munitions, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles being launched each night at Ukraine.
“Although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them,” he said, the “sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Nigel Farage’s regular column for the Telegraph to end
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Nigel Farage will no longer write a regular column for the Telegraph, becoming the latest prominent rightwing figure to leave the title’s roster under its new ownership.
The Reform UK leader wrote for the broadsheet as recently as last week, condemning the first budget of Andy Burnham’s premiership and pledging to “scrap benefits for foreigners, abolish net zero targets” and “slash foreign aid”.
However, the Guardian understands that his contract to write regularly for the title is to end.
Farage did not write for the Telegraph for a fixed number of columns a week or month. However, he contributed to the title regularly and was paid a retainer for doing so.
There appears to be a dispute over the reasons behind the termination of the contract, which paid Farage about £4,000 a month, according to the register of MPs’ financial interests.
Sources suggested that Axel Springer, the Telegraph’s new German owner, has decided not to renew it.
However, sources close to Farage said the Reform leader submitted his resignation on Friday, as he did not like the direction that the Telegraph was moving in.
The news comes after it emerged last week that Allison Pearson, a writer firmly on the right wing of the Telegraph’s regular columnists, was understood to be in negotiations about leaving the title.
The end of Farage’s regular column will further fuel speculation over the political direction of the Telegraph under Axel Springer. It is hoping to use the title to make inroads into the US market as a centre-right, pro-free speech challenger to the Wall Street Journal.
It also comes after concern from some inside the Telegraph over its links to Reform UK. The title has traditionally been closely associated with the Conservative party.
There was unease among some staff about Reform’s repeated use of the Telegraph for “spoiler” stories: a media tactic designed to pre-empt a problematic story by placing a more sympathetic version with a rival title.
Some insiders also disapproved of a piece about a journalist travelling to Britain on a small boat. It later emerged the journalist in question was a Reform member and activist.
The paper also features columns by the former Sunday Times political editor Isabel Oakeshott, the partner of Reform’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, and an open supporter of many Reform UK policies.
Farage’s previous columns have urged Telegraph readers to “vote Reform and help me help you get our country back”, warning them it could be their “last chance”.
Another defended Reform’s acceptance of two unprecedented £36m donations from the crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne.
“Both donors have stated plainly that they want nothing in return,” he wrote. “No peerage, no knighthood, no government contracts. They simply believe Britain needs change and that Reform UK is the only party prepared to deliver it.”
The end of Farage’s regular column-writing comes as Axel Springer has set out plans for mass redundancies across the business, including the newsroom. Its sports and culture sections appear to have been hit hard.
The cuts have angered staff after earlier suggestions from Mathias Döpfner, the billionaire chief executive of Axel Springer, that the titles could not cut their way to growth.
Many expect the cuts to soon be accompanied by plans to grow the Telegraph’s operations in the US, though many staff have been confused by the strategy set out so far.
Farage’s departure follows anger on the right and among Pearson’s supporters over the apparent decision to end her column.
Alex Phillips, a former Brexit party politician and current presenter on Rupert Murdoch’s TalkTV, said the Telegraph was “a political bloodbath with some of the most talented leading commentators of our day brutally axed before the paper veers left”.
“Wake up,” she wrote. “The long slow communist takeover of Europe is currently on steroids.”
It appears that the Telegraph will also stop publishing Pearson’s podcast Planet Normal, which she co-hosts with economics writer Liam Halligan. Halligan announced his Sunday Telegraph column had also been scrapped as part of Axel Springer’s cuts.
A Telegraph source said they were not able to comment on individual employment matters.
The Telegraph Media Group’s latest accounts showed it had slumped to a £4m loss last year as a result of legal fees connected to its lengthy ownership saga and the revaluing of assets. Its revenue had also fallen slightly from 2024 to £273.2m.
However, the accounts of Telegraph Media Group Holdings also revealed it had made an underlying pre-tax operating profit of about £48m.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: EU charges TikTok with failing to protect users’ mental health
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model.
Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”.
The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation, which can lead to anxiety, sadness, worsen existing eating disorders or mental health problems.
Officials said their investigation focused on legal content, where a single video might not be problematic, but the cumulative effect of watching scores of them on one theme could damage users’ mental health.
TikTok’s safeguards to mitigate the risks of “rabbit-hole effects” – where users are served narrow and repetitive content to keep them engaged – were found to be ineffective. For example, officials said, if a user checked a “not interested” button on a video about eating patterns, the algorithm would still offer them similar content on diet and body image. Similarly, refreshing a feed only provided a brief respite from a stream of content on one topic, it found.
“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” said the European Commission’s lead official on tech policy, Henna Virkkunen. “TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ wellbeing, including those of minors.”
In response, a TikTok spokesperson said: “The commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety.
“We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience.”
The company argues that its policies prohibit content that promotes disordered eating and risky weight-management behaviours. It also says that more than 79 million users in the EU used its “not interested” or keyword filters to screen out unwanted content in the first six months of 2026.
The Molly Rose Foundation, which was set up in memory of 14-year-old Molly Russell, who took her own life in 2017 after being exposed to a torrent of harmful online content, welcomed what it called the landmark findings “to seek to hold TikTok to account for the way their algorithm drives young people down rabbit holes of despair”.
A survey for the charity earlier this year found that nearly half of girls and a third of all UK teenagers saw suicide, self-harm and eating-disorder content on social media in a week.
The foundation called on the UK regulator, Ofcom, to open an investigation into TikTok’s “extremely damaging” algorithm.
The EU investigation strikes at TikTok’s business model, which is built on keeping users scrolling as long as possible.
EU officials want TikTok to change the design of its ForYou feed, to give users greater control over the content they see.
“We are addressing a business model,” a commission official told reporters, saying that a business model focused mainly on engagement “can potentially create a risk” especially for minors and vulnerable adults.
The findings are part of a broader investigation launched in February 2024 under the Digital Services Act, which obliges large internet companies to take action to prevent a wide range of harms, from disinformation to damage to mental health.
The commission has already found the company violated EU rules over its “addictive design” for features such as infinite scroll. The company said at the time “the commission’s preliminary findings present a categorically false and entirely meritless depiction of our platform” and that it would challenge the findings.
A complaint about lack of transparency over who paid for TikTok’s advertising was resolved when the company made binding commitments to change its policies last December.
TikTok, which now has a chance to examine the investigation file and mount a defence, could agree to change its recommender system to avoid a fine.
If EU officials uphold the finding, the company could be fined up to 6% of its global worldwide turnover.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump again calls for prosecution of Mary Peltola as turmoil grows over Alaska campaign investigation – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
On the campaign stage in South Carolina, Trump again calls for prosecution of Mary Peltola
Speaking to a campaign audience in South Carolina, Donald Trump reiterated his belief that Mary Peltola should be criminally prosecuted and disqualified from the Alaska Senate contest.
“This is voter fraud at the highest level,” Trump said of the Peltola campaign’s alleged scheme to recruited a man who shared the name of her Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan, to run, all in a bid to peel away votes.
Trump added that Peltola “should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted, and so should the fake Dan Sullivan”.
“I think it’s a criminal act, what they did,” Trump said.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, confirmed on Thursday that his campaign is no longer airing an attack ad that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr Amy Acton.
Donald Trump called again for Democrat Mary Peltola to be criminally prosecuted and disqualified from the Alaska Senate race for her campaign allegedly recruiting a man named Dan Sullivan to run against Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed will campaign on Sunday in Detroit with Haley Stevens, the congresswoman he narrowly defeated to win the Democratic party’s nomination in August.
Tom Hoyle, who achieved instant viral fame on Thursday by comparing Trump supporters to a cult in a live interview with Fox News before the president’s rally in South Carolina, was removed from the venue by three Secret Service agents.
Trump lashed out at a Reuters reporter who asked him why he just canceled a planned appearance at a rally in Kansas on Saturday in support of a embattled Republican senator, Dr Roger Marshall. “You’re sick to ask that question,” the president said.
Michigan Democrats Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens to campaign together in Detroit - report
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed will campaign on Sunday in Detroit with Haley Stevens, the congresswoman he narrowly defeated to win the Democratic party’s nomination in August, the Associated Press reports.
The joint appearance — their first since a Democratic unity breakfast days after the August primary — comes after Stevens’s fiancé, Jason Turkish, appeared at a campaign event for Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan on Wednesday and told reporters that he was voting for the Republican, not El-Sayed.
The two former rivals will reportedly be joined by Jim Clyburn, an influential Black congressman from South Carolina who had endorsed and campaigned for Stevens in the primary, at a get-out-the-vote event at a Detroit church.
Stevens appeared on CNN on Wednesday night and to say that, unlike her fiancé, she would be voting for El-Sayed. But she expressed what she called the reservations of Bl;ack and Jewish voters who had supported her in the primary. She urged El-Sayed to respond to what she said were ads that angered Black and Jewish voters by taking down one tongue-in-cheek ad that features Tucker Carlson saying he would not vote for Rogers, and denouncing another, made by an outside group founded by commentator Cenk Uygur, which blames US aid to Israel for high food prices.
El-Sayed campaign already said that the second ad, posted online last week by Uygur, the uncle of streamer Hasan Piker, was “not affiliated in any way” with him or his candidacy. The was not even made in support of El-Sayed, but repurposed from one originally produced in 2024 for Uygur’s own, short-lived presidential campaign.
While Vivek Ramaswamy suggested that his campaign had not bowed to pressure when it stopped running an attack ad featuring the estranged, troubled mother of his rival for Ohio governor, Dr Amy Acton, some Democrats are not convinced.
On social media, Hakeem Jeffries, the New York congressman in line to be Speaker of the House should Democrats win control in next week’s midterms, posted: “Vivek Ramaswamy just pulled down his sick ad. These MAGA extremists are on the run. Keep. The. Pressure. On.”
Vivek Ramaswamy confirms campaign is no longer running ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother
Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, confirmed on Thursday that his campaign is no longer airing an attack ad that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr Amy Acton.
The ad prompted a wave of revulsion since Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, lost custody of her daughter in 1978, when her second husband, Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her daughter between the ages of 10 and 12.
Asked by a reporter in Vandalia, Ohio if his campaign had stopped running the ad, Ramaswamy said: “It ran to completion and we put up four other ads.”
“But what I will say is that for all of the discussion around 30-second ads, I would love, even for this final close, for this campaign to really be about policy,” Ramaswamy added, before criticizing his opponent for not debating him.
Ramaswamy’s campaign had announced last week that it would spend $4m to broadcast the ad, despite criticism from Democrats and Republicans after court records showed that Acton’s mother, who called her daughter “a liar”, had fled the state with her husband when her daughter accused him of rape.
In an interview with the anti-abortion group Operation Rescue in 2020, when Acton was leading Ohio’s response to the Covid pandemic, Acton’s mother said that she was aware that Cledith Arthur had previously been accused of raping his own daughter before she married him.
Ramaswamy’s reference to “30-second ads” referred to the length of the ad after his campaign edited down the original 60-second version, to remove the allegation from Acton’s mother that her daughter had lied about the family having lived in a tent with Arthur when she was a child. Court records from the time indicated that Cledith Arthur had, indeed, lived in a tent at the time of his arrest on rape charges.
Donald Trump repeatedly defended the ad, including at a rally with Ramaswamy on Wednesday, while refusing to acknowledge that the serious child rape allegation was relevant to the credibility of Acton’s mother.
Reporting from NBC News and Zeteo suggests that Acton’s mother has suffered from mental health challenges and was found living in her car with dozens of cats, which troubled some people involved in producing the ad for Ramaswamy’s campaign.
Ramaswamy’s ad was also defend byJD Vance, his Yale law school classmate, despite the vice-president’s previously expressed disdain for empowering “childless cat ladies.”
“How far will Vivek Ramaswamy go?” Acton’s campaign asked in a new campaign ad on the controversy released earlier on Thursday. “To become governor, he’ll smear his opponent for being raped by her stepfather when she was just 10 years old – exploiting the sexual abuse of a child and spending millions lying to you about it,” the ad warns Ohio voters.
Acton also addressed the attack ad at an event on Thursday. “You’ve probably all heard by now, if you didn’t know, a little bit about my childhood,” she told supporters. “My brother and I experienced a lot of things, a lot of abuse and a lot of neglect. We were frequent flyers in children’s services, ended up living in a tent in the middle of winter.”
“My opponent has now chosen to exploit my childhood intentionally,” she continued. “He’s doing it in a desperate attempt to save his struggling campaign. But I’ll tell you, Mr Ramaswamy, it’s not going to work.”
Trump has Qatari-gifted Air Force One fly low over White House Halloween party, scaring some Washington DC residents
Donald Trump is so proud of the $400m luxury jet he received as a gift from the nation of Qatar, to use as Air Force One, that he frequently orders its pilots to show it off, by flying the Boeing 747-8 low over events he attends, including political rallies, Fourth of July celebrations and, on Thursday, the White House Halloween party.
The roar of a huge jet flying very low over the nation’s capital, and heading for the White House, as the president handed out candy to children on the South Lawn, was greeted with whoops of delight from some revelers who were perhaps aware of the planned flyover, but it alarmed many Washington DC residents who were not.
The fact that the jet is painted not in the traditional light blue, but in a dark blue and gold livery that resembles several commercial airlines, including the failed Trump Shuttle, might have added to fears from some residents who posted images and comments on social media indicating that they feared an air disaster or a terrorist attack was underway.
Man who compared Trump supporters to cult members live on Fox News says he was ejected from rally by Secret Service
Tom Hoyle, who achieved instant viral fame on Thursday by comparing Donald Trump supporters to a cult in a live interview with Fox News before the president’s rally in South Carolina, told the Guardian that he was quickly removed from the venue by three Secret Service agents.
Hoyle, 57, explained in a phone interview that he was offended to have received an invitation to what he called the president’s “Nazi rally” in a text sent to his screen-printing business’s phone earlier this week.
He accepted the invitation, he said, with the intention of “screaming vulgarities” at Trump during his speech.
As he was waiting inside the relatively small venue in Rock Hill, South Carolina, however, he was approached by the Fox News correspondent Lucas Tomlinson.
Hoyle said he agreed, and then had just a few seconds to “come up with something not vulgar” to say on air and express his point that most Americans do not support Trump. (“It’s all a charade,” he told the Guardian later, calling Maga Republicans a minority of voters, but a very loud one.)
When Tomlinson then asked Hoyle “why are you here this morning?” he responded by comparing the assembled Trump supporters to members of a cult who committed mass suicide in 1978 by following their leader’s order to drink cyanide-laced fruit punch in Jonestown, Guyana (giving rise to the phrase that true believers “drink the Kool-Aid”).
“Well, the late 70s, I was a little too young to get involved and go to South America for the Jonestown massacre, but this is as close as I’ll ever get, so that’s why I’m here,” Hoyle said.
“Wait, the Jonestown massacre?” Tomlinson asked.
“That’s right,” Hoyle replied. “There’s nothing like seeing a cult right up front, man.”
“All right, so maybe this is not a Trump supporter,” Tomlinson told the studio before stepping away to find someone else to interview.
Before the camera moved, Hoyle took the opportunity to point to his cap and plug his business, MadPark Designs in Charlotte, North Carolina.
Hoyle said after he was ejected from the venue by the Secret Service, he spoke with a group of college student protesting against the president outside.
Speaking to the Guardian later, Hoyle pointed out that his business is in the same office park as a Customs and Border Protection office in Charlotte, adding that he has regularly told officers involved in Trump’s immigration crackdown what he thinks of them to their faces.
Trump lashes out at Reuters reporter who asked why he canceled rally in Kansas
After his return from South Carolina, Donald Trump lashed out at a Reuters reporter who asked him why he just canceled a planned appearance at a rally in Kansas on Saturday in support of a embattled Republican senator, Dr Roger Marshall.
After the reporter inquired about Trump’s health, and Trump said he was well, the reporter asked: “So you not going to Kansas has nothing to do with you being sick of travel?”
With a look of disgust, Trump responded: “Oh, you’re sick to ask that question.
“You are a sick guy. Reuters is terrible,” the president added.
Then, stepping away to address other reporters, Trump said: “Can you imagine? Look at this dope. Look at this guy, he’s way out of shape.”
“He comes to me, ‘Sir, you’re not going to go to Kansas.’ I’m not going to Kansas because he’s doing very well. I’m going to do a tele-rally,” Trump continued, imitating the reporter and suggesting that Marshall no longer needs his help to win his Senate race.
“He said, ‘what’s the reason’, after doing what, 28? He says ‘what’s the reason for this, sir, that you’re not going to Kansas?’” the president continued, recapping the exchange for journalists who had just witnessed it for themselves.
“You know what the reason is? I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump went on. “I’m going to Florida tomorrow, and I’ll do- if something else comes up – but he said, ‘You’re not going to Kansas, sir, are you feeling well?’ You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect,” the president said, with indignation.
“You are disgusting,” Trump said, turning back to the Reuters reporter. “Put yourself in shape – you look like hell.”
He then ended the discussion and walked away from the press corps.
Trump administration subpoenas local election officials in California – report
The New York Times reports that the Trump administration has issued federal grand jury subpoenas to local election officials in California, opening a criminal investigation as part of a White House campaign to pre-emptively cast the results of the midterm elections in the nation’s largest state as fraudulent.
According to copies of the subpoenas obtained by the Times, the investigation is an effort to promote the unsubstantiated claim that thousands of noncitizens are on California’s voter rolls, and that elections in states run by Democrats are rigged against Republicans.
JD Vance writes to top Iranian security official in sign Washington has not abandoned diplomacy
Patrick Wintour
Hopes of averting a major new conflagration between Iran and the US soon after Tuesday’s midterm elections could rest on Iran’s response to a personal letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, offering to restart diplomacy.
The letter, written after predominantly Qatari mediation, was sent to the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, on Sunday. It requires Tehran to agree to make commitments on its nuclear programme at the start of a process that would lead to the opening of the strait of Hormuz within seven days in return for US sanctions relief.
A reply is imminent, but Iran is reluctant to give upfront and irreversible commitments on its nuclear programme, such as exporting its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country, if the compensatory US steps, such as lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports, are reversible.
Republicans escalated calls to investigate Mary Peltola’s alleged ballot-stacking scheme. Donald Trump, JD Vance and other Republicans echoed the president’s calls to criminally investigate Peltola for recruiting a man with the same name as her opponent to join the Alaska Senate race.
Alaska’s governor went one step further, ordering an investigation into Peltola. “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Mike Dunleavy, the governor, said in a post on X. “Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.”
A new CNN poll found that Democrats are leading Senate races in Texas and Michigan. The poll found that James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed led by a significant margin over their Republican opponents. But it turned up no clear leader in Maine, once thought a likely Democratic pickup, or Kansas, a deep red state where the race has turned unexpectedly competitive.
New reporting indicates Trump aided Flávio Bolsonaro’s flight from Brazil to the US. According to the New York Times, the president ordered Bolsonaro, the defeated right-wing candidate for Brazil’s presidential election, to be allowed into the US on temporary status. A White House official also arranged the flight that brought Bolsonaro to Miami.
Trump, campaigning today in South Carolina, canceled another planned rally in Kansas. The president opted not to appear in-person at a rally in Kansas on Saturday, instead opting to focus on participating in remote tele-rallies. Other slated campaign appearances in Florida and Iowa are set to continue as planned.
Trump ditches plan to attend Kansas rally in Saturday
President Trump has canceled one of his last scheduled campaign stops before the midterm elections next week, axing his plans to appear at a rally in Kansas.
The planned stop in Salina, Kansas, would’ve come as Republicans seek to fend off a surprise challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, who polls have found could flip the normally deep-red seat currently held by incumbent Roger Marshall.
Instead of appearing in Kansas, Trump will instead partake in a remote tele-rally for Marshall.
Trump’s other slated appearances through the weekend – including one in Florida and another in Iowa – are still expected to go ahead as planned.
New Mexico’s Deb Haaland poised to be first female Native American governor
With a comfortable lead in the polls, Deb Haaland, a former congresswoman and interior secretary under Joe Biden, is set to become the first Native American woman to serve as governor in US history.
Her campaign has energized New Mexico’s Indigenous communities. But while the historic nature of her potential victory isn’t lost on her, Haaland says the hectic final stretch of her campaign has pushed it to the back of her mind.
“Sometimes I forget about the fact that I would be the first Native woman,” Haaland said in a recent interview. “We’re in the throes of this statewide campaign and it’s so busy and we’re trying to be everywhere all at once.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Wanted: new No 10 adviser to help citizens deal with rise of AI
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham is to recruit a number of advisers to plug gaps in No 10, including an expert on how AI will affect society.
The roles advertised by Downing Street give a glimpse into the biggest challenges facing the prime minister – and what he has decided to prioritise.
The new hires will flesh out the threadbare No 10 policy unit – where many of the roles are still vacant after Keir Starmer’s departure. Senior sources have said the prime minister wanted to take time to recruit advisers.
The adviser on AI, who will be expected to have “deep expertise” in the sector, will be expected to lead preparations for the impact of the AI boom on the workforce, amid significant concerns for lower-level professional services jobs, in particular for new graduates.
They will also be expected to be the main adviser to Burnham on frontier AI, the effects and benefits of AI in public service transformation and other major societal impacts.
Several cabinet ministers have openly expressed concerns about the UK’s readiness for the impact of AI on the workforce and economy, as well as the dangers of unregulated systems.
In his Labour conference speech on 28 September, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said there were “daunting” dangers of AI, saying they could not allow technological advances “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.
Burnham will also hire an adviser to develop policy on greater public control over everyday essentials – with a roving brief across transport, energy, housing, water and the environment.
The adviser will be asked to focus on the cost of living. The job advert specifically demands an individual who can “bring challenge and external perspectives into policy development”.
Burnham is known to be frustrated with the cautious and limited options presented to him by Whitehall on areas where he is seeking greater public control.
The Guardian reported on Tuesday that Burnham had told officials to rip up their plans on how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical choices for what to do with the stricken company, including options that could cost more taxpayer money or carry higher legal risk.
Burnham will also recruit an economic adviser to replace Starmer’s aide, Minouche Shafik. The job, which will examine growth and macroeconomic policy, requires “a strong understanding of the economic, fiscal and political context shaping government decision-making”.
Before he became prime minister, Burnham took advice from Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, as well as from Richard Hughes, a former chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, and Jim O’Neill, a cross-bench peer and former Treasury minister.
However, none have agreed to take roles in No 10. Haldane and O’Neill have been critical of Burnham’s economic approach since he entered government, particularly on increased public spending and a lack of growth-oriented policies.
Other roles will include a new adviser on Scotland, an adviser on work and welfare who will report to the new growth director, as well as another post working across immigration, security and justice, looking at cross-border crime, exploitation and illegal migration.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘Local services are vital’: Former rough sleepers on what helped them off the streets
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Martin Fletcher had been homeless for more than 20 years after being made redundant before he finally got accommodation in Sunderland in 2024.
What was the one thing that finally ended his rough sleeping and sofa surfing? “My mindset, mainly,” the 61-year-old said. “The realisation that I was getting old and I couldn’t live like this for ever. And also help from a charity who didn’t judge, who didn’t bombard me with forms – they made me a cup of tea and built up a picture of what I needed and helped me get back on track.”
That charity was Basis Sunderland’s drop-in service for housing support, which closed its doors in July for lack of funding.
Fletcher found this devastating: “How are they going to end rough sleeping when services like this are closing? You’ve got to remember, unless people want to come in off the streets, it won’t happen. They said they did it during Covid but they didn’t – I was still on the streets. And not all homelessness is visible. So these local services are vital.”
Andy Burnham, who had announced plans in July to end rough sleeping and offer everyone in need a bed by Christmas, hosted a summit on the issue on Monday.
The prime minister told the Downing Street event this commitment would be backed by a further £432m to sustain the support into next year. A number of charities had raised concerns that people would simply end up back on the streets after Christmas. Burnham said he was “bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts”.
Those who work in the homelessness sector have warned there is no easy solution. The Guardian has spoken to several formerly homeless people to find out what helped them back into housing, sometimes after decades of sleeping on the streets.
Amy Bell, 37, was street homeless and struggling with heroin addiction for seven years between 2013 and 2020. She said she hit “rock bottom” when her council said it could offer her only a voucher for a two-man tent, which she “cried herself to sleep in at night”.
The next morning, workers employed by the same council put her tent and all her belongings in the bin because it was classed as litter. Borrowing a phone from a Citizens Advice centre, she secured a place at a hostel for a few weeks, which enabled her to reconnect with a local drug treatment service, get a phone with a sim card and start to rebuild.
She said being offered a bed in a hostel, even though she was still taking drugs, was the key to getting her off the streets. “The hostel system is broken. You are basically set up to fail,” she added.
“They don’t accommodate people with addiction problems, and that’s who it should be for. Eventually you will do something that shows you are still using and they ban you. It doesn’t take long to get kicked out of all of them. And then you’re left with nothing.”
Bell said for Burnham to succeed in abolishing rough sleeping he must get rid of the “ridiculous bureaucracy” that stops people from accessing support.
“Everything is done by app now. When you’re homeless, you don’t have that – believe me, if you get a decent phone, you sell it,” she said. “The days of being able to walk into the Citizens Advice bureau or the jobcentre don’t exist any more. Homeless people need a real-life person to help them.”
Others the Guardian spoke to said they moved from England to Scotland because it was easier to get help there after it abolished the priority needs test in 2012. According to Crisis, Scotland has some of the most progressive homelessness rights in the world.
Tony* became homeless after being released from prison in 2024. He told his probation officer he had nowhere to go but was simply advised to contact a council homelessness team the day of his release.
No housing was available and he ended up sleeping in a tent in the woods. “I was a prison leaver, I hadn’t made myself intentionally homeless, but there was nothing. The support was nonexistent,” he said. “I was telling my probation officer where I’m sleeping at our weekly meetings but they didn’t help.”
A chance meeting led him to the Salvation Army, where he has been living in supported accommodation for the past two years. With evidence suggesting the amount of people being released from prison into homelessness is on the rise, Tony said the government must deal with this issue if it wanted to end rough sleeping.
“I was in for three years, and they only started talking to me about accommodation 10 days before I was released,” he said. “If I’d been set up with a bedsit or something like that, the government would have paid less in the long run. I would have begrudgingly gone to a hostel but that wasn’t even offered. Something has to change.”
* Some names have been changed to protect anonymity

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: I know the dangers a wounded Trump presents – this is how the UK should deal with him now | Kim Darroch
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Election nights are party time in Washington. The bars and restaurants fill up and the city rocks. For diplomats, it’s an opportunity – but it’s also a long night, as you trek across the party scene in search of insight and illumination. Invariably, it has its moments. I recall being at the Washington Post party on the night of the presidential election on 8 November 2016. Washington is an overwhelmingly Democrat city and the atmosphere was raucously optimistic, reflecting Hillary Clinton’s small but consistent lead in the polls. As the first results came in a shocked hush fell across the room. People gathered in small, murmuring groups. Within 30 minutes, half the guests had left.
In contrast, I recall speaking to Nancy Pelosi, the queen of the Democrats, at a watch party on 6 November 2018, for the midterms during Trump’s first presidency. I asked her what I should put in my overnight report to London, given that most results wouldn’t be in. She said, with striking confidence, that I should predict that the Democrats would retake the House of Representatives. She was right: the Democrats flipped 41 Republican seats. It gave Pelosi a second term as speaker of the House and gave the world the enjoyable theatre of her sitting directly behind Trump at his State of the Union speeches, rolling her eyes at the bombast.
So what judgments will the current generation of British diplomats have made about the extraordinary political earthquake of Tuesday night, and its implications for British interests and the handling of our most important bilateral relationship for the next two years?
The starting point has to be the scale of this victory. The blue tsunami has swept the Democrats into ownership of the House, the Senate and the majority of governors’ mansions across the country. To a real estate guy such as Donald Trump, imagine how galling it must be to lose so much property in one night: the Monopoly board almost swept clean. The Democrats ended their lockout from rural states by taking the cornfields of Iowa. After a succession of “close, but no cigar” elections, they finally took a Senate seat in Texas. And they even won in Kansas, which hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. In short, it is beyond the Democrats’ wildest dreams and the most comprehensive rejection conceivable of the president’s policies and actions of the last two years.
Now we are left to wonder how this bloodbath will affect Trump’s behaviour over the remaining 26 months and 14 days of his presidency. The Washington insider gossip after his 2018 defeat was that Trump had taken it badly; he felt humiliated and was casting around for people to blame. Well, this is a much worse beating. So expect the Trump woodchipper to be fired up. Pete Hegseth first in the hopper? Or the chief of staff, Susie Wiles?
But never mind Trump’s hurt feelings: what about the stuff that matters to us? As JD Vance has pointed out – at some risk to his personal relationship with the president – the conflict with Iran and its impact on global energy prices was a big part of this election disaster.
The problem for Trump is that he hasn’t got an obvious exit ramp. Negotiations are taking place with Iran via intermediaries. US demands seem to change every day, but they centre on ending the Iranian nuclear programme and the destruction of what Trump calls the “nuclear dust” – Iran’s stock of 440kg of highly enriched uranium. But the Iranians are demanding a huge amount in return – security guarantees, the end of the US naval blockade, an end to sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian assets, a reduction of US forces in the region and even, by some accounts, the strategic prize of sovereignty over the strait of Hormuz. And they think they can outlast the Americans: after all, they live there while the Americans are just visiting.
So perhaps there will be a deal with the midterms out of the way. But equally, given how far apart the parties are, this might drag on, compounding the economic damage for all of us. And the bombing might restart: the Israelis clearly want this, and Trump seems to be keeping his options open, moving more military hardware to the region. No one knows which way he will jump – least of all perhaps Trump himself.
As for Ukraine, for whatever reason (and the conspiracy theories abound), Trump has always appeared to blame Volodymyr Zelenskyy rather than Vladimir Putin for the war. I think he will continue to advocate a peace settlement involving Ukraine giving up all of the Donbas (including the territory Putin has failed to capture) and promising never to join Nato or the EU. Zelenskyy will refuse to sign up to this. So, absent some surprise Putin concessions – of which there have been none to date – this too could drag on and on.
Then we have the continuing possibility of new tariffs. Trump has argued for tariffs for more than 40 years. They will remain his instrument of choice for coercion or punishment. He might use them against Europe if we displease him in any way – for example, by refusing to follow US policy on China, by regulating AI, or by raising new taxes on US tech companies.
So there is no shortage of risks. And there may be more in the pipeline. The loss of Congress will mean Trump is heavily constrained on domestic policy: expect endless fights, vetoes and deadlocks. But he will still have a relatively free hand on foreign policy. And he will want to do things: a deal with Putin, conceivably sacrificing Ukraine, to get US hands on Russia’s energy resources and rare earths; a big trade deal with China; perhaps regime change in Cuba. European and British interests will not figure in his calculations, any more than they did in the conflict with Iran.
The UK embassy will be advising how best to handle this badly wounded president; how to influence his moves and steer him away from decisions that impact on the wellbeing of the UK. My advice would be to carry on pretty much as before, with one important qualification. We are seeing the beginning of the end of the Trump era. Power is already draining away from him: the vultures are circling. But this is not a man who will settle for just raging at the dying of the light; he will light bonfires to ward it off.
So we have to be careful not to appear to be distancing ourselves or moving on from Trump. His antennae are finely tuned to pick up signals of disrespect. This doesn’t mean turning up the dial on sucking up. But it does mean talking to him intensively, arguably even more so than at present, about the issues that matter to us – Iran, Ukraine, the future of Nato, the global economy. And we should resist the temptation to be seen to be cultivating possible successors from either side of the US political spectrum. Trump needs to believe that we recognise what is actually the case: that he is the president and will call the shots until 20 January 2029.
- 
  Kim Darroch was British ambassador to the US from 2016 to 2019, and is author of Collateral Damage: Britain, America and Europe in the Age of Trump

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK will not put tariffs on Chinese vehicles, says Jonathan Reynolds
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The business secretary has hit back at European demands for British tariffs on Chinese imports, saying the government will not change its trade rules because of pressure from Brussels.
Jonathan Reynolds warned that the government would not bow to calls from other countries for the UK to hit Chinese vehicles with import taxes, despite political pressure to align with the EU in exchange for deeper future economic ties.
The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024 and last Friday agreed a 350,000 a year quota on Chinese hybrid cars amid fears cheaper alternatives are causing deindustrialisation and job losses.
Reynolds conceded that levying sanctions on Chinese goods was an option in the future, but he dismissed concerns from Brussels that the UK could provide a back door to the European market.
His comments highlight the divisions that remain between the UK and EU on trade and industrial policy, which could derail the prime minister’s attempts to move closer to Brussels.
“I just want to be clear: when we make any trade decision in terms of trade defence tariffs in relation to the EU, that’s based on the UK interest – it’s not based on any other country asking for that,” said Reynolds during a trade trip to India.
“In 2024, [we] looked at this issue carefully, and we keep it under review depending on what the needs of industry are … But it comes down to what is the fundamental nature of the UK automotive sector. It’s an export-led sector, so that’s what I’ve got to take into account.”
With Europe having imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese electric cars, some believe that the UK has opened an alternative route into the EU for Chinese companies setting up in the UK to sell into the bloc.
Nissan, for instance, has agreed to look at building cars in northern England for the Chinese manufacturer Chery.
Reynolds rebutted those accusations, however, saying: “The UK currently has no major Chinese manufacturer based in its automotive sector, so we’re not making vehicles here and sending them to the single market through some sort of back door.”
His comments raise the stakes ahead of intense final weeks of negotiations before the long-awaited UK-EU summit, which Andy Burnham confirmed this week would be held in Brussels on 20 November.
The prime minister told the Commons on Monday he wanted a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s place in Europe, as he framed the summit as a possible first step to EU membership.
The new Made in Europe trade rules aim to protect European companies from subsidised Chinese imports, but British manufacturers worry they will also be shut out of supply chains.
The issue will not formally be on the agenda at the November summit, but British officials are hoping to use those talks to shape the European legislation.
Diplomats on both sides of the Channel say the summit will now be an early test of whether Burnham’s desire for a “real reset” in UK-EU relations is likely to bear fruit.
One EU official said this week that the UK’s negotiating position would determine whether it was worth pursuing more fundamental changes such as British access to the single market, a new customs union or re-accession.
Some in Brussels have been pushing for Britain to levy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in return for getting access to the European market under the new trade rules.
Reynolds has previously dismissed such an option in part because of the risk that Beijing could hit the UK with reciprocal tariffs, damaging British companies such as Jaguar Land Rover.
He said it would be to Europe’s detriment if it did not admit the UK into the scheme. “If you look at the impact analysis of such a policy, the consequences for the EU [of] excluding the UK are much more difficult,” he said.
“This is not just in the UK’s interest; it’s not in the EU’s interest because obviously we have integrated supply chains.”
Reynolds said the summit was an important milestone in EU-UK relations but also insisted that new trading terms for electricity, emissions and food and drink products would be a major achievement in themselves.
Speaking from a two-day trade delegation to Delhi and Mumbai, he acknowledged that the landmark free trade agreement he helped strike last year with India would become defunct if Britain does rejoin the EU.
“Obviously, if you enter those arrangements, you are doing things collectively. So there would be trade relationships with the UK that were based on Europe, the EU as a whole – that is how the European Union works in terms of its relationship.
“That’s why obviously when we were part of it, we didn’t have these separate bespoke arrangements.”
But he insisted that it remained worth continuing to push to broaden the scope of the agreement, as he unveiled a series of UK-India investments which officials say are worth over £1bn to the UK over the next 15 years.
The deal has already begun to reduce the price of Scotch whisky in Indian shops, after tariffs were reduced from 150% to 75%. Now British officials are keen to free up trade in services as well as goods, for example, pushing for both countries to recognise each other’s legal qualifications.
“There are some specific things regarding who can practice law and in which area,” Reynolds said. “I am confident over the medium to long term that this will improve over time.”
He added: “We’ve got to be cognisant of this long-term position with the EU. But frankly, there’s a job to be done here and now, which we’re doing.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Europe’s central bank chief, Christine Lagarde, steps down for ‘freedom of speech’
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.
Ending months of speculation about her future at the European Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president in March rather than October next year because the rules of neutrality that governed her job prevented her from influencing debate about financial and economics affairs.
She spoke at the end of a press conference to explain the ECB’s decision to hold interest rates – maintaining its key deposit rate at 2.5% – despite inflation climbing to 3.8% last month, its highest since September 2023.
Lagarde said: “I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters.”
The former managing director of the International Monetary Fund has been tipped as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab, stepped down last year after being accused of financial and ethical misconduct, which he denies.
Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is struggling with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.
The European Council made up of EU heads of state appoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone.
There has been speculation that Lagarde, a former finance minister of France, has been encouraged to quit early by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, so her successor can be appointed before the possibility of a far-right or far-left presidential candidate being elected to the Élysée Palace. Lagarde will also be able to participate in next April’s elections.
She noted that ECB officials were bound by strict rules on not appearing partisan. “We have an obligation of neutrality; we comment on the situation with the focus on monetary policy,” Lagarde said, adding that the mandate was “the price we pay for being independent”.
Lagarde said she no longer felt comfortable staying silent on broader global issues. “I’m interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation,” she said, without elaborating.
Drawing on more than two decades in international economic and financial roles, she said she had more to contribute. “There are things that I can say – whether people will listen or not is another story. But I feel that I should say those things and I cannot do so in my current position.”
To reassure markets and staff that her early departure would not disrupt the central bank’s operations, she added: “A process has already started to identify my successor.” She said there were “plenty of excellent candidates.”
Macron said on Thursday that the succession at the ECB must be prepared in “an orderly and balanced way” with European partners, and also expressed his deep gratitude to Lagarde for her action during her tenure.
Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank, said: “The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027.
“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Élysée Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”
Lagarde joined the ECB in late 2019, shortly before the start of the Covid pandemic. During her tenure the central bank has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war, Donald Trump’s trade war and his war in the Middle East.
Lagarde was wearing two plasters on her face in her video message, which she said was because of “a small surgery earlier in the week”. She added: “Follow doctors’ orders and get your skin checked regularly.”
