SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: One thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemy | Jane Martinson
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
While the merits of a so-called Britannia shield to protect Britain from missiles and drones are debatable, the Conservatives’ proposal did achieve one thing last week: the very idea of the shield was used to anoint a political leader.
In a significant development, little observed amid the hullaballoo of news events, Kemi Badenoch’s uncosted, pie-in-the-sky plans to build a £10bn anti-missile system were enthusiastically heralded by the rightwing press. It was not just a matter of the plans themselves being lauded, even by outlets that must know them to be ridiculous. More significant is what it said about the champion chosen by these media organisations in their offensive against the Labour government and Andy Burnham.
The Sun splashed a smiling Badenoch across its front page with a banner headline calling her the “Iron Dome Lady”; the Express paraded her in a power suit and a union jack. The Daily Mail, meanwhile, hailed the Tories for seeking to “protect the nation’s skies” and sealed the plans with its “Don’t Leave Britain Defenceless” campaign stamp. Even wartime leaders could not hope for better, unquestioning coverage from battle-aligned, nation-rallying propaganda sheets.
The slavish Badenoch coverage is significant so soon after Burnham’s first conference speech as prime minister. It marks the moment when much of the rightwing press has returned to its traditional Tory-supporting ways after years of flirting with – and outright eulogising – Nigel Farage and his now scandal-hit Reform UK party. It also suggests a back-to-basics return to the economy as the chief battleground for this fight, and not the madder excesses of the war on woke that has recently consumed them.
The praise for Badenoch, who was also recently treated to an all-expenses paid trip to Greece to meet Rupert Murdoch and executives from the Sun and Times-owning News Corp, suggests that she has cemented a position as the rightwing press’s best political hope of beating Burnham.
The search for a suitable champion has assumed a growing urgency because the prime minister has so far proved hard to leave a mark on. “Red Andy”, the early attack line, has not been widely used since the June byelection in Makerfield. The Mail may have dubbed Burnham’s first conference speech “the most Left-wing speech delivered by a modern British prime minister”, but in recent weeks only the Telegraph’s Allister Heath has fired the “Red Andy” missile in a column that called plans for pension reform, a social care system and all talk of a return to the European Union, “mad, nasty and shockingly extreme”.
This coverage reminds Alastair Campbell of his early years advising Tony Blair when he was depicted either as a “useless Bambi or Stalin”, he tells me. “They can’t decide if [Burnham] is a useless Paddington Bear or red in tooth and claw,” says Campbell. “They just can’t work him out yet.” A member of the loathed liberal elite or outright Trot?
There are a few factors that are making it difficult for the rightwing press to get the full measure of their enemy – including Burnham’s trajectory from New Labour luvvy to working-class champion, the King of the North. Labour advisers also cite the fact that Burnham’s inner circle, in contrast to his predecessors, has also been relatively leak- and conflict-free, leaving rightwing combatants with fewer vulnerabilities to exploit.
This is the calm before the storm, of course, with Burnham’s opponents gearing up for the budget and the inevitable controversies on 28 October. “The press are probing his defences,” Tom Baldwin, a former Labour party adviser, tells me. “They’ll keep trying, of course, and the chances are that one of their missiles will eventually hit a target.”
Amid rising fuel prices, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns over jobs, the back-to-the-future nature of this debate – indeed the back-to-the-Tory-future nature of it – is hardly surprising. Burnham has assaulted shibboleths. He has vowed to reverse “40 years of failure” with his pledge to repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on public ownership of water companies, to abolish the Tory version of the right-to-buy housing scheme, and to restore a sense of common good to Britain. To the right, this is unconscionable. Dan Hodges in the Mail, praising Badenoch’s “best speech yet”, wrote that the country faces a choice between Burnham’s “unashamed 1970s-style socialism” and the Tory leaders’ “bold attempt to reappropriate and recondition Margaret Thatcher’s radical conservatism”.
Although the rightwing outlets fight a similar battle against Labour, they do so for varying reasons. Some of those are ideological, but commercial imperatives also fuel their fervour. The 1970s and 80s marked a golden age for newspapers, when millions of loyal readers gave them heft and profits. With sales and readership figures now at a fraction of their peak in the late 80s, the Sun (which claimed sales of 3.8m per day in 1987) and several other titles no longer publish their numbers, focusing instead on online reach. In dwindling markets, the strategy is to stay competitive by aligning with, or perhaps exacerbating, the prevailing wave of political populism.
The Sun has struggled more than the Mail with the shift online. It has also struggled more with Burnham because of its coverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, in which it falsely blamed Liverpool supporters for a crush that killed 97 people. According to Baldwin, citing well-placed sources, Burnham may become the first prime minister since the Labour leader Jim Callaghan to refuse requests for exclusive interviews and articles in Rupert Murdoch’s biggest tabloid.
The right’s battle-camp has the additional problem that Burnham himself is proving quite a wily opponent. The prime minister spends 10 minutes a day with his social media team before posting to his nearly 1m followers on Instagram and more than 700,000 on TikTok. His short-form videos on fuel prices and the triple lock don’t seem to target younger voters, but they are a way of bypassing a negative narrative – or what Campbell calls “the madness of the rightwing press”.
Burnham could opt to go his own way, to ignore the hostile rightwing outlets altogether. But in a democracy, that would be no more ethical for Labour than it is for Reform UK, which has barred press critics. David Yelland, the editor of the Sun when it put Tony Blair on its front page with the headline “Is THIS the most dangerous man in Britain?”, tells me it would also be unwise. The power of the rightwing press is diminished, he says; they are “toothless tigers in a jungle full of new dangers – dangers as lethal for them as the rest of us, by which I mean AI and what comes next”. But, “the truth is the Tory press still has influence over the political and media classes … it can still set the weather”.
And as we know from famous battles past, the weather can be a decisive factor. The side that copes with it best usually wins.
- 
  Jane Martinson is an academic and Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group, and writes in a personal capacity

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: No 10 plays down UK joining EU single market after Burnham suggests referendum would be needed – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham has claimed that a debate on the UK’s future relationship with the EU could “bring people together who voted in different ways” in 2016. Brexit had not “played out” like it was promised to the public, he said in an interview on ITV’s Good Morning Britain. But he subsequently caused some confusion by seeming to imply that he would only take the country back into the EU single market after a referendum. (See 2pm.) Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey discuss this more in the latest episode of our Politics Weekly UK podcast.
Capita’s attempt to improve its performance over the running of the Civil Service pension scheme has been labelled as “abysmal” by a Cabinet Office minister. Speaking in the Commons, Sally Jameson said the outsourcing giant had failed to improve after thousands of civil servants had been left waiting for payments and retirement quotes. As the Press Association reports, Jameson said she would not rule out in-sourcing the pension scheme’s management after calls from MPs and unions. She said:
Since taking up this role I have met with the CEO and his senior team twice, and on two occasions I have expressed in no uncertain terms my outrage at their performance throughout this contract.
We were promised, and I quote, ‘the most AI-enabled pensions service’, and it’s fair to say that Capita have comprehensively failed to deliver on that commitment.
This progress overall has been abysmal. Complex issues remain unresolved for too long, 1,800 cases for over a year and while some individuals have more than one case, there is too many members and family left waiting in limbo.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has pledged to provide answers to Henry Nowak’s family, as she announced an independent review into the student’s murder. (See 4.07pm.)
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.
Badenoch claims Labour 'all over the place on defence spending' in light of Burnham interview
Kemi Badenoch posted this on social media about Andy Burnham’s comments about defence spending in his Good Morning Britain interview this morning. (See 10.32am.)
The government are all over the place on defence spending. I don’t think Andy Burnham realises he commits to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 in this interview...his Defence Secretary won’t even make that commitment!
When the government are saying Britain needs to be ready for war in 1000 days, hitting a defence spending target in 2035 is too late. Getting to 3% by 2030 means spending the money to be ready NOW, not in 9 years time.
That makes two comments in TV interviews today where Burnham seemed to go beyond what he intended in an answer. The other was what he said about a referendum on joining the single market. (See 2pm.)
During his press conference, Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s Treasury spokesperson claimed that his party’s plan to bring back imperial measures might be good for growth because it could help exports to the US. (See 2.52pm.)
Jernick is right to say that some of the words used in the US are the same. But, as a reader has pointed out, in the US customary system, although the terminology may be identifcal, the units of volume are actually different. A British imperial pint is not the same as a US pint. Jenrick’s policy won’t help exporters who think otherwise.
Mahmood announces review into murder of Henry Nowak, to be carried out by former Tory justice secretary Alex Chalk
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has pledged to provide answers to Henry Nowak’s family, as she announced an independent review into the student’s murder, the Press Association reports. PA says:
The review will be led by former lord chancellor Alex Chalk and will look at “any missed opportunities to intervene”, Mahmood told the Commons.
The 18-year-old died after being fatally stabbed by Vickrum Digwa in Southampton on 3 December 2025. Nowak was handcuffed as he lay dying, after Digwa, a Sikh, falsely accused him of racial abuse. In police body-worn camera footage Nowak can be heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replies: “Don’t think you have, mate.”
At Home Office questions in the Commons, Mahmood said: “I can announce an independent review led by a former lord chancellor, the right honourable Alex Chalk KC. It will investigate what was known about the perpetrator, including any missed opportunities to intervene. It will look at the Nowak family’s experience of the criminal justice system and whether they were supported in the manner they should have been.
“Once the Independent Office for Police Conduct has concluded its investigation into the police response, this review will also consider the actions of the IOPC and, if necessary, the police.
“The full terms of reference have been published today, and an initial report will be submitted to me within five months.
“We must get to the truth of what happened before, during, and after that awful night, and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate.
“We owe that to Henry and to all who loved him. They deserve answers, and this review will provide them.”
Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years on 1 June this year, for Mr Nowak’s murder.
As Paul Brand from ITV reports, Nowak’s family have welcomed the review, saying they hoped it would “finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought too hard for”.
Q: Is Reform UK still committed to its Britannia Card policy, which would allow non-doms to avoid UK taxes in return for paying £250,000?
Jenrick said current government policy was chasing away wealthy and talented people. He went on:
Reform set out a policy a year ago. Could we do better than that? I think we actually could do, because I believe that if we enacted these policies (see 12.46pm and 2.42m), if we got a sense of excitement back into the British economy, then we might even be able to charge more than £250,000. And so we’ll be saying more about that in the near future.
Farage defends Reform UK's plan to cut capital gains tax for cryptocurrency assets
Q; Are you still committed to cutting capital gains tax on cryptocurrency assets from 24% to 10%? (Reform UK’s two biggest donors are both crypto billionaires.)
Farage defended the proposals. He said:
You’ve got the choice on crypto. You can leave it to the Wild West. You can leave it completely unregulated. You can leave it where the scammers could operate freely, where people get ripped off, and where the Inland Revenue or HMRC earned virtually nothing. Or you can bring it under regulatory control.
And this is the irony of crypto. I’m the one arguing for regulation and protection for consumers on crypto.
Farage said between 5 million and 7 million people in Britain had cryptocurrency assets. That was more than the number of people owning shares in companies, he said. He went on
So I want it brought under a protective umbrella. And I want a tax rate that makes people declare what their income is. Hence the incentive to do that, bring crypto in from the outside.
Q: What do you think about banking taxes going up in the budget?
Farage said he did not love the banks. He was debanked by one back, and another 10 refused to have him as a customer, he said.
But he claimed bank taxes were already higher than in any other comparable nation. He said it might be possible to squeeze “a bit more” out of the sector. He went on:
Loathsome as I think some of their practices are … I do not want a tax rate that makes the banks leave London, because that will make all of us poorer.
Farage said he think the staying out campaign would win a referendum on rejoining the EU “very comfortably indeed”.
He went on:
People may be frustrated that their hopes were not delivered. I’m one of those.
But a referendum on rejoining? £41bn a year rough estimate of contribution? Commitment to free movement of people? Commitment ultimately to joining the euro?
I can’t see any situation in which the British people vote for that.
Q: This morning Andy Burnham implied free movement could be part of any future deal with the EU, and then No 10 rowed back. What do you think is going on?
Farage said:
He’s all over the place on this and we’re beginning to learn we can’t trust him.
Referring to the forthcoming UK-EU summit, he said:
What I’m saying is [Burnham] must not agree to anything at that summit without putting to the people in a general election. And if he does that and wins a general election, then he has some mandate to proceed with moving on to closer links with Europe. But I do not believe that anybody could rejoin the European Union without putting it back to the British people.
He also he would be happy to fight an election with rejoining the EU a campaign issue.
Farage defends close ally calling Badenoch 'Nigerian scammer'
Q: [From the Daily Telegraph] Do you think Raheem Kassam was being racist when he called Kemi Badenoch a Nigerian scammer? (Kassam used to work as Nigel Farage’s chief of staff in Ukip, and he is still a close ally and supporter.)
In response, Farage turned on the questioner.
Britain’s going broke and you’re asking about what somebody who’s an adjunct of the party says on social media. It shows frankly, the level that we sink to with these debates.
I thought the use of the word scammer was very accurate because she says things often that simply are not true. It’s almost their instinctive response to things. It’s to say things that simply aren’t true.
Farage says he would bury hatchet with Tories and campaign with them in referendum on joining EU
Q: If there is a second referendum on Brexit, will you form a coalition with the Tories to campaign against rejoining?
Farage said the first referendum showe there were “different constituency audiences” and the leave campaign succeeded because it appealed to different groups, like Labour leavers, Tory leavers and Ukip leavers. He goes on:
It was actually the fact that it was a grand coalition that made it succeed. So I don’t think there’ll be any question, in an issue like that, of burying hatchets.
Farage also said they would stress they were fighting for “independence”. He said he would like to use that description more often.
Farage sarcastically describes parliamentary commissioner for standards as 'utterly unimpeachable'
Q: Are you preparing for a second byelection in Claction (in the event of the parliamentary investigation leading to a recall election)?
Farage replied:
If I comment on that, I’ll be in breach of rules. And, as we all know, our standards, procedure, and our wonderful standards commissioner, are utterly unimpeachable people in absolutely every single way. Thank you so much. What a complete and utter farce the whole thing is.
Q: What would you say to Tory claims that many of the plans in your document are policies that they have already announced? Like cracking down on bogus degrees.
Farage points out that, even if they are promoting these ideas now, the Tories did not do these things when they were in power.
Q: Do you think voters want a bit more positivity?
Farage says Andy Burnham is positive. He explains:
Has [Burnham] got a positive spin? Yes. Is he more engaging than Keir Starmer? Yes. Does he appear a bit more normal than Keir Starmer? Yes.
But what does he actually stand for? And if he wants to unite the country, the one way not to do it is to rerun all the arguments from the referendum ten years ago. And what happened to what he said to the people of Makerfield just a few months ago?
So I begin to genuinely doubt his sincerity. I really, really do.
Farage describes parliamentary investigation into claims he broke Commons rules as a 'farce'
Q: What do you say to Andy Burnham claiming that dealing with illegal migration has become harder since Brexit?
Farage says what Burnham is saying is not true. Under the Dublin convention, which applied to the UK when the UK was in the EU, Britain had to take back more asylum seekers from other countries than it was able to send back, he claims.
Q: Have you any update on the investigation into you by the parliamentary commissioner for standards?
Farage says this topic is “a gem”. He says journalists are allowed to ask about this, but, under the parliamentary rules, Farage is in breach if he even menions publicly that an investigation is taking place.
He goes on:
There are some who think that standards are now being used as a political tool. You may very well think that; I couldn’t possibly comment.
Farage says the process is a “farce”. He adds sarcastically:
He’ll judge at some point, but I’ve no doubt he’ll be fiercely independent.
Q: [From Serena Barker-Singh from Sky News] How to you respond to Andy Burnham implying people like you lied about the benefits of Brexit?
Farage claims Adam Boulton, the former Sky News political editor, used to say Farage was the only leading person on the leave side who never lied about the potential benefits of Brexit.
I would say to the prime minister the opportunities of Brexit have not been delivered. This was the chance of a great escape from a failing European single market, which in terms of foreign direct investment growth and every other metric you could look at was failing …
We’ve not had anything like the potential that Brexit could have delivered. Was it the right thing to do? Undoubtedly. And what would rejoining be? Utterly moronic.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola delays campaign stops after car crash
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Mary Peltola, a Democrat who is running for Alaska’s lone US Senate seat, and her family suffered minor injuries in a car crash while driving to a campaign stop on Saturday, her campaign said.
The family was on its way to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet when another vehicle crashed into the one transporting Peltola and her family, her campaign said in a statement on Sunday. Peltola required medical attention after the collision.
“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits,” Cheryl Bruce, Peltola’s campaign manager, said in a statement. “Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover.”
Bruce added: “Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families.”
Police responded to a “multi-vehicle collision” at about 6.55pm on Saturday, according to the Anchorage police department. Peltola’s family and the occupant of a second vehicle were taken to a local hospital “with non-life-threatening injuries”, according to the authorities, while the occupant of a third vehicle refused medical transport.
“The circumstances of the collision are under investigation,” reads a statement from the police department.
Peltola, an Alaska Native and former congresswoman, is challenging Republican incumbent senator Dan Sullivan, hoping to become the first Democrat in nearly two decades to represent the state in the Senate. Both candidates have tried to rally support from Alaska Native voters, a key constituency in the high-stakes race that has become one of the most watched in the nation.
On Friday, Donald Trump ordered the justice department to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Sullivan loses. The lawsuit cites potential confusion with another Republican candidate who is listed on the ranked-choice ballot as Daniel J Sullivan Jr, who is a retired schoolteacher.
Peltola’s incident delayed what her campaign announced as the “Alaska Always tour,” an eight-stop push through the last week before election day. Her campaign said she will resume events on Tuesday, with a stop in Homer, Alaska.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump’s appearance at Georgia rally disrupted by anti-ICE protesters – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Donald Trump’s speech to a small crowd of supporters in Dalton, Georgia, was just disrupted by three protesters holding up signs against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), who were forced out of the crowd by Trump supporters, including a man wearing a yellow Gadsden flag as a cape.
Two of the signs denounced the idea of sending ICE officer to the polls on election day, which the administration has refused to rule out.
After he began speaking again, Trump praised “the woman in the yellow cape”, apparently referring, incorrectly, to the man draped in a yellow Gadsden flag, with the slogan Don’t Tread on Me, who was among the first to confront the anti-ICE activists.
“She went up there, ripped them out of their seats and threw them the hell out of here. Where’s the woman with the yellow cape, then? She was great,” Trump said.
“I love the woman with the yellow cape. She was right on there. She’s pushing them around, slapping the guy around,” he added.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Katie Zacharia confirmed that her brief tenure as White House press secretary is over in a social media post filled with fulsome praise for Donald Trump.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez denounced attempts by Trump and other Republicans to smear Abdul El-Sayed, by falsely claiming that he is linked to the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood, as clearly “racist”.
Before Trump visited Georgia on Friday to campaign against him, Democratic senator Jon Ossoff said that he would be “delighted for the president to come every day between now and the election”.
Speaking in Georgia, Trump spent most of his time defending his record as president, rather than discussing Republican candidates at the rally who are up for election next month. Much of what he said was simply not true.
Trump’s speech to a small crowd of supporters in Dalton, Georgia, was disrupted by three protesters holding up signs against Immigration and Customs Enforcement, who were forced out of the crowd by Trump supporters, including a man wearing a yellow Gadsden flag as a cape who Trump mistook for a woman.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez denounces Trump's 'racist' lie about Abdul El-Sayed
During a visit to Michigan on Friday to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate, New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez denounced attempts by Donald Trump and other Republicans to smear El-Sayed, by falsely claiming that he is linked to the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood, as clearly “racist”.
On Thursday, Trump recorded a social media video in the Oval Office in which he lied that El-Sayed, an American physician born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrant parents, is “a Muslim Brotherhood member”. There is no evidence that El-Sayed is or ever was part of that Islamist movement in Egypt.
El-Sayed has said that reports that his birth mother might have been associated with the group as a student in the 1970s, a decade before his birth, which have been pushed by a conspiracy theorist close to Trump, do not mean that he has “ties” to the group.
El-Sayed, who was raised by his father and stepmother – and grandparents – told NBC News on Wednesday, “I wasn’t raised by my mother,” and has never talked to her about her days as a student activist in Egypt, when she might, or might not, have been associated with the Islamist opposition to Egypt’s dictatorship.
After she ate at a Culver’s in Michigan Thursday, Ocasio-Cortez was asked to comment on the smear by a reporter for TMZ. “On the scale between real and racist, where does this whole Muslim Brotherhood thing fit?” the reporter asked.
“I think it it falls into racist, very clearly,” the progressive congresswoman replied.
She went on to comment on El-Sayed’s distance from his mother, and argued that he is not defined by whatever political associations his relatives in Egypt might have had in the past.
“As someone who is familiar with Abdul’s story – he’s talked about this – it’s a very vulnerable thing,” Ocasion-Cortez said. “When Abdul was born, his parents separated very shortly afterwards and his mom left and so he was raised by his dad.”
“I think what’s hard about this is that people are, you know, throwing really painful and insulting and racist stuff around, but it also hits, you know, a little boy in Detroit that grew up without his mom,” she added.
“It doesn’t define Abdul at all,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “How many of us have had a family member that has either dealt with addiction or gotten in trouble or what have you and they are distant or estranged or what have you and that has nothing to do with you as a person?” she asked.
“The fact of the matter, none of this has to do with Abdul,” she argued. “ And if you take any person and zoom out far enough, with every person that they’ve known or grown up with, of course you’re going find whatever you’re going find.”
“It’s just got nothing to do with him,” she said. “He’s he’s one of the most patriotic people I’ve ever met.”
Katie Zacharia posts resignation statement saying it 'was an honor' to work for 'kind, wonderful, gracious' Trump
Katie Zacharia confirmed that her brief tenure as White House press secretary is over in a social media post filled with fulsome praise for Donald Trump.
“President Trump is such a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. There’s nobody who will ever come close to making America great the way he has and is,” Zacharia wrote on X. “It was an honor to work for him.”
In a similarly worded message posted on Instagram she added: “I wish more Americans appreciated him.”
Zacharia later edited the text of her post on X to match the one on Instagram.
Zacharia’s post was accompanied, on both platforms, by a photograph of her standing beside a seated Trump in the Oval Office – and a blurred out map of what looked to be part of an island on his desk.
Fox News, which played a central role in convincing the viewer-in-chief, Trump, that Zacharia was not up for the job, first reported the statement.
Zacharia stumbled through surprisingly tough interviews with the Fox host Sean Hannityon Thursday night, and with three Fox morning hosts, including Hannity’s fiance, Ainsley Earhardt, on Friday.
As he left the White House on Friday without Zacharia, Trump mentioned that he had seen both of those “rough” interviews.
California elections officials under threat of prosecution from Trump
The Trump administration is escalating its fight with California ahead of next month’s midterm elections, warning that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.
The letter on Friday from senior justice department officials and obtained first by the Associated Press is the latest salvo in an ongoing tussle with heavily Democratic California, coming just a day after the Trump administration sued the state to prevent it from counting mail-in ballots from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
“The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime – and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful,” warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the justice department.
It adds: “If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.”
The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles county counsel’s office and also is copied to the California secretary of state, Shirley Weber, and the Los Angeles county registrar, Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice.
Capitol Police warned congressional offices on Friday to be on watch for suspicious mail, after several members of Congress reported receiving envelopes containing unknown substances or other suspicious packages this week.
Among them was Washington representative Pramila Jayapal, a Democrat.
“This seemingly deliberate and widespread attack on our democracy and elections is unacceptable,” said in a Friday statement.
Maxwell Frost, a Democratic congressman who represents Orlando, Florida, said his office was evacuated Friday due to a suspicious package.
And California representative Jimmy Panetta, also a Democrat, told KRON4 a staffer in his Santa Cruz district office opened mail that contained a “white powdery substance.”
“My priority is the safety and security of my staff and, thankfully, she and the other staff have been initially cleared by medical officials,” Panetta said.
The FBI is investigating the letters, officials said Thursday.
After wrapping up his rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump is now off to a Republican National Committee fundraiser in Palm Beach, Florida. The event is closed to press.
And so Katie Zacharia joins the mayfly ranks of Liz Truss, Anthony Scaramucci, New Coke, CNN+ and Quibi. To say she burned twice as bright and half as long would be too kind. She went out like a firework on a soggy night.
The White House confirmed on Friday that Zacharia is leaving her role as press secretary after just five days on the job. No one was surprised after a lacklustre press briefing debut and scrutiny over her legal credentials.
But even more importantly, Zacharia lived by the sword and died in the one arena that Donald Trump truly cares about: television.
She reportedly got the job by closely monitoring the US president’s public schedule and tracked his active hours on Truth Social to predict exactly when he would be watching TV. She then timed her own appearances on air to make sure she caught his eye. The fact that she fitted the glossy blond aesthetic from what Trump calls “central casting” also helped.
But TV also proved her undoing. On Thursday, Zacharia gave a series of interviews to Trump-friendly outlets in a desperate bid for redemption. Instead, she sealed her own fate with more hapless performances.
She must have expected Fox News host Sean Hannity, who has even spoken at Trump rallies, to give her an easy ride. But even he was sceptical when she admitted she had “stepped up to the plate with very little prep time” for the first briefing. Hannity asked: “Am I hearing that you think the staff should have prepped you better?”
Zacharia rejected the notion that she had only taken questions from conservative outlets, incorrectly asserting that the Daily Mail is “not known to be a conservative outlet”. Hannity also quizzed her about her dubious legal credentials. “Why not just say, ‘I went to Pepperdine law school, and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn’t pass?’”
Zacharia tried again on Fox & Friends but ran into host Lawrence Jones, who said: “You know, Katie, it’s been a tough week for you. It’s not an easy job to be the press secretary and you never want to be the story.”
He also asked: “Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?” Zacharia responded, “I’m standing here,” referring to the fact that she was speaking from the White House north lawn.
Her exit hours later was met with widespread ridicule – and a measure of human compassion for someone whom Trump had subjected to a very public humiliation.
Trump plays old clip from CNN polling analyst who said last night 'Trump’s numbers are absolutely garbage'
Donald Trump has concluded his lengthy speech to hundreds of supporters in Dalton, Georgia, wrapping up just short of the one hour and 40 minute mark.
Close to the end of the remarks, Trump asked his aides to play a video clip for the crowd, which showed a CNN polling analyst, Harry Enten, pointing out that the president was still popular with voters who describe themselves as “MAGA Republicans.”
Trump has played this clip, from an August broadcast, at multiple stops on his current campaign tour, as if to block out less flattering recent polls that find him at record-low approval ratings from the public as a whole.
In a more recent segment broadcast on Thursday morning, that Trump did not play for the crowd, Enten explained to CNN viewers this week that a new Fox News poll shows that Trump’s overall approval rating has fallen to 36%, with 64% disapproving of the job he has done as president.
As Enten noted, the most dramatic shift was among voters under 30 surveyed by Fox. In October 2024, that demographic had a net positive approval of Trump of plus-3. Now, the same group disapproves of Trump by 50 points.
On Thursday night, Enten was asked on another CNN show about Trump’s current standing in polls and said this: “Trump’s numbers are absolutely garbage, they’re trash.”
“He has the highest disapproval rating of all time when it comes to inflation going into a midterm election,” Enten continued. “In fact he has the worst inflation net approval ratings that I’ve ever seen for any president, we’re talking all the way back to James Earl Carter. He’s the first guy ever to hit minus 50 points or worse on the net inflation.”
Trump repeats lie that Abdul El-Sayed is 'a member of the Muslim Brotherhood'
During his speech in Georgia, which has blown past the 90-minute mark, Donald Trump just repeated the lie he has told multiple times this week about Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, telling supporters that the Michigan Senate candidate is “a member of the Muslim Brotherhood”.
Despite Trump’s false statement, there is no evidence that El-Sayed, the US-born son of Egyptian immigrant parents, is a member of the Egyptian Islamist opposition group. El-Sayed has flatly denied that he has any ties to the Egyptian group.
Trump made this false claim on Thursday in public remarks and in a video message recorded in the Oval Office and posted on the president’s social media platform.
As if to make the anti-Muslim racism of his message entirely clear, the president has insisted on referring to Abdul El-Sayed as “Mohammed” each time he’s told this lie.
In Georgia, Trump rails against Ossoff who said he would be 'delighted for the president to come every day between now and the election'
As Donald Trump continues to rail against senator Jon Ossoff at his rally in Georgia, it is worth noting that Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent and a fierce Trump critic, said on Thursday that he would be “delighted for the president to come every day between now and the election”.
Speaking on MS Now, Ossoff said Trump was welcome to campaign against him in Georgia because “the public is turning against this administration.”
“They see, on the one hand, the total incompetence,” Ossoff continued. “The nation plunged recklessly into a war that they don’t know how to win or to end, a global energy crisis, record high diesel prices, record high prices for healthcare.”
“It costs more today than ever before in our country’s history to fill up your truck, to stock your fridge, to power your home,” the Democratic senator continued. “And then everybody can see that at the same time, the first families raking in billions of dollars from all over the world. The president’s adorning his office in gold. People are fed up and they’ve had enough.”
Trump repeats false claim about praise from Saudi king
Donald Trump’s remarks to supporters in Georgia are mainly a rehash of previous speeches, filled with false claims we have debunked repeatedly, suggesting that the president is not a regular reader of the Guardian.
“Less than two years ago, our country was dead. Now we have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” Trump said, before claiming, as he has in the past, that this was an observation made to him by the Saudi king during his visit to that country last year.
“So that statement was true. The king of Saudi Arabia, when I was over there, he said, ‘A short time ago, you had – you were a laughingstock’ – meaning our country was a laughingstock, all the way, all the way around the world, everybody was laughing at the USA,” Trump said. “‘And in a very short period of time, you made it the hottest country,’” the president continued, attributing this remark to the Saudi king.
As the Guardian has reported previously, Trump did not meet the Saudi king, who is elderly and not often seen in public, during his visit last year. Instead, he was hosted by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. There is also no evidence that the Saudi prince made this statement to Trump, but there is video of Trump making a version of that claim to Prince Mohammed during an address to a US-Saudi investment event in Riyadh on 13 May 2025.
“The days of economic misery under the last administration are rapidly giving way to the greatest economy in the history of the world,” Trump said before directly addressing the crown prince in the audience. “We are rocking. The United States is the hottest country, with the exception of your country, I have to say, right? … No Mohammed… You’re hotter. At least as long as I’m up here, you’re hotter. But groceries, gasoline, energy and all other prices are down with no inflation. We have no inflation.”
Two weeks after his return to the US, Trump began saying that this observation had been made not by him, but to him. “I went to Saudi Arabia,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on 28 May 2025. “The king told me, he said, ‘you got the hottest com-’ we have the hottest country in the world right now.,” Trump said. “Six months ago this country was stone cold dead. We had a dead country.”
As he repeated the story, again and again, Trump began to also attribute his own claim, that the US was “dead” under Joe Biden, to the Saudi king as well. In remarks at the Nato summit in the Hague in June 2025, Trump insisted that the Saudi king had told him: “A year ago, your country was dead. You had a deadhead running it. You had a country that was dead”.
Since then, Trump has repeated the tale dozens of times.
Trump repeats imaginary tale about being blamed for high prices on second day of his term
Speaking in Georgia, Donald Trump is spending most of his time defending his record as president, rather than discussing Republican candidates at the rally who are up for election next month.
Much of what he said was simply not true.
To take one example, the president repeated an entirely imaginary story he has repeated frequently in recent weeks, about how he was supposedly blamed for high prices by reporters on the second day of his term, in January 2025.
“When I came in, it was January 20th. I came in and on January 21st I had a news conference and some of those same people were at the news conference and they were screaming at me. I was only there for less than one day, substantially less than one day. And I’m having a news conference. I thought it would be a victorious conference. I thought the fake news would be saying, ‘Oh, sir, what a great race you ran,’” Trump said.
“My first news conference, January 21st. So I take office on the 20th. I figured maybe I won’t have a news conference. So the next day I have a news conference and I’m waiting for accolades from the press. And they said, what about the cost of eggs? What about the cost of beef?” Trump claimed.
In fact, a review of the transcript from that news conference reveals that no such exchange took place on 21 January 2025, when he was mainly pressed on the pardons he signed the day before for Capitol rioters convicted of violence against police officers on January 6 2021, in support of his attempt to stay in power despite losing the 2020 election.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Brazil publishes first global ‘roadmap’ for phasing out fossil fuels
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
All countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now without needing to wait for new technologies or economic changes, Brazil’s government has said ahead of a global climate summit.
Brazil, the host of last year’s UN climate conference, set out the world’s first global “roadmap” for phasing out fossil fuels on Tuesday, showing that countries could boost their economies and pull people out of poverty while breaking the link with coal, oil and gas.
But Joeri Rogelj, a professor of climate science and policy at Imperial College London, said that although the Brazilian roadmaps represented a step forward, they were limited. “The roadmaps are valuable but fall short of clearly indicating the pace of change needed by including no timeline or key benchmarks,” he said.
“Because of this omission, they still leave much to be imagined about what is needed to achieve the Paris agreement’s ultimate goal: limiting global warming to well below 2C, and preferably to 1.5C, to avoid dangerous climate harm.”
André Corrêa do Lago, Brazil’s president of the Cop30 summit, said the roadmaps were intended to help move the annual UN Cops away from their previous focus on negotiating global agreements to tackle the climate crisis, and on to implementing the targets that had already been agreed. Cop31 takes place in Antalya, Turkey, this month.
“They are documents of implementation,” Corrêa do Lago told the Guardian in an interview. “There is a different group of people that negotiate and that implement. The problem we’ve had at many Cops is to think that the same people who negotiate might also need to coordinate the implementation – this is not the case.”
He said the roadmaps should be taken up by ministries of finance, transportation, energy and infrastructure to work on how they could be implemented in each country.
Brazil hosted the Cop30 summit last November in the coastal city of Belém, in the Amazon rainforest, where a bitter dispute broke out over whether the final set of resolutions should include pledges on fossil fuels. As a compromise, the presidency agreed to produce two roadmaps, one on “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just orderly and equitable manner” and the other on halting and reversing deforestation.
These roadmaps are separate from similarly named plans from governments that met after Cop30 at a conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, in April, to discuss the transition away from fossil fuels. At that conference, nearly 60 countries formed a new “coalition of the willing”, separate to Cops, to set out their own national roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels. Several countries have since produced national plans, including Germany, France and the Netherlands.
The roadmaps produced by governments under the Santa Marta initiative are much more specific and prescriptive than Brazil’s, as each of those is written by the national government responsible for implementing the policies recommended.
The Brazilian roadmaps only set out steps that are possible. They are not binding, they contain no deadlines or milestones for actions, and they leave it to countries themselves to “diagnose” their degree of dependence on fossil fuels and select steps to reduce it.
“Every country will have a different rhythm [for moving away from fossil fuels] – it’s very important to concentrate on the diagnoses of countries’ circumstances,” Corrêa do Lago said. “Based on these diagnoses, they can choose their levers [of policy] and implement the transition.”
Among the steps Brazil suggests is for oil and gas producers to urgently cut the flaring and venting of gas from extraction sites. Methane is a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, so this would have an immediate impact. Other steps are for countries to reduce their subsidies to fossil fuel use or production, and building up renewable generation.
The roadmap on deforestation notes the large sums that are expected to be needed to help poor countries with heavily forested areas such as the Amazon, the Congo rainforests and south-east Asian tropical forests that are under threat from fires and palm oil exploitation.
About $300bn is likely to be needed every year for forests by 2030, and $500bn a year by 2050, according to the roadmap, citing UN figures. The current amounts available fall far short at about $85bn a year.
At Cop30 last year, Brazil set up the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a fund aiming to preserve forests, which raised about $7bn from various countries including a £400m loan from the UK.
The deforestation roadmap also notes the importance of regulating trade between forested countries and consumer countries. At present, there are few trade checks to stop unscrupulous companies from selling goods from deforested areas.
In some cases, deforestation has appeared to be condoned or encouraged by local or even national administrations. Indonesia is being sued by civil society groups for “gross negligence” over the record-breaking fires over the last few months that have cleared swathes of forest and destroyed wildlife habitats, most likely to be replaced by palm oil plantations.
Brazil was able to publish the roadmaps after its president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won a fourth election term just over a week ago. In the last four years under Lula, deforestation rates have fallen by about 70%. His defeated opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, had been expected if elected to return to his father’s policies of rampant exploitation of the Amazon rainforest.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.
But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink, accused the Ukrainian military of violating the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a social media post.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser, said on the Telegram app that the country is “physically unable” to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drone operations.
Ukraine’s general staff and defence ministry did not immediately comment.
The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.
The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.
The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.
However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”
Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.
The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”
There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.
Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need.”
The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.
When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”
He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.
Reuters contributed reporting

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: overdue, but proceed with care | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The German philosopher GWF Hegel famously evoked the owl of Minerva when discussing the historical wisdom that comes through hindsight. This autumn, she has flown tirelessly over the landscape of British politics. Party conference season was dominated by conflicting Labour and Conservative accounts of the 1970s and 80s. And a decade after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, Andy Burnham this week abandoned all equivocation over the damage – economic but also strategic – that resulted from that decision.
Having declared that it is time to “face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good”, Mr Burnham told the House of Commons on Monday that it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to explore all options for closer relations with Brussels. Though he confirmed that in this parliament he will honour the red lines in Sir Keir Starmer’s Labour manifesto, all bets will subsequently be off.
A long-delayed reset summit, Mr Burnham also announced, will take place next month with deals on food and drink and youth mobility to be negotiated. The former Labour leader Neil Kinnock asserted to an Italian newspaper on Tuesday that the prime minister’s “obvious” eventual objective was to rejoin.
That might well be contested in Downing Street. But as has become the norm in this overture phase of Mr Burnham’s premiership, his Commons statement was bracingly expansive and forthright. It also had the signal virtue of being correct in its diagnosis and prescription. Nevertheless, the reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk.
Labour’s hyper-caution over revisiting the EU relationship has increasingly been at odds with polls indicating a substantial majority of the public supports closer ties. But the devil will be in the detail. In the red wall, in particular, much will depend on the prime minister’s undoubted persuasive powers. The need to undo the economic self-harm of Brexit was not something that Mr Burnham chose to emphasise while campaigning for his seat in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield.
For its part, the EU itself is in flux and may have new red lines of its own. Responding to a more menacing geopolitical environment, Brussels is contemplating deeper coordination in areas such as defence and economic policy. The direction of travel is already evident in the “Made in Europe” strategy, which threatens to leave British-based car manufacturers out in the cold.
As that risk illustrates, it is overwhelmingly in Britain’s interests to be acting in concert with the EU, rather than flailing in sorry isolation on the sidelines. Following the visceral mutual distrust of the Tory Brexit years, Sir Keir restored a basic if circumscribed civility to relations between the UK and the EU. Mr Burnham’s boldness can now open up new possibilities down the line for “a real reset”, to use the formulation of one EU diplomat.
It will not have escaped Mr Burnham’s notice that such a prospect would unite progressive Britain behind it, and could significantly boost Labour’s percentage vote share. His overriding early theme has been the need to rectify the political “wrong turns” of past decades. Beginning the long task of doing so on Brexit is brave, but it promises significant dividends for his premiership and, much more importantly, the country.
-

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Oleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have ‘frank’ call with Putin
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A local ceasefire in a southern Ukrainian city under Russian occupation appeared to be holding on Tuesday, with both sides ceasing drone attacks ahead of an apparent evacuation of about 2,000 trapped and desperate civilians.
The temporary truce began at 3am in Russian-controlled Oleshky. The city sits on the Dnipro River and is about 3 miles (5km) from Kherson, a larger city on the opposite bank. Ukrainian troops recaptured Kherson in autumn 2022.
Witnesses reported that the deadly frontline across the river was quiet for the first time in four years. The pause in fighting is due to last until 11pm on Sunday, Ukrainian officials said, and represents a significant if limited moment of de-escalation.
Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, held what they described as a “frank and substantive” phone call with Vladimir Putin about efforts to end the war in Ukraine. Støre indicated afterwards that big differences remained.
The two Nordic leaders said the call – a rare instance of direct contact between Putin and western leaders – was linked to upcoming talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US, expected to take place in Abu Dhabi next month.
The ceasefire in Oleshky appears to be an attempt by the Kremlin to curry favour with Donald Trump before the trilateral meeting and next week’s US midterm elections. The first lady, Melania Trump, requested the humanitarian mission, and in a post on X said it was brought forward by two days to allow the delivery of critical aid.
Its geographical scope had been extended beyond Oleshky “within the Kherson region”, she added, to provide safe passage for convoys. Calls for a ceasefire were also issued by Pope Leo, the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe.
Between 1,500 and 2,000 people in the city have been living under a complete blockade by Russia. The last delivery of food to stores was in May, and many people are now starving and eating weeds. The Ukrainian military has airdropped food using drones but locals say Russian security forces detain anyone who takes it.
Russian soldiers have mined roads and use ruined buildings to coordinate round-the-clock strikes against Kherson. Some Oleshky residents have managed to escape, walking or cycling past bodies lying on the street and the burnt-out shells of vehicles.
Ukrainian observers say the Kremlin is planning a major propaganda tour this week in which Kyiv is blamed for Oleshky’s destruction. Trump-supporting US media channels have been invited to witness the evacuation, in which buses will take residents to occupied Crimea and Russia.
Ksenia Arkhipova, who fled the city in 2022 and now, as a volunteer, helps others leave, said some residents have told her they fear Russian officials may “filter out” evacuees with pro-Ukraine views.
“People say they are genuinely afraid that the Russians will check their phones and look for evidence of Ukrainian relatives or ties to the Armed Forces of Ukraine – something they have done repeatedly in other occupied territories,” Arkhipova told the Associated Press.
The ceasefire does not extend to other parts of Ukraine. Overnight, Russia bombarded Kyiv with drones and ballistic missiles, killing at least one person and injuring 15. It hit a university campus, wounding students, as well as a bridge over the Dnipro and metro infrastructure. Ten other regions came under fire.
The bridge remains closed to traffic, but some commuters walked across it to get to work. Writing on social media, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia “must stop dragging out this war” and said he welcomed European attempts to end it.
He said Stubb and Støre had briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas clearly conveyed to the Russian leadership the need for genuine steps towards de-escalation, particularly when it comes to our energy sector and infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote.
The Finnish-Norwegian initiative comes amid growing efforts by some European nations to establish a direct channel of communication with Moscow and secure a stronger European voice in negotiations. Stubb and Støre said they took part in the call as leaders of their respective countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe as a whole.
European governments remain divided over whether direct engagement with Putin is worthwhile, given Russia’s maximalist demands remain stubbornly unchanged. There is little agreement on who should lead such talks. Stubb is seen by some EU officials as a candidate.
The divisions were laid bare shortly after news of the call emerged, when Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, criticised the move. “I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not agreed with any of us,” Frederiksen said.
She added: “I see no signs that Russia wants peace with Europe – neither in the hybrid warfare it wages every day, nor in Ukraine, where brutal and aggressive strikes continue daily, claiming many lives.”
Russia’s foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, said the Europeans had offered “nothing new”, and were simply trying to insert themselves in the negotiation process.
This month Putin said he was willing to resume peace talks, but only on Russia’s hardline terms. They include the handover of the entire eastern Donbas region, including parts Russia has been unable to seize since 2014, as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces.
Last week Zelenskyy said he was open to a peace agreement that would freeze the war along the current frontlines. “Yes, we are ready to stop this war as soon as possible,” he said in an interview with ABC News. He made clear that Ukraine would not recognise land seized and occupied by Russia as Russian.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Most Europeans want action to tackle climate crisis but not at any cost, poll shows
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Europeans believe human-made climate change is real, a survey has shown, with most feeling action must be taken soon – as long as they do not have to sacrifice too much to achieve it.
The YouGov poll of six European countries showed between 69% (Germany) and 80% (France) of respondents believed the climate was changing, with few (1%-4%) denying it and 14-20% believing it was changing, but not as a result of human activity.
Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent and scientists say human-driven climate breakdown through the burning of fossil fuels is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and destructive storms.
Days before the Cop31 climate conference in Turkey, the polling showed vast majorities (79-89%) in Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK thought countries would combat the crisis more effectively by working internationally.
Those in the EU were more likely to say that climate action decisions should be made at EU rather than national level, a feeling shared by 50-54% of respondents in France, Italy and Germany as well as 61% in Denmark and 64% in Spain.
Majorities of between 65% and 83% in each country surveyed said they were worried about the climate crisis, including 23%-42% who were “very worried”. YouGov noted an uptick in concern during this summer’s heatwaves.
In April, 74% of respondents in France said they were worried about the climate crisis but that figure was up to 83% by mid-August and still at that level last month.
The number of French people who were “very worried” about climate change also rose, from 28% in April to a record high of 42% in August, a level it held last month. Concern in other countries spiked in August but has since dipped.
In Germany, for example, the number very concerned rose from 27% in April to 40% in August but has now fallen back to 31%. Concern remained relatively stable in Denmark, at 66%-69% “worried” and 20%-23% “very worried”.
Across the six countries surveyed, respondents mostly (45%-63%) thought it was not too late to avert the worst impacts of the climate crisis but that it would require a drastic change in approach. Only 11%-24% believed it was already too late.
Between 9% and 20% said they thought current measures would be enough to prevent the most serious impacts. But in terms of what climate actions had support, those not directly affecting people’s lives were the most popular.
Measures such as planting more trees, subsidising energy efficiency, banning single-use plastics and taxing big emitters were all favoured, while increasing fuel duty, limiting meat and dairy, taxing air fares and banning new petrol and diesel cars were opposed.
A similar pattern emerged when respondents were asked what steps they would be prepared to take: cheap and easy actions such as creating green space at home and eating only seasonal fruit and vegetables were popular, but not shopping exclusively secondhand or paying more for flights.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The measure slipped into UK budget that could protect spending on children, youth and rough sleeping | Heather Stewart
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
John Healey’s debut budget was far from a blockbuster, but it may come to be remembered for the birth of a plucky new character in the tax and spend universe – little PDEL.
It may not have the charm of Disney’s Wall-E, but PDEL (pronounced P-Del), or preventative departmental expenditure limit, to give it its full name, marks a welcome, and potentially very consequential, addition.
The chancellor made clear that ahead of what the Institute for Fiscal Studies has said will be a “brutal” spending review next year, the Treasury is prepared to ringfence the budget for preventive policies.
The impetus for the move came partly from No 10. Andy Burnham knows that to achieve some of the missions closest to his heart, such as tackling rough sleeping, he will have to make the argument that it’s worth spending more upfront to save the state in the longer term.
It’s an intuitive idea, yet it’s not how the government tends to think about spending – and it’s certainly not how the Treasury makes decisions.
In the cut and thrust of a spending review, a process in which the Treasury’s power over the public purse is at its most muscular, individual departments are under pressure to show how they will save money from their own budgets.
Yet many of society’s greatest challenges have impacts across several departments. The future savings made by spending on, say, family hubs, may show up years in the future, and across several other departments – in the welfare bill, the health budget, even the criminal justice system.
In a 2023 paper that introduced the idea of PDEL, the thinktank Demos identified £22bn of costs to government that it claimed could have been averted by preventive programmes.
“For decades, governments have talked about the importance of prevention, but the system has consistently rewarded spending on dealing with crises rather than stopping them from happening in the first place,” said Demos’s chief executive, Polly Curtis.
In the Treasury documents that accompany the spending review, and more importantly in the months of wrangling beforehand, PDEL will have its own storyline, alongside RDEL – day-to-day, or “resource” spending for each department, and CDEL – investment.
It sounds technical, and it is – but we have plenty of evidence that the way public spending is categorised changes the way it is debated and understood.
Before Labour came to power in 1997, day-to-day spending and investment were not formally separated in the public finances, but Gordon Brown was rightly keen for long-term investment and day-to-day spending to be considered separately.
Disaggregating RDEL and CDEL allowed him to set the “golden rule” – that it was fine for the government to borrow to invest, but current spending should be covered by taxation.
Separating out capital spending didn’t prevent the Tories raiding it repeatedly during the austerity years – and indeed, Whitehall departments have just been asked to cut back future capital budgets to fund the defence investment plan.
But it does allow additional scrutiny, and a new kind of conversation about which areas of public spending are most important.
Demos’s argument is that some kinds of day-to-day spending, while not “investment”, in strict accounting terms, are worth protecting, because scrapping them could bring short-term cash benefits but carry net costs to the government over time.
Gavin Kelly, the chief executive of the Nuffield Foundation, which funds social research, says the shift to thinking about preventive spending makes sense now, because we have better data to inform policymakers.
He points to a series of IFS studies, funded by Nuffield, which showed Labour’s Sure Start centres boosted children’s education performance, increased their future wages, and even reduced hospital admissions, for example.
“Over the last decade, we’ve become more able to forensically link datasets across different aspects of services, illuminating how decisions in one public service can go on to impact other services and outcomes. That wasn’t possible in the same way in the past. The agility of decision-making about how and where we spend has not kept up with some of these data advances.”
Healey offered precious few details in the budget as to how PDEL will be defined but the Treasury says departments will have to make the argument for individual projects to be considered as preventive.
Rough sleeping is one area it highlights. Alan Milburn appears poised to make a similar argument in his soon-to-be-published review into young people not in education, employment or training, saying that money spent now on employment support potentially saves future costs on welfare, health and housing. Demos also highlights early mental health support and obesity prevention.
It does not seem beyond the bounds of possibility that, if defined tightly enough, preventive spending could even come to be considered “investment,” for the purposes of the fiscal rules, though the Treasury says that is not the plan.
That would mean the government being prepared to borrow today to fund projects it strongly believes would save money over time – a similar logic to the argument for investment in bridges or roads, but with a more social slant.
However, no amount of accounting tweaks can disguise the fact that, based on the figures Healey set out in the budget, next year’s spending review – which could take place as late as the autumn – looks impossibly tough.
He clearly hopes better news will come along, to ease the squeeze. But you can’t ringfence your way out of what the IFS reckons is £27bn-worth of spending pressures.
Against that bleak narrative arc, it remains to be seen if PDEL can play a starring role, or turns out to be just a side character. But perhaps it can at least help to bring some longer-term thinking to bear.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Healey’s budget cuts mean Britain is likely to miss green heating targets
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Britain is unlikely to hit its targets on green heating after the cuts announced by John Healey this week, experts have warned, as critics of Ed Miliband claim the former energy secretary’s green agenda is being dismantled.
The chancellor unveiled more than £3bn worth of cuts to the energy department’s budget this week, much of which will pay for higher defence spending.
One casualty of the cuts is the government’s scheme to subsidise heat pumps, leading to warnings that clean heating ambitions are being undermined.
Some believe the cuts are evidence of a broader shift away from the pro-renewables agenda pushed by Miliband and his successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh. However, energy department sources insisted the government’s longer-term changes will incentivise people to move towards cleaner power sources and benefit the overall green agenda.
Andrew Sissons, a director at the research charity Nesta, said: “After the cuts announced on Wednesday, it is very difficult to see how we can hit our clean heating targets. It is even possible that a Labour government will be the first to miss the targets it has signed up to in the current carbon budget.”
Healey announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments.
Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps.
Under the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, and was planning to increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30.
The plan forms a key part of the UK’s programme to clean up its heating networks and hit its overall emissions reduction targets. However, ministers said on Wednesday the scheme’s funding would rise only in line with inflation, meaning the number of installations is likely to stagnate or rise much more slowly than previously planned.
“It’s disappointing – so frustrating,” said Ed Matthew, the director of the UK programme at the thinktank E3G. “We are behind a lot of other countries in rolling out heat pumps and we need a sea change in take-up to change that.”
The cuts to heat pump subsidies came alongside about £250m of other cuts to the warm homes plan, £500m worth of cuts to hydrogen schemes, and £200m to funding for carbon capture and storage technology – all projects once championed by Miliband.
Healey also announced that renewable projects would only be approved in future if they could be shown to bring costs down and were ready to be connected with the grid. Officials insist the government remains committed to its target of having clean power by 2030, though many experts believe that will be impossible under the new system.
One government source said: “This is probably the most significant shift we have seen in energy policy since we came to office. The emphasis now is on cost, not just building to make sure there is enough capacity to hit our green targets.”
Paul Ovenden, a former adviser to Keir Starmer, said: “It is fascinating to see the energy capital budgets being raided to fund defence – this is the bones of Ed Miliband’s project being picked clean.
“This was something that has been discussed in government before – but Miliband always won that argument. Now he’s not in that department any more, it’s happened.”
Ovenden added: “Had he not helped to oust Starmer and Reeves, he’d probably be in post still and it wouldn’t have been possible.”
But allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever. They pointed out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed.
They also said the government’s intention to change energy markets so electricity prices are no longer so attached to gas prices would help encourage consumers to move away from fossil fuels.
One source said: “Ed and Miatta have both made affordability their focus. It would be wrong to suggest that prioritising cost is in any way a shift away from the green agenda.”
A spokesperson for the energy department said: “Over the last two years, we have made considerable progress, thanks to the momentum of clean power 2030, seeing £110bn of private-sector investment announced and securing enough clean power for over 20m homes.
“We are committed to making the most of clean, homegrown power and meeting our heat pump target to protect consumers from volatile fossil fuel prices.”
