SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by lack of expertise, report says
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship.
An audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised.
“Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit, published on Wednesday, reads.
The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says.
It cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China.
Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, says Ipac, pointing to budget cuts as an additional problem.
Ipac counts almost 50 MPs among its members, including from Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National party, the Greens and Reform.
Ipac member and former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”.
A UK government spokesperson said that while working with China presented opportunities, “we are also clear-eyed about the threats China poses, and national security is the first duty of government”.
“We will cooperate with China where we can while meeting any challenges head-on,” they added.
The Chinese embassy in London said Ipac’s “sole agenda is to manufacture falsehoods, mislead the public, and undermine China’s relations with other countries”.
The report “distorts the facts” and “is not even worth refuting”, it added.
While the Ipac report accepts that “disengagement is not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies and human rights.
The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains.
Emerging technologies such as AI represent “another front we’re potentially facing”, Labour’s Dame Meg Hillier said at the launch, with the report identifying areas of concern such as disinformation and surveillance capabilities.
The climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment.
“Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium-term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says.
The government conducted its own audit of the UK-China relationship in late 2024 but has said it cannot publish most of the detail for fear of damaging national interests.
But Evan Fowler, author of the Ipac report, said that a public audit was important “because engagement with China doesn’t just happen at the government level”.
It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London.
However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China.
“Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said.
“You can’t teach really important things in a classroom; you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump administration asks Washington to set aside hundreds of ballots from suspected noncitizen voters
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Trump administration on Monday asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it alleges are registered to vote without US citizenship, less than two weeks after making a similar demand in California.
The announcement is the latest sign of the administration’s attempts to sow doubts about the election or its outcome in states with races that will help determine control of the US Senate and House.
In a letter to Washington secretary of state Steve Hobbs, the justice department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by more than 400 people in prior elections. It asked the state to set aside any ballots they might cast in next month’s midterm elections until state officials can confirm they are legally eligible to vote. The state has more than 5 million registered voters, and the state issues mail ballots to all of them.
At a news conference, Charles Neil Floyd, the acting US attorney in Seattle, said he believed the 405 voters identified so far represented “the tip of the iceberg”.
“Because of limitations the state has placed on our investigation, we’ve only been able to uncover a fraction of the total number,” he said.
Hobbs said he was reviewing the justice department’s request. His office noted that the data shared by the department included the last time each of the 405 people voted. One was in 1994.
“The timing of this request – one week before the general election – is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results,” Hobbs said.
Much of the list was built based on “recent contacts” with suspected noncitizens, Floyd said, because federal officers are now routinely checking to see if the people they interact with are registered to vote.
Without access to those state records, proving someone illegally voted will be difficult, Floyd said. The justice department has demanded information including addresses, dates of birth, driver’s license numbers and partial social security numbers.
The effort is the latest by the administration to identify noncitizen voters, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine public confidence in elections.
Meanwhile, Washington officials have noted that changes in US Postal Service operations have disenfranchised thousands of legitimate voters.
The Washington request marks the third time this month that the justice department has brought a direct state challenge as voting is under way. All three states – Washington, California and Alaska – have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in the country's Capitol.
The race for Washington’s third congressional district is one of the most competitive in the country in this year’s midterm elections. Democrats are counting on congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez winning reelection as crucial to their strategy of retaking the majority in the House. She has won twice in a district that also has supported the president each time he’s been on the ballot.
The justice department sued California as part of a similar attempt to require the state to set aside mail ballots from up to 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. Another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win.
In California, a panel of federal appellate judges heard rare Sunday arguments and questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Department of Justice’s demand. On Monday, they declined to rule on the expedited timeline the justice department requested and sent it back to a lower court.
The elections clause of the US constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections.
Los Angeles county assistant registrar-recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that her staff went through a sample of 200 records from the Trump administration’s list. They found the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, people with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States.
California state officials touted the appeals court’s decision on Monday as a victory for voting rights. The state’s attorney general Rob Bonta vowed to “fight back against the administration’s unlawful overreach at every turn”. California governor Gavin Newsom meanwhile accused Trump of an assault on democracy.
The justice department told Washington it anticipates sending the state an additional list of people it suspects are not citizens prior to election day. It also noted that some of the people it suspects registered without citizenship may have since become naturalized.
Nick Robins-Early contributed reporting.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content: A protest in London against the development of the Jackdaw and Rosebank fields. Campaigners used court action last year to halt the gas and oil projects. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA protest in London against the development of the Jackdaw and Rosebank fields. Campaigners used court action last year to halt the gas and oil projects. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockExplainerWhat does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?Decision has implications for household energy bills, the UK economy and the climate crisis Andy Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drilling About four years and six energy secretaries after it was given the green light, the Jackdaw gasfield is to be given consent on Wednesday to begin production 150 miles east of Aberdeen.So what will this long-awaited decision mean for the Labour party, household bills, the economy and the climate crisis?Does this break a Labour manifesto promise?No, because although the party vowed to “not issue new licences to explore new fields” in the hydrocarbon-rich basin, it made clear it would honour licences granted before it came to power.These fields include Jackdaw, which was granted a licence in 2022, and the larger Rosebank oilfield west of Shetland, which was approved the following year.Oil and gas licences give broad permission to explore an area for fossil fuels but consent is still needed to extract them. Although Jackdaw and Rosebank had both, they were blocked from starting production after a legal challenge by campaigners at Greenpeace and Uplift early last year.That ruling compelled the companies behind the project to resubmit their applications with extra information on the climate impact of the fuels produced.Jackdaw is owned and operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norway’s state oil company, Equinor. Adura also hopes to develop Rosebank in conjunction with Ithaca Energy. A decision on Rosebank’s new application for consent is expected soon.View image in fullscreenThe North Sea is an ageing hydrocarbon basin in terminal decline, while still offering economic benefits. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianWill the Jackdaw decision lower energy bills?Probably not. Household bills are based on the price of gas in the UK wholesale market, which is determined by international prices that have surged amid disruptions to global supplies.These have included the loss of Russian flows to Europe and disruption to Gulf exports to buyers around the world – shocks far too big for the relatively small output from Jackdaw to outweigh.The Tories have claimed drilling could still help to lower bills under their plans to use tax revenues to cut VAT on gas and electricity bills for three years. However, this does not mean energy costs are fundamentally lower – or sustainable.Meanwhile, Labour has cut VAT from electricity bills from this month until next March and ministers are understood to be planning to offer billions in energy bill support for low-income households at next week’s budget.What about the UK’s carbon emissions?Gas from Jackdaw could release between 23.6m and 35.8m tonnes of CO2 equivalent over its 11-year operational lifespan, but the carbon impact of new North Sea fields is “not clear cut”. That’s the view of the Committee on Climate Change (CCC), which advises the government on meeting its legally binding climate targets.There are two sorts of emission to consider: firstly the “scope 1 and 2” kind, created from getting fossil fuels out of the ground and transporting them to users. These are relatively low in the British North Sea and make up about 3% of the UK’s total. In fact, the CCC has said there might be “emissions advantages” to the switch because scope 1 and 2 emissions from UK gas are by some estimates four times lower than from US and Gulf fossil gas imports.The second, far bigger impact is from the “scope 3” emissions created from burning the fossil fuel. Although Jackdaw’s gas would release CO2 when used in homes, businesses, factories and power plants, there is no evidence it would lead to higher overall gas consumption.As Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said in July: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from.” A better way to reduce UK emissions would be to replace gas boilers and fossil fuel vehicles with electric alternatives powered by low-carbon sources.What about the impact on global emissions?Here too, the answer is unclear. Some academics have suggested that more UK oil and gas would push up fossil fuel production globally unless output fell elsewhere.In 2024, the CCC said new fossil fuel developments would have a “minimal impact on UK carbon budgets” but that if others followed the UK’s lead in increasing production the cumulative impact could lead to “an oversupply that would pose a risk” to international targets.It urged the UK government to “reassess whether further exploration for new sources of fossil fuels” was aligned with its global climate obligations. This supports the government’s ban on new licences but would not rule out Jackdaw – which is not a new source.Moreover, a global oversupply of fossil fuels does not necessarily lead to greater emissions. In 2025, China’s crude oil imports hit a record 11m barrels a day but its emissions continued to fall because it was building its crude stocks to a record high of 1.4bn barrels.In short, emissions are largely due to energy consumption, not energy production. So if consumption continues to decline, emissions will fall regardless of the amount of fossil fuels made available in the global market.Where does this leave the UK’s climate agenda?Green groups have argued that allowing North Sea developments to move ahead would undermine the UK’s role as a climate leader and weaken its ability to use climate diplomacy to encourage other nations to adopt green energy policies.However, their opposition has been focused less on Jackdaw and more on the impact of the larger Rosebank scheme, which Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary turned foreign secretary, described as “climate vandalism” while he was in opposition. If the government goes on to also give consent for this project it could fuel accusations of climate hypocrisy at the top of the cabinet, undermining the UK’s ambition to be a global climate leader.John Gummer argued as CCC chair in 2022 that an end to UK exploration “would send a clear signal to investors and consumers” and “help the UK in its diplomatic efforts to strengthen climate ambition internationally”.So what might the economic benefits be?The North Sea is an ageing hydrocarbon basin in terminal decline but supporting new projects still offers economic benefits, including higher tax revenues from oil and gas companies, income tax from well-paid workers and job creation within the industry and its supply chain.Offshore Energies UK, an industry body, has promised the government that approving both Jackdaw and Rosebank could provide £1.4bn in tax revenues by 2029, rising to £3.8bn by 2034. It has also claimed the fields could support a peak of more than 3,500 jobs during the construction phase and 880 jobs with an average salary of £85,850 over the lifetime of the fields.Green groups reject these figures, arguing they overstate the economic benefits. Regardless, they are still relatively modest in the context of the broader economy.Given the disputed impact, why is the debate so febrile?The North Sea has become a totemic issue. For some, the basin is steeped in nostalgia for a long-gone period of British economic success and innovation, while for others it is a reminder of the UK’s longstanding contribution to the climate crisis and its responsibility to take action.“It has sucked all the oxygen out of the debate around what to do about climate change,” the CCC’s former chief executive, Chris Stark, told the New Statesman in 2024. “It means we haven’t got the political capital to deploy on the heat pump story, or the electric vehicle story. That’s where the action needs to be.”Explore more on these topicsOilOil and gas companiesGreenpeaceScotlandClimate crisisLabourEnergy industryexplainersShareReuse this content

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Eight of England’s nine water companies still failing on environment, report finds
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has summoned water industry bosses to Whitehall after a report found that the environmental performance of the big companies has worsened despite investment.
“People are sick of excuses,” Dame Angela said, after the Environment Agency joined the Drinking Water Inspectorate, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat for a joint report that rated eight of the nine water companies in England as “poor” or “requiring improvement”.
There were 74 serious pollution incidents, the category that causes significant harm to the environment, the report said. That was just one fewer than the previous year, despite billions of pounds of investment, bans on bosses’ bonuses and a public outcry. The watchdog’s environmental performance assessment ratings of water companies added up to 16 “stars” out of a possible 36, a fall from 19 the previous year, and the lowest score since the process began.
Changes could be imposed on the industry, Eagle warned: “Water companies have let the public down time and time again, and today’s report is further proof that root-and-branch reform cannot wait.”
The UK is one of only two countries in the world where the provision of water is fully privatised. The other is Chile, where water privatisation was imposed in the 1980s by a military dictatorship.
Overall, there were 2,666 pollution incidents in England in 2025 – a 40% increase on 2016, the EA said. Thames Water had the most, followed by Anglian Water, United Utilities, Yorkshire Water and Southern Water.
The Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Eagle was preparing to take “further action”, with “tougher consequences” for executives at failing companies.
Defra said it would “set out a clear set of improvement actions”, such as “tackling leakage”, “reductions in pollution incidents” and “improving customer satisfaction”. Rules that took effect last year would block bonuses for executives at companies receiving a one-star rating.
Environmental campaigners called for stronger action. “This is a system that rewards shareholders and creditors while our rivers, wildlife and bill payers lose out,” said James Wallace, the chief executive of River Action.
Thames Water, the worst offender, ought to go into special administration immediately, he said. “Ministers must end the failed privatisation experiment, review alternative models including public ownership, and give regulators the power to make polluters pay not the public.”
The four agencies have pooled their data in a joint report for the first time – a step towards combining currently fragmented regulatory responsibilities under a single watchdog. But Richard Benwell, the chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said a new regulator “must be more than a merger of existing institutions”.
“It needs a clear legal duty to restore nature, strong environmental targets and the powers and resources to enforce the law across the water industry, industrial agriculture, and chemical companies,” he said.
Water UK, the industry trade body, said: “Today’s report shows the lowest level of leakage in history, as well as other areas of good performance. However, the fact remains that the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough.
“While more than half of all pollution incidents last year were caused by blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies, there is clearly more work to do.
“It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth and end sewage entering rivers and seas.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Can curry nights and canny advisers help Healey deliver a budget for everyday people?
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Every Sunday night, the chancellor, John Healey, slips next door to Andy Burnham’s Downing Street flat where they order a curry and chew over politics on the prime minister’s sofa.
An Indian takeaway is one of the totemic issues in British politics, a “treat” fewer people can afford, like a pint at the football or soft play for the kids.
Healey has promised to give Britain’s battered consumers “breathing space” in next week’s budget, but three months after taking on the job, the new chancellor also hopes to buy himself time.
Key decisions will be postponed until a spending review at some point next year – including when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence: the issue that prompted Healey’s resignation as defence secretary in June, hastening Keir Starmer’s departure.
The weekly curry summit is a chance, as some aides see it, to separate Healey from cautious Treasury officials, and get him to kick around the politics.
With just a few days to go before the budget, every adviser and official remarks on how closely the prime minister is involved: not just in decision-making, but in the process and politics – unlike Starmer.
“Keir wanted to be presented with three ideas and then pick one,” one aide says. “But, actually, in politics, sometimes you need to bash things around and come up with ideas. And that Sunday night is a bit of that – wrestling with some of Britain’s problems.”
The budget on 28 October – and the public response – will set the course for what comes next. Much of the Burnham project depends on how it is received. “After this we will be in election mode,” one aide says. That may not mean an imminent snap election, but few people believe Burnham will go longer than May 2028.
There will be another big presence in the budget – Rachel Reeves. More and more Labour strategists mention a growing gratitude to Healey’s Treasury predecessor, who had often been previously seen as a symbol of the party’s missteps.
“She made the mistakes, yes, but she left us a Labour Treasury,” one adviser says. “It’s a very different ballgame to stepping straight into a Conservative Treasury, I think we realise that now.
“And she had to take those massive decisions early on and do a big tax and spend budget because public services were on their knees and it was a crisis we had to start to fix. But from that point, now we can start to think about other priorities.”
In Bangkok last week, where Healey attended the International Monetary Fund annual meetings, Reeves’s tax and spending plans meant the UK was praised as the only G7 country with a plan to tackle its budget deficit – and urged to “stay the course”.
The IMF also revised up its forecast for UK growth for 2026 – reflecting the economy’s better-than-expected performance, despite the effects of the Iran war.
Healey’s presence in Thailand was brief. He eschewed the public discussions on the state of the global economy that Reeves enjoyed, leaving speechmaking to the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who took the opportunity of the global gathering to set out Britain’s plans for its presidency of the G20 next year.
Healey, who as ever travelled with a bottle of HP sauce in his luggage, managed to find time to film an excruciating social media video with Miliband, riding a tuk-tuk through the hectic night-time streets of the Thai capital while discussing their favourite snacks.
Back in the UK, he has told Treasury staff that when he is drafting the budget he is thinking about people in the small towns and villages in his constituency in South Yorkshire. But there is a particular character to those smaller towns – home to small businesses and self-employed sole traders, rather than big industry or public services.
It is these people, in particular, say sources close to Healey, whom he hopes to protect and give “breathing space” – perhaps a veiled acknowledgment that small businesses have borne too much of the brunt of some of Labour’s tax and regulations in the early years of this parliament.
“He has spent a lot of the time thinking about the cost of business and cost of doing business – something that’s driven him quite heavily,” one source says.
Treasury insiders say Healey is more formal in meetings than Reeves; and that his past stint in Whitehall’s most powerful department means he understands how to manage its bright civil servants.
He has urged officials to come up with innovative solutions to the challenge of handing over more tax revenue to regional mayoralties – an idea first announced by Reeves, but given impetus by Burnham’s pro-devolution agenda. “It’s the biggest challenge that they’ve had for a really long time. And you can see the groupthink sometimes – but you can also see the spark in these really clever people,” says one adviser.
When it comes to economic strategy, Healey has inherited some of Reeves’s advisers, including the tax expert Spencer Thompson, and hired Ravinder Athwal, the author of Labour’s 2024 manifesto. Healey’s chief of staff, Will Straw, a senior figure in the Remain campaign back in 2016, is viewed as a canny political operator.
Yet like Reeves before him, Healey seems to lack a figure who combines economic expertise with political heft: the equivalent of Ed Balls in Gordon Brown’s Treasury, or Rupert Harrison in George Osborne’s. Burnham’s No 10 is also advertising for political advisers with economic backgrounds, including a specialist in macroeconomics and growth.
Though aides are keen to stress the closeness of Burnham and Healey, their different approaches have led to early whispers about tensions in their partnership. “I am not sure how we reconcile the end of 40 years of neoliberalism and the approach of this chancellor,” one Labour adviser says.
A government minister adds that the central question Healey has to answer in drawing up the budget is how much tax and spending policy should be adjusted in response to the damage wreaked on the public finances by the Iran war.
The chancellor’s answer appears to be: as little as possible – with the hope that by the time of a spending review, the geopolitical situation has improved, and with it, the public finances.
Donald Trump’s Middle East adventure has pushed up inflation, and in turn the interest rate the UK government must pay servicing its £3tn debt-pile.
These higher interest costs are likely to have more than offset the benefits of higher-than-expected economic growth in bumper tax revenues – perhaps halving the £24bn headroom Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules.
Healey is expected to allow the headroom to take some of the strain and opt for a low-key budget statement – raising a few billions in taxes, including on banks, and giving some of that away again to households.
He is likely to opt for a relatively modest energy support package, of perhaps £1.5bn – “targeted and temporary”, as the IMF has urged.
But with the Bank of England widely expected to raise interest rates the following week, hitting mortgage borrowers; inflation expected to top 4% in the new year, and the energy price cap rising by perhaps another 16% in January, consumers may not feel particularly grateful.
Some senior Labour figures have urged Healey to be more blunt about the connection between rising costs at home and Trump’s Iran war.
Advocates of more generous energy support argue it could cut bills – and hence inflation – alleviating some of the pressure on the Bank to hike interest rates and convince voters Burnham is making a fresh start.
“He needs to do something big and bold enough for the public to think, this is why we’ve got a new prime minister and chancellor,” says Michael Jacobs, an emeritus professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield and a former adviser to Brown. “I think the public will be bewildered by a steady as she goes budget.”
Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, says it will not have gone unnoticed in Downing Street that the riots on the streets of France have been partly driven by the soaring cost of living.
“If you’re the Treasury, if you’re the prime minister, you’re certainly looking across the pond at the growing unrest around the cost of living, tensions on that front,” he says. “Clearly we’re in a different place to France but if there are some low-hanging fruit – temporary measures – across the next two or three-quarters, it could go a long way.”
The latest consumer confidence data, which was published on Friday, shows a sharp slide into pessimism, amid what the consultancy GfK, which collects the figures, calls “relentless cost-of-living pressures”, even before winter bites.
If cash-strapped households have to start cutting back on little pleasures like that occasional takeaway, there must be a risk the “breathing space” voters seem to have been prepared to offer Burnham’s government, may not last much beyond the budget.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on a migration U-turn: it still leaves unfair changes intact | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Shabana Mahmood has made a partial retreat on her policy to lengthen the wait for some foreign workers who were soon to be eligible for settlement in the UK. But while the home secretary lost the argument in cabinet on a particularly damaging aspect of her proposals, she has won the larger battle that settlement ought to be based not just on residency but also on how much tax has been paid, English language proficiency and the “character” of applicants. Significantly, she has also won the “full support” of the prime minister for this approach.
The home secretary plans to double the standard qualifying period for settlement from five to 10 years for most workers. Importantly, she dropped the proposed 15-year qualifying period for some workers in occupations below graduate level. That is a good thing. Differences in pay, however, should not determine how soon people can put down secure roots. The Home Office’s own figures suggest that a person earning £41,700 makes a similarly positive lifetime fiscal contribution as someone earning £50,271. But the former has to wait five years longer to qualify for settlement than the latter. It is only three years for foreign workers who make enough to be in the top 2% of earners – about £125,000.
It was right that Britain recruited people to perform essential care work after the pandemic to fill gaps in the workforce. But it was wrong for Ms Mahmood to propose using the poor remuneration of that work to delay their permanent place in society. Ms Mahmood’s concession corrects that for some people. But it will cause insecurity for others. Those who came to this country between 2022 and 2025, meet their care worker visa conditions and are paid £25,000 or more will still be able to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) – effectively permanent residency – after five years. The Home Office says that that could cover as many as 146,000 care workers and 136,000 dependants.
However, those who do not meet the requirements will have to get another five-year “health and social care” visa before applying for ILR. The care sector has been beset by allegations that unscrupulous employers have exploited migrant staff by taking advantage of their vulnerable visa status. The government is less clear about how it will be able to tell whether earnings had been deliberately kept low by unprincipled firms.
On asylum, Ms Mahmood makes settlement depend on how people reached Britain. Those admitted through “safe and legal” routes can settle after five years; others face much longer waits – up to 30 years for “illegal entry” by small boat, even after their need for protection has been recognised. But the UN says that refugees cannot apply directly for UK resettlement. Ministers must explain how penalising people for failing to use a route largely unavailable to them amounts to fair play.
Ms Mahmood’s plans are a step towards a Gastarbeiter Britain. The guest-worker logic of the home secretary’s proposals – like that of postwar West Germany – is to admit foreigners to fill labour shortages in lower-earning work while keeping their membership of society conditional. Calling this integration seems a stretch. Settling down, changing jobs at will and planning a family life are how people put down roots. Ms Mahmood’s plans are likely to frustrate the integration that she says she wants.
-

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing Institute
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute.
The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson.
The institute is the UK’s leading AI research body and is under new leadership after the government, its main source of funding, demanded a strategic shift.
“As AI becomes more embedded in critical services, in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control, or that could be restricted or even switched off,” said Williamson.
In June Washington temporarily blocked the release outside the US of Anthropic’s latest models, and has reportedly asked leading AI labs to withhold their models from being tested by the UK’s AI Security Institute until they have been examined by AISI’s US counterpart.
“We’ve seen now that both political and commercial pressures mean we may not have access [to AI] in all the circumstances when we want it. That is not a place where a nation wants to be,” he said.
Williamson added: “There’s a set of circumstances where it would be a good idea for us to have something that we don’t have to ask other people’s permission to use.”
He said national resilience would be a focus of ATI’s work amid concern about the geopolitical situation and the risk posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.
Those concerns were highlighted last month by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announcing a new national centre to tackle state-backed disinformation, and Anthropic predicting the technology had a greater than 10% chance of wiping out humanity by 2030.
“It’s a moment when national resilience is definitely what the country needs and it’s definitely a thing I think the Turing institute can help with,” he said.
“We are facing a more adversarial world, more frequent shocks to our critical infrastructure and now powerful AI amplifying these threats. To strengthen national resilience, the Turing will focus on securing critical systems against disruption, countering threats from AI itself and helping to shape the right strategic AI capability for the UK.”
Williamson said the institute could assist in building such resilience by helping produce uses for AI “for the public good”, working on areas from weather forecasting to farming, as well as helping spot disinformation. Referring to state-led disinformation campaigns, he said: “It’s very dangerous for the state of democracy and it’s an area that we can monitor.”
Williamson is the former head of His Majesty’s Government Communications Centre, a secretive government body that makes gadgets for UK spy agencies and counts Alan Turing – the second world war codebreaker and AI pioneer after which ATI is named – among its former staff.
Williamson said it had become clear in recent months that the UK needed “more agency on access to technology” and a stronger sovereign position in AI. “It feels pretty uncomfortable if you don’t have some control or ability to use technologies when you want them, and also harder to imagine how you build an economy on the top of stuff that can disappear,” he said.
In recent weeks Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, have urged Europe to be more self-sufficient in AI, with Lagarde speaking about the threat of being “cut off” from US and Chinese technology.
Williamson cited China as another reason for boosting domestic AI, amid concerns that Chinese-made systems might not “coincide with our values”. He said: “Try asking some of these models about some events in the recent past in China and you’re not going to get an answer that’s particularly helpful if you’re doing GCSE history.”
“This is the defining technology of our time. We want to be able to shape that technology … in a way that accords with who we are and our values,” he said, adding that while ATI and the UK probably could not match the financial resources of major AI labs, they could still produce “nationally owned IP” or smaller models that could be made available to startups.
“We can be ambitious here without trying to copy what frontier labs are doing,” he said.
Williamson said ATI, a registered charity, could be an “objective and helpful” arbiter of concerns about AI, including existential threat. “A national institute should be an active partner to government and the public more generally in helping to navigate some of this stuff.”
He said there was a “a lot of stuff being tossed around” on the existential threat risk that “is not always well grounded in science”. Referring to the penchant among some in the sector for expressing the risk of AI-triggered extinction in percentage terms, he said: “I’m not sure it’s helpful trying to assign particular percentages to it because I have not seen anyone show me a convincing evidence of how they’ve arrived at the number they then start throwing around.”
Williamson indicated that the focus on national resilience would enable ATI to keep doing work on the environment that Keir Starmer’s government had wanted to sideline. In 2025 the then technology secretary, Peter Kyle, wrote to ATI’s chair demanding the institute switch its main focus to defence and security. Williamson’s predecessor Jean Innes resigned soon afterwards.
“For me climate is as much a national security issue as defence. For me, it [national resilience] is a frame that enables us to cover the range of threats and opportunities to the UK,” he said.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Reform UK launches its own ‘newspaper’ with Farage on front page
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Reform UK has launched what it is calling a newspaper, featuring large pictures of Nigel Farage, which the party hopes will replace mainstream media for its supporters.
Though the party is hiring qualified journalists to write its newspapers, the only “reporter” credited with writing articles is Farage, the party leader.
Political parties often put out pamphlets made to look like newspapers in local areas during elections, but it is unusual for a party to put out a paper nationally, year-round. The party has said it wishes to build a “significant national publishing operation” as well as its TV channel hosted on YouTube.
In his first column for the publication, Farage writes: “We have had enough of what we say and do being distorted by the media. So instead, we want to talk to you directly, and make sure that you get our message straight from the Reformer.”
Its front-page story features a photograph of Farage smiling and posing with a labrador, with the headline “Nigel Farage: we will fix broken Britain”.
Other stories include “Clacton result: Farage 22,239, Establishment 0.” This refers to the byelection called by Farage after he resigned his Essex seat following revelations about an undeclared £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. The gift was revealed by the Guardian earlier this summer. The other main parties declined to stand in the ensuing byelection, with the result that Farage’s main opponent was Count Binface.
One piece advertises Reform’s plan to use the Royal Navy to send back migrants who travel across the Channel in small boats. It says: “A Reform UK government will launch Operation Fortress. Prime Minister Nigel Farage will order the Royal Navy to stop the boats and return the illegal immigrants to France. Not one will make it to Britain.” Military experts have criticised this plan, saying the navy should not be used as a ferry service.
Other articles include a short tribute to Ann Widdecombe, the Reform politician who was killed in her home in July, featuring a quote from Farage, and another piece by Farage in which he vows to declare a national emergency should he become prime minister. Other features include updates on local Reform politicians’ progress on filling in potholes and picking up litter.
Reform insiders said the first edition was “rushed” and to expect more news and features in subsequent editions, coming monthly.
Roles at the publication are still open, with 12 journalist jobs including executive editor, website editor and multimedia reporters/producers advertised online.
Reform sources said they thought the newspapers, being delivered to homes across Britain and available in the lobby of the party’s Westminster office, would drive up membership rates. Those who join the party using the cut-out form included in the newspaper are offered a free mug and badge.
Rather than being kept on the news stands in the lobby of Millbank Tower, where Reform has its headquarters, the Reformer is kept behind the desk at reception and available on request. The party says the paper has been sent to 15 million people across the country.
Readers of the publication are also urged to sign up as Reform candidates in the May 2027 local elections.
A report by Printweek revealed that the paper has been printed by Walstead Group, which has contracts with several of the UK’s leading newspapers including the Sunday Times and Sun on Sunday.
The paper is reportedly being led by Mick Hume, the founder and former editor of the online libertarian-right politics magazine Spiked, and is part of Reform’s drive to build a “national publishing operation” with a digital newsroom and expanded video content.
Though the first edition of the free paper does not appear to contain any exclusive news stories, budding reporters hoping to join the Reformer need to be able to produce scoops.
A job advert states: “Reform UK is building a seven-day digital newsroom at its Westminster headquarters and is looking for hard-working, NCTJ-qualified multimedia reporter/producers who can report, write and publish high-quality content at speed. The role sits at the heart of the party’s ambition to build the Reform UK website into a significant national publishing operation.”
It adds that applicants need to come up with original stories “rather than relying solely on rewriting or republishing material already available elsewhere”.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Rogue UK energy bosses and brokers face crackdown on mis-selling
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Energy bosses in the UK will have their bonuses curtailed when suppliers and brokers break the rules under a crackdown on mis-selling.
Through the energy independence bill, which will be introduced on Wednesday, Ofgem will be given new powers to order compensation, impose fines and ban rogue operators that have pushed businesses and households into overpriced contracts.
Companies with a business energy supply contract often use a broker to secure their deal, but – unlike the intermediaries who market mortgages or insurance deals – these energy middlemen are largely unregulated.
The government said rogue brokers had been able to push small businesses into overpriced energy contracts while pocketing hidden commissions, leaving companies paying more than they should.
These energy brokers and price comparison services will now be brought under Ofgem’s remit. The move is expected to save businesses more than £100m a year from hidden commissions and mis-selling.
The watchdog will also be given powers to crack down on payments to bosses who have “rewarded themselves while customers suffer”.
It follows public outrage over huge bonus payouts to executives despite investigations into the treatment of vulnerable customers.
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “People work hard for their money. They shouldn’t be ripped off by energy companies or forced to fight for fair treatment when things go wrong.
“When energy bosses fail their customers, they shouldn’t be walking away with bumper bonuses while families and businesses pick up the bill.”
The bill, which was announced in the king’s speech and is expected to set out more details on the government’s plans to transition to clean energy, comes as ministers face criticism over the green agenda.
John Healey recently unveiled more than £3bn of cuts to the energy department’s budget, much of which will pay for higher defence spending.
The chancellor also said he would veto new offshore wind projects if they did not lower bills, adding to concerns that the government was moving away from the pro-renewables agenda. However, the government says it is still committed to its target of clean power by 2030.
As part of the new bill, local authorities will be given stronger powers to tackle landlords who fail to meet energy efficiency standards, including fines of up to £30,000.
Since 2020, it has been illegal to let properties with energy performance certificate ratings below E, unless the landlord can show that it is exempt.
The government will also use the bill to introduce a moratorium on fracking by ending new licensing onshore in England. Fracking, which involves pumping liquid underground at high pressure to crack rock and release trapped oil or gas, is controversial because of its links to earthquakes and fears it could contaminate the water table.
It was banned by the Conservative government in 2019. However, in 2022, Liz Truss used her brief tenure as prime minister to overturn the ban, prompting widespread anger.
The minister for climate transition, Katie White, said the government was “putting communities first and protecting them from the risks of earthquakes and unsafe drilling”.
The moratorium will not include lower-volume fracking operations or “proppant squeeze”, which the fracking industry says is not a form of fracking. However, Tony Bosworth, an energy campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said this was an attempt to “creep in through the back door under a different name”.
The government said the low-volume activities were not under the scope of the ban and it was not aware of evidence that they posed the same risks as high-volume fracking.
Prof Stuart Haszeldine of the University of Edinburgh has said that earthquakes caused by lower-volume fracking can be as large and unpredictable as those caused by high-volume fracking.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘Digital hostile environment’: AI secretly being embedded across Home Office, report claims
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research.
Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG).
It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool.
Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry.
The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric.
It says AI is being trialled and tested in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall freedom of information requests and redact disclosures. Successive governments are criticised for pushing an ideology that reduces complex human cases to a technical problem that can be fixed.
The report raises concerns about “reducing people to data points” and replicating the hostile environment first envisaged by Theresa May as home secretary in 2012. “Relying on AI to decide who gets to stay here and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move,” it states.
Open Rights Group is calling on the government to regulate AI and ban uses that are undemocratic and risk human rights violations, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications.
It also wants more transparency and stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools.
Ribeiro-Addy said: “In spite of questions and requests, the Home Office has been reluctant to publish the documents that would explain how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. The department has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks.”
Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said: “Migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. We urgently need transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “Use of artificial intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.
“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims.
“We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their rollout.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Audi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearance
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally with Donald Trump just days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions of dollars of investment in battleground state Georgia.
Gernot Döllner joined Trump on stage after the US president gave a speech criticised by the head of an elected body of employees at Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, as being full of “racism, sexism, transphobia [and] contempt for democracy”.
Daniela Cavallo, the head of the VW works council, added that anyone who heard Trump’s speech and then saw that Döllner had become an active participant in the event must “sink into the ground with shame”, according to internal company communications released to German media.
She said the investment deal and Döllner’s appearance showed VW’s management had allowed itself to be “turned into a puppet in the propaganda show of a highly dubious political figure”.
Isabel Cademartori, the transport spokesperson for Germany’s Social Democrats – part of the country’s ruling coalition – called Döllner’s actions a “disgrace”. She added this was particularly so “in view of the history of the Volkswagen Group”, in an apparent reference to VW’s founding as a showcase company under the Nazis.
A spokesperson for the German government declined to comment on the matter, calling it “a business decision regarding where the company invests and, in this case, where the company’s chief executive appears”.
Döllner and Trump announced to the crowd on Saturday that Audi would spend $4bn to build its first factory in the US and create 4,500 jobs, even as VW aims to slash tens of thousands of positions and close plants in Germany.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Döllner said at the rally in Perry near Macon, in a highly unusual move for a European executive during a hard-fought US electoral campaign.
He called the plans, which foresee factory construction starting next year and car production beginning in the 2030s, “a long-term investment because we believe in the American market”.
Audi is the only premium car manufacturer without its own factory in the US, making it particularly vulnerable to Trump’s punishing 15% import tariffs, which cost it an estimated €1.2bn last year. The Macon plant would build 200,000 SUVs annually.
The head of the powerful German trade union IG Metall, Christiane Benner, called Döllner’s US appearance “extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company, but above all of Audi’s employees”.
She accused Döllner of being in “flagrant breach” of the company’s code of conduct, “which expressly requires political neutrality in the run-up to elections”.
She warned that any major investment like the Macon plant would have to go before VW’s supervisory board. Benner is the board’s deputy chair.
Volkswagen is locked in a battle between management and labour over a push to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the downsizing on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as US tariffs and the expensive transition to electric vehicles.
Its German factories are under particular pressure to drive down costs, with Audi’s facility in Neckarsulm, which employs 15,000 people, among four VW plants threatened with closure from early next decade.
“Each site must do its part in terms of competitiveness and the long-term strength of Audi,” a company spokesperson said.
Trump is deeply unpopular in Germany and has riled its political mainstream by vocally backing the far-right Alternative für Deutschland. The AfD is the country’s most popular party, according to polls, and has actively courted Trump’s support.
The 3 November election in Georgia could be decisive in the Democrats’ battle to regain a majority in the Senate. The incumbent senator, Jon Ossoff, is fighting a tough re-election battle against Republican challenger Mike Collins, in a state Trump won in 2024.
Trump has argued ahead of the midterms that his tariffs on car imports are helping the US economy.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Burnham aims for ‘quite radical change’ in support for young people
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The government is aiming for “quite radical change” in the way young people are supported, Andy Burnham has said, indicating this could include tougher rules for benefits as well as notably more help with everything from finding work to mental health.
In media interviews before the release of the second report by the former minister Alan Milburn on reducing the numbers of young people not in work, education or training, Burnham said his mission was “rethinking childhood” from the early years onwards.
Milburn’s review, due to be published this month, will call for ambitious efforts to help young people get jobs and training, and is expected to recommend moves to limit access to some benefits for people who refuse to engage.
The first part of his review, published in May and intended to set out the scale of the problem, said about one in eight young people – 1 million – were not working or in training. It blamed a series of largely structural factors, including inequality, the modern labour market and mental health.
This was “an issue of huge societal importance”, Burnham said in one of the interviews, with Times Radio. “If you leave young people in their 20s without hope, that is a dangerous thing to do,” he said. “People need to have a path. And I think if we look to the roots of this, I don’t think we have done enough to support young people growing up in a very different world to the one that many of us grew up in. The support hasn’t been there.”
He said Milburn’s report was not “a narrow consideration of just the benefits system … It’s got to be a root and branch review of childhood and how we support young people on their way in life.”
Asked if this could involve cutting some benefits, he replied: “I am prepared to take difficult decisions because I can’t accept the idea that we have a million or more young people in their 20s on benefits. It’s not good for them. It’s not good for anybody. So there does need to be quite radical change in the way we support young people.”
Likening the idea to the proposal to change the triple-lock system of guaranteed pension increases while at the same time bringing in a new system for adult social care, Burnham said the reappraisal of young people’s opportunities would begin in early years.
He said: “Too many young people are not school-ready when they come to school. And the evidence is many don’t catch up. If they’re not ready to learn in reception class, that gap stays all the way through the school system. So it’s part of this. It is about rethinking childhood, in every aspect of it.”
In a separate interview with the BBC, Burnham said he could not promise when the overall benefits bill would start to decrease, as there was a need to invest. “What will have to go up first is the spending on support for young people,” he said, noting this may mean having to “reprioritise” some money. But he said the overall bill would go down in time.
Asked if this would happen in this parliament, he said: “You do it in a way that’s sustainable. And if it could be this parliament – as soon as possible is the thing I would say to you.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Obama condemns comments by ‘border czar’ that Ilhan Omar could ‘of course’ be denaturalized
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Former US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s “border czar” that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of her citizenship and deport her.
Obama wrote Sunday morning, on X, that “the full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.”
He urged all Americans to defend Omar, regardless of their political beliefs, adding: “if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her – or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.” Obama, too, has had his citizenship scrutinized by Trump, who more than a decade ago fueled false conspiracy theories that Obama was born in Kenya and therefore not eligible to be president.
Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, was asked on Saturday by a Fox News host whether the investigation into Omar could involve “denaturalizing and then deporting her”, Homan answered: “Of course”.
“If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody,” Homan said. “We’ve done it before. It’s a long, tedious process, but it’s been done before.
“And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen.”
Homan’s comments were the first remarks explicitly mentioning denaturalization and deportation in connection with Omar that were attributed by name to a top Trump administration official since federal agents raided the Minnesota US House representative’s home on 12 October.
The search of Omar’s home sparked major backlash and accusations that the Trump administration was weaponizing the federal government to target a political rival whom the president and his supporters have openly fantasized about denaturalizing and deporting.
The federal government’s investigation into the most prominent Somali American in the US is to see whether Omar or her family violated any laws when obtaining her citizenship. The investigation was launched only weeks before the November midterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.
Homan also seemed to imply during his Fox News appearance that the federal government is investigating Omar for other allegations – but refused to give details.
“I’m not going to go there,” Homan said. “I know things, but that’s a question for the FBI.”
Omar – a naturalized US citizen from Somalia – was a child when her father filled out the immigration paperwork which the federal government is evidently scrutinizing. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, died in June 2020.
Obama stated in his post on X that Omar arrived in the US with her father when she was 12, and five years later, when her father became a naturalized citizen, she became one, too, because she was 17. (An 18-year-old would have had to apply for citizenship separately, he noted.)
“Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen,” he wrote. “Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone – all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.”
In a letter after her home was searched, Omar’s attorneys accused the US justice department of potentially influencing an election in violation of longstanding internal policy.
The move to investigate Omar came amid a heightened offensive by the administration in pursuit of its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown. In addition to funneling resources and deploying droves of officials to arrest, detain and deport undocumented immigrants throughout the country, the administration has also escalated its on offensive on legal migration.
The administration has been pursuing dozens of cases nationwide in which they are attempting to denaturalize Americans born outside of the US, who they claim fraudulently obtained their citizenship.
As Homan alluded to on Sunday, the lengthy denaturalization process requires a federal investigation and drawn-out court proceedings.
Nonetheless, as of April, the US justice department had reportedly identified nearly 400 foreign-born citizens that it sought to investigate.
The investigation into Omar follows unsubstantiated accusations by rightwing figures who support Trump that she obtained her citizenship fraudulently. Omar denies the accusations, which also include allegations that her ex-husband is her brother, whom she only married so he could obtain immigration status in the US.
The federal government reportedly seized Omar’s phone during the raid on her home and has issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives.
Omar’s attorneys have demanded that the federal government return her property and preserve any audio or video taken during the search.
Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was eight and spent years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She and her family came to the US in the 1990s, and she became a naturalized US citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers.
There is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, said her attorneys’ letter, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Even veterans at the Department of Justice expressed shock over the targeting of Omar, according to reporting by NBC News. “I was astounded to see a search of a sitting congressperson this close to an election,” said Peter Carr, a former career justice department spokesperson, NBC News reported.
“Historically, the department has been very adamant that politics plays no role in investigative decisions they make and they try very hard to avoid taking overt actions that might even have the perception of influencing an election.”
After the raid on her home, Omar posted on X that she was “ok”.
“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar also wrote. She said: “Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns” for years – and “this is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”
“I will not be silenced,” Omar added.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK hospitality sector to offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people out of work
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Bars, clubs and restaurants will offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years in an effort to give them a first step on the ladder into work.
The move comes before the publication of a report on Neets by the former health secretary Alan Milburn, who has warned that the number of young people not in work or education in the UK could rise to 1.25 million over the next five years unless ministers intervene.
His full review into Britain’s crisis in youth unemployment, including recommendations to the government about how to tackle the crisis, is expected soon after the autumn budget on 28 October.
Working with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), hospitality businesses including the restaurant chains Wagamama, Nando’s and Burger King, the hotel chain Premier Inn and pub chains including Fuller’s and Mitchells & Butlers will offer Neets aged 18 to 24 placements of up to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”.
The initiative, which will be launched by Andy Burnham during a visit to a hospitality venue on Thursday, comes after the DWP announced a similar scheme for retailers including Marks & Spencer, Asda, Pets at Home and the John Lewis Partnership last month.
The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said the scheme would help young people “get their first step on the ladder” and build their careers. “With the UK employment rate now the second highest in the G7, this will unlock 100,000 jobs and connect young people with employers ready to take them on and help them build a brighter future,” he said.
Lucy Powell, the education secretary, is expected to announce a review of school exclusion changes, after research showed that students who are persistently absent from school are nearly four times more likely to end up unemployed and not in education or training.
A consultation will gather views on measures to support students at risk of exclusion, improve integration into the classroom and help children stay engaged in the classroom.
Powell said: “Absence and exclusion are too often a path to disengagement, with increased risks of becoming Neet. Too many young people who fall out of education risk being permanently left on the sidelines of work and opportunity.”
Milburn has signalled that Britain’s benefits system should be overhauled, alongside measures to boost job support, training and apprenticeships. Ministers are understood to be considering sweeping changes to the welfare system, including scrapping a critical disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.
Milburn has previously argued that a national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work.
The chancellor, John Healey, has indicated a readiness to curtail the government’s rising benefits bill, while McFadden has said there is a moral and economic case to shake up the welfare system, as the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances.
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has made demands for cuts to welfare a central plank of her attacks on the government, telling Burnham in prime minister’s questions (PMQs) on Wednesday that he should cut welfare to fund higher defence spending.
But ministers will be wary of going head to head with Labour MPs, and will hope to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion that forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive | Heather Stewart
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to “end 40 years of neoliberalism”. But as he prepares for his first budget on Wednesday, his government is yet to let go of one of its most tedious cliches: red tape.
In the run-up to the chancellor John Healey’s high-stakes Commons address, the government issued a press release last week promising his plans would include measures to “slash the red tape choking firms”.
Named after the tape once used to tie up government bills, and popularised by the historian Thomas Carlyle, the phrase is straight from the neoliberal playbook and has long outlived its usefulness.
Getting the interfering state out of the way of the wealth creators was a trope of Thatcher and Reaganite economics, and on this side of the pond it has been repeated ad nauseam by every government since.
Thatcher unleashed the City with her “big bang” deregulation drive, and her successor John Major was enthusiastic about “hacking back the jungle of red tape”. It was the man he appointed for the job – Michael Heseltine – who coined what has become the most hackneyed description of this particular approach: the “bonfire of red tape”.
With Labour back in power, Gordon Brown celebrated a light-tough regulatory regime for the UK’s hard-driving financial sector – until the Treasury had to bail out the banks after the 2008 financial crisis.
Boris Johnson wanted to unfetter Britain’s businesses from “Brussels bureaucracy” and waffled on during the Brexit campaign about bendy bananas. Yet, after Brexit, business groups said their members would rather comply with longstanding EU standards in many areas than adopt an entirely new UK regime. And bananas are no more or less bendy than before.
Rachel Reeves had a more unpleasantly graphic way of making a similar point, referring to regulation as a “boot on the neck” of British business.
There is nothing wrong with ensuring the interaction between business and the state is smooth. But even during the early years of neoliberalism, the free market good, regulation bad dichotomy was always unhelpful, for several reasons.
First, good regulation – a robust competition regime, for example – is essential to make markets work well. And even most enthusiasts for a laissez-faire approach would acknowledge the need for some basic quality standards – for food and medicines, for example.
When it comes to the labour market, Labour has unashamedly adopted a pro-regulation stance. Its Employment Rights Act is the most significant increase in workers’ rights in a generation – but it inevitably, and deliberately, increases the rules firms must follow.
That is to the benefit, ministers rightly argue, of low-paid employees trapped in insecure work. But a bonfire of red tape it is not. Labour posing as a champion of deregulation will seem unconvincing, given that context.
Second, and ironically, the march of neoliberalism itself is a reason regulation has mushroomed in recent decades. As the Labour MP Yuan Yang argued in a recent lecture for the journal Renewal, as the state retreated from providing important services, watchdog institutions to oversee the private sector became necessary.
As she put it: “The neoliberal illusion, that privatisation liberated markets from state interference, obscures the reality that the state already significantly controls our privatised utilities, but through a maze of arm’s length regulatory agencies which operate outside democratic influence.”
For the water sector, privatised in 1989, these include Ofwat, which sets bills (with the Competition and Markets Authority acting as an appeals body in the event of a dispute); the Drinking Water Inspectorate; the Environment Agency; and the Consumer Council for Water.
Yet, as Yang points out, none are responsible for drawing up a coherent plan for the sector as a whole. “Everyone knows how this story ends: with our rivers polluted and our water infrastructure dangerously lacking.”
Hacking away at the regulatory thicket fails to deal with the structural features of the economy that make the rules necessary in the first place.
Mat Lawrence, the director of the thinktank Common Wealth and author of The Productive State, a policy paper influential among those close to Burnham, calls this “the regulatory state”. He cites affordable housing targets for private developers as another example of regulation taking the place of stuff the state once did itself.
The third reason the endless red tape discourse is unhelpful is one raised by Mike Clancy, the general secretary of the Prospect union, which represents workers at many of the regulators.
He has urged the government to lay off these often not lavishly paid staff, who are trying to do their jobs with stretched resources. “Regulators continue to be labelled as ‘blockers’ despite the vital work they do keeping us safe and protecting our natural environment,” he said.
Prospect has been urging the government to ditch a promise to “cut the administrative burden” of regulation by 25% by the end of the parliament, arguing it is arbitrary and potentially counterproductive.
Finally, we would all benefit from some over-mighty businesses being reined in by regulation, not least the tech firms, which insouciantly concede that their AI agents have been busting through safety controls and may be about to start spawning spontaneously.
Embracing the tired idea that red tape is “choking” business is hardly likely to help the government make the case for the more stringent approach that is clearly necessary.
As it happens, Bonfire Night is almost upon us. If Burnham really wants to embrace a different approach to the economy, he could start by consigning the phrase “red tape” to the flames.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Public sector an ‘afterthought’ to North Sea oil jobs, says Unison leader
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The leader of the UK’s biggest trade union has called for the same political focus to be given to NHS, education and care sector workers as there has been on those employed in North Sea oil and gas.
Andrea Egan, the general secretary of Unison, said too often public sector workers were treated as an “afterthought” by the government compared with the “massive political focus” on protecting jobs in the North Sea.
“There’s no question it is vital for oil and gas workers to be guaranteed secure, well-paid jobs in the industries of the future,” Egan said. “But public service workers, in contrast, often seem like an afterthought for ministers. What about the thousands of jobs cut in recent years across local government, the NHS and education? Care workers, nurses, teaching assistants.”
North Sea oil and gas has been in the headlines again in recent weeks after the government gave the go ahead to the Jackdaw gasfield following huge pressure from the fossil fuel industry and rightwing politicians – in the UK and abroad.
The decision caused anger among climate campaigners and scientists, as well as many Labour supporters, who argue that extracting more fossil fuels will further escalate the crisis and do nothing to reduce bills, significantly improve energy security or halt the long-term decline in jobs in the sector. A final government decision on the more controversial Rosebank oilfield is expected before the end of the year.
After Wednesday’s budget, which factored in the project’s approval in its forecast, the Guardian revealed some Labour MPs were lobbying Andy Burnham and John Healey not to overrule the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, if she decided to block Rosebank.
Egan said approving Jackdaw was “a serious misstep from the government” and sent the wrong signal about the UK’s climate commitments. She said ministers should instead focus on creating secure, well-paid jobs in the renewable sector for oil and gas workers and give similar support to the millions of employees in the public sector, which has also been hit by severe cuts in recent years.
“It’s time for the government to get its priorities straight: invest in clean energy, invest in the public services that communities rely on – to the benefit of us all.”
There is a split among the UK’s main trade unions on allowing fossil fuel companies to drill in the North Sea. Unite and GMB, which represent many oil and gas workers, back more licences, while Unison and the National Education Union oppose more drilling as part of a wider drive to create long term sustainable jobs and tackle the climate crisis.
One concern among unions is that jobs in the rapidly growing renewables sector are often not unionised and therefore not as secure or well paid as in those in the oil and gas sector.
However, last week Unison announced a new recognition deal with the UK’s largest energy company, Octopus Energy, known as a progressive organisation with a focus on renewable energy.
The GMB union had been attempting to gain recognition at Octopus but the company said Unison “stood out for its commitment to the energy transition”.
Egan said it was an important step to securing good, secure jobs in the renewable sector. “Unison is proud to be leading the way as the clean energy union. We urgently need more well-paid, unionised jobs and to transition away from fossil fuels at pace. This agreement is a step in the right direction on both counts.”
