SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Shall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yet | Polly Toynbee
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
When I hear that word again, a shudder runs down my spine. I want to groan, hold my head in my hands and wail. The horror! No, never again, not another referendum. But the idea is back in play as Andy Burnham looks for ways to reverse a decade of economic stagnation.
As the prime minister dared to unlock the door to a Brussels reunion, you could hear Ode to Joy burst out from all remainers. But the prospect of a re-run of the most self-destructive vote in our history is dismaying.
Remember that morning a decade ago. First came Sunderland’s 12.20am result, a 61.3% vote to leave, but there was still hope for remainers … until the BBC’s 4.40am verdict that leave had won. In that second a great rift tore across the country. Remainers, dubbed remoaners, never recovered. UK politics became a circus: we who paraded as the west’s strong and stable “mother of parliaments” ran wildly through seven prime ministers in 10 years. Both Labour and Tory parties were wrecked by the most shattering event of our political lifetime. It is a wound neither has dared to reopen.
Only now Burnham has finally broken the spell of Brexit silence, aiming to rejoin, while the Tories will stay in the wilderness until they repent the Brexit disaster they inflicted on the country.
As Burnham sets out to explore all the options, outriders scout the way back in. Making the strong case for full EU membership, IPPR, the thinktank closest to Labour, has published a weighty report this week on how it can happen and why it must: we need it for prosperity, security and democracy. It has left us dangerously alone and friendless in a world of great power blocs. Our once reliable ally, the US, is never to be fully trusted again now we know what its people are capable of voting for. And so the warmth of familiar democracies across the Channel looks welcoming (at least for now). Make this bid to rejoin about who we are, bonding with where we belong, emotionally and historically. We have discovered “sovereignty” is a mirage: every treaty and trade deal requires sharing it with allies.
Within a year, a majority of people in the UK thought Brexit was a mistake (not quite the same as regretting their own vote). Now we know that Brexit has robbed us of a walloping 8% of GDP. IPPR and Persuasion UK polling finds 52% want to rejoin, 29% to stay out. Support grows by the year, partly as older people drop off their perches and young pro-Europeans join the electoral roll. As the IPPR tested every option from Keir Starmer’s slight reset to full membership, the least popular was leaving things as they are. The current Boris Johnson/Lord Frost deal is so dysfunctional that Burnham says keeping it would be a “dereliction of duty”. As ever ignoring the public mood, last year Kemi Badenoch wrote to the EU ambassador warning that, if elected, she would repeal any change, an act of near-treason that could sabotage negotiations in Brussels that start next month. Watch Michael Gove, arch-Brexit manipulator, telling the Guardian’s Aditya Chakrabortty he regrets nothing, blaming others for failing to capitalise on those illusory Brexit benefits. Would that bleating work? I think not.
But is this shift to 52% v 29% strong enough to dare throw the dice and risk everything? No, not quite yet. The IPPR admits it is still “soft”, and there are familiar echoes of what happened last time. After years in which it felt as if we could talk about nothing else, the EU now has reassuringly low salience. But that’s just as it was until Ukip and Tory Brexiters turbocharged what had been a non-issue. As before, polling figures that encouraged David Cameron to breeze arrogantly into a referendum looked sufficient to someone who assumed he would win. This time we know better. Prepare for Dominic Cummings et al rising from their coffins with Brexit defibrillators to shock new life into the issue. Nigel Farage was at it on Sunday, claiming the EU would charge Britain £42bn a year to rejoin.
Testing arguments for both sides, this report reveals traps to avoid and what people like about rejoining. Red lights flash over joining the euro, scrapping our other trade deals, giving up fishing rights and high contributions to the EU budget. Top of the most effective reasons for rejoining is passport queues. Second comes security: Ukraine has exposed this dangerous Trump/Putin world. Third is the need to bring lost foreign investment back to Britain.
But reasoned, fact-based focus groups in a calm and rational atmosphere can’t begin to replicate the monstrous lies, fabrications and devilry of a TikTok, Instagram and X referendum campaign. Remember the £350m-a-week bus, the Turks are coming, immigration will end and, best of all, “take back control”. Of what? Everything! That’s what referendums do.
So not yet. The case for joining has to be powerfully made, the argument won overwhelmingly for allied EU forces to circle the wagons against what Peter Ricketts, ex-national security adviser, along with the head of MI5, warns are “more reckless, more dangerous” cyber-attacks on vital services, such as energy, water, transport, banking or air traffic control. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, meeting with the EU home affairs commissioner today to restore data cooperation on crime and migration is a reminder of how insanely self-destructive Brexit was.
In a decade, Britain has changed. Though Brexiters will threaten floods of migrants storming the border on joining the EU, IPPR polling shows freedom of movement no longer alarms voters as it once did. The cost of living is now the top national concern, not immigration. Look how poorer countries have caught up to us: per capita income in Bucharest, Romania’s capital, is far higher than Sunderland’s.
But the EU has changed too. The question is what kind of Europe we would join if Marine Le Pen and the Alternative für Deutschland became its new axis of power. Here’s the answer: that would make joining even more urgent, to be inside to influence what we can, bolstering the democrats. Staying out leaves us powerless.
This report sets to work on the campaign Burnham ignited when he proposed going “all the way”. The goal is clear and the need is growing urgent. As the EU ambassador told the Guardian’s Patrick Wintour, the ball is in our court. Brussels, he said, is “ready to engage”, once Britain decides what it wants.
Let’s decide, but proceed with extreme caution. Would you risk the next general election by putting this into Labour’s manifesto, certain to become the right’s battle-flag? Yes, when a strong pro-EU campaign makes it winnable. But there should be no referendum until public opinion is so solid that it would be a mere rubber-stamping of the overwhelming public will.
- 
  Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: US maternity wards face wave of closures as Medicaid cuts kick in
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Maternity wards across the United States are facing a wave of closures as cuts to federal Medicaid funding take effect, experts have warned.
According to analysis by the non-profit Protect Our Care, 52 maternity wards have closed since the HR1 bill was announced in July 2025, with a further eight having announced their upcoming closure.
The bill, which will fully come into effect in the new year, will result in many adults covered through Medicaid having to meet new work requirements and being subject to more frequent eligibility checks, while there will be less federal funding for states for Medicaid.
Hospitals which have already permanently closed their maternity wards include the Centra Southside Community hospital in Virginia and St Mary’s Sacred Heart hospital in rural north-east Georgia, which both cited upcoming federal policy changes to Medicaid as a reason.
Experts are expecting to see more closures of maternity units in the run-up to and after the federal changes to Medicaid come into effect in the new year.
“We’re deeply concerned that these changes already have and will continue to worsen an already serious maternity care crisis,” said Erin Jones, senior director of legislative and strategic counsel of the non-profit March of Dimes. “Reduced funding and restrictions on how states finance Medicaid will put additional pressure on state budgets and hospitals, increasing the risk that communities lose essential maternity services and specialized providers close to home.”
She added that the consequences for maternity care would be particularly devastating within rural communities. The non-profit has identified 31 at-risk rural hospitals with labor and delivery services, with their possible closure leaving 96 counties without a labor and delivery unit.
“Losing these services means fewer places to deliver safely and fewer options for pregnancies requiring specialized care,” Jones added.
About 40% of births in the US are paid for by Medicaid, while the country has one of the highest maternal mortality rates among high-income nations, at a rate of 17.9 deaths per 100,000 live births, according to the latest Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) figures.
Benjamin Sommers, a professor of healthcare economics at the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, said the changes to Medicaid would “absolutely” affect women who are pregnant and specialist pregnancy organizations.
“It’s not true that this law in any way protects Medicaid for pregnant mothers, for low-income parents. It adds financial strain to the providers and the insurance program that they rely on,” he said.
Sommers, who was deputy assistant secretary for health policy under Joe Biden, said although the new work requirements for Medicaid are supposed to exempt pregnant women, his research has shown that many women are not enrolled in the Medicaid pregnancy pathway, meaning the state might not know that they’re pregnant.
He added: “Someone could be enrolled through Medicaid expansion, they could get pregnant and they could mistakenly think – because they heard it on the news that this law doesn’t affect pregnant people – [they’re] fine, and it turns out the state doesn’t know they’re pregnant and they lose coverage.”
Vaishu Jawahar, director of policy and programs at Protect Our Care, added: “When you’re cutting Medicaid by a trillion dollars, you’re cutting this money from hospitals. So these hospitals are going into the red and being forced to make hard decisions, which usually results in maternity wards being closed as they are extremely expensive to run.”
Meanwhile, in early 2025, the entirety of the CDC’s pregnancy risk assessment monitoring system team, which oversees a population-based surveillance system collecting data on women’s experiences before, during and after pregnancy, was placed on administrative leave by the Trump administration.
According to an upcoming report authored by academics and former CDC staff, seen by the Guardian, these actions by the federal government disrupted the collection and management of “one of the nation’s most important sources of population-based information on pre-pregnancy, pregnancy, postpartum experiences, and maternal and infant health” which has existed for over four decades.
“There are no other datasets like it. Teams like mine used to have access to this data before the portal was shut down, and so now there’s no way to study the more recent trends in maternal and infant health,” said Rita Hamad, professor of social epidemiology and public policy at the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health and co-author of the report.
“Now we’re very worried that the cuts to US safety net policies or barriers that keep people able to access those programmes are going to have detrimental effects on maternal and infant health.”
She added: “I think we’re going to see those geographical and maternal disparities widening. Or we’re not going to see it because we don’t have the data, but that’s what is going to happen.
The Department for Health and Human Services has been contacted by the Guardian.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Migration is a moral issue for Burnham – but is he trying to please everyone?
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
While out on the campaign trail in Makerfield, Andy Burnham gave a glimpse into where he might land on Labour’s plans for immigration reform, which had already been decried by the left of the party as unfair while described on the right as electorally necessary.
Asked what he thought of Reform’s attack on “open borders Andy” – Nigel Farage’s early attempt to define him as soft on migration – the then Manchester mayor dismissed the charge as “ridiculous” and went on the defensive.
“I’m not like that. You know me. I was in the Home Office under Tony Blair, and actually, it was my job to return people. That was my specific role,” he said while out knocking on doors in the constituency.
“I used to have to travel to governments around the world and persuade them to take back planes of people who had come here with no basis to stay, so you know, I’ve never have been shy of getting to grips with these difficult issues.”
But Burnham wasn’t just pitching to the Reform-inclined voters he needed to win the seat; he was already charting whatever path he might need to take if he made it to Downing Street.
While he was supportive of attempts by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, to limit legal and illegal migration, which had been criticised by some senior Labour figures as un-British, Burnham wanted to reframe the changes.
“I think there’s a different way of thinking about it that might in the end get you to a better position, and one that restores public confidence,” he said.
The prime minister’s political allies say he regards migration as a moral issue, showing people who’ve lost faith in politics that the government does have control over the UK’s borders and is prepared to do something about it.
But he also wants to tell a positive story about the contribution of migration to the country, they say. Weeks after arriving in No 10, the Guardian revealed that social care workers could be exempted from the plans as he looked for ways to relieve pressure on the sector.
In an interview with ITV this week, Burnham again tried to make the case. “When you have planned migration, it’s difficult to say if it’s too high or too low,” he said, arguing that migrants help plug “gaps in the economy”.
In the end, Mahmood’s reforms came with a significant carve-out for almost 300,000 care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) after five years.
In a further compromise to those on the Labour benches feeling squeamish, those deemed to be making a “strong contribution” to the UK – high earners, those with strong British connections or who work in health and teaching – will also be able to settle in five years.
But that Burnham delivered the bulk of Mahmood’s hardline reforms should not come as a surprise. The prime minister, steeped in the politics of the “red wall”, understands better than many the salience of the issue with voters.
The most rigorous of the new rules first drawn up a year ago by the Home Office – retrospective changes for many migrants, and forcing small boats arrivals to face up to 30 years before applying for settlement – are still there.
How they land with the public (which polling suggests supports a doubling of the waiting time for most migrants to 10 years) now depends in part on whether ministers can convince them it’s about people making a contribution, rather than a U-turn forced by their own side.
The Conservatives and Reform, unsurprisingly, are already pushing the latter narrative, Farage describing the care workers carve-out as “the beginning of the capitulation” on borders.
Burnham is, equally predictably, arguing that it’s about fairness. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier,” he said.
“Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.”
But Burnham’s words did not come in the Commons chamber or at a press conference standing alongside Mahmood or even as part of his prolific social media output.
They were instead issued in a press release, after the government chose to push ahead with the sensitive policy announcement while he was out of the country – travelling to the Commonwealth leaders summit in Antigua.
The plans are still likely to face criticism from some on either wing of the Labour party – for going too far or not far enough – although plenty of former critics do now appear to be on board. But without an obvious vote to coalesce around, any major rebellion looks unlikely.
Mahmood’s bigger challenge will be convincing the public. She will need Burnham, who has praised her for “gripping this problem”, to help her to do so. But the prime minister will have to accept, on an issue as divisive as this, he won’t be able to please everyone.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘Profound anger’ among black voters over Kemi Badenoch’s slavery remarks
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has caused “profound anger, hurt and disbelief” among many black voters with her comments about transatlantic slavery, according to the chair of Operation Black Vote (OBV), who urged the prime minister, Andy Burnham, to apologise for Britain’s involvement without delay.
David Weaver, a former government adviser, said the Labour and Tory leaders risked alienating black voters with their handling of the issue of a state apology for slavery, while saying Badenoch’s remarks showed a “troubling absence of moral leadership”.
In a week in which the UK political agenda was dominated by postcolonial legacies, Badenoch said Burnham should not apologise for Britain’s historical role in slavery “because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash”, while criticising Commonwealth leaders on X.
Burnham, while saying he was open to making a formal apology on behalf of the British state, has ruled out reparations. Weaver said he welcomed the prime minister’s apparent willingness to apologise, but said the government’s “almost reflexive insistence” that any apology must come with assurances “reparations are off the table” was concerning.
Weaver said only the prime minister had the power to address the hurt felt by descendant communities and show Britain had the “moral courage to apologise without qualification”.
But he said Badenoch’s comments highlighted wider concerns about the UK’s political climate, adding: “At Operation Black Vote, we are hearing profound anger, hurt and disbelief.”
He added: “For us, this is not an abstract historical debate. It concerns our families, our heritage and our humanity. Political leaders should not underestimate the depth of feeling within black communities or their democratic power.”
Weaver said that in seeking an apology, Commonwealth nations wanted recognition of continuing colonial legacies that hampered development, and that Badenoch’s comments were “profoundly insulting”.
This week marked the second anniversary of Badenoch becoming the first black woman to lead a major British political party. OBV, a national, non-partisan civil rights group founded in 1996, welcomed her historic achievement in becoming Tory leader in 2024.
Meanwhile, although black voters were more likely than any other voters to have backed Labour in the 2024 general election, Weaver said OBV had found they felt “despondent” with the party and “taken for granted”, in particular over its handling of the consequences of the Windrush scandal.
Weaver added: “All parties should understand that to not apologise for slavery, the worst crime against humanity, is an insult. An apology should not have to be begged for. It should be an expression of genuine remorse and moral responsibility, not a carefully managed political statement designed to demonstrate toughness or avoid obligation.
“Reparative justice is not just about money. Ending an injustice does not erase responsibility for perpetrating it. We must ask why acknowledging this particular historical injustice remains so difficult and whether deeper racial attitudes continue to shape the debate.”
Badenoch, who has advocated a “colour-blind” approach to race, has long argued that people from ethnic minorities should be free to express differing views on race without being accused of betraying their communities.
But while attempting to frame herself as a unifier, Badenoch has given roles to the hard-right politician Rupert Lowe, Katie Lam – the MP who said a “large number” of legal migrants “need to go home” – and the former neo-Nazi Joshua Bonehill-Paine, while outlining plans to scrap the public sector equality duty and leave the European court of human rights.
Weaver said: “She’s the leader of the Conservative party. That’s a big deal. She’s got a high popularity rating and can be very effective. But many black voters tell us there’s a lot of mistrust for her lack of empathy – and because she will sometimes say things her white counterparts could not say and get away with it. So she becomes the front for unacceptable views on race.
“The current state of public discourse – and the silence when it comes to challenging it – contributes to a sense among black communities that they are being treated with contempt across the political spectrum.
“This is not just about Badenoch. Just because you’re black doesn’t mean you have to hold a particular point of view. But your heritage, whether you are white or black, does not place your views beyond challenge. An apology for slavery is about humanity and decency and seeing people’s worth. Andy Burnham must do the right thing – and soon.”
Downing Street and the Conservative party were approached for comment. Commonwealth leaders have said the UK has agreed to “structured dialogue” in the next year.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Local devolution decisions rest solely with Scotland and Wales, first ministers tell Burnham
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Scotland and Wales’s first ministers have told Andy Burnham that decisions on local devolution rest solely with their parliaments, in response to the prime minister’s push to extend English-style regional powers across the UK.
After Burnham held discussions in Glasgow with John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth about localised employment and reindustrialisation powers, Downing Street characterised the talks as constructive.
However, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, caused friction before the summit by criticising Swinney’s government for hoarding powers it acquired from Westminster rather than devolving them further.
Streeting told BBC Scotland: “One of the critiques we have … is that for the Scottish government, devolution is often about transferring power, responsibility, resources from Westminster to Holyrood and the challenge Andy Burnham is setting out is: ‘What about devolving more power also from Holyrood to local government across Scotland?’”
Northern Ireland’s first minister, Michelle O’Neill, had also been due at the talks, but did not attend after a political row between Sinn Féin and the DUP. Burnham said it was “disappointing” she was not there.
The prime minister said he hoped to have all four UK nations moving at the same pace on devolution, particularly on efforts outlined in Wednesday’s budget to give mayors in England more powers over tax revenues.
“There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind,” Burnham said. “I don’t want to see Wales left behind, but also, crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.”
Ap Iorwerth said he had pushed Burnham on his wish to have more powers for his government.
He added: “I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd.”
Swinney’s comments after the summit took a similar line, saying he would “work constructively and collaboratively” in devolving more powers to his government, while adding that Burnham had assured him “that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour”.
Despite the emollient tone, tensions remain. Shortly before the summit, ap Iorwerth said Burnham’s first budget, which the Welsh government said amounted to a real-terms funding cut for the country, showed the prime minister was “not serious about Wales”.
Plaid Cymru, which won May’s Senedd elections, putting nationalists in office in all three of the UK’s Celtic nations for the first time, has already formally asked Burnham to give Wales the same devolved powers as Scotland.
The SNP-led government is frequently irritated by comments such as those by Streeting, characterised by one Scottish official as “lecturing us on devolution”.
Separately, Lee Waters, who was a minister in the Labour-led Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until the elections in May, told the Guardian that Burnham, who was the Greater Manchester mayor before becoming prime minister, should not try to impose an English-style mayoral model on Wales, as “we are not comparing like with like”.
He said: “The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas.
“Transposing an English mayoral worldview on to a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends.
“Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘A direct cultural threat’: your questions on the rise of the right across Europe answered
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Support for far-right parties has been growing across Europe, with radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany.
The Guardian reported this year that nearly a quarter of voters in Europe voted for far-right parties in their most recent national elections, a fivefold increase since 1995.
In Germany, Alternative für Deutschland recently booked a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Elsewhere, though – in the Netherlands, in Hungary and in Sweden, where the Sweden Democrats lost vote share – far-right parties have suffered defeats. But their ideas – and their influence on mainstream politics – are today clearly visible across the continent, notably on policies around immigration and law-and-order.
The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year.
How might these elections shape the political future of Europe? What is the impact of their policies – and what might prevent their continuing rise?
The Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley has reported for the Guardian from 23 of the EU’s 27 member states, while Europe community affairs correspondent Ashifa Kassam was on the ground in Sweden and Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state to speak with people ahead of the elections.
Jon and Ashifa answered questions about their reporting and experiences. Read the Q&A below.
One user asked: It’s no secret in Europe that Donald Trump and his allies are funding far-right parties all over the continent. Trump is unpopular enough in Europe that even the majority of people planning to vote for the AfD et al despise him. So how can so many Europeans who hate Trump still vote for the far right?
Jon Henley: You’re absolutely right about the Trump administration’s efforts to promote far right parties in Europe. That was made very plain in the US National Security Strategy policy document last year – I wrote about that here.
But while there may be an ideological affinity between European far right and nationalist voters on issues like anti-immigration, hostility toward the EU, and softer stances on Russia, Trump’s “America First” policies (demands re Greenland, tariff threats, etc.) and constant unpredictability pose major problems for far-right leaders trying to look credible in Europe, because they scare all European voters – including far-right voters.
Leaders including Giorgia Meloni in Italy and Marine Le Pen in France have openly criticised Trump and distanced themselves from his more erratic pronouncements, conspiracy claims and hostility toward European security.
European far-right voters’ support for Trump varies from country to country but is broadly low – clearly peace and security in Europe matter more than anti-immigration sentiment. Ultimately, nation-first means putting your nation first, and Trump has made clear that the US’s interests are not Europe’s interests.
The evidence would seem to suggest that many of Europe’s far-right voters think their own far-right parties will be more responsible as regards (many of) those issues – though whether they actually will be or not is moot, of course.
00000000000000000000 asked: How do you measure when a grassroots movement represents a genuine structural shift versus an isolated vocal minority?
Ashifa Kassam: Our jobs involve covering a wide range of community actions, whether it’s people fighting back against datacentres, protests against tourism, or the vandalisation of mobile phone masts by people who seemingly linked them to the coronavirus pandemic.
Oftentimes the reporting starts small and local. For example, perhaps it’s focused tightly on a protest against tourists in Barcelona or a push to restrict cruise ship dockings in Dubrovnik. From there, myself and the editors often continue to watch these movements and their reach; are politicians responding in any way? Are others joining in? Will the movements lead to policy changes? These are the kinds of questions that I tend to consider when deciding how much to make of the grassroots movements and how much coverage to give them.
At times it’s been incredible to see just where these movements will go, whether it’s the housing protests in Spain that led to snap general elections or the opposition movement that coalesced around Péter Magyar in Hungary in 2024 and which, more than a year later, saw him oust Viktor Orbán from power.
Gramoun-kal asked: Can the EU survive the rise of the extreme right? What if AfD and RN get into power at the same time?
Jon Henley: One of the very few upsides of Brexit is that hardly any European far right parties now want their countries to leave the EU. Instead, they want to “transform it from within”, turning it more into a looser “Europe of nations”.
But that’s not to say the EU would not be considerably weakened by, say, a President Le Pen, who could paralyse decision-making, challenge the supremacy of EU law and push a “France First” agenda undermining the single market and Schengen free-travel zone and opposing EU expansion, climate action, etc.
I’m not sure there’s any imminent risk of the AfD coming to national power in Germany (and if Le Pen wins France’s presidential election, which isn’t certain but looks highly plausible, she is also unlikely to have a parliamentary majority, which will limit her room for manoeuvre).
Plus, the AfD is too extreme even for the RN – Le Pen’s outfit (which kicked the AfD out of its European parliament grouping a while ago over various issues including comments to the effect that not all Nazis were bad), has repeatedly made it clear it is not an ally of the German party and does not share its views on eg. “remigration” – the mass deportation of immigrants.
But for sure – if Spain, Italy, France and Poland all see far-right parties in government after elections due over the next 12 months or so, the EU will face some major challenges. I don’t think it will collapse, but it will certainly find it even harder to reach agreement on many major issues than it already does, and so move (even) more slowly. Natalie Tocci wrote a great comment piece about this.
OrangeSpaceMan5 asked: Do you see Nato and the EU disintegrating if we see Far-Right victories across Britain, Germany and France?
Jon Henley: No, I don’t see the EU and Nato disintegrating, just becoming a lot more complicated/difficult to run … The EU could be “eroded from within” above all by far right-led governments using their veto (as Orbán did with Hungary) in major decisions like the EU budget, EU enlargement, the green deal, etc. They may well also simply ignore EU law, as Orbán also did. And for Nato, see previous answer – it would survive but become more paralysed in terms of longer term decision making.
Ashifa Kassam: I think we saw a glimpse of how complicated things can become in the European parliament after an EU vote earlier this year aimed at increasing deportations. The immediate aftermath laid bare just how deeply polarised the EU has already become, as right-wing MEPs chanted “send them back” and centre-left and left-wing MEPs shot back with “Shame on you.”
ElendX asked: Why and how have the left and centre parties failed to respond to the concerns of the electorate? How do they now need to respond?
Ashifa Kassam: What comes to mind immediately is the housing crisis in Spain and beyond. It’s been just over two weeks now since the Spanish protests and encampments over the housing crisis burst into public view, laying bare the long-simmering anger over soaring housing costs.
I think it’s an issue that has long been overlooked by many left and centre parties across Europe, even as vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected, and analysts warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. Last year I spoke to Jaume Collboni, the Socialist mayor of Barcelona, who (along with 21 mayors across Europe) are urging the EU to treat the surging housing costs as a “new pandemic” by unleashing billions in funding to boost affordable housing and give mayors a seat at the table to ensure measures capable of tackling housing speculation. Speaking to me, Collboni warned: “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse.”
I also think left and centre parties have done little to address the precariousness of the labour market, ie. the rise of gig jobs and, in many cases, the deterioration of public services. If you keep an eye on the Eurobarometer, the cost of living constantly ranks among the top concerns for people across Europe, hinting at the idea that this could be fertile territory for politicians to focus on. Immigration, in contrast, was in 7th place in the most recent survey.
Jon Henley: I think broadly speaking mainstream parties have failed to adequately address people’s concerns about the cost of living, declining public services (healthcare, education, transport), economic/job security, etc. – as I said above, fear of/anger at some kind of “loss of status” is one of the key drivers of the far right vote. (I’m not suggesting that’s easy – it clearly isn’t, economies are struggling.)
I’d also add that far-right parties are clearly extremely effective at exploiting voters’ concerns politically, including by pointing the finger at the group they think are most to blame and promising to fix things by getting rid of them.
And I’d also note that mainstream parties really have not helped themselves by adopting far-right parties’ framing on several issues in hopes of hanging on to disillusioned voters – electoral evidence shows that almost never works, mainly because, as Marine Le Pen’s father Jean-Marie put it, people tend to prefer the original to the copy.
Dc740 asked: Did you measure any change in online activity for extremist parties like Vox in Spain after the Yandex datacentre was targeted by Ukraine?
Ashifa Kassam: Funny you should ask – earlier this week, I sent out queries on this to several research groups, so it’s something we’re looking into. It’s a really interesting question. Last week, in an interview with news site Eldiario.es, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez was asked whether he was worried about foreign interference in the elections given his high profile opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza and the US-Israeli attack on Iran. His answer: “Yes, and not only by nations, but also by non-state actors.”
Capitao_barbosa asked: How much foreign funding, especially from Russia and America, is being funnelled to these parties? And can we value how much indirect support (bots, disinformation by state actors, algorithm meddling on X, etc.) they are receiving?
Jon Henley: Our data team looked at this question a couple of years ago, before the last European parliament elections. They concluded a quarter of all private money donated to political parties in the EU was going to far-right, far-left and populist movements – aided by the fact that only a quarter of EU countries require parties to identify private donors – with €97m (about one in every seven private donation euros across the EU) going to far-right parties.
A European parliament report from 2023 estimated that about $1.18bn in funding towards organisations targeting LGBTQ+ rights and promoting traditional family policies flowed into Europe from 2019 to 2023, and a 2022 declassified US intelligence assessment found the Russian government had covertly funnelled at least $300m to foreign political parties, often in Europe, from 2014.
Ashifa Kassam: We’ve also had some recent reporting on the flow of funds from the US. In July, the Guardian reported that Donald Trump’s state department intended to allocate $12m to organisations in the UK founded by prominent conservatives. Of these funds, $7m was to go to 878, a thinktank that describes itself as being devoted to “the rediscovery of our ancient culture” and “ending mass migration.”
In July, the state department issued a notice of funding, offering grants for organisations and institutions interested in promoting what it described as “civilisational self-confidence in Europe”.
While research out of Europe, such as the Munich-based Ifo Institute, has found “no correlation” between migration and higher crime rates, the US state department notice suggested it was hoping the grants would lead to outcomes including reports on the impact of mass migration on local safety and tools to analyse impact of mass migration on democratic institutions.
One user asked: How serious would you describe the threat these far-right parties pose to democracy? And to what extent do you think there is a collaboration between them and powerful social media personalities or state sponsored online social media propaganda?
Jon Henley: Some far right parties definitely pose more of a threat to democracy than others. Political scientists divide far-right parties into those that essentially operate within basic democratic norms (“radical right” parties), and those that seek to overturn the system, to the extent even of condoning violence (“extreme right” parties).
If we take one example, AfD in Germany could be described as extreme right in some respects (and some local branches are indeed classified as such by German domestic intelligence). Some of its positions are in clear contradiction with liberal democracy: it is openly racist, homophobic, misogynistic. It believes citizens should be ranked by its own warped criteria, including ethnicity, gender and religious belief. It flirts continually with Nazi rhetoric, imagery and symbolism.
On this question I recommend this column by Cas Mudde, a top scholar of populism and the far right, after AfD won in the recent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. He argues that mainstream parties have to wake up to the fact that they are not in a battle that’s about vote share and elections, it’s about democracy itself.
Ashifa Kassam: I would add that we’ve seen some fairly high-profile examples of collaboration, from Elon Musk’s repeated endorsements of the AfD on X to his 2025 X talk with the party’s co-leader, Alice Weidel. The Guardian has also regularly explored the interplay between the far right and social media, such as a 2025 investigation that looked at how a network of far-right Facebook groups had become an “engine of radicalisation” by exposing hundreds of thousands of people in Britain to racist and extremist disinformation.
KilmaSelth asked: Do you think the hard right parties tend to moderate as they approach power, or do they maintain their radicalism?
Jon Henley: Based on Meloni and Le Pen, I would for a long time have said yes – Meloni basically struck a bargain to get elected in which she promised to be responsible on the economy, in the EU and as regards foreign policy, as long as she could do her culture-wars stuff domestically. Le Pen has spent years “detoxifying” the National Rally and kicking out over-radical undesirables. But if you look at AfD, they haven’t moderated their language at all – if anything, they’ve hardened it – and it manifestly is not doing them any harm. And as Meloni and Le Pen have moderated their positions, we’ve started to see them being outflanked on their right, by the likes of Roberto Vannacci and his National Future in Italy and Eric Zemmour’s Reconquête in France. So I think we may be heading into a period where the former far right is effectively now part of the political landscape, like “regular” parties that will sometimes win and sometimes lose elections, and will be increasingly challenged on their right by more extreme elements.
Ashifa Kassam: Vox offers another way to look at this question, as the party was founded in 2013 by disgruntled members of the conservative People’s party (PP). Its leader, Santiago Abascal, is a career politician who was among those who saw an opportunity to push further on the right flank of Spanish politics when it came to Catalan separatism, immigration, abortion and LGBTQ+ rights. It was a hardline stance that was often (but not always) diluted when Abascal was part of the PP; now as a separate party, they’ve seized on their electoral momentum in some regions to push the party to heed their agenda.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Democrat Troy Jackson defeats Susan Collins to win Maine US Senate seat in blow to Republicans
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Democrat Troy Jackson has won Maine’s US Senate race, toppling five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins in one of the biggest upsets of the 2026 midterms.
Jackson, 58, unseated Collins – who has been in the Senate since 1997 – in a closely fought, and often rancorous, race characterized by mutual accusations of corruption and clashes over living costs in the predominantly rural state.
The victory delivers Democrats one of their most coveted pickup opportunities this midterm cycle, and brings an end to Collins’ nearly three-decade tenure in Washington.
A lumberjack by trade and former state senate president, Jackson sought to break down Collins’ carefully crafted image as a moderate Republican willing to break with the Donald Trump, painting her instead as a loyal supporter of the president.
Jackson, who ran on a platform of progressive economic populism, had argued that Collins emboldened Trump’s agenda through critical votes, like confirming Brett Kavanaugh, the conservative supreme court justice – which paved the way for overturning the constitutional right to an abortion in the US.
Collins, meanwhile, cast Jackson as ideologically inconsistent and lacking the experience needed to deliver for Maine at the federal level.
As the only Senate Republican running in a state that Trump lost in 2024, Collins also argued that her independence and influence had delivered tangible results for Maine. She often pointed to the millions of federal dollars she had helped steer home as chair of the Senate appropriations committee.
Both of the nominees were courting a swathe of Mainers who were comfortable splitting the ticket in 2020 – voting for Joe Biden as president and sending Collins back to Washington for another term.
Maine has been hit hard by soaring fuel costs tied to Trump’s war with Iran and record-high heating oil prices, which began squeezing voters as temperatures fell in the weeks before the election. The state has also faced the pain of the administration’s sweeping tariffs, which have affected several of Maine’s most critical industries.
The Senate saw a dramatic midterm cycle as the first Democratic nominee, Graham Platner, an oysterman and former marine, was forced to drop out amid a cascade of scandals that culminated in an allegation of sexual assault and rape, which he denied. Collins repeatedly sought to tie Jackson to Platner’s brand of progressivism, noting the two had campaigned together during Jackson’s unsuccessful gubernatorial bid earlier in the year.
Maine Democrats had just weeks to organize a special convention to select a replacement for Platner. After Jackson won, he had just 101 days to mount a Senate campaign.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence | George Monbiot
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
What a world we live in. Imagine: gangs dragging civil servants off commuter trains and beating them up because they handed government data jobs to the wrong contractor – and the government is changing its procurement decisions as a result. Well, OK, it might not have happened yet, but it’s only a matter of time. As the former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson asks: “Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices?” No, I absolutely don’t want the latter, and it’s always good to get ahead of trouble.
But then I remember there are two common meanings of mob rule. One is intimidation by crowds of thugs. The other is a pejorative term for democracy. And while I’ve yet to see government procurement practices in the UK determined by pitchforks and flaming torches, democratic transparency could be a genuine threat to certain contractors. One might have hoped that Watson, who once took on the Murdoch empire, would have recognised the distinction. But then again, one might have hoped that Watson would not have taken a job as a senior vice-president at Palantir.
Over the past few years, this US company has been worming its way into the British state. It has landed contracts worth hundreds of millions with the Ministry of Defence, several police forces, the Financial Conduct Authority, the atomic weapons establishment and the NHS. Its superpower, according to a deep investigation by Peter Geoghegan and Lucas Amin in the London Review of Books, is that it is “willing to spend more on securing political access than almost all of its British and continental competitors”. It made abundant use of Peter Mandelson’s company Global Counsel, which seems, in turn, to have made abundant use of the UK’s remarkably flimsy lobbying laws. Watson is one of more than 30 former UK ministers and officials Palantir now employs.
Palantir’s contracts might have been awarded lawfully, but some of us might question the ways in which doors were opened for it. These include an unrecorded meeting between Boris Johnson, Dominic Cummings and the co-founder of Palantir, Peter Thiel, in Downing Street in 2019. It was invited back to Downing Street when the Covid-19 pandemic began a few months later, and was working in the NHS within days, on a contract for which it charged only £1. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, has criticised such loss-leaders, which can quickly lead to reliance on a company, at which point it can name its price.
Another controversial meeting was brokered by Mandelson in 2025, when he was UK ambassador to the US. Keir Starmer visited Palantir’s showroom in Washington, where he met the company’s global and UK chief executives, Alex Karp and Louis Mosley. They talked about defence spending. No 10, Geoghegan and Amin tell us, “refused to say whether Starmer knew that Palantir was a client of Global Counsel, in which Mandelson still held a stake of around a fifth at the time. The meeting was never declared on transparency registers.” A few months later, Palantir secured a £241m contract with the Ministry of Defence, without an open tender.
Now we learn that Martha Dalton, a key player in Andy Burnham’s campaign to win the Makerfield byelection, enabling him to become prime minister, was on unpaid leave from the lobbying company she co-founded, Lodestone. Lodestone had done extensive work for Palantir. And the Financial Times reports that Samantha Jones, then the lead non-executive director on the board of the health department, was an adviser to one of Palantir’s partners when the company was bidding for its huge and controversial NHS contract. Now she is permanent secretary in the same department.
There have been repeated allegations that some of Palantir’s products are rubbish. But, as the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committee warns, government agencies can quickly succumb to “vendor lock-in”: once you start using them, it can be very hard to stop.
Thiel, has claimed that “the NHS makes people sick”, and that we should “just rip the whole thing from the ground and start over”. The company is deeply embedded in the Trump administration, where it supplies software that helps ICE find undocumented people. It also works for the Israeli government on identifying targets in Gaza. When Karp was confronted by a protester who told him that “Palantir kills Palestinians”, he replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”
This is the company handling our critical information. After official denials, it turns out that NHS England has granted Palantir “unlimited access” to patient data. This is a huge issue. Identifiable patient data is supposed to be visible only to people directly involved in a patient’s care, or who have received the patient’s informed consent. There are widespread concerns about how this and other datasets might be used.
So, as Palantir runs into ever-greater controversy, it’s not hard to see why it might have hired Watson, who, with Burnham, was a minister in Gordon Brown’s government. I wouldn’t presume to speculate about what attracted Watson to the multibillion-dollar company.
In July, the government’s ethics and integrity commission recommended a major shake-up, enabling us to see all the encounters between lobbyists and ministers, aides and senior officials. I’ve heard this call many times before. The pattern is always the same: a scandal, followed by a call to action, followed by … little or nothing.
Before he became prime minister, David Cameron noted that lobbying “has tainted our politics for too long”. He would shine “the light of transparency” on it. Instead, he oversaw an act that was “more loophole than law”. It did nothing to protect us from lobbying by people such as Cameron – pulling strings, once out of office, among his old colleagues, to try to drum up government business for the bank Greensill .
You could almost believe that the real purpose of government was to do the bidding of corporations, foreign states and the ultra-rich. You could almost believe that some government ministers may have an eye on future opportunities when they resist effective reform.
So this is another key test for Burnham. Will he allow the mob rule of private business to keep dominating our lives, or will he ensure that government is for the people?
- 
  George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Employers to be forced to put salaries on job ads, Andy Burnham announces
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Employers will be forced to publish salaries on job adverts, Andy Burnham has announced, in an effort to empower both employees and jobseekers.
The prime minister said his government would bring in a legal requirement for companies to say what they pay when listing new jobs, which campaigners say will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay.
Burnham said the move would help deal with the frustration of applying for a job without knowing the salary, while officials say that publicising pay will help those in work know if they are being paid fairly in comparison with others.
The prime minister said: “Whether you’re a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it. That’s why we will make it a legal requirement for all employers to say what you pay.
“But breaking down barriers is only one part of the job. We also need businesses to open more doors and give young people the experience and confidence to take that first step into the world of work.”
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said: “Anyone who’s searched for a job knows how frustrating it is to read ‘competitive salary’.”
Burnham has spent much of his first few months in power announcing a series of “small fixes” to help improve people’s daily lives, while promising more radical change to come. The changes have included removing VAT from electricity bills, reducing bus fares and a £100 council-tax rebate.
The prime minister is working on a 10-year plan for ending what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism”, which is expected to include more fundamental changes, such as bringing utilities under public control. He said this week the plan’s publication could be delayed until next year, having originally been expected next month.
Ministers first consulted in July on a series of moves to improve how equal pay laws work. That document also proposed greater equality protections for disabled people and ethnic minorities, but ministers have not yet set out their final plans on those points.
They have promised further policy changes to help young people into work in response to a review by the former minister Alan Milburn to be published in the coming weeks.
Recent research by the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development found less than half of employers always published salaries ranges on job adverts, while less than a fifth always published specific salaries.
Experts say omitting pay details from job adverts makes it harder for young people to know which jobs to apply for, and makes it easier for employers to offer lower pay to some candidates, including women.
The government said 93% of businesses responded positively to the consultation. Ministers have not yet decided exactly what information will have to be published, which size of company will have to comply, or how it will be enforced.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: King tells Commonwealth leaders that Britain’s role in slave trade was ‘shameful’ but stops short of apology – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The King has told Commonwealth leaders the transatlantic slave trade “fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow”, but did not offer an apology. As the Press Association reports, in his address to presidents and prime ministers, Charles said his commitment was growing to find ways to “address the wrongs of the past with action for the future”. He delivered his speech against the background of Andy Burnham announcing a change in long-established government policy and making an offer of talks on a slavery apology but not financial reparations. The King told the leaders of the Commonwealth’s 56 member states meeting in Antigua:
Our history inspires us, can appal us, yet it can always teach us. We cannot change the actions of those who came before us. We can, however, learn from the past.
The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth. As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.
And yet history also teaches us that evil need not have the last word; that character and courage can combine to overcome the most monstrous injustice, as they did with the determination to end international trade in enslaved people, in which the Royal Navy played such a leading role.
The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future.
Here is John Crace’s sketch of Kemi Badenoch’s speech and Q&A with journalists this morning.
And this is how it starts.
HMS Wellington. A decommissioned Grimsby-class sloop from the second world war. A warship that has been moored on the Thames, going nowhere for the best part of 80 years. Today’s venue for the leader of the opposition to explain why the Conservative party hollowed out defence spending throughout their time in office. Sorry. Scrub that. To welcome in a brave new world order. Come aboard the good ship Badenoch. There are times when you wonder if the Tory media team have been infiltrated by Labour HQ. Still, we might as well enjoy it while we can.
Burnham claims Badenoch 'misreading public mood' in her opposition to negotiating new relationship with EU
Andy Burnham has accused critics of his proposed new trade deal with the EU of “misreading the public mood”.
As the Guardian reports, a deal to remove Brexit checks on imports and exports of food and animal products has now been agreed. At a summit in Brussels later this month, the EU and the UK will also be discussing deals covering emissions trading and youth mobility.
Speaking to reporters this morning, Kemi Badenoch said she could not say whether or not she would back the deal covering food products because she had not seen the detail. (See 10.38am.) And she said she was not opposed to a renegotiation per se, because she thought the EU-UK trade relationship needed “constant negotiating”.
But she also said she thought any proposal from Burnham was likely “to make things worse, not better”, and she said dynamic alignment with the EU on regulation was a “red line” that would be unacceptable to the Tories. As the Guardian report says, the deal that has been agreed does require dynamic alignment on sanitary and phytosanitary regulation.
Burnham said that the Treasury had confirmed in recent days that agreements under negotiation ahead of a summit later this month could raise GDP by 0.4% – up from the previous estimate of 0.3%.
And, in an interview with The Economist, he also hit back at Badenoch for criticising his attempts to forge a new relationship with the EU. He said:
I think it’s interesting because I sense, since conference, that there is an appetite to discuss it. And those who are making the argument over ‘Oh my goodness, don’t open up this psychodrama’ are misreading the public mood in my view.
Referring to the economic benefits of the deal being discussed at the summit later this month, he said:
A deal could add up to 0.4% to GDP. Now, that is a number that you cannot ignore.
The British and Australian governments have backed a joint agreement at the Commonwealth summit on working together to tackle threats directed at parliamentarians, especially women. Here is an extract.
We commit to working together with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, with the Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians, and with countries from across the Commonwealth to bring together technology, expertise and practical solutions to help protect parliamentarians from online abuse and support democratic participation across the Commonwealth. We’ll hold the first forum in 2027 and will engage all those in the Commonwealth who share these values.
There are a range of software tools that are being trialled in our parliaments and around the world, and we welcome and encourage this innovation.
While we work to change attitudes, restore respectful debate and return people’s choice, in the short term we can commit to take steps together to protect our democracies.
MSPs call for review of law allowing people with just temporary rights to be living in Scotland to be elected to Holyrood
Severin Carrell
Severin Carrell is the Guardian’s Scotland editor.
MSPs at Holyrood have called on Scottish ministers to review a law which allowed the Indian-born student Q Manivannan to win a seat at Holyrood in May, claiming public confidence in parliament was “fragile”.
The standards, procedures and public appointments committee said in a report that the rationale for allowing people with limited rights to be in the UK was “simply not clear” and had “run ahead of what the public want”.
Under the Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Act 2025, overseas citizens with the legal right to live in Scotland can stand for Holyrood and local councils, even if their rights are temporary.
There was an outcry led by the Conservatives and Reform UK in May when Manivannan was elected as a Scottish Greens list MSP for Edinburgh and Lothians East. A successful PhD candidate at St Andrews, it emerged their student visa was due to expire at the end of 2026. They have since been granted a three-year graduate visa, giving them right to remain until the end of 2029.
Jenny Minto, the Scottish National party MSP who chairs the committee, and who voted in favour of the reforms last year, said public sentiment appears to have swung against the policy. She said:
It is vital that Scotland has elected representatives who look like the communities they represent. This diversity helps build trust in our elected institutions.
But we know that this trust is fragile, and so careful consideration needs to be given to all electoral reform that comes before us.
Reform UK was delighted by the committee’s recommendation, which follows proposals by ministers to extend the right to Commonwealth citizens, but the Scottish Greens said it was regressive. The Scottish Greens said:
There are thousands of people with limited leave to remain who live and work in Scotland and have made a home here, including Commonwealth citizens. They should be able to stand for our parliament and councils.
MSPs backed this change unanimously at the time, including the convenor and deputy convenor of the committee. It would be a regrettable backwards step for representation and democracy if Scotland was to roll back on this commitment.
Burnham claims he cares less about criticism from newspapers than previous PMs did
Andy Burnham has said that he cares less about what the newspapers say about him than previous prime ministers did.
In one of his interviews with Daniel Hewitt for the ITV documentary being shown tonight about his first 100 days in office, Burnham was asked if he cared less about what papers like the Daily Mail and the Sun said about him than some of his predecessors did. Burnham replied: “Definitely.”
He said:
I left Westminster for a reason. I got fed up with commentators deciding things down there and then the whole world [being] meant to believe what they believe. Well, sorry, the world’s not like that anymore.
Burnham also defended prioritising social media more instead. He said:
People want more involvement, more understanding of the way politics is being done and that’s what I’m bringing. And hopefully it connects with people, particularly younger people, who may have felt quite distant from politics.
In another interview for the programme, Burnham rejected the suggestion that he was ruthless. Explaining why he did not like the description, he said:
Determined, I definitely would say that [I am] determined. I will come back and back and back at something. I’ve always been like that. Ruthless to me says you just have a disregard for everybody else. And that wouldn’t be me. But I am determined.
Burnham also revealed that, since becoming PM, he continues to go running regularly – and that this is often when his “best thoughts” occur. He explained:
If you’re asking me about what’s the thing that makes it work, I go running and I’ve not stopped my running. It’s when my mind goes a bit into neutral. And I feel then I get my best thoughts in those moments.
You know, all of a sudden, "Oh, that, yeah, I’ll do that.’ Or a particularly intractable problem that you’ve been thinking and worrying about – all of a sudden, I’ve been out on a run sometimes, and you just think, ‘Ah, that’s the way I’ll go into that one.’
Reform UK councillor charged with 12 counts of rape and multiple other offences
Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council has been charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child, Peter Walker reports.
Charles ended his speech urging Commonwealth leaders to “recommit … to a Commonwealth in which our young people can look to the future with greater confidence and purpose”.
Charles said he was glad climate proposals were being considered at Chogm.
Here in the Caribbean, as in so many parts of our Commonwealth, climate change is not some distant prospect. It is an alarming reality.
As we know, large ocean states have contributed little to the causes of climate change, and yet they are among those bearing the greatest cost.
If we mobilise climate finance through the private sector and with the leveraging capacity of the public sector, we can drive investment into climate resilience.
Nature herself is an essential form of capital that sustains our prosperity and well-being. And yet we have persisted for too long to live off nature’s capital, rather than her income.
To restore nature is therefore not to choose our environment over our economy. It is to invest in the very foundations of our economy, not to mention our security.
Charles said Commonwealth values have never been more important.
What unites this extraordinary and unique group of countries even more deeply is our values of democracy and the rule of law, of respect, equal dignity and human rights, of sustainable development, of peace and security. These values have never been more important, contested as they are on so many fronts, and they guide us to action.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme.
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”.
 
 
 “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

Trump focuses closing message on anti-Muslim racism, with attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib
Donald Trump made anti-Muslim racism a focus of his attacks on Democrats in remarks in Kansas on Monday, with attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, and gratuitous mentions of Barack Obama’s middle name.
“Democrats are the party of Abdul Mohammad El-Sayed,” Trump said of the Michigan Senate candidate.
The president then repeated his riff about what a brilliant move it was for him to stop using El-Sayed’s first name and instead call him “Mohammed El-Sayed”, to better stoke Islamophobia.
“You know, he got very upset because I called him Mohammad. I just felt like it. Somebody said, ‘How did you do that?’ I said, ‘I’m the president, I can call him whatever the hell I want’”, Trump said.
“And actually his middle name is Mohammad,” the president added, before adding: “One good thing if you call somebody from that part of the world Mohammad, you’re about 65% sure to get it right. So if you have any problem with names, just call the guy Mohammad.”
El-Sayed responded to Trump mocking his name at a previous rally by writing on social media: “He says the name just fine when he’s begging the Qataris for a personal jet or the Saudis for funding for his son-in-law’s private equity firm.”
Despite being in Kansas to campaign for Republican senator Roger Marshall, Trump returned again and again to attacks on El-Sayed, and brought up two Muslim congresswoman, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, who are also not from Kansas.
He also lied that both El-Sayed and his sister are members of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist opposition group in Egypt, a wild claim that is not supported by any evidence at all but is repeated almost daily by the president.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
