Donald Trump has taken the stage in Corinth, Mississippi at a rally in support of Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, and began by suggesting that he is determined to reverse the historical pattern that midterm elections almost always go against the party of the president elected two years earlier.
In a hoarse voice, Trump claimed that his rallies have “totally changed the dialogue” around the campaign.
“For some reason, presidents don’t do well in the midterm, no matter how good they are, even if they’re great, like us,” Trump said. “But I will say, nobody has ever campaigned- nobody’s ever campaigned like I have for midterms.”
The president’s remarks are ongoing, and so far have mostly moved on from attacks on the Democratic nominee for Senate, Scott Colom, who was campaigning outside the arena before the rally, speaking to Trump supporters on line for the event, to repeating his claim that the US is experiencing a “golden age” of prosperity. The president did not mention high inflation and gasoline prices, caused by his tariffs on imported goods and the war he started with Iran.
A three-judge panel of a US appeals court on Monday ruled 2-1 against the Trump administration, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely noncitizens.
The two judges who concurred on the majority decision were Mark Bennett, who was nominated to the bench by Donald Trump in 2018, and Gabriel Sanchez, who was nominated by Joe Biden in 2021. The dissenting judge, Patrick Bumatay, was also nominated by Trump.
The justice department charged former FBI director James Comey on Monday with two counts of leaking information related to national defense, the third time the Trump administration has filed criminal charges against one of Donald Trump’s most despised foes.
The charges, filed in federal court in Washington DC, provide few details about what Comey is alleged to have leaked. The government alleges that the former FBI director leaked the information in 2016 and conspired with an unnamed person to give the information to a national news outlet.
Patrick Fitzgerald, Comey’s attorney, said the charges were related to a 5 October 2016 New York Times article that had already been investigated by prosecutors. The case was filed through a criminal maneuver known as an “information” – meaning it was not approved by a grand jury. While prosecutors will eventually have to have the charges approved by a grand jury, filing the charges through an information appears to have been an effort to quickly get the criminal charges in against Comey before the 10-year statute of limitations expires.
“Ten years after the article was published, the government filed an ‘information’ against Mr Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes he did not commit,” Fitzgerald said in a statement.
In a court filing unsealed on Monday, Comey’s lawyers argued the indictment should be dismissed because the statute of limitations had expired and it had been twice investigated and determined no charges should be filed. They also argued that the law required an indictment, not an information, within the 10-year statute of limitations.
NAACP denounces 'blatantly racist attacks' in Michigan Senate race
In a statement released on Monday, the president of the NAACP, Derrick Johnson, denounced a wave of Islamophobic attacks on Dr Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, from Republicans, including Donald Trump.
Johnson said:
“The blatantly racist attacks surrounding the Michigan Senate race are unacceptable and disgusting. It’s the same ugly, divisive tactics we’ve seen used during the darkest chapters of the South’s history. Race should never be used as a tool to scare anybody or try to prevent them from voting their conscience. This behavior is grotesque and undemocratic, and cannot under any circumstance be tolerated from anyone holding or seeking elected office.”
Trump lashes out at Obama for joking 'he's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory'
Before boarding Air Force One to fly to Mississippi for a campaign rally on Monday, Donald Trump was asked to respond to his predecessor, Barack Obama, joking over the weekend that his renovation of the White House, with “gold everywhere”, has “the White House looking like Saddam Hussein open a Cheesecake Factory.”
While rightwing media outlets have tried to cast Obama’s joke as a jibe at patrons of the restaurant chain – despite a report that his own family frequented the chain during his presidency – Cara Castronuova, a former reality TV fitness trainer now covering the White House for LindellTV, seemed to get confused about the talking point when she asked Trump for comment.
“Do you have a response to Obama,” she asked, “who made fun of the Cheesecake Factory, comparing it to the White House?”
“I’ve taken care of the White House. I fixed it with the finest artisans in the world. We’ve reskinned it. It was in horrible shape,” Trump said, in part.
“Guys like Obama, they would pass the front door, they’d see the broken masonry; they’d see the broken- the beautiful pilasters that were all broken, for years they were broken, and he wouldn’t notice because he doesn’t notice that,” Trump said. “He doesn’t notice dirt and filth that hadn’t been cleaned, where the walls hadn’t been cleaned for years. He doesn’t notice areas that haven’t been painted.”
“So it’s very easy for me to do,” Trump continued. “I do it very very simply because it’s my nature. You know, I’m a very clean person, and the White House was in terrible shape.”
“We have to explain that to Obama because he doesn’t understand it, because he’s not a smart guy,” Trump went on. “We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly.
“Guys like Obama don’t see it. You don’t see dirt. He doesn’t see filth. He doesn’t see broken ornaments on a building,” Trump added.
The president then turned to the camera to address Obama directly through the lens. “The White House - to president Obama – is a symbol of America. It has to be clean. The columns can’t be broken. The bricks can’t be falling off from under the plaster. And for you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president.”
In Waterville, a town of around 16,000 people, Troy Jackson took the stage at a local theater, just a week before the midterm elections where he’s hoping to oust Susan Collins, the long-serving Republican incumbent, in the US Senate.
He was joined on stage by Elizabeth Warren, the Democratic senator from Massachusetts, who rallied the crowd of about 150.
“You know, we’ve had a medical emergency in Washington. Every Republican in the United States Senate has had their spine surgically removed,” Warren said, while blasting the Trump administration’s agenda, which has seen the price of gas and heating oil skyrocket across the country as the war with Iran continues.
Mainers are feeling the pinch acutely, particularly as the state braces for winter, where temperatures will soon drop to below freezing.
“Why is all this happening? Because people wanted more money. Billionaires had to have more money. I mean, it just doesn’t make any sense,” Jackson said. “It could end Tuesday … when we take the Senate.”
The US Senate race in Maine is neck-and-neck, with most polls showing Jackson and Collins virtually tied. In each recent election, however, Collins has defied political gravity, and defied the odds while branding herself as an independent comfortable breaking with the rest of her party (and Trump by extension). Jackson is banking on the deep-seated anti-Trump animus that’s sweeping the country to pull off an upset.
Trump makes baseless claim Lula's victory in Brazil 'looked like another rigged election'
Speaking to reporters as he left for a campaign rally in Mississippi on Monday, Donald Trump said that the comeback victory of Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, over his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, “looked like another rigged election, frankly.”
“It was a terrible look, for the world,” Trump said, apparently referring to the court-ordered extension in voting hours after widespread reports that supporters of the president had been hindered in getting to the polls by public transportation outages.
“You know, elections have to be indisputable — and it looked very bad to me,” the US president added. “It looked so corrupt.”
None of the reporters in the limited press pool, after reporters from CNN and Politico were again blocked from taking part, pointed out to Trump that Brazil’s supreme court only extended voting hours across the nation by two hours after requests from both candidates.
The correspondent who was questioning Trump was Cara Castronuova a former reality TV fitness trainer now covering the White House for LindellTV, the streaming platform created by Mike Lindell, the election conspiracy theorist pillow salesman.
As our colleagues in Brazil reported earlier, the president of Brazil’s electoral court, justice Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed by the Bolsonaro’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, said that extending voting hours had caused “no change” to the election result.
Asked if he intended to intervene in any way, Trump said: “Well, I’m not running Brazil. I’m running the USA. And I just thought that the election was – I like Lula. I get along with him very well. I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated. The extension given was very strange.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: ‘A despicable betrayal’: Democrats incensed by Haley Stevens’s endorsement of Mike Rogers
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Democrat Haley Stevens’s shocking last-minute endorsement of Mike Rogers, the Michigan Republican Senate candidate, in the run-up to Tuesday’s midterm elections has sparked fierce backlash from members of her party.
Stevens, who narrowly lost in the Democratic primary for Senate to Abdul El-Sayed, announced her support for Rogers after a feud with the El-Sayed campaign over an outside group’s advertisement, which blamed the high cost of living on US support for Israel.
Stevens had said she would appear at a campaign event if he denounced the advertisement. El-Sayed’s campaign disinvited her.
Following the extraordinary public rupture on Sunday, El-Sayed’s campaign said it raised more than $2.4m, a fundraising record in the final days of a race that could determine control of the US senate. The Democrat’s campaign said more than 26,000 people contributed for the first time on Sunday.
New York Democrat Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, described Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers as “a despicable betrayal”.
“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors,” Schumer posted on social media.
Nancy Pelosi, the Democratic former House speaker, posted that Stevens had “chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement”.
The New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, said that “working class people’s lives are on the ballot on Tuesday”.
“Haley Stevens just betrayed them by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against,” Mamdani posted.
Stevens refused to clearly explain what led to her endorsement of Rogers in an interview with Anderson Cooper on CNN Sunday evening. “I’m just casting my one vote this way,” Stevens said, while insisting she still wanted Democrats to win the majority on election day.
“I am not trying to upset anyone,” she added. “I’m just being honest with my constituents and what I’m hearing from people, and in fact, I’ve been hearing from a ton of Dems, Anderson, who said: ‘Thank you, this is how we felt; we haven’t liked this campaign; it’s painful.’”
Cooper pressed Stevens, questioning whether being disinvited from El-Sayed’s campaign event triggered her endorsement of Rogers. At one point, Stevens refused to answer the question, allowing several seconds of silence to air.
Stevens has continued to defend her decision as she faces accusations of betrayal from Democrats, including calls for her expulsion from the House caucus. Several members of her congressional staff resigned in protest. In an interview on Monday, she compared herself with Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman, a one-time progressive who now frequently breaks with his party, especially over supporting Israel.
“You see a Democrat from Pennsylvania, you know, his name’s a lightning rod in the party. His name’s Fetterman,” she told conservative commentator Scott Jennings. “They say the same thing about him.”
Curtis Hertel, the chair the Michigan Democratic party, said in a post that Stevens was not a member of the party “nor will she be in the future”.
A Detroit journalist, Sam Robinson, shared a video in which Hertel was asked why he thought Stevens made the endorsement.
“Obviously there are sour grapes from the election, but there is no reasonable explanation for this. I have known Haley Stevens for a long time, and I know what she has fought for her in her career, and this is the antithesis of all of that,” Hertel said.
Debbie Dingell, a veteran Michigan House Democrat, dismissed Stevens’s endorsement as a distraction from voters’ concerns about the cost of living.
“That’s what they’re talking about, not Congresswoman Stevens’ continued efforts to get attention,” she said in a statement.
On MS Now on Sunday, El-Sayed encouraged undecided Michigan voters to stand with him to protect democracy in the United States. “The divide in our politics isn’t left versus right; the divide in our politics is the people who are locked out versus the people who are locking them out,” El-Sayed said.
Speaking to Fox News on Monday, Rogers praised Stevens for her endorsement. “I know Democrats are thumping their chest and saying she has done something other than courageous,” he said. “It was nothing but courageous.”
Charlotte Clymer, a blogger and activist who supports Democrats, told the Guardian she had considered Stevens a friend for several years, and said the congresswoman’s decision to back Rogers “is like endorsing Donald Trump”.
“This is like living through a bad dream. It really is,” Clymer said. “If you had told me there’d be a sitting Democratic member of Congress who would switch like this, Haley would not have come to mind.”
She called Stevens a lawmaker of “strident integrity” who has stood up for LGBTQ+ rights, unions and abortion access. As tensions rose with the El-Sayed campaign Clymer said that on on Saturday she texted Stevens, who replied with messages assuring her she still supported the Democratic nominee. Clymer said she texted again after Stevens released a video endorsing Rogers on Sunday, but has not heard back.
“It really is bizarre. It feels like there [is] a body snatcher moment. Someone has kidnapped Haley Stevens and replaced her with a completely different person,” Clymer said.
Meanwhile, Trump praised Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers on his platform Truth Social and described her as a “highly respected Democrat”. He again cheered Stevens during a campaign rally on Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa, and encouraged her to switch parties.
“I’d love her to join the Republican party, actually, I think that could happen maybe. But she showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the great people of Michigan,” Trump said.
When asked about Trump praising her, Stevens told CNN: “Well, I impeached him twice,” before criticizing Republicans for being “really focused on just letting Trump be the dictator”.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite | Gaby Hinsliff
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Another morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway.
In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back.
And therein lies the challenge to the government’s hopes of AI helping to transform the machinery of the state on the cheap, saving not only time but billions of pounds in public money. It’s early days, but AI seems not so much to be streamlining public service delivery as gumming it up – partly because, as was once the case with email, the public is using it right back at them.
In a Substack post last week, the former civil servant Sam Freedman noted that governments around the world seem to be experiencing unusual surges in complaints, requests and responses to regulatory and official bodies since the adoption of ChatGPT. It’s the same story in the courts, with employment tribunal cases in England, Scotland and Wales reportedly rising by 39% in a year thanks in part to claimants using AI to draft claims, while magistrates and judges face a wave of people who can’t afford lawyers using ChatGPT to build cases that often don’t make sense. And all of this needs patient disentangling by a human, on the grounds that just because a defendant is citing precedents that don’t exist, it doesn’t mean there isn’t a genuine grievance buried in there somewhere.
Whitehall special advisers complain of departments drowning in AI-generated freedom of information requests, an abuse of a system originally intended to empower individuals. MPs’ offices are similarly swamped by AI-generated letters, all of which need to be read by humans for fear of missing something important from a constituent.
How long before public consultations on changing the law become so spammed by slop that they are in essence useless as a measure of what the country actually thinks? There’s a fine line between the noble aim of making it easier for individuals to interact with an otherwise remote state, and making it so easy that the result is an uncontrollable firehose of meaningless machine-generated guff.
The obvious answer to this kind of AI flooding is getting AI tools to detect or sift it, but that doesn’t always work when dealing with potentially vulnerable human beings. Constituents who use AI to express themselves in more fancy-sounding language when writing to their MP, for example, still have the right to expect a personal response from a human being.
Employers who thought they were being smart by getting AI to sift job applications, meanwhile, are reaping what they sowed, as resentful applicants automate their end of things too and spray-gun applications across the board, rather than concentrating on the jobs they really want. Now neither side can separate the wheat from an avalanche of chaff.
The risk of paralysis is likely only to increase if the public starts adopting agentic AI in the kind of numbers big tech fondly imagines. Early adopters might well find agents save them time and hassle. But shortcuts stop being shortcuts once everyone else is using them too, and risk turning into bottlenecks instead. Think of cars, which have vastly shortened journey times compared with travelling by horseback, except in cities at rush hour when too many other people are also trying to shorten theirs. By 2018, central London daytime traffic was moving on average at just over 7mph – about the same speed as a trotting pony.
Historically, humans have always learned to develop ways around problems of our own making. We have spam filters for email, congestion charges to keep cars out of cities, and in the long term we could well figure out what kind of frictions we need to put back in the system to make it possible to live with the impact of AI.
But for now a useful rule of thumb, if improbable claims start to be made for savings due to AI, will be that more isn’t always better; faster and easier isn’t always more convenient; and time saved in one section of public services has a horrible habit of popping up in another one. Let the Whac-A-Mole begin.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Pentagon says Trump and Hegseth spoke about decision not to livestream execution ahead of announcement
The Pentagon has also now responded to Donald Trump’s decision to cancel the livestream of the execution of Nidal Hasan.
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said:
President Trump and Secretary Hegseth spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan’s execution ahead of the Truth Social announcement.The Secretary supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Donald Trump lied to Michigan voters about Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, calling the American physician “a Muslim Brotherhood member” in a video message recorded in the Oval Office.
Elected officials in Oregon and lawmakers in Washington DC have expressed dismay at the school shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon on Thursday, in which a 16-year-old attacker killed at least three children and one adult before being fatally shot by a community member.
Speaking to reporters in Virginia on Thursday, the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, claimed that the measles outbreak that has killed at least six people in Pennsylvania was caused by the suspension of vaccination against the disease during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Trump administration sued the state of California and its election officials, seeking to compel the state to not count ballots cast by 20,000 registered California voters whom the Department of Homeland Security suspects might not be citizens.
Trump said that the execution of Nidal Hasan, the US army doctor who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, would not be livestreamed.
Trump lies about Abdul El-Sayed in social media appeal to Michigan voters, falsely accusing candidate of being 'a Muslim Brotherhood member'
Donald Trump lied to Michigan voters about Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, calling the American physician “a Muslim Brotherhood member” in a video message recorded in the Oval Office and posted on the president’s social media platform on Thursday.
As if to make the anti-Muslim racism of his message entirely clear, the president insisted on referring to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” repeatedly.
Trump acknowledged that El-Sayed, the Michigan-born son of Egyptian immigrant parents, has flatly denied having any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Egyptian Islamist social and political movement, before adding, without any explanation at all: “all you have to do is look at his past correspondence”.
While it was not clear what “correspondence” Trump seems to think would contradict El-Sayed’s denial, and there is no evidence at all that the Michigan doctor is a member of the Egyptian group, the president might have been referring to a letter El-Sayed reportedly signed in 2012, in which prominent Egyptian-Americans who supported the revolution that deposed Egypt’s dictator Hosni Mubarak urged the president elected that year, Mohamed Morsi, to keep elements of the old regime from seizing power. Morsi, a former Muslim Brotherhood member, was deposed in a military coup months later.
“Don’t vote for Mohammed El-Sayed,” Trump urged Michigan voters at the end of his nakedly Islamophobic video. “He’s not for us and he hates our country.”
Elected officials react to school shooting in Oregon
Elected officials in Oregon and lawmakers in Washington DC have expressed dismay at the school shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon on Thursday, in which a 16-year-old attacker killed at least three children and one adult before being fatally shot by a community member.
“They’re killing our babies. Shredding our kids with lead. Forcing us to live in fear,” congresswoman Janelle Bynum, who represents the city, said in a statement. “I feel this deep, deep, deep in my soul. Our whole community does. Our whole state does.And the whole nation should.”
“Our babies are supposed to do arts and crafts at school, not use their desks as cover from gunfire. They’re supposed to make friends, not mourn them,” she continued. “This is every parent’s worst fear. My heart and my prayers and everything else I got is with the families at Silver Rail Elementary. When will it end?”
“All Oregonians mourn this loss today,” the state’s governor, Tina Kotek, said at a news conference in Bend. “This is a horrible day. No parent should have to have this kind of day and no community should have to live through this kind of day.”
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want to you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” she added.
Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, the leader of the Democratic minority in the House, wrote: “Heartbroken by the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Oregon. Praying for the children, families and educators affected by this tragedy. We must end the scourge of gun violence in America.”
House Republicans repeated a familiar formula in response to mass shootings, writing in a statement “Our thoughts and prayers are with the victims and their families.”
Order to limit Ukraine's access to SpaceX’s satellite internet system came from inside White House - report
Citing two US officials and a western official, Reuters reports that an order to limit Ukraine’s access to Starlink satellite internet terminals, used for battlefield communications and drone operations, came from inside the White House.
According to the Reuters report:
The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.
The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.
Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.
A White House official denied that Donald Trump had ordered the Pentagon to limit Starshield for Ukraine this week, which disrupted its ability to hit Russian targets, telling the news agency: “No such request was ever made by the president.”
The White House did not say if another administration official might have made the request.
Questions are mounting about Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, who told Guardian reporter Shrai Popat that only six days passed between the moment she first received a call from the White House and when she stepped up to the podium for her very first briefing.
Zacharia has offered up little intel on how she plans to take on the role, responding that it is “unknown” how often she will brief the press or speak to reporters. That’s not all that’s unknown, however, information about Zacharia’s work history and experience is also a bit fuzzy.
While she’s been referred to as an attorney by the president, she reportedly failed the California bar exam after graduating from Pepperdine University’s law school in 2011.
As Shrai Popat reports:
After her time in China, there is a 10-year gap on Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile. Wired reported on Thursday that during that period she worked as an “affiliate marketer” for Beachbody, a multi-level marketing company she described to the outlet as “sort of a pyramid scheme”.
She later served as “general counsel” for Fix California, a conservative group founded by Ric Grenell, a longtime Trump ally and the special presidential envoy for special missions. The Guardian has approached both Zhong Lun and Fix California seeking additional details about Zacharia’s legal roles at the organizations.
One thing is for certain, however, and a look at other Trump appointees shows it’s often a credential that outranks experience. Championing her history as a “devoted fan of Maga”, he said she has “an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning”.
RFK Jr tries to blame measles outbreak on failure to vaccinate children during Covid-19 shutdowns
Speaking to reporters in Virginia on Thursday, the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, claimed that the measles outbreak that has killed at least six people in Pennsylvania was caused by the suspension of vaccination against the disease during the Covid-19 pandemic.
After an event focused on efforts to address a shortage of health care providers in the US, a reporter asked Kennedy, the former leader of an anti-vaccination group, if he believes that the number of measles deaths in Pennsylvania “is acceptable”.
When a press aide interrupted to say the question was off-topic, the reporter said, “he’s the highest-ranking health official in the country; he can answer that question. He’s a cabinet secretary.”
“We’ve done better than- we’re having a global measles outbreak right now,” Kennedy replied. “It’s all over the world, and the measles outbreak is occurring because so many people went unvaccinated during the Covid pandemic.
“And this is something that Anthony Fauci, in fact, predicted,” Kennedy added, before referring, imprecisely, to an entry in a private journal kept by Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, on 6 May 2020, about the “unintended consequences” of shutdowns to stop the spread of the coronavirus. “He said: ‘We’re gonna kill more people from measles than we save from Covid ‘cause we’re shutting down measles vaccination programs,’” Kennedy said.
What Fauci wrote at that early stage of the shutdowns, as discussions about when to end the restrictions in the US were underway, was that more than “1 million children worldwide have missed their measles vaccinations because of the shutdown. This is terrible and needs to be addressed since on that basis alone, there would be far, far more excess deaths from measles among children than coronavirus deaths among children.”
On Thursday, Kennedy claimed that that pause in childhood vaccination, not fears about vaccines spread by anti-vaccine activists like him, was the cause of the current outbreak.
“So now, six years later”, Kennedy said, “we have a global outbreak.
“We have done better, and particularly my administration has done better, at controlling the outbreak than any other country in the world,” Kennedy claimed. “We’ve had 4,000 measles cases this year. Mexico, which is a third of our population, had 20,000. Canada has 7,000, has a third, or one-eighth of our population. In Europe, they’ve had 135,000 cases. So we’re doing better at controlling it than any country in the world.”
He then pivoted to blaming the severity of the Pennsylvania outbreak on the state’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro.
“Unfortunately, in Pennsylvania”, Kennedy said, “the governor- the only state where the governor would not accept CDC Epi-Aid,” referring to the shorthand for a CDC investigation of an epidemic.
In August, Shapiro said that he blamed Kennedy for spreading anti-vaccine misinformation.
Trump says John Cornyn and Karl Rove will be to blame if Republican Ken Paxton loses Texas Senate race
As public polling suggests that the Texas Senate candidate Donald Trump endorsed, Ken Paxton, could lose a seat Republicans have held since 1961 to Democrat James Talarico, the president on Thursday tried to preemptively shift the blame away from himself and on to two other Republicans: Senator John Cornyn and former Karl Rove.
Writing on social media, Trump lashed out at Cornyn, who lost a bitter Republican primary battle after Trump endorsed Paxton, and Rove, a veteran Republican campaign strategist who left college to work for the party during the Watergate scandal and went on to get George W Bush elected president.
Trump accused Cornyn and Rove or “doing everything possible to make it hard for” Paxton “to win”.
The president, who spends much of his day watching Fox News, bitterly complained that Rove, a Fox News contributor, “shouldn’t be allowed to spew his jealousy on” the rightwing network created by a former adviser to Richard Nixon to help elect Republicans.
“If Ken Paxton loses”, Trump added, “it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career.”
Trump, who is not on the midterm ballot, then boasted about how well he had done in the previous election in Texas, using information he said he had gotten from Fox News.
Trump administration sues California to block counting of mail ballots from 20,000 registered voters
The Trump administration sued the state of California and its election officials on Thursday, seeking to compel the state to not count ballots cast by 20,000 registered California voters whom the Department of Homeland Security suspects might not be citizens.
Officials in California named in the suit rejected the demand, which the state’s governor, Gavin Newsom, called “a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day.
“The courts have made clear that the federal government has no role in how a state carries out its election process, and now, in the middle of Californians voting, they have asked local officials – who do a damn good job defending democracy – to violate federal law,” the governor added.
In a letter to the Department of Justice, California’s secretary of state, Shirley Weber, noted that the federal government did not explain the methodology it used to compile the list of 20,000 voters who had been sent mail ballots for the midterm elections. Setting ballots cast by those voters aside, Weber said, would violate federal and state law.
Weber also pointed out that a similar list of suspected noncitizen voters in Nevada had been shown to be entirely wrong. “DHS initially alleged that Nevada’s voter roll included nearly 16,000 potential non-citizens,” Weber wrote. “However, after working with the State of Nevada, DHS officials failed to establish that a single non-citizen was on the voter rolls.”
Dean Logan, the registrar of the state’s largest county, Los Angeles, with 5.8 million registered voters, said in a statement that his office received a thumb drive from the federal government two days ago, said to include a list of 20,000 alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls, with a “hand written note providing a password”.
Logan said that his office did not open the thumb drive, since “we do not consider the device a secure medium.” The secretary of state’s office said the password was written “on a sticky note”.
“Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established – and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching,” Logan added.
Experts have warned for years that a DHS database that flags people who were once immigrants to the US is not a reliable method of finding current noncitizens, since it is not updated when people become naturalized citizens.
According to a 2024 data analysis from the USC Dornsife Equity Research Institute, 5.7 million Californians are naturalized US citizens, including 1.3 million who became citizens since 2015.
The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service are investigating letters sent to state officials and election offices across the country containing an “unknown substance”.
Just weeks before November’s US midterm elections, election officers in Louisiana and Oklahoma received envelopes containing a powdery substance, leading to evacuations. A similar package containing white powder was also sent to the Ohio secretary of state, but the US Postal Service intercepted the package.
The US Senate sergeant at arms, who serves as chief law enforcement for the Senate, informed members of the upper chamber on Thursday of the investigation in a message, obtained by the Associated Press.
The notice said law enforcement officials were working to intercept additional mail, but it is possible some could reach their destination. Federal authorities have urged recipients to treat the mail as “potentially hazardous”.
Brendan Donahue, a senior official with the US Postal Inspection Service, confirmed the investigation into the suspicious mailings during a press conference on Thursday. “We are committed to protecting our nation’s election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable,” Donahue said.
The US Postal Inspection Service referred the Guardian to the FBI.
In a statement, the FBI said it would not confirm specific instances but said that it was “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State office and their related election officers” alongside the US Postal Inspection Service.
“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the FBI said. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”
The FBI declined to comment on what the purported substance may have been.
Donald Trump has said that the execution of Nidal Hasan, the US army doctor who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, would not be livestreamed. The decision, issued via a post on Truth Social, comes after bipartisan backlash to defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement that Hasan’s execution by firing squad, would be broadcast online.“Many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” Trump wrote on Thursday. “He [Hasan] will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.”
Following the news, lawmakers from both parties welcomed the decision. “Good. So sick to have ever considered this,” wrote Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, on X. Meanwhile, Republican Senator John Curtis of Iowa, said “this is the right move, both for the loved ones of the victims and for the country.”
The Pentagon has said that Hegseth and Trump are “completely aligned” about the decision to not livestream the execution. In the statement to the Guardian, Sean Parnell, the chief defense department spokesperson said that Hegseth and the president spoke before the Truth Social announcement, and the press secretary supports Trump’s decision.
Key voting groups including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans are increasingly disenchanted with Donald Trump’s economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian. The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three-quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one. By its typical definition, the US is not currently experiencing a recession. More here
While Donald Trump announced on Thursday he was cancelling Pete Hegseth’s recently announced plans to livestream the military execution of Nidal Hasan, because “many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die”. There were, however, some fans of Hegseth’s now-scotched idea: the rightwing religious figures who have long backed his career.
The de facto leader of Hegseth’s theocratic Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), Douglas Wilson, welcomed the announcement.
Wilson, the Idaho pastor who co-founded CREC, has promoted capital punishment as biblically authorized for decades. Last Friday he told Religion News that he prefers “public executions to those conducted in the recesses of a prison somewhere in the middle of the night”, adding that “executions in the scriptures were public”.
Wilson told the outlet that public executions can “turn into a circus”.
Wilson told the Guardian that “I support the execution of Hasan, and prefer public executions to private”, adding: “I prefer the older forms, like a firing squad, as opposed to attempts to ‘medicalize’ it, as with the recent botched execution by injection in Tennessee.”
He did stipulate that “the Pentagon has the responsibility to head off ghoulish behavior by some means”, but admitted: “That will be challenging with a live stream.”
Wilson wrote that he had not spoken to Hegseth nor anyone in his department about the issue.
Wilson and his religious allies are at odds with some other religious leaders, including Pope Leo and the archbishop to the US military, Timothy Broglio, both of whom have condemned Hegseth’s plans.
But CREC pastors, whose church in Washington DC Hegseth attends, have for years advocated the death penalty for many perceived moral infractions including adultery, abortion and homosexuality, and a podcaster from Hegseth’s former church has repeatedly called for executions to be public. Several have expressed hostility to Muslims and Islam, with one calling Allah a “demon God”.
Ilhan Omar’s office did not confirm to the Guardian whether the congresswoman’s phone has been seized, per reporting. But a spokesperson reiterated that the ongoing investigation is “politically motivated and an escalation of Trump’s personal vendetta” against the congresswoman.
“He [Trump] has lied about her family, about her immigration history, and about her love of this country. But the truth is that Trump’s push to strip her of her citizenship and deport her has no basis in the law and has no precedent,” the spokesperson added. “This isn’t a legitimate law enforcement action – it is an authoritarian move to silence an opponent right before an election where he and his party will be rejected by Americans in historic proportions.”
As more emerges about the raid by federal agents on Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s DC home, an unlikely defender has emerged in the form of Marjorie Taylor Greene.
The former Republican representative, now estranged from her party after falling out over the handling of the Epstein files and the Gaza war, took to social media to say that while she and Omar are not aligned on many issues, she questioned how the investigation would “bring gas down under $2, make health insurance freaking affordable, make a family’s weekly grocery bill make sense, and stop sending our beloved military off to fight for another fucking foreign war???”
Greene, who previously introduced a resolution in early 2024 to censure Omar over “treasonous” statements about US-Somali relations, said that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) probe was futile.
“People are so sick and tired of the bullshit,” she wrote on X. “When you dumb mf’ers at the WH actually release the Epstein files and lock up the pedophiles and rapists you all hang out with, then we will start paying attention.”
A reminder that federal authorities investigating Omar have reportedly seized her phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, a person briefed on the inquiry told the Associated Press. Markwayne Mullin previously suggested that agents are examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
We’re keeping an eye on the press conference between Pete Hegseth and his UK counterpart, Wes Streeting at the Pentagon. The pair are currently on the steps of the Department of Defense.
In the Rose Garden today, Donald Trump joked that “one of those beautiful robots” which they could make “look just like” the president could be sent out to campaign on his behalf.
“You wouldn’t know the difference. They make them pretty good. Send them out on the trail. I could sit home and watch them on television,” Trump said. “But, I love doing it.”
This comes as the president is in the middle of a midterm campaign blitz, to stump for everal Republican nominees across the country. After stops in Alaska, Arizona and Montana so far this week, the president will head to Georgia tomorrow, and Kentucky this weekend.
Trump will also head to Iowa on 22 October and 1 November, according to the chair of the Iowa Republicans.
Pentagon says Trump and Hegseth spoke about decision not to livestream execution ahead of announcement
The Pentagon has also now responded to Donald Trump’s decision to cancel the livestream of the execution of Nidal Hasan.
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said:
President Trump and Secretary Hegseth spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan’s execution ahead of the Truth Social announcement.The Secretary supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned.
UK defence secretary Wes Streeting emphasizes importance of standing with Ukraine as he speaks in Washington DC
Britain’s defence secretary Wes Streeting has stressed the importance of standing with Ukraine in its defence against Russia amid mounting fears over the United States’ commitment to Kyiv, the Press Association reports.
During his first visit to Washington in the role, Streeting warned that if Vladimir Putin’s aggression was rewarded, “the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent.”
Streeting is expected to meet his US counterpart PeteHegseth in a bid to strengthen ties that have been strained by issues including DonaldTrump’s stance on Kyiv and the widening US-Nato rift.
Streeting said today that the UK and US must strengthen their defence partnership to confront growing threats at a time when “it is not yet clear if this century will be defined by freedom or tyranny”.
Speaking at an event held by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies and the Royal United Services Institute, he said:
Britain and America have never been content to simply watch history unfold. At defining moments, we have helped determine its course.
The front line for freedom today can be found in Ukraine.
He continued:
Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent.
So standing with Ukraine is not a choice between our values and our self-interest. It is a recognition that ultimately they are inseparable.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Shabana Mahmood has been accused of launching a “perfunctory political gimmick” by the Eritrean government in a row over the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals.
After the home secretary threatened to block all Eritreans from entering the UK unless a returns deal was agreed, the country’s embassy claimed the UK had failed to engage in “meaningful and appropriate” dialogue.
The spat began on Thursday morning when the Home Office claimed the east African country had abruptly withdrawn cooperation on the return of unwanted citizens earlier this year.
From Thursday, diplomats from the east African country also face restrictions on their movement outside London and VIPs will be stripped of access to fast-track visas as preferential processing is scrapped.
It prompted a statement from Eritrea’s north London embassy “categorically” rejecting Mahmood’s claims.
“Despite Eritrea’s repeated requests for constructive discussion with relevant UK authorities on the dignified return of its citizens, the UK has shown no interest to engage in meaningful and appropriate dialogue,” it said.
Describing the home secretary’s decision as regrettable, the statement added: “The act is nothing more than a perfunctory political gimmick. The fact is, the UK has not issued a single visa to an Eritrean official since 2023.”
UK government officials denied this. They insisted a confirmed exemption from immigration control for an Eritrean official took place as recently as August 2026.
Sources said Eritrea previously cooperated with the UK on returns between 2024 and March 2026, while the UK has repeatedly sought to engage with Eritrean authorities, including repeatedly offering to send a Home Office delegation to Asmara to discuss returns.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “The Eritrean government’s press notice misrepresents the UK’s position and contains numerous factual inaccuracies.”
Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals.
Mahmood said on Thursday morning: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.
“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK. I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.”
The move followed similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025.
Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the DRC faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February.
In March, ministers also placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the home secretary accused them of exploiting Britain’s generosity to claim asylum.
Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were also halted, as were work visas for Afghans.
Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality.
After the success of the previous sanction threats, Mahmood warned other countries that they faced similar visa restrictions if they continued to refuse to take back their criminals, illegal migrants and rejected asylum seekers.
India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Somalia, Egypt and Gabon have been identified as resistant to taking back illegal migrants and could face sanctions.
Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said roughly 7,000 applications for asylum came from Eritreans, about 8% of the total.
About 84% were successful on first application and more would be successful on appeal, she said.
“There are different types of threats that can be made such as stopping student visas, or stopping visit visas. It will be interesting to see what kind of impact this has on the number of returns.”
Reacting to Mahmood’s announcement, one Eritrean asylum seeker said any returnees would “be put in prison and may never be able to get out”.
The advocacy group Justice for Eritreans condemned the announcement. “Many Eritreans have fled indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and severe human rights abuses,” it said. “These risks cannot be ignored for the sake of immigration targets. Refugee protection is a legal responsibility, not a political bargaining tool.”
UN experts say the human rights situation in Eritrea continues to be dire. Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, the special rapporteur on human rights in Eritrea, said there were no signs of meaningful improvement in the country’s human rights situation.
“There remain reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity continue in Eritrea,” he said when launching a report this year into the human rights situation.
“Regrettably, the core human rights issues that prompted the creation of this mandate 14 years ago remain mostly unresolved.
“The ongoing systematic, and widespread enforced disappearance and prolonged incommunicado detention without charge or trial, torture, and the persecution of political opponents, journalists, and members of religious communities remain central features of governance in Eritrea.”
Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International’s policy lead on refugee and migrant rights, said: “As Amnesty and others have documented, Eritrea has an appalling human rights record.
“It has not become any less unsafe following the election in this country of a Labour government in 2024 or Shabana Mahmood beginning her term at the Home Office in 2025.”
Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “Severe political repression and widespread human rights abuses are the reason people are forced to flee Eritrea, and are, in the vast majority of cases, recognised by our government as in need of support.
“It’s imperative that this policy only targets the Eritrean authorities, and does not undermine the UK’s moral and legal duty to provide protection to those who need it.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s ‘politically motivated’ requests for Falklands oil arrests
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off the Falkland Islands.
With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war with Argentina in 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation.
A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated.
It is understood the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working in the Falklands.
An oil project known as Sea Lion in the North Falkland Basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors.
In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood.
Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.”
She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”
It is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character.
Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year.
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has told MPs that the UK will protect businesses working in the Falklands from pressure from Argentina through measures under protection of trading interests (PTI) legislation.
The legislation allows the UK to issue orders and directions forbidding British individuals and companies from complying with specific foreign laws or trade controls. It also opens up the possibility that those affected by Argentinian legal pressure could claim damages in UK courts.
Miliband said: “The UK’s support for the Falkland Islands is steadfast. Argentina’s attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion.
“We will always stand up for the Falkland Islanders, their right to determine their own future, and their right to pursue legitimate economic development.”
The intensity of Argentinian pressure relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by the then Argentinian dictator, Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation.
Milei has initiated criminal proceedings against the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration, which are the core companies in the offshore Sea Lion project.
A draft national sovereignty bill introduced to Argentina’s congress would further expand the scope of sanctions to affiliates of those companies, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers.
The bill additionally contains clauses that could target those involved in the fishing industry in the Falklands, which makes up a large part of the islands’ economy. The archipelago is 300 miles (500km) east of the southern Patagonian coast of Argentina.
Workers in the oil and fisheries sectors on the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – are understood to be concerned that they could be targeted should they travel, particularly to South America, where there is support for Buenos Aires’s sovereignty claim.
In a tandem move to kill off Sea Lion, Argentina is expected within 24 hours to escalate further its dispute with the UK by requesting arbitration under annex VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (Unclos) over the oil project.
On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline to stop the project or face such legal action. The deadline passed on Monday and Argentinian newspapers said an application for arbitration would follow.
Under it, Buenos Aires will claim the UK is in breach of a UN resolution inviting the parties to negotiate over the sovereignty dispute and refrain from “unilateral modifications” to the situation. It will be seeking a binding ruling that the UK must stop the drilling. However, UK government sources are confident that Unclos will not wade into a sovereignty dispute.
At a public meeting on Monday evening, one of the Falkland Islands’ assembly members, Dean Dent, told constituents that the UK government was working hard on a tough response to the Argentinian Unclos threat.
“The UK government has assembled quite an in-depth team of legal advisers, KCs – that is the first step,” he said. “There have been four recent similar cases where a case of sovereignty has been taken to Unclos and all four were disregarded by the tribunal as all four cases were a sovereignty issue, not a maritime issue.”
The UK government is expected to be increasingly muscular in its approach to Argentina in the coming days. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Monday that he had raised the issue and “the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British” with the US president, Donald Trump.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Poland looks to economic heights in a country transformed since Soviet days
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Above the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso tower overlooks Joseph Stalin’s gift to Poland that has divided opinion for decades.
For some, the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science is a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history.
For the managers of the Varso – completed four years ago, as the tallest building in the EU – with its 310m-high spire rising symbolically above its Stalinist neighbour, it is a waypoint on Poland’s rapid path to economic prosperity.
“We look down on it,” says Cezary Błaszczyk, the managing director of HB Reavis in Poland, which owns the tower, gesturing at the palace opposite. A few months ago a slackline walker traversed the 500m gap between the buildings. “It was a symbolic walk from the past to the future,” says his colleague Natalia Kasperska.
“Since we are higher and taller than the Palace of Culture, we treat it as: ‘We got over communism, and now we are a country with a strong economy,’” Błaszczyk says.
Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.
National income surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, ranking Poland among the world’s 20 largest economies. International Monetary Fund projections show income per capita will soon overtake Japan and Spain.
“Four decades ago, we were in – excuse my English – deep, deep shit,” says Marcin Bosacki, the Polish deputy foreign minister.
Stirring a cup of tea and lemon in his opulent Warsaw office, he recalls queueing after school in the 1980s for up to five hours to buy butter and meat as the communist government imposed martial law.
However, the Gdańsk shipworkers’ Solidarność movement and Pope John Paul II’s 1979 pilgrimage to his home country paved the way for Poland’s transition to democracy in 1990 and an “economic miracle”. Integration with western institutions, including Nato in 1999 and EU accession in 2004, also helped.
For years, many Poles chose to emigrate to earn more abroad, in a brain drain accelerated by EU membership. Polish plumbers became shorthand in Britain for foreign labour amid the political battles over EU freedom of movement before the Brexit vote.
Now Britons are increasingly likely to have their taps fixed by Romanians and Bulgarians, after a surge in the number of Polish nationals leaving. In each year since 2021, when Brexit was enacted after a year-long transition period, twice as many Poles left the UK than arrived.
Meanwhile, Germany recorded more non-Germans moving to Poland in 2024 than heading in the opposite direction for the first time on record.
On the Varso’s 44th floor, in the Warsaw practice of Foster + Partners, Jedrzej Kolesinski and Krzysztof Gornicki are among those returnees. Both moved to London in their 20s to work in the British architecture firm’s head office – where they led the design team behind the tower they now occupy.
Gornicki says Poland has changed dramatically in the years he was away. He always wanted to return to contribute to the country, and raising a family near his parents in a safe, green city that is more affordable than London also has its plus points. Now the pair are working to design Warsaw’s new airport – the biggest greenfield infrastructure project in Europe.
“You can work globally from one location. In London we worked on projects from North America to Asia … right now, we’re doing the same thing, just from Warsaw.”
On the streets below the Varso, the sights and sounds of progress are unmistakable. Modern electric trams glide past skyscrapers, there are cranes and construction work, giant advertising boards, and dockless e-scooters.
The traditional working-class bar mleczny (milk bars) still do a roaring trade serving beetroot soup and Polish dumplings. But at the oldest, Prasowy, orders are taken on a digital touchscreen.
Once an asphalt desert designed for columns of Soviet tanks, the old Parade Square surrounding the palace has had a green makeover. Further development is planned to bolster Warsaw’s bid for the 2040 summer Olympics.
There are also growing pains. Just as the facades of Warsaw’s medieval old town – rebuilt from the rubble of the second world war – conceal 20th-century concrete, Poland’s stellar growth obscures tensions. The influx of global capital has driven up living costs, squeezing out poor Varsovians. Income inequality is among the highest in Europe, while growing political divisions set the stage for a fractious general election next year.
Convergence with the west also presents a novel challenge for a country with a reputation as a low-cost hub within the EU.
For years Poland’s cheap, skilled workforce attracted companies such as Volkswagen to build cars, Cadbury to make chocolate and banks such as JP Morgan to open global support centres. At €19.10 (£16.10) an hour, average labour costs (wages, taxes and other costs) are still half the level of Germany and France, but the gap is closing.
Since 2004, the average monthly wage has more than tripled in nominal terms to 8,904 złoty (£1,723) last year. The net monthly salary in Warsaw has risen by 120% since 2016, according to Deutsche Bank, lifting it above Rome and Lisbon. A meal for two in the capital now costs more than in Tokyo and the price of a cappuccino has doubled.
Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Kraków, says Poles deserve their reputation as hard workers. But now the country must focus on working smarter, in higher-value-added manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services.
“The next phase will depend less on catching up, and more on productivity. We don’t have labour cost advantage at all. We need to focus on productivity, technology, cheaper energy and better regulation.”
He is, however, concerned about the tensions in Polish politics. Divisions between the nationalist president, Karol Nawrocki, and Donald Tusk’s liberal government have grown increasingly acrimonious. Meanwhile, fringe far-right parties together hold a fifth of public support. Poland is also investing heavily in defence and energy security – aiming to boost economic growth in the process – amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement.
“People may put trust in someone else that has a magic remedy. [But] there is no magic remedy. We need to be super careful in terms of believing there is a secret sauce that will magically change things,” Brzoska says.
“In my opinion – unfortunately for all of us – we still need to work hard.”
As part of its growth plans, Poland is pushing to become a regional tech hub, bolstered by a $1bn investment fund backed by public and private capital to support tech startups and AI companies. The number of high-growth firms is rising, including ElevenLabs, an $11bn AI audio generation and voice cloning company named after 11 November – Poland’s national independence day.
There are strong foundations for its ambition. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s annual programme for international student assessment (Pisa) scores ranks Poland equal to the UK among the top countries in Europe and globally for maths, while a greater share of adults have higher education qualifications than in Germany.
On the eastern side of the Vistula River in the gritty and creative working-class district of Praga, the campus of the games company CD Projekt Red shows the progress being made.
As the developer behind the smash hit games series The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077, the company started life in the 1990s as an importer of CD games made by US publishers.
Michał Nowakowski, its co-chief executive, says this was about the limit of Polish ambition in the early days. Now he competes globally to attract coders, games developers and graphic designers.
“In the late 90s and early 2000s I feel there was a massive inferiority complex. Among everybody who was young, you wanted to catch up with the west.”
Growing up in the 1980s, his family were expelled from Poland in the period of martial law. He recalls visiting London aged 15 and being “blown away” by the Virgin megastore and British culture. “I could never imagine Poland being like it.”
Within a generation, though, he says this attitude would be alien to his own children. “For young people now they have no inferiority complex. They don’t stop and think: ‘Can we be as good as Brits, French, Spanish?’ It’s not holding them back.
“We have really good universities and skills teaching people. I think that can take us to unprecedented heights as a country.
“We’re a proper-sized country. Not too small, not too big; no inferiority complex any more. There’s nothing holding us back.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Senior Reform official cast doubt over legality of huge donations
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A senior Reform UK official raised questions about whether major donations from billionaire backers Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo would be legal under the proposed new foreign donors cap three months before they gave £72m to the party.
James Orr, who was then Reform UK’s head of policy and a Cambridge professor, discussed potential difficulties around future donations from Harborne and Delo in undercover footage captured by the investigative reporting group Verbatim.
A reporter was posing as a potential donor when Orr talked to him about “filling the war chest in anticipation” of tougher donations rules, describing it as the establishment trying to “kneecap” the party.
Orr was suspended as Reform’s head of policy last month after Channel 4 broadcast some of Verbatim’s undercover filming in which he appeared to discuss ways to get around funding laws to allow donations from a US-based donor.
The matter is under police investigation and he remains suspended, although Reform has released its own report clearing Orr and another official of wrongdoing.
The new footage has been shared with the Guardian after a public debate about whether the two £36m donations from Harborne and Delo to Reform UK will be allowed under the cap. The party maintains the donations are legal, pointing out that the retrospective overseas donor cap has not yet been passed into law.
In the footage, recorded in July this year, Orr expressed doubt about whether Delo and Harborne would still be able to donate given that, when it does become law, the £100,000 overseas donor cap is to cover party donations dating back to March this year.
Orr believed Delo would probably meet the residency test as long as he was not required to have been a tax resident, in which case he would be “stuffed”. He said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge” in terms of avoiding the overseas cap and he “can’t do anything for 12 months” after moving back.
Harborne had been living in Thailand until he registered to vote in Hampshire this summer, and Delo has long been resident in Hong Kong, though he has been on the UK domestic register for some years.
The new law will limit overseas donors to giving £100,000 a year to a political party. It will apply to donations made after March 2026, and will require any domestic donor who wants to give more than £100,000 to have been resident in the UK for at least a year.
In the discussion, Orr was recorded as saying the party was too reliant on Harborne and Delo as “two big whales”. He said the new law was “a retrospective law, which is unheard of. So, we’re going to challenge it in the courts.”
Orr added: “We’ll push it through judicial review. And then … so, we’ll have a big fight. But, yeah, the last few days we’ve been working hard on just filling the war chest as best we can, in anticipation of something quite brutal.”
On whether the two men would be caught by the overseas cap, he said: “I mean, there’s going to be a huge fight over that. But Ben, I think it’s probably OK, because I think he is … it depends on how they legislate it, they might just say, you must have been tax domiciled here for X period of time, in which case Ben is stuffed.”
Orr went on to say: “It depends what … test for moving back you apply. So, under the common law, there’s a two-limb test, which is actually quite a – not a stringent one. It’s a factual thing, a factual matrix test.
“How much time you spend in England, do you have a house here, can you vote, do you have any bills that you pay, you know, it’s quite kind of, it’s not tax … So, on that test, Ben meets it, I think. And then the second then is intention. Do you intend to stay, so, evidence that you intend to stay …”
Having debated whether Delo would meet the test, Orr said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge”. The Reform official said he would move back to the UK. “But, if he does move back, there’s 12 – he can’t pay – he can’t do anything for 12 months. And, it looks as if they will bring that in.”
In his chat with the undercover reporter, Orr also referred to the “complicated backstory” of Delo, a British-born billionaire who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business. He was later pardoned by Donald Trump.
Orr also spoke about having spent time on a boat with Ben Delo in the Peloponnese this summer, talking of mixing work and a holiday in Greece, saying: “We went from Athens down to Ben’s boat in Porto Cheli.” Lawyers for Delo said he did not own a yacht.
A Reform UK spokesperson said: “We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back.”
Orr did not respond to a request for comment. He has previously denied wrongdoing in relation to electoral laws on overseas funding and dismissed Verbatim as “politically motivated actors trying to discredit a political opponent through dubious legal means”.
Lawyers for Harborne described Orr’s comments as private speculation that would not be appropriate to comment on and did not represent established facts. Delo’s lawyers did not respond substantively, saying he would not be drawn into speculation about a conversation he was not party to, or the legal effect of a law yet to be passed. They later added that he had taken extensive legal advice on his donations and had previously set out his rationale for making them.
Reform has previously said it intends to take legal action against Verbatim and its directors over the undercover filming.
