SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Zelenskyy says 40 now confirmed dead after ‘insane’ Russian attack on school – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
40 killed, more than 30 missing after 'insane' Russian attack on Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy – fresh back from his meetings in Germany yesterday and today – has offered an update on the search and rescue operations after the Russian strike on a school in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region on Monday.
40 people have been confirmed dead, with fears that more than 30 may still be under the rubble, Zelenskyy said.
“Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack. But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response. Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that 40 people were confirmed dead and more than 30 missing after “insane” Russian attack on a school in Ukraine on Monday (14:44), just days before key trilateral peace talks with the US and Russia.
Zelenskyy continues his trip of Europe and after visiting Germany where he was hosted by chancellor Friedrich Merz, he is now expected in Spain.
His comments came as the EU hosted key technical talks with the US, some EU countries, Nato, and the World Bank on Ukraine (10:05).
Following the US midterm elections, some European leaders expressed hopes that the result will put Donald Trump under pressure to make progress in talks with Moscow and Kyiv (12:18, 12:57, 14:31).
But some leaders also expressed concerns about the political consequences of the vote (11:31, 11:55, 12:45).
In other news,
Montenegro could be in a position to join the European Union as early as 2028 with accession negotiations concluded by the end of this year, after the bloc praised the country for advancing “the reforms needed” to complete the process (13:33).
If you are after more reactions to the US midterm elections, you can follow our US live blog here:
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Ukraine's Zelenskyy lands in Spain for talks with key Ibero-American leaders
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has landed in Spain, where he is expected to take part in talks with key leaders from Spain and Latin America, as well as the UN secretary-general and the European Council president, according to Spain’s El País newspaper.
The paper reported that Zelenskyy will take part in “several high-level meetings” on the sidelines of the Ibero-American summit in Madrid, hosted by Spain’s embattled prime minister Pedro Sánchez.
Argetina’s controversial president Javier Milei is believed to be among the guests. Portugal will be represented by PM Luís Montenegro.
Just like in Berlin, Zelenskyy’s trip was kept secret until his plane touched down for security reasons, El País said.
French blood banks hacked in latest cyber-attack on Europe
Jon Henley
Europe correspondent
In other news, France’s national blood service has said hackers accessed control systems and boosted temperatures at three cold stores stocking vital blood products, in an apparent escalation of recent cyber-attacks on fridges and freezers across Europe.
The French blood service (EFS) saidtemperature and defrosting thresholds had been raised to “very high levels” in the attack, adding that its alarm systems had allowed technicians to intervene before the products were compromised.
The EFS is France’s public blood transfusion operator, collecting, testing, preparing and distributing products such as blood, plasma and platelets to more than 1,900 hospitals around the country. It supports more than a million patients a year.
Here is some more on how Italy’s far-right prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who once had good relations with Donald Trump, dismissed questions about the midterm election results, telling journalists “let’s talk about America another time”.
Meloni, wearing a red suit, had been door-stepped while attending a ceremony in central Rome on Wednesday to mark Italy’s national unity and armed forces day and didn’t welcome the journalistic focus on the US midterms.
“I see you’re very interested in the celebration of the republic and the Armed Forces,” she said sarcastically.
Meloni had positioned herself as a key European ally to Trump until April, when the pair fell out, firstly over Italy’s refusal to support the US-Israeli war in Italy and then because of Trump’s extraordinary broadside against Pope Leo in reaction to the pontiff’s condemnation of the war.
They had appeared to be getting relations back on track at the G7 summit in June before Trump claimed Meloni had begged him to take a photo with him - a story Meloni said was a “a total invention”.
Italy’s foreign minister Antonio Tajani did instead comment on the midterms, saying Italy’s relationship with the US “remains unchanged regardless of who is in government or the parliamentary situation”.
In an interview with the Rome-based newspaper, Il Messaggero, Tajani said “we have never been Trumpians” and “Meloni isn’t a Maga supporter either – heaven forbid!”
The League, which is led by joint deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini, who until fairly recently continuously praised Trump, said in a statement:
“When a population votes, their vote must always be respected and understood.”
The party also expressed hope that the outcome would speed-up efforts to end wars and restore peace.
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that “US voters have made their choice clear”, commenting on the country’s midterms election results.
She said she hoped Congress would continue to support Ukraine and put more pressure on Russia.
“I hope that the new Congress... will continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia,” Kallas said, adding that Europe and the United States “are much stronger together” in pushing Moscow to end its war.
The European Union has offered fresh hope for Serbia’s membership talks if the election-winning student movement there forms a government willing to strengthen democracy.
The election of a diverse student-led opposition movement could provide an opening for a reset with the most influential of the western Balkan countries in line at Europe’s door, AP reported.
“Now Serbia has the chance for a fresh start,” enlargement commissioner Marta Kos told EU lawmakers as she debriefed them on the report.
“The new Serbian government has an opportunity to turn the page, strengthen democratic institutions and fundamental rights and take the necessary steps to advance on Serbia’s accession path,” she added.
Serbia could progress rapidly under a government with strong political will but membership currently looks years away.
It comes as the the European Commission said in its enlargement report that Montenegro is on track to become the EU’s 28th member in 2028 (see post 12.33) - and that Albania and Moldova could join the following year.
However, Ukraine is unlikely to meet the conditions for joining before the end of the decade.
40 killed, more than 30 missing after 'insane' Russian attack on Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy – fresh back from his meetings in Germany yesterday and today – has offered an update on the search and rescue operations after the Russian strike on a school in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region on Monday.
40 people have been confirmed dead, with fears that more than 30 may still be under the rubble, Zelenskyy said.
“Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack. But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response. Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered.”
Germany's Wadephul sees both 'continuity and change' after US midterms, hopes for breakthrough on Ukraine
German foreign minister Johann Wadephul has said the results of the US midterm elections will mean some “continuity” in Germany’s relations with the Trump administration, but also a “change” in ties with the US Democrats as he hoped to see some breakthrough on Ukraine.
Berlin will “continue to seek common ground” with the Trump administration, “striving for compromise” on key issues in the face of global challenges.
But these elections “also signal change” as the Democratic Party’s success – which he noted was “of a magnitude rare in American history” – will “likely seek to shift the political discourse in the US.”
He said he did not “any complications” arising from this result, and noted that the political engagement will now need to be “broader” and “perhaps even more interesting in certain aspects.”
He said many foreign policy issues featured prominently in the US elections, including tariffs and the war in Iran.
Wadephul added that he hoped for “more dialogue in Congress, across party lines, about what can be done collectively to support Ukraine.
“I think they’ve been holding back on that issue for quite some time now during the election campaign,” he said.
“I also know that in both chambers – and within both parties – there are staunch supporters of Ukraine who clearly recognise that this Russian war of aggression threatens not only security and freedom in Europe but also in the United States.”
Montenegro could sign EU accession treaty in mid 2027, European Commission says
The European Union could conclude accession negotiations with Montenegro by the end of this year and could sign an accession treaty with the country as soon as June 2027, the European Commission said, as reported by Reuters.
“For the first time since 2011, when the EU closed accession negotiations with Croatia, the EU is in a position to soon close accession negotiations with another candidate country, Montenegro,” the EU’s executive said in its annual enlargement policy report.
“This is testament to Montenegro’s sustained efforts to advance on the European path and implement the reforms needed to turn EU membership into reality,” it said, adding that “it considers that accession negotiations could realistically be closed by the end of 2026”.
If the accession treaty gets signed in mid-2027, Montenegro could join the bloc as early as 2028, German news agency dpa says.
Joining the bloc requires all current 27 member countries to ratify an accession treaty.
Kremlin says it hopes midterm results do not affect Trump's 'peacemaking efforts'
Meanwhile, the Kremlin said that it hopes that the results of the US midterm elections will not impact what it said were president Donald Trump’s “peacemaking efforts" on Ukraine, Reuters said.
In comments broadcast by Russian state media, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said:
“We are sincerely counting on [Trump] continuing his peacemaking efforts.“
'Governing in the US will be almost impossible,' Belgian defence ministers worries
Belgian defence minister Theo Francken has warned that “governing in the US will be almost impossible in the coming years,” but said that Europe’s priorities should be on trade, Ukraine and Nato.
Writing on X, he said in a post translated by Reuters:
“Governing in the United States will be almost impossible in the coming years given the level of internal division and polarisation. As a European politician I will mainly look of course to trade policies, support to Ukraine and Nato.”
'Democracy won in America,' Tusk declares alongside Czech Republic's Babiš
Czech prime minister Andrej Babiš is in Warsaw today, meeting with Poland’s Donald Tusk, and unsurprisingly both leaders were asked for their thoughts on the US elections.
Babiš briefly chuckled in response to the question, before saying the results were “as expected,” but stressed the significance of the Republican party losing in places like Texas, where they “ruled for decades.”
He said that Trump will still have “major competence,” and he hoped that the US president would use them to focus on the issues that he promised he’d resolve: ending the Russian invasion on Ukraine and the crisis in the Hormuz strait.
“I am not expecting some sort of major change … but let’s see what he comes up with. What we need … is to end these two wars,” he said, stressing their costs for Europe.
Poland’s Tusk declares: “Today, democracy won in America.”
“Democracy is amazing; I love democracy, it’s a beautiful thing,” he said, absolutely beaming.
He then added:
“I hope that the result will stabilise the situation also in our region, but then Trump is still the president. … My advice would be not to overuse the veto … as a sort of method of governing,” an apparent domestic swipe at Poland’s opposition president and Trump ally, Karol Nawrocki, with whom he is locked in a bitter dispute over the country’s constitutional court.
'Either he decides to rise above fray and tone down involvement, or he doesn't,' French finance minister says
French finance minister Roland Lescure also responded to the result in the US, discussing what the next steps of the US president, Donald Trump, could be.
Here are his comments, via Reuters:
“Either he decides to rise above the fray – acknowledging that changes are necessary, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly affect people – and, I might add, he tones down his international involvement; or he does not.“
Frankly, this is something we will need to keep an eye on in the coming days.“
Germany's Pistorius congratulates Democrats on 'historic victory' in US midterms
German defence minister Boris Pistorius has congratulated the US Democeats “from the bottom of his heart” on their win last night, Dlf reported.
Deutsche Welle’s chief political correspondent Nina-Haase-Trobridge posted a longer clip of his comments at the Berlin Security Conference, with Pistorius acknowledging a “historic victory” for the Democrats.
“So for us this means we will continue our relationship based on trust and cooperation with the administration. … And, like in the past, we will have a close working relationship with the Democrats,” he said, quoted by the journalist.
“As for what we can expect now, that remains to be seen. It depends, to some extent, on what the American president intends to do following these elections,” he said in response to a question from Politico’s Rixa Fürsen.
'A powerful political signal about a change of course,' Norway's Støre says
Meanwhile, Norwegian PM Jonas Gahr Støre told Reuters:
“This is a powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters.
Voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy.“
'We'll talk about America some other time,' Meloni tells reporters
Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, who also clashed with Trump in recent months, wasn’t in the mood to offer any reaction to the US elections this morning, as she told reporters, via Corriere:
“We’ll talk about America some other time. Right now, it’s Armed Forces Day, 4 November.”
But opposition politicians celebrated the result, with former prime minister Matteo Renzi calling it “wonderful” and a response to Trump’s “abuse” of his position.
“Trump has another two years to go, but the Maga movement has been severely weakened, if not defeated.”
MEP Sandro Gozi said the electorate’s verdict “offers renewed hope that the next two years will mark the beginning of the end of the Trump era.”
Meanwhile, Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski ridiculed the Polish right, which has been supportive of Trump since his return to the office.
Paraphrasing Jesus’s words from the Bible (sic!), he said:
“Truly I tell you, before the rooster crows, they will disown him three times”
He also took swipe at US billionaire Elon Musk who donated hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican campaigns, reposting his comment from one of their previous clashes, saying:
“See, big man, politics is harder than you thought.”
For what it’s worth, Musk also appeared to see a funny side in his involvement in the campaign, saying:
“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”
Spain's Sánchez hails progressive fightback in the US 'against hate,' draws parallels with Spain
Sam Jones
in Madrid
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results in the US, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.
“Yesterday, American society voted against the policies that only impoverish,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”
Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added:
“It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”
Morning opening: EU to lead talks on support for Ukraine with US, Nato, partners
Jakub Krupa
With most eyes still on the US this morning, Brussels is quietly getting on with the task of leading on discussions about the next round of support for Ukraine.
The European Commission will hold talks with the US, France, Germany, Britain, Nato, and the World Bank, looking what can be done to help Kyiv throughout the winter and how to support the US-led peace process with the upcoming negotiations in Abu Dhabi.
Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff said US negotiators would meet with their European partners in Brussels.
Their talks come after another night of heavy attacks on Ukraine, hitting power stations in Kyiv and Zhytomyr and a cargo vessel at sea near Odesa.
I will also bring you any European reactions to the midterms in the US, although many politicians (while quietly amused or relieved) may choose to stay silent to not risk Donald Trump’s wrath.
Let’s see what the day brings.
It’s Wednesday, 4 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Ukraine thankful that intelligence on missile strikes ‘works now’, says Zelenskyy – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Ukraine is thankful that intelligence on missile strikes 'works now,' Zelenskyy says
Zelenskyy says the talks covered security guarantees, among others, and he hopes to hear Russia’s response tomorrow.
He says Ukraine needs “strong security guarantees after the war ends.”
He also pointedly says that he is thankful that intelligence sharing “works now” (that’s my emphasis), and it helps with responding to any Russian attacks against Ukraine.
US envoy Witkoff to travel to Russia with new ideas discussed with Ukraine, Europe - summary
Jakub Krupa
US peace envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to St Petersburg on Wednesday to relay to Russia some new peace proposals discussed with Ukraine, Norway’s prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre said after hosting the US-Ukraine talks in Oslo (19:06).
The leaders discussed a number of contentious issues, including possible ceasefires, energy, and security guarantees (19:13).
Zelenskyy also confirmed that Ukraine is “now” again receiving US intelligence about Russia’s strikes (19:22), after his earlier discussions with US secretary of state Marco Rubio (19:10, 19:16).
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggestedthat any final peace deal would require a trilateral summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, as some outstanding issues are of such gravity that “only the leaders” can resolve them (19:10).
Zelenskyy stressed that “Ukraine wants peace more than anyone,” but insisted “nothing [gets discussed] about Ukraine without Ukraine.”
Finland’s influential president Alexander Stubb said today’s talks put the peace process “back on track” with good progress “on a technical level,” as he hoped for a good outcome from Witkoff’s discussions with Russia on Wednesday (19:13, 19:28).
A further summary of earlier events today is here.
Peace process 'back on track,' hopeful Stubb says ahead of Witkoff's talks with Russia
In his closing comments, Finland’s Stubb says “it was a good day for peace,” as he acknowledges that “the top priority of the US administration is to find a peaceful solution to Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine.”
He repeats that they “have made a lot of progress under the radar in the past week or so.”
“I feel that the process is back on track, and we’ll continue to work on it together with our European friends.
The key, of course, will be, what kind of messages Steve Witkoff will be able to get from St Petersburg tomorrow. But I think today was a success, and tomorrow is a new day. Hopefully we don’t do any backtrack[ing].”
'Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,' Zelenskyy insists
Zelenskyy gets asked if today’s meeting changes his view that the US is trying to pressure Ukraine to capitulate, and reports of a possible US, China, Russia trilateral meeting.
He stresses the principle of “nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine.”
“So I don’t know what about the trilateral meeting will be between America, China and, Russia? It’s up to them. But of course, if this is about Ukraine, our future, it can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations.”
He says the talks between Ukraine, Europe and the US have been constructive, “and we will see what will be tomorrow” in St. Petersburg.
Norway’s Støre repeats his positive lines on today’s talks which he says allowed both sides to “straighten out a few things and to agree that what matters now is to look ahead.”
He pointedly thanks Witkoff and hopes for a good outcome from his talks with Russia tomorrow (which he curiously says will be in Moscow, not St Petersburg, as said earlier).
“We are on a certain track, but war is unpredictable. It doesn’t follow a plan. And that’s why from time to time, we have to use, some cool diplomatic political brains to get our thinking back on track and our planning back on track.”
Ukraine is thankful that intelligence on missile strikes 'works now,' Zelenskyy says
Zelenskyy says the talks covered security guarantees, among others, and he hopes to hear Russia’s response tomorrow.
He says Ukraine needs “strong security guarantees after the war ends.”
He also pointedly says that he is thankful that intelligence sharing “works now” (that’s my emphasis), and it helps with responding to any Russian attacks against Ukraine.
Norway’s Støre jumps in to respond to a question on why Witkoff is not answering questions with the three other leaders.
He diplomatically points out that “this is a press conference among political leaders,” hinting that Witkoff is essentially of a different diplomatic rank.
But more broadly, he talks about the process, and the need for Europe “to be at the table.”
“To succeed, to achieve a last and fair piece, we need an equation of us, Ukraine, Russia and Europe and basically also other key countries, because this is a war with huge ramifications.”
He says he and Stubb don’t talk “on behalf of Europe,” but both countries, neighbours of Russia, have a deep understanding of the challenges faced by Europe.
Finland’s Stubb jumps in to add that they just work “in the back office” of the talks to support their progress.
He says Norway and Finland take part “because we believe in international law, but also based on self-interest” as Russia’s neighbours with “our history with Russia.”
“We’ll see what happens after tomorrow in Saint Petersburg. It’s very important that the American negotiators and President Trump stay engaged.”
Zelenskyy hints at further talks with US Rubio in the next 48 hours
Asked about his confidence in doing deal with Trump, Zelenskyy is very diplomatic.
He goes back to his conversation with Rubio earlier today, and says it was the right channel to discuss “sensitive issues” such as Stalink, interceptors, and intelligence sharing.
He says he hopes to talk with Rubio again in the next 48 hours.
In the Q&A, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy gets asked about his concessions and whether he is losing the war now.
He says the discussions revolved around “sensitive” issues, but he wants to “push as quick as possible to end this war” and focus next discussions on reconstruction.
He insists “we are not losing the war,” but concedes that “we are losing people and time,” as “our children do not have real life, childhood.”
He says “that is why we need to end this war as quick as possible.”
'Peace requires patience, but unfortunately war does not wait,' Stubb says as he hails 'genuine progress'
Finland’s Stubb says he believes today’s talks achieved some “genuine” progress “on two levels: … the short term and the big picture.”
“We found some elements of peace which will be taken forward to Saint Petersburg tomorrow.”
He says the discussions focused on “key issues such as air defence, energy installations, and partial ceasefires, such as those on energy and food security,” building on discussions in Miami.
Stubb says he understand “there has been a lot of noise” but “on a technical level, I feel that we are on the same page, and the next steps are about how we get there.”
“In my experience, peace requires patience, but unfortunately war does not wait. People are dying every day and each day. Our job is to do what we can to end it. And I think today was a step in the right direction.”
'Ukraine wants peace more than anyone,' Zelenskyy says as he calls for trilateral meeting with US, Russia
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy is up next.
He thanks Norway for hosting the talks, and Finland’s Stubb for joining the process.
He says today’s talk with the US were “important” as he says all parties need to “keep talking at all levels and work together on the decisions needed to end this war.”
He thanks US secretary of state Marco Rubio for their earlier phone call conversation, too.
He says:
“Ukraine wants peace more than anyone. It was Russia who started this war, and the decision to keep the killing going is Russia’s choice and Russia’s alone.”
He adds:
“We are working to find a solution. I thought we have some clear ideas on how to get to peace, and we are united with our European partners in this effort, and we want the Americans to take these ideas to the Russians.”
He says he wants a trilateral meeting of the leaders – that’s Trump, Putin and himself – because there are issues that “only the leaders” can resolve.
Norway’s Støre hails 'positive' meeting with Witkoff flying to Russia to discuss proposals tomorrow
Norway’s Støre is the first to speak.
He says Norway remains supportive of Ukraine, and “we have always made it clear there will be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine.”
He thanks Trump’s envoys Witkoff and Kushner for joining the talks, and says:
“We believe that peace is possible and necessary for Ukraine and for Europe and for the entire world. We have hosted today, I would say, good and constructive talks, necessary after events of the last week. We have agreed that working together is crucial.”
He says US’s Witkoff will fly to St. Petersburg tomorrow to relay the result of today’s proposals to Russia, and “possibly pave the way for a meeting at the leaders’ level.”
“We have discussed today issues linked to security for Ukraine, prosperity plan after the war; issues related to territory and issues related to sanctions and questions related to European security order in the aftermath of this war.”
We are waiting for press conference after Ukraine-US talks in Oslo
Jakub Krupa
We are now pausing our coverageas we wait for the Ukraine-US talks in Oslo to wrap up.
I will be back when the leaders of Ukraine, Norway and Finland show up for their press conference, which is currently expected around 6pm UK (7pm Oslo). We will bring you the presser live here.
In the meantime, here’s the summary of the day so far:
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in Oslo, holding talks with the US peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, with the Norwegian PM Støre and Finnish president Stubb also attending (12:23, 13:22, 16:06).
French authorities said that military forces will be deployed to reinforce “massive” police presence during the upcoming protests on Saturday (15:29, 15:57), as they framed the worsening situation as a choice between “violence and the Republic.”
Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto warned that city riots, seen also in the Italian city of Milan, are part of a broader “hybrid war” against the west, with younger people radicalising through the use of social media platforms (15:21), with the Italian government planning to approve new security measures (14:27).
In other news,
EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the bloc’s relationship with the UK is of “vital importance in the current geopolitical, security and economic context,” as he set out the bloc’s expectations ahead of next month’s EU-UK summit on 20 November (11:44).
UN human rights chief condemns protests violence, worries about 'excessive use of force' by authorities
Meanwhile, UN Human Rights chief Volker Türk has condemned “all acts of violence” during the last week’s protests in Albania, Belgium, France, Italy and Portugal, and called on all parties to “reduce tensions and prevent further violence.”
In a statement he insisted that “the best and only way forward is inclusive and safe dialogue.”
Türk continued:
“People have the right to protest peacefully, and to have their voices heard. States must facilitate these rights.
I deplore the actions of those exploiting protests to commit acts of violence and vandalism against public and private property. They should be held individually accountable.
I am concerned by reports of unnecessary and excessive use of force against protesters, including children. States must ensure that any law enforcement response remains lawful, necessary and proportionate. Allegations of unlawful use of force must be investigated promptly, effectively and independently, with accountability and effective remedies for victims.
I note some steps already taken by authorities to investigate incidents and ease tensions. I further urge States to engage protesters, particularly young people, in meaningful, inclusive and constructive dialogue, and to take concrete steps to address legitimate and fundamental human rights concerns over education, public services, housing, the rising cost of living and inequality.”
A short press release issued by the police quoted the head of investigation at the North Jutland force saying that “this is a case we are taking very seriously.”
The case focuses on suspected cooperation with foreign intelligence and has been brought forward in partnership with the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, the police said, without disclosing more detail.
The two men – which DR says are aged 18 and 21 – were arrested yesterday, and a preliminary court hearing is now getting under way.
But DR notes that the case is unusual given the hearing is taking place outside of regular court hours.
The incident comes less than a month after the Danish defence intelligence service issued a report warning against Russia’s activities.
For what it’s worth, we are expecting to hear from Zelenskyy, Stubb and Støre after today’s talks, probably around 6pm UK time (7pm Oslo).
We will bring you the key lines here, alongside a live stream to follow along.
In the last few minutes, Zelenskyy posted a video from today’s talks alongside the Norwegian and Finnish leaders, saying:
“Jonas, Alex, thank you for your unwavering support and DAILY attention to protecting lives. We are stronger together. Thank you, Norway! Thank you, Finland!”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Covid as cost of living bites
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.
With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.
Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.
The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.
The latest snapshot represents a marked change from the summer, when GfK said a “Burnham bounce”, along with a strong World Cup run by the men’s England football team and sunny weather, lifted the mood of consumers in its long-running monthly survey.
Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said: “Relentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”
It comes as consumers face a fresh squeeze on living standards triggered by the unfolding war in the Middle East. Petrol and diesel prices have surged close to record highs and energy bills have increased in advance of a difficult winter for households already feeling the pinch from years of price increases.
Over the past five years analysis by the Trades Union Congress shows that UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.
With less than a week before his tax and spending speech to the Commons, the chancellor is under pressure to take action to support households amid warnings that consumer energy bills could reach £2,000 a year from January for the typical household.
Healey has pledged to use his statement to announce “breathing space” measures to ease the pressure. However, he has also warned that the government has limited resources to intervene as the Middle East conflict pushes the UK’s borrowing costs to the highest level in decades.
Official figures released on Wednesday show headline inflation rose by more than expected to 3.5% last month, while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn.
In a double blow for the chancellor, the twin pieces of bad news underscore the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure.
According to the latest figures from GfK, consumers became less confident about the strength of their own personal finances, as well as the general outlook for the British economy at large.
The major purchase index fell by 14 points to -22 in October, suggesting that consumers could be bracing to cut back on spending over the winter months to make room in their finances for higher energy bills.
Separate figures from the CBI show investment intentions among manufacturing businesses were subdued as cost pressures remained high in the three months to October.
Manufacturing output is expected to stabilise in the next three months, according to the lobby group’s latest Industrial Trends Survey. However, cost pressures for businesses remained elevated.
Cameron Martin, senior economist at the CBI, said: “If the government wants to meaningfully tackle the cost of living, it must give manufacturers the breathing space to invest and drive the productivity growth needed to sustain rising real wages.
“Next week’s budget must deliver this by cutting business electricity costs, reducing labour costs and reforming business rates to support rather than hinder investment and growth.”
The Treasury has been approached for comment.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump tells Texas campaign rally crowd he’s rolling back environmental rules to curb methane pollution – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Speaking in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Donald Trump announced a rollback of federal rules issued by the Biden administration in 2023 to force oil and gas companies to cut their emissions of methane, a “super pollutant” gas that traps heat in the atmosphere.
“Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators.
In a press release, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator, Lee Zeldin, priased what he called Trump’s move “to end the war on oil and natural gas” by revising oil and natural gas regulations under the Clean Air Act.
According to the EPA, the proposal is expected to save $45bn in costs to consumers and businesses, including small businesses operating marginal wells, and produce an estimated 210m additional barrels of oil and 1.41tn cubic feet of natural gas.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Faced with widespread voter discontent over the spike in oil prices since he attacked Iran, Donald Trump staged his rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on Tuesday alongside a vast oil tanker, the Angerona, which, the president said, had just arrived from Venezuela bearing a personal gift for him: a million barrels of oil.
A senior State Department official told the Associated Press that the US will “will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States.”
In his remarks to supporters in Lubbock, Texas Trump attacked James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, for having shown compassion for transgender children who demonstrated for their rights at the Texas state capitol in 2023.
Trump lied that “our gasoline prices are lower than when Barack Hussein Obama- our oil prices, gasoline, lower than they were with Obama”.
Democratic congressman demands to know if Trump administration helped Flávio Bolsonaro flee justice in Brazil
As we await confirmation of a BBC report that Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right Brazilian senator who lost a presidential election on Sunday, has arrived in Florida, fleeing corruption investigations in Brazil, one Democratic lawmaker has rejected the idea of giving him asylum.
“Losing an election is not grounds for asylum,” congressman Joaquin Castro, a Texas Democrat posted. “Yet the Trump Administration is giving Flávio Bolsonaro safe haven in the United States. In Brazil, he is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and currency evasion, and was ordered to surrender his passports. The Trump Administration owes Congress answers on its role helping Bolsonaro flee Brazil in contravention of Brazilian law.”
As the Brazilian journalist Octavio Guedesobserved on Brazilian television on Tuesday, Bolsonaro “is not fleeing a dictatorship.”
“Flávio Bolsonaro is fleeing a country in which he ran for office freely—a country where his brother is a senator, another brother is a federal deputy, his party holds a majority in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, and his stepmother is a senator,” Guedes said.
“He is fleeing a country where 59 million people went to the polls and freely cast their votes for him. In short, he is fleeing a democracy. He is fleeing a reckoning with the justice system.”
Speaking in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Donald Trump announced a rollback of federal rules issued by the Biden administration in 2023 to force oil and gas companies to cut their emissions of methane, a “super pollutant” gas that traps heat in the atmosphere.
“Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators.
In a press release, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator, Lee Zeldin, priased what he called Trump’s move “to end the war on oil and natural gas” by revising oil and natural gas regulations under the Clean Air Act.
According to the EPA, the proposal is expected to save $45bn in costs to consumers and businesses, including small businesses operating marginal wells, and produce an estimated 210m additional barrels of oil and 1.41tn cubic feet of natural gas.
Trump lies that gasoline prices are lower now than when Obama was president
Speaking in defense of his record as president in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Donald Trump once again claimed that his war on Iran was necessary to stop Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, despite a US intelligence finding that Iran stopped pursuing nuclear weapons in 2003.
The president then told a more blatant lie. “With all of this that we’re doing, our gasoline prices are lower than when Barack Hussein Obama- our oil prices, gasoline, lower than they were with Obama, and a guy named Crooked Joe Biden.”
In fact, the current national average for a gallon of regular gasoline in the US is now $4.27, up from $3.05 a year ago, before Trump started the war with Iran that has spiked fuel prices globally. A gallon of gasoline never rose above $4.17 during the Obama administration, and was under $2.50 for a quarter of his time in office, including his the last three years of his second term.
As Reuters reports, the price has now averaged $3.472 since Trump took office in January 2025, passing the $3.471-per-gallon average for Biden’s term, according to data from the AAA.
In Lubbock, Texas, Trump attacks Talarico for showing compassion for transgender children
In his remarks to supporters in Lubbock, Texas on Tuesday, Donald Trump attacked James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, for having shown compassion for transgender children who demonstrated for their rights at the Texas state capitol in 2023.
The president began by repeating a string of false claims about Talarico and then insisted, falsely, that the Democrat, who is Presbyterian seminarian, said that “God is transgender”.
In fact, as a selection of statements from Talarico that Trump played for his rally crowd showed, what the state lawmaker actually said, during an October 2021 debate on a Texas bill barring trans children from competing on school sports teams, was that “God is nonbinary”.
“The first two lines of the Bible, the first two lines in Genesis use two different Hebrew words to describe God – one is the masculine Hebrew noun for divinity, the second is the feminine Hebrew noun for spirit. God is both masculine and feminine and everything in between. God is non-binary,” Talarico said.
In Genesis 1:26 and 1:27, Talarico added, “God speaks of God’s self in the plural, saying ‘Let us make human beings in our image, to be like us’. That’s the infinite multitude of God, the masculine, the feminine and everything in between. Trans children are God’s children, made in God’s own image, there’s nothing wrong with them nothing at all.”
Trump’s summary of those remarks was to claim this: “He actually said that if Jesus Christ himself came and visited the Texas legislature, Jesus would be promoting sex changes for little children.”
Trump also attacked Talarico for saying, “that he loves transgender children”.
This is a highly misleading reference to comments Talarico made on a podcast in 2023, when he told the host about how impressed he had been by a group of young trans activists and their parents who had come to the Texas legislature to protest a bill that would deny trans children life-saving health care. After they were removed from the gallery, Talarico said, “there was video of one of the law enforcement officers violently throwing down one of those trans activists outside the House chamber”.
At the end of the podcast, during a lightening round, when the host asked Talarico to name one thing he hates, he said: “I hate people who are not willing to change their mind”.
Asked then to name one thing that he loves, Talarico paused a moment and said: “Um, I love… and I just say this because it’s on my mind, the trans children who showed up yesterday at the state capitol to advocate for their humanity; they shouldn’t have to but it was an inspiration to watch.”
This is the statement that JD Vance, Trump’s vice-president, has used to suggest, mockingly, that Talarico’s internet search history must be obscene.
Apparently unaware of its origin, Trump once again uses the phrase ‘to the victor belong the spoils’ to claim Venezuela's oil
Faced with widespread voter discontent over the spike in oil prices since he attacked Iran, Donald Trump staged his rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on Tuesday alongside a vast oil tanker, the Angerona, which, the president said, had just arrived from Venezuela bearing a personal gift for him: a million barrels of oil.
The president told reporters before the event that he intends to re-gift the oil, giving it to the people of the United States of America.
During his remarks, Trump pointed to the tanker, which can hold an estimated 800,000 barrels of oil, and said: “See that little ship out there? It’s got one million barrels of oil on it from Venezuela.”
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” Trump continued. “‘To the victor belong to spoils’, right?” he added, referring to a phrase he has used in the past to suggest the US has a rightful claim to Venezuela’s oil since US forces kidnapped its leader.
Trump first used the phrase in public during an April 2011 appearance on Fox News, when he told the host Bill O’Reilly that, if elected president, he would not withdraw US troops from Iraq but redeploy them to secure its oil fields.
“In the old days, when you had wars, you win, right? You win. ‘To the victor belong the spoils’. So when we go to Iraq, we spend $1.4 trillion so far and thousands of lives are lost … and we’re going to leave,” Trump said. “I like the old system better: You won a war, you stay there, and you keep the oil. And you know, then those people will not have died in vain.”
“You stay and protect the oil, and you take the oil and you take whatever is necessary for them and you take what’s necessary for us and we pay our self back $1.5 trillion or more,” Trump added.
Since the US military operation seized Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro, Trump has repeatedly used the same phrase to lay claim to the country’s oil, but the president appears to be unaware of its original meaning.
The phrase was first used in 1832 by New York senator William L. Marcy during a speech in defense of president Andrew Jackson’s right to reward his supporters with appointments to public office, arguing that “to the victor belong the spoils of the enemy.”
The phrase gave rise to describing the system of political patronage as “the spoils system”.
US will grant visas to defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro - report
A senior State Department official told the Associated Press on Tuesday that the US will “will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States.”
Bolsonaro, a rightwing Brazilian senator who lost a presidential election on Sunday to Brazil’s incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.
As our colleagues Tiago Rogero and Tom Phillips report from Brazil:
A report by the news website Metrópoles, citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.
Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.
Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that he was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.
“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.
The younger Bolsonaro, who had Donald Trump’s tacit support, had been under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in Brazil and had been ordered to surrender his passport.
Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.
Standing before a birthday cake on the day he turned 81, Lula called it “shameful” that his rival had fled the country.
‘This is what the Bolsonaro family is like,” the president said. “Brazil is their second country, the US is their first.”
US Federal Election Commission’s website targeted by hackers - report
Reuters reports that the US Federal Election Commission’s website has been targeted by a hacker or hackers, disrupting the agency’s electronic filings system to disclose campaign spending a week before the midterm elections.
In a statement to the news agency, the FEC said, “at this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service.” The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said users could still search the website for past reports. It declined further comment on the outage.
The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters’ ability to cast ballots, although it will keep information on how much political groups are spending on specific races from the public as they cast ballots.
“We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily shut down our web facing services,” an FEC electronic filings officer said in an email seen by Reuters.
In Texas, Trump repeats a stream of false claims and screens misleading edit of CNN polling data segment
Near the end of his speech to a Republican campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, Donald Trump just screened two short clips, edited from longer CNN segments first broadcast in August and September, highlighting polling data that flatters him.
As we have reported previously, screening these brief clips has become a routine part of Trump’s argument as he tries to convince supporters, and perhaps himself, that he is far more popular than other polling suggests.
The clips, however, were created by editing out negative information the president does not want his supporters to hear.
The first clip is 43 seconds of CNN’s chief data analyst, Harry Enten, showing viewers in September that Trump remains very popular with self-described “Maga Republicans,” which is to say people who describe themselves as loyal to his Make America Great Again movement.
“Maga GOP on Trump. In the 2024 election versus Kamala Harris, he got 99% of the Maga GOP vote—perhaps surprisingly, I might have thought it’d be 100%, but it was 99% percent,” Enten said in the first part of the clip. “Compare that to his approval rating now with the Maga GOP. It’s 98%; that is, there’s been no real decline in Maga support.”
“Look, now in terms of the congressional vote, 98% of them say they’re going to be voting for House Republican candidates,” Enten added. “So, that support is actually really holding up strong. It’s really, really strong when it comes to Maga GOP and Republicans holding on to that vote.”
However, a look at the full 14-minute segment broadcast in late September shows that what the White House edited out was Enten carefully explaining that Trump’s approval rating among Republicans who do not describe themselves as Maga loyalists had suffered a sharp drop, plunging from +56 points in the 2024 election to just +7 points in September 2026.
“You know, when it comes to non-Maga, this is where we’ve absolutely seen Donald Trump’s numbers plummet into the ocean,” Enten said, in a part of the report Trump did not screen at the rally.
The president also screened for his supporters a portion of a prior CNN segment, from August of this year, in which Enten showed viewers that according to polling conducted in May, Trump was, at that time, called the president Republicans most admire by 53% of Republicans, ahead of Ronald Reagan at 18% and Abraham Lincoln at 8%.
Trump is so fond of these two cherry-picked pieces of data, from months ago, that he included both in his 1,300-word social-media tirade against the comedian Bill Maher on Sunday.
Trump cited the data as supposed proof that Maher was wrong to say that the president is unpopular. “I have High Ratings and, more importantly, he said that I’m losing the support and approval of the Republican Party when, in fact, CNN just came out with a Poll showing that I’m at 98 and 99% support within the Republican Party, an All Time Record High,” Trump wrote.
Given that the president has repeatedly screened the clip of Enten clearly saying these were his ratings with Maga Republicans, not the party as a whole, this is not the evidence that he seems to think it is.
Addressing the crowd in Corpus Christi, Trump said that he was expecting the price of oil to spike even higher than it has when he launched the war in Iran – and he was still willing to go ahead with it.
“I knew that oil would go up,” Trump told the crowd in Corpus Christi. “I actually thought it would go up two or three time higher, and I was still willing to do it.”
The stark rise in gas and diesel prices, a product of Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the war’s opening days, has been a major source of grievance against Republicans going into the 2024 midterms.
During his address, Trump stated, as he has before, that gas prices were set to drop imminently, and that he views the temporary economic strain facing Americans as a worthwhile sacrifice to dismantle Iran’s military and prevent it from obtaining a nuclear weapons. A lasting deal to end the war and realize either of those goals long-term has, so far, remained elusive through months of fighting.
Trump flaunts Venezuelan oil shipments at campaign event in Corpus Christi, talks of making Venezuela '51st state'
Trump has taken the stage in Corpus Christi, Texas, the first of two campaign events in the state he’ll be speaking at today.
He started off by gesturing to an oil tanker docked just outside the campaign event, filled, he said, with Venezuelan crude – a product of the deal his administration inked with Venezuela’s new, US-pliant leadership.
“The oil in the ships outside is being provided to the United States at zero cost to the American taxpayer,” Trump said.
US forces launched a surprise incursion into Venezuela to seize its former leader, Nicólas Maduro, in January, dragging him to the US to face criminal charges. Since his ouster, his former Vice President, Delcy Rodriguez, ruling with the Trump administration’s blessing, has agreed to deals that would funnel vast shares of the nation’s oil wealth to US coffers.
Trump spoke of his relationship with Venezuela in unsparing terms, as a conqueror extracting resources from a defeated nation.
He described the oil as being the byproduct of “our big victory in our recent war with Venezuela,” and repeated a phrase he used while addressing the United Nations last month about his toppling of Maduro: “To the victor belong the spoils.”
Trump continued: “We’re bringing out a lot of oil for ourselves, a lot.”
He went on to say, repeatedly, that the US should make Venezuela the 51st US state.
“It will become a prosperous country, and who knows, maybe someday soon it will become a prosperous 51st state. That’s possible. Let’s make it the 51st state, and instead of a president, we’ll have an election for a governor.”
Trump’s remarks about Venezuela’s oil shipments come against the backdrop of surging oil prices downstream of the war in Iran. At several point in his remarks, Trump has vowed that gas prices are set to drop precipitously any day now.
Trump is campaigning in Texas alongside Marco Rubio and a tanker of Venezuelan oil. The President is making two stops in Texas, one in Corpus Christi and another in Lubbock, to try and rally voters behind Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton. Paxton is fending off a stiff challenge from Democrat James Talarico, which risks putting one of the state’s Senate seats back in Democrat hands for the first time in decades.
Vance attacked Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign rally in Michigan. While Trump was in Texas, his vice president returned to Michigan to stump for Republican Mike Rogers, and to bash his opponent, Abdul El-Sayed. Vance, who has traded words for months with El-Sayed online and at campaign rallies, connected the progressive candidate to recent mass protests in Paris, accusing El-Sayed of endorsing similar unrest in the United States.
US Senator Chris Murphy condemned Republican attacks on Muslim Americans. Murphy, responding to a clip of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. dismissing Arab contributions to art and science, said that remarks like those served to “delegimatize Muslim Americans - not just as citizens but as humans.” He continued: “these increasingly hysterical attacks are a prelude to Republicans bringing us to a very, very dark place after the election.”
Trump said he would accept the midterm election results “if they’re honest.” The remark, given to reporters en route to Texas, seemed to allude to the possibility Trump might deem results of the midterms fraudulent if they aren’t in his favor. But he also said he saw a path to working with a Democratic majority in Congress, if Republicans were to lose control of the legislative branch in November.
Voters in Israel are turning out for an election that will decide whether Benjamin Netanyahu will remain in charge of the country. Netanyahu is facing his first serious election test since the October 7 attacks and the start of the wars in Gaza and Iran. The results of that election will shape who, exactly, the Trump administration will be working with as it seeks to settle those conflicts.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Britain cannot deal effectively with geopolitical crises without rejoining EU, says thinktank
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Britain cannot deal effectively with geopolitical crises such as Russian aggression and political turmoil in the US without rejoining the EU, according to an influential thinktank.
The Institute for Public Policy Research has become the latest organisation with ties to the Labour party to call for the UK to re-enter the bloc, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to examine all possible options.
The paper, which comes weeks after a similar one from the Tony Blair Institute, adds to growing pressure on the prime minister to back re-entry once his review is over.
Harry Quilter-Pinner, the IPPR’s executive director, said: “The government has made important progress in repairing relations with Europe, but a series of individual deals will not be enough. There is one option which is best for the UK’s relationship with Europe – membership of the EU.
“That does not mean announcing another referendum tomorrow. But this means starting work to move towards this destination, building political support at home and in Europe.”
The IPPR argues that the position taken by the former prime minister Keir Starmer – that the UK should seek closer ties with the EU but not contemplate joining a single market or the bloc as a whole – puts the UK at a disadvantage at a time of global change.
It says Russian expansionism, the lack of reliability from the US as an international partner and increased assertiveness from Beijing mean that the UK should reinforce its power by joining other European nations rather than trying to go it alone.
The paper says: “Sovereignty without the ability to act on it is not autonomy; hedging between larger powers is, at best, a strategy for survival rather than for success.”
It argues that so much has changed since Britain left the EU in 2020 that this would not count as rejoining, but becoming a member of a wholly new European Union. Most voters would be willing to support such a position, it says, citing new polling showing 52% of voters back reentering the union, compared with 29% who oppose such a move.
Voters were likely to be attracted by the promise of shorter queues at passport control in particular, which comes out considerably ahead of economic benefits and the chance to live and work in the EU as potential benefits of membership.
However, they were also likely to be dissuaded by aggressive messaging on migration, with the percentage in favour falling from 52% to 47% once voters are told that rejoining would “open the floodgates” to more migrants. Such a message proved more effective in the polling than one focused on “freedom of movement”, which failed to change the minds of many voters.
The flurry of thinktank reports comes after Burnham signalled he wanted a rethink of Britain’s policy on the EU, announcing at Labour conference he would commission a review of all the options available.
Though the prime minister has not stated his own view as part of that review, he previously told the Guardian he wanted the UK to re-enter the bloc in his lifetime.
Many in government support the idea of rejoining, but worry it could boost support for Nigel Farage and his Reform UK party, which are struggling to overcome controversies over funding and racist views expressed by some party candidates.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.
“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.
Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.
Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.
On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.
The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.
Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.
In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.
Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.
The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.
As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”
He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.
The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.
The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.
The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.
In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”
The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.
In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.
In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.
“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”
Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.
His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.
Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Burnham says ‘too much time is wasted in those dramas’ when asked about Scottish independence – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Burnham on Scottish independence: 'Too much time is wasted in those dramas'
Following his speech, Burnham is taking questions from the media.
When asked by the BBC whether his approach with devolution will make him more or less likely the last prime minister of the United Kingdom, he said: “Obviously, I don’t want to be that.”
The SNP has been pushing for a path to Scottish independence, which the prime minister has repeatedly ruled out.
Burnham added:
I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions.
In my view, people in Scotland are suffering the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else. And I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people.
Right now, too much time is wasted in those dramas. It consumes too much energy.”
We’re going to wind down our UK politics coverage now, heres a quick list of some of todays top lines:
Andy Burnham has declared that he is making a “serious and genuine offer” to the Scottish government in order to put more control “in the hands of local people” through devolution. Burnham, giving a speech in Lanarkshire, stated that he was open to working with first minister John Swinney, even though the two have “a different view” on Scottish independence.
The deputy first ministers for Scotland and Wales both spoke at the SNP conference taking place in Aberdeen, with Plaid Cymru’s Sioned Williams praising the victories both parties enjoyed in May and her Scottish counterpart, Jenny Gilruth, claiming that “Westminster’s time is coming to an end”.
The Guardian understands that chancellor John Healey is poised to tax Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget to help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has labelled Andy Burnham’s devolution plans as a “waste of time”, stating Holyrood “have the powers that they need” and that they have done “absolutely nothing” with the ones that they do have. Badenoch made the comments during her own trip to Paisley in Scotland, where she posed in front of a mural for noted England enthusiast William Wallace.
The Campaign for Real Ale (Camra) has criticised Andy Burnham and Labour for their attempts to block a bill that would afford extra protections for historic pubs, calling the efforts an “absolute disgrace.”
The protections, put forward in a bill by Conservative MP Mike Wood, would have given pubs in England a “legal shield” from unlawful redevelopment, with the 2023 destruction of the Crooked House, which was located in Wood’s Kingswinford and South Staffordshire constituency, cited as an example of what can be avoided.
The bill was “talked out” on Friday, as a five-hour debate involving a group of Labour MPs prevented its second reading from taking place before the 2.30pm cut-off time.
Wood accused Labour of filibustering to prevent the bill from passing, saying, “This was Andy Burnham’s first test of whether he means what he says on pubs, and he’s flunked it.”
Paul Ainsworth, the national planning policy adviser for Camra, accused the government of blocking the bill, which he said was “an absolute disgrace”, and urged the government to “put laws in place to preserve our heritage and protect pubs from being converted or demolished against the wishes of local communities.”
Next up in Aberdeen, Gilruth’s Welsh opposite number, Sioned Williams, spoke about the connections that bind the two countries as well and claimed that they shared the same dream of independence.
Williams congratulated the SNP for their own victory in May and echoed Gilruth’s sentiment that the success of national parties in all three countries could spell the end of the UK, claiming that “the stars aligned in Wales, Scotland, and the north of Ireland, and the UK constitution now sits in a very different constellation.”
Scottish deputy first minister: 'Westminster's time is coming to an end'
Back to Scottish news, day two of the SNP conference has kicked off in Aberdeen with deputy first minister Jenny Gilruth taking the stage first.
Gilruth took the opportunity to congratulate Plaid Cymru, the SNP’s sister party, for their victory in the May Senedd elections, pointing out that it meant that “Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland are now led by first ministers who believe in independence from the UK.”
Gilruth also reminded the crowd of the meeting that took place between the three nations’ first ministers in Cardiff in September, claiming that it was “the clearest possible sign yet that Westminster’s time is coming to an end.”
In other news today, pornography that depicts strangulation and incestuous relationships will be banned in England and Wales from early November, the government has announced.
The content will be outlawed from 6 November after cross-party pressure prompted ministers to announce new legislation earlier this year.
Online pornography depicting strangulation or suffocation, sex between people who are related or pretending to be related, or when somebody is pretending to be a child under 16, will be illegal.
The justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said: “This isn’t about criminalising harmless sexual preferences. But porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people.
“Content that normalises, or even glorifies, violence against women is dangerous and can blur the line with what is acceptable in real life.”
Burnham says he accepts Swinney 'has a different view' on Scottish independence
Continuing on the theme of Scottish independence, Burnham was asked by the Daily Record whether he was categorically ruling out a second referendum during his premiership.
The prime minister said:
I think unions of countries are better because you can face a challenging world in a more confident and stronger way, in my view, when you collaborate and you work together.
That is my view, I communicated it to the [Scottish] first secretary very clearly.
He has a different view, but let’s accept there’s a different view there and then work on together what we can agree on.
My view won’t be changing, but let’s now move forward where we can make some progress.”
Burnham on Scottish independence: 'Too much time is wasted in those dramas'
Following his speech, Burnham is taking questions from the media.
When asked by the BBC whether his approach with devolution will make him more or less likely the last prime minister of the United Kingdom, he said: “Obviously, I don’t want to be that.”
The SNP has been pushing for a path to Scottish independence, which the prime minister has repeatedly ruled out.
Burnham added:
I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions.
In my view, people in Scotland are suffering the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else. And I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people.
Right now, too much time is wasted in those dramas. It consumes too much energy.”
Burnham's devolution plans 'a waste of time,' says Badenoch
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister’s plans to devolve more powers to Scottish towns and regions is a “waste of time”.
During her own visit to Scotland, at the Malcom Group near Glasgow, Badenoch said: “I think that this is yet again a waste of time discussion.
“This naval gazing about Holyrood powers and constitutional settlements and should we have another referendum and should have more councils – they all have the powers that they need.”
She said the discussion should instead be on what the Scottish government is doing with its powers, which she believed was “absolutely nothing”.
She told Sky News: “What are they doing on education? What are they doing on health? They’ve got no answers.”
Here she is standing in front of a mural of Mel Gibson’s William Wallace who famously led a rebellion against English rule:
Burham has finished his speech, which lasted about 35 minutes. I could just about hear him on the hot mic saying “sorry that went on a bit” as he shook someone’s hand off camera.
'If we don't move now, Scotland could lose out,' says Burnham
The prime minister said he is making a “serious and genuine offer” to the Scottish government to put more control “in the hands of local people”.
He said:
We need to look at the resources and decision-making powers that sit at the regional level in Scotland, so that no Scottish city regions are left behind.
I know the Scottish government has announced a long term programme for local government reform.
But if you ask me, we’ve got to move faster … if we don’t move now, Scotland could lose out.
There is a risk that some of the towns and cities become underpowered when some of the towns and cities of the north of England are going the other way and starting to power up. I don’t want to see that as prime minister.”
