SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Andy Burnham outlines new rules to outlaw ‘rip-off’ private parking fines
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Drivers will get a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their parking session ends before they face a fine under new rules for private car parks that Andy Burnham said were designed to outlaw “rip-off” charges.
In the latest in a series of “everyday fixes” to ease the cost of living and give consumers a “fairer” deal, the prime minister said a new official code of practice for the industry meant motorists in England, Scotland and Wales would enjoy a range of new rights.
The consumer body Which? said the “long overdue” rules appeared to fall well short of what was needed to help drivers fight back against private parking “cowboys”, however.
Each year in the UK, private firms dish out millions of parking tickets, and the number has been climbing. In August, the RAC said the number issued rose 17% in a year to reach a record 16.9m in 2025-26.
Complaints about poor behaviour by some operators are rife, and campaigners say reform is years overdue. Legislation was passed in early 2019, and an official code of practice was unveiled by the then government in early 2022 – but lasted less than six months after legal challenges by several parking firms forced it to be withdrawn.
In a fresh push, a new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday, though it is unclear when this will take effect. Ministers said they would look to bring the code into force “as soon as possible”.
New rights for drivers include “a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park, and 10 minutes to leave once their session ends”.
The government is sticking with the existing industry maximum parking charge of £100 despite calls to halve it. Which? said: “It is particularly concerning that the government has shied away from a £50 price cap.” The consumer body had called for a maximum £50 fine, and this was also the amount at which some charges were capped under the withdrawn code.
Meanwhile, fines will be scrapped on appeal for “honest mistakes”, such as stopping briefly to check directions, and for situations such as a medical emergency, vehicle breakdown or broken ticket machine.
For “smaller slip-ups”, such as forgetting to display a parking permit or entering the wrong vehicle’s registration, the government said drivers would face a maximum charge of £20 on appeal. This appears to be a less generous system than under the original rules: the code that was withdrawn required the cancellation of a parking charge “in all mitigating circumstances”.
Which? said the government had also shied away from an independent appeals body “that could rein in the industry’s worst practices” and had failed to take action on private parking debt recovery fees, which it said were regularly added without motorists’ knowledge and pushed unfair charges even higher.
On the latter point, the government has promised to consult on these fees – which are added when a fine becomes overdue – “as soon as possible next year”. These fees are currently capped at £70, and the consultation will look at whether they should be cut or scrapped altogether.
Burnham said: “Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.
“These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them. We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Vivek Ramaswamy discontinues attack ad that prompted wave of revulsion
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, confirmed on Thursday that his campaign is no longer airing an attack ad that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.
The ad prompted a wave of revulsion since Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, lost custody of her daughter in 1978, when her second husband, Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her daughter between the ages of 10 and 12.
Asked by a reporter in Vandalia, Ohio if his campaign had stopped running the ad, Ramaswamy said: “It ran to completion and we put up four other ads.”
“But what I will say is that for all of the discussion around 30-second ads, I would love, even for this final close, for this campaign to really be about policy,” Ramaswamy added, before criticizing his opponent for not debating him.
Ramaswamy’s campaign had announced last week that it would spend $4m to broadcast the ad, despite criticism from Democrats and Republicans after court records showed that Acton’s mother, who called her daughter “a liar”, had fled the state with her husband when her daughter accused him of rape.
In an interview with the anti-abortion group Operation Rescue in 2020, when Acton was leading Ohio’s response to the Covid pandemic, Acton’s mother said that she was aware that, before she married him, Cledith Arthur had previously been accused of raping his own daughter.
Ramaswamy’s reference to “30-second ads” referred to the length of the ad after his campaign edited the original 60-second version, to remove the allegation from Acton’s mother that her daughter had lied about the family having lived in a tent with Arthur when she was a child.
Court records from the time indicated that Cledith Arthur had, indeed, lived in a tent at the time of his arrest on rape charges.
Donald Trump repeatedly defended the ad, including at a rally with Ramaswamy on Wednesday, while refusing to acknowledge that the serious child rape allegation was relevant to the credibility of Acton’s mother.
Reporting from NBC News and Zeteo suggests that Acton’s mother has suffered from mental health challenges and was found living in her car with dozens of cats, which troubled some people involved in producing the ad for Ramaswamy’s campaign.
“How far will Vivek Ramaswamy go?” Acton’s campaign asked in a new ad on the controversy released earlier on Thursday. “To become governor, he’ll smear his opponent for being raped by her stepfather when she was just 10 years old – exploiting the sexual abuse of a child and spending millions lying to you about it,” the ad warns Ohio voters.
Acton also addressed Ramaswamy’s attack ad at an event on Thursday. “You’ve probably all heard by now, if you didn’t know, a little bit about my childhood,” she told supporters. “My brother and I experienced a lot of things, a lot of abuse and a lot of neglect. We were frequent flyers in children’s services, ended up living in a tent in the middle of winter.”
“My opponent has now chosen to exploit my childhood intentionally,” she continued. “He’s doing it in a desperate attempt to save his struggling campaign. But I’ll tell you, Mr Ramaswamy, it’s not going to work.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Seven reported bomb threats against European flights confirmed as false alarms – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
At least seven flights and a cruise ship in Europe received bomb threats, causing disruption at airports although no devices were discovered. At least two flights to Warsaw, two to Sofia, two to Rome and one to Murcia airport in Spain were subjected to the threats on Tuesday and another flight to Sofia had been threatened a day earlier. 
An airport in Warsaw was briefly shut and the Italian Air Force accompanied one of the flights to Rome, while an Israel-bound cruise ship was searched for bombs in Greece.
Authorities diverted a LOT flight from London that was meant to land at Warsaw’s Chopin airport to nearby Modlin airport, which was closed and then reopened after the plane was searched and no device was found. Another Warsaw-bound flight, an SAS flight from Copenhagen, landed at Chopin as scheduled. Chopin airport said no device was found and the airport remained operational.
Bomb threats were made against planes traveling from Milan/Bergamo and Dublin to Sofia, Bulgaria’s transport ministry said in a statement to Reuters. Both landed safely and no explosive devices were found on inspection.
The Bergamo flight was operated by Wizz Air and was carrying 176 passengers, the statement said. The Dublin flight, operated by Ryanair, had 186 passengers on board. Bulgarian news agency BTA had earlier quoted an interior ministry official as saying a flight from Israel had been affected, but authorities later said this was not the case.
In Murcia in southeastern Spain, parts of an airport were cordoned off after a bomb threat was reported on a Ryanair flight from Manchester. Officials said the report proved to be a hoax, and the airport resumed normal operations after authorities found no explosives on board.
Two other Ryanair flights - one from Lisbon and another from Dublin - were searched at Rome’s Fiumicino airport following bomb threats, said a source from airport operator ADR. The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force until it landed. The alert was cleared and the airport continued to operate as usual with no effects on other flights, the person said.
An explosives detection dog and a diver searched the Panama-flagged Crown Iris cruise ship on the Greek island of Syros after an unknown person said an explosive device had been attached to the boat’s hull, authorities said. Initial checks found no explosive device with coast guard specialists expected to carry out further inspections before the ship could resume its voyage.
Meanwhile, Czech public media workers went on a one-day strike to protest a government plan to overhaul how public broadcasters are funded. The legislation, led by populist billionaire turned prime minister Andrej Babiš, has been criticised as threatening the independence of the media organisations.
Russia bombarded Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in waves on Tuesday, knocking out power to swathes of the country with dozens of missiles and hundreds of drones, a week before US-brokered peace talks were due to resume.
At a press conference in Berlin with German chancellor Friedrich Merz, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack showed that Moscow was intent on killing people instead of building on the humanitarian ceasefire in and around Oleshky.
Merz warned thatthe outcome of the war in Ukraine “will determine European security for a long time to come.” He said Germany will be coordinating with France and the UK, and will host a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin later this month.
The European Commission will host a meeting regarding Ukraine with representatives from the United States, Ukraine and its key European allies on Wednesday, Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho said. “So tomorrow the European Commission will host a meeting with representatives from Ukraine, from the United States, France, Germany, the UK, Nato and the World Bank and this meeting will build on earlier talks that took place in Miami,” Pinho told reporters in Brussels.
Bomb threat prompts checks on Israel-bound cruise ship in Greek port
A bomb threat to an Israel-bound cruise ship prompted a security operation at the Greek island port of Syros after an unknown person claimed an explosive device had been attached to its hull, Greek authorities said.
The Panama-flagged Crown Iris was due to sail to Haifa carrying 940 passengers and 597 crew members when the threat was received, Reuters reported.
Coast guard personnel assisted by an explosives detection dog and a private diver searched the vessel, while a special coast guard unit was deployed to the scene.
Initial checks found no explosive device. Coast guard specialists are expected to arrive at 9.30pm (7.30pm GMT) to carry out further inspections before the ship can resume its voyage.
Czech public media workers strike over government plan to overhaul funding
Here are some images from earlier today as Czech public media workers went on a one-day strike to protest a government plan to overhaul how public broadcasters are funded.
The legislation, led by populist billionaire turned prime minister Andrej Babiš, has been criticised as threatening the independence of the media organisations. The plan led to street protests in Prague last month.
Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television would be financed from the state budget, not from an existing system of regular fees from individuals, households and businesses. The media would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could likely lead to staff layoffs, limited production and program cancellations.
Critics say the overhaul would give the ruling three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under prime minister Robert Fico and in Hungary before former prime minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
Michal Kubal, chief news editor at Czech Television, said the strike today is unprecedented in the history of Czech public service media.
On their TV screens, Czech residents on Tuesday saw an announcement saying:
We are doing everything we can to ensure that we can continue to provide a public service in its full scope and quality in the future.
The UK government confirmed that two of the planes affected had departed from British airports.
A spokesperson said:
The UK has one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we’ve seen today.
Our world-leading police and intelligence agencies work closely every day to keep us safe, using the tools they have to assess and respond to potential threats.
Bulgaria confirms bomb threats against flights from Bergamo, Dublin, not Israel
There is also an update from Bulgaria, with the country’s transport ministry telling Reuters the bomb threats were actually made against two planes from Bergamo in Italy and Dublin in Ireland, and not from Israel as previously reported.
That brings the total to seven planes (that we know of).
Back to Berlin, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy also rejects Russia’s suggestion of a meeting in Moscow as “counterproductive.” He says what’s needed is serious talks, and not a gimmick.
He also insists that Russia has no advantage on the frontline at the moment.
Merz then adds that the 19 November meeting will decide further support for Ukraine in 2027, and that concludes the press.
Two false bomb threats reported on Italy-bound Ryanair flights
Meanwhile, two more false bomb threats were reported in Italy involving Ryanair flights from Lisbon and Dublin to Rome’s Fiumicino Airport, according to the Italian newspapers La Repubblica and Corriere della Sera.
The plane from Dublin was escorted by two Italian air force fighter jets, newspaper reported.
In both cases, routine checks were confirmed as negative, meaning no threat was identified, SkyTG24 said.
That brings the total of flights affected by false alarms today to at least six, up from four reported earlier (that we know of).
Security guarantees, Ukraine reconstructions, energy and Black Sea truce to be discussed in Abu Dhabi, Zelenskyy says
Asked about his expectations for the Abu Dhabi talks, Zelenskyy says he hopes to see future security guarantees for Ukraine to be covered, alongside a “prosperity package” that would help with the reconstruction of Ukraine.
He also says he hopes to discuss a proposal on energy, Black Sea truce, which is “in the interest of not only Ukraine, but also Russia and various nations in Africa.”
He reiterates that “there can be no stable peace unless Europe is at the negotiating table.”
Merz for his part says that “it is crucial for Russia to finally engage in serious negotiations.”
Europe remains 'crucial' for ending the war in Ukraine, Zelenskyy says, as he confirms Abu Dhabi talks
Responding, Zelenskyy thanks Germany for its continued help, including on air defence, and says that while many people will be following the events in the US today’s midterm elections, “the role of Europe – and specifically Germany – remains crucial.”
He says he briefed Merz on the latest attacks on Ukraine.
He also confirms the upcoming Abu Dhabi talks on 10-11 November (11:21), which he says hopefully “will pave the way for a trilateral meeting at the level of heads of states and government.”
He also confirms further talks on Ukraine will be held in Brussels on Wednesday (12:41), as per the European Commission’s announcement earlier, and that the coalition of the willing will meet in Berlin on 19 November.
Merz declares Germany will keep supporting Ukraine as he warns about Russia's attacks, impact of Black Sea strikes on food security
Germany’s Merz begins by saying Zelenskyy’s visit comes “at a critical moment” as Russian attacks on Ukraine continued with “undiminished – indeed, increasing – severity and ruthlessness.”
He says Ukraine “can continue to rely on Germany,” with more support from Berlin in the coming months, including on air defence, energy, and broader winter-related aid.
Merz also warns that the outcome of the war in Ukraine “will determine European security for a long time to come.”
He says Germany will be coordinating with France and the UK, and will host a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin later this month.
The German chancellor also talks of growing concerns about the broader effects of the continuing war, including a potential “global food crisis” triggered by Russia’s continued attacks on trading routes in the Black Sea.
He says the upcoming Abu Dhabi talks are “the right step forward,” and Europe hopes to play its part.
In the meantime, Berlin and partners will “increase the pressure on Moscow and continue to support Ukraine,” he says.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).
Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.
The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.
Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.
The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.
It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”
Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.
Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.
The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.
Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?
“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.
“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”
Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: British people don’t need to apologise for slavery – but the government does | Olivette Otele
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Departing from his predecessors’ stances, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, surprised us all when he stated he was open to listening to calls for an apology for the UK’s role in centuries of transatlantic enslavement. King Charles is expected to speak with “unflinching honesty” and “sincere sorrow” about the UK’s role in the transatlantic slave trade at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda today. Burnham was quick to add that financial reparations were off the table. But he was in favour of discussions about debt restructuring – one of the key concerns of the Caribbean community (Caricom) and the African Union. The opposition, led by Kemi Badenoch, argued that apologies were a distraction.
Beyond political bickering and point-scoring lies a deeper question. Why does Britain struggle to fully understand its colonial past and to grapple with the negative impact of its legacies? One the one hand, the country celebrates its historical conquests as far back as the Battle of Hastings and applauds the wealth that derived from the products of colonisation, such as cotton. On the other, it refuses to accept that harm was caused to populations whose lands it forcefully occupied – and that the trafficking of African captives has changed how we think and what we assume about different racial groups to this day.
The king and the PM clearly understand that Caribbean countries, and the Commonwealth as a whole, are among Britain’s most important relationships. The group of 56 Commonwealth countries represents about a third of the world’s population with more than 2.7 billion people. Because of their historical links to Britain, these countries play an important role in the UK’s global influence and soft power. Refusing to apologise and work together towards a reparatory justice plan is a diplomatic and political mistake. In the long run, it also has a knock-on effect on trading partnerships, as Burnham seems to acknowledge.
The question of repair continues to be framed along the lines of financial compensation. That framing fails to consider how the past is weighing on the present and future of British citizens. Repairing includes building a society that is honest about its traumas and ready to work towards reconciliation. In these times of recession, drawing on existing resources could help address points raised by Caricom and the African Union. For example, the return of cultural heritage could be facilitated by having a discussion in parliament about the British Museum Act 1963 and the National Heritage Act 1983, which prevent the British Museum, Natural History Museum, V&A and Science Museum from permanently returning certain objects from their collections.
A fair reparatory justice plan would help tackle issues such as education, climate justice, health inequality and so on. Perhaps the PM has been paying attention to Caricom’s focus on green energy and climate resilience. His pledge of £40m to Caribbean projects is a very significant step towards mending fences and furthering dialogue on climate justice. Education could also be an important part of the plan precisely because part of the British public doesn’t understand why apologies are required, let alone why taxpayers should pay the bill for financial reparations at a time of national and even global economic recession. Lack of knowledge – of how the trafficking of African captives for more than 300 years helped shape British institutions such as parliament, the Church of England, universities, the banking system, royal societies and so on – has led many to wonder why they should apologise for their ancestors.
Transatlantic enslavement centuries ago relied on the labour of enslaved Africans, and it made Britain very wealthy. The institution of slavery classified populations based on a racist hierarchy. It developed the so-called scientific racism of the 19th century, which led to the 21st-century eugenicists’ stances that still influence current debate about belonging and identity.
Tracie Jolliff, an organisational development consultant who specialises in dismantling systemic racism, puts it like this: “There appears to be a collective amnesia when it comes to harms towards people with black skins as compared to other atrocities that have been well documented. Racism still shapes the way the descendants of those same African people are treated today.”
For Jolliff, the ideas that informed and perpetuated transatlantic enslavement never went away; they simply morphed into more subtle, but still life-limiting structural racism. The evidence and outcomes of that can be seen in the ways that British citizens who are black are disadvantaged in housing, health, education and the criminal justice system. Similarly, Marvin Rees, a former mayor of Bristol who is involved with the Repair Campaign, says, “Individuals today are not responsible for their ancestors’ wrongdoings. It is, however, important to make a link between individuals and institutions. Individuals inherited institutions and institutions bestowed advantages.”
Arguments that position reparations as a subject of the distant past are overlooking the facts. UK taxpayers have been paying back the colossal sum that compensated the owners of enslaved people after the Abolition Act 1833 – a bill that was only repaid in full in 2015. It’s not British people who should apologise, but the British government that used taxpayers’ money to compensate those who profited from trading in people.
Because of the legacies of this trade, many descendants of those responsible for transatlantic enslavement are still part of the financial elite of this world. Some of them, like the Heirs of Slavery, are attempting to engage with the question. The UK government should work with families whose ancestors received compensation in 1837 and who are ready to work towards a restorative justice plan – and with institutions such as the Church of England, Lloyd’s of London and universities that have started to do the work. Combining resources is the way forward now.
Black communities who have their life chances negatively affected by systemic racism were also paying the bill for the owners of their ancestors until 2015. So, if the debt to the slavers can endure without question into this century, surely repair for the legacies of ongoing systemic injustices should be dealt with on similar terms.
- 
  Olivette Otele is a historian and distinguished research professor of the legacies and memory of slavery at Soas University of London

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
British officials reportedly insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned that Andy Burnham would not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.
Currently, slavery reparations is not on the official agenda of the Commonwealth Heads of Government (Chogm) summit, which begins on Sunday.
Trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and investment in opportunities for young people are among the stated priorities for the 56-nation bloc spanning Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Americas, the Pacific and Europe.
“My understanding from informed circles is that Britain was vehement not to have the matter on the agenda. The British officials – and in that regard they were joined by the Canadian officials – were even raising the prospect that if it is on the agenda the prime minister of Britain wouldn’t go,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.
“They also started to circulate this untruth that India didn’t want it on the agenda, but that was not so at all. India was very supportive at the UN general assembly resolution on March 25th, 2026. So they were spreading this false word about India.”
Gonsalves said that the relentless campaign by Caribbean nations, amplified by a growing regional and global reparations movement, has propelled reparatory justice to the heart of the political conversation at the meeting.
“Because of what happened at the UN, because of what happened in Africa, what happened in the Caribbean, and all the work which is taking place in Britain itself too, inside of the British parliament, inside of the British Labour party, both in the Commons and the House of Lords, it is an issue which you can’t duck any more,” he said.
He added: “The danger of not putting it formally on the agenda is what we see happening now, that everybody who could have foreseen, whether or not it’s formally on the agenda, even the nature of how the discussions take place at the Commonwealth, and certainly in the retreats, it would have been raised.”
Gonsalves said while the actual structured dialoguewas unlikely to happen at Chogm, it was expected that when the leaders met in their private retreat, the format and details of the dialogue would be discussed.
He said: “The British government, they’re coming, kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue. But at least they’re coming.”
An FCDO spokesperson said: “We categorically reject this completely untrue accusation. The UK has approached this conversation in good faith, and we have at no point told any other Chogm member what should not be on an agenda.
“Our position on reparations is clear but this government respects the right of others to raise matters as they wish.”
Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, had described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations”, adding that reparatory justice was “the number one item” for the Caribbean as Commonwealth leaders gather in the region.
On Friday there was a historic shift in Britain’s position when the British prime minister went further than any of his predecessors by agreeing to structured dialogue and to consider an apology.
Though Caribbean governments and campaigners welcomed Burnham’s announcement, made in an op-ed for the Guardian, it was clear that agreeing on forms of reparations was still a priority for the region.
Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, welcomed Burnham’s statement and called for a Commonwealth subcommittee to work out the details of the dialogue over the next six to 12 months.
“I’m happy that finally the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been, where the British government is involved, because that’s the state we are dealing with,” he said.
Ali said the talks should move beyond attempting to put a price on the indignity of slavery and towards addressing its developmental consequences.
“How do we identify a system of support where the UK government, with its financial institutions, can sit with countries … and work on a development pathway, identify development gaps, whether in health, education, social services, infrastructure?”
Barbados’s prime minister, Mia Mottley, thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground”, while making clear that the two sides remained divided. “On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she said.
Mottley identified an apology, investment in health and education, tackling systemic poverty and inequality, and fairer debt terms among areas where agreement could be reached.
The Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, said the talks were not simply about “historical remembrance” but “the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress”.
As the meeting kicks off on Sunday, the 45th anniversary of Antigua and Barbuda’s independence from British colonial rule, King Charles is indicating he will not follow Burnham and offer a full apology, there is still a sense that the reparations fight is far from over.
King Charles and Burnham will be greeted with protests as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend Chogm events.
On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be clear: there will be calls for an apology and reparations.
On Sunday Kemi Badenoch told broadcasters that an apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade would be a “navel-gazing distraction”, describing slavery as an evil “in which people from every continent and region participated”.
“I would really like to sit down with my dear sister Kemi and explain to her so that she could get an understanding of what we are talking about,” Gonsalves said, adding that he would like to discuss how reparatory justice could help heal some of the fractures arising from Britain’s multicultural and ethnic tensions.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: US has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says Zelenskyy
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday after a meeting with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway.
He said Ukraine was again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which were seemingly suspended last week by the White House. “Now it works. It’s great,” he said, adding that the US move would save lives.
The Ukrainian president said: “It’s very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles] is coming. So we are thankful to the American side.”
Witkoff will on Wednesday meet Russian president Vladimir Putin after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Zelenskyy in Norway. The US envoy would aim to “create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations”, a US official told Reuters.
The talks in Oslo took place amid the worst crisis in US-Ukraine relations since Putin’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Donald Trump has bitterly accused Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and has said Ukraine needs a new leader.
On Tuesday Trump again suggested Zelenskyy was the main obstacle to an agreement. “We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office,” he said.
Trump also said he had asked Putin to release Stephen Hubbard – an American taken prisoner by Russian forces in occupied Ukraine – in a further sign of his growing public alliance with Moscow.
The US president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined Witkoff and Zelenskyy by video for the talks. Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, also took part, alongside EU and British security officials.
Zelenskyy said he had held a “positive” phone call earlier with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. Asked if Ukraine was now losing the war, after recent hostile US actions, Zelenskyy replied: “Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It’s a pity.”
He said he had raised with Rubio restrictions imposed last week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s satellite internet service. The slowdown has crippled Ukraine’s ability to launch mid-range drone strikes on Russian battlefield positions.
Zelenskyy said he had offered to stop Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries – a key Trump demand – if the US provided Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriots to Kyiv paid for by other countries, leaving Kyiv more vulnerable than ever to air attacks.
Speaking on Tuesday, Zelenskyy also said he opposed a trilateral summit floated by Putin, which would see the Russian leader, Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, meet next month to strike a Ukraine deal. Zelenskyy would be shut out, the Wall Street Journal reported.
“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in Oslo. He added: “If it’s about Ukraine and our future it can only be acceptable when we are at the table of negotiations.”
The Washington-Kyiv crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced he was lifting US sanctions on Russian diesel, in an attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He then announced an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv implemented for several days but Russia ignored.
Despite this, Trump has bitterly rounded on Zelenskyy. He has effectively positioned the US as Russia’s ally, favouring Moscow over Kyiv, to the dismay of America’s pro-Ukrainian European and British backers. The US’s peace proposals have largely echoed Russia’s maximalist demands.
The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators had been honest brokers in the peace efforts. Witkoff has held numerous meetings with Putin in Moscow, while so far visiting Kyiv only once.
“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin’s terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine”, Kallas said.
Tuesday’s talks came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”.
US officials have denied this but have failed to explain convincingly why satellite communication services were curtailed or intelligence sharing temporarily cut off.
Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio insisted nothing had changed. He said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and were needed in other parts of the world, as well as for the US’s own defence. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he insisted.
At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. They included passengers who were travelling on the Kyiv to Odesa highway. A Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of the victims was the driver of a shuttle bus, which was on its way from the capital to a military cemetery.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The Guardian view on AI safety: the push for global regulation must advance | Editorial
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Organisations around the world scrambled on Thursday to fix critical flaws in PHP, the software that powers much of the web. The vulnerabilities could allow attackers to take control of affected servers. Some websites were taken offline as a precaution while fixes were installed. The paradox is that while AI helped researchers uncover the flaw, it also threatens to accelerate the ability to exploit it. Amazon said that it had detected an attempt before the public disclosure of the PHP flaws.
What the episode highlights is AI’s central role in security – and not always for the right reasons. OpenAI’s models have also been responsible for two alarming hacks this year – a security breach of an Australian health department website and a raid by a swarm of AI bots on Hugging Face, an AI services platform. Citing those incidents, the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, warned that a similar cyber-attack on the UK is “likely, if not inevitable”.
Britain is not uniquely vulnerable. In some respects it is more advanced than many countries in grasping the scale of the challenge. The London-based AI Security Institute is internationally recognised as an authority in a rapidly evolving field. A cybersecurity bill to protect critical digital infrastructure is going through parliament.
As Mr Narayan concedes, national governments face limits in protecting their citizens from a global threat. Having Donald Trump in the White House makes the international challenge harder. The US president has rejected calls for international negotiations on AI regulation. He is even dismissive when the bosses of US technology companies recognise the need for external monitoring and ask for statutory guardrails on their own activities.
Mr Trump takes the view that America’s lead at the most advanced frontier of AI is a national strategic asset that would be compromised if other nations, and China in particular, were allowed to set the pace of advancement. In the president’s eyes it is a race for global supremacy and only losers urge caution. “Whoever wins AI, wins,” he has said. That is a disturbingly reckless approach to technology that, in some of the more apocalyptic prognoses, has the potential to destroy humankind. Even in more circumspect scenarios, the risk of some catastrophic incident or severe economic shock caused by the malicious or accidental use of AI is growing at a rate that more responsible leaders than Mr Trump cannot afford to ignore.
Andy Burnham has said that he intends to put AI at the top of the agenda when the UK holds the G20 presidency for the first half of next year. In his speech at the Labour party conference earlier this month, the prime minister compared his role to the global leadership position that Gordon Brown took on as the chair of the G20 in early 2009, coordinating a response to the financial crisis.
But the world looks very different in 2026. Mr Burnham’s convening power will not move a US administration that treats historic allies and multilateral institutions with contempt. That is not a reason to abandon the ambition. The drive to build some global regulatory architecture has to advance. If Mr Trump cannot be moved by care for humanity, this week’s PHP emergency should remind him that America’s technological lead offers no protection from disruption. Shielding US citizens and businesses from such turmoil requires international cooperation that a race for AI supremacy puts at risk.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Trump claims US will end military aid to Israel by end of this year
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this year in a surprise election day announcement that appeared to be targeted at voters sceptical of US support for Israel and the war in Gaza.
In a phone interview with Fox News as voting began on Tuesday morning, the US president said the US would cut nearly $4bn (£2.96bn) in military aid to Israel because “they don’t need it”.
“We were giving them $4bn … But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” he said.
Trump also indicated that he had decided to end the aid – which he claimed would be replaced by arms sales to Israel instead – because it had become a popular criticism of US foreign policy led by outspoken candidates including the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad talking point.”
During the interview, Trump claimed that the abrupt ending of aid was proposed by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “We give them $4bn of things and money, and they don’t need it,” he said. “And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
Netanyahu had previously suggested tapering off US military aid to Israel over the next decade, but Trump’s announcement on Tuesday would significantly accelerate that timeline.
Israeli officials appeared to be taken by surprise by the announcement, and leading members of the opposition said it showed the damage that Netanyahu had done to the US-Israel relationship. The announcement comes at a crucial moment after Netanyahu’s party lost its majority in the Knesset in last week’s elections and the opposition is trying to cobble together a coalition to replace him.
“The fact that the security establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning about a change in the strategic relationship framework through the media highlights just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a genuine danger,” said Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right rival to Netanyahu who is seeking to replace him as prime minister. “We can no longer rely on him and must replace him.”
“A responsible prime minister would have fought to increase American aid, not dismantle it,” wrote Yair Golan, the head of the Democrats opposition party. “Netanyahu is deepening the security and economic crisis, putting Israel’s future at risk.”
Israel received most of the approximately $3.8bn in 2025 as foreign military financing grants that allow the country to buy US military hardware including F-35 fighter jets. Another $500m was given for joint missile defence programmes.
Trump’s announcement on Tuesday appeared timed to affect the outcome of the midterm elections, in which US foreign policy and support for Israel have played an unusually important role in key races, including the Michigan senatorial race where El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed would become the country’s first Muslim senator if he is elected.
A Quinnipiac University poll released in September showed that 48% of Americans believed that the US was too supportive of Israel, and other recent polls have shown a historic shift away from US support for Israel and Netanyahu’s government.
Anger over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has helped usher in a wave of progressive Democratic candidates including El-Sayed, and Trump’s vice-president, JD Vance, has openly accused Israel of trying to sabotage US negotiations with Iran. In a June interview with the New York Times, Vance said of Israel’s foreign policy: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have.”
During his Fox News interview, Trump spoke warmly about Netanyahu and also boasted about his own popularity in Israel. “If people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” he said.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Christian nationalism in Britain is being driven largely by people who rarely attend church and are more concerned with defending the country’s Christian heritage, according to research.
The report, by the thinktank Theos, identified five different groups within the UK in a survey that looked at their attitudes to Christianity and Britishness.
The group whose views most closely resembled Christian nationalism, termed “identity integrationists” by the researchers, accounted for 11% of respondents, making it the smallest of the five groups.
Although 81% of this group identified as Christian, just 13% attended church weekly, only slightly above the 11% average across the population surveyed. Less than a third (31%) prayed weekly, while 47% expressed an interest in the Bible.
The group was strongly hostile to immigration and Islam. Just 19% agreed that Christian values required welcoming and supporting asylum seekers, while 30% supported the equal treatment of religions in public life.
In contrast, another group in the survey with high levels of Christian affiliation, were considerably more religiously observant and less hostile to immigration and religious diversity. They comprised 13% of respondents.
Among these “belief integrationists”, 31% attended church weekly, 46% prayed weekly and 62% expressed an interest in the Bible.
Almost half (48%) agreed that Christian values required welcoming and supporting asylum seekers, while 63% supported the equal treatment of religions in public life.
Although they are the group containing the highest proportion of practising Christians, only 18% of belief integrationists think that defending Britain’s Christian culture and heritage is important for being Christian, compared with 90% of the Christian nationalist group.
At a time when crosses have been carried at Unite the Kingdom rallies and crowds have chanted “Christ is King” at protests, the research challenges the idea that the growing prominence of Christian nationalism in Britain reflects a revival of Christianity.
Instead, the findings suggest that Christianity is increasingly being invoked as a marker of British identity amid wider anxieties about immigration, Islam and cultural change.
The results are based on a survey of 1,765 adults conducted in April 2026, which identified five distinct groups according to their attitudes towards Christianity and British national identity.
More than half of Britons surveyed (55%) said they would be unhappy if their local church closed and became a mosque, including 37% who would be very unhappy.
More than a third (37%) agreed with the conspiracy theory that the white population of Europe was being deliberately replaced by migrants from Muslim countries, sometimes known as the ‘great replacement’ theory.
Nick Spencer, a senior fellow at Theos and one of the report’s authors, suggested that the difference between the two most highly affiliated Christian groups’ attitudes towards asylum seekers might partly reflect their religious practice and ethnic composition.
The more practising Christian group were the most ethnically diverse of the five groups, with 20% identifying as non-white, while identity integrationists were among the least diverse.
Spencer added that there was also “a difference between Christianity as an idea and Christianity as an embodied practice”.
“If it matters enough for you to haul yourself out of bed on a Sunday morning, to spend time with people who you don’t choose – you don’t choose who you’re sitting next to in the pew, you don’t choose who’s next to you in the communion rail – it becomes a bit more human and more humane.”
Arun Arora, Church of England bishop of Kirkstall in Leeds, said the distinction between cultural Christianity and practising faith was central to understanding the findings.
“What is it to be a disciple? It’s threefold: deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow me,” he said.
“And what I think’s interesting about the nationalists is that they want to take up the cross at marches, and display it, but there’s less of an interest in denying themselves and following Jesus.”
He argued that the lessons for church leaders weren’t just to encourage church attendance, but to be out in the community.
“If as the church we’re going to wait for people to come into the ark to be saved, to use Noah’s ark analogy, then we’re going to be waiting a while,” he said.
“Whereas the responsibility for us is to bring that full gospel message of discipleship, of what that requires, the costly nature of discipleship, to be able to expound and articulate that, and the passionate love of God for his people, and his world, and not just those who carry certain passports.”
The Rev Dr Helen Paynter, a theologian who has researched the far right’s use of Christianity, said the findings highlighted the responsibility of churches to welcome people across the political spectrum.
But, she added: “The church is and has been since its inception a multi-ethnic, multinational group, and may not rightly be equated with any nationality or ethnicity. In fact, the ‘average’ Christian in the world today is poor, female and black.”
For Paynter, one of most important findings is the starkly different attitudes evidenced by those who are practising Christians, compared with those who claim the label.
“The Christian faith is not just an identity that we can put on like a coat; it involves an encounter with transcendence which must be transformative of all our values.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: If the PM reboots the UK for working-class people, unions will be with him. But the time for talking is over | Andrea Egan
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
After Keir Starmer, things could only get better inside Labour. But Andy Burnham’s arrival as party leader and prime minister didn’t just clear that low bar. It was a cause for hope, especially for those of us in the trade union movement. That’s less because Burnham is streets ahead of his predecessor as a politician – although he is – and more about just how radically the new prime minister has framed his project for the country.
I’ve been active in the labour movement for almost four decades. In that time, I cannot count how many times I’ve heard talk of reversing the devastation wreaked by Margaret Thatcher. For socialists and grassroots trade union activists, this kind of political thinking is bread and butter. But not so much for a Labour prime minister.
Tony Blair, between torching the Middle East and taking a hammer to our civil liberties, infamously came to build upon Thatcher’s legacy rather than bury it. Gordon Brown and Starmer were more set against the Thatcherite fracturing of our society than Blair. But they both continued to inhabit the political cage she built: the idea that there is no alternative.
Before now, the only major party leader ideologically opposed to neoliberalism in a remotely serious way was Jeremy Corbyn, who drew up a programme that would have started to undo the rule of the market. But it wasn’t to be. So in beginning his premiership by insisting that there is, in fact, an alternative way of organising our economy and society to the neoliberal one, Burnham marked a historic shift.
This kind of talk isn’t cheap. How the prime minister has articulated his vision really matters, both because it has challenged the assumptions that have shaped our politics for decades and because the analysis is fundamentally correct. Virtually every aspect of this country’s malaise, as Burnham powerfully explained to Kemi Badenoch, can be traced back to the “wrong turns” taken in the 1980s.
But the flip side for Burnham is that his diagnosis doesn’t leave any doubt about what Labour must do in government. To measure up to his own ambitions, the party will have to implement changes to the structure of our economy unseen since the immediate postwar period. At a minimum, that means bringing sectors into public ownership and investing on a huge scale to rebuild a social fabric – our public services, infrastructure and collective life – that has been shredded.
Many of the Burnham government’s measures so far have been welcome. Banking quick wins that don’t require wrangling with the Treasury but signal you are on the side of the people was a sensible approach for the early days. Labour’s steady improvement in the polls reflects that. But four decades of neoliberalism won’t be ended through Google Maps updates of petrol prices, or even with measures to provide breathing room in the face of the cost of living crisis.
Following up a bold, historical diagnosis with piecemeal measures just isn’t politically sustainable. From US wars to the climate crisis, the factors making essentials ever more unaffordable are out of control. Without the radical action the prime minister has called for, then, the lives of our people and communities are going to keep getting worse, rapidly. And the stakes remain high: it’s the far right that will benefit if this project fails.
So the budget must be the moment that the prime minister’s programme starts to match his rhetoric. Unison is clear about that, and so are my colleagues across the trade union movement. We’re not expecting neoliberalism to have melted away by the time John Healey finishes reading out his statement. But we are demanding serious measures that actually begin to improve workers’ lives.
We expect a big, multiyear funding plan to restore investment and wages in our public services – alongside kicking profiteering vultures out of the public sector through bringing services back in-house. These measures should be funded by finally making the wealthy few pay their fair share of tax. It’s imperative that the prime minister and chancellor defy pressure from the business lobby and the rightwing media to reject changes such as equalising income and capital gains tax.
The decades-long political settlement the prime minister has rightly defined himself against might have impoverished the vast majority, but there were some winners. And those who have profited handsomely from neoliberalism will fight tooth and nail against any attempt to actually break with it.
So, if the prime minister sticks with his historic ambition to remake Britain in the interests of the working class, it won’t be easy. But the trade union movement will be by his side. There’s no dodging a battle with the vested interests committed to keeping things as they are – and the budget is the place to begin.
- 
  Andrea Egan is the general secretary of Unison

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Tennessee national guard trained guns on dying man after guard member shot him, video shows
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Tennessee national guard troops in Memphis last summer trained their handguns on a man as he lay dying on a sidewalk after a guard member shot him in the back, video released Monday by county prosecutors shows.
A Memphis police officer can be heard in the footage from an officer’s body camera calling for an ambulance and then asking the troops: “Hey, you guys got a medical kit or anything?”
The Shelby county district attorney’s office released the videos, which also include footage from stationary cameras and a cellphone from a bystander, as the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation continues its investigation into the 5 July shooting of Tyrin Johnson.
Johnson, 20, who had been armed, died at the scene from a single gunshot wound, according to investigators. An autopsy report shared by Johnson’s family found that he was shot in the back, contradicting police and national guard accounts that said he was facing the guard members with a gun when they fired at him.
The footage did not show Johnson’s initial encounter with the guard members or them firing at him.
The guard members were part of a federal taskforce created by Donald Trump, who last year sent troops and federal agents to Democratic-run cities that he described as overrun with crime. Tennessee’s Republican governor Bill Lee had deployed the guard to support the effort. The task force was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July.
District attorney Steve Mulroy said he has not yet decided whether to file charges in connection with the death.
A spokesperson for the Tennessee national guard did not immediately respond to email and phone messages seeking comment. Ed Yarbrough, an attorney for the two guard members, said they have no comment at this time.
Authorities said the troops were responding with local police to reports of gunshots at about 4am when they began pursuing an armed man fleeing on foot.
Footage from stationary street cameras shows a person in dark clothing firing shots through an empty parking lot at three people walking on a sidewalk. Two Memphis police officers hear gunshots nearby and start walking and then running in that direction, a body camera worn by one of the officers shows. The officers say on their radio that they are pursuing a man who is running and armed with a gun.
The video, which is blurry from the officer’s movement, captures yelling and the sound of a single gunshot, followed by several additional gunshot noises.
A Tennessee national guard report obtained by the Associated Press via a public records request said two guard members responded to the Memphis police radio call, left their vehicle and approached the suspect, who “rounded on them and pointed a tan handgun at them”. Both guard members fired their service weapons – M17 handguns – and Memphis police arrived shortly after, the report stated.
Police body camera footage shows guard members at the scene shouting “Hands!” and “Turn over!” as they point their handguns at a man lying on his back on the sidewalk.
André C Wharton, an attorney for Johnson’s family, noted that the videos do not show the moments immediately before the shooting, or the shooting itself.
“This investigation must stay focused on the moment the guardsman fired the fatal shot and whether that action was reasonable,” Wharton said.
Johnson was the father of a young child and was preparing to help lead the family construction business, his grandfather, Evaniel Johnson, said.
At least six guard members were on the scene immediately after the shooting, the body camera video shows. One can be seen moving a handgun that is on the ground until a police officer tells him to leave it alone. An officer calls for an ambulance over the radio, and a guard member begins to cut off the man’s shirt just before the video ends.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship had become a political liability.
Trump’s 11th-hour suggestion, on election morning, that he would cut military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, as he put it, “they don’t need it”, was condemned across the board – with pro-Palestinian advocates dismissing it as “desperate” and pro-Israel ones as “unserious”.
Trump’s suggestion that he would replace nearly $4bn in annual military aid with arms sales signaled little would change in practice – the funding would continue and it would be harder to track. But it was still a notable recognition by the president of just how much support for Israel has tanked against the backdrop of the latest war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, been widely described as a genocide, and reshaped US politics in ways unthinkable just three years ago.
Indeed, come January, the US House will include an army doctor who went on a medical mission in Gaza, a lawyer who was fired by her firm over a blogpost criticizing Israel’s war, a Jewish lawmaker who was recently detained by Israeli forces while helping Palestinians harvest olives in the occupied West Bank, and a community organizer who participated in a pro-Palestine student encampment and scored one of the primary season’s most stunning upsets under the banner “babies, not bombs”.
Pro-Palestinian candidates – including Palestinian-American ones – have won downballot races. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim to be elected to the US Senate, following a campaign that saw more than $40m spent by Aipac in an effort to defeat him, last-minute drama, and unprecedented levels of Islamophobic rhetoric and bigotry.
“The old bipartisan consensus on Israel is over,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, said. Without that consensus in place, the next Congress could push a number of measures, from an arms embargo on Israel to sanctions against violent settlers and officials – though Trump would retain veto power to block them.
The vote was also a rejection of Trump’s war in Iran – something even JD Vance said on Wednesday was “obvious to almost everyone”. Foreign policy issues rarely determine US elections – that is, until those issues have a direct effect on Americans’ lives at home.
“Americans were reminded of the failures of the Iran war with every visit to the gas station and grocery store,” said Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine/Israel Program at the Arab Center Washington DC. “Israel is a central piece of that story.”
Across the country, and up and down the ballot, unabashedly pro-Palestinian candidates defeated pro-Israel ones despite groups like Aipac pouring tens of millions of dollars into a failed attempt to reverse Israel’s collapsing standing among US voters. Last month, Aipac acknowledged its open support was hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them, and announced it would stop making direct endorsements and contributions – a remarkable admission even if one with little practical consequence.
The victories of El-Sayed and several other candidates whom the right sought to cast as antisemitic over their support for Palestinians also marked a significant rejection of the narrative that pro-Israel voices and the Trump administration have relentlessly advanced over the last three years – that criticism of Israel is, by default, antisemitic.
“They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” El-Sayed, who has continued to speak plainly about his support for Palestinians despite coming under enormous pressure over it, said during his acceptance speech. “If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self determination, that’s not hate, it’s love.”
In Michigan, El-Sayed won a majority of Jewish voters, according to exit polls. Despite warnings that Jews would leave the Democratic party en masse over its shifts on Israel, J Street said its polling found that 72% of Jews voted for Democrats on Tuesday, even though the Republican party increased its share of the Jewish vote since 2024..
This does not mean that the Democratic party is unified on Israel and Palestine and or in opposition to foreign wars.
For decades, the party has “excluded or marginalized anyone whose progressive values extend to support for Palestine”, Lara Friedman, the president of the Foundation for Middle East Peace, said. “American voters, organizers, and a cohort of enormously talented candidates came together and kicked the door down.”
Matt Duss, executive vice-president of the Center for International Policy and a former foreign policy aide to Senator Bernie Sanders, said that the Democrats now must seize the opportunity to become the party opposed to war.
“Trump ran and won as an anti-war candidate in 2024, because unfortunately Democrats left that lane wide open for him,” he said. “The question is: will Democrats finally get it? Will they finally realize that Americans are tired of war and want a new foreign policy?”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Nigel’s ‘chiselled cheekbones’ make the news – Reform’s the Reformer, digested by John Crace
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
THE REFORMER
Welcome to your new super, soaraway Reformer. The paper that aims to take you back to the 1950s with all the stories that the mainstream media don’t want you to read. Free to all patriots. And those who happen to have found a copy on the floor of the bus.
A message from the editor, Nigel Farage
We are living in dangerous times. The chances of finding an immigrant ahead of you in the supermarket checkout queue have never been higher. Now more than ever you need a newspaper you can trust. One that isn’t afraid to tell you the truth about Broken Britain, and where you can find a grievance on every page. So let me introduce you to the Reformer team. There’s me, Nigel. I’m the editor-in-chief. And then there are seven or eight other nobodies whose names escape me. Here is my promise to you. If you are not fully satisfied with the Reformer in the first 100 days then I will sack all the people I have already forgotten.
FARMING IN CRISIS
by Nigel Farage, agriculture editor
A sensational report that has been hushed up by establishment figures linked to the European Union reveals that migrants are responsible for the failure of this summer’s harvest. The report, which has been leaked to the Reformer by a source who wishes to go by the name of Nigel, reveals that officials have tried to blame the crop failure on climate change. “It’s a total scandal,” said Nigel. “What’s been going on is that immigrants have been bringing their hot weather over to the UK with them in small boats. Global warming is a hoax perpetuated by leftwing politicians who want to encourage unlimited illegal immigration. But there’s no denying the facts. Back in the days when you seldom saw a black or brown face, British summers were much cooler. It’s time for everyone to start telling the truth.”
FOREIGNERS INCREASE THE WELFARE BILL
by Nigel Farage, home affairs editor
In one of the country’s biggest surveys of two families, the Reformer can exclusively report that white people much prefer to live next to white people. The families in question say their lives are being made a misery by having a man called Zia Yusuf as their next door neighbour. “It’s got nothing to do with Zia being a brown Muslim,” said Trevor Bloke. “I don’t care what colour or religion he is. What’s intolerable is that he is a deeply unpleasant person who goes out of his way to be rude to everyone. He thinks he owns the whole street. We all just wish he would leave. It’s doing my head in. I’m now on maximum Pip payments for my anxiety and I can no longer work.”
HOW TO SPOT A NIGERIAN SCAMMER
by Nigel Farage, consumer affairs editor
We’ve all had it. An email from someone who is clearly black. A telephone call from someone who is also clearly black. You know they are black because deep down, every black person wants to try to scam your bank account. Not a nice feeling when you’ve just been transferred £5m as a gift from a Thai-based billionaire. It’s the new something-for-nothing society. Say what you like about Oswald Mosley, but he would never have tolerated such behaviour. Now we just accept that immigrants are trying to take over our country. What is the easiest way to spot a Nigerian scammer? Just go to the House of Commons. There you will find the criminal mastermind. A woman called Kemi. She claims to be the leader of the opposition, but all she really wants are your credit card details.
INTERVIEW OF THE MONTH: NIGEL FARAGE
Our features editor, Nigel Farage, interviews Nigel Farage. With additional reporting by Nigel Farage
It’s late afternoon in autumn. The sun streams through the window, its rays dancing off Nigel’s chiselled cheekbones. Nigel is at his most relaxed, mainly because he has just sent his valet, Richard Tice, to the off-licence for a third bottle of champagne. He smiles kindly at me. Reform are well ahead in the polls in third place and he is busy putting the finishing touches to his first speech as prime minister. “Tell me, Nigel,” I say. “Why is it that God has sent you down into the world to save Great Britain from all the illegal immigrants? Please can you also talk me through your magnificent byelection victory against a comedian with a bin on his head?”
Continues for another 1,500 words …
HARRY’S GOLDEN BOOTS
by Nigel Farage, football editor
In a stunning triumph for Brexit Britain, England’s Harry Kane has seen off countless other black and foreign footballers to be crowned the world’s best footballer in a glittering Ballon d’Or ceremony in London. Speaking exclusively to Reform, Kane’s best friend, Nigel Farage, said: “It’s about time a white Englishman won this. Harry would never have been able to do this if we hadn’t left the European Union. Just think what might have happened if footballers had freedom of movement. Harry might have ended up playing for some deadbeat team like Bayern Munich. Then he would have remained an unknown. So, really, Harry owes it all to me.”
THE READERS’ CHAMPION
by Nigel Farage, agony uncle
Dear Nigel, I recently got married and it should have been the happiest day of my life. Instead it became the worst. First, discovered that the man who had promised me he was rich enough to be worth divorcing my first husband for had only bought premium economy seats for our honeymoon in the US. Then I discovered that British Airways – a disgrace of a national carrier – had deliberately delayed the departure of our plane to maximise our inconvenience and then lost an item of luggage. My husband, Thicky Dicky, as I affectionately call him, yelled: “Don’t you know who I am?” and the person on the desk said: “We know exactly who you are.” Please help us seek redress. Yours, Isabel Oakeshott, Dubai
Dear Isabel, I am sorry to hear your distressing story. Please send me £80 and I will do a Cameo video calling for every foreign-looking baggage handler at Heathrow to be sacked. PS: BA is now owned by a private Spanish company.
RACIST OF THE MONTH
by Nigel Farage, competitions’ editor
Call 0800 001 for Tommy Robinson who has recently been found guilty of harassing journalists in a massive miscarriage of justice.
Call 0800 002 for cheeky chappy Raheem Kassam, who asked the Guardian to correct a sketch that said he had deleted a racist tweet.
Calls will cost £5 plus normal charges. Winners will receive something worthless in bitcoin.
BOOK OF THE MONTH
by Nigel Farage, literary editor
My Struggle, by Nigel Farage.
In which the Reform leader hilariously recounts the ways he made antisemitic remarks in front of Jewish boys at school on his way to becoming the most consequential politician of the last 200 years.
‘Almost as good as Liz Truss’s Bank Job’ – the Guardian
POTHOLE OF THE MONTH
by Nigel Farage, transport editor
In the first of an ongoing series, Nigel Farage,discusses his favourite pothole and how he got it filled. “There was this fantastic pothole near my house in Kent,” he said. “We filled it up with loads of dead immigrants and the rubber of small boats the navy had sunk in the Channel.” Doing good with a smile on your face. That’s the Reform way.
TRAVEL NEWS
by Nigel Farage, the Reformer’s eye-in-the-sky
Avoid travelling on the M6 north of Birmingham. Traffic is at a standstill due to too many foreigners driving on English roads. It’s a nightmare. And I can promise you that I will stop all immigrants driving when I become prime minister.
TV LISTINGS
by Nigel Farage, media editor
1. Anything from GB News.
2. ITV: a charming documentary in which almost everyone at Reform HQ is found to be racist.
3. Channel 4: a brilliant drama in which Farage and friends pretend they are trying to take illegal donations. With hilarious consequences for everyone.
CRYPTIC CROSSWORD CLUE
compiled by Nigel Farage
Robert Jenrick confused Newark MP (6 letters, anag. Beginning with W)
