SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: British people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy Burnham
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
On 28 October 1787, Thomas Clarkson pushed through the crowds to reach the pulpit of Manchester Cathedral. A campaigner for abolishing slavery, he spoke urgently about the horrors of the slave trade and the humanity of enslaved people. “He drinks the cup of sorrow,” Clarkson said. “And he drinks it at our hands.”
During Black History Month, these are the stories it is important to remember. They show us the complicated truth of our history. Thousands of people in Manchester signed a petition against slavery after Clarkson’s sermon. And yet Manchester’s cotton industry was built on the labour of enslaved people. There are similar stories up and down the nation. We are a country where brave people led the way in abolishing slavery, but we are also a country that participated in the trade in human lives.
The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.
Our history is intertwined with countries that are now our allies, particularly in the Commonwealth. Next week, I will attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm). In an increasingly divided and dangerous world, our family of nations in the Commonwealth is vital to our interests: a beacon of stability, strength and security. Together we can face down shared challenges. We can seize opportunities for trade and economic collaboration. We can strengthen our respective countries and share our values to build a safer world for us all.
But facing a changing world together requires us to stand on firm foundations. To meet those challenges of the future, we need to face up to the past. For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function.
Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.
So we are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.
Some have called for financial reparations for the slave trade. I do not believe that is the right answer. I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.
My focus is on building a future where people at home and abroad live in greater peace and prosperity.
So we will bring to the Chogm our determination to tackle the issues that affect people across our Commonwealth family and beyond.
Today, debt-servicing costs in the poorest and most vulnerable countries are at their highest in more than 25 years. More than 40% of these countries spend more on interest repayments than on health. I want to launch a new drive on debt, working with our global partners to help those countries repay over a longer time period and with better rates. That is why the chancellor, foreign secretary and I have asked Gordon Brown, who will join us at the Chogm, to help with this work.
We will also support the energy transition in the face of the climate crisis. And we will build on the incredible work being done to educate women and girls, give smaller countries a louder voice on the world stage, and end global poverty and inequality.
I want us to build stronger relationships with each other and renew the relevance of the Commonwealth in a new era. We do that by facing our past together and focusing on a future where every person living within it has equality, security and hope.
We stand on the shoulders of those such as Thomas Clarkson and the many ordinary people who spoke out for justice and humanity.
In 1862, at the height of the American civil war, Manchester was the cotton capital of the world. In a vote at the Free Trade Hall, the humble cotton workers resolved that they would no longer handle slave-picked cotton. Their actions helped end the civil war, prompting Abraham Lincoln to write to them praising their “sublime Christian heroism”.
It is so often the case in British history that huge injustices ignored by the powers-that-be are eventually overturned by ordinary people. Those Manchester cotton workers represent that proud British tradition, and I will take inspiration from them as we go forward into our new dialogue.
- 
  Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Ramaswamy accuses Acton of 'lying' about attack ad, but court records contradict claim made by Acton's mother in ad
Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, accused his Democratic opponent, Dr Amy Acton, of “lying about lying” in her outraged response to an attack ad released by his campaign.
“We ran an ad about lying,” Ramaswamy argued on Friday, “it had nothing to do with childhood abuse”. Instead, the Republican claimed, his opponent was lying “about her history”.
The Ramaswamy campaign ad features Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing the daughter she lost custody of in 1978, after her second husband was charged with raping her then 12-year-old daughter, of lying about her childhood.
According to police and court documents obtained by the Associated Press, Arthur’s second husband, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter in July 1978, after Acton’s biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978, when Acton was between 10 and 12 years old.
Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty and was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. Donna Arthur fled the state with her husband, who later died.
Philip Stearns, Acton’s brother, said in a statement denouncing the ad that after his stepfather was arrested “and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.”
In the attack ad, Donna Arthur called her daughter “a liar” and said “she lies about her past; she says she grew up living in a tent, none of that is true.” That part of the ad uses stock video of a tent that had previously appeared in a biographical ad from Acton’s campaign, in which the candidate described her troubled upbringing. “I think it was somewhere off Route 7,” the candidate recalls. “I was 12, and we were living in a tent.”
A copy of the 1978 arrest warrant for Cledith Arthur, posted online on Friday by Nick Evans, a reporter for the Ohio Capital Journal, suggests that Acton was telling the truth. The warrant lists a campground off Ohio Route 7 in Rogers, Ohio as Cledith Arthur’s address.
“In 1982, after the Arthurs had skipped bail and fled Ohio, a deputy attempted to serve a warrant at” the same campground, Evans reports. “In a hand written note, the deputy relays that the park’s manager said Arthur ‘has not camped here for over two years.’”
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day, but we will be back on Saturday. Here are the latest developments:
Donald Trump started his day by lashing out at a female White House correspondent who asked him “Do the sexual abuse allegations mean nothing to you, sir?”, as the president refused to admit that the credibility of a woman featured in Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad was fatally undermined by the fact that she sided with the man charged with raping her 12-year-old daughter.
Democrat Mary Peltola, the former Alaska congresswoman running for Senate against the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, and an independent candidate named Daniel Sullivan, told MS Now that the justice department lawsuit to block the certification of Alaska’s results if the Republican incumbent loses “is clearly corruption.”
Ramaswamy accused Acton, of “lying about lying” in her outraged response to the attack ad released by his campaign. But a copy of the 1978 arrest warrant for Cledith Arthur, Acton’s then-stepfather, suggests that Acton was telling the truth.
After lashing out at a reporter who pressed him on ignoring sexual abuse, Trump ends his day with a softball question from a friendly outlet
Donald Trump started his day by lashing out at a female White House correspondent who asked him “Do the sexual abuse allegations mean nothing to you, sir?”, as the president refused to admit that the credibility of a woman featured in Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad was fatally undermined by the fact that she sided with the man charged with raping her 12-year-old daughter.
Trump insisted that the ad, in which the mother of Dr Amy Acton, a Democrat running for Ohio governor, called her estranged daughter a liar, was valid, even though Acton’s mother had lost custody of her children in 1978, when her second husband was charged with raping her daughter.
“A mother is saying, ‘Don’t put my daughter there because she’s a terrible person and she’s a liar’. Why shouldn’t somebody use that?” Trump said.
“But do the sexual abuse allegations mean nothing to you, sir?” Monica Alba of NBC News asked.
As he tried to ignore her and press on with his point that the ad was damning, Alba repeated: “But do sexual abuse allegations make no difference?
“Wait, wait, wait, wait. Slow down. Who are you with? Who you with?” Trump asked.
After Alba identified her network and Trump criticized it, she said again: “But there are very serious sexual abuse allegations.”
“Quiet,” Trump said.
“They make no difference to you?” Alba asked again.
“Isn’t she a fresh person?” Trump asked another reporter, before turning to Alba and saying: “You’re a horrible little reporter, aren’t you?”
After pressing ahead with his talking point that the observations of a mother must be valuable, Trump turned back to Alba and asked: “Why wouldn’t you listen to a mother that says that? Why wouldn’t you listen, Miss NBC?”
“She stayed with a stepfather-” Alba began.
“Wait a minute, quiet,” Trump said. “I don’t know anything about a stepfather.”
Alba continued: “who was charged with raping his stepdaughter in 1978, sir.”
“You just keep talking,” Trump told her.
“I am answering you, sir.,” she replied.
“I don’t know anything about stepfathers,” the president repeated and then reiterated that the allegation of sexual abuse did, in fact, mean nothing to him.
That evening, instead of taking questions from nonpartisan outlets, Trump limited his last exchange of the day to a single softball question from a reporter from the rightwing news channel Real America’s Voice, who told the president his rally was fun and then asked him to trash FBI officials his administration accuses of helping suppress reports about Hunter Biden’s laptop in 2020.
Peltola calls federal lawsuit to block Alaska results should she win 'a very desperate attempt to cling to power'
Democrat Mary Peltola, the former Alaska congresswoman running for Senate against the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, and an independent candidate named Daniel Sullivan, told MS Now on Friday that the justice department lawsuit to block the certification of Alaska’s results if the Republican incumbent loses “is clearly corruption.”
The federal intervention Donald Trumpsays he ordered, on the premise that some voters might mistakenly vote for the wrong Dan Sullivan, “is not playing well with Alaskans at all,” Peltola said.
“It’s sending a message that Dan Sullivan does not believe that Alaskans are sophisticated enough to know exactly who they’re voting for and what the implications of their vote is,” she added. “I mean, Alaskans are very dialed into this race because 24 hours a day, the Pacs are running ads and attack ads. So there’s no room for anybody to not be thinking about this Senate race.”
“This is clearly a very desperate attempt to cling to power,” Peltola said of her Trump-endorsed Republican rival, “using his allies in Washington, DC to rig the system even further.”
Peltola also noted that the ballot in Alaska’s Senate race clearly “says incumbent” next to Dan Sullivan’s name, “so there just isn’t much room for confusion on the ballot.”
Because Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, any voters who are confused as to which Dan or Daniel Sullivan they want in office, could simply rank both of them and no other candidate.
Peltola was interviewed by the host Nicole Wallace, a former communications director in George W Bush’s White House who, as a senior adviser to the McCain-Palin campaign in 2008, tried to convince Americans that Sarah Palin was ready to be president.
“I’ve spent a little bit of time in Alaska,” Wallace noted at the start of the interview, causing Peltola to chuckle.
“I feel remorse for my role in the final weeks of the McCain-Palin effort,” Wallace said in 2020, “that I was part of an effort to suggest in interviews and otherwise that she was ready to be president if she had to step in to that role.”
Abdul El-Sayed to run new ad on Fox News and Newsmax filled with praise for him from Fox News and Newsmax hosts
Dr Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat battling a Republican opponent and rightwing media for a seat in the US Senate, announced on Friday that he is buying ad time on Fox News and Newsmax to run a new ad filled with praise for him from Fox News and Newsmax hosts.
At the start of the ad, El-Sayed tells voters who get their news from the rightwing outlets: “We agree on a lot: Washington is a corrupt swamp; the big corporations and elites run the show there, and it raises our costs; release the Epstein files; and yeah, free speech is under attack, and we should Make America Healthy Again, stop wasting our tax dollars on overseas wars and end bad trade deals.”
Then he introduces a package of clips from the rightwing hosts and podcasters by saying, “Don’t want to take my word for it? How about some folks you know a little bit better?”
The ad then cuts together grudging and genuine praise for the Democrat from: the Fox hosts Jesse Waters, Ainsley Earhardt, Jessica Tarlov and Lara Trump; Newsmax host Lidia Curanaj; Saagar Enjeti on Tucker Carlson’s podcast and former Republican congresswoman-turned-podcaster Nancy Mace.
'We’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran', Trump tells Florida crowd
Donald Trump casually hinted at likely US military action against Cuba during a campaign rally in Fort Myers, Florida on Friday.
About midway through his 90 minute speech, as he described the toll inflicted on Iran by the Pentagon, Trump’s remarks were interrupted by a supporter shouting “What about Cuba?”
“He wants to know what about Cuba. Give me a break,” Trump said. “Don’t worry, we’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran. We’ll just- we’ll do a little stopover”.
“Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is we’re going to come back from Iran,” Trump went on, making a swerving gesture with his hand. “Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast, they’ll raise up their hands and then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”
“We’ll have Marco – Marco!” he continued. “We don’t even have to stop, we could just put him in there and he’ll figure it out.”
Trump has dropped similar hints about a US regime change operation on more than a dozen occasions this year.
Minutes after the president stopped speaking, Rubio, his secretary of state, urged Cubans to collaborate with US spies to topple their own government.
“To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time,” Rubio posted. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA.”
The top US diplomat, whose parents left Cuba for the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete” meaning separate, rather than “discreet” meaning private or secret.
Ramaswamy campaign staffers blame candidate for attack ad - report
Amid the bipartisan backlash against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, for running an attack ad against his Democratic rival in the Ohio governor race, Amy Acton, which features Acton’s estranged mother, Ramaswamy campaign staffers are blaming the candidate for the ad, Axios correspondent Marc Caputotold MS Now on Friday.
“From what we understand at Axios, Ramaswamy was the one who wanted the ad and his campaign didn’t,” Caputo said. “So what they did is, they wanted to show him that it wasn’t popular. And nowadays when you test an ad, you send people an email or a text message with a copy of the ad for them to rate it. Someone saw that ad; they got polled. They screen-capped it, screen-recorded and published it online, and it just got the most negative reception I’ve seen in a very long time.”

At Florida rally, Trump again shows CNN video on his support from Maga Republicans
Before Donald Trump finished his remarks in Florida, he took a moment to show supporters one of his favorite clips – part of a segment from CNN, in which the network’s chief data analyst, Harry Enten, discussed the fact that recent polling shows Trump’s support among self-described “Maga Republicans” had only declined from 99% to 98% since 2024.
Given that Maga Republicans are people who define themselves as supporters of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, that is perhaps unsurprising. What Trump failed to mention is that the same CNN analyst has more recently tracked the sharp decline in Trump’s support among Republicans, and the broader public.
Donald Trump touted the justice department lawsuit that attempts to block the Senate race certification in Alaska, if the incumbent Republican that he has endorsed there loses. “I’m the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters ahead of a campaign rally in Florida. More here
Without evidence, the president claimed that Daniel J Sullivan, the retired schoolteacher and registered Republican running against the incumbent GOP senator Daniel S Sullivan,was “put up” by Democrats to siphon the vote against the Trump-endorsed candidate. A reminder that both Sullivans (no relation to one another)will be competing against Mary Peltola, the former Democratic congresswoman, who is currently leading in many polls against the incumbent Sullivan.
Earlier, Trump doubled down on his support for Vivek Ramaswamy’s widely condemned ad that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent in the Ohio governor’s race,Amy Acton. “If my mother said bad things about me, do you think the Democrats would put it up? I think so, but my mother thought I was wonderful,” Trump said in response to Monica Alba, a reporter from NBC News.
Outside the White House on Friday, Trump scolded Alba, the reporter who followed up with questions about Acton’s childhood, and whether that changed the president’s perspective on the ad. “You’re a horrible little reporter, aren’t you?” Trump said, while continuing to ignore the myriad questions about the number of Republicans who have disavowed the ad. A reminder that Acton was removed from her mother’s care when she was 12, after her stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her. Her mother, Donna Arthur, fled the state with her husband, before his trial, and remained married to him until his death in 2004.

As we bring you the news about the justice department lawsuit against Alaska, that Donald Trump said he ordered, the president doubled down on his baseless claims that the ballot for US Senate Alaska is an attempt to confuse voters.
A reminder that there are two Dan Sullivans up for election in the pivotal race. Dan S Sullivan, the Trump-backed Republican incumbent, will face Dan J Sullivan, the retired schoolteacher who is also a registered Republican. On stage, Trump suggested again, without evidence, that this is a move orchestrated to boost Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee.
“So the Democrats maybe here they’re not so dumb … It’s cheating like hell, but it’s not the dumbest thing in the world,” Trump said.
Susan Collins announces tariff exemptions on Canadian products ahead of competitive re-election race in Maine
Susan Collins, the vulnerable Republican senator in Maine vying for a sixth term in office, said that she had secured additional tariffs exemptions on Canadian products that are crucial to her state’s agricultural industries.
“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said in a statement. “In my repeated conversations with ambassador [Jamieson] Greer, secretary [Howard] Lutnick, and other senior administration officials, I have asked for tariff relief for these important products.”
Collins has positioned herself as a moderate Republican, comfortable breaking with Donald Trump, and touted the millions in federal funds she’s directed back to Maine as chair of the powerful Senate appropriations committee.
Throughout campaigning the GOP incumbent has distanced herself from many of the administration’s unpopular policies – particularly in a state that Trump has lost in the past three presidential elections.
In one of the Senate debates against her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, Collins said she has been “the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada”.
“Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friend,” she said.
Today, Collins said that she will “continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada”.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report that the administration was expected to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a bid to help Collins in the final stretch of the campaigning.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Labour has got the message – developing nations suffer most from bond market turmoil | Heather Stewart
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
From Washington to Paris, London to Tokyo, policymakers in every large economy have been counting the costs of bond market turmoil in recent weeks. But the brunt of the pain is being borne by heavily indebted developing countries that have little hope of influencing the whims of global investors, but pay the price regardless.
Markets have responded to the war in the Middle East, and a spendthrift White House, by dumping government bonds – driving up borrowing costs just about everywhere.
Finance ministers and central bankers gathering in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank may be loth to point the finger at Donald Trump’s regime, but all are at least in part hostage to the US president’s war plans.
That has made what was already a perilous situation even worse – just as the world is battling an energy crisis, and as developing countries urgently need to invest in adapting to the climate emergency.
Even before the latest market gyrations, experts calculated that debt servicing costs absorbed 45% of government revenues in the global south, and 70% in low-income countries. That crowds out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future.
There have been growing demands for reform of the framework for international debt in recent years, including from African Union heads of state, and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa.
The G20 – the forum in which Gordon Brown coordinated a global fiscal stimulus package in the depths of the financial crisis in spring 2009 – is meant to be an important body for discussing international economic issues. With a much wider membership than the G7, it has coordinated previous efforts on debt, including establishing the IMF-administered Common Framework, to which struggling countries can apply, and suspending repayments for hard-hit borrowers during the Covid crisis.
However, this year’s chair has been Trump’s US, which has placed much more emphasis on other aspects of the G20’s remit, including promoting global economic growth – somewhat ironically, given the main obstacle to achieving it is the war on Iran.
Next year, the presidency falls to the UK, and Labour has made clear it will have different priorities. These will include seeking a global agreement on AI regulation, which seems a faint hope but is clearly worth pursuing.
The UK also intends to put unsustainable debt on the agenda. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who will be in Bangkok, told Labour conference delegates last month: “Friends, I promise this. We will use our G20 presidency next year to meet our responsibilities and mobilise the world, building on the great achievements on debt and development of the last Labour government.”
He was referring to 2005, when Brown and Tony Blair rode the vociferous Make Poverty History movement to the Gleneagles G8 summit and beyond, securing significant debt relief for more than 30 countries.
As the development minister, Kirsty McNeill, herself a veteran of that campaign, said recently, the circumstances now are very different, for two reasons. First, she said, “we’re now dealing with private creditors – the debt isn’t held by us. So that is quite a big shift.” And second, she suggested it was harder now to delineate a group of countries clearly deserving of support.
“There isn’t this really clear demarcation between the very poor world and the very rich world that was true when I was starting out, and it was just a much starker and therefore more readily told story because the antagonists and the protagonists were just much clearer,” she told an event at the Labour conference.
Yet she and other ministers have made clear they are open to proposals – and ready to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind making progress on this formidable challenge.
One ambitious plan drawn up by the thinktank Development Finance International (DFI) and shared with the government would involve 27 of the most heavily burdened countries being given a 10-year “holiday” during which their debt service costs would be slashed to below 10% of their revenues.
Implemented by cutting interest rates and extending loan terms rather than writing off debt altogether, the $13bn-a-year cost would fall primarily on private creditors – which might have to be coaxed, cajoled, perhaps even legislated into taking part, as in previous debt relief initiatives.
The “hope initiative” also envisages potential relief for another six small island developing states that do not meet the threshold on the basis of their debt burden but are regularly battered by natural disasters. These could be offered a five-year “holiday” from the moment of the next extreme weather event they face, at the cost of a further $700m a year.
An even more expansive version would embrace another five countries, including Pakistan and Angola.
Crucially, because the international financial institutions – including the IMF and the World Bank – tend to be preferred creditors, only chipping in when other help is exhausted, the costs to them would be relatively low.
Echoing Andy Burnham’s slogan – so far confined to the domestic sphere – Matthew Martin, DFI’s executive director and the author of the plan, says: “Let’s bring hope back to the poorest countries in the world, through an ambitious but financially and politically feasible initiative, which will free up $13bn for them to spend on their climate and development goals.”
It remains to be seen how bold the government is prepared to be in setting its G20 agenda, but the groundwork is being done.
Labour trashed its reputation as a champion for international development when Keir Starmer took the axe to aid spending to pay for defence. Perhaps 2027 could be the year Burnham starts to rebuild it.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: A decade of magical thinking since Brexit has taught me that it’s always OK to hope for better | Zoe Williams
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
However sunny your disposition, it wears you down, 10 straight years of being asked to accept facts about Brexit that aren’t true: 52% as an “overwhelming majority”; a flaky, half-baked referendum as the endpoint of purest democracy; the severance of a complicated trading and geopolitical relationship that took decades to build as the dawn of a new prosperity. All such nonsense, all delivered with such conviction, by such a wide variety of sources, many of them self-describing as impartial, that in the end you just surrender to it. None of it magically becomes true, don’t be silly. It’s more that you come to accept that everyone else talks nonsense now.
Nobody get too excited – just because Andy Burnham has reopened a debate that upside-down world said couldn’t be reopened, it doesn’t mean the UK is on the brink of coming to its senses. I have no idea what’s going to happen; all I can say for certain is that times have changed more than I realised. The pro-Brexit crew have updated their arguments. They no longer say leaving the EU will bring untold riches, and they never even namecheck all the control we were meant to have taken back. They rarely mention any immigration benefits because that unwieldy issue now has a life of its own – or, to put that more simply, it turns out that in or out of the European Union, we can still fight about our borders like rats in a sack.
Instead, they have a new narrative, and these are its contours. Remain sympathisers are apparently very divided. Some of us want freedom of movement, especially for young people, while others of us just want our trading relationships rebuilt with our nearest gigantic market. Different remainers again wish for greater collaboration on security and defence with nations who share our values. Those who can be trusted, for example, to oppose Vladimir Putin and his war of aggression, rather than opposing him on a Tuesday and calling him a great guy by Thursday. Some of us just miss the days when we made coherent, continent-wide decisions about the climate emergency. Given that degrees of global heating observe no nationality and pick no favourites, given that people who believe in scientific evidence tend to get on quite well together, however stark that evidence is, it would be quite relaxing to club together, no?
All these different interest groups, I’ve heard it said by those who defend the status quo, can cooperate from a distance, but sooner or later, the remain coalition will fall apart. Here, I rediscover the certainty I thought I’d lost for ever in the post-2016 melee: there is absolutely no way will we fall apart. We are a match made in heaven. I have a fair idea which of those issues I care about the most, between climate, young people, defence and trade, but seriously, this is like choosing my favourite song on Surfer Rosa (the Pixies album), or adjudicating my favourite guest at the wedding of, say, my sister. In the joy of the moment, my preferences could take a backseat. I’d really just want everyone to have a good time.
There’s one other new rhetorical strain: Brexit supporters point to Europe and say, that place is on fire. It’s not a blip caused by arson-happy French protesters, nor the housing-impoverished Spanish, it’s not a peculiarity of new German political movements, nor rage at the policing tactics of the Portuguese. Everyone, everywhere, is absolutely furious. Would this not be a good time to keep our distance? This might be the weakest argument of all, since all it underscores is that the cost of living crisis affects us all; the wars in Ukraine and Iran have hit everyone; the long tail of the financial crash and subsequent austerity has left no one unscathed; the disfigurement of the housing market was only temporarily a London thing, a Madrid thing – sooner or later, it would be an everywhere thing, and later’s where we are. There is no isolationist course that protects you from civic unrest, unless you can miraculously protect yourself from the conditions driving it. And those conditions were not made in Strasbourg.
Again, if a decade of magical thinking has taught me anything, it’s that predictions are futile, and however absurd an argument looks, you can’t bank on toppling it. But these fresh lines are so weak it’s almost endearing.
Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Briton threatened with deportation from Sweden over Brexit rules goes into hiding
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A seriously ill British man living in Sweden has been forced into hiding amid fears he will be deported as a result of what he says is a government Brexit residency error.
Mark Smith, 60, who has had heart attacks, strokes, severe headaches and chronically high blood pressure that has been difficult to treat, was told on the phone he should leave Sweden by 17 October as he was an “alien” without permission to stay.
Terrified of deportation, he and his wife have moved out of their home in Falkenberg, in south-west Sweden, to a caravan park. “We are in hiding, we daren’t go back to our apartment. We are scared to go out as we don’t know if the police will come and take us,” Smith said.
A court ruled on 12 October that a decision on deportation would not be suspended but gave him until 20 October to “submit his application for a retrial” in relation to “the grounds for the decision on indefinite deportation”.
Smith has been in Sweden since 2017 and says he was told by authorities he did not need to do anything to stay after Brexit in 2020. He worked, had private health insurance, supported his wife and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority, as required under Swedish rules.
He was unaware, however, that Sweden was among 13 of the 27 EU member states that required Britons living in the country before Brexit to make a formal application to remain. Other countries, such as Spain, did not opt for that system and just required Britons to declare they were a resident.
Smith said: “I asked the tax authorities three times on different occasions if I had to do anything because of Brexit and they said no, telling me I had to wait for five years to apply for permanent residency.
“Because it was the tax authority, a government body, I took it for granted that what they told me was correct,” he added.
David Milstead, a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights activist working through the Brits in Sweden group, said Smith’s case was typical of many Britons living in Sweden.
Milstead said: “Mark’s experience is far from unusual. I have encountered many British citizens who actively sought information from the Swedish authorities about their residence rights after Brexit, only to receive vague, unhelpful answers, sometimes being told that they needed to do nothing.”
They include the 78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas, whose husband also inquired about Brexit residency and was told by the tax authorities there was nothing to do, and who is now fighting a removal order.
Smith had a minor heart attack on Wednesday night but wanted his situation publicised because he said the British government needed to know what was happening to expats in Sweden, “not just to me but others”.
His wife, Petra, said his health conditions had left him so vulnerable she was not sure “if he will last until Christmas”.
She said: “He has been told he can’t drive, he can’t fly – what do they expect him to do? Get up and walk to England? Come on, Sweden, we need to step back from all of this and be better.”
After 12 years together, she said deportation would be devastating for her and her 15-year-old son who has special needs, who Smith co-parents. “It is wrong what they are doing, I feel ashamed to be Swedish. What they are doing is racist to British people,” Petra said.
Milstead said Smith’s case was “depressingly familiar” and should warrant the urgent attention of the European Commission, which has previously said Sweden was not breaking any laws.
“A gentleman with Mark’s serious health conditions should not be having to fight deportation. It is difficult to understand how the European Commission has concluded that Sweden’s treatment of late applications under the [Brexit] withdrawal agreement does not warrant a challenge,” he said.
“Sweden stands out so starkly from other EU countries, and there are serious questions that remain unanswered, particularly about proportionality and the treatment of vulnerable people. These are precisely the kinds of cases where the protections of the withdrawal agreement ought to matter most.”
The Scandinavian country has found itself under mounting pressure over its approach to the withdrawal agreements having deported 458 Britons, including one man who had been in the country since he was 10 years old, and a 65-year-old man married to a Swede with no family or property in the UK.
Sweden has also issued removal orders to a man with dementia who is in 24-hour care and who has been in the country for 25 years.
Under the legally binding treaty, it was agreed governments would communicate the Brexit residency rules, consider late applications on reasonable grounds, and exercise “proportionate” decisions including in the case of vulnerable people.
Smith’s troubles began in 2021 when he started to get ill and applied for sickness benefit. He was told by officials that he should have applied for post-Brexit residency. The couple immediately did so; they recall making the application at the end of 2021, in time for Sweden’s 31 December 2021 deadline.
They waited more than two years to hear back and when they did it was a rejection on the grounds that they were not married and therefore did not have a family connection to merit his residency in Sweden.
They were married in 2023 and had been living together since 2017.
It is not clear if Smith applied for the specific Brexit residency or through the usual immigration route, an important difference and one that may not have been made clear to British protected by the withdrawal agreement. Family connections are not a criteria under free movement rights, which apply to any individual regardless of marital status, so campaigners believe they have a strong case.
Smith said: “We were so much in love, we lived together, we did everything together, even now we hold hands walking down the streets. We wanted to get married, we wanted to do it the right way. I wanted to ask Petra’s father for permission and have him give her away, but two weeks after he gave me permission to marry his daughter, he passed.
“So we were looking into marriage but things just kept happening. But we don’t understand why this matters.”
They also said they had not been given the full court paperwork from the first case appealing against the migration agency’s decision, so they appealed to a higher courtwithout the full arguments against them.
After speaking to a judge this week, Petra has had assurances that all the paperwork will be sent to them by post, but they feel angry that they were not apprised of the information that the migration agency was arguing before the courts.
Sweden’s migration agency has said there is no evidence Sweden has taken an extreme approach to the withdrawal agreement.
The UK Foreign Office has raised concerns about Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement with the European Commission on numerous occasions, but has been told Sweden is not breaching the agreement.
A spokesperson said: “We are in touch with Mr Smith and are providing consular support. We know this is a distressing and challenging time for those concerned and we are urgently raising the situation with both the Swedish authorities and the European Commission.”
The Foreign Office welcomed a statement by Sweden’s former migration minister Johan Forssell in August that Sweden would examine “additional measures” that would address the issue of Brexit deportation, and a similar declaration by Magdalena Andersson, who is on track to form the new government.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Rubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political change
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying “now is the time” moments after Donald Trump told a Friday rally for candidates in south Florida that US warships could intervene in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.
The US secretary of state, in his social media post addressed “to those who seek to create positive change”, urged Cubans to capitalize on Trump’s plans. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said.
The top US diplomat, whose parents left Cuba for the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete”, meaning separate, rather than “discreet”, meaning private or secret.
Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days before midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the US war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.
“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”
Havana on Friday mocked the “desperation” of the US following the comments made by Rubio and Trump.
“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban deputy foreign minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.
“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”
Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.
In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of US military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it”.
Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba had been a national security threat for years because of its ties to US adversaries and that Trump was intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wanted to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the US could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.
Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a 29 September interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.
“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.
“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”
Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the US side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.
During his address to the United Nations general assembly last month, Trump said Rubio – son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership – was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.
Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal”, adding: “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”
Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.
Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk , and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have immigrated, many to the United States.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.
The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.
Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.
As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.
Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.
Trump the deal-maker
Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.
But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.
The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.
“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.
But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.
“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.
In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.
As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward
Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.
“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.
His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”
If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.

That’s the number of trees Mumbai’s municipal authorities authorised to be felled over five months this year, to make way for development works, according to the Indian Express. Of these, about 3,500 will be permanently removed, while the rest will be replanted elsewhere.
Vibe check
Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.
“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Britain stands behind Zelenskyy, says Streeting after Trump’s call for new leader in Ukraine
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Britain stands behind Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the defence secretary has said, after Donald Trump called for the Ukrainian president to be replaced and the US announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel.
Wes Streeting said Ukrainians alone should be able to decide who leads their country as he indicated Trump was facing domestic political pressure over fuel prices before next month’s midterm elections.
Asked on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether Britain supported Zelenskyy staying in office, Streeting said: “We are in no doubt that the aggressor here was Vladimir Putin. He is the person who chose to start this war. He is the person who could end this war tomorrow, and he chooses not to. So, we stand with Ukraine. We stand with President Zelenskyy.”
Trump said on Saturday that Ukraine should get a new leader capable of reaching a peace agreement, accusing Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for increasing American diesel prices.
Zelenskyy condemned the diesel agreement as a gift to Putin, warning that increased Russian energy revenues would help finance the war against Ukraine.
Trump has been facing rising political pressure over the economic fallout from the war with Iran, which has driven up global energy prices weeks before Americans vote in the midterm elections.
Soaring fuel costs have hit Americans and added to wider inflation, damaging Trump’s standing with voters. The squeeze is felt particularly in agricultural states such as Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio where farmers depend on diesel to operate machinery and transport their produce.
These traditionally Republican-leaning states battling rising cost of living pressures will create a headache for Trump, whose party is trying to hold on to its majorities.
Streeting told Sky News on Sunday: “Let’s be candid about this: midterms are coming up, cost of living is an issue. No doubt President Trump is feeling the same pressure that lots of leaders are facing in terms of wanting to ease cost of living pressures, energy prices.
“I think it’s just a political reality, isn’t it? We would obviously prefer a stronger approach on sanctions.”
Streeting sought to avoid a deeper public confrontation with Washington, insisting Britain’s priority was to maintain western unity. “Let’s not overstate the impact of President Trump’s decision on purchasing oil from Russia and let’s not also understate US support for Ukraine,” he said.
In a phone call with Zelenskyy on Saturday, Andy Burnham, the prime minister, restated his “complete solidarity” with Ukraine.
Downing Street said the leaders had agreed to meet in person in the coming days. Burnham has also pledged to strengthen sanctions against Russia, while both called for an immediate energy ceasefire.
Gen Sir Richard Barrons, one of the authors of Britain’s strategic defence review, warned that Trump’s Russian diesel deal would lead to more Ukrainian deaths by helping Moscow fund its war.
He told Sky News that money from Russian oil and gas was used to pay for the “missiles and drones that it fires at Ukraine”. Asked if the deal would mean more Ukrainians being killed, he said “for sure”, adding that security interests were being “sacrificed on the altar of an election”.
Meanwhile, Streeting said Britain was not currently considering offensive military operations against the Houthis, after an attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh, Saudi’s capital, killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others.
Streeting said he had been discussing further military assistance with Saudia Arabia, and he declined to categorically rule out future involvement. Asked on the BBC whether Britain could join US offensive operations, he said: “That’s not what we’re looking at, at this stage,” insisting there was no military solution to the conflict.
The defence secretary described the overnight attack as a “shocking escalation” and said the UK was already providing air-to-air refuelling and ground-based air defence support.
Streeting said he had spoken to his Saudi counterpart on several occasions in recent weeks about what further support Britain could provide. “I think there is clearly more to do, as evidenced by what we saw last night,” he said.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Democrats rebuke federal raid of Ilhan Omar’s home: ‘rogue abuse of power’
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Ilhan Omar’s Democratic colleagues have condemned federal agents’ search of the Minnesota congresswoman’s home on Monday morning, describing it as “deeply disturbing” and emblematic of the Trump administration’s “corrupt weaponization” of the US government.
House Democratic leaders, including minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, party whip Katherine Clark and caucus chair Pete Aguilar, issued a joint statement excoriating the president for the search.
“The Trump administration’s raid on congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against [the president’s] adversaries,” their statement said.
“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations. Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected member of Congress and her family.”
The Democratic leaders vowed to “deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power” from the US Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, the latter of which oversees immigration enforcement.
Citing unnamed sources “close to the investigation”, Fox News – which is typically friendly with the Trump administration – reported that the search on Omar’s home pertained to a criminal fraud investigation concerning her immigration paperwork. Omar’s late father filled out that paperwork when Omar, a Somali-born, naturalized US citizen, was a child.
California representative Ro Khanna also condemned Monday’s search, saying: “It is simply chilling that they are targeting political opponents this way, and it is disturbing that they are targeting Muslim Americans and a Muslim American legislator. Any decent American needs to stand up and speak out.”
Sydney Kamlager-Dove, Khanna’s fellow Democrat and California representative, called the search “fascism in the extreme”.
“This is an unadulterated abuse of power,” Kamlager-Dove said. “Trump is weaponizing the federal government to escalate his racist attacks against [representative] Omar, undermine her ahead of the midterms [on 3 November], and distract from his failures as president.”
Pramila Jayapal, a Democratic House member from Washington state, similarly called the search of Omar’s home a “disgusting abuse of power from an out of control president” facing widespread public disapproval from high living costs amid the war in Iran that he helped start alongside Israel in February.
“To use federal law enforcement resources to raid the home of a sitting Member of Congress weeks before an election is a dangerous sign of an authoritarian president who will stop at nothing to distract you from his deep unpopularity with the American people,” Jayapal added.
Jayapal’s statement alluded to years of unsubstantiated rumors from Trump and others about Omar and her family, including the accusation that her ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is in fact her brother – and that the marriage was part of an effort to earn him immigration status. Omar has denied those rumors.
The Illinois representative Delia C Ramirez called for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to be dismantled. Omar “has not backed down, so now they are using DHS and the federal government to target and persecute her”, Ramirez said in a post on X.
“This is an absolute abuse of power and unacceptable. We must strip them of their weapons. We must dismantle DHS.”
Similarly, Greg Casar, a Democratic representative from Texas, wrote that the Trump administration is targeting Omar “because he thinks it’ll help his [Republican] party” during the midterms, when it is expected to lose seats in Congress.
“Ilhan Omar stands up and won’t let Trump do whatever he wants to our country,” Casar said. “It’s up to us to do the same.”
The Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the US’s largest Muslim civil rights organization, also spoke out against the search of Omar’s home, saying: “We strongly condemn this unconscionable raid on her home for what it is: an obvious act of political persecution.”
Criticizing the Trump administration’s handling of files pertaining to Jeffrey Epstein’s child sex-trafficking network as well as the president’s pardons for those who attacked the US Capitol in early 2021, Cair said the justice department “could clearly [not] care less about fighting crime and is instead focused on conducting a witch hunt”.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Judge rebuffs Trump DoJ’s bid to force California to set aside 20,000 ballots
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A federal judge declined to order California election officials to segregate and not count ballots from people the Trump administration claimed were non-citizens, rebuffing a legally thin request from the justice department that appeared designed to cast doubt over the results of the midterms.
The ruling from US district judge David Carter, nominated to the federal bench by Bill Clinton, comes about two weeks after the justice department delivered a USB drive to election officials in Los Angeles and Sacramento that it said contained the names of 20,000 non-citizens on the state’s voter rolls. There are more than 23 million registered voters in California and non-citizen voting is extremely rare.
“This case is about the right of every American citizen to vote in a free and fair election,” Carter wrote in his Wednesday evening ruling. “Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”
“In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign,” Carter continued. “But California and its people are sovereign, too.”
The justice department gave officials just 48 hours to review the list and said it would sue the state if officials did not sequester ballots from those whose citizenship it could not confirm. The department refused to provide more details about its methodology and Los Angeles officials found preliminary indicators the list was inaccurate. The justice department then sued California on 15 October to try and force the state to sequester the ballots and verify citizenship.
If the justice department’s request were granted, Carter wrote, it would likely violate a 1993 law that requires states to strike ineligible voters from its official lists no later than 90 days before an election.
California election officials have said they cannot verify the citizenship of those on the agency’s list before election day. Carter chastised the justice department’s directive as risking the disenfranchisement of thousands of voters. “A ballot segregated, in effect, would be a ballot removed,” Carter wrote.
The justice department separately has threatened to prosecute election officials in the state if they tabulate ballots from non-citizens. Such a move would be without a legal basis, Sam Trepel, a former prosecutor at the justice department, wrote in a blogpost this month. After filing the lawsuit, the Trump administration began providing lists to other counties of suspected non-citizen voters. When election officials began reviewing them, they found the department had flagged voters who were not on the rolls and had provided insufficient information to verify their citizenship status, according to CalMatters.
Carter’s ruling came after the justice department tried to bypass him entirely. After Carter set a 27 October hearing on the justice department’s emergency motion, the department took the unusual step of appealing to the US court of appeals for the ninth circuit, saying Carter was not considering the case fast enough. A panel of ninth circuit judges ruled 2-1 against the justice department earlier this week.
Legal experts have been skeptical about the justice department’s efforts in California since the outset. In July, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced it had identified up to 190,000 non-citizens on California voter rolls. The DHS did not provide more details to the state until after ballots had already gone out in the state.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Carter wrote in his Wednesday opinion. “This Court declines to be a party to such process.”
Uwa Ede-Osifo contribued reporting

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”
Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.
Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.
She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”
Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.
“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”
Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.
Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.
The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”
Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.
Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.
“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”
Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.
In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”
Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Abdul El-Sayed’s Republican rival Mike Rogers
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, in an extraordinary rebuke of her party’s nominee on the eve of the midterm elections.
Her endorsement came in a video posted to X after she attended an event with Rogers at the predominantly Black Perfecting church in Detroit on Sunday. Stevens’s endorsement was the culmination of an escalating feud between the former primary rivals – primarily over support for Israel – that has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests of the cycle.
The endorsement was met with immediate pushback from Democrats, who condemned Stevens for her “betrayal”.
Michigan’s Democratic party chair Curtis Hertel said: “Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers – a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda – shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about. We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us.”
Some of the people who worked for Stevens’s campaign also reportedly quit following her Rogers endorsement. Her long-time chief of staff, Justin German, and her communications director, Logan Basch, were among those who left, according to CNN correspondent Manu Raju.
German later released a statement on behalf of Stevens’ campaign team endorsing El-Sayed: “As Haley Stevens’ Chief of staff for eight years, I speak on behalf of our team in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate. This election is too important to sow division or stand on the sidelines. We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’ decision to support Mike Rogers.”
Fallout over Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers continued Sunday, with figures from the progressive left stepping up to back El-Sayed.
Bernie Sanders joined the controversy, attacking Stevens for what Democrats view as an extraordinary betrayal after Stevens accepted El-Sayed’s narrow victory over her in Michigan’s Democrat senate primaries.
“Rep. Haley Stevens’ staff is right to resign in disgust,” Sanders posted on X. “They understand that the election in Michigan is far more important than Haley’s fragile ego and that all of us must stand together to elect Abdul, defeat Rogers and end the Republican rubber-stamp control of the Senate.”
Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, said Stevens had “betrayed” working class people “by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against”.
In his first public comments since Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers, El-Sayed told reporters at a press conference outside of a rally he held on Sunday, the very same rally that Stevens had earlier been disinvited from attending, “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.” He added, “I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.
“If you are somebody who believes that we should stand up to hate, and you have watched this last campaign, I think we probably would not want to support Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and JD Vance,” he said.
But Stevens’s political pivot earned her praise from Donald Trump, someone whose policies she has an entire page on her website dedicated to denouncing.
Trump, during his rally in Iowa, heaped praise on Stevens for turning against El-Sayed, urging her to join the GOP. “It was an incredible thing,” Trump said. “I’d love her to join the Republican party. I think that could happen.”
Stevens had lost by a close margin in this year’s primary, and for months had refused to openly campaign for El-Sayed, as had his other opponent Mallory McMorrow. But top Democrats had brokered the truce between El-Sayed and Stevens. After the two had sparred viciously in the primary campaign Stevens extended him a tepid endorsement, and this weekend was scheduled to join El-Sayed at a predominantly Black church in Detroit’s North End.
Those plans have quickly unraveled over an issue that divided Stevens and El-Sayed perhaps more than any other: Israel.
Later last week, Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, made clear that her appearance alongside El-Sayed was preconditioned on his denouncing of an outside group’s campaign ad that had blamed US support of Israel for the rising cost of living. El-Sayed declined the request, accusing Stevens of needlessly reopening debates from a settled primary.
As the vicious political firestorm has unfolded, Democratic commentators have also pointed out that Stevens’s fiance, Jason Turkish, has been condemning El-Sayed publicly while supporting Rogers. Turkish, who is also vocally pro-Israel, has donated heavily to Democrats in the past, but this year also donated to Republican candidates including Susan Collins.
California governor Gavin Newsom said on the political talkshow 2WAY that Stevens “went another 180 degrees overnight, so something was going on there”.
“She’s been successful at taking our eye off the ball and that’s why I understand party leadership condemning it ... This may be curiously the October surprise of sorts,” he added.
Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer also responded negatively to the endorsement. Schumer’s campaign account called it a “despicable betrayal” from Stevens in a statement, but continued to push for unity among Democrats.
“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors. We Democrats equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans. These attacks are evidence of the total bankruptcy of the Republican Party today, who resort to ugly and un-American fearmongering because they have nothing to offer on the problems that concern people today.”
