SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Andy Bloke appears vaguely normal on Gogglebox – but Kemi dodged a bullet
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
On nights like this a man can feel like he’s slipped through the looking-glass. I’m sitting on the sofa watching the TV, poised to make some gags about the prime minister and the mayor of Liverpool, who are themselves sitting on a sofa at No 10, poised to make some gags about what they are watching on TV.
Life doesn’t get more meta. The saving grace is that this episode of Gogglebox is a charity special for Stand Up to Cancer. Andy Burnham has requested that any journalist writing about the programme makes a donation to SU2C. I’m happy to oblige. Cancer is costing me a great deal more than money.
Meet Andy Bloke and his best mate, Steve Bloke. Two career politicians who still manage to look and sound vaguely normal. Not totally normal, mind. In real life, Steve Bloke would have said to Andy Bloke: “This is a total shithole you’re living in.” And Andy Bloke would have replied: “I know. It’s been a complete tip since Boris was here. You can’t get rid of the stains.”
You can’t deny that Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke are naturals at this. Not so bland that you want to turn off, a genuine connection with one another and a sense of fun that can’t be faked. Kemi Badenoch is reportedly annoyed she wasn’t invited on the programme.
The reality is that she’s dodged a bullet. Kemi just doesn’t have the woman of the people shtick. It’s something you’ve either got or you haven’t and she really doesn’t. If you let her on Gogglebox the only laugh you would get from her would be if she was livestreaming an execution from the US.
Mind you, it’s a slow burn. At first Andy and Steve look like they are feeling their way into the programme. But then so do the other celebs, Joe Lycett and his aunties, Stanley Tucci and his wife, Felicity, and Paul Whitehouse and Lenny Rush. The bantz feels a bit contrived and Andy Bloke – a Cambridge English grad – fails to recognise a photo of Margaret Atwood.
If Steve Bloke had been more on the ball, he’d have taken the piss mercilessly. But Andy and Steve are nothing if not a team. They’ve got each other’s backs and bond over filling in the blanks on members of the royal household in Only Connect.
“The king will be pleased with me at our next weekly meeting,” says Andy Bloke. He probably will be. I suspect Camilla will have made Charles watch this. The Man of the People meets the King of the People.
Halfway through, we get a reminder that this isn’t all about the laughs. There is the story of Callum who died at the age of 16 from brain cancer. Then the story of a woman whose mother died of pancreatic cancer when she was 11, was diagnosed with cervical cancer shortly after her child was born and whose husband died of bowel cancer a week after diagnosis. Sometimes shit really does happen to good people. All the celebs were fighting back tears. Andy was no exception.
“I’d like to see Match of the Day,” says Paul Whitehouse. “Why? To hear how crap Spurs are?” Lenny joked. Careful, Lenny, careful. We might be past the watershed but it’s still way too early for gags about Spurs.
But some football would have been nice. Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke would have been in their element. You could have made an entire programme of the pair of them pissing themselves laughing as Manchester United were beaten 4-1 by Como in the Champions League. It might even have earned a Bafta nomination.
For some reason, Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke were excluded from watching an X-rated natural history about some young birds that haven’t yet learned to fly and are so dim that they literally just stand there as tortoises eat them alive. Well, not all. One bird managed to hop on top of a tortoise shell. Though not before the tortoise had taken a chunk out of a wing. A happy ending of sorts. The celebs couldn’t quite believe they were being forced to watch such ultra-violence.
Normal service was resumed with a mercifully brief excerpt from Strictly Come Dancing. Brief because none of the real celebs had any idea who the celebrity contestants were. Andy Bloke admitted he still had PTSD from watching Ed Balls crashing around the dancefloor. Steve Bloke wisely helped himself to another beer. Maybe this was the way they used to do business when Andy Bloke was also a mayor.
We ended on an upbeat note. The Celebrity Traitors. Steve Bloke had no idea what was going on so Andy Bloke tried to fill him in as they cracked up over some crisps, pork scratchings and Skips. Me neither. I guess that was one were you had to be in the room.
“You should be quite good at this,” Andy Bloke said, encouragingly. “You can generally spot the wrong ’un in the room.” I guess that depends on how often you’ve been in the same room as Michael Gove.
Claudia Winkleman was announcing that the murder would be done in plain sight by boring a Faithful to death. Steve Bloke had the solution. Just make them watch the proceedings in the House of Commons. Boom boom.
Neither Steve nor Andy Bloke had much to say about Ross Kemp’s worrying levels of paranoia or Jerry Hall’s complete charisma bypass. How do you bore someone who is already boring? That could have been a question for Only Connect. Maybe we had come full circle. Or perhaps their gags about Rupert Murdoch got cut in the editing suite.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Epstein files take back seat in midterms but experts say issue has not gone away
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
As US voters head to the polls for crucial and fraught midterm elections, some survivors’ advocates in the Jeffrey Epstein investigation have expressed concern that the scandal could recede into the background.
Political experts believe, however, the Epstein issue is not going away permanently and that many voters can balance day-to-day concerns such as affordability and AI with the scandal involving the late financier and accused sex trafficker whose social circle was widespread among America’s elite.
“My greatest concern is not that the public will forget Jeffrey Epstein, but that the politicians and institutions responsible for accountability will use the chaos of world events as an excuse to move on,” said Spencer Kuvin of Goldlaw, who has represented multiple Epstein survivors.
Kuvin added: “Wars, economic crises and political controversies may dominate the headlines, but they do not erase the suffering of the victims or the unanswered questions about how Epstein and his powerful associates were allowed to operate for decades.
“Justice should not have an expiration date, and it certainly should not be dictated by the news cycle. We cannot allow the Epstein scandal to become yesterday’s news simply because today’s headlines are more urgent.”
Kuvin called for the US government to continue releasing Epstein files – which many have said were excluded from allegedly incomplete disclosures – and for Congress to demand accountability.
“It has been disappointing to have seen attention diverted from Jeffrey Epstein in the past year,” said Jennifer Freeman of Marsh Law, who represents numerous Epstein survivors in litigation surrounding his sexual abuse of teenage girls.
Freeman, however, expressed optimism about the long-term prospects of justice for survivors, saying: “While public attention may have shifted from the Epstein case, given the electoral cycle, I am confident it will command concentration and accountability shortly again.”
Freeman noted that she was continuing to pursue a lawsuit against the US government for alleged negligence “in repeatedly, for decades, dropping the ball on investigating and prosecuting Epstein”. She is also litigating a class-action lawsuit against his estate related to his collection and production of child sex abuse images.
Political experts said that Epstein might get less attention from campaigning politicians and voters, but that it was probably a temporary dip, not a permanent drop-off.
“It really does feel like everything is on fire. I think people can care about several things at once, but what’s directly affecting their lives tends to take priority,” Brittany Martinez, a Republican strategist who works as acting director of Principles First, said. “When they’re worried about gas prices, living costs and whether their government is working for them, that can push Epstein out of the immediate conversation.
“I don’t think the questions or the demand for answers have gone away; they’re just competing for attention. So I’d expect to hear less about it for stretches, rather than see it disappear altogether.”
“There’s just something every day with Trump,” said Shawn Donahue, clinical associate professor in the University at Buffalo’s department of political science.
For Donahue, timing also plays a key role. The US Congress has been in recess and without members on the House floor, so there’s not any discussion of the Epstein Files Transparency Act’s proposed new iteration. This bill, the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, seeks to address what advocates have said are shortfalls in the present EFTA – such as an absence of enforcement mechanisms.
“It kind of feels like whenever Congress comes back into session, this probably starts to become more of an issue again, and especially if Democrats are looking at being in control of one or maybe both chambers of Congress,” Donahue said.
Should Democrats win the house, as polls project, Donahue expects they will swiftly “put Republicans on the spot” with Epstein. “Democrats are ready to start on the investigation from day one.”
For Julie Roginsky, who co-founded the non-profit Lift Our Voices and pursued a sexual harassment lawsuit against the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes, the significance of Epstein among voters has not gone away.
“I think Epstein is part of the reason that Trump’s numbers are at record lows. I think it’s something that was one of the issues where even Maga Republicans broke with him,” Roginsky said. “I think that if Democrats do get control of at least one house of Congress this year, then starting next year, you’re going to see a lot more conversation about survivors and about Epstein.”
Congressional supporters of survivors said they would keep fighting for truth and justice.
“This is bigger than a moment. It’s a reckoning, and Americans are ready to have this conversation about power, abuse, and who gets protected,” the Democratic New Mexico representative Teresa Leger Fernández said in a statement. “Of course, Americans will vote with their pocketbooks. They’re worried about groceries, gas, and making rent. But they won’t forget that this president was Epstein’s friend and tried to hide the truth from them.
“The survivors have fought for decades to be heard. Our responsibility is to keep fighting alongside them, get the truth out, and hold those responsible accountable. That responsibility doesn’t disappear when the headlines change.”
The Massachusetts Democratic representative Ayanna Pressley said in a statement: “Justice for survivors of Epstein’s abuse has been a prominent issue amongst the electorate because people of conscience see through the cover-ups of the Trump Administration and demand accountability – that won’t change no matter how much they try to flood the zone and distract us.”
Pressley and fellow representatives Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross recently introduced legislation to address survivors’ financial burdens.
The New Mexico Democratic senator Ben Ray Luján similarly commented that whatever might be unfolding, he would keep pushing for the files to be released in full despite the Department of Justice insisting they have released all Epstein investigative files required under the law.
“We cannot lose sight of the need to release the full Epstein files, hold those responsible accountable, and ensure survivors receive the justice they deserve,” Luján said.
Asked for comment, the White House insisted Trump had advocated for survivors.
“Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein. And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him,” the White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement.
The statement then claimed that several Democrats had yet to explain why they were soliciting money and meetings from Epstein after he was a convicted sex offender.
As for the Department of Justice, the department maintains they have complied with disclosure requirements under the original EFTA. They also rejected claims by New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, that the justice department had not been helping the state’s investigation.
“The Epstein Files Transparency Act does not require, and the protective orders in place in the Southern District of New York do not permit, disclosure of victim-identifying information carte blanche, and New Mexico has provided no lawful basis to justify such sweeping disclosures,” the department said in a statement. “Protecting victim privacy remains a top priority for the Department, and neither [legal] requests nor a desire to cooperate outweighs that privacy. DOJ remains available to assist New Mexico’s investigation consistent with the law and binding court orders.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Burnham to double spending on homelessness amid drive to end rough sleeping by Christmas
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Andy Burnham is to double spending on ending rough sleeping to almost £900m by the end of the current parliament, as he steps up efforts to get people off the streets by Christmas.
The prime minister has pledged to offer every rough sleeper in England a safe route off the streets or wider support as a central part of his premiership.
As he prepared for a Downing Street summit on ending rough sleeping on Monday, Burnham said the budget would bring a further £432m commitment to helping to tackle homelessness.
The sum is on top of an initial £442m from Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government budgets that will be allocated to the problem before March 2027.
Speaking ahead of the meeting, which will bring together charities and businesses, Burnham said: “Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life. It’s a thing governments either choose to accept or don’t.
“Well, I don’t accept it. That’s why we’re doubling funding so that people aren’t just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this parliament too.
“But we can’t do it alone. If we’re going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this. So today we’re bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts.”
Burnham’s mission to end rough sleeping is already under way with just two months to go before his deadline. There are specialist outreach teams and new accommodation spaces operating in Coventry, and further provision is being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden over the coming weeks.
The additional funding is being provided in an attempt to solve the problem of rough sleeping in the longer term. As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced schemes such as A Bed Every Night to offer emergency accommodation, but while the number of rough sleepers fell, it then began to increase again.
Burnham has previously said this was because “we were the only place providing that level of support and, understandably, people then travelled to Greater Manchester to access that support”.
He has said ending rough sleeping across the country will only be possible “if all areas are pulling in the same direction, and that’s what this funding is designed to achieve”.
The prime minister’s rough sleeping summit on Monday will bring together businesses, charities, housing providers and local leaders as they attempt to create more lasting changes.
Alongside the government, other organisations are making pledges towards solving the problem, with the National Housing Federation working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.
Virgin Media O2 will provide practical digital support to frontline organisations, while the charities St Mungo’s and Haircuts4Homeless will work with L’Oréal on hair salons and wellbeing provision for those who have been sleeping rough.
Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said it was a “big ambition” and the government would “not back down from making sure everyone has the offer of a route off the streets this Christmas”.
She said: “The first step is giving people a roof over their head and freedom from the nightly struggle to find somewhere safe to sleep. But Christmas is only the beginning and that’s why we will keep working together to tackle the root causes of homelessness and end rough sleeping for good.”
The homelessness charity Shelter welcomed the announcement. Its acting CEO, Mairi MacRae, said the funding showed “the government understands that a safe home is not a privilege, it is a necessity”.
However, the Conservatives dismissed the move, with Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, accusing the government of wanting to spend too much money on ending rough sleeping.
“Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester,” she said. “Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers’ money and more empty promises.”
Referring to the chancellor, Lam said: “[John] Healey must use his budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices. Instead of piling more costs on to hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers’ money.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this summer from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Dolomites, the Italian army has said.
The devices, which included Italian artillery shells and French mortar bombs, were removed and defused by the army’s Julia Alpine brigade, according to a statement.
The weapons originated from the white war, a battle between the Austro-Hungarian army and Italian troops across treacherous and bitterly cold terrain between 1915 and 1918.
More than a century later, hikers reported several sightings of bombs during the summer, mostly in the area of Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley in eastern Trentino. The soldiers then conducted an extensive sweep there and across other high-altitude and glacier locations in the Trentino Alto Adige region of the Dolomites.
They recovered and neutralised 250 explosives, including “18 Italian 75mm artillery shells and 37 Thevetot mortar shells – a French-made device that was also supplied to the Italian royal army during the first world war”, the Julia Alpine brigade.
It is not the first time that relics of the white war have emerged from melting glaciers, whose retreat has accelerated over more than decade.
“It is very much a consequence of global heating,” said Stefano Morosini, a professor at the University of Bergamo and the coordinator of heritage projects at Stelvio national park, where some of the explosives were also found.
“In recent years, at the end of each summer, these dangerous artefacts emerge and each year there is a higher number. They have been conserved by the ice for more than 100 years. Some had already exploded but many hadn’t, so now when they re-emerge, they are very, very dangerous.”
The advice to hikers and mountaineers is to “never touch any type of explosive device you might find, regardless of where it is located” and to promptly report any discovery to police.
Fought mainly in the Dolomites of Trentino Alto-Adige and the Alps of the Lombardy region, the white war was a period of history frozen in time until the 1990s, when global heating started to reveal an assortment of perfectly preserved relics, including weapons, sledges, letters and diaries.
A wooden barracks that had been dug into a cave on the top of Mount Scorluzzo, a 3,095-metre (10,154ft) peak overlooking the Stelvio pass, reappeared in 2015 after the ice which had sealed it off for almost a century completely melted.
The shelter had been hastily locked up when the first world war ended in November 1918, and the soldiers abandoned most of their belongings. Beds made of straw as well as clothes, lanterns, newspapers, postcards, coins, and tinned food were found well preserved inside.
A white war museum to host the relics is scheduled to open in Bormio in June 2027.
The white war is thought to have claimed more than a million lives, although the majority of soldiers were believed to have been killed by avalanches, falling down mountains or hypothermia.
Dozens of corpses, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice over the past 15 years.
The relatives of an Italian soldier were able to bury him in 2017 after documents revealing his identity were found with his body on Presena glacier.
Morosini said the intense summer heat was making access to the glaciers in the Dolomites less safe. Eleven people died when a huge mass of the Marmolada glacier broke off in 2022.
“It is becoming more and more impossible to access the glaciers during the summer because of the very long heatwave at high altitude,” he said.
“If you come to the area, you can see how fast the glaciers are retreating and how strong the impact of climate change is.”

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Budget 2026: £100 energy payment for millions and rise in bank tax as watchdog warns on stalling living standards – as it happened
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
OBR: living standards forecast to rise by just 1% over whole post-Covid decade
The OBR report says RHDI (real household disposable income – one measure of living standards) is rising at a record slow rate – less than 0.1% per decade. That means, by the end of the decade, it will be just 1% higher than its pre-Covid level, it says.
Our central forecast represents a continuation of the historically weak growth in RHDI per person since the global financial crisis. Chart 2.7 shows the rolling 10-year average annual growth in RHDI per person. This slowed significantly in the aftermath of the financial crisis, due to lower growth in productivity and real wages. Growth reached a historic low over the 10 years to 2025-26, averaging just ¼ per cent a year, and we expect it to fall further in the near term. By 2029-30, our central forecast sees growth over the prior 10 years averaging less than 0.1 per cent a year. As a result, 10 years on from the onset of the pandemic, RHDI per person would be just 1 per cent higher than its pre-pandemic level.
Here are comments on the budget from a Guardian panel, comprising Polly Toynbee, Hettie O’Brien, Rohan Sathyamoorthy, Kevin Cashman, Nik, and John McDonnell.
And here is Polly’s conclusion.
Is this the “growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” Andy Burnham promises? No, not yet, not yet … Wait for his 10-year plan, spending review and an election with a new manifesto. And hope.
Jim O’Neill, the former Goldman Sachs chief economist and a Treasury minister under David Cameron, told the PM programme that he thought it was sensible for John Healey not to “rock the boat” with this budget. He said his old City friends were pleasantly surprised by what was in it.
My friends in my old world of business and investing, from the ones that have contacted me, every single one of them has been slightly positively surprised by what was announced today.
Treasury minister Torsten Bell rejects charge budget lacks 'ending 40 years of neoliberalism' ambition
Torsten Bell, the Treasury minister, has just finished an interview on Radio 4’s PM programme. Asked about claims (like this one, assuming the MP is being sarcastic, or ours at 8.50am) that the budget did not live up to Andy Burnham’s ambitions to end 40 years of neoliberalism, Bell said he did not accept that. In many areas, the government was taking a very different approach, he argued. He said Margaret Thatcher hollowed out local government, while today’s fiscal devolution roadmap will reverse that. He also said the proposals to change the way energy pricing works (see 12.50pm) would transformative.
Here is a chart from the fiscal devolution roadmap document setting out what rules will change, and when.
MSAs are mayoral strategic authorities, and FSA are foundation strategic authorities, equivalent bodies which do not have a mayor to lead them.
Minister dismisses as 'garbage' Tory and Lib Dem claims that defence spending actually being cut
A Treasury minister has dismissed as “garbage” opposition claims that the small print in the budget book shows that John Healey is actually cutting defence spending.
The budget red book says that, while £42.6bn had been set aside for MoD spending in 2027-28, that has now been revised down to £41.1bn.
The Treasury says this is because less money than expected is needed for pensions. But James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, said that not allocating the unused money for other areas of defence spending was “a complete dereliction of duty from the chancellor”.
And James MacClearly, the Lib Dem defence spokesperson, made the same argument. He said:
It is disgraceful that after pitching Labour as serious on defence, Healey and [Wes] Streeting are cutting the military’s resource budget by nearly £1bn next year. This will leave our troops worse off and undermine our security.
In response, Torsten Bell, a Treasury minister, posted this on social media.
Absolute garbage - this is a technical change that happens when public sector pension contributions change. There’s no impact on defence spending power & the Tories used the same mechanism in govt. What does matter for defence spending? The chancellor, who has increased it
Today’s ‘picky bits’ budget has pushed tough decisions into next year, says Tim Sarson, head of tax policy at KPMG UK:
“When it comes to tax rises, as expected with his options limited by the 2024 manifesto, the chancellor was left with a pick and mix or ‘picky bits’ approach.
Overall the announcements today will raise £7bn per year by 2031-32 with some winners and losers including a widely trailed bank surcharge, which came in lower than expected at 3% and further taxes on the gambling sector
James Smith, ING’s developed markets economist in the UK, says the budget has left more questions than answers.
Those questions include:
How will the government account for higher inflation in departmental budgets? How will it fund defence? Both questions were left unanswered today. The government’s overall spending pot for government departments was left largely unchanged later this decade, despite a higher path for inflation and the chancellor’s reaffirmed commitment to 3% Nato spending by 2030. Implicitly, that pledge is being funded by squeezing other areas of government; the OBR’s numbers imply real-terms cuts of 2.6% a year for unprotected departments later this decade.
That almost certainly won’t happen – and this is before you take social care or any of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s other bold policies into account.
These thorny issues have been punted into 2027, potentially in the autumn, when the government will have to unveil its long-awaited spending review.
The NewEconomicsFoundation says the budget is a missed opportunity to bring down inflation, through more ambitious cost of living measures.
They say:
The chancellor has missed an opportunity to bring down inflation rates, according to analysis from the New Economics Foundation (NEF). The research suggests a more ambitious package of cost-of-living policies would take inflation from the OBR’s projected 3.64% to 2.88% by June 2027.
But CapitalEconomics say the chancellor has done enough to keep the markets on side.
Today’s UK budget announcement has proven the non-event that newly-minted Chancellor Healey had signalled in advance. While his first budget is hardly inspiring, it contrasts favourably with the initial efforts of some of his recent predecessors.
By sticking to a gradual fiscal tightening path, and to the expectations set over the past couple of months for a muddle-through budget, Healey has probably done enough to keep the Gilt market on side for now.
We think that Gilt yields will fall over the coming year as the UK’s fiscal risk premium remains contained and the Bank of England policy takes a less hawkish path than money markets discount.
Ministerial direction needed for £6.5bn loan for Ukraine after export finance agency warns of 'exceptionally high' risk of default
The government needed to issue a ministerial direction to get UK Export Finance to approve a £3bn increase in lending for Ukraine, it emerged today. This is a procedure that happens when a civil servant judges that a decision is not justified under normal responsible public spending rules, and insists that it can only go ahead if a minister explicitly overrules the objections.
In his letter explaining the need for a ministerial direction, Tim Reid, UKEF’s chief executive, argued that this was not a core obligation for the agency (which is there to help British exporters, not to fight Russia) and that the risk of the £6.5bn not being paid back was too high.
Reid said:
UKEF has played a significant role in delivering the government’s support to Ukraine by staying on cover with £3.5bn of capacity to provide export finance, supporting strategically important transactions including the supply of nuclear fuel, reconstruction of critical infrastructure and air-defence missiles. These have supported Ukraine’s resilience at a critical time while also creating jobs and industrial capacity across the UK.
However, the financial risks associated with UKEF providing support in Ukraine remain far beyond those that we would normally be willing to accept. The probability of default and expected loss is exceptionally high …
UKEF is close to capacity against its existing £3.5bn limit. You have now asked me to consider a £3bn increase in UKEF’s cover limit, taking UKEF’s Ukraine country risk limit to £6.5bn.
In response, Jonathan Reynolds, the business secetary, said he was issuing a ministerial direction because “the United Kingdom has been steadfast in its support for Ukraine’s defence, economic resilience and long-term recovery, and I consider UKEF’s support to be an important component of that wider effort.”
OBR: Employment Rights Act will have negative impact on economy
Labour’s Employment Rights Act is likely to have a negative impact on the economy, the OBR says today.
This is the first time that the OBR has assessed the potential economic impacts of the ERA, which received royal assent at the end of last year.
And the fiscal watchdog has concluded the ERA will probably have a negative impact on potential output, though it isn’t making an explicit assessment today.
The OBR says:
Our analysis suggests that the ERA will likely have a negative economic impact from negative impacts on businesses, particularly through increased uncertainty, lost flexibility and higher labour related costs, which will more than offset any potential positive impact on worker productivity.
That fits with the government’s own analysis, which said the reforms could cost businesses up to £5bn a year.
How budget includes £10bn in extra support for Ukraine
Earlier John Healey got an endorsement for what he said about defence spending from Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general. (See 2.15pm.)
George Robertson, the former Nato secretary general and the lead author of the strategic defence review, has also welcomed Healey’s defence announcements. (See 1.30pm.) He said:
John Healey is acting in the national interest – and has done exactly what he said was needed for defence in his resignation letter, by setting a headmark for 3% in 2030.”
I am strongly in favour of innovative ways of financing defence – and this is a credible route to get more into UK defence. Today’s annoucements strengthens UK leadership in Nato once again.
In his speech Healey announced an extra £10bn in economic support for Ukraine. This Treasury news release explains where that money is going. It says:
The £10bn package includes £7bn of economic support being made available over three years, including up to £5.5bn of World Bank guarantees and a £500m grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association’s crisis facility, mobilising £1.5bn of support for Ukraine.
Alongside this, there will be a £3bn increase in UK Export Finance (UKEF) capacity for Ukraine, prioritised for military support. It will bring the total UKEF support to £6.5bn.
What business organisations are saying about budget
Business groups have given the budget a mixed reaction.
Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the CBI, welcomed some measures, but argued John Healey should have done more for growth. She said
On the face of it, this budget lacks the bold moves that would have made it easier for firms to invest, hire and grow.
At a time of exceptional geopolitical pressures, using some fiscal headroom to absorb genuine short-term shocks is preferable to loading additional permanent costs onto business and weakening investment.
Slowing the convergence of youth rates with the national living wage is a sensible move in face of the Neets crisis and current labour market pressures. But the chancellor could have gone further. Reducing the cost of hiring by increasing the employer NICs threshold would have given firms more space to create entry-level jobs and boost employment.
Jonathan Geldart, director general at the Institute of Directors, said his members were relieved.
Business leaders will be relieved that the chancellor’s budget included no nasty surprises, having been conditioned in previous budgets to expect the worst. We very much welcome the numerous measures intended to support British start-ups and scale-ups, such as the new Founders’ Relief, Young Entrepreneurs Allowance and EMI2 [enterprise management incentive] share incentives (as well as support for small brewers).
What might at first blush be a case of small beer today could start adding up to something promising in the future.
But Tina McKenzie, national chair of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), said the budget was a disappointment.
This budget should have been the moment to help small businesses with the soaring costs holding them back, and the taxes restricting job creation. Instead, they got nothing to ease sky-high energy bills and nothing to make hiring someone more affordable, while the increase in business rates relief excludes too many.
A JP Morgan spokesperson has criticised the decision to hike the UK’s bank tax today, arguing that targeting one of the UK’s most lucrative sectors “lacks principle”:
“We are committed to the country, and we recognise the cost of living challenges there and the global economic headwinds that it faces, but to single out this industry for additional taxes again, one of the UK’s biggest generators of growth and jobs, lacks principle.
“It also overlooks that the banking industry operates in a highly competitive global marketplace.”
But despite the bank’s disappointment, JP Morgan is due to charge ahead with its £3bn new UK HQ, according to a source familiar with the matter.
What opposition parties are saying about the budget
Kemi Badenoch’s reaction to the budget on behalf of the Conservative party was covered earlier, at 2.11pm. Here is some reaction from other oppostion parties.
The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, told MPs that John Healey should have done more to address the problems with Brexit. He said:
I do think this budget will be more defined by Labour’s red lines on Europe and the Conservatives’ Brexit red tape, rather than faster growth.
And at the root of so much of what’s gone wrong in our country – the cost of living crisis, higher taxes, broken public services, empty high streets, the lack of jobs and opportunity – at the root of all of that is the lack of economic growth.
Our economy is being held back. British business is being held back, and it’s been held back above all by the terrible damage of the Conservative Brexit deal.
Ellie Chowns, the Green party Treasury spokesperson, said the budget was lacking in ambition.
You’d have thought that, after going to the trouble of ousting the last PM, taking his job, and installing a brand-new chancellor, Andy Burnham would be keen to ensure Labour displayed a bit more ambition at today’s budget than it did under his predecessor.
Unfortunately, what Britain actually saw today was a business-as-usual budget which failed to engage with the real issues facing our country – choosing to tinker round the edges, rather than properly taxing extreme wealth and profits, making essentials genuinely and permanently affordable, or investing in our long-term climate resilience.
There was no discussion of the climate crisis in Healey’s speech today, nor any new investment in renewables and climate adaptation, despite the devastating impact of this summer’s deadly heatwaves and wildfires on our communities, public services, and economy.
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said Britain was broke. In a post on social media, he said:
These are the stats John Healey doesn’t want you to read.
Unemployment will rise to 5% in 2027.
The tax burden is going up AGAIN to the highest since WW2.
By 2031 we’ll be spending £160bn/year on debt interest alone – up £36bn/year …
We are on a fiscal knife-edge. Britain is Broke. Britain needs Reform.
Kirsty Blackman, the SNP’s economy spokesperson at Westminster, said this was not a budget for Scotland. She said:
The UK Budget shows the Labour government doesn’t get Scotland – and isn’t doing anywhere near enough to protect people from the looming cost of living emergency this winter.
This isn’t a budget that a Scottish chancellor would have delivered. Instead of providing meaningful help, it has abandoned families in the face of soaring bills and has imposed another betrayal on Scotland’s energy – with the decision to scrap Scottish carbon capture funding.
Andy Burnham promised to cut the cost of living but every major household bill has increased on his watch – and the UK budget completely fails to address the scale of the challenge families are now facing.
Ben Lake, Plaid Cymru’s economic spokeperson at Westminster, said Wales was just an afterthought in the budget.
Today’s budget was UK Labour’s opportunity to prove that Wales is more than an afterthought in Treasury decisions. Instead, it appears to have delivered the worst funding settlement for Wales in years.
After months of promises about a new relationship with Wales and a new approach from the Treasury, the question many people will be asking is – where is the ambition
The chancellor chose not to announce what Wales would receive in consequentials from this budget. Buried in the documents is around £450 million of additional funding spread over three years. That falls well short of keeping pace with inflation and risks forcing the kind of spending reductions Wales experienced during the worst years of Tory cuts.
UK gambling firms' value jumps after chancellor resisted large duty hike
Rob Davies
Machine games duty (MGD) is the tax levied on slot machines found in bookmakers, casinos, bingo halls and adult gaming centres (AGCs). The chancellor faced calls to double the rate of MGD from 20% to 40%, a policy backed by one of his predecessors, Gordon Brown.
Amid fierce lobbying from gambling firms, which issued dire warnings of thousands of job cuts, Healey opted for a more modest rise to 25% today. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.
Investors responded with relief, adding £240m to the combined stock market value of Entain (Ladbrokes/Coral), Evoke (William Hill), RankGroup (Mecca Bingo/Grosvenor Casinos) and Playtech (designer of slot machine games). Entain said the MGC hike will cost it £25m, which it expects to be able to mitigate, including by shop closures. Betfred boss Fred Done, whose family took a £30m dividend from their betting empire earlier this year, also warned that closures and job losses would follow.
The chancellor singled out AGCs, sometimes known as “slot farms” for particular attention. As well as the duty rise, they will also be excluded - along with vape shops - from business rates relief available to retail and hospitality businesses.
Burnham rules out general election in the next year
Andy Burnham has ruled out calling a snap general election in the next year amid ongoing speculation (including among economists and investors) that he could seek to consolidate his position.
He said he was thinking “about people” and not “my own party and its prospects”, Press Association reports.
The prime minister was asked if he would call an election in the next year as he visited a community centre in central London after the Budget.
He said:
“I don’t know how many times I’ve done this now, but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months.
“I have said repeatedly since coming into this job, I’m not thinking about myself. I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects.
“I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them to have that care for people, which I spoke about on my first day in Downing Street.”
He added that he was “leading from the front” and “putting Britain on a different path”.
He said:
“We’ve got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage.”
Several City economists are suggesting that today’s budget may be teeing up an early general election.
AndrewWishart, senior UK economist at Berenberg, suggests there is a 40% chance of a general election before the end of 2027.
He points out that this would allow Labour to discard its previous manifesto commitments not to raise taxes on working people.
Wishart says:
The big questions, about how to fund a national social care service and a £15bn increase in defence spending by 2030 remain unanswered. The government will hope that the combination of a decline in gilt yields a reduction in transfer payments to those with disabilities and efficiency savings enable them to fund their priorities without a major increase in taxes. It’s just about possible, but pretty unlikely and requires tax hikes pencilled in for the back end of the parliament to come in, potentially just before the next general election.
More ambition would require a new mandate without the manifesto constraint on tax, achieved by via a general election. We put the chances of one before the end of next year at about 40%.”
Eoin O’Callaghan, macro strategist at Wellington Management, says there is a “significant question mark” over the credibility of the projections, including the biig squeeze on departmental spending in a few year’s time.
Like last autumn’s budget they incorporate an unrealistic real term freeze in departmental spending in 2029-30, after the next election. And they now incorporate an even more challenging 3% real terms cut to next year’s departmental spending too to help offset rising interest rate and unfunded public sector pensions costs. The forecasts are also predicated on nominal growth staying relatively elevated close to 4% throughout the forecast.
“That may not concern the market for now. But it highlights how challenging the UK public finances are. How difficult the fiscal decisions ahead of this government are. And why there is a risk of early elections given the tough spending decisions ahead.”
BenjaminJones, Invesco’s Global Head of Research, predicts speculation about an early election will continue to build:
“After two blockbuster, tax-hiking budgets, investors will welcome this more ‘steady as she goes’ package from the new Labour Chancellor. Against a backdrop of rising gilt yields and geopolitical uncertainty, Healey’s decision to limit spending increases and tax rises shows sensible caution.
His opening comments were clearly aimed to ease bond market fears. However, many of the difficult fiscal choices - such as delivering welfare savings and boosting Defence spending - have been postponed until the Spending Review next year, which will continue to fuel speculation of an early election.
John Healey announced a first-time buyer ISA in his speech. This is what the Treasury says about how it will work.
The government will introduce a new FTB ISA from April 2029. The product will replace the Lifetime ISA (LISA) for new savers and provide a 25% government bonus, paid on withdrawal, towards the purchase of a first home worth up to £450,000. The maximum value of the bonus will be capped at £20,000. Existing LISA holders will be able to continue contributing to and using their accounts under the current rules. In addition, the government will reduce the withdrawal charge for existing LISA holders who use their savings to purchase a first home above the £450,000 property price cap.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: Exiled opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to rapturous reception in Venezuela
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
The Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, has announced she has returned to Venezuela almost a year after she left the country to receive the Nobel peace prize.
“I’m here. With you,” she wrote on X on Sunday lunchtime.
Her close ally Edmundo González, who is in exile, confirmed her arrival. “Venezuela! I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil,” he posted on social media.
“Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!” he said, adding that he too would soon return.
It was not immediately clear how Machado, 59, had managed to return to Venezuela but footage on social media showed she was in Barquisimeto, the capital of Lara state, which is about 220 miles west of the capital, Caracas.
Images showed her surrounded by supporters holding mobile phones in the Sanctuary of the Divine Shepherdess church.
Footage posted on social media by her close ally Pedro Urruchurtu showed hundreds of supporters gathered outside the church to greet her, shouting: “Freedom! Freedom! Freedom!”
After leaving the church, it took Machado – festooned in rosaries handed to her by followers – eight hours to reach Caracas because of massive crowds lining and blocking streets and highways.
Tens of thousands of cheering supporters greeted Machado as she made her way to the capital on Sunday night. “This country is giving lessons to everyone,” she shouted as her convoy entered Caracas, leaning out of the sunroof to shake hands and hug raucous supporters.
“For the reunion of every family, for freedom of every political prisoner, for the freedom of Venezuela,” she wrote on social media.
The Trump administration had reportedly opposed Machado’s return, believing her presence would complicate the cosy relationship it has struck up with the interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, since abducting her former boss, Nicolás Maduro, in January.
Machado and Rodríguez are political arch-rivals.
Machado slipped out of Venezuela last December – a few weeks before Maduro’s capture – and in recent months has reportedly made more than half a dozen failed attempts to return home, including after the devastating earthquake that hit the northern coast in June.
After Maduro was seized, many had expected Donald Trump to give Machado his blessing to take power. Her movement is widely believed to have beaten Maduro in the 2024 presidential election, but he refused to hand over power.
Instead the US president embraced Rodríguez, Maduro’s vice-president, who now governs a country widely seen as a US protectorate.
Machado has repeatedly heaped praise on Trump for launching the operation to remove Maduro, and gave him her 2025 Nobel peace prize medal, which she had been awarded for her peaceful challenge to Venezuela’s authoritarian government.
Asked by reporters on Sunday about her return, Trump said: “I don’t know anything about it, but I think she’s a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel prize, so how can I say anything else?
“I hope she’s safe. She’s a very nice woman. But we’re doing very well in Venezuela.”
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed credit for creating the conditions that allowed Machado’s safe return after 10 months in exile.
Her return “is the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile”, he said.
From Barquisimeto, Machado headed east through the state of Yaracuy towards Caracas in a convoy of vehicles. Images released by aides show her reaching out from a car’s sunroof towards dozens of supporters who had gathered at the roadside to see her.
Members of Venezuela’s government have long hinted that Machado would be arrested if she tried to return as a result of her years-long struggle for political change. But there was no sign of the security services bothering her on Sunday as she moved towards the capital, perhaps suggesting Washington had sanctioned her return and instructed Rodríguez’s government not to react.
Machado has called for fresh presidential elections to be held by July 2027, but it is unclear whether the Trump administration supports that timeline given the lucrative partnership it has struck up with Rodríguez.
Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Venezuela in August, subsequently describing the agreement as the spoils of January’s brief “war”.

SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_title: After the ITV exposé, see Reform’s fixation with ‘hate preachers’ as the stinking hypocrisy it really is | Owen Jones
SELECT *\r\nFROM \"dimArticle\" da\r\nWH.article_content:
Who are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists? As the head of MI5 warns that anti-migrant haters are increasingly considering terrorist attacks, it is surely a question we must ask. After all, the role of hate preachers in Islamist terrorism has long been debated.
After the London Bridge Islamist terrorist attack in 2017, Nigel Farage demanded that Sadiq Khan – “as the first Muslim mayor of London” – declare that he would do all he could “to work with the Muslim community to drive out the extremist preachers from our mosques” and to fight radicalisation in schools and prisons. More recently, he suggested that Muslim parents in the United Arab Emirates feared sending their children to study in British universities “given the risk of radicalisation here”. His colleague Suella Braverman agrees. “There should be zero tolerance for hate preachers in mosques or radicalising imams in prisons,” she says.
And what of Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s self-styled shadow chancellor, who warns of “terrorist influencers and radicalising inmates” in prisons and demands “complete zero tolerance on hate preachers”?
Yet on the very day of MI5’s warning, Jenrick declared that Royal Marines would be deployed to turn back migrants in the Channel – and that “if they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so”. Here was one of Britain’s most prominent politicians injecting violence into our already deeply toxic debate about immigration.
Farage sought to backtrack on Jenrick’s behalf, claiming force “would be used only if soldiers were fired at” and insisting that Jenrick had been “utterly misconstrued”. This made little sense: the Home Office said last year that it had no record of firearms being brought in via small boats over the previous seven years.
Not that long ago, there was supposed to be a strict demarcation between the mainstream right and extremists. No longer. Consider the ITV investigation, screened last night, that exposed Reform councillors describing Asian families as “parasites” and Black children as “animals”. Another spoke of training young men to round up migrants “street by street, house by house”. One spoke of holding asylum seekers in “concentration camps”. Another Reform figure spoke of criminals facing “Sunday morning rose garden executions”. Some of these individuals have since stood down. But while the leaders of Reform have not yet plunged to such extreme depths, what effect might their own words have on impressionable people?
Consider that last week, Jenrick appeared on the YouTube channel of former GB News presenter Dan Wootton, a supporter of both Tommy Robinson and the anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas, the latter of whom he calls “a British hero”.
Take the anti-migrant protests outside hotels housing asylum seekers. Last August, Jenrick turned up to such a demonstration in Epping, Essex, where far-right activists were also present, praising the “peaceful, patriotic protesters”. A month earlier, following clashes which left eight police officers injured, Braverman insisted the protests had been “largely … peaceful”. Farage, meanwhile, warned that Britain was close to “civil disobedience on a vast scale” and said he understood the anger in Epping: “You bet your life I do.”
Asked about Thomas’s group, Patriot Platform, Jenrick sympathised with masked protesters, arguing that, without a face covering, “you can lose your job, you can be cancelled”. When he was pushed on whether he would accept Robinson supporters into Reform, Jenrick’s response was telling. “Ultimately [it’s] not my call who comes into the party, that’s for Nigel and others in the party to determine,” he said. “But look, I want to build as broad a coalition as possible of people who share my values, who want us to fix this country.” How to square this with Jenrick’s denunciation of Islamist hate preachers?
In the recent past, Reform politicians – Farage, Jenrick and Braverman among them – have described migrants arriving in small boats as an “invasion”. It is the language of war: a nation under siege, an enemy to be repelled. It is hardly a leap for fearful people to conclude that those who resort to violence are not really dangerous extremists, but patriots defending their country.
We can hardly forget that Farage called for “pure, cold rage” in response to alleged police failings over the murder of Henry Nowak. Hours later, violence erupted on the streets of Southampton. He increasingly embraces the language of white resentment, claiming that “anti-whiteness is institutionalised into every aspect of public life”, calling diversity policies a form of “social cleansing” and warning of white Britons becoming a minority by the end of the century. Such rhetoric echoes the “great replacement” conspiracy theory, which argues that white people are being deliberately displaced by mass immigration.
Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, meanwhile, describes Conservative and Labour politicians as “traitors to their country”, warning – without elaboration – that a “reckoning is coming”.
None of these statements constitute a direct incitement to violence. But taken together, they can conjure up a terrifying picture in impressionable minds: a nation and a people under attack, its own political leaders conspiring in its destruction and time running out to save it.
This can’t be divorced from rightwing media outlets echoing and amplifying such rhetoric. We’ve already had the far-right uprising of August 2024, when racist mobs assaulted people of colour in the streets, attacked mosques and migrant-owned businesses, and tried to burn down hotels housing asylum seekers. We’ve had far-right terrorist attacks, such as the neo-Nazi attempted murder of an Eritrean man in 2024, the firebombing of an immigration centre in Dover in 2022, the attack on the Finsbury Park mosque in 2017 and the murder of Jo Cox a year earlier.
None made a dent on the national discourse. It has only become cruder, more toxic and more inflammatory. So, with all we know, time to ask again. Who are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists?
- 
  Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West, is out now. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.
